Definition from research

Chapter 3 · Faith and Doubt

  • While Miss MacIntosh acknowledges God, she does not believe in extravagant religious fantasies or promises of an afterlife.
  • She sees life itself as a sufficient test and believes in accepting one’s lot without illusions.

Chapter 7 · Mystery and Suspicion

  • The deaths of Josh and his brother Rudolph are shrouded in mystery and accusations of murder, highlighting themes of betrayal and concealed violence.
  • The locked door and fire incident suggest murder but remain unproven, emphasizing distrust and ambiguity.

Chapter 8 · Isolation and Mystery

  • The setting (a spectral village at night, broken fences, a flooded yard with refuse, and a mysterious woman who hides from strangers) creates a sense of isolation and secrets.
  • The village itself appears ghost-like, with empty streets, wooden geese, and flickering lights, symbolizing a place suspended between life and death.

Chapter 12 · The Limits of Human Understanding and Divine Mystery

  • Vera reflects on the limitations of human knowledge, emphasizing that humans are not omniscient and should not try to tamper with God’s mysteries.
  • God is portrayed as remorseful over creation’s imperfections, but humans are advised to focus on their own lives rather than cosmic mysteries.

Chapter 12

  • “filled with the greatest remorse”: “And it repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart” (Genesis 6:6).

Chapter 19 · Faith and Morality

  • Her Christian beliefs, criticism of gambling, and chained Bible contrast with the ominous presence of the cards and other symbols of fate, indicating internal conflicts or tensions between belief and fate.

Chapter 20 · Spiritual and Existential Questions

  • The narrative moves toward existential and spiritual reflection, pondering God’s nature, the problem of creation, and the place of suffering and imperfection in the divine order.
  • Vera likens the “baldness” and loss to a profound experience, possibly greater than mere mortal wisdom or aging, invoking biblical and mythological imagery.
  • The chapter closes with a meditation on life failing before one’s eyes and the idea of seeing something no one “should see and live to relate.”

Chapter 21 · The Devil and Deception

  • The narrative includes reflections on evil’s many forms, warning against being deceived by charming appearances (“The Devil does not always wear horns”).
  • The Devil is described metaphorically as “God’s ape,” emphasizing the complexity of good and evil and the danger of superficial judgments.

Chapter 25

  • “who did not believe in Heaven except as a state of mind”: The concept of heaven “as a state of mind” originates from interpretations of Jesus’ teachings, particularly the phrase “the kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:21), which suggests that a state of peace, love and spiritual fulfillment can be achieved here on Earth through one’s mindset and actions, rather than being solely a place one goes to after death (Leo Tolstoy took the verse for the title of The Kingdom of God Is Within You, 1894); this interpretation is often associated with mystical or spiritual traditions that emphasize inner consciousness and personal transformation. It captures a key existential and metaphysical perspective in the novel, emphasizing the internal, often ambiguous nature of spiritual experience over fixed external realities.
  • “his existence which she denied”: Proving existence through denial refers to a philosophical concept where the act of actively denying something’s existence can inadvertently reveal its presence, often used in arguments where the very act of trying to refute something implies its reality, particularly in discussions about abstract concepts like God or the nature of consciousness. In his Proslogion (1078), Anselm answers “the fool” who “hath said in his heart, There is no God” (Psalm 14:1): to deny God, the fool must first understand “that than which nothing greater can be conceived,” and such a being, Anselm argued, must exist in reality as well as in the mind. This concept can be misused to manipulate arguments by implying that simply denying a claim equates to its truth, which is a logical fallacy.

Chapter 25 · Faith and Doubt

  • Mr. Spitzer lacks faith in an afterlife, which contributes to his hesitant living.
  • His brother’s suicide suggests a belief in an afterlife or at least a finality that Mr. Spitzer cannot embrace.
  • The tension between hope and despair permeates the narrative.

Chapter 29 · The Mystery of Origin and Existence

  • The chapter speculates on the origins of butterflies and existence itself.
  • Questions arise about whether butterflies predate time and space or came from cosmic or otherworldly realms.
  • This reflects broader metaphysical inquiry into creation, existence, and the nature of the divine.

Chapter 29 · The Role of God and the Divine

  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates the nature of God, presenting a multifaceted and paradoxical image of divinity.
  • God is the King of Light, “opposed… by the necessary King of Darkness,” who must “create… bless, absolve, curse, forgive,” and is elusive beyond human comprehension.
  • The divine is intertwined with the symbolism of butterflies and the cosmic order.

Chapter 29 · Reflections on God and Creation

  • The multifaceted nature of God and the mystery of creation, mirrored in the symbolism of butterflies.

Chapter 30 · The Cosmic and the Mystical

  • Frequent cosmic imagery: stars, planets, moons, constellations, and celestial events.
  • Catherine’s dialogue with cosmic elements (stars, waves, tides) reflects a mystical quest for meaning beyond the earthly.

Chapter 44 · Mystery and the Human Heart

  • The suffragette is depicted as a repository of secrets and confidences, receiving the hidden sorrows and loves of others even as her own heart remains obscure.
  • The novel questions whether anyone can truly understand love, life, or ambition, suggesting these remain inscrutable mysteries.
  • The idea that knowing without experiencing, knowing love without loving, or death without dying, might be a deeper form of understanding is proposed.

Chapter 45 · Mysticism and Symbolism

  • The chapter is rich with symbolic imagery: mountains, clouds, snow, stars, fireflies, sea shells, the moon, and butterflies.
  • These symbols often blur the boundary between reality and hallucination, reflecting Mr. Spitzer’s and Cousin Hannah’s fractured consciousness.
  • The narrative suggests the possibility of existence beyond physical death, through memory, spirit, or cosmic forces.

Chapter 49 · The Cosmic and the Mystical

  • The cosmos, stars, and celestial imagery permeate the text, emphasizing vastness, mystery, and the unknowable.
  • Mr. Spitzer imagines his existence woven into universal patterns, yet feels lost and disoriented within them.
  • The narrative contemplates the idea of multiple dimensions, alternate realities, and the eternal recurrence of life and death.

Chapter 65 · Faith, Salvation, and Doubt

  • The chapter explores the tension between religious fervor, spiritual hope, and personal doubt.
  • Mr. Bonebreaker’s apocalyptic preaching contrasts with Miss MacIntosh’s pragmatic and skeptical attitude.
  • Her rejection of his God and his ultimate flight from her when confronted with her full reality illustrates this tension.

Chapter 69 · The Supernatural and Reality

  • The narrative blurs lines between reality and the supernatural with ghostly figures, haunted rooms, and symbolic presences.
  • The landlord’s tall tales and Mr. Weed’s shadow complicate the story’s realism.

Chapter 72 · Mystery and the Unseen

  • The unborn child, the stillborn babies, and the hidden layers of Esther’s life symbolize the mysteries of existence and creation.
  • References to shadows, ghosts, and invisible presences underscore this motif.

Chapter 74 · Mystery and Ambiguity

  • The narrative blurs reality and memory. Esther’s story is full of mysteries: the paternity of her children, the nature of her pregnancies, and the actions of the detective.
  • The repeated motif of “stillborn” children and the detective’s ambiguous role deepen this theme.

Chapter 75 · The Body and the Supernatural

  • Esther’s body is a site of suffering and mystery; her miscarriages are described in surreal terms (e.g., “mud baby,” “marble statue,” “ectoplasm”).
  • The dead babies return as ghostly figures, sometimes walking, sometimes lying in boats, symbolizing unresolved grief and the supernatural intrusion into her life.

Chapter 77 · Mystery and the Unknown

  • The nature of Esther’s pregnancies, the deaths, and the detective’s role create a pervasive sense of mystery.
  • The chapter explores the limits of understanding and the unknowable facets of human experience.

Chapter 80 · Life, Death, and the Supernatural

  • The narrative blurs boundaries between life and death, as Esther communicates with spirits and imagines an “other world” parallel to this one.
  • Her miscarriages and stillborn children are depicted as ghostly presences and delicate entities like moths, feathers, and snowflakes.
  • Walter exists both as a living child and a spectral presence haunting her conscience.

Definition from research

Chapter 6 · Identity and Duality

  • Madge struggles with her identity, feeling split between her past self, her present, and the “other” face she must become.
  • The motif of doubles: Madge and Jacqueline, life and death, waking and sleeping.
  • Madge’s painted face and changing appearances symbolize the fluidity and fragility of identity.

Chapter 14 · Memory, Identity, and Duality

  • The chapter explores fractured identities, especially through the figure of Mr. Spitzer and his deceased brother.
  • Catherine perceives multiple overlapping realities and versions of Mr. Spitzer, reflecting her confusion and the blurred boundaries of life and death.
  • The motif of “four Mr. Spitzers” suggests layered selves and mirrored images, raising questions about selfhood and existence.

Chapter 18

  • “such a man as is hidden in the woman”: Jung named the woman within the man the anima, and the man within the woman the animus.

Chapter 18 · Duality of Human Nature: The Secret Man and Woman

  • The concept that within every woman is a secret man, and within every man, a secret woman.
  • This duality is visualized through the phantom lover who is neither fully man nor woman but an “angelic demon” representing the hidden self.

Chapter 25 · Identity and Duality

  • The twin brothers symbolize duality: life/death, faith/faithlessness, decisiveness/hesitation.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s identity is fractured, as he carries both his own life and that of his dead brother.
  • The confusion over who he is and who he might become reflects existential uncertainty.

Chapter 26 · Duality of Human Nature

  • Through the contrast between Joachim and his twin brother Peron, the duality of restraint versus impulsiveness, order versus chaos, and life versus death is examined.

Chapter 35 · Unity and the Fragmented Self

  • Catherine is “this fragmented ego, these fragmentations of partial selves, of splintered mirrors and partial images.”
  • Her selves include “the look-out in the crow’s-nest… the lady in the phaeton, the figurehead in the foam.”
  • Hannah seemed never to have “divided herself… into opposing factions, warring camps, the battle raging in her own breasts.”
  • “Yet the extremities of faith in anything might always beget, my mother knew, its opposite.”
  • Mr. Spitzer acknowledges “at all times, two truths, neither of which should be true.”

Chapter 39 · Duality of Reality and Imagination

  • Catherine exists simultaneously in multiple realms: physical, mental, spiritual.
  • She is described as living through dreams and hallucinations, often unable to distinguish between real visits and imagined ones (e.g., the visit from Cousin Freemount-Snowden).
  • Her imagination is described as “all there was,” compensating for isolation and loss.

Chapter 41 · Life and Death as Intertwined States

  • Catherine insists there is little difference between life and death, “only an infinitesimal difference… a hair’s breadth.”
  • Her spirit moves beyond the physical body, engaging in multiple selves and journeys that may never return, implying immortality is linked to loss and absence.
  • Death is not final; rather, it is a transformation or continuation of life in another form or realm.

Chapter 47 · Love and Death as Intertwined Realities

  • Love is portrayed as transitory and dying, yet death is equated with a dark lover who embraces and consumes the beloved.
  • The idea that death is not an end but a transformation or continuation, possibly into another life or state.

Chapter 54 · Duality of Identity and Madness

  • Mr. Spitzer oscillates between his own identity and that of his brother, sometimes confused about who he truly is. The chapter explores the thin line between sanity and madness, with Joachim embodying order and Peron chaos, yet both are reflections of each other.

Chapter 55 · Duality and Mirror Imagery

  • The chapter repeatedly emphasizes twins, mirrors, and reflections: twin portraits, twin gardens, twin portraits of historical figures, and the divided house.
  • Symbolizes the split between order (Joachim) and chaos (Peron), reason and passion, life and death.
  • The mirroring extends to the psychological level where the brothers are halves of one whole, each incomplete without the other.

Chapter 73

  • “married to a twin whose identical twin was married to no one”: Twins who change places in the night echo the Spitzer twins, Joachim and Peron, one never sure which of the two he is.
  • “the evening star and the morning star were one star”: The evening star and the morning star are both the planet Venus, called Hesperus at dusk and Phosphorus at dawn; the Greeks credited Pythagoras or Parmenides with discovering they were one. In 1892 the philosopher Gottlob Frege made “the morning star is the evening star” his famous example of two names with one meaning.

  • Miss MacIntosh’s perspective on love is pragmatic and grounded; love is about seeing and hearing another in daylight and tested by harsh experience.

  • Vera emphasizes that true love remains constant despite changing circumstances. Love “does not ebb, does not wane,” symbolizing an ideal of permanence in an impermanent world.
  • This eternal love contrasts with the physical and emotional struggles depicted, underscoring a spiritual or emotional steadfastness.

Chapter 21 · Love and Identity

  • Highlights Vera’s struggle to reconcile ideal love with the imperfect reality of human beings.

Chapter 22

  • “those who fall in love are always blind”: “But love is blind, and lovers cannot see” (The Merchant of Venice 2.6).
  • “her old dollar watch which was given to her by her dead love”: The silver-dollar watch of Chapter 19.

Chapter 31

  • “in love with no man on earth but with a fleeting shadow, the mere shadow of a man”: Shadows in scripture and Shakespeare.

Chapter 31 · Love and Shadows

  • Catherine’s love is portrayed as a love for a shadow, a phantom rather than a living man.

Chapter 38 · Love and Absence

  • Love is portrayed as an unfulfilled, silent, and distant force.
  • Catherine loves an absent, dead man whose love, she believes, was expressed through silence and neglect rather than conventional gestures.
  • Peron’s love is described as “his love greater than his hatred” but unexpressed, a “dead love which never was and never would be real,” paradoxically eternal.
  • Cousin Hannah is described as never having loved, or only loving the “image of the dead,” though she weeps at a snowflake or a rustling skirt.

Chapter 42 · Love and Isolation

  • Despite her militant exterior, Cousin Hannah harbors hidden loves and intimacies. The narrative hints at secret lovers, lost opportunities for human connection, and the loneliness of a life lived in opposition to societal norms.

Chapter 43 · Love and Loss

  • The suffragette expresses deep, eternal love in her delirium, though the identity of lover and beloved is unclear.
  • Love and death blur together, raising the question of whether death extinguishes love or transforms it. Her last whispered words ask, “should love be extinguished by death?”
  • The paradox of love’s endurance beyond death is a poignant motif.

Chapter 44 · Love and Loss

  • Despite being a fierce fighter for women’s rights, Cousin Hannah is shown to be deeply haunted by a lost love, which shapes much of her life and final moments.
  • Her dying cries for her “love,” “little snowdrop,” and her search for a “skirt” symbolize a yearning for something lost, possibly innocence, identity, or a personal connection.
  • The narrative suggests that her suffrage activism was motivated by personal heartbreak, intertwining public struggle with private grief.

Chapter 45 · Love and Its Ambivalence

  • Love is portrayed as an unattainable ideal.
  • Cousin Hannah’s love life is marked by loss, guilt, and a yearning for a final answer that never comes.
  • Cousin Hannah’s lamentations at her deathbed emphasize her betrayal of love (whether by herself or by fate) and her eternal search for her lost love.

Chapter 46 · Love Beyond Mortality

  • Hannah’s message is that love transcends mortal bounds, aiming for an immortal love. This idea recurs as Mr. Spitzer contemplates the power and persistence of love even after death, and the paradox that those who have loved have also died, and vice versa.

Chapter 47 · Love and Death as Intertwined Realities

  • Love is portrayed as transitory and dying, yet death is equated with a dark lover who embraces and consumes the beloved.
  • The idea that death is not an end but a transformation or continuation, possibly into another life or state.

Chapter 48

  • “an arrowsmith to make that arrow which should reach this heart”: Cupid carries two arrows, one tipped with gold to kindle love and one with lead to put it to flight (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1).
  • “all these little deaths which were like love”: La petite mort, “the little death,” is the French phrase for the swoon of love.
  • “Perhaps there was only the bridge”: “There is a land of the living and a land of the dead and the bridge is love, the only survival, the only meaning” (Thornton Wilder, The Bridge of San Luis Rey, 1927). In Zoroastrian belief the dead cross the Chinvat Bridge, wide for the righteous and narrow as a blade for the wicked.

Chapter 52 · Love and Loss

  • Central to the narrative is the motif of lost love, symbolized by the suffragette’s lost skirt and her search for love that may never be found or may be forever elusive. Love is portrayed as inseparable from death, an eternal quest that transcends time.

Chapter 64

  • “Was it a woman or a man?”: Vera asks without assuming, and Miss MacIntosh answers that there was no man, only “a beautiful dancing girl.” Her one love was a woman.

Chapter 64 · Love and Loss

  • Miss MacIntosh’s reflections on Lorena and her own life reveal deep emotional wounds.
  • The absence of romantic fulfillment and the loss of connections highlight themes of regret and yearning.

Chapter 65

  • “Love is blind”: The saying, meaning that love overlooks faults, is ancient; Plato wrote that the lover is blind about the beloved (Laws 731e). In English, Chaucer has “For love is blynd alday, and may nat see” (“The Merchant’s Tale”), and Shakespeare’s Jessica says, “But love is blind, and lovers cannot see / The pretty follies that themselves commit” (The Merchant of Venice, 2.6).

Chapter 76

  • “by Cupid, the blind god of love”: In classical mythology, Cupid is the god of desire, erotic love, attraction and affection. “And therefore is wing’d Cupid painted blind” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream, 1.1).

Chapter 82

  • “Man loves a silent woman”: In Ben Jonson’s comedy Epicoene, or The Silent Woman (1609), Morose, who cannot bear noise, marries a bride for her silence; once wed, she talks without stopping.

Chapter 82 · Love Beyond Death

  • Mr. Spitzer’s confession of being Peron and his love for Catherine after her death touches on eternal love transcending mortality.

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • “upon which boxer would triumph, the black or the white”: In 1908 Jack Johnson became the first Black heavyweight champion of the world, and white promoters spent years searching for a “Great White Hope” to beat him. When Johnson defeated the former champion James J. Jeffries in 1910, riots broke out in cities across the country. Mr. Spitzer lays “his bet on the black man.”

Chapter 3 · Social Order and Class

  • Miss MacIntosh rejects aristocratic airs and illusions of grandeur.
  • She advocates for the dignity of simple people and honest labor.

Chapter 5 · Political and Social Decay

  • The bus-driver’s tirades against Democrats reflect frustration with political corruption and societal decline.
  • The country is depicted as a “dead country,” with broken roads, empty towns, and lost hopes.

Chapter 8 · Skepticism Toward Institutions

  • The bus-driver’s distrust of “old Doc,” politicians, and even the concept of God highlights disillusionment with traditional authorities and systems.
  • Medical science is portrayed as outmoded and helpless in the face of mortality.

Chapter 8 · Social Stigma and Reputation

  • Beatrice Fitzgerald’s character embodies themes of social judgment, stigma (being called a prostitute), and resilience.
  • The conflicting opinions of Madge and Homer reveal the complexity of social roles and the harshness of gossip

Chapter 10 · Social Roles and Expectations

  • Miss MacIntosh’s resignation to a life without marriage and Vera’s reflections reveal societal pressures on women.
  • The notion that “none would have her” contrasts with Vera’s hope for unexpected companionship.

Chapter 11

  • “Admiral Peary”: Robert E. Peary claimed the North Pole in 1909 and was made a rear admiral in 1911. Matthew Henson, the Black explorer beside him, by his own account reached the spot first and got little credit for decades. In 1897 Peary brought six Inuit from Greenland to New York for the American Museum of Natural History, and four died within months. The museum staged a fake burial for the boy Minik while it kept his father Qisuk’s skeleton.
  • “colder than Boston society”: John Collins Bossidy’s toast (1910): “And this is good old Boston, / The home of the bean and the cod, / Where the Lowells talk only to Cabots, / And the Cabots talk only to God.”

Chapter 14

  • “The black coachman had had no wages for years”: The history of domestic work in the United States is deeply intertwined with the exploitation of Black women, men, and immigrant laborers through systemic racism, limited economic opportunities, and discriminatory labor practices. Enslaved Black women performed essential, unpaid domestic labor before emancipation, with conditions often leading to sexual abuse and the work continuing in a similar vein after abolition. For both Black and immigrant workers, this path was one of few available options, resulting in low pay, long hours, and a lack of protections, while modern policies continue to perpetuate a cycle of vulnerability.
  • “the black coachman with the white, rolling eyes”: The “white, rolling eyes” are the stock caricature of minstrel shows and early films, which made Black servants figures of fear and comedy.
  • “imaginary street Arabs”: “Street Arab” was the Victorian name for homeless children, a slur drawn from the image of Arabs as rootless wanderers.
  • “Mrs. Astor could not go, and Mrs. Vanderbilt would not be seen”: Mrs. Astor is Caroline Schermerhorn Astor, a famous American socialite who led the Four Hundred, the list of New York society in the Gilded Age. Mrs. Vanderbilt is likely Grace Graham Wilson Vanderbilt, another American socialite of the Vanderbilt family. In 1883 Alva Vanderbilt’s costume ball forced Mrs. Astor to call on the Vanderbilts, a famous defeat for old society.
  • “what had become of the color line?”: W. E. B. Du Bois: “The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line” (The Souls of Black Folk, 1903). Catherine has just turned the coachman white and the horses black.
  • “a long weekend in Newport”: Newport, Rhode Island, where Gilded Age families summered in marble “cottages.”

Chapter 14 · Race and Servitude

  • The black coachman is unpaid, nameless, and ordered to serve in death.
  • He is described by the minstrel-show stereotype of “white, rolling eyes.”
  • Catherine’s slip, “the carriage and the white coachman and the four black horses, what had become of the color line?” turns the whole arrangement inside out.

Chapter 17

  • “some Irish hooligan or drunken sailor”: “Hooligan” came into use in 1890s London, said to be from a rowdy Irish family named Houlihan. The word carries the era’s contempt for the Irish poor.

Chapter 19

  • “the cap of a sleeping car porter”: After the Civil War, the Pullman Company hired Black men, many of them formerly enslaved, as sleeping car porters. They worked long hours for low pay and tips, and passengers called every one of them “George,” after George Pullman. A. Philip Randolph organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters in 1925, and in 1937 it won “the first major labor agreement between a Black union and a corporation” (Smithsonian Magazine, February 18, 2025).

Chapter 22

  • “a needle-workers’ strike or a new garment union”: In the “Uprising of the 20,000” (1909), shirtwaist makers in New York, most of them young immigrant women, struck for months. The International Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Union was founded in 1900.
  • “a fall in sea island cotton”: Sea Island cotton, a long-staple variety cultivated on coastal islands of South Carolina and Georgia, was intimately linked to the institution of slavery. Its high quality and demand made it a lucrative crop, but its production relied entirely on the forced labor of enslaved Africans. The Sea Island cotton industry thrived from the late 1700s to the late 19th century, fueled by the brutal exploitation of enslaved people. The cultivation, harvesting, and processing of Sea Island cotton were entirely dependent on the labor of enslaved Africans. The Civil War ended slavery, but not the crop. Sea Island cotton was grown by freedpeople and others until it was “no longer economically viable by the 1910s,” and the boll weevil, arriving in the 1910s and 1920s, dealt the “final blow” (South Carolina Encyclopedia, “Cotton”).
  • “How does the other half live?”: Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890). The conservative opinion in the Wikipedia article, that immigrants chose to live in slums as a stepping stone to living in America, is ludicrous. It is very convenient that slum lords would argue we need slums. Any conservative minority has been paid to have that conservative opinion in the US, from history up to the present. Riis’s autobiography, The Making of an American (1901), shows the nuance: he may have had prejudices against certain ethnicities, as racism has always been a thing, but that doesn’t explain that slums are necessary for the working class.
  • “The mill workers were striking”: In the Lawrence textile strike of 1912, the “Bread and Roses” strike, women and children of more than twenty nationalities walked out of the mills.
  • “a baseball autographed by a dead St. Louis Cardinal”: Young mentioned the St. Louis Cardinals and the Cardinals/Dodgers rivalry and this mention seems to be through the lens of racism. During this period, after the 1942 season, Branch Rickey, who had built up the Cardinals farm system as their general manager, moved to become the Dodgers’ general manager. In 1947, after Rickey broke the color line by signing Jackie Robinson to the Dodgers, there were rumors that southerners playing for the Cardinals were planning to boycott games against the Dodgers, although the players later denied it. In general, the Cardinals were latecomers to integration. Front-office executive Bing Devine said the owner from 1947 to 1953, Fred Saigh, refused to sign black players. There was a widespread belief that St. Louis was, in many ways, a Southern city. In the mid-1950s many of its stores and restaurants refused to serve black customers. The Cardinals, with baseball’s largest radio network blanketing the Midwest and South, had cultivated white Southern fans. Their ballpark was also the last in the majors to abolish segregated seating. Because of their lack of black players, the Cardinals’ play suffered on the field tremendously in the 1950s. Meanwhile, with the success of Robinson, the Dodgers doubled down on the opportunity to sign players of color from the Negro leagues. In the subsequent years after their pennant-winning season in 1947, they would sign Don Newcombe, Roy Campanella, and Jim Gilliam from the Negro leagues, adding to an already tremendous team. The Dodgers made the World Series in 1949, 1952, 1953, 1955, 1956, and 1959 (winning championships in 1955 and 1959) and were a historic pennant race away from making it in 1951, in part because they were the first to accept African American players. The 1951 season included a 14-game winning streak for the Dodgers against the Cardinals, the longest such streak in the rivalry. (Wikipedia)
  • “shirts going in job lots, slightly damaged by fire and flood”: May refer to the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in 1911 in New York City which killed 146 workers because a door to one stairway was locked, and the fire escape collapsed. Firefighters’ ladders couldn’t reach the upper floors. Workers, mostly all women, jumped to their deaths. The tragedy led to New York’s Factory Investigating Commission and its safety laws (1911-15).
  • “an old Jew’s pawn shop under the sign of the three golden balls”: The three golden balls were the sign of a pawnbroker. They come from the arms of the Medici and the legend of St. Nicholas’s three bags of gold. Young’s “old Jew’s pawn shop” draws on an old antisemitic stereotype. Medieval Christian law barred Jews from most trades and left them moneylending, and then despised them for it.

Chapter 23 · Historical and Cultural Reflections

  • References to historical figures such as Emperor Constantine, Benjamin Franklin, and President Garfield serve as symbols of human folly or misguided progress.
  • The chapter also evokes images from ancient times and myths (e.g., Helen of Troy, Ulysses) to illustrate timeless human experiences affected by modern changes.

Chapter 24

  • “she should send her gold-turbaned blackamoor”: “Blackamoor” figures, carved and gilded Black servants in turbans, were a fashion of European decorative art. They turned enslaved people into ornaments.

Chapter 26

  • “he had hesitantly called to leave his engraved calling card, to pay, in fact, his respects to the new owners”: Leaving an engraved calling card was the ritual of a nineteenth-century social call.
  • “sleeping car porters with golden roosters on their heads”: Pullman sleeping-car porters were Black men, many of them formerly enslaved, hired by the Pullman Company from 1867 for low wages and long hours, and passengers called every one of them “George.” The Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, led by A. Philip Randolph, was founded in 1925.

Chapter 30

  • “Moroccan pirates returning from raids upon the sleeping coast of Spain with beautiful captive girls”: The Barbary corsairs of Salé and Algiers raided the coasts of Europe and sold captives into slavery.

Chapter 37

  • “not even, as Mr. Spitzer sometimes remarked, a Chinaman’s chance”: A “Chinaman’s chance,” no chance at all, is a racist American phrase of the late nineteenth century. California’s Supreme Court had ruled in People v. Hall (1854) that Chinese people could not testify against whites, and the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 barred them from the country.

Chapter 45 · Public Versus Private Life

  • Cousin Hannah was a public hero, a suffragette with noble deeds and a fiery spirit, yet her private life was marked by confusion, betrayal, and unfulfilled love.
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on how public memory tends to forget the complexity of individuals, often reducing them to symbols or monuments.
  • Cousin Hannah had a “double life,” perhaps even a “triple life,” that no one truly understood.

Chapter 49

  • “only an old night porter riding with her”: Pullman sleeping-car porters were almost all Black men, many of them formerly enslaved or the sons of the enslaved; passengers called every porter “George,” after George Pullman, and they worked long hours for low pay and tips until they organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters under A. Philip Randolph in 1925. “Black as the ace of spades” was a common racist simile; see the ace of spades in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “had done to Indians in their lonely tepees”: The United States has never been held legally to account for genocidal acts against its Indigenous peoples, though many historians and academics describe the Mystic massacre (1637), the Trail of Tears (1838-1839), the Sand Creek Massacre (1864), and the Mendocino War (1859) as genocidal. Roxanne Dunbar-Ortiz states that U.S. history, as well as inherited Indigenous trauma, cannot be understood without dealing with the genocide the United States committed against Indigenous peoples (An Indigenous Peoples’ History of the United States, 2014). From the colonial period through the founding of the United States and into the twentieth century, it entailed torture, terror, sexual abuse, massacres, systematic military occupations, removals of Indigenous peoples from their ancestral territories, the forced removal of Native American children to military-like boarding schools, allotment, and a policy of termination. During Pontiac’s War, General Jeffery Amherst wrote to Colonel Henry Bouquet, “You will Do well to try to Innoculate the Indians by means of Blanketts, as well as to try Every other method that can serve to Extirpate this Execrable Race” (July 16, 1763), part of a broader genocidal attitude displayed toward Native Americans during the colonization of the Americas. Under the Indian Vaccination Act of 1832, Secretary of War Lewis Cass ordered that no surgeon be sent higher up the Missouri than the Mandans, leaving the upper Missouri nations unvaccinated, and when smallpox swept the northern plains in 1837 it killed thousands of Mandans, Hidatsas, Arikaras, Assiniboines, Crees, and Blackfeet (J. Diane Pearson, “Lewis Cass and the Politics of Disease: The Indian Vaccination Act of 1832,” Wicazo Sa Review 18, no. 2, 2003). The United States has to date undertaken no truth commission and built no memorial for the genocide of Indigenous people, and it does not acknowledge or compensate for the historical violence of westward expansion. American museums such as the Smithsonian Institution do not dedicate a section to the genocide; in 2013 the National Congress of American Indians passed a resolution to create a space for a National American Indian Holocaust Museum inside the Smithsonian, but it was ignored (Wikipedia). After the Family Planning Services and Population Research Act of 1970, the Indian Health Service sterilized thousands of Native American women, many without informed consent: a 1976 General Accounting Office report found 3,406 sterilizations in just four of its twelve areas from 1973 to 1976, and by some estimates a quarter or more of Native American women of childbearing age were sterilized (Jane Lawrence, “The Indian Health Service and the Sterilization of Native American Women,” American Indian Quarterly 24, no. 3, 2000). In 1977 Marie Sanchez, chief tribal judge on the Northern Cheyenne Indian Reservation, told a United Nations conference on the Indigenous peoples of the Americas in Geneva that Native American women suffered involuntary sterilization, which she equated with modern genocide.
  • “the black eunuch and the white”: In the Ottoman palace the harem was guarded by Black eunuchs under the Kızlar Ağası, their chief, and the outer palace by white eunuchs.

Chapter 50

  • “Come in, Blackamoor”: Blackamoor is an old, racist English word for a Black African. Figures of Black servants in livery and turbans, called blackamoors, were fashionable decorations in European and American houses; the opium lady greets the human-sized blackbird with it.
  • There is an actual case. Henrietta Lacks, a Black woman treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins in 1951, had cells taken without her knowledge or consent; they became HeLa, the first immortal human cell line and an important source of medical data. Neither she nor her family was compensated, and the family did not learn of the cell line until the 1970s (Rebecca Skloot, The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks, 2010). Its use for medical research and for commercial purposes continues to raise concerns about privacy and patients’ rights; in 2023 her estate settled a lawsuit against a company that had sold the cells.

Chapter 51

  • “a mandarin with a long cue”: The queue was forced on Han Chinese men by the Manchu Qing rulers in 1645 on pain of death, and Western caricature later made it a racist emblem of the Chinese.

Chapter 54

  • “an Indian stockade”: During the forced removal of the Cherokee people, also known as the Trail of Tears, stockades were built to hold them captive before their westward journey to Indian Territory. These stockades were often overcrowded, lacked adequate sanitation and food, and were plagued by disease. A stockade camp at Rattlesnake Springs in Tennessee held many Cherokees awaiting relocation, and it was the site of the final Cherokee council before their departure. The Treaty of Greenville, which concluded a period of conflict between the United States and Native American tribes in the Ohio region, was signed at a large stockade in Greenville, Ohio.
  • “Indian massacre!”: “Indian massacre” The phrase eventually became commonly used to also describe mass killings of American Indians. Killings described as “massacres” often had an element of indiscriminate targeting, barbarism, or genocidal intent. According to historian Jeffrey Ostler, “Any discussion of genocide must, of course, eventually consider the so-called Indian Wars, the term commonly used for U.S. Army campaigns to subjugate Indian nations of the American West beginning in the 1860s. In an older historiography, key events in this history were narrated as battles. It is now more common for scholars to refer to these events as massacres. This is especially so of a Colorado territorial militia’s slaughter of Cheyennes at Sand Creek (1864) and the army’s slaughter of Shoshones at Bear River (1863), Blackfeet on the Marias River (1870), and Lakotas at Wounded Knee (1890). Some scholars have begun referring to these events as “genocidal massacres,” defined as the annihilation of a portion of a larger group, sometimes to provide a lesson to the larger group.” In The Wild Frontier: Atrocities during the American-Indian War from Jamestown Colony to Wounded Knee, lawyer William M. Osborn compiled a list of alleged and actual atrocities in what would eventually become the continental United States, from first contact in 1511 until 1890. His parameters for inclusion included the intentional and indiscriminate murder, torture, or mutilation of civilians, the wounded, and prisoners. His list included 7,193 people who died from atrocities perpetrated by those of European descent, and 9,156 people who died from atrocities perpetrated by Native Americans. In An American Genocide, The United States and the California Catastrophe, 1846-1873, historian Benjamin Madley recorded the numbers of killings of California Indians between 1846 and 1873. He found evidence that during this period, at least 9,400 to 16,000 California Indians were killed by non-Indians. Most of these killings occurred in what he said were more than 370 massacres (defined by him as the “intentional killing of five or more disarmed combatants or largely unarmed noncombatants, including women, children, and prisoners, whether in the context of a battle or otherwise”).
  • “Gold Dust Scouring Twins”: were fictional, racially stereotypical black children who served as mascots for Fairbanks’ Gold Dust washing powder from the 1890s until 1960. Created by the N.K. Fairbanks Company, the twins, “Goldie” and “Dusty,” were depicted doing household chores and promoting the slogan “Let the Gold Dust Twins do your Work.” They were a highly successful, albeit controversial, marketing tool, appearing on packaging, in print, and eventually on a popular radio show, becoming as famous as other racially insensitive brands.

Chapter 55

  • Shut out of most work by law and prejudice, many Chinese immigrants ran hand laundries, whose painted signs in Chinese characters Young calls mystical.
  • “the hitching posts which were little black boys with golden turbans”: “little black boys with golden turbans” The earliest versions of lawn jockeys, used as hitching posts, were created in the 1850s or early 1860s. There are several legends about the black lawn jockeys. The Jim Crow Museum of Racist Memorabilia writes that “there is very little, if any, primary source material for the claim that lawn jockeys were used as signaling devices for escaping slaves on the Underground Railroad.” It is featured in two stories: Raymond Chandler’s 1942 Philip Marlowe novel, The High Window, and a short story by Flannery O’Connor in 1955, The Artificial Nigger. The story suggests that people are not intrinsically racist: rather, racist views are handed down from generation to generation because some people stand to profit from racism. O’Connor said that it was her favorite story she had written.

Chapter 57

  • “would always be a Boston Abolitionist”: Boston abolitionists, active from the 1830s to the Civil War, included prominent figures like William Lloyd Garrison, Wendell Phillips, and Lewis Hayden, who formed societies like the New England Anti-Slavery Society and published the anti-slavery newspaper The Liberator. These activists, both Black and white, organized and rallied against slavery, often facing violent opposition from anti-abolitionist mobs in the city. They also supported the Underground Railroad, assisted fugitive slaves, and pushed for social justice within their communities, eventually contributing to the eventual end of slavery.

Chapter 65

  • “Why should the black men, the railroad porters, the shoe-shiners”: The history of returning enslaved people to Africa, known as the Back-to-Africa Movement, involved efforts by groups like the American Colonization Society (ACS) in the 19th century to send freed slaves to colonies like Liberia and Sierra Leone, aiming to create homelands for Black people in Africa. While supported by some, including President Lincoln at times, it faced strong opposition from many African Americans who saw it as racist and a way to strengthen slavery, with thousands settling in Liberia before the Civil War despite harsh conditions and high mortality. Founded in 1816 by white elites, the ACS established Liberia (settled 1822) as a colony for freed U.S. slaves, modeled partly on British efforts in Sierra Leone. Paul Cuffee was an early proponent who, in 1815, transported free Black people to Sierra Leone, envisioning trade and immigration. The British settled formerly enslaved people in Sierra Leone starting in the late 1780s, a model the ACS followed.
  • In the Bible, Ham, one of Noah’s three sons, had four sons: Cush, Mizraim, Phut, and Canaan, who became ancestors of peoples in Africa and the Middle East, particularly Ethiopia, Egypt, Libya, and Canaan (modern Israel/Palestine). The story in Genesis details how Ham saw his father Noah naked while drunk, leading Noah to curse Ham’s son, Canaan, rather than Ham himself, a narrative known as the Curse of Ham. After the Flood, Noah became drunk and lay uncovered in his tent. Ham saw his father’s nakedness and told his brothers, Shem and Japheth. Shem and Japheth, however, respectfully covered Noah without looking. Noah, upon waking, cursed Canaan (Ham’s son) to be a “servant of servants” to his brothers (Genesis 9:25, KJV), a passage later misused to justify slavery. In the American South the Curse of Ham was preached as God’s own warrant for enslaving Africans, and Mr. Bonebreaker still calls Black men “the sons of Ham.”

Chapter 66

  • In 1897 Peary brought six Inuit from Greenland to New York, where four of them died, among them Qisuk; the American Museum of Natural History staged a false burial for his son, Minik, and kept Qisuk’s skeleton. Its remains were returned to Greenland in 1993.
  • “followed by this Pinkerton agent”: The Pinkerton National Detective Agency, founded in Chicago by Allan Pinkerton in 1850, hired Kate Warne in 1856, the first woman detective in America. Pinkertons were also hired by mill and mine owners to spy on and break strikes, as at Homestead in 1892.
  • “At the head of Wall Street”: From 1711 to 1762 New York’s municipal slave market stood on Wall Street. See the Wall Street broker in the Chapter 54 resources.
  • Peter Stuyvesant, the Dutch director-general of New Amsterdam, is buried there (1672). In 1654 he tried to turn away twenty-three Jewish refugees from Brazil, and the Dutch West India Company overruled him; he also held enslaved Africans.
  • “who have no social security”: The Social Security Act of 1935 created old-age pensions in the United States. Miss MacIntosh, always saving for her old age, gives the poor old fish none.

Chapter 66 · Stock Exchange

  • A place of illusionary wealth and human folly; also a site where she confronts capitalism and socialism.

Chapter 67

  • “These heathen Chinee”: “The Heathen Chinee” was the popular name of Bret Harte’s poem “Plain Language from Truthful James” (1870). Harte meant to mock the white cardsharps who cheat a Chinese player, but the phrase became an anti-Chinese slur, sung and shouted during the agitation that led to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882.
  • “A Chinaman’s chance” meant no chance at all. Chinese workers were given the most dangerous work on the railroads and in the mines, and in People v. Hall (1854) the California Supreme Court ruled that a Chinese witness could not testify against a white man.

Chapter 69

  • “a very little black man who had no tongue but had swallowed a diamond”: At the Kimberley diamond mines in South Africa, from 1885 Black miners were locked in closed compounds, searched naked, and held and dosed with purgatives before they left, to recover any diamonds they had swallowed.
  • “Hagenbeck’s out of Berlin”: Hagenbeck’s out of Berlin may refer to The Tierpark Hagenbeck zoo in Stellingen, Hamburg, Germany. The collection began in 1863 with animals that belonged to Carl Hagenbeck Sr., a fishmonger who became an amateur animal collector. The park itself was founded by Carl Hagenbeck Jr. in 1907. It is known for being the first zoo to use open enclosures surrounded by moats, rather than barred cages, to better approximate animals’ natural environments. Among his collections, however, were also human beings whom he exhibited in “human zoos.” The private zoo is still run by the Hagenbeck family. Hagenbeck’s was based in Hamburg, not Berlin. From 1874 it exhibited Sámi, Nubians, Inuit, and other peoples in its “ethnological shows.”

Chapter 70

  • “She was descended from three signers of the Declaration of Independence”: Lineage societies such as the Daughters of the American Revolution (1890) made descent from the founders a mark of status. In 1939 the DAR barred the Black contralto Marian Anderson from singing at its Constitution Hall, and Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from it in protest.
  • “It would admit both Jews and Negroes”: Catherine’s hotel “would admit both Jews and Negroes.” Jews and African Americans could not freely stay in hotels in the US until the passage of federal and state laws that banned discrimination in public accommodations, which was enforced with the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was a landmark piece of legislation that explicitly prohibited racial discrimination in public places, such as hotels, and this was the first time that Jewish people were also protected from discrimination in public places. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibited discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in public accommodations like hotels, restaurants, and theaters. In the pre-1964 era, many hotels openly discriminated against both African Americans and Jews, often barring them from the premises entirely or requiring them to stay in separate, inferior accommodations. This was particularly true in the South, where discriminatory practices were widespread, even after the Civil War. In 1877 the banker Joseph Seligman was turned away from the Grand Union Hotel at Saratoga Springs because he was a Jew, and resorts advertised themselves as “restricted.” From 1936 Black travelers carried Victor Hugo Green’s Negro Motorist Green Book to find where they could sleep.

Chapter 71

  • Prejudice against Italian immigrants ran deep: in 1891 a New Orleans mob lynched eleven Italian Americans, the largest mass lynching in American history, and in 1927 Massachusetts executed the anarchists Sacco and Vanzetti after a trial many believed unjust.
  • “Tom Swift in the Land of Giants”: Tom Swift in the Land of Giants may refer to a book in the various Tom Swift book series. All books are credited to the pseudonym Victor Appleton while the character was created by Edward Stratemeyer for his book packaging house, the Stratemeyer Syndicate. Tom Swift is the main character of six series of American juvenile science fiction and adventure novels that emphasize science, invention, and technology. The books contain heavy racism, depicting Africans as brutish, uncivilized animals, and the white protagonist as their paternal savior. The Tom Swift books have been credited with assisting the success of American science fiction and with establishing stories focusing on brilliant scientists and inventors as a basic cultural myth. The series uses many adverbs and the phrase Tom Swiftly or Tom Swifty was coined to describe a book that uses many adverbs. Tom Swift’s fictional inventions have apparently inspired several actual inventions. A number of scientists, inventors, and science fiction writers have also credited Tom Swift with inspiring them.
  • “The President’s Daughter”: There are two books by this name. One published by Nan Britton in 1927 is a memoir, detailing her affair with President Warren G. Harding. The second is Clotel; or, The President’s Daughter (1853) by William Wells Brown, about the enslaved daughters of Thomas Jefferson, the first novel published by an African American.
  • “They want an American Pope”: Vatican conspiracy theories are conspiracy theories that concern the Pope or the Roman Catholic Church. A majority of the theories allege that the Church and its representatives are secretly controlling secular society with a Satanic agenda for global domination. In the 1920s the Ku Klux Klan in Indiana enrolled perhaps a quarter of a million members, preaching against Catholics, Jews, and Black Americans and holding the state government until its leader, D. C. Stephenson, was convicted in 1925 of the rape and murder of Madge Oberholtzer.
  • “There are no Negroes in this county, for the sun will not set on a Negro’s head here”: Such places were called sundown towns: Black people had to be gone by nightfall or risk violence. Indiana had scores of them. See the Kentucky lynching in the Chapter 68 resources.
  • “We don’t want mulattoes”: Indiana forbade marriage between white and Black people from its first years until 1965; the Supreme Court struck down the last such laws in Loving v. Virginia (1967).
  • “There’s a nigger in the woodpile somewhere”: In the English language, negro, is a term historically used to denote persons considered to be of Black African heritage. The word negro means the color black in both Spanish and in Portuguese, where English took it from. The term can be construed as offensive, inoffensive, or completely neutral, largely depending on the region or country where it is used. It has various equivalents in other languages of Europe. In the English language, the word nigger typically is an ethnic slur used against black people, especially African Americans. Because it is considered extremely offensive, even if only mentioned and not used as a slur, it is often referred to by the euphemism, the N-word. It became a racist insult by the 20th century. Accordingly, it began to disappear from general popular culture. Its inclusion in classic works of literature has sparked controversy and ongoing debate. The phrase, meaning a hidden catch, dates from the 1840s and is said to come from fugitive slaves hidden in woodpiles on their way north.

Chapter 71 · Social and Cultural Tensions

  • The hotel reflects a microcosm of social prejudice and conflict.
  • The widow’s rant reveals anti-Semitism, racism, and political resentment, referencing Hitler, Roosevelt, and local attitudes.

Chapter 72

  • “thank you, George Washington”: George Washington was an aggressive surveyor and land speculator who acquired over 50,000 acres, often on indigenous lands, earning him the name “Town Destroyer” (Conotocarious) from the Iroquois. He was a lifelong, large-scale slaveholder, inheriting ten enslaved people at age eleven and later controlling over 300, while navigating brutal, disease-ridden early frontier life.

Chapter 73

  • In 1904 the St. Louis World’s Fair put Ota Benga, a Mbuti man from the Congo, on display in its anthropology exhibit, and in 1906 the Bronx Zoo caged him in its monkey house until Black ministers forced his release. He died by suicide in Lynchburg, Virginia, in 1916.
  • “there had been thirty rounds”: Glove fights once ran long: on July 4, 1910, in Reno, Jack Johnson, the first Black heavyweight champion, knocked out Jim Jeffries, the “Great White Hope,” in the fifteenth round of a fight scheduled for forty-five. Riots broke out in some two dozen places, most of them white mobs attacking Black Americans; between 11 and 26 people were killed, among them a Black man lynched in Wheeling, West Virginia, for driving an expensive car (Wikipedia). New York’s Walker Law of 1920 capped bouts at fifteen rounds.

Chapter 74

  • On Hispaniola Columbus enslaved the Taíno; in 1495 he shipped some 500 to Spain to be sold, and about 200 died on the voyage. In 1500 he was arrested for his cruelty as governor and sent home in chains.

Chapter 74 · Societal Judgment and Isolation

  • Esther fears the court trial, anticipating gossip, blame, and misunderstanding from the community.
  • She is alienated and misunderstood, with the jury and townspeople serving as a metaphor for harsh societal judgment.

Chapter 75

  • “They had thrown the stillborn into the river above the dam”: This may refer to the Mississippi Burning Case on August 4, 1964, FBI agents discovered the bodies of three civil rights workers (James Chaney, Michael Schwerner, and Andrew Goodman) buried in an earthen dam on a farm in Neshoba County, MS. The workers had been murdered by members of the Ku Klux Klan and a local deputy sheriff on June 21, 1964, and their bodies were buried within the construction of the dam. The novel was published in 1965.
  • Joel Chandler Harris, a white Georgia journalist, took the tales from Black storytellers, some of them enslaved on the Turnwold plantation where he worked as a boy, and put them in the mouth of Uncle Remus, a contented old former slave of white Southern fantasy.

Chapter 76

  • In King Leopold II’s Congo Free State (1885 to 1908), villagers who failed to meet rubber quotas were flogged, held hostage, and killed, and soldiers cut off hands as proof of the bullets they had used.

Chapter 77

  • “exhibit N, a Negro, the night, a noose”: The night, the noose, and the rope that follows at R: the alphabet calls up lynching. The Tuskegee Institute recorded 4,743 lynchings in the United States from 1882 to 1968; 3,446 of the dead were Black.
  • “But he only dealt with the deaths of little white children”: When Young wrote this the civil rights movement had been going on since 1954.

Chapter 77 · Racism and Social Injustice

  • The white Chicago detective is interested only in the deaths of white children, ignoring black children’s deaths, revealing racial prejudice and societal neglect.

Chapter 78

  • “partly Irish and partly Indian and maybe even had a Negro streak”: Indiana outlawed marriage between white and Black people for most of its history and repealed the ban only in 1965, two years before Loving v. Virginia (1967) ended such laws everywhere.

Chapter 79

  • “this old concubine walking between her parents”: Concubinage in the U.S. was primarily defined by the sexual exploitation of enslaved Black women by white owners, alongside localized systems like plaçage in Louisiana. These coerced, non-marital relationships were driven by power imbalances, racial prohibitions on marriage (anti-miscegenation laws), and the economic value of offspring.
  • “this large-fisted, ugly woman who had brought the life and the shadow”: The intermediary woman who facilitated Esther Longtree’s conception is a complex and symbolically potent figure whose role resonates deeply when analyzed alongside the historical context of Black Americans’ civil rights struggles in the United States. This woman is described vividly and somewhat grotesquely as a large, dark, misshapen figure with broad, earth-stained hands, wearing men’s shoes, a man’s hat, and coat. She is a foreigner, someone with a strange accent, and carries an aura of mystery and hardship, possibly linked to an old crime or exile. She is neither kind nor gentle but is methodical, fierce, and patient, walking back and forth between Esther’s parents with a silver spoon, the instrument used to impregnate Esther’s mother over the course of seven years. This woman embodies a liminal, almost mythic figure: part man, part woman, part shadow crossing boundaries between genders, generations, and roles. She is the “go-between” in a domestic and biological triangle that is itself fractured and barren, symbolizing the failure of natural union and the intrusion of a painful, unnatural process. The intermediary woman’s outsider status (foreign, dark, and stigmatized) can be read as emblematic of the marginalized Black American figure during the civil rights era. Like the go-between, Black Americans were often seen as “other,” standing apart from the mainstream, burdened by historical injustices and systemic exclusion. Yet, this figure is also crucial to the creation of life, a bearer of possibility and transformation despite the cruelty and hardship she embodies. Similarly, Black Americans’ struggle was against a backdrop of oppression but also one of profound resilience and the potential to create new social realities. Esther’s conception through an intermediary and a silver spoon, rather than through a natural marital union, parallels the forced and unnatural social conditions imposed upon Black Americans (segregation, disenfranchisement, and systemic violence) that distorted natural human relations and family structures. The intermediary’s role in bridging a distance or barrier between two barren parents mirrors the social barriers (legal, racial, and cultural) that Black Americans sought to overcome in their fight for civil rights. The intermediary woman’s presence between Esther’s parents and her shadow-like figure evoke the heavy legacy of slavery, segregation, and historical trauma that Black Americans carried. Esther herself, born of this unnatural and painful process, embodies the complex identity born from a fractured past. The intermediary’s shadow, her “darkness,” and the violence implicit in the conception process reflect the historical violence and the pain of inheritance that civil rights activism sought to confront and transcend. The intermediary woman subverts traditional gender and familial roles by acting as the agent of conception in an unconventional way. This subversion can be seen as analogous to the civil rights movement’s challenge to established power structures and norms. The movement demanded recognition and redefinition of identity, agency, and rights, much as the intermediary woman’s presence disrupts the conventional narrative of family and birth. The intermediary is simultaneously a figure of cruelty and care, oppression and agency. She is paid for her role, yet wields a strange power over the life created. This duality reflects the complex dynamics in civil rights struggles, where oppressed communities both suffered under systemic injustice and exercised profound agency in shaping their destinies. The intermediary woman in Esther Longtree’s conception is a richly layered symbol and explores themes of alienation, unnaturalness, and painful mediation that resonate powerfully with the historical and social conditions of Black Americans fighting for civil rights. She embodies the barriers to natural unity imposed by history and society, yet also the endurance and complexity of life born from hardship and estrangement. Her figure invites reflection on the intersections of race, gender, power, and identity in a fractured world.
  • “This third person, this dark woman”: A “dark woman” who assisted with births may refer to the following: 1) the Biblical midwife Shiphrah, one of the “Hebrew midwives” of Exodus 1:15, though some readers have taken her and Puah for Egyptians. Shiphrah, along with her colleague Puah, defied the Pharaoh’s order to kill newborn Hebrew males. 2) Biddy Mason, who was born into slavery, was a midwife and advocate for other enslaved people in 19th-century California. After gaining her freedom, she became a successful entrepreneur and philanthropist. 3) Margaret Charles Smith was an African American midwife in Alabama who delivered over 3,000 babies during a career spanning over 30 years, often in rural areas with limited healthcare access. 4) Mary Francis Hill Coley was a midwife from Georgia who delivered over 3,000 babies during her career. Her work was featured in the 1952 documentary, All My Babies. 5) Susie Carey was a third-generation midwife featured in a photograph at the National Museum of African American History and Culture. 6) Sarah Hudson Grant was a Black Southern midwife whose work is remembered today.

Chapter 80

  • “as black as the ace of spades”: “Negro” was the standard, accepted, and often respectful term for people of African descent in the U.S., evolving from slavery-era usage to a self-identifying term supported by leaders like W.E.B. Du Bois. It was used by the U.S. Census from 1950, though it later became associated with Jim Crow, declining in favor of “Black” by the late 1960s. “Negro” was used by the U.S. Census for much of the twentieth century.
  • “He had fled for fear the white people would see him and kill him”: Interracial marriage in the United States has only been legal since the 1967 U.S. Supreme Court decision Loving v. Virginia that held anti-miscegenation laws were unconstitutional by the 14th Amendment established in 1868. The court’s landmark decision has been commemorated and celebrated every year on the Loving Day, June 12th. The number of interracial marriages in 1967 was three percent. The first interracial marriage in what is today the United States was that of Pocahontas, who married tobacco planter John Rolfe in 1614. The first ever law prohibiting interracial marriage was passed by Maryland in 1691. The Quaker Zephaniah Kingsley married, outside the US, a black enslaved woman that he bought in Cuba. He also had three black common-law enslaved wives. He freed all four. They had to flee Florida for Haiti when it became a US territory. The prospect of black men marrying white women terrified many Americans before the Civil War. It was magnified into the greatest threat to society. The first legal black-white marriage in the United States was that of African-American professor William G. Allen and a white student, Mary King, in 1853. When their plans to marry were announced, Allen narrowly escaped being lynched. Their marriage was secret, and they left the country immediately for England, never to return. In 1957 actor Sammy Davis Jr. faced backlash for his relationship with a white woman, actress Kim Novak. In 1958, Davis briefly married a black woman, actress and dancer Loray White, to protect himself from mob violence.
  • “He had gone farther North”: In the Great Migration, some six million Black Southerners moved north and west between 1910 and 1970, fleeing lynching and Jim Crow.
  • “mother, I go to a fine school with the white children now”: In Brown v. Board of Education (1954) the Supreme Court struck down segregated public schools; in the 1930s a Black child like Walter was barred from white schools across the South and kept out of many in the North.
  • Black jockeys were driven from the track after 1900; Jimmy Winkfield, who won the Derby in 1901 and 1902, was the last Black jockey to win it.

Chapter 80 · Race and Identity

  • Walter’s father was a black man, described metaphorically as “the prince of Africa” and “as black as the ace of spades.”
  • Esther’s shock and societal stigma over this interracial relationship and child profoundly impact her life.
  • Walter’s blackness is a symbolic and literal source of conflict, shame, love, and fear for Esther, reflecting broader themes of racial tension and identity.

Chapter 81

  • “In death, all persons were black as Negroes on slabs”: His contempt reaches past the Jews: even the drowned are, to him, “black as Negroes on slabs.”

Chapter 82

  • “When the white girls turned their faces away from him”: This sudden inclusion of a Negro woman plays into the Magical Negro trope in cinema, television, and literature. The character often has no past but simply appears one day to help the white protagonist. They usually have some sort of vague magical power. The character is patient and wise, often dispensing various words of wisdom. Racism historians Francisco Bethencourt and John Beusterien trace the trope to the Spanish comedias de negros of the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries. The Magical Negro stereotype serves as a plot device to help the white protagonist get out of trouble, typically through helping the white character recognize his own faults, overcome them and teaching him to be a better person. Although the character may have magical powers, their magic is used to help and enlighten a white male character. (Wikipedia)

In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 7, Chapter 8, Chapter 17, Chapter 24, Chapter 33, Chapter 36, Chapter 38, Chapter 39, Chapter 54, Chapter 56, Chapter 69, Chapter 70, Chapter 71

Definition from research

Chapter 2 · Madness and Sanity

  • Catherine’s mental state is ambiguous; she is at times lucid, at times delusional.
  • Opium and drugs regulate her condition, creating a "scheduled madness" that preserves her life.
  • Her madness is a form of self-preservation and rebellion against a brutal world.

Chapter 7

  • “A fool, Lear in the storm”: In Shakespeare’s King Lear, the “storm” is both a physical and metaphorical force. Lear is exposed to a violent natural storm on the heath, symbolizing his internal turmoil and the chaos of his kingdom after he disowns his loyal supporters and his loving daughter Cordelia. This exposure forces him to confront his own mortality and the suffering of others, leading to a shift in his perspective and, ultimately, a descent into madness. It is a metaphorical description that situates old Doc in the tradition of tragic figures overwhelmed by chaos, emphasizing themes of madness, vulnerability, and existential struggle that run through the novel.
  • “Crazier than fifty mad men playing at badminton in an insane asylum”: Despite the shared space and activity, each player struggles individually while staff, guards, and others look on for their amusement. The phrase underscores the sense of profound disorientation and madness that pervades the novel, particularly embodied in old Doc, caught between life and death, reality and dream.
  • “All these old cretins”: Cretinism, stunted growth and mind from a lack of iodine, was common in the Great Lakes “goiter belt” until iodized salt came to Michigan in 1924.
  • “because it didn’t have its right mind. It was an idiot”: Idiot, imbecile, and moron were official medical categories, ranked by the eugenicist Henry Goddard in 1910.
  • “grew up with the water on her brain”: Hydrocephalus. Before shunts were developed in the 1950s, children with it were often called idiots and put away.

Chapter 8

  • “Delirium tremens, mocking birds, snakes”: The shaking delirium of alcohol withdrawal often brings visions of snakes and crawling things.
  • “Barmy, old Doc is, screw loose, unhinged, off his head”: Moses’s strings of synonyms, mad words here and later “Trunk, bole, hulk, skeleton,” read like the lists in Roget’s Thesaurus (1852).
  • “Mad as a March hare”: Hares run wild in their March mating season. Lewis Carroll’s March Hare (1865) keeps the mad tea party.

Chapter 17 · Fear and Madness

  • The setting at midnight, the eerie descriptions, and the “zero hour” evoke a sense of dread.
  • Vera’s fear escalates into a violent struggle, suggesting a descent into madness and trauma.
  • The chapter explores how strange events can “leave us mad” or shatter sanity.

Chapter 24 · Madness and Sanity

  • The novel delves into how prolonged exposure to Catherine’s dreams affects the servants, leading some to lose their grip on reality and adopt bizarre identities or behaviors (e.g., thinking they serve Wellington or living among cuckoo clocks).
  • This theme raises questions about the fragile line between sanity and madness in a closed, surreal environment.

Chapter 33

  • “none for the place, none for the person”: Doctors test whether a patient is “oriented to person, place, and time.”

Chapter 33 · Catherine’s Conversations with Invisible Figures

  • Demonstrates her detachment from consensus reality.
  • Mr. Spitzer could not hear the answer she heard, “though apparently what the other person said was quite rational.”

Chapter 36

  • “Hers was undoubtedly the logic of madness”: “Though this be madness, yet there is method in’t” (Shakespeare, Hamlet 2.2).

Chapter 36 · Memory versus Imagination

  • The chapter explores the fragile line between memory and imagination.
  • “It seemed to him that she had never distinguished between imagination and memory, the thinnest line sometimes dividing them.”
  • Catherine struggles to separate what is remembered from what is imagined or dreamed.
  • This blurring reflects the human difficulty in holding onto a fixed identity or past, especially after loss.
  • “Hers was undoubtedly the logic of madness, as he had many times pointed out.”

Chapter 38

  • “most people, it had been Mr. Spitzer’s unfortunate observation, were at some level disoriented”: Doctors still test whether a patient is “oriented” to person, place, and time, the same three matters Mr. Spitzer names.
  • “Lunacy reigned supreme”: Lunacy comes from the Latin luna, the moon, which was long believed to cause madness.

Chapter 38 · Labyrinthine Streets and Changing Signs

  • Symbolize confusion about identity and reality.

Chapter 39 · Illness and Madness

  • Catherine’s opium use and mental state are central to her experience.
  • She is aware of her insanity and the limitations imposed by it.
  • Madness is depicted as both a torment and a source of her vivid imagination and insight.

Chapter 54 · Duality of Identity and Madness

  • Mr. Spitzer oscillates between his own identity and that of his brother, sometimes confused about who he truly is. The chapter explores the thin line between sanity and madness, with Joachim embodying order and Peron chaos, yet both are reflections of each other.

Chapter 56 · Madness and Sanity

  • Madness is presented ambiguously as both a form of death and a form of life, sustaining illusion and preventing the advance of time.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s mental state deteriorates as he questions who controls him, who “tailored” his existence, and whether he is merely a puppet or a phantom.
  • His inability to distinguish between reality and imagination is a symbol of his psychological collapse.

Chapter 69 · Isolation and Madness

  • The doctor’s madness and isolation are emphasized through his anguished monologues and the strange, disruptive presence of Sarah.
  • The landlord and Vera observe these events as somewhat detached witnesses, enhancing the sense of alienation.

Chapter 70 · Madness and Sanity

  • Mrs. Hogden’s behavior is perceived as madness, yet she retains a shrewd awareness and control.
  • The narrative questions who is truly mad: the woman or those rejecting her.
  • Madness is portrayed both as a social stigma and a complex psychological state.

Chapter 71 · Madness and Reality

  • Dr. O’Leary’s madness blurs the lines between reality and hallucination.
  • The presence of imaginary babies and patients reflects the struggle to grasp meaning in a chaotic world.
  • Vera questions her own perception, wondering if she too is dreaming.

In the research: Chapter 12, Chapter 15, Chapter 16, Chapter 30, Chapter 35

Definition from research

Chapter 12 · Freedom, Innocence, and Joy

  • There is a moment of profound joy and freedom as Vera walks out into the night, celebrating the beauty and unity of nature.
  • This freedom is described as innocence and clarity of vision, untainted by past sorrow or fear.
  • Vera feels connected to the natural world, sensing stars, flowers, and animals as real and meaningful.

Chapter 15 · Youth and Experience versus Adult Convention

  • Vera experiences a moment of awakening, realizing the vastness and complexity of life beyond the restrictive, controlled world she has known.
  • She contrasts her youthful desire for experience and freedom with the narrow, methodical, and often fearful mindset of the adults, especially Miss MacIntosh.
  • The tension between youthful exploration and adult caution is central: Vera laughs at the warnings and rules, craving life’s fullness despite risks.

Chapter 16

  • “The fierce, exultant pride that was mine”: In “What Is It with Women and Horses?” (Intelligent Horsemanship, 2019), Dr. Rosie Jones-McVey, drawing on her PhD research among British horsewomen, writes: “In Victorian novels, as well as in the more modern genre of pony-girl books, it is often aboard a horse that girls find their wings, often proving some snot-nosed boy wrong in the process, or enabling them to escape various romantic dramas and find solace in the barn. Just like the pony-girl books, many of my participants’ life stories entwined horseyness with coming-of-age stories. Horses were the means through which many women first acted in a truly independent way, often pursuing equestrian endeavours despite/without their parents, or else, proudly taking up adult-like responsibilities in being the teacher, pilot, and carer of their ponies, rather than the one being looked after and told what to do.” She argues that horses give many women a space for independence and self-assertion that their everyday lives do not.

Chapter 16 · Imagination and Childhood Freedom

  • Vera’s ride on Falada is a metaphor for freedom and escape from her restrictive life.
  • The imaginative descriptions of the pony’s capabilities and their adventures reflect the boundless nature of a child’s mind.

Chapter 30 · Adventure and Escape

  • Cousin Hannah embodies the spirit of adventure, traveling to forbidden places and surviving countless dangers.
  • Her life serves as a counterpoint to Catherine’s static, opium-induced dreaming.
  • The recurring imagery of ships, deserts, and mountains emphasizes journeys both physical and metaphysical.

Chapter 35 · Freedom and Emancipation

  • Cousin Hannah embodies the fight for women’s rights and freedom from traditional roles.
  • Her life is a metaphor for breaking boundaries: social, geographic, and existential.
  • The suffrage movement is portrayed as her husband, her master, and her true love.
