Definition from research

Chapter 1 · Vera reflects on the nature of memory, illusion, and the human soul

  • The idea that individuality is an illusion and that every heart, soul, and face is interconnected.
  • The metaphor of ships passing in the night, representing fleeting human connections.
  • Vera’s lifelong search for tangible truth and connection, which has often evaded her, leaving only illusions and disconnected images.

Chapter 1 · Vera Cartwheel’s Personal Quest and History

  • Vera reveals herself as searching for a lost companion, Miss MacIntosh, an old nursemaid who symbolized stability, truth, and moral guidance in Vera’s life.
  • Miss MacIntosh is described as a simple, practical woman with a broken nose and red hair, who rejected illusions and fanciful dreams in favor of truth to nature. She was a grounding figure during Vera’s turbulent childhood amid a family haunted by opium and dreams.
  • Vera has wandered through various cities, employment, and social strata, always searching for Miss MacIntosh who had disappeared or died. This search is both literal and symbolic of Vera’s deeper quest for meaning, love, and truth.
  • Vera contrasts the opulent but empty grandeur of her mother’s house, filled with ghosts and illusions, with the plain, unpretentious life Miss MacIntosh led by the sea. This contrast highlights the theme of reality versus illusion in the narrative.
  • Vera contemplates the ephemeral nature of life, the inevitability of death, and the elusive quest for light and meaning in a world filled with darkness and dreams that fail.
  • Vera’s journey is both physical and spiritual, seeking a reality not distorted by illusion.
  • The narrative questions what is real, suggesting individuality and perception may be illusory.
  • The human condition is described as one of alienation, with fleeting and often failed attempts at connection.
  • The past haunts the present, and memory is both a source of pain and a guide.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s simple life contrasts with grand illusions, suggesting truth lies in everyday reality.

Chapter 2 · Memory and Forgetting

  • Catherine’s memories are fragmented, clouded, and often replaced by fantasy.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s forgetfulness contrasts with her photographic recall of his movements and lost incidents.
  • The past is both a refuge and a source of pain since she relives moments that never fully happened.

Chapter 4 · The Burden of the Past and Hope for Renewal

  • Vera acknowledges the haunting presence of past memories and illusions but expresses hope for a new life free from these obsessions.
  • She envisions a future where the "dead past would be buried," and she would awaken to the "blessed events" of life, including natural death after a long life filled with love and community.
  • The chapter ends with a reflection on the necessity of turning away from the insubstantial past towards the reality of life, even though it is fraught with disappointment and loss.

Chapter 6 · Memory and Forgetting

  • The tension between remembering and forgetting is prominent.
  • Madge tries to hold onto memories but is haunted by the past she cannot fully grasp.
  • Memory is unreliable, fragmented, and painful.

Chapter 8 · Memory and the Passage of Time

  • Vera reflects on the idea that drowning people relive their lives in moments before death, but here the memories seem fragmented and possibly belong to others.
  • The blending of past and present, and the uncertainty of reality and memory, permeate the narrative.

Chapter 11 · Memory and Loss

  • Catherine’s dream denies loss, imagining a universe where things are lost but not lost forever.
  • This suggests a coping mechanism for dealing with grief or fading consciousness.

Chapter 12

  • “each clock having been stopped at a different hour”: In Dickens’s Great Expectations (1861), Miss Havisham stops every clock at twenty minutes to nine, the hour she was jilted, and never leaves her room. Mourners once stopped the clocks at a death.

Chapter 13 · Memory and Change

  • Miss MacIntosh, once a familiar figure, will henceforth be seen as almost a stranger due to Vera’s new awareness.
  • Vera anticipates that all memories and familiar objects will be differently understood, weighted with new meanings.
  • This reflects the theme that memory is mutable and that new knowledge reshapes how the past, and people once thought known, are perceived.

Chapter 14 · Memory, Identity, and Duality

  • The chapter explores fractured identities, especially through the figure of Mr. Spitzer and his deceased brother.
  • Catherine perceives multiple overlapping realities and versions of Mr. Spitzer, reflecting her confusion and the blurred boundaries of life and death.
  • The motif of “four Mr. Spitzers” suggests layered selves and mirrored images, raising questions about selfhood and existence.

Chapter 14 · Family Legacy and Betrayal

  • Catherine suspects Mr. Spitzer of betraying the black coachman and mishandling her will and the family estate.
  • There is a theme of lost inheritance, broken promises, and the failure of caretakers to uphold traditions.

Chapter 16 · Memory and Identity

  • Vera reflects on her orphanhood, her lack of parents, and her future hopes.
  • She shares her secrets aloud, many of which she herself is only understanding as she speaks.

Chapter 16 · Death and Legacy

  • The imagery of marble statues, tombs, and silent fountains suggests mortality and the passage of time.
  • Falada’s pedigree connects him to historical and mythical lineage, suggesting the persistence of memory and identity beyond death.

Chapter 17 · Memory and Perception

  • Vera recalls past moments with Miss MacIntosh, contrasting them with the present terrifying vision.
  • There is an awareness that memory and perception can deceive or change over time.
  • Vera’s reflections on proverbs and parables hint at larger philosophical questions.

Chapter 18 · Memory and its Limitations

  • Memory is depicted as incomplete, evolving, and surrounded by the unknown.
  • Vera questions the accuracy of remembered events, hinting that memory may omit or alter essential details.
  • The idea that “the dream is never complete” and that new realities arise from what is missing in memory.

Chapter 22 · Memory and Forgetfulness

  • The sea, a recurring motif, is described as both full of “wrinkles” and yet possibly without memory. This paradox symbolizes the blurred lines between remembering and forgetting, life and oblivion.

Chapter 23 · Historical and Cultural Reflections

  • References to historical figures such as Emperor Constantine, Benjamin Franklin, and President Garfield serve as symbols of human folly or misguided progress.
  • The chapter also evokes images from ancient times and myths (e.g., Helen of Troy, Ulysses) to illustrate timeless human experiences affected by modern changes.

Chapter 23 · Historical References

  • Serve to question accepted narratives and human progress.

Chapter 25 · Memory and Forgetting

  • Memory is unreliable, often blending with imagination or dream.
  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with recalling events accurately and questions the nature of his own existence.
  • The dead are both remembered and forgotten, complicating the notion of legacy.

Chapter 26 · Memory versus Oblivion

  • Mr. Spitzer contrasts Catherine’s desire for memory with his own preference for oblivion after death, questioning what form of afterlife or peace is truly desirable.

Chapter 27 · Time and Memory

  • Time is portrayed as fluid, unreliable, and artificial.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s broken and inherited watches symbolize the fractured nature of time and memory.
  • The struggle with remembering and forgetting is a persistent motif, especially in relation to Mr. Spitzer’s brother’s death.

Chapter 28 · Memory and Identity

  • Mr. Spitzer’s struggle to understand “the actual man he was” highlights the elusive nature of self-knowledge and the effect of loss on personal identity.
  • Memory serves as a bridge to the past and as a means to preserve continuity, especially through his recollections of his brother.
  • The chapter suggests that memory may be deceptive or limited, with “things not possible” entering the mind through “the deceived memory of the unknown.”

Chapter 29 · Memory, Loss, and Mourning

  • Mr. Spitzer mourns his dead brother Peron, whose life was full of mystery and volatility.
  • His butterfly memories serve as a means to keep his brother’s essence alive, reflecting the human struggle to grasp and preserve fleeting moments.
  • The grief is profound yet hidden, affecting Mr. Spitzer’s mental state deeply.

Chapter 30 · Memory and the Past

  • The narrative dwells on historical figures and events (e.g., Russian czar’s murder, archdukes’ assassinations, Saladin, Solymon the Magnificent).
  • Cousin Hannah’s knowledge spans centuries and cultures, emphasizing the weight of history and memory.
  • Catherine’s longing for her lost husband and her imaginary invitations for card games with ancestors suggest an attempt to connect with the past.

Chapter 31 · Memory and Legacy

  • Mr. Spitzer’s grief and his attempts to memorialize Cousin Hannah illustrate struggles with remembering and forgetting.
  • “She had said that my mother was in love with no man on earth but with a fleeting shadow…” Emphasizes the theme of elusive love and the tension between reality and illusion.

Chapter 33 · Memory and Illusion

  • Catherine’s memories are described as “beautifully inaccurate,” blending fact with fantasy.
  • She often confuses time, place, and people, exemplifying the fragility of human memory.
  • Memories of her wedding are surreal, involving images like bats, owls, icy landscapes, and ambiguous bridegrooms.
  • The narrative suggests memory as a form of dream or illusion that can persist beyond life.

Chapter 35 · Memory and Legacy

  • The chapter meditates on how people are remembered after death.
  • Cousin Hannah remains vivid in memory, more alive in death than in life.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s legacy is one of bitterness and inertia, suggesting that memory favors the bold.

Chapter 36 · Memory versus Imagination

  • The chapter explores the fragile line between memory and imagination.
  • “It seemed to him that she had never distinguished between imagination and memory, the thinnest line sometimes dividing them.”
  • Catherine struggles to separate what is remembered from what is imagined or dreamed.
  • This blurring reflects the human difficulty in holding onto a fixed identity or past, especially after loss.
  • “Hers was undoubtedly the logic of madness, as he had many times pointed out.”

Chapter 37 · Memory and Oblivion

  • Catherine fears the loss of memory and self-awareness.
  • There is a contemplation of a “land of infinite greyness” where nothing remains: no memory, image, or ego.
  • This fear underlies her refusal to fully surrender to death or oblivion.

Chapter 38 · Memory and Reality

  • The chapter blurs the lines between memory, dream, and reality.
  • Catherine’s recollections are described as “inaccurate,” “clouded,” and “untrustworthy,” reflecting the elusive nature of truth.
  • The narrative questions the reliability of memory and whether dreams may contain a deeper accuracy than factual truth.
  • Time is fluid, with events and identities slipping and merging, e.g., Catherine confusing visitors or historical periods.

Chapter 39 · The Role of Memory and History

  • Catherine recalls historical figures and events with intimate detail, blending fact and fantasy.
  • Her memory is selective, fragmented, and often symbolic.
  • This reflects the human tendency to reconstruct identity and meaning through past narratives.

Chapter 40 · Memory, Dream, and Reality

  • The chapter blurs the boundaries between what is remembered, what is dreamed, and what is real.
  • Time is non-linear; events and voices intermingle without chronological order, reflecting Catherine’s fragmented memory and dream state.
  • Catherine frequently questions the reality of her experiences, wandering “not only the known world but the unknown world which she knew so very well because no one knew the unknown.”

Chapter 41 · Memory, Identity, and Self

  • Identity is fluid; Catherine can be many persons at once, sometimes failing to recognize herself.
  • Memories and past experiences collapse into moments without clear distinctions between past and present.
  • She grapples with who she is, where she is, and what form she might take after death.

Chapter 42 · Memory and Legacy

  • Cousin Hannah’s fading fame and forgotten battles symbolize how history erases even the greatest struggles. Mr. Spitzer’s reflections reveal the tension between public recognition and private sorrow, as well as the difficulty of preserving true legacy.

Chapter 43 · Memory, Identity, and Illusion

  • The suffragette’s past is fragmented and elusive, mixing real and imagined events.
  • Both characters wrestle with who they are and who others have been.
  • Dreams and memories flow outside of linear time, suggesting the permeability of identity.
  • Reality and illusion are intertwined; the suffragette’s visions may be symbolic rather than literal truth.

Chapter 44 · Death and Memory

  • Death is portrayed as a transformative and mysterious force, an eternal transmutation where forms change but essence remains.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s reflections suggest that death does not erase a person but deepens the mystery of their existence.
  • The chapter explores how memory is fragile; great lives and deeds can be forgotten, and the true nature of a person might never be fully known.

Chapter 45 · Memory, Identity, and the Passing of Time

  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with memory’s frailty, likening it to fleeting natural phenomena.
  • The chapter meditates on the dissolution of identity.
  • Cousin Hannah’s secret life and true self remain ambiguous, veiled in clouds and mystery, reflecting the difficulty of truly knowing another person, especially after death.

Chapter 46 · Memory and Oblivion

  • The chapter addresses how history, fame, and memory are fleeting. Cousin Hannah, despite her great achievements, is largely forgotten by the world, illustrating the tension between individual legacy and collective memory.

Chapter 47 · Memory, Identity, and Loss

  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with memory and identity, feeling lost between two worlds, unable to anchor himself or find certainty.
  • The elusive nature of memory and the impossibility of fully capturing or commemorating a lost love.

Chapter 48 · Memory, Lost Meaning, and the Music of Existence

  • The chapter frequently references music as a metaphor for life’s meaning and its transient, often elusive nature. Missing notes, echoes, and lost music symbolize forgotten memories or lost meaning in life and death.
  • The idea that the greatest music might be that which has no clear meaning, symbolizing the ineffability of existence.

Chapter 49 · Memory and Forgetfulness

  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with remembering and forgetting, his past and identity constantly shifting.

  • He questions the reliability of memory, pondering if he ever truly lived or if life was just a “mistaken dream.”

Chapter 53 · Life, Death, and Memory

  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates death not as an end but a transformation and continuation beyond physical existence. The boundaries between life and death blur, as love and memory maintain connections beyond mortality. He mourns his brother, yet also mourns himself, reflecting on the theme of grief diffused over time.

Chapter 54 · Memory, Time, and Reality

  • Time is fluid and non-linear. Newspapers are dated years ago but read as current; streets and cities shift; memories and experiences overlap. This challenges the concept of objective reality and highlights the fragility of memory.

Chapter 55 · Memory and Identity

  • Joachim’s identity is fragmented; his memory is unreliable, altered by grief and loss.
  • He questions whether he is himself or his brother, and whether he is awake or dreaming.

Chapter 57 · Debt and the Past

  • The persistent tailor’s bill symbolizes the unpayable debts of the past and the burden of memory. Mr. Spitzer’s attempts to pay or deny the debt represent his inability to move beyond grief and the past.

Chapter 58 · Memory and the Past

  • Mr. Spitzer’s reflections evoke buried childhood memories and a past nearly lost to time. His thoughts on his dead brother and old sportsmen convey a deep sense of mourning and nostalgia. The music, described as an old, nearly forgotten waltz, symbolizes this connection to the past and the fading of cultural memory.

Chapter 59 · Time and Memory

  • Time is depicted as fluid and unreliable; Mr. Spitzer experiences memories of vanished streets, people, and moments.
  • His experience of time is cyclical and elusive, with the past, present, and future intermingling.

Chapter 59 · On Memory and Loss

  • Memory holds both joy and pain; past pleasures become present pains.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s awareness of his own fading perceptions underscores the themes of loss and impermanence.

Chapter 60 · Memory, Imagination, and the Unconscious

  • The text weaves memories, hallucinations, and dreams, blurring boundaries between past and present, real and imagined.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s recollections of his dead brother and the imagined music he never wrote suggest themes of loss, regret, and the elusive nature of artistic creation.

  • The persistence of memory and identity beyond physical existence.

  • The cyclical nature of seasons (autumn, winter, spring) parallels Esther’s repeated pregnancies and losses, symbolizing the persistence of trauma and hope over time.

Chapter 3 · Discipline, Labor, and Practicality

  • Life is portrayed as a testing ground requiring discipline, hard work, and acceptance of necessary deprivations.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s emphasis on practical tasks (mending clothes, building fires) and physical exercise reflect this ethos.

Chapter 3 · Social Order and Class

  • Miss MacIntosh rejects aristocratic airs and illusions of grandeur.
  • She advocates for the dignity of simple people and honest labor.

Chapter 9 · Discipline and Domesticity

  • Miss MacIntosh’s rigorous training prepares Vera for the traditional female role of housekeeping and marriage.
  • Emphasis on practical skills (sewing, household chores) contrasts with Vera’s imaginative inner life.
  • The discipline is strict, yet there is an undercurrent of rebellion and dissatisfaction.

Chapter 12

  • “a place for everything”: “A place for everything, and everything in its place,” the old household rule.

Chapter 14 · Law and Order versus Chaos

  • Mr. Spitzer embodies legal order but is portrayed as overwhelmed by the disorder of life and his own ghosts.
  • Catherine’s world is chaotic, filled with shifting images, ghosts, and memories that resist neat categorization.

Chapter 15 · Youth and Experience versus Adult Convention

  • Vera experiences a moment of awakening, realizing the vastness and complexity of life beyond the restrictive, controlled world she has known.
  • She contrasts her youthful desire for experience and freedom with the narrow, methodical, and often fearful mindset of the adults, especially Miss MacIntosh.
  • The tension between youthful exploration and adult caution is central: Vera laughs at the warnings and rules, craving life’s fullness despite risks.

Chapter 18 · Return to Normalcy and the Persistence of Routine

  • Miss MacIntosh insists that the strange night is a dream and that normal life will resume with the morning.
  • The repeated references to daily routines, domestic tasks, and practical lessons reflect the human need to cling to order amid chaos.

Chapter 22 · Routine versus Inner Turmoil

  • Vera experiences deep emotional fatigue and existential questioning, feeling trapped in repetitive, meaningless tasks imposed by Miss MacIntosh’s rigid routine. The contrast highlights the human struggle between external order and internal chaos.

Chapter 22 · Knowledge and Education

  • The insistence on memorizing Biblical genealogies, current events, geography, and sports reflects a traditional, perhaps oppressive, approach to learning as a way to impose order and meaning in a chaotic world.

Chapter 23 · Common Sense and the Middle Way

  • She values common sense and the “middle brow,” the average life, as a guiding principle.
  • Despite her philosophical musings on vast, cosmic issues, she prides herself on practicality and sensibility.

Chapter 23 · Nature and the Cosmic Order

  • The novel references natural phenomena such as glaciers, tides, northern stars, and the changing seasons.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s talk about ice floes, winter preparations, and the Arctic environment symbolizes the fragility and impermanence of existence.
  • There is a tension between the cosmic, the remote, and the immediate, everyday life.

Chapter 37 · Order and Chance

  • “Order, had she not always said, was a mad man’s dream, the maddest dream of all.”
  • She asks “how should we live except by accident, for were we not already dead.”
  • The music shakes “the enamelled heavens and the earth like a dice box,” and she sees “stars marked like dice.”

Chapter 40 · Time and Order

  • The chapter challenges conventional notions of time and causality (“the echo came before the song,” “death came before life”).
  • Time is cyclical, layered, and full of “refractions” and “oblique passages,” making logic and sequence unreliable.

Chapter 42 · The Search for Meaning Amid Chaos

  • Mr. Spitzer’s obsession with lost ships and records symbolizes humanity’s quest for order and meaning despite the inherent chaos of existence. The lost ships, passengers, and forgotten histories mirror Cousin Hannah’s own forgotten life.

Chapter 51

  • “he might change rivers in their course”: Mr. Spitzer’s fear is the butterfly effect of chaos theory: small, subtle causes yielding large, unpredictable consequences in a complex, interwoven reality. Chaos theory studies systems, like weather or ecosystems, so sensitive to their starting conditions that a tiny change can lead to vastly different outcomes, though underlying patterns, feedback loops, and self-organization remain (Wikipedia). The meteorologist Edward Lorenz named the effect in a 1972 talk, “Predictability: Does the Flap of a Butterfly’s Wings in Brazil Set Off a Tornado in Texas?” Ray Bradbury had already imagined it in “A Sound of Thunder” (1952), where a time traveler steps on a butterfly and changes history. “For the chaos had its pattern.”

Chapter 55 · Order versus Chaos

  • Joachim’s life is governed by plans, maps, and precise arrangements designed to exclude chance and disorder.
  • Peron’s life is the antithesis: reckless, chaotic, and unpredictable.
  • The tension between these forces creates conflict and tragedy, illustrating the human struggle to balance these aspects.

Chapter 70 · Decay and Disorder

  • Her physical smell and appearance evoke decay (rotted apples, dead flies).
  • The disorder she brings contrasts with the previously orderly household.
  • Symbolizes the intrusion of chaos into a controlled environment.

  • Catherine’s dream involves figures like Rameses I, II, and III, representing fragmented selves and layered identities.

  • “partitioned into many selves without his knowing it”: The Egyptians held that a person was made of many parts: the ka, the life force; the ba, the soul that flies from the tomb; the name; the shadow; and the heart, weighed at judgment.

  • The chapter explores fractured identities, especially through the figure of Mr. Spitzer and his deceased brother.

  • The motif of “four Mr. Spitzers” suggests layered selves and mirrored images, raising questions about selfhood and existence.

Chapter 16 · Memory and Identity

  • Vera reflects on her orphanhood, her lack of parents, and her future hopes.
  • She shares her secrets aloud, many of which she herself is only understanding as she speaks.

Chapter 17 · Identity and Transformation

  • Miss MacIntosh’s sudden baldness and altered demeanor symbolize a profound change, calling into question the stability of identity.
  • Vera’s inability to accept this change reflects a struggle with understanding the self and others.

  • The “mask” everyone wears shields them from their true selves, leading to isolation and existential loneliness.

Chapter 20 · Identity and Self-Perception

  • Miss MacIntosh’s lack of “intuitive imagination” and her common sense shield her from the deeper, visionary truths Vera perceives; she is “content with things just as they were” and would deny or not suspect the “empty vision” beyond the commonplace.
  • Vera’s internal conflict involves a desire to pretend normalcy to protect both Miss MacIntosh and herself from confronting the full reality of her condition.
  • There is also a complex emotional dynamic, where Vera simultaneously sees her as an “obstacle” to her happiness and as someone deeply significant, a secret lover or cause of her “vain pursuits.”

Chapter 25 · Identity and Duality

  • The twin brothers symbolize duality: life/death, faith/faithlessness, decisiveness/hesitation.

  • The confusion over who he is and who he might become reflects existential uncertainty.

Chapter 27 · Dignity and Self-Image

  • Mr. Spitzer is deeply concerned with preserving his dignity and avoiding ridicule.
  • His physicality (notably his size) and the fear of losing control over his image are recurring concerns.

Chapter 27 · Calling Cards and Passport

  • His calling cards, out-dated passport, and scroll of silent music are what he carries so that the world will know him from his brother.

Chapter 28 · Memory and Identity

  • Mr. Spitzer’s struggle to understand “the actual man he was” highlights the elusive nature of self-knowledge and the effect of loss on personal identity.
  • Memory serves as a bridge to the past and as a means to preserve continuity, especially through his recollections of his brother.
  • The chapter suggests that memory may be deceptive or limited, with “things not possible” entering the mind through “the deceived memory of the unknown.”

Chapter 29 · Multiplicity of the Soul

  • The idea of multiple souls or a divided self, reflecting Mr. Spitzer’s sense of identity and the presence of his brother’s spirit within him.

Chapter 34 · Identity and Loneliness

  • Catherine feels isolated, spouseless, and robbed of love, reflecting a deep sense of loneliness and alienation.
  • Cousin Hannah represents a contrasting figure of strength and defiance, yet also one marked by solitude and an almost otherworldly existence.

  • Catherine is “this fragmented ego, these fragmentations of partial selves, of splintered mirrors and partial images.”
  • Her selves include “the look-out in the crow’s-nest… the lady in the phaeton, the figurehead in the foam.”
  • Hannah seemed never to have “divided herself… into opposing factions, warring camps, the battle raging in her own breasts.”
  • “Yet the extremities of faith in anything might always beget, my mother knew, its opposite.”
  • Mr. Spitzer acknowledges “at all times, two truths, neither of which should be true.”

Chapter 36 · Identity and Fragmentation

  • Characters experience fragmented selves, double lives, or counterfeit identities.
  • The death of a twin brother creates a split in Mr. Spitzer’s identity.
  • Cousin Hannah’s identity transcends death and conventional existence, becoming fluid and ambiguous.

Chapter 37 · Identity and Transformation

  • Identity is unstable and mutable, with images of people changing genders, faces, or even species. “One saw that God was dog.”
  • This theme questions the essence of self, suggesting that we might be composites of many selves or none at all.
  • The recurring motif of masks, doubles, and shifting forms highlights the fracturing or multiplicity of identity.

Chapter 39 · Fragmented Identity and Multiplicity of Selves

  • Catherine perceives herself as many selves, sometimes contradictory, never unified.
  • She contemplates which self is true or dominant, fearing that choosing one would mean losing the many fascinating false selves that sustain her.
  • This fragmentation extends to her questioning of self-knowledge and sanity, recognizing her madness but finding it integral to her existence.

Chapter 40 · Identity and Multiplicity of Self

  • Catherine perceives herself as many selves, reflections, and chimeras, sometimes unable to distinguish her true self from her images or memories.
  • This multiplicity reflects the complexity of identity within the realms of memory, dream, and consciousness.

Chapter 41 · Memory, Identity, and Self

  • Identity is fluid; Catherine can be many persons at once, sometimes failing to recognize herself.
  • Memories and past experiences collapse into moments without clear distinctions between past and present.
  • She grapples with who she is, where she is, and what form she might take after death.

Chapter 42 · Identity and Transformation

  • Hannah’s multiple identities (Hannah, Hamid, Al Hamid, Great Moor) and her shifting roles reflect the multiplicity of self and the transformative power of myth and legend. Mr. Spitzer’s own uncertainty about his identity parallels this theme.

Chapter 43 · Memory, Identity, and Illusion

  • The suffragette’s past is fragmented and elusive, mixing real and imagined events.
  • Both characters wrestle with who they are and who others have been.
  • Dreams and memories flow outside of linear time, suggesting the permeability of identity.
  • Reality and illusion are intertwined; the suffragette’s visions may be symbolic rather than literal truth.

Chapter 45 · Memory, Identity, and the Passing of Time

  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with memory’s frailty, likening it to fleeting natural phenomena.
  • The chapter meditates on the dissolution of identity.
  • Cousin Hannah’s secret life and true self remain ambiguous, veiled in clouds and mystery, reflecting the difficulty of truly knowing another person, especially after death.

Chapter 46 · Identity and Masks

  • The motif of masks and clothing in dreams suggests that identity is always layered, never fully naked or transparent. Ghosts and memories are always clothed in some form, and this applies to living beings as well.

Chapter 47 · Memory, Identity, and Loss

  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with memory and identity, feeling lost between two worlds, unable to anchor himself or find certainty.
  • The elusive nature of memory and the impossibility of fully capturing or commemorating a lost love.

Chapter 48 · Identity and Self-Consciousness

  • Mr. Spitzer questions the nature of identity, whether the self remains unchanged after death, and how one can recognize oneself or others beyond life.
  • The possibility that he and his brother might be one and the same or that identity is fragmented and uncertain.

Chapter 49 · Identity and Self-Perception

  • There is a profound ambiguity regarding Mr. Spitzer’s identity, “He knew not whether he was himself or an image contained within an image.”
  • The motif of doubling, shadows, and reflections recurs, contributing to his fragmented self-understanding.
  • He often quarrels with himself or his shadow, suggesting an internal conflict and fractured self.

  • Mr. Spitzer experiences a world where “everything seemed off key and out of course” and where familiar structures (rooms, stars, chairs) multiply or dissolve, making it impossible to distinguish reality from dream or hallucination.

  • Mr. Spitzer is described as a man of many parts, many identities, reflecting a fragmented self that cannot be pinned down to a single essence.
  • There are references to his “dead twin,” suggesting a duality or multiplicity of selves.
  • His confusion over who he is (lawyer, doctor, musician, lamp-lighter) which symbolizes the fluidity and elusiveness of identity.

  • The chapter is permeated with questions of identity, both Mr. Spitzer’s and the suffragette’s. Mr. Spitzer struggles to know who he is or whether he is a ghostly twin. The suffragette’s identity remains veiled, indicated by symbols like veils, masks, and cloud fusions.

Chapter 53 · Identity and Duality

  • The chapter explores the paradox of the two brothers’ overlapping identities. Joachim as the “pale replica” of Peron, and Peron as an elusive, many-personality figure. The idea that Joachim might be Peron and vice versa underlines the instability of self and questions the fixity of identity.

Chapter 54 · Duality of Identity and Madness

  • Mr. Spitzer oscillates between his own identity and that of his brother, sometimes confused about who he truly is. The chapter explores the thin line between sanity and madness, with Joachim embodying order and Peron chaos, yet both are reflections of each other.

Chapter 55 · Memory and Identity

  • Joachim’s identity is fragmented; his memory is unreliable, altered by grief and loss.
  • He questions whether he is himself or his brother, and whether he is awake or dreaming.
  • His life is a continuous search for meaning in the past and the present, often blurred and confused.

  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with his identity, feeling like a shadow or a poor copy of his brother, or even a puppet controlled by unknown forces.

Reality itself is depicted as made from “sticks” or tools, with identity shaped by perspective and imagination.

  • “He knew only that in order to be what one was one must be what one was not”: To be himself, Mr. Spitzer, the living brother who carries the dead one, must also be his brother, his shadow, his opposite: identity holds what it is not.

  • The text contrasts Esther’s experiences with societal expectations of men and women, highlighting gendered double standards, especially concerning sexuality, motherhood, and blame.

  • Walter’s blackness is a symbolic and literal source of conflict, shame, love, and fear for Esther, reflecting broader themes of racial tension and identity.

  • “The shadow created the light, but the light created the shadow”: Miss MacIntosh, the practical nursemaid, sides with the light and with facts faced plainly.   • “the Big Ben alarm clock”: The Big Ben was the Western Clock Company’s alarm clock, sold from 1909 and the first alarm clock advertised across the country (1910). It takes its name from the great bell in London.
  • “though time was an illusion, it was not the illusion of servants”: Einstein wrote in 1955 that the distinction between past, present, and future “is only a stubbornly persistent illusion.” Servants still had to rise on time.

  • The inevitability of winter and death is anticipated, reflecting on the cycles of life.

  • “he lived in a forest of cuckoo clocks”: The cuckoo clock came from the Black Forest of Germany in the eighteenth century.

  • Cuckoo clocks and elephants represent distorted time and impossible realities within the servants’ transformed perceptions.

  • The narrative challenges linear notions of time. Catherine’s journey is described as transcending death and time, visiting Cousin Hannah when both are bed-ridden or dead. Dreams and waking reality blur, reflecting a mystical view of existence where farewell is “a matter of opinion as to the time, the place, the person.”

In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 3, Chapter 5, Chapter 6, Chapter 7, Chapter 8, Chapter 9, Chapter 10, Chapter 11, Chapter 12, Chapter 13, Chapter 14, Chapter 15, Chapter 16, Chapter 17, Chapter 18, Chapter 19, Chapter 20, Chapter 21, Chapter 22, Chapter 24, Chapter 25, Chapter 26, Chapter 27, Chapter 29, Chapter 30, Chapter 31, Chapter 32, Chapter 33, Chapter 34, Chapter 35, Chapter 36, Chapter 37, Chapter 38, Chapter 39, Chapter 40, Chapter 41, Chapter 42, Chapter 43, Chapter 44, Chapter 45, Chapter 46, Chapter 47, Chapter 48, Chapter 49, Chapter 51, Chapter 52, Chapter 53, Chapter 54, Chapter 55, Chapter 56, Chapter 57, Chapter 58, Chapter 59, Chapter 61, Chapter 62, Chapter 63, Chapter 65, Chapter 66, Chapter 68, Chapter 69, Chapter 70, Chapter 72, Chapter 73, Chapter 76, Chapter 78, Chapter 79, Chapter 81

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • “great frogs with jewels in their foreheads”: An old belief held that the toad carried a precious stone, the toadstone, in its head, a cure for poison. Shakespeare used it in As You Like It: “Sweet are the uses of adversity, / Which, like the toad, ugly and venomous, / Wears yet a precious jewel in his head.”
  • “such as a dusty sparrow falling”: Jesus says of the sparrows, “one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father” (Matthew 10:29), and Hamlet answers his friend’s fears with “There is special providence in the fall of a sparrow.” Catherine later counts “falling sparrows, falling leaves, drops of water, grains of sand.”
  • “If ears could see, if eyes could hear”: Bottom wakes from his enchanted night in A Midsummer Night’s Dream with the senses mixed up: “The eye of man hath not heard, the ear of man hath not seen, man’s hand is not able to taste, his tongue to conceive, nor his heart to report, what my dream was.” Bottom is parodying 1 Corinthians 2:9.

Chapter 3

  • “She dismissed the insubstantial fabric of the dream”: The phrase echoes Prospero in Shakespeare’s The Tempest: “And, like the baseless fabric of this vision, . . . this insubstantial pageant faded, / Leave not a rack behind. We are such stuff / As dreams are made on.”
  • “those who died but once, those who could not afford to die twice”: Julius Caesar says in Shakespeare’s play, “Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once.”
  • “our good works should not live after us”: Miss MacIntosh reverses Mark Antony in Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar: “The evil that men do lives after them; / The good is oft interred with their bones.”

Chapter 5

  • “seeing the breath on the mirror where there was no breath, the feather move where there was no feather”: Holding a mirror or a feather to the lips was the old test for death. King Lear, holding the dead Cordelia, calls, “Lend me a looking-glass; / If that her breath will mist or stain the stone, / Why, then she lives,” and then, “This feather stirs; she lives!”
  • “this womb of time”: Iago says, “There are many events in the womb of time which will be delivered” (Othello 1.3).
  • “in his second childhood”: In Shakespeare’s As You Like It, Jaques’s seven ages of man end in “second childishness and mere oblivion.”

Chapter 6

  • “To thine own self be true, and it will follow as the day the night”: Polonius gives this advice to his son Laertes in Hamlet (1.3): “This above all: to thine own self be true, / And it must follow, as the night the day, / Thou canst not then be false to any man.” Homer gets it backwards, “as the day the night.”
  • “come to the wedding feast and had stayed for the funeral”: Hamlet reversed: “the funeral baked meats / Did coldly furnish forth the marriage tables” (Hamlet 1.2).
  • “it had not been a marriage of true souls”: Shakespeare’s Sonnet 116: “Let me not to the marriage of true minds / Admit impediments. Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds.” Later Madge asks whether love can “alter.”
  • “Oh, Romeo, oh, Romeo!”: Juliet’s “O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?” (Romeo and Juliet 2.2).
  • “love is blind”: “But love is blind, and lovers cannot see” (The Merchant of Venice 2.6).
  • “Ding, dong, bell”: Ariel’s song for a drowned father in The Tempest: “Full fathom five thy father lies . . . Ding-dong, bell.” Madge’s father drowned. The nursery rhyme “Ding, dong, bell, / Pussy’s in the well” also ends in drowning.
  • “She was Juliet, and I was Romeo”: In the play Romeo kisses Juliet, believing her dead, and drinks poison before she wakes from the sleeping potion.

Chapter 7

  • “A fool, Lear in the storm”: In Shakespeare’s King Lear, the “storm” is both a physical and metaphorical force. Lear is exposed to a violent natural storm on the heath, symbolizing his internal turmoil and the chaos of his kingdom after he disowns his loyal supporters and his loving daughter Cordelia. This exposure forces him to confront his own mortality and the suffering of others, leading to a shift in his perspective and, ultimately, a descent into madness. It is a metaphorical description that situates old Doc in the tradition of tragic figures overwhelmed by chaos, emphasizing themes of madness, vulnerability, and existential struggle that run through the novel.
  • “I know old Gertrude from away back”: Gertrude may be named after the character in Hamlet by Shakespeare. Both Gertrudes embody the tragic consequences of familial and marital complexities: Miss MacIntosh’s Gertrude through literal murder and madness, Shakespeare’s Gertrude through moral ambiguity and political betrayal. They both represent the fragility of women’s positions within patriarchal and violent family systems, caught between roles as wives, mothers, and individuals subjected to forces beyond their control. Their characters explore themes of guilt, innocence, and the ambiguity of human motives, complicating simplistic moral judgments. Both have a presence associated with death and decay, whether physical or psychological, underscoring the novel’s and play’s meditation on mortality.
  • “no lock which could not be opened at last by the locksmith”: The proverb “Love laughs at locksmiths” comes from Shakespeare’s Venus and Adonis.
  • “the drunken sexton who used to dance a merry jig when anybody died”: Hamlet’s gravedigger sings at his work: “Has this fellow no feeling of his business, that he sings at grave-making?” (Hamlet 5.1).
  • “It was that skull the children played with”: “Alas, poor Yorick!” Hamlet holds the jester’s skull (Hamlet 5.1).
  • “She was Mrs. Hathaway, and she became Mrs. Hathaway”: Shakespeare’s wife was Anne Hathaway, a fitting married name for a Gertrude straight out of Hamlet.

Chapter 7

  • “I know old Gertrude from away back”: Gertrude may be named after the character in Hamlet by Shakespeare. Both Gertrudes embody the tragic consequences of familial and marital complexities: Miss MacIntosh’s Gertrude through literal murder and madness, Shakespeare’s Gertrude through moral ambiguity and political betrayal. They both represent the fragility of women’s positions within patriarchal and violent family systems, caught between roles as wives, mothers, and individuals subjected to forces beyond their control. Their characters explore themes of guilt, innocence, and the ambiguity of human motives, complicating simplistic moral judgments. Both have a presence associated with death and decay, whether physical or psychological, underscoring the novel’s and play’s meditation on mortality.

Chapter 7

  • “What did he expect, marrying his brother’s wife”: Levirate marriage is the custom where the brother of a deceased man is obliged to marry his brother’s widow. (Wikipedia) Deuteronomy 25:5 commands it, and Leviticus 20:21 forbids it. Henry VIII used Leviticus to end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, his brother’s widow. In Shakespeare’s Hamlet, Gertrude, Hamlet’s mother, marries her husband’s brother Claudius after the king’s death. Since women were completely dependent on their father, brother, or husband, they did not have much choice. In order to not be destitute they had to be attached. Even now women are poorer at retirement with less savings mainly because of missed years of income raising children. Social Security was partly founded to take care of these widows who wrote letters to FDR.

Chapter 8

  • “What happened to Julius Caesar?”: Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. He was stabbed in the Senate in 44 B.C. by conspirators including Brutus, his friend, and Shakespeare gave him the words “Et tu, Brute?”
  • “Cyclops, men whose heads do grow beneath their shoulders”: Othello tells of “the Anthropophagi, and men whose heads / Do grow beneath their shoulders” (Othello 1.3). The Cyclops is the one-eyed giant of the Odyssey, like one-eyed Beatrice.

Chapter 9

  • “the canker eats the rose”: “And loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud” (Shakespeare, Sonnet 35).
  • “all local habitations and all names”: The poet “gives to airy nothing / A local habitation and a name” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream 5.1).

Chapter 10

  • “his brother worm who was under the ground”: Job says “to the worm, Thou art my mother, and my sister” (Job 17:14), and Hamlet says, “Your worm is your only emperor for diet” (Hamlet 4.3).
  • “What is man but a poor, two-legged animal?”: Plato defined man as a featherless biped, and Diogenes answered with a plucked chicken. Lear calls man “such a poor, bare, forked animal” (King Lear 3.4).
  • “Porpoises shall eat the drowned sailor. The waters of this world shall close over his head”: The preacher gives the bride and groom a sailor’s burial at sea. Milton’s “Lycidas” (1638) mourns a friend drowned in the Irish Sea, and Ariel sings of a drowned father in The Tempest: “Full fathom five thy father lies.” The line foreshadows Miss MacIntosh lost in the waves.

Chapter 11

  • “Pericles”: Pericles (c. 495-429 BC) led Athens in its golden age and had the Parthenon built.
  • “a society of night devoted exclusively to atheistic propositions”: “The school of night” comes from Love’s Labour’s Lost (4.3): “Black is the badge of hell, / The hue of dungeons and the school of night.” The phrase became a name for Raleigh’s circle with Thomas Harriot and Christopher Marlowe, men accused of doubting Genesis and God. In 1594 an inquiry at Cerne Abbas examined charges of atheism against Raleigh’s circle.

Chapter 12

Chapter 13

  • “Ben Jonson”: Ben Jonson was a significant early modern English poet and playwright, known for his satirical comedies, masques, and poetry. He was a contemporary of Shakespeare, received a royal pension in 1616, which has led some to call him England’s first Poet Laureate, and is celebrated for plays like Volpone (a dark comedy about greed and corruption) and The Alchemist (a satire about fraud and human folly). “To Celia,” also known as “Drink to me only with thine eyes,” is a famous love song by Ben Jonson, first published in his 1616 collection The Forest. (Wikipedia)
  • “fixed like the North star”: “But I am constant as the northern star, / Of whose true-fix’d and resting quality / There is no fellow in the firmament” (Julius Caesar 3.1).
  • “my mother feigned death”: Juliet drinks the Friar’s potion to lie as if dead (Romeo and Juliet 4.1).
  • “not even the creaking of starlight”: Aristotle reports the Pythagorean answer: the spheres do make music, and people do not hear it because they have heard it since birth (On the Heavens 2.9). Lorenzo tells Jessica, “Such harmony is in immortal souls; / But whilst this muddy vesture of decay / Doth grossly close it in, we cannot hear it” (The Merchant of Venice 5.1).

  • “but what was a name?”: “What’s in a name? That which we call a rose / By any other word would smell as sweet” (Romeo and Juliet 2.2). Catherine says it of a servant whose name no one kept.

Chapter 15

  • “Man was but a poor, forked animal”: Lear: “unaccommodated man is no more but such a poor, bare, forked animal as thou art” (King Lear 3.4).

  • “still water runs deep”: “Still waters run deep” is a proverb of Latin origin now commonly taken to mean that a placid exterior hides a passionate or subtle nature. Formerly it also carried the warning that silent people are dangerous, as in Suffolk’s comment on a fellow lord in Shakespeare’s Henry VI, Part 2: “Smooth runs the water where the brook is deep” (3.1). (Wikipedia)

  • “a rose by any other name would smell as sweet”: Romeo and Juliet 2.2. Catherine forgot the coachman’s name in Chapter 14, while Mr. Spitzer believes “all things were in their names.”

Chapter 17

  • “her corset stays sticking out like the quills of an angry porcupine”: The Ghost tells Hamlet his tale would make “each particular hair to stand on end, / Like quills upon the fretful porpentine” (Hamlet 1.5). A few lines later, “My hair crawled,” and soon Vera’s hair stands “on end.”
  • “that zero hour, the hour of midnight when strangest things do often happen”: “Zero hour” was the soldiers’ name for the hour of attack in the First World War. “’Tis now the very witching time of night, / When churchyards yawn” (Hamlet 3.2).
  • “who knows not the grinning skull?”: Yorick’s skull: “Where be your gibes now?… Not one now, to mock your own grinning?” (Hamlet 5.1).

Chapter 18

An old man’s love is a young maid’s sorrow”: Both lines are old proverbs, often found in folk traditions and songs, particularly in the context of warnings against marrying old men, as in the ballad “Maids When You’re Young Never Wed an Old Man” (Ballad Index). John Heywood’s Proverbs (1546) has the other side: “Better to be an old man’s darling than a young man’s warling.”

In Romeo and Juliet, the Nurse warns Romeo not to “lead her into a fool’s paradise” (2.4). Miss MacIntosh tells Vera she was “living in a fool’s paradise, and now you know there is no answer.”

Young follows with “The true love wears an old shirt and is familiar.”
  • “where was Shakespeare?”: William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet and actor.
  • “Watchman, what of the night? Who goes there?”: “Watchman, what of the night?” (Isaiah 21:11), and the opening of Hamlet, “Who’s there?”
  • “Out, out, brief candle!”: “Out, out, brief candle! / Life’s but a walking shadow” (Macbeth 5.5).

  • “most men are conceived in the night and die with the ebbing of the tide”: In Dickens’s David Copperfield (1850), Mr. Peggotty says of the dying Barkis, “People can’t die, along the coast, except when the tide’s pretty nigh out.” Falstaff died “ev’n at the turning o’ th’ tide” (Henry V 2.3).

Chapter 21 · Love as Eternal and Unchanging

  • Vera emphasizes that true love remains constant despite changing circumstances. Love “does not ebb, does not wane,” symbolizing an ideal of permanence in an impermanent world.
  • This eternal love contrasts with the physical and emotional struggles depicted, underscoring a spiritual or emotional steadfastness.

Chapter 22

  • “I know no Greek, less Latin, less Hebrew”: Ben Jonson said Shakespeare had “small Latine, and lesse Greeke” (First Folio, 1623).

  • “It takes more than clothes to make the man”: It means that a person’s character, personality, and true worth cannot be judged solely by their appearance or what they wear. A person’s inner qualities and actions are what truly define them, not just their outward appearance. This saying directly contradicts the proverb “clothes make the man.” Polonius: “the apparel oft proclaims the man” (Hamlet 1.3).

  • “where Childe Roland had blown his horn before a dark tower”: Childe Roland is a character in a poem by Robert Browning. The character Roland in the poem makes a journey to the Dark Tower much like the journey of Pilgrim’s Progress and the Divine Comedy. The name Child Roland comes from the Shakespeare play King Lear Act 3 Scene 4 Lines 195-197. Browning’s poem is “Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came” (1855), and it ends with the horn: “Dauntless the slug-horn to my lips I set, / And blew. ‘Childe Roland to the Dark Tower came.’” The horn also recalls Roland of The Song of Roland, who blew his horn Oliphant at Roncevaux (778).

Matthew Arnold called Oxford the “home of lost causes” (Essays in Criticism, 1865), and “a thing of naught” is Flute’s phrase in A Midsummer Night’s Dream (4.2).

Hamlet’s players perform a dumb-show before The Murder of Gonzago (3.2). (Wikipedia)

Chapter 43 · Black Moor / Blackamoor

  • “out, out of this life”: “Out, out, brief candle! / Life’s but a walking shadow” (Macbeth 5.5). Mr. Spitzer speaks it with a match burning in his hand.

  • “for this life was a long rehearsal of music for the silence”: Life is a rehearsal, a practice, for the silence of death. The “music” is the experience of a life, passing and temporary; the “silence” is death, where all of it ceases, and which “could surely not answer or reproach.” Socrates says that “the true philosophers, Simmias, are always occupied in the practice of dying” (Plato, Phaedo 67e, trans.   • “Perhaps he was translated”: “By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death” (Hebrews 11:5); to be translated is to be carried to heaven without dying. “Bless thee, Bottom, bless thee! thou art translated” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream 3.1).

Chapter 49

  • “the griffin with its wings of gold”: Griffins were said to guard the gold of the far north (Herodotus 3.116). “The smallest worm will turn being trodden on” (Henry VI, Part 3, 2.2), but this worm never turned.

Chapter 51

  • Eros is a concept in ancient Greek philosophy referring to sensual or passionate love. It has been used in philosophy and psychology as an equivalent to life energy. “Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind; / And therefore is wing’d Cupid painted blind” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream 1.1).

Chapter 52

  • “that old jack of all trades who was the master of none”: The saying “Jack of all trades, master of none” grew from older forms; in 1592 Robert Greene sneered at the young Shakespeare as a Johannes factotum, a Jack of all trades.
  • “she could not have worn her heart upon her sleeve”: Iago says in Shakespeare’s Othello, “But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve / For daws to peck at” (1.1).
  • “Love knew no age”: Jessica says in Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice, “But love is blind, and lovers cannot see / The pretty follies that themselves commit” (2.6). Cupid was sometimes depicted blindfolded; Erwin Panofsky traced the image in “Blind Cupid,” in Studies in Iconology (1939).

Chapter 53

  • “old Dan Cupid, the wizened cherub, the blind god of love”: Dan was an old title of respect, from the Latin dominus; Berowne calls him “Dan Cupid” in Shakespeare’s Love’s Labour’s Lost (3.1). See blind Cupid in the Chapter 52 resources.
  • “a queen of the desert sands had played billiards”: The “queen of the desert” who played pool may refer to Cleopatra in Shakespeare’s play Antony and Cleopatra where she is bored and asks Charmian to play billiards. “Let it alone; let’s to billiards: come, Charmian” (2.5), an anachronism, since billiards is a much later game.

This is similar to the plot line in the Shakespeare play Hamlet where the ghost is Hamlet’s dead father.

Chapter 54

  • “his wife had cuckolded him”: A cuckold is the husband of an adulterous wife (or partner for unmarried companions); the wife of an adulterous husband is a cuckquean. In biology, a cuckold is a male who unwittingly invests parental effort in juveniles who are not genetically his offspring. A husband who is aware of and tolerates his wife’s infidelity is sometimes called a wittol or wittold. The slang term bull refers to the dominant man who has relations with the cuckold’s partner.
  • Lord Banquo is a character in Shakespeare’s play MacBeth. He is at first an ally of Macbeth and they meet the Three Witches together. After prophesying that Macbeth will become king, the witches tell Banquo that he will not be king himself, but that his descendants will be. Later, Macbeth in his lust for power sees Banquo as a threat and has him murdered by three hired assassins.
  • “My kingdom for a horse”: “A horse! a horse! my kingdom for a horse!” cries Richard at Bosworth (Shakespeare, Richard III 5.4).

Chapter 55

  • “Should the alteration recognize that it was altered?”: Young turns Shakespeare’s “Love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds” (William Shakespeare, Sonnet 116, 1609).
  • “cast off, as he would say, these mortal coils”: “When we have shuffled off this mortal coil, / Must give us pause” (William Shakespeare, Hamlet, 3.1).

Chapter 56

  • “all kinds of head coverings including the ass’s head”: In Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, Puck gives the weaver Bottom an ass’s head, and Titania, under a love spell, falls in love with him (3.1).
  • “the glass of fashion and the powdered fop”: Ophelia remembers Hamlet as “The glass of fashion and the mould of form” (William Shakespeare, Hamlet, 3.1).
  • “How often had he died”: “Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once” (William Shakespeare, Julius Caesar, 2.2).
  • “The mandrakes screamed”: The mandrake root, forked like a human body, was said to shriek when pulled from the ground and to kill or madden whoever heard it: “shrieks like mandrakes torn out of the earth, / That living mortals, hearing them, run mad” (William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet, 4.3).
  • “Those were pearls that were his eyes”: Ariel sings of the drowned king: “Full fathom five thy father lies; / Of his bones are coral made; / Those are pearls that were his eyes” (William Shakespeare, The Tempest, 1.2).

Chapter 57

  • “alert interest and baited breath”: Young’s spelling puns on the usual phrase, from Shylock: “With bated breath and whispering humbleness” (William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, 1.3). Bated means held back, abated.
  • “knowing, also, that dark is fair, that fair is dark”: “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” (William Shakespeare, Macbeth, 1.1).
  • “He had seen a cloud like a great skull”: Compare Hamlet teasing Polonius: “Do you see yonder cloud that’s almost in shape of a camel?” (William Shakespeare, Hamlet, 3.2).

Chapter 58

  • “killing the song sparrow in his fall”: “There is special providence in the fall of a sparrow” (William Shakespeare, Hamlet, 5.2), after “one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father” (Matthew 10:29, KJV).
  • “a tree with its bare branches filled with singing birds”: Young reverses Shakespeare’s winter tree: “Bare ruin’d choirs, where late the sweet birds sang” (William Shakespeare, Sonnet 73, 1609).
  • “they were those who wore their hearts upon their sleeves”: “I will wear my heart upon my sleeve / For daws to peck at” (William Shakespeare, Othello, 1.1).
  • “the star lilies swimming through dark waters”: Young’s star lilies are crinoids, sea lilies and feather stars, animals that look like flowers. A feather star begins life on a stalk like a lily and then breaks free and swims. Their “sea-change” is Ariel’s: “Nothing of him that doth fade / But doth suffer a sea-change / Into something rich and strange” (William Shakespeare, The Tempest, 1.2).

Chapter 59

  • “the red rose of the sun or the white rose of the moon”: Compare the Temple Garden scene of Henry VI, Part 1, where the lords of York pluck white roses and the lords of Lancaster red, the start of the Wars of the Roses (William Shakespeare, 2.4).
  • “this undiscovered shore”: Compare Hamlet’s “undiscover’d country from whose bourn / No traveller returns” (William Shakespeare, Hamlet, 3.1).
  • “that which has a local habitation and a name”: The poet “gives to airy nothing / A local habitation and a name” (William Shakespeare, A Midsummer Night’s Dream, 5.1).

Chapter 61

  • “a silver helmet with beaver down to hide his face”: The beaver is the face guard of a helmet; of the ghost of Hamlet’s father, “he wore his beaver up” (William Shakespeare, Hamlet, 1.2).
  • “Abusing of God’s patience and the king’s English” (William Shakespeare, The Merry Wives of Windsor, 1.4).

Chapter 62

  • “add to his music of aubade and serenade his nocturne”: Aubade is a song or poem that greets the dawn, traditionally a morning love song about lovers parting at daybreak. The term, from the Old Occitan word auba meaning “dawn,” can also refer to morning music or a song sung outdoors at dawn as a compliment. The concept has been used in literature for centuries, notably in medieval France, and also appears as a subject for visual art, like the Picasso painting The Aubade. “It was the nightingale, and not the lark” (William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet, 3.5).

Chapter 63

  • “a kind of fool’s paradise”: “If ye should lead her into a fool’s paradise” (William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet, 2.4).
  • “There shall be bare and ruined choirs”: “Bare ruined choirs, where late the sweet birds sang” (William Shakespeare, Sonnet 73).
  • “it’s a wise child who knows his own father”: Shakespeare turns the proverb around: “It is a wise father that knows his own child” (The Merchant of Venice, 2.2).
  • “Here’s the livid skull that might be any fool’s or king’s”: “Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio” (William Shakespeare, Hamlet, 5.1).
  • “a plague, a plague, a light, a light!”: Compare “A plague o’ both your houses!” (Romeo and Juliet, 3.1) and the king’s cry “Give me some light. Away!” (Hamlet, 3.2).

Chapter 65

  • “Romeo and Juliet, Paul and Virginia, Eloise and Abelard, Tristram and the white Yseult”: Romeo and Juliet is a tragedy written by William Shakespeare early in his career about two young Italian star-crossed lovers whose deaths ultimately reconcile their feuding families. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 66

  • “born in Denmark hard by the castle of Elsinore”: The description situates his origin geographically and culturally: he is from Denmark, specifically near Elsinore Castle, which is famously known as the setting of Shakespeare’s play Hamlet. Elsinore Castle is a real fortress located in Helsingør, Denmark. Like Hamlet, he is a Dane marked by tragedy: he “had left home because of a great tragedy.”

Chapter 68

  • “Dark Lady was winning”: The racehorse’s name recalls the “Dark Lady” of Shakespeare’s Sonnets 127 to 152, the mysterious woman of the poet’s desire.
  • “the mandrakes screaming when they are pulled up by the roots”: This folklore is based on the mandrake plant which is a hallucinogenic and narcotic. It is said that it grows from the blood of a hanged man and the tuber can resemble a human form. Forensic medicine does record erection and the discharge of semen in some deaths by hanging, and the folklore of the gallows mandrake grew from it. Juliet fears “shrieks like mandrakes’ torn out of the earth” (Romeo and Juliet 4.3), and in Genesis Rachel trades for Leah’s mandrakes to bear a child (Genesis 30:14-16).

Chapter 69

  • “a canker in the rose immortal”: “And loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud” (Shakespeare, Sonnet 35). Compare Blake’s “The Sick Rose” (1794), destroyed by “The invisible worm.”
  • “a wormwood”: Culturally wormwood has been used in the Christian Bible to connote something incredibly bitter. In the Book of Revelation it is used as the name of the star. In Hamlet, he uses the word wormwood to describe the situation he believes is going on with his family. “And the name of the star is called Wormwood” (Revelation 8:11, KJV).

Chapter 70

  • “A rose by any other name would smell as sweet”: “What’s in a name? that which we call a rose / By any other name would smell as sweet” (Romeo and Juliet 2.2). Mr. Spitzer answers the same way at the end of the chapter: “What’s in a name?”

Chapter 72

  • “Johnny-jump-ups springing in her path”: The Johnny-jump-up, the wild pansy, is also called heartsease; in A Midsummer Night’s Dream it is love-in-idleness, whose juice makes the sleeper love the first creature seen on waking (2.1).

Chapter 73

  • “too, too solid for his tastes”: “O, that this too too solid flesh would melt, / Thaw and resolve itself into a dew!” (Hamlet, 1.2). Dew falls all through this chapter.

Chapter 76

  • “thin as a comma sleeping in the womb of time”: “There are many events in the womb of time which will be delivered” (Iago, Othello, 1.3).
  • “by Cupid, the blind god of love”: In classical mythology, Cupid is the god of desire, erotic love, attraction and affection. “And therefore is wing’d Cupid painted blind” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream, 1.1).

Chapter 78

  • “Poor, poor little thing, poor little other one who would have loved her mother so much, Rosemary”: “There’s rosemary, that’s for remembrance; pray, love, remember” (Ophelia, Hamlet, 4.5). Esther’s mother remembers Rosemary all her life.

Chapter 79

  • “the times were out of joint and she the dead”: “The time is out of joint: O cursed spite, / That ever I was born to set it right!” (Hamlet, 1.5).
  • “The bleeding hand of a dead child, lifting, might testify against her”: By the old ordeal of the bier, a murdered body was believed to bleed afresh when its murderer came near. In Richard III, Henry VI’s corpse bleeds before Gloucester: “Dead Henry’s wounds / Open their congeal’d mouths and bleed afresh!” (1.2).

Chapter 81

  • “gently rocking in the vasty deep”: “I can call spirits from the vasty deep. / Why, so can I, or so can any man; / But will they come when you do call for them?” (Henry IV, Part 1, 3.1).
