Chapter 4

  • “The voice of the turtle-dove was not heard in all that land, for the golden bowl was broken and the wheel broken at the cistern”: The lady reverses the Song of Solomon, “the voice of the turtle is heard in our land” (2:12), and quotes Ecclesiastes 12:6, “or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern.” That chapter of Ecclesiastes describes old age and failing senses, “and all the daughters of musick shall be brought low,” which fits the deaf old people. Henry James took the title of his novel The Golden Bowl (1904) from it.

Chapter 6

  • “Remember Thy Creator in the Days of Thy Youth Ere the Evil Days Come on Thee”: Ecclesiastes 12:1, a favorite verse for girls’ needlework samplers.
  • “Oh, a little birdie told me”: “A bird of the air shall carry the voice” (Ecclesiastes 10:20).

Chapter 9

  • “It would be better to celebrate, not the day we were born into this world but the day we were born out of it”: “The day of death than the day of one’s birth” (Ecclesiastes 7:1).
  • “One died in his full strength. Another died in bitterness of soul. How died the wise man?”: Job 21:23-25, and “how dieth the wise man? as the fool” (Ecclesiastes 2:16).

Chapter 15

  • “that old Ecclesiastes and of Exodus and of the Farmer’s Almanac”: The Old Farmer’s Almanac, published since 1792, with weather forecasts, planting tables, and proverbs.

Chapter 20

  • “Better were two heads than one”: “Two heads are better than one,” in John Heywood’s proverbs (1546), and “Two are better than one” (Ecclesiastes 4:9).

Chapter 25

  • “as no man knew the time of his birth, no man knew when he died”: “For man also knoweth not his time” (Ecclesiastes 9:12).

Chapter 31

  • “in love with no man on earth but with a fleeting shadow, the mere shadow of a man”: Shadows in scripture and Shakespeare.

Chapter 32

  • “Death is that which is caused by our partial knowledge”: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Corinthians 13:9-10).

Chapter 35

  • “swifter in the race”: “The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong… but time and chance happeneth to them all” (Ecclesiastes 9:11).

Chapter 41

  • “what happens to one must happen to all”: “And I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all” (Ecclesiastes 2:14).

Chapter 47

  • “neither to stay nor to depart”: “To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: A time to be born, and a time to die” (Ecclesiastes 3:1-2).

Chapter 48

  • “It seemed better not to know that which was unknowable”: Mr. Spitzer chooses humility before mystery: to try to grasp the ultimate things, death and what follows it, may be futile or even harmful, and it is better to live without the burden of complete understanding. Keats called this negative capability, “when man is capable of being in uncertainties, Mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact & reason” (letter to George and Tom Keats, December 1817). “For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1:18).

Chapter 63

  • “and if ever the golden bowl is broken, or the wheel at the cistern”: “Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern” (Ecclesiastes 12:6, KJV). Miss MacIntosh breaks off and adds, “The Bible exaggerates.”
  • “killed by the oldest preacher, he with the flaming hair”: “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2, KJV).

Chapter 64

  • “Vanity, vanity, all is vanity, sayeth the poet”: Ecclesiastes 1:2-11 “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.” This phrase conveys the preacher’s meditation on the fleeting nature of worldly things and human endeavors under the sun. It expresses the idea that much of what people strive for (wealth, wisdom, pleasure) is ultimately empty or futile because it does not provide lasting meaning or satisfaction. It is used by Miss MacIntosh to reflect on the futility and emptiness she perceives in life, especially in relation to her own condition and experiences. The phrase captures a sense of existential weariness and the recognition that many pursuits and concerns, such as appearances, social acceptance, or even personal desires, are ultimately transient and meaningless. Miss MacIntosh calls the Preacher a poet.
  • “the golden bowl was broken”: See the golden bowl of Ecclesiastes 12:6 in the Chapter 63 resources.

Chapter 65

  • “the serpent bite without enchantment”: “Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment” (Ecclesiastes 10:11, KJV).

Chapter 67

  • “The generations of buzzards do go on”: “One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever” (Ecclesiastes 1:4, KJV).

Chapter 69

Easton’s Bible Dictionary (1897) explains that the “head of the corner” is the topstone, and Zechariah 4:7 says, “he shall bring forth the headstone thereof with shoutings, crying, Grace, grace unto it.” The headstone signifies strength, stability, and alignment. Specifically, it’s often associated with Jesus Christ, who is described as the cornerstone upon which believers are built. In a broader sense, headstones can also refer to memorial markers at graves, symbolizing remembrance and faith. (Psalm 118:22; Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7; Genesis 28:18-22; Joshua 4:1-8).

Vera’s narrative continuously navigates between dreamlike confusion and the search for meaning or “ultimate harmony.” Miss MacIntosh represents order and common sense amid the chaos of Catherine’s opium-induced visions and the fragmented lives of other characters. The novel portrays characters with fragmented selves: Vera’s own complex consciousness, Miss MacIntosh’s evolving physical and psychological state (including her baldness and amputated breast), and the multiple personae like Cousin Hannah and Mrs. Hogden. The novel’s intense focus on female embodiment, sexuality, motherhood, loss, and survival complements critical perspectives on misogyny and sexual politics. Cousin Hannah, “an organizer of chaos,” takes up the part these myths assign to woman and turns it against the order men have made.

Women are often depicted as enduring various forms of hardship, including prolonged stress and instability, without succumbing to their circumstances. Some believe that societal expectations and responsibilities, like caregiving, can contribute to women developing a strong ability to persevere through difficulties. This concept is reflected in literature and cultural narratives, where women are often portrayed as resilient characters who face challenges with strength and fortitude. While men often dominate in shorter, more intense endurance events, women demonstrate strong performance in longer distances, particularly ultra-endurance activities. This is partly attributed to potential physiological advantages, such as efficient fat utilization and greater fatigue resistance in women during prolonged exercise. Psychological factors like strong mental resilience and consistent pacing strategies are also believed to contribute to women’s success in these events. It is important to acknowledge that the experiences of endurance and resilience differ based on individual circumstances and intersectional factors like race and culture. For instance, Black women in horror narratives are described as “Enduring Women” (Kinitra D. Brooks, “The Importance of Neglected Intersections: Race and Gender in Contemporary Zombie Texts and Theories,” African American Review 47, no. 4, 2014) who face different and more persistent threats than the traditional “Final Girl” (Carol J. Clover, Men, Women, and Chain Saws, 1992), highlighting the complexities of navigating misogynoir and societal challenges. It is crucial to recognize the importance of understanding resilience within the context of women’s lived experiences and the societal factors that influence their well-being.

It illustrates that God judges wickedness and sin but also provides a way for salvation for those who are righteous, like Noah, and those who have faith. The story highlights themes of God’s faithfulness through the covenant of the rainbow, and in Christian theology, the ark is often seen as a foreshadowing of Christ as the ultimate source of salvation. Forensic medicine does record erection and the discharge of semen in some deaths by hanging, and the folklore of the gallows mandrake grew from it. The garment, likely a regal tunic with long sleeves, signified Joseph’s special status and set him apart, though it also provoked envy, highlighting themes of favoritism, betrayal, and God’s guiding purpose through hardship. “Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children… and he made him a coat of many colours” (Genesis 37:3, KJV).

The name has deep roots in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, maintaining timeless popularity across cultures. “As for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be” (Genesis 17:15, KJV).

Rape has been used as a plot device in literature and other media. It has been criticized for using rape as a metaphor that displaces the actual, violent and traumatic act of rape. It is considered misogynistic in the way female rape victims continue to be cast as collateral damage and the assault and rape of women is used as a plot point in a narrative that is fundamentally about men. Young is making this about Esther and showing how things would be different if she were a man. Young makes many references to mythology. The struggle to escape from sexual pursuit is one of the most popular motifs of Greek mythology: Persephone, Callisto, Daphne, Europa, Io, etc. Greek mythology depicts women as vulnerable to assault, able to escape only through death, or metamorphosis like Daphne who becomes a laurel tree. The consequence of fleeing sexual violence is another type of force on the body, the loss of the human form where women who survive sexual violence become pregnant, and when gods as the rapists, produce a hero child. The Chicago detective takes Esther for a corpse, then feels her pulse, finds her heartbeat, and rapes her. Chione in Greek mythology was said to be so beautiful that she was the object of a thousand men’s desire. Hermes put Chione into a deep sleep with his wand and proceeded to rape her. Since Young has said Esther is the mother of us all and Mr. Spitzer as the father of us all, these could be archetypes for Adam and Eve and possibly Lilith. In On the Origin of the World, part of the Nag Hammadi Library, the rulers of the world rape the earthly Eve, and she bears their children. In the midrash Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, Samael, riding the serpent, seduces Eve and fathers Cain; later Kabbalah makes Lilith, Adam’s first wife, Samael’s bride. The Talmud says that in the years Adam was apart from Eve he fathered spirits, demons, and lilin (Eruvin 18b).

Chapter 2

  • New England spinsters like Susan B. Anthony and Louisa May Alcott, were famous. Spinsters in general were celebrated for their “uncompromising morality.” Spinster was an honorary term for a woman who earned money spinning wool. They were regarded as “highly moral and fully womanly creatures'' and many documented in their journals that they “remained unmarried not because of individual shortcomings but because they didn’t find the one ‘who could be all things to the heart.”

Chapter 13

  • “the Venus was bearded by patriarchal fog”: Velázquez’s Venus at Her Mirror (1647-51), the Rokeby Venus, hangs in the National Gallery, London. On March 10, 1914, the suffragette Mary Richardson slashed it with a meat cleaver. “I have tried to destroy the picture of the most beautiful woman in mythological history as a protest against the Government for destroying Mrs Pankhurst, who is the most beautiful character in modern history. Justice is an element of beauty as much as colour and outline on canvas. Mrs Pankhurst seeks to procure justice for womanhood, and for this she is being slowly murdered by a Government of Iscariot politicians. If there is an outcry against my deed, let every one remember that such an outcry is an hypocrisy so long as they allow the destruction of Mrs Pankhurst and other beautiful living women, and that until the public cease to countenance human destruction the stones cast against me for the destruction of this picture are each an evidence against them of artistic as well as moral and political humbug and hypocrisy.” (Mary Richardson’s statement, The Times, London, March 11, 1914).

Chapter 30

  • “Because of the loss of a skirt”: Young told Studs Terkel that this came from an Alpine story in which two bloomer girls shed their skirts at a summit, and the younger, going back for hers, was lost: “the lady lost her life for a skirt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See the Chapter 31 resources.
  • “so many foreign and domestic wars for the emancipation of woman”: The white women’s suffrage movement, primarily organized and led by middle-class educated white women, focused on gaining voting rights for white women, culminating in the passage of the 19th Amendment in 1920. The movement came out of the abolitionist movement with leaders being: Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony, Alice Paul, Carrie Chapman Catt, and Sojourner Truth (who played a significant role in the movement’s background). Suffragists employed various tactics, including lobbying, organizing marches and parades, and civil disobedience. After decades of activism, the 19th Amendment to the US Constitution was ratified in 1920 granting some women the right to vote. On paper the 19th Amendment covered all women. In practice it did not secure the vote for women of color. Black women in the South were kept from the polls by poll taxes, literacy tests, and terror. Native American women were not citizens until 1924. Asian immigrant women could not become citizens until 1952. It wasn’t until the Voting Rights Act of 1965 until all women’s voting rights were protected.

Chapter 31

  • “girding her loins with suffrage like that iron girdle worn by a great Crusader’s wife”: “Gird up now thy loins like a man” (Job 38:3). The chastity belt of Crusaders’ wives is largely a legend of later centuries.
  • “Here lies one who searched all her life for her dead love, a body covered by the snow”: Young told Studs Terkel that Cousin Hannah came partly from an Alpine story in which two bloomer girls shed their skirts at a summit, and the younger, going back for hers, was lost: “the lady lost her life for a skirt.” She also drew on Margaret Fuller, who drowned off Fire Island in 1850 within reach of a sandbar (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See the Chapter 30 resources.

Chapter 32

  • “to fly her skirts on tallest mountain peaks”: Young’s Alpine story of the two bloomer girls who shed their skirts on a summit, one lost going back for hers.
  • “picketing in a cold, sleet rain in front of a skirt factory”: The Silent Sentinels of the National Woman’s Party picketed the White House in all weathers from January 1917, and many were jailed. In the 1912 Lawrence, Massachusetts, “Bread and Roses” strike, women mill workers marched through the New England winter. Charles Studin’s suffragist, Young’s source for Cousin Hannah, “chained herself to a lamppost in front of the White House” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “challenging the conductor to a duel”: Studin’s suffragist “challenged a British prime minister to a duel and the prime minister refused to bear arms against the lady” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 32 · Cousin Hannah as a Warrior and Adventurer

  • Cousin Hannah is depicted as a forceful, uncompromising woman, a “great captain” who went “brandishing her sword like a cane even when there was no one” and preferred “the strident clash of arms, the pitched battle against man.”
  • Her sword symbolizes her militant feminism and unyielding fight against patriarchal oppression. The sword, usually a weapon of war and honor, here is also described metaphorically as a cane, suggesting both her authority and perhaps a certain defiance despite solitude. The image of her as a “veteran of so many winter campaigns, desert marches through burning sands” evokes the harshness of her battles, both literal and metaphorical.

Chapter 34

  • “this cynical suffrage captain”: Through Cousin Hannah, Marguerite Young is not speaking about the futility of suffrage even though it was a long fought battle that has not been fully documented. In The Dialectic of Sex, Firestone quotes Carrie Chapman Catt: “To get the word ‘male’ in effect out of the Constitution cost the women of the country fifty-two years of pauseless campaign… During that time they were forced to conduct 56 campaigns of referenda to male voters, 480 campaigns to get legislatures to submit suffrage amendments to voters, 47 campaigns to get state constitutional conventions to write woman suffrage into state constitutions, 277 campaigns to get state party conventions to include woman suffrage planks, 30 campaigns to get presidential party conventions to adopt woman suffrage planks in party platforms and 19 successive campaigns with 19 successive Congresses” (Carrie Chapman Catt and Nettie Rogers Shuler, Woman Suffrage and Politics, 1923, as quoted in Shulamith Firestone, The Dialectic of Sex, 1970). Firestone adds, “Thus defeat was so frequent, and victory so rare—and then achieved by such bare margins—that even to read about the struggle for suffrage is exhausting, let alone to have lived through it and fought for it.” In light of this Cousin Hannah’s relentless energy is seen as not disproportionate to the women’s suffrage movement. Cousin Hannah’s attitude to marriage and men (at least the outward appearance) would reflect the fundamental struggle. Again from The Dialectic of Sex, “To make both women and children totally independent would be to eliminate not just the patriarchal nuclear family, but the biological family itself” (Shulamith Firestone, The Dialectic of Sex, 1970).

Chapter 35

  • “even a British prime minister to quail”: Young’s source for Cousin Hannah, a suffragist “battle-axe” described by Charles Studin, a founder of the NAACP, “challenged a British prime minister to a duel and the prime minister refused to bear arms against the lady” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “She had wished to overthrow man, both as to the marital state”: The suffrage movement did not oppose marriage. The anti-suffrage movement opposed suffrage because it feared that women would be “masculinized” and that this in turn would “feminize” men. Under coverture, after marriage the man and woman became one legal unit that the man controlled. Women in many cases were not allowed to own property, sign contracts, earn a salary, or enter education without their husbands’ permission.
  • Gertrude Bell crossed these deserts and helped draw the borders of Iraq in 1921, yet by 1909 she was honorary secretary of the Women’s National Anti-Suffrage League.
  • “She had wished to rescue the slave, not only the economic slave but also the slave of love”: Cousin Hannah’s struggle is presented in terms of gender emancipation and suffrage activism. The economic slavery she aims to end is linked to the patriarchal and marital structures. Her battle is against male dominance and the social and domestic oppression of women.

Chapter 35 · Freedom and Emancipation

  • Cousin Hannah embodies the fight for women’s rights and freedom from traditional roles.
  • Her life is a metaphor for breaking boundaries: social, geographic, and existential.
  • The suffrage movement is portrayed as her husband, her master, and her true love.

Chapter 36

  • “the queen of the strong-minded”: “Strong-minded women” was a common nineteenth-century name, often a sneer, for advocates of women’s rights.

Chapter 38

  • “The lonely cause of suffrage had seemed to my mother to be quite unworthy”: Catherine does not believe in suffrage, and that was common among rich, white women from elite social and political backgrounds at the time. They argued that it would disrupt gender roles and the family structure, doubted women’s political capacity, and opposed broader progressive reforms such as prohibition. Racism drove them too, for they feared the vote would spread to women of color. They argued that it would simply double the size of the electorate without adding any new value or perspective. Opposition also came from business and industry since it may lead to increased regulation and reforms that would hurt their profits.
  • On May 21, 1914, Emmeline Pankhurst was arrested at the palace gates as suffragettes tried to bring a petition to King George V.

Chapter 38 · Sacrifice and Activism

  • Cousin Hannah embodies sacrifice for a cause, dedicating her life to suffrage and battling societal “ogres.”
  • Her life is one of relentless struggle and fortitude, marked by physical and emotional trials.
  • Catherine contrasts this with her own withdrawal and guilt for not engaging in such struggles.

Chapter 39

  • “the rational suffrage movement”: Cousin Hannah is described as being part of the “avant-garde” women’s suffrage movement, and that is a real thing. Its most famous figure, Inez Milholland Boissevain (1886-1916), led the 1913 suffrage parade in Washington, D.C., in a flowing white cloak on a white horse. A lawyer and peace activist, she belonged to the Greenwich Village circle of progressives and socialists around The Masses, a magazine that combined art, satire, and political commentary, along with Dorothy Day, Crystal Eastman, and Louise Bryant.

Chapter 41

  • “riding her white horse through a cloud”: Inez Milholland rode a white horse at the head of the 1913 suffrage parade in Washington.
  • “trooping her suffrage colors of rose on white”: The real suffrage colors were purple, white, and gold for the National Woman’s Party, yellow for the National American Woman Suffrage Association, and purple, white, and green for the British suffragettes. In Tennessee in August 1920, when the last state needed ratified the Nineteenth Amendment, “Supporters of suffrage wore yellow roses in public; the anti-suffragists wore red roses,” in “what became known as the War of the Roses” (National Constitution Center, “The man and his mom who gave women the vote”). Hannah’s “red rose of her blood” was, in Tennessee, the flower of her enemies.
  • “patriarchal suffrage captain”: Cousin Hannah is given this oxymoron title “patriarchal suffrage captain.” Patriarchy is a system of social organization where men hold the primary power and authority versus suffrage which is the fundamental right of all to vote which would lead to all citizens having the power to influence political decisions and hold leaders accountable. The paradox is suggesting that someone who holds patriarchal power but is also advocating for or leading a movement that challenges this very power structure.

Chapter 42

  • “But she had outlived her fame”: Cousin Hannah dying in obscurity is reminiscent of Shulamith Firestone’s funeral where mourners grappled with the idea that a whole generation of feminists had been unable to thrive in the world they had done so much to create (Susan Faludi, “Death of a Revolutionary,” The New Yorker, April 15, 2013).
  • The British burned Boer farms and held Boer women and children and Black Africans in concentration camps, where some 26,000 Boers, most of them children, and at least 14,000 Black Africans died. Emily Hobhouse exposed the camps, and the suffrage leader Millicent Fawcett headed the women’s commission sent to inspect them in 1901 (Thomas Pakenham, The Boer War, 1979).
  • Sixteen-year-old Sybil Ludington is said to have ridden some forty miles through what is now Putnam County, New York, on the night of April 26, 1777, to rouse her father’s militia after the British burned Danbury. The story first appeared in print in Martha J. Lamb’s History of the City of New York (1880), and Paula D. Hunt found no reliable evidence of the ride from the time (“Sybil Ludington, the Female Paul Revere: The Making of a Revolutionary War Heroine,” New England Quarterly 88, no. 2, 2015).
  • “Cousin Hannah as the great bloomer girl”: Amelia Bloomer’s The Lily promoted the loose trousers worn under a short skirt in 1851, and the costume took her name. See Young’s account to Studs Terkel of the bloomer girls who shed their skirts, in the Chapter 38 resources.
  • “leading the needle workers to strike albeit she was the owner of a mill”: In the Uprising of the 20,000, the New York shirtwaist strike of 1909, wealthy women such as Alva Belmont and Anne Morgan, the “mink brigade,” paid bail and fees for the strikers. Earlier, the Lowell mill girls of Massachusetts turned out in 1834 and 1836. Harriet Hanson Robinson, who led her room out at eleven, became a suffragist (Harriet H. Robinson, Loom and Spindle, 1898).
  • “the narrow channels of a lost cause”: Suffrage for women took a hundred years and many rights for women while Young was alive were not in place. Women and children were still property. Seeing again the erosion of these rights and the incompleteness of them worldwide (2025 saw Bangladesh Islamists protesting the expansion of human rights to women and a general attempt at rolling back gender rights for most parts of the world) one can see where there has to be a complete love (obsession) for something that might never be achieved in one lifetime.
  • “organized the pickets around an old town clock”: See the Silent Sentinels of the National Woman’s Party, who picketed the White House in 1917, in the Chapter 32 resources. Arrested pickets were beaten and choked at the Occoquan Workhouse on the “Night of Terror,” November 14-15, 1917, and Alice Paul was force-fed.
  • “No slave might wait on the great Abolitionist”: The suffrage movement grew out of abolition. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott met at the World Anti-Slavery Convention in London in 1840, where the women delegates were refused seats, and they called the Seneca Falls convention in 1848.

Chapter 43

  • “the dead cast no vote”: Padding the rolls with the names of the dead, the “graveyard vote,” was an old charge against city machines such as Tammany Hall. Mr. Spitzer’s brother believed otherwise, and Mr. Spitzer, who has not “been inside a ballot box for years,” sits at the deathbed of a suffrage captain.
  • “In heaven the black rooster lays the egg, and the white hen crows”: An old proverb says “A whistling woman and a crowing hen are neither fit for God nor men.” It was used against women who spoke out of their expected place, which makes a crowing hen a fitting image for a suffragette. A rooster laying an egg was considered unnatural and dangerous. Medieval legend held that a rooster’s egg hatched the basilisk, and in Basel in 1474 a rooster accused of laying an egg was tried and burned (E. P. Evans, The Criminal Prosecution and Capital Punishment of Animals, 1906). Hannah’s heaven reverses the order of the barnyard. The hen crows, “and none shall stop her.”
  • Bloomers are divided women’s garments for the lower body. They were developed in the 19th century as a healthful and comfortable alternative to the heavy, constricting dresses worn by American women (Wikipedia). They take their name from their best-known advocate, the women’s rights activist Amelia Bloomer. It became a symbol of women’s rights in the early 1850s. See Amelia Bloomer in the Chapter 42 resources.

Chapter 44

  • “that great bloomer girl”: Lucy Stone and other suffragists adopted the Bloomer costume, which consisted of a knee-length skirt worn over trousers or pantaloons, in the early 1850s. Stone loved the comfort and practicality of the outfit and wore it both at home and in public for about three years. However, the Bloomer costume attracted significant public scrutiny and ridicule, and critics of the women’s rights movement often focused on the reformers’ attire rather than their arguments for suffrage and other reforms. By late 1853, many prominent suffragists, including Elizabeth Cady Stanton, abandoned the Bloomer costume due to the negative attention it generated. Stanton persuaded Stone to follow suit. Stone resumed wearing long skirts, although she never again wore the restrictive corsets and voluminous dresses of the fashionable style. Other notable suffragists like Susan B. Anthony also stopped wearing Bloomers around the same time. Amelia Bloomer, the editor of The Lily newspaper and namesake of the costume, continued to wear it until 1858. Only Elizabeth Smith Miller, who had helped popularize the style, continued to wear bloomers longer, until 1861 (Wikipedia). See Amelia Bloomer in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “the white feather of cowardice”: In August 1914 Admiral Charles Penrose-Fitzgerald founded the Order of the White Feather, whose women handed white feathers to men out of uniform. Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst turned the WSPU from the vote to recruiting, and Sylvia Pankhurst wrote that their followers handed out feathers to young men in civilian dress (E. Sylvia Pankhurst, The Home Front, 1932).
  • “this old maid”: In Henry James’s The Bostonians (1886), the Boston suffragist Olive Chancellor loves the young speaker Verena Tarrant. Two women who made a home together came to be called a Boston marriage.

Chapter 45

  • “this great father of suffrage”: Young named her own sources for Cousin Hannah (see the Chapter 30 resources and the Chapter 31 resources), and Susan B. Anthony and her sister, Hannah, offer a historical comparison. Mr. Spitzer described Cousin Hannah as “this great father of suffrage.” Susan B. Anthony’s father was the first one in the family to become interested in the women’s suffrage movement. She was interested in social reform. She was a teacher and was paid less than her male counterparts (then as now). Anthony said, “I wasn’t ready to vote, didn’t want to vote, but I did want equal pay for equal work.” The family started out as Quakers and Anthony claimed to be a Quaker but the father moved away from the order to join the Unitarian Church. They were abolitionists and temperance advocates and had the likes of Frederick Douglass speak at their house. She formed a partnership with Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucy Stone. Stanton kept a room for her at her house where she also spent most of her life working with her. Anthony and Stanton went on to write the History of Woman Suffrage. Anthony said this kind of work, “makes me feel growly all the time... No warhorse ever panted for the rush of battle more than I for outside work. I love to make history but hate to write it.” Anthony did not believe in her writing skills which mostly went to Stanton. Most of her quotes come from speeches and lectures. Anthony did not live to see the ratification of the 19th Amendment or equal rights. “There have been others also just as true and devoted to the cause—I wish I could name every one—but with such women consecrating their lives, failure is impossible!” “Now, after 40 years of agitation, the idea is beginning to prevail that women were created for themselves, for their own happiness, and for the welfare of the world.” Back to her religion. It is a mixed bag in that they moved to being Unitarian although proud of her Quaker roots. She was involved with the Friends of Human Progress that included “Christians, Jews, Mahammedans, and Pagans.” She tried to start her own Free church where all were welcome. She later, according to Stanton, became agnostic. “Work and worship are one with me. I can not imagine a God of the universe made happy by my getting down on my knees and calling him ‘great.’” When Anthony’s sister Hannah was on her deathbed, she asked Susan to talk about the great beyond, but Anthony later wrote, “I could not dash her faith with my doubts, nor could I pretend a faith I had not; so I was silent in the dread presence of death.” Hannah was known for her domestic nature, but also for her full sympathy with the reforms championed by her sister. As a teen, Anthony went to parties, and she had offers of marriage when she was older, but there is no record of her ever having a serious romance. Anthony loved children, however, and helped raise the children in the Stanton household. As a young worker in the women’s rights movement, Anthony expressed frustration when some of her co-workers began to marry and have children, sharply curtailing their ability to work for the understaffed movement (Wikipedia). When Lucy Stone abandoned her pledge to stay single, Anthony’s scolding remarks caused a temporary rupture in their friendship. It was a bit more than a temporary rupture. They both formed separate suffrage movements. Anthony wanted a federal constitutional amendment. Stone wanted a more gradual state-by-state approach. Anthony opposed the 15th Amendment because it did not grant everyone the right to vote. Stone supported it as a stepping stone. It was 20 years before their two organizations worked together again. Stone worked out with her husband a separate but equal marriage where Stone retained rights to her property and finances and her personal liberty. Lucy Stone wore bloomers. She also kept her name. They publicly declared their commitment to equality and rejected the idea of a wife’s legal subordination. Journalists repeatedly asked Anthony to explain why she never married. She answered one by saying, “It always happened that the men I wanted were those I could not get, and those who wanted me I wouldn’t have.” To another, she answered, “I never found the man who was necessary to my happiness. I was very well as I was.” To a third she said, “I never felt I could give up my life of freedom to become a man’s housekeeper. When I was young, if a girl married poor, she became a housekeeper and a drudge. If she married wealth she became a pet and a doll. Just think, had I married at twenty, I would have been a drudge or a doll for fifty-nine years. Think of it!” In a speech in 1877, Anthony predicted “an epoch of single women. If women will not accept marriage with subjugation, nor men proffer it without, there is, there can be, no alternative. The woman who will not be ruled must live without marriage.”
  • “the innumerable coal mine strikes she had helped to start”: Mary Harris “Mother” Jones organized coal miners’ strikes from the 1890s into the 1920s. She put her class before suffrage and is reported to have said, “you don’t need the vote to raise hell!” (Russell E. Smith, “March of the Mill Children,” Social Service Review 41, no. 3, 1967, 298). To suffragists who called her anti, she answered, “I’m not an anti to anything which brings freedom to my class” (The Autobiography of Mother Jones, 1925, 203).

Chapter 46

  • “surely the greatest ever known among ladies”: Real suffragists climbed too. Annie Smith Peck made the first ascent of Huascarán’s north peak in 1908 and planted a “VOTES FOR WOMEN” flag on Coropuna in Peru in 1911. Fanny Bullock Workman of Massachusetts was photographed in the Karakoram about 1912 holding a newspaper headed “Votes for Women.”

Chapter 47

  • “What could he do for that old bloomer girl”: See Amelia Bloomer in the Chapter 42 resources.

Chapter 50

  • Hyphenated double surnames began among the British aristocracy as a way to keep a family name and inheritance alive when there was no male heir, and spread to the Victorian upper middle class. In the United States wives took their husbands’ names; the suffragist Lucy Stone kept her own at her marriage in 1855, and the Lucy Stone League, founded by Ruth Hale in 1921, urged women to do the same. Second-wave feminists of the 1960s and 1970s made the hyphenated name a common choice, and states removed barriers to keeping a birth name on passports, bank accounts, and other documents. For the old suffragette captain “the hyphen was all.” (Wikipedia)

Chapter 52

  • Young told Studs Terkel that she found the skirt in “the history of British mountain climbing”: one of the original bloomer girls and her companion climbed an Alpine peak to shout “Vive la femme,” took off their skirts at the top where no one could see them, and on the way down the younger, “the acolyte as I call her,” went back for the skirt she had left on the other side of the peak and never returned. Cousin Hannah “is haunted all her life by the ghostly rustle of the skirt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). In the novel the girl is her “apostle.” In 1858 Julia Archibald Holmes, a suffragist, climbed Pikes Peak in Colorado in a bloomer costume, the first recorded ascent by a woman.
  • “She had chained herself to a lamp-post”: Chaining was a signature suffrage protest. In January 1908 Edith New and Olivia Smith chained themselves to the railings of 10 Downing Street and shouted “Votes for Women!” so that Flora Drummond and Mary Macarthur could slip inside. On 28 October 1908 Muriel Matters and Helen Fox of the Women’s Freedom League chained themselves to the grille of the Ladies’ Gallery in the House of Commons, and the section of grille had to be removed with them still attached. Young’s source, Charles Studin’s suffragist, “chained herself to a lamppost in front of the White House” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). Chaining herself to a lamp post, she makes herself a public fixture, visible and accountable, a woman who takes control of her fate even while bound by it.
  • “this old bloomer girl”: Elizabeth Smith Miller wore loose trousers under a short skirt in Seneca Falls in 1851, and Amelia Bloomer championed the costume in The Lily, her temperance and women’s rights paper, so that it took her name. Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony wore it for a time before ridicule drove most women back into long skirts.

Chapter 52 · Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • Cousin Hannah fought “for the overthrow of man” and urged all ladies to “divest themselves of excess luggage,” yet her forty trunks hold only wedding gowns. Mr. Spitzer cannot tell whether she dreamed of being the bridegroom or the bride, and he decides the world need not know.

Chapter 53

  • “he had been a woman masquerading as a man”: Young’s ward-heeler has a real counterpart. Murray Hall, a Tammany Hall politician in New York who worked the 13th Senatorial District for some twenty-five years, lived as a man for about forty years, married twice, and voted at a time when no woman in New York could. When Hall died of breast cancer in January 1901, the discovery that Hall had been born female made headlines across the country, and Hall was buried in women’s clothing with none of the political colleagues at the funeral (Smithsonian Magazine, “The Mystery of Murray Hall”).

Chapter 54

  • “nearly knocked down by a lady cyclist”: The bicycle craze of the 1890s gave women a new freedom, and new clothes to ride in. Susan B. Anthony told Nellie Bly in 1896, “Let me tell you what I think of bicycling. I think it has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world” (New York World, 2 February 1896).

Chapter 64

  • “her red bloomer leg”: Red bloomers, named after reformer Amelia Bloomer, emerged in the 1850s as a radical symbol of women’s dress reform for health and freedom, featuring loose trousers under a short skirt for mobility, but faced public scorn as “unwomanly” and threatening gender norms, leading many suffragists to adopt less controversial symbols like a red shawl, though bloomers persisted as gym/cycling wear.

In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 11, Chapter 18, Chapter 20, Chapter 22, Chapter 23, Chapter 24, Chapter 28, Chapter 29, Chapter 30, Chapter 31, Chapter 32, Chapter 33, Chapter 35, Chapter 40, Chapter 41, Chapter 42, Chapter 44, Chapter 45, Chapter 48, Chapter 50, Chapter 52, Chapter 54, Chapter 55, Chapter 59, Chapter 61, Chapter 64, Chapter 65, Chapter 66, Chapter 74, Chapter 75, Chapter 81, Chapter 82

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • Marco Polo was an Italian explorer who traveled through Asia along the Silk Road between 1271 and 1295.

Chapter 2

  • Admiral Robert Peary was an American explorer and US Navy officer who made several expeditions to the Arctic.

Chapter 2

  • Ernest Shackleton was an Irish Antarctic explorer.

Chapter 11

  • “the proud, cold, utterly snobbish Queen Maud Mountains”: The Queen Maud Mountains rise at the head of the Ross Ice Shelf, on the south edge of the Ross Sea. Roald Amundsen found them in 1911 on his way to the South Pole and named them for Queen Maud of Norway, a daughter of King Edward VII of England. Queen Maud Land is a different region of Antarctica, claimed by Norway.
  • The Ross Sea, a deep bay of the Southern Ocean, is named for James Clark Ross, who sailed into it in 1841.
  • “Sir Walter Raleigh in his marvelous white satin suit embroidered with seed pearls”: Sir Walter Raleigh (c. 1552-1618) was an English statesman, soldier, spy, writer, poet, and explorer. (Wikipedia) He was famous at Elizabeth’s court for the pearls and jewels on his clothes, even his shoes.
  • “Admiral Peary”: Robert E. Peary claimed the North Pole in 1909 and was made a rear admiral in 1911. Matthew Henson, the Black explorer beside him, by his own account reached the spot first and got little credit for decades. In 1897 Peary brought six Inuit from Greenland to New York for the American Museum of Natural History, and four died within months. The museum staged a fake burial for the boy Minik while it kept his father Qisuk’s skeleton.

Chapter 18

  • “the rose at the North Pole is the rose immortal”: In a spiritual sense it signifies the coexistence of death and eternal life, the presence of enduring beauty and essence in a world otherwise marked by loss, coldness, and transience. It evokes a mystical, almost sacred dimension beneath the surface of harsh reality or an eternal “rose” blooming in the frozen heart of the North Pole.
  • A compass rose, sometimes called a rose of the winds, is the diagram of directions on maps and nautical charts, and medieval mariners were expected to name all 32 of its points. It is also the emblem of the worldwide Anglican Communion. (Wikipedia) There are two North Poles, magnetic and true.

Chapter 20

  • “haunted rays of Aurora Borealis”: The northern lights. The Latin name, “northern dawn,” joins Aurora, the Roman goddess of the dawn, and Boreas, the north wind, and is usually credited to Galileo (1619).

Chapter 22

  • “Where’s old Jessup Land, far to the North?”: The Arctic Jesup Land, named for Morris K. Jesup, president of the Peary Arctic Club, like Cape Morris Jesup in Greenland.
  • “Where’s Herbert Island?”: Herbert Island lies off northwest Greenland, near Thule, a walrus-hunting ground.
  • “Where is Queen Maud Mountains”: Roald Amundsen named them in 1911, on his way to the South Pole, for Queen Maud of Norway.

Chapter 23

  • “is Baffin Bay?”: Baffin Bay is located between Baffin Island and the west coast of Greenland. It is named for William Baffin, who charted it in 1616.
  • “It’s always well”: An igloo (Inuktitut iglu, “house”) is built of snow blocks.
  • “the latitude and longitude in which may be located the Austral Islands, ice-locked Baffin Bay or the Magnetic Pole”: The Austral Islands are in French Polynesia. James Clark Ross reached the North Magnetic Pole in 1831.

Chapter 24

  • “Admiral Peary was to be put into the blue room”: Admiral Robert Peary.

Chapter 28

  • “perhaps the Antarctic Queen Maud Mountains”: The Queen Maud Mountains are a major group of mountains in the Antarctic. Roald Amundsen named them in 1911 for Queen Maud of Norway, on his way to the South Pole.

Chapter 29

  • “Did it come through the strings of the golden lyre of the stars”: The constellations Lyra, Sagittarius (the archer), Argo Navis, and Centaurus. The Small Magellanic Cloud is a dwarf galaxy, named for Magellan’s crew, who described it on the first voyage around the world (1519-22).

Chapter 30

  • “disguised as an Arab king”: There were female explorers in the Middle East: Gertrude Bell (a British explorer, archaeologist, and writer) and Freya Stark who was another British explorer and writer. Other explorers: Isabella Bird, Lady Anne Blunt, Lady Hester Stanhope. Isabelle Eberhardt (1877-1904) rode the Sahara dressed as an Arab man, and Lady Hester Stanhope lived among the Arabs in men’s dress.
  • “sailing in the six months’ darkness”: The polar night, when the sun does not rise for months near the poles.

Chapter 30 · Mountains and Deserts

  • Represent challenges, isolation, and spiritual journeys.

Chapter 31 · The Desert and the Alps

  • The Desert and the Alps symbolize harsh trials, isolation, and spiritual quests. Cousin Hannah’s travels through these landscapes symbolize her restless spirit and adventurous life.

Chapter 32

  • “colder than the Weddell Sea”: The Weddell Sea is part of the Southern Ocean off Antarctica. It is named for the sealer James Weddell, who sailed into it in 1823, and its pack ice crushed Shackleton’s Endurance in 1915.
  • “Had she come from Manitoba, Hudson’s Bay, Cape Reprieve, the Laurentian Shield”: The Canadian Far North.
  • “Had she found the Northwest Passage”: Northwest Passage is the sea route between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans through the Arctic Ocean. Sir John Franklin’s expedition was lost seeking it in 1845, and Roald Amundsen first sailed through it in the Gjøa, 1903-1906.

Chapter 33

  • “great balloon ascensionists who long ago had descended to earth, dragging their shrouds and cords”: Salomon Andrée set out by balloon for the North Pole in 1897 and vanished. The bodies and diaries of his party were found on White Island in 1930.
  • “a great many formal king penguins, a great many melancholy seals”: King penguins live only in the far south, and seals in both polar seas, so “the bipolar illusion” means of both poles.

  • “why so many great Antarctic explorers had left home”: Richard E. Byrd named Marie Byrd Land in Antarctica for his wife, Marie, in 1929.
  • “even like Queen Maud Mountains”: Roald Amundsen named the range for Queen Maud of Norway in November 1911, as his party climbed the Axel Heiberg Glacier toward the South Pole.

Chapter 40

  • Eskimo is Young’s word. Many Inuit and Yupik people now reject it.
  • They are named for Ferdinand Magellan, whose crew recorded them on the first circumnavigation of the world (1519-1522).
  • “Christolpho Colombo”: Christolpho Colombo or Christopher Columbus was an Italian explorer and navigator who completed four voyages across the Atlantic Ocean.
  • “balloonists who had not been sighted for years”: S. A. Andrée’s balloon expedition to the North Pole vanished in 1897. The men’s last camp was found on White Island in 1930.

Chapter 41

  • “like Balboa discovering the Pacific Ocean”: Balboa may refer to Vasco Núñez de Balboa, the Spanish explorer who crossed the Isthmus of Panama and in 1513 became the first European to see the Pacific from the Americas.

Chapter 44

  • “mountains of the moon”: Ptolemy placed the Mountains of the Moon at the source of the Nile.

Chapter 45

  • “some distant roof- top of the world”: The Pamirs and the Tibetan plateau are called the Roof of the World.

Chapter 48

  • “like Stanley, find his Livingston”: Sir Henry Morton Stanley was a Welsh-American journalist and explorer of Central Africa. Sent by the New York Herald to find the missionary David Livingstone, he found him at Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika in November 1871 and reported greeting him, “Dr. Livingstone, I presume?” (How I Found Livingstone, 1872). The pages of Stanley’s diary for that meeting were torn out, and his biographer Tim Jeal doubts the words were said (Stanley: The Impossible Life of Africa’s Greatest Explorer, 2007). David Livingstone was an explorer of Africa and one of the most popular British heroes of the Victorian Era.
  • “holes in ice swallowing the sled”: Sir John Franklin’s expedition of 1845 in search of the Northwest Passage was lost when its ships, Erebus and Terror, were locked in the ice; all 129 men died.

Chapter 50

  • “perhaps the poles themselves had flown”: A geographic pole is either of the two points where Earth’s axis of rotation meets its surface, the North Pole in the Arctic Ocean and the South Pole in Antarctica. The poles wander by a few meters over a few years, partly from the Chandler wobble, a free oscillation with a period of about 433 days, but for maps they are taken as fixed, the points where the lines of longitude meet. (Wikipedia) See the reversals of the magnetic poles in the Chapter 42 resources.

While “Laplander” was historically used to refer to people from the region of Lapland, it’s now more respectful to use the term Sami or the endonym their specific language group uses, such as Northern Sámi.

Admiral Perry is probably Robert E. Peary, the Arctic explorer who claimed to have reached the North Pole in 1909 and was made a rear admiral in 1911; Commodore Matthew Perry, who opened Japan to American ships in 1854, never sailed to the ends of the earth.

Chapter 66

  • “Who was Captain Cook?”: Miss MacIntosh’s “Captain Cook” is Dr. Frederick A. Cook (1865-1940), the American who claimed to have reached the North Pole in April 1908, a year before Peary. The University of Copenhagen rejected his records in 1909. In 1923 he was convicted of mail fraud for promoting oil stocks in Texas, served his sentence at Leavenworth until his parole in 1930, and was pardoned by President Franklin Roosevelt in 1940. Young merges him with Captain James Cook, the British navigator.
  • “it was Captain Cook and not Commander Peary”: Commander Peary or Robert Peary was an American explorer and officer in the United States Navy who made several expeditions to the Arctic in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He is best known for, in April 1909, leading an expedition that claimed to be the first to have reached the geographic North Pole. Explorer Matthew Henson, part of the expedition, is thought to have reached what they believed to be the North Pole narrowly before Peary. (Wikipedia) Peary’s backers were the Peary Arctic Club of wealthy New Yorkers, and the National Geographic Society endorsed his claim.
  • “Where is the Bering Sea?”: The Bering Sea and Strait are named for Vitus Bering (1681-1741), a Dane in Russian service who sailed them in 1728 and died on what is now Bering Island in 1741. The explorer of this chapter is a Dane too.

  • “Far above King William Land, at the Magnetic Pole”: King William Land, also called King William Island, is an island in the Kitikmeot Region of Nunavut, which is part of the Arctic Archipelago. (Wikipedia) Franklin’s lost expedition perished near King William Island in 1845-1848, and James Clark Ross first reached the North Magnetic Pole nearby, on the Boothia Peninsula, in 1831.
  • “the nights were six months long where they would go”: At the North Pole itself the sun sets near the September equinox and does not rise again until the March equinox, so the night there is about six months long.

Chapter 1

  • Jehovah’s Witnesses is a millenarian (the belief by a religious, social, or political group or movement in a coming fundamental transformation of society, after which "all things will be changed") restorationist (is the belief that Christianity has been or should be restored along the lines of what is known about the apostolic early church, which restorationists see as the search for a purer and more ancient form of the religion) Christian denomination with nontrinitarian (is a form of Christianity that rejects the mainstream Christian doctrine of the Trinity: the belief that God is three distinct hypostases or persons who are coeternal, coequal, and indivisibly united in one being, or essence) beliefs distinct from mainstream Christianity. Jehovah's Witnesses are best known for their door-to-door preaching, distributing literature such as The Watchtower and Awake!, and for refusing military service, refusal to salute state symbols and blood transfusions. They consider the use of God's name vital for proper worship. They reject Trinitarianism, inherent immortality of the soul, and hellfire, which they consider to be unscriptural doctrines. They do not observe Christmas, Easter, birthdays or other holidays and customs they consider to have pagan origins incompatible with Christianity. They prefer to use their own Bible translation, the New World Translation of the Holy Scriptures, although their literature occasionally quotes and cites other Bible translations. Adherents commonly refer to their body of beliefs as "The Truth" and consider themselves to be "in the Truth". They consider "human society" to be morally corrupt and under the influence of Satan, and most limit their social interaction with non-Witnesses. Congregational disciplinary actions include disfellowshipping, their term for formal expulsion and shunning, a last resort for what they consider serious offenses. Chapter 1

Psalm 43:3 is a prayer asking God for His guiding light and truth. Micah 7:8 expresses hope that even in darkness, the Lord will be a light. Ephesians 5:14 encourages those who are spiritually asleep to wake up and receive Christ's light.   • The Pilgrim's Progress from This World, to That Which Is to Come is a 1678 Christian allegory written by John Bunyan. It is commonly regarded as one of the most significant works of Protestant devotional literature and of wider early modern English literature. It has been translated into more than 200 languages and has never been out of print. It appeared in Dutch in 1681, in German in 1703 and in Swedish in 1727. The first North American edition was issued in 1681. It has also been cited as the first novel written in English. According to literary editor Robert McCrum, "there's no book in English, apart from the Bible, to equal Bunyan's masterpiece for the range of its readership, or its influence on writers as diverse as William Hogarth, C. S. Lewis, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Herman Melville, Charles Dickens, Louisa May Alcott, George Bernard Shaw, William Thackeray, Charlotte Bronte, Mark Twain, John Steinbeck and Enid Blyton.” The lyrics of the hymn "To be a Pilgrim" are based on the novel.

Chapter 3

  • “whether a camel shall enter through the needle’s eye or a rich man through the gates of heaven” - is a metaphor used in both the Bible and the Qur'an. It emphasizes the difficulty, or even impossibility, of a wealthy person achieving salvation through their own means. The phrase uses the image of a camel, a large animal, being unable to pass through the tiny eye of a needle to illustrate the immense challenge for a rich person to enter heaven. The saying appears in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, often in the context of Jesus speaking to a rich young man who is unwilling to give up his possessions to follow him. The Quran also uses this metaphor in Surah Al-A'raf (7:40), stating that those who reject God's signs will not enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle.

The language used in describing a lamplighter is someone who holds dreams and stars. The lamplighter stands as a symbol of hope, constancy, and the pursuit of clarity in a world that is otherwise engulfed by darkness, illusion, and uncertainty. He is a guardian figure who attempts to bring light, both literal and metaphorical, into Vera's chaotic and dreamlike existence.

The story of Lazarus's raising highlights the close relationship between Jesus and his friends, as well as Jesus's power over death. The miracle was a powerful sign of Jesus's divine authority and his identity as the Messiah as well as a symbol of the promise of eternal life through faith in Jesus. Lazarus in this context represents Vera's yearning for a new beginning, a restored life beyond the illusions and failures of the past, where she can experience reality as it is lived by ordinary people, with the natural rhythms of life and death, love, and community.

(Wikipedia) "Jezebel" in this context represents a symbol of moral judgment and inner conflict within the bus-driver's troubled psyche during a moment of dark reflection and suffering.

Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John in the chapter symbolize the four passengers as spiritual or angelic figures, evoking the Four Evangelists and thus linking the narrative to themes of spiritual journey, life, death, and cosmic judgment.

This statement highlights the theme of authentic love as acceptance and compassion for the whole person, including their imperfections and vulnerabilities. It contrasts with superficial or idealized love, which might only appreciate a partial or idealized image. The “truest love” is grounded in reality, acknowledging the full truth of the beloved. In the context of the chapter, Vera (the narrator) reflects on the nature of love and marriage, and the idea that true love involves a deep understanding and acceptance of the other person. Miss MacIntosh, who values common sense and reality, would likely agree with this view, emphasizing love based on truth rather than illusion or fantasy. The phrase captures a central insight into the nature of love as something that embraces the whole self (the light and the dark, the certain and the uncertain) and that this kind of love is the most meaningful and enduring.

It captures the paradox that those closest to us, who may offer care and safety, can also inflict pain and disappointment. The imagery implies vulnerability and the complicated nature of love and trust with those who protect have the power to hurt as well. The phrase conveys the idea that protection and harm are often intertwined in human relationships, emphasizing the complexity and sometimes painful duality of intimacy.

This phrase marks a moment of profound questioning or a crisis point in the narrative where the comforting presence of God is deeply questioned or felt to be absent, confronting the characters with the mystery of existence and the silence in the face of suffering.

Something once living and vibrant but now scorched, fragile, and destined to wither away. The Israelites’ long journey is often attributed to their disobedience, doubt, and lack of faith in God’s leadership. God led them by a longer route to protect them from enemies and allow them time to develop their faith and trust: “God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near; for God said, Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war” (Exodus 13:17), and “your children shall wander in the wilderness forty years” (Numbers 14:33).

Chapter 20 · Biblical and Mythological References

  • “one who had not built her house upon shifting sands”: “A foolish man, which built his house upon the sand” (Matthew 7:26).
  • “the road to Hell, as she had often grimly said, is very broad and very wide and is paved with bones and good intentions”: “Wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction” (Matthew 7:13). Samuel Johnson said “Hell is paved with good intentions” (Boswell’s Life of Johnson, 1775). Miss MacIntosh repeats it at the end of the chapter: “the highway to Hell is paved with more good intentions than shining cobblestones.”
  • “life is this valley of dry bones”: “The hand of the Lord… set me down in the midst of the valley which was full of bones… Can these bones live?” (Ezekiel 37:1-3).
  • “The Devil could quote his Scriptures, too, chapter and verse for his purpose”: “The devil can cite Scripture for his purpose” (The Merchant of Venice 1.3). In the temptation, Satan quotes Psalm 91 to Christ (Matthew 4:6).
  • “some there are who still confuse the brothers, he who fell”: Both are called the morning star: Lucifer, “son of the morning” (Isaiah 14:12), and Christ, “the bright and morning star” (Revelation 22:16).
  • “He might appear as the angel transfixed by light or as the angel of darkness”: “For Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14), as in Chapter 17.
  • “The King James version of the Bible was not to be trusted because made for the vanity of earthly kings”: The King James Version of the Bible was not the first English language version of the Bible, but the culmination of extensive translation activity (some illegal!) in the 1500s. This began with the work of William Tyndale and the printing of the first English New Testament in 1526. Following a tumultuous 75 years, James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603, joining the two crowns. Three main English Bibles were in use: the Bishops’ Bible (Church of England), the Geneva Bible (Protestants), and the Rheims New Testament (1582, Roman Catholic Church), causing much confusion and dissension. To settle disagreements over reforms in the Church of England and respond to pressure from the Puritans, King James in 1604 approved a new translation of the Bible, primarily because he knew that it would reinforce his image as a political and spiritual leader. He approved six companies of translators, 54 men in all, of whom 47 are known to have worked on it, to prepare the new translation, using previous English Bible translation work, and using the best Hebrew, Greek, and Latin texts and manuscripts. The completed King James Version was first published in 1611. These first editions were large pulpit Bibles (folios) to be read in churches, but were followed within a year by the printing of smaller versions (quartos) for personal use. Though slow to be adopted in the English-speaking world and to replace the more popular Geneva Bible, from the mid-1600s to the late 20th century, the King James Version was the Bible of the English-speaking church (Encyclopaedia Britannica). The translators’ dedication addresses “the most high and mighty Prince James,” the kind of flattery Miss MacIntosh distrusts.
