  • “plucked up into the bosom of Abraham”: “The beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom” (Luke 16:22).
  • “bearded human lions in their dens”: Daniel in the lions’ den (Daniel 6), and Scott’s “to beard the lion in his den” (Marmion, 1808).
  • “in love with no man on earth but with a fleeting shadow, the mere shadow of a man”: Shadows in scripture and Shakespeare.
  • “for what were earthly riches, great castles and lonely towers”: Luke 12:16-21, the Parable of the Rich Fool, shows how wealth can be a distraction from the true purpose of life. “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?” (Luke 12:20). Mr. Spitzer’s reflections echo the parable’s warning against greed and misplaced security.
  • “The rose of Sharon is growing in a desert place”: “I am the rose of Sharon” (Song of Solomon 2:1), and “the desert shall… blossom as the rose” (Isaiah 35:1).
  • “her search for the external man”: “Though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

Chapter 32

  • “to invite her enemy to a banquet, to ease his suspicions with goblets of wine”: Judith feasted with Holofernes until he lay drunk, then “smote twice upon his neck with all her might, and she took away his head from him” (Judith 13:8, Apocrypha, King James Version).
  • “as she had lived by the sword, should have died by one sharp blow”: “All they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Matthew 26:52).
  • “the walls might crumble at a lonely trumpet’s sound”: “When the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat” (Joshua 6:20).
  • “the valleys of dry bones”: “The valley which was full of bones… O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD” (Ezekiel 37:1, 4).
  • “Death is that which is caused by our partial knowledge”: “For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Corinthians 13:9-10).

Chapter 33

  • “what ghostly hand had guided the great printer’s devil”: “In the same hour came forth fingers of a man’s hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall” (Daniel 5:5), the writing at Belshazzar’s feast.
  • “The bride had been a door. The bridegroom had been a key”: Christ says “I am the door” (John 10:9) and holds “the key of David” (Revelation 3:7), and the Church is “the bride, the Lamb’s wife” (Revelation 21:9).
  • “though she seemed to remember that he had been at her wedding”: “He that hath the bride is the bridegroom: but the friend of the bridegroom, which standeth and heareth him, rejoiceth greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice: this my joy therefore is fulfilled” (John 3:29). Mr. Spitzer is the friend at the wedding.
  • “except that the door was closed”: The Parable of the Ten Virgins (Matthew 25:1-13). It symbolizes spiritual readiness, and those that are able to enter the wedding feast. This imagery is rooted in Jewish wedding customs, where the bridegroom’s arrival was a central event, and the bride and her attendants would go out to meet him. The bridegroom came, “and the door was shut” (Matthew 25:10). “Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh” (Matthew 25:13).

Chapter 34

  • “a parable in unknown tongues”: “He that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God” (1 Corinthians 14:2).
  • “Cousin Hannah had exceeded these human dimensions by many dazzling cubits”: “Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?” (Matthew 6:27).
  • “the inner light and the outer darkness”: “Cast out into outer darkness” (Matthew 8:12). George Fox’s Quakers spoke of the Inner Light, God’s light in every soul.

Chapter 35

  • “one who had seen the burning bush”: “And he looked, and, behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed” (Exodus 3:2).
  • “a plague of fiery locusts, those who have no king”: “The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands” (Proverbs 30:27). The locusts of Revelation do have one: “they had a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit” (Revelation 9:11).

Chapter 36

  • “Had not the heavens divided, splitting apart”: “And the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together” (Revelation 6:14) marks the destruction of the old world order, as the heavens are seen as being destroyed and replaced with a new creation. Surah Ar-Rahman (55:37) describes the heavens splitting apart and becoming rose-red like burnt oil. At Jesus’s baptism by John the Baptist, “he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit like a dove descending upon him” (Mark 1:10).
  • “that door of death which, though very narrow”: “Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it” (Matthew 7:14).
  • “One should not know one’s mother’s face, one’s father’s face”: “Now the brother shall betray the brother to death, and the father the son; and children shall rise up against their parents” (Mark 13:12), among the signs of the end.

Chapter 37

  • “Her head was eaten by great birds”: “The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it” (Proverbs 30:17).
  • “The last conch trumpet had already blown”: Triton blew his conch to call back the waters of the flood (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1). “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible” (1 Corinthians 15:52).

Chapter 38

  • “Babylon is fallen, is fallen” (Isaiah 21:9).
  • “the heavenly bridegroom none should see”: “Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him” (Matthew 25:6).
  • “Cousin Hannah must have believed that the dead were silent”: “The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence” (Psalm 115:17).

Chapter 39

  • “the spokes of the wheels of her carriage were sleeping cherubim”: “And when I looked, behold the four wheels by the cherubims, one wheel by one cherub, and another wheel by another cherub” (Ezekiel 10:9).
  • Gloucester has lost thousands of fishermen to the sea. Its Fisherman’s Memorial (1925) bears the words “They that go down to the sea in ships” (Psalm 107:23).
  • “many cubits adding to dazzling cubits”: “Which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature?” (Matthew 6:27).
  • “for surely he was her prince of the East”: The black coachman is in Catherine’s dreams as her “prince of the East” which refers to Lucifer, the light bringer, Venus, morning star. The black coachman is “wound in his cloth of gold.” “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” (Isaiah 14:12).
  • “In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain” (Daniel 5:30).
  • “instead of wandering stars”: “Wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever” (Jude 1:13).

Chapter 40

  • “as if it were she who had driven the sun against the clouded net, stopping time”: “And the sun stood still, and the moon stayed” (Joshua 10:13).
  • “the king of the Medes”: King of the Medes may refer to Darius the Mede who is mentioned in the Hebrew Bible in the Book of Daniel as a King of Babylon but is not known to history.
  • “that she listened for hours to Ahaseuris, the Wandering Jew”: Ahaseuris or Ahasuerus is the name of a king, the husband of Esther, in the Book of Esther from the Bible. A German pamphlet of 1602 gave the same name to the Wandering Jew, and Young follows it.
  • Solomon made pillars and harps of almug trees (1 Kings 10:12), often identified as red sandalwood.
  • “Avaunt, villains, knaves, blackamoors, blackbirds, Boanerges”: Avaunt means to move away, depart. Boanerges is a vociferous preacher or orator. A nickname applied by Jesus to James and John in Mark 3. “Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17).
  • “A horse knew what the horseman did not know”: Balaam’s ass saw what Balaam could not: “And the ass saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand” (Numbers 22:23).
  • “as if the truth were mighty and would prevail”: “Magna est veritas, et praevalet,” “great is truth, and it prevails” (1 Esdras 4:41, Vulgate).

Chapter 42

  • “Should the lost locate the lost?”: “For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19:10).
  • “the great lamp-lighter going his rounds”: God and light have been closely linked in the Bible. Lamps are lit in many religions around the world, as at Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, and at Hanukkah. Maria Susanna Cummins’s The Lamplighter (1854) was a bestseller. It is about an orphan that is taken in by a lamplighter and raised with love and taught virtue and religious faith.
  • “No one net could ever drag in all the stars”: “The kingdom of heaven is like unto a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind” (Matthew 13:47).
  • Hannah, from the Hebrew for grace, is the mother of Samuel in 1 Samuel 1.
  • “struck fear and trembling”: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2:12), the source of Kierkegaard’s title Fear and Trembling (1843).
  • “the difference between right and left”: Nineveh held “more than sixscore thousand persons that cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand” (Jonah 4:11).
  • “Where, he wondered, was the great tent-maker now?”: Omar Khayyam’s name means tentmaker.
  • “with their faces covered like Ahaseuris”: Ahaseuris or Ahasureus was a king and the husband of Esther in the Bible. In Esther it is Haman’s face that is covered as he is condemned: “As the word went out of the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face” (Esther 7:8). See the Ahasuerus entry in the Chapter 40 resources.
  • “might there be resurrection and eternal life”: “I am the resurrection, and the life” (John 11:25).
  • Mr. Spitzer’s ideal is the resurrection of the body of the Apostles’ Creed: “It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (1 Corinthians 15:44).
  • “waiting for the spirit to return”: “I will return into my house from whence I came out; and when he is come, he findeth it empty, swept, and garnished” (Matthew 12:44).
  • “came like a thief in the night”: “The day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2).
  • “where was now her armor of virtue”: See “the whole armour of God” (Ephesians 6:11) in the Chapter 20 resources.
  • “should not all be as brides going to the bridegroom”: “Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him” (Matthew 25:6).
  • “the void calling to the void”: “Deep calleth unto deep” (Psalm 42:7).
  • “Oh, is there no pavilion to hide me from the storm?”: “For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion” (Psalm 27:5), and “thou shalt keep them secretly in a pavilion from the strife of tongues” (Psalm 31:20).

Chapter 43

  • “Are they the hooded thirteen apostles?”: The twelve apostles included Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus. Matthias was chosen to take his place (Acts 1:26), and Paul, who came later, is often called the thirteenth apostle. Jesus and the twelve made thirteen at the Last Supper, one root of the old superstition that thirteen at table is unlucky, and Hannah’s “hooded thirteen apostles” picketing the town clock carry that ominous number. In the Eastern tradition there may have been as many as seventy apostles, the seventy whom Jesus “sent them two and two before his face” (Luke 10:1).
  • “Am I the anvil which is struck or the hammer which strikes?”: In Isaiah 41:7 the craftsmen are encouraged with a job well done when the hammer and anvil work together to make an object. In context the object is an idol, and the prophet is mocking people who build their own gods. Elsewhere the hammer both makes and destroys: “Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces?” (Jeremiah 23:29), and Jael kills Sisera with a hammer and a tent nail (Judges 4:21).
  • “Is that the rooster crowing?”: “Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Matthew 26:34). Hannah, who denied her love, hears the rooster at the end.
  • “Shall I put on this body and this love?”: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53).
  • “Oh, is she in the shadowed valley”: “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil” (Psalm 23:4).

Chapter 44

  • “There was not the eye of a sparrow”: “Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father” (Matthew 10:29).
  • “a seed of buried hope to move mountains”: “If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove” (Matthew 17:20).
  • “bearding the sleeping lion in its den”: To beard the lion in its den means to attack someone on their own ground or subject. David told Saul that when a lion took a lamb, “I caught him by his beard, and smote him, and slew him” (1 Samuel 17:35). Here the sleeping lion is Cousin Hannah, “this great anchorite of suffrage.”
  • “Is this your second coming?”: “And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven” (Matthew 24:30). See Yeats’s “The Second Coming” in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “Is this as it was, ever will be?”: See the Gloria Patri, “As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be,” in the Chapter 10 resources.
  • “Judas cock”: The Judas cock may refer to the Book of the Cock/Rooster which was probably written in the 400s or 500s in Arabic or Greek and used by Ethiopian Christians who have and use the text during Holy Week activities. It describes the final three days of Jesus’s life, including a sequence where he reanimated a previously roasted rooster that He sent to spy on Judas Iscariot when he (Judas) was plotting to betray Jesus. The rooster informed Jesus and his disciples of the plan. Among other events, the Book of the Rooster describes Saul of Tarsus’ participation in the arrest, abuse and crucifixion of Jesus, the betrayal of Jesus by a female relative of Judas, a debate between Pilate and Herod about the culpability of Jesus, Mary’s grief, John the Evangelist witnessing the crucifixion of Jesus, the conversations Jesus had with the two thieves he was crucified alongside Gestas (Awsēmobyā) and Demas (Salikonilidākki) and references to other miracles that Jesus performed during his life. The rooster may be based on the Ziz of Jewish mythology, a giant bird. Like the Gospel of Judas from the second century, the Book of the Rooster attempts to explain the betrayal of Judas before the Last Supper, an act which is traditionally seen as abrupt or lacking reason (Wikipedia).

Chapter 45

  • “Is it on the mountain slope or in the valley of the shadow?”: See Psalm 23:4 in the Chapter 43 resources.
  • “angels rolling away the stones of tombs”: “For the angel of the Lord descended from heaven, and came and rolled back the stone from the door” (Matthew 28:2).
  • “It would be neither the anchor nor the heart”: The anchor on a gravestone is hope: “Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast” (Hebrews 6:19).
  • “the Greeks and Medes, the Persians”: “The law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” (Daniel 6:8).
  • “Forgive the cloud which knows not what it whispers”: “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).
  • Icarus flew too near the sun and fell into the sea (Ovid, Metamorphoses 8), and “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” (Isaiah 14:12).
  • “For love is strong as death” (Song of Solomon 8:6). See the Liebestod of Tristan und Isolde in the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “he who loves shall lose himself in love as in death”: “For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it” (Matthew 16:25; see also John 12:25). The loss of self in love is not presented as purely tragic but as an essential part of the human condition and the search for connection beyond isolation.

Chapter 46

  • “the silver sheep’s bell which had once rung to the lost sheep”: “What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?” (Luke 15:4).
  • “Have you seen my lady—or my lord?”: “I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth… The watchmen that go about the city found me: to whom I said, Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?” (Song of Solomon 3:2-3).
  • “the surveyor with his plummet line”: “The Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand” (Amos 7:7).

Chapter 47

  • “some small Moses in his mollusk boat”: “And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes… and she laid it in the flags by the river’s brink” (Exodus 2:3). Moses is an important prophet in Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Druze faith, Baha’i faith and other Abrahamic religions.
  • “through which he had lived, moved, gathered weight”: “For in him we live, and move, and have our being” (Acts 17:28).
  • “there was no Savior upon these waters”: When Peter sinks on the waters he cries, “Lord, save me. And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him” (Matthew 14:30-31). It underscores the stark reality that sometimes there is no rescue, no reprieve, no saving grace, only the merciless, indifferent “waters” that engulf all.
  • “the king with many crowns”: “His eyes were as a flame of fire, and on his head were many crowns” (Revelation 19:12).
  • “when all which had been lost should be found”: “For this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found” (Luke 15:32), the parable of the Prodigal Son.
  • “Should the reprobate be pure as snow”: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18), and “If I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean; yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch” (Job 9:30-31). See the ace of spades in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “Better that her cruel lord should never have plowed this stony land”: “Some fell upon stony places, where they had not much earth” (Matthew 13:5).

Chapter 48

  • “through clouds of eye witnesses”: “Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight” (Hebrews 12:1).
  • “drawing all things unto themselves”: “And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me” (John 12:32).
  • “certainly not by those who were the living, for they were dead”: “Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22).
  • “He had gone down in darkness and in whirlwind”: The reverse of Elijah’s ascent: “and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven” (2 Kings 2:11).
  • “His star had fallen, never again to rise”: “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” (Isaiah 14:12). Lucifer, Latin for “light-bearer,” is the morning star, the planet Venus, which the Greeks called Phosphorus and which heralds the dawn. The verse was addressed to the king of Babylon, but Christian tradition, reading it in Jerome’s Latin, made Lucifer a name for Satan, the angel who fell from heaven.
  • “Perhaps he was the stowaway”: “But Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep” (Jonah 1:5).
  • “only by losing life did one win life”: “For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it” (Matthew 16:25).
  • “Perhaps he was translated”: “By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death” (Hebrews 11:5); to be translated is to be carried to heaven without dying. “Bless thee, Bottom, bless thee! thou art translated” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream 3.1).

Chapter 49

  • “the twelve Apostles in their long white robes and the thirteenth Apostle”: The twelve Apostles are Jesus’s apostles. The thirteenth Apostle may refer to Judas Iscariot, who was replaced after his suicide when lots were drawn and Matthias was chosen (Acts 1:23-26). Paul, called apart from the Twelve, is often named the thirteenth apostle, and Mary Magdalene was called “the apostle to the apostles.” The emperor Constantine had himself buried among memorials to the Twelve in his Church of the Holy Apostles and was called the thirteenth apostle.
  • “But why should any man weep if the heavens wept for him?”: In the Bible God grieves and Jesus weeps: “it grieved him at his heart” (Genesis 6:6); “Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears” (Jeremiah 9:1); “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). In the Book of Moses of the Latter-day Saints, “the God of heaven looked upon the residue of the people, and he wept” (Moses 7:28). The Quran says of Pharaoh’s drowned people, “And the heaven and the earth wept not for them” (44:29, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, 1930), and the Egyptians said the Nile rose with the tears of Isis for Osiris (Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.32.18).
  • “He wept for others who wept not for him”: “Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children” (Luke 23:28). To weep for himself seems an excess to Mr. Spitzer, who is already “dead or dying to this world, this world dying,” so he turns his sorrow outward to others who do not mourn him in return: a solitary, unreciprocated mourner and witness caught between life and death.
  • “Is thy light shining, or hast thy spirit departed upon the evening wind?”: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick… Let your light so shine before men” (Matthew 5:15-16). Mr. Spitzer asks whether the inner light, the vital spirit, still shines or has already departed upon the evening wind, the approach of darkness and death.
  • “She is melted in the fiery furnace of man’s disbelief”: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego were cast “into the midst of the burning fiery furnace” and walked out unharmed (Daniel 3:23-27). Martha is not spared.
  • “the dove of God like that which flew up through Mary’s skirts”: The Holy Spirit descends “in a bodily shape like a dove” (Luke 3:22), and in paintings of the Annunciation a dove brings the conception to Mary. See the three trinitarian minutes, above.
  • “Every Martha must have her Mary”: “Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part” (Luke 10:41-42); the sisters of Lazarus appear again in John 11. Martha is associated with active service and worldly duties, Mary with contemplative devotion and the inner life. For every Martha bearing the burdens of the world there is a Mary who embodies grace and hope; here Mary is “that snow-white pigeon with the red-rose breast who used to come to her through miles of clouds.” The pairing holds loss, maternal suffering, spiritual yearning, and the interplay of outer and inner life.

Chapter 50

  • “begot this pearl with the light burning within”: A pearl forms when an oyster coats an irritant with layer upon layer of nacre; the grain of sand of legend is rarely the cause, more often a parasite or a bit of tissue. “The kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matthew 13:45-46).
  • “that earth which swallows the horse and the rider”: “The horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:1), and “the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up” (Numbers 16:32).
  • “a light upon the water”: “Who layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters: who maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind” (Psalm 104:3).
  • “the mere flyleaf stuck between two passages or testaments”: In the King James Bible of 1611 the Apocrypha, books such as 2 Esdras that are outside the Hebrew canon, were printed between the Old and New Testaments; Mr. Spitzer, who “was not of this margin, canon, text” but “the apocryphal firefly,” is that leaf between.
  • “between the patriarch and the cloud or water bird”: “Also he sent forth a dove from him, to see if the waters were abated from off the face of the ground” (Genesis 8:8).
  • “stuck between the millstone above him and the millstone below him”: “No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man’s life to pledge” (Deuteronomy 24:6), and “Though the mills of God grind slowly, yet they grind exceeding small” (Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, “Retribution,” 1846).

Chapter 51

  • “the hounds of Nimrod barking through clouds”: “He was a mighty hunter before the LORD” (Genesis 10:9). A nimrod is now a skillful hunter, or, in later American slang, an inept person. The huntsman of the stars is Orion; see the Chapter 49 resources.
  • “some old lazar with his tinkling bell”: Lepers in the Middle Ages had to warn of their approach with a bell or clapper; lazar comes from the beggar Lazarus, “full of sores” (Luke 16:20).
  • “Did not the live coal burn upon his lips”: “Then flew one of the seraphims unto me, having a live coal in his hand… And he laid it upon my mouth, and said, Lo, this hath touched thy lips; and thine iniquity is taken away” (Isaiah 6:6-7).
  • “that darkened glass through which he might view his own eclipse”: “For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). Eclipses were watched through smoked or darkened glass.
  • “like Gabriel blowing his horn”: The Bible says “the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised” (1 Corinthians 15:52) but does not name the trumpeter; Gabriel’s horn is later tradition.
  • “The copestone was missing like the arch of the sky”: “The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner” (Psalm 118:22).
  • “the silks of the universe being torn in two”: “And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom” (Matthew 27:51).
  • “We were all transmuted while we lived”: “We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye” (1 Corinthians 15:51-52).

Chapter 52

  • “like the infant Moses sleeping in his little boat among the reeds”: “And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes, and daubed it with slime and with pitch, and put the child therein; and she laid it in the flags by the river’s brink” (Exodus 2:3, KJV). Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew son cast into the river (Exodus 1:22), and three women, his mother, his sister, and Pharaoh’s daughter, saved him.
  • “I might fish up a minor prophet”: The twelve Minor Prophets of the Bible, Hosea through Malachi, are called minor for the shortness of their books, not their importance. Their message is judgment and salvation, social justice and the treatment of the poor, and concern for divine judgment in the future. One of them was fished up indeed: “And the LORD spake unto the fish, and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land” (Jonah 2:10, KJV).
  • “The mountains skipped about like rams”: “The mountains skipped like rams, and the little hills like lambs” (Psalm 114:4, KJV).
  • “Perhaps she was the ladder personality”: “And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it” (Genesis 28:12, KJV).
  • “a four-faced cherub one hundred cubits high”: “And every one had four faces, and every one had four wings” (Ezekiel 1:6, KJV).
  • “in creation there was division as in division there was creation”: Genesis tells creation as a series of divisions: “and God divided the light from the darkness” (Genesis 1:4, KJV). Life begins the same way: in nearly all animals the fertilized egg, or zygote, splits again and again, a process called cleavage.
  • “Who knew the womb of a snowflake?”: “Hath the rain a father? or who hath begotten the drops of dew? Out of whose womb came the ice? and the hoary frost of heaven, who hath gendered it?” (Job 38:28-29, KJV).
  • “where none had moved over the face of the waters”: “And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters” (Genesis 1:2, KJV).
  • “who should find the doors which held back the sea”: “Or who shut up the sea with doors, when it brake forth, as if it had issued out of the womb?” (Job 38:8, KJV). Young follows it at once: “The sea flowed like the waters from the womb.”

The Greek word translated “servant” is diakonos, deacon, and she is the only woman so named in the Bible; Paul trusted her to carry his letter to Rome. Where modern translations of 1 Timothy 3:11 speak of women deacons, the King James Version has “Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things.” In Greek mythology Phoebe was a Titaness, grandmother of Apollo and Artemis; the name means bright.
  • “cut down in the flower of their youth”: “He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not” (Job 14:2, KJV).
  • “she might endure the birth of nothing”: “We have been with child, we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind” (Isaiah 26:18, KJV).

Chapter 75

  • “Nothing was brought to light that had been hidden”: Esther reverses the Gospel: “For there is nothing hid, which shall not be manifested; neither was any thing kept secret, but that it should come abroad” (Mark 4:22, KJV).

Chapter 77

  • “Who had killed the heavens, rolling them up like a scroll”: “And all the host of heaven shall be dissolved, and the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll” (Isaiah 34:4, KJV).
  • “raped by a thief in the night”: “For yourselves know perfectly that the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2, KJV).
  • “the Song of Songs of the sterility which is the creation”: The Song of Songs is an erotic poem. It is unique within the Hebrew Bible in that it celebrates sexual love. The two are in harmony, each desiring the other and rejoicing in sexual intimacy. Jewish tradition reads it as an allegory of the relationship between God and Israel In Christianity, it is treated as an allegory celebrating the love between God and Church or Christ and his bride, the Church. The Christian church’s interpretation of the Song is evidence of God’s love for his people, both collectively and individually. Over time a moral element and the bride as Virgin Mary were added. It is unique in that these conclusions are not found in the overtly theological books of the Bible. Those books reveal an imbalance in the relationship between God and man, but Song of Songs is a theological metaphor in which the two partners are equals, bound in a committed relationship. In modern times the poem has attracted the attention of feminist biblical critics, with Phyllis Trible’s “Depatriarchalizing in Biblical Interpretation” (1973) and the Feminist Companion to the Bible series edited by Athalya Brenner and Carole Fontaine.
  • “Exhibit A, the agony, exhibit B, the birthday”: Esther’s alphabet of accusation echoes the New England Primer (about 1690), the first schoolbook of American children, whose alphabet begins with guilt: “In Adam’s Fall / We sinned all.”
  • “a wall of brass between her and the bodies of creation”: “And I will make thee unto this people a fenced brasen wall” (Jeremiah 15:20, KJV).

Chapter 78

  • “that needle’s eye through which the camel shall not pass”: “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God” (Matthew 19:24, KJV). See also the Chapter 72 resources.
  • “the swaddling clothes which she had buried”: “And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger” (Luke 2:7, KJV).
  • “kicking against them all, against the traces”: “It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks” (Acts 9:5, KJV), said of Saul, the persecutor, before he became Paul; the pricks are the goads that drive an ox.
  • “She was not born innocent and stainless”: “Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psalm 51:5, KJV). Augustine, in the first book of his Confessions, saw sin even in the jealous infant at the breast; the doctrine of original sin holds that every child is born guilty.
  • “her having killed somebody without shedding of blood”: “And almost all things are by the law purged with blood; and without shedding of blood is no remission” (Hebrews 9:22, KJV).

Chapter 79

  • “After all, her own was the virgin birth”: The Immaculate Conception is the belief that the Virgin Mary was free of original sin from the moment of her conception. Original sin is the Christian doctrine that holds that humans, through the fact of birth, inherit a tainted nature in need of regeneration and a proclivity to sinful conduct. According to Christian apocryphal and Islamic tradition, Saint Anne was the mother of Mary and the maternal grandmother of Jesus. Saint Anne appears as the mother of Mary in the late 2nd-century Gospel of James. Saint Anne and her husband, Joachim, are infertile, but God hears their prayers and Mary is conceived. The conception is claimed to occur without sexual intercourse between Saint Anne and Joachim, which fits well with the Gospel of James’ persistent emphasis on Mary’s sacred purity, but the story does not advance the idea of an immaculate conception. The Orthodox Church claims that Mary was conceived by her parents in the same way everyone is conceived. Anne (Hannah in Arabic) is recognized as a highly spiritual woman and as the mother of Mary. In the Quran she is described as childless until her old age. One day, Hannah saw a bird feeding its young while sitting in the shade of a tree, which awakened her desire to have children of her own. She prayed for a child and eventually conceived. Joachim (Imran in Arabic) died before the child was born. Expecting the child to be male, Hannah vowed to dedicate him to isolation and service in the Second Temple. However, Hannah bore a daughter instead, and named her Mary. Her words upon delivering Mary reflect her status as a great mystic, realizing that while she had wanted a son, this daughter was God’s gift to her. She said: “My Lord! Truly, I brought her forth, a female. And God is greater in knowledge of what she brought forth. And the male is not like the female” (Quran 3:36). So her Lord received her with the very best acceptance. And her bringing forth caused the very best to develop in her. Joachim was a rich and pious man, who regularly gave to the poor. At the temple, Joachim’s sacrifice was rejected, so the couple’s childlessness was interpreted as a sign of divine displeasure. Joachim consequently withdrew to the desert, where he fasted and did penance for 40 days. Angels then appeared to both Joachim and Anne to promise them a child. Joachim later returned to Jerusalem and embraced Anne at the city gate, located in the Walls of Jerusalem. An ancient belief held that a child born of an elderly mother who had given up hope of having offspring was destined for great things. Joachim is named as the patron saint of fathers, grandfathers, grandparents, married couples, cabinet makers, and linen traders. “The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee” (Luke 1:35, KJV).
  • “A dove of God, she had read somewhere, impregnated Mary”: According to Christian theology, Mary was not impregnated by a literal bird like a dove, but rather conceived Jesus through the power of the Holy Spirit. While artistic depictions sometimes show a dove (a symbol of the Holy Spirit) during the Annunciation, this is a symbolic representation. At Christ’s baptism the Spirit descended “like a dove” (Matthew 3:16, KJV).
  • “that Christ was the youngest brother”: The Gospels make Jesus the eldest: “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James, and Joses, and of Juda, and Simon? and are not his sisters here with us?” (Mark 6:3, KJV).
  • “in the twinkling of an eye”:
  • “Her innocency had been spoiled by men, women, children”: “I will wash mine hands in innocency” (Psalm 26:6, KJV); innocency is the King James word.

Chapter 80

  • “she had been swallowed by the earth”: “And the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up” (Numbers 16:32, KJV); “and it vomited out Jonah upon the dry land” (Jonah 2:10, KJV).
  • “Now the first would not be the last”: “So the last shall be first, and the first last” (Matthew 20:16, KJV).
  • “Some sins, if they were sins, had left no stains”: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18, KJV).
  • “Where is black white”: “Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness” (Isaiah 5:20, KJV).

Chapter 81

  • “Saturn stood still in the glassy heavens”: “Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon” (Joshua 10:12, KJV).
  • “a voice saying to jump from the high places”: “If thou be the Son of God, cast thyself down: for it is written, He shall give his angels charge concerning thee” (Matthew 4:6, KJV), the devil’s temptation on the pinnacle of the temple.

Chapter 82

  • “Thou hast wrapped me in Thy fleece”: The hymns Miss MacIntosh sings reveal a profound spiritual dimension to her character. While she keeps her doubt to herself (“Her doubt was her own wound”) and will not be “the stumbling block in another’s path,” these songs from her childhood represent an enduring, if conflicted, faith. They expose her inner struggles with vulnerability, physical and emotional wounds, and the existential human condition of being lost and in need of guidance. These moments of singing, even as she performs mundane tasks, highlight the tension between her practical life and her deep, unarticulated spiritual longings, demonstrating that her common sense and brusqueness are often a defense against profound personal suffering and a search for meaning in a chaotic world.
  • “when Gabriel blew his horn”: “For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16, KJV); The Bible does not name the angel who sounds the last trump; the spiritual “Blow Your Trumpet, Gabriel,” printed in Slave Songs of the United States (1867), gives it to Gabriel.

In the research: Chapter 42, Chapter 68, Chapter 71, Chapter 77, Chapter 80

Definition from research

Chapter 42

  • Frederick Douglass answered at the American Equal Rights Association in May 1869: “When women, because they are women, are hunted down through the cities of New York and New Orleans; when they are dragged from their houses and hung upon lamp-posts… then they will have an urgency to obtain the ballot equal to our own” (History of Woman Suffrage, vol. 2, 1882, 382).

Chapter 68

  • Oliver Moore was lynched in North Carolina in 1930. Oliver Moore was accused of assaulting two young white girls, Ethel, age 5, and Lucile Morgan, age 7, daughters of Mr. and Mrs. E. F. Morgan, who lived on the county line between Wilson and Edgecombe Counties, on the night of 18 July 1930. Moore evaded capture for nearly a month but was finally caught and arrested on 15 August 1930 and jailed in Tarboro, NC, in the county jail. At around midnight on 18 August 1930, a mob of masked men broke Moore out of jail and took to a wooded area on the Wilson-Edgecombe County line just inside Wilson County not far from the scene of the alleged assault, hung him from a tree with a rope around his chest, and shot him repeatedly until he was dead. By the next morning when it appears this photo was taken, thousands of people from all around the area had gathered to view the lynching aftermath and Moore’s body hanging riddled with bullets from the tree.
  • “as a young man in Kentucky”: Rainey Bethea, a young Black man, was hanged in Owensboro, Kentucky, on August 14, 1936, for the rape of Lischia Edwards, a seventy-year-old white woman; he was charged with rape and not murder, which under Kentucky law allowed a public hanging. About 20,000 people came, many because the sheriff, Florence Thompson, a widow who had succeeded her husband, was to spring the trap; in the end a former policeman, Arthur Hash, did it. It was the last public execution in the United States. See the Equal Justice Initiative’s report Lynching in America (2015).
  • “The Negro was hanged for sleeping with a white woman”: This is a story told by the Christian hangman Mr. Weed about a botched lynching of a Black man in Kentucky. According to the tale, the man was hanged for the accusation of sleeping with a white woman, an accusation that, as the hangman himself says, was false: “as he surely never did.” The hangman describes how the man was cut down from the noose a split second too soon, meaning he was still technically alive and was later seen pushing a baby buggy, frightening the local white community. The hangman reflects on the “inefficiency” of the hanging, suggesting that his role was to make death as swift and painless as possible, but here the man suffered unnecessarily by surviving the hanging. This passage echoes real historical accounts of lynching in the United States, particularly in the South, where Black men were often falsely accused of crimes, especially of violating racial codes like alleged relations with white women. Lynchings were extrajudicial killings by mobs, commonly by hanging, sometimes with brutal torture. There are documented cases where victims were cut down prematurely or survived the initial hanging, leading to further suffering before death or even escape, heightening the terror of such acts. The passage metaphorically highlights the cruelty and injustice of these acts, along with the hangman’s conflicted role: he sees himself as a Christian bringing mercy through a swift death, yet is part of a brutal system that perpetuates racial violence and injustice. The “unofficially alive” status of the man symbolizes the liminal, tortured state of lynching victims: condemned by society, yet clinging to life in a world that refuses them justice or dignity. This passage serves as a fictional reflection on historical racial violence in America, underscoring the themes of injustice, suffering, and moral ambiguity surrounding lynching and the societal roles that participated in or failed to prevent such atrocities.
  • In Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases (1892), Ida B. Wells showed that the charge of rape or of relations with a white woman was the usual pretext for lynching Black men, and was usually false.
  • “Who would want to be unofficially alive?”: In 1946 Louisiana’s portable electric chair failed to kill Willie Francis, a Black teenager of seventeen; the Supreme Court allowed the state to try again (Louisiana ex rel. Francis v. Resweber, 1947), and he was executed that May.
  • “Away down in Mississippi, they are using a portable electric chair”: Mississippi’s portable electric chair, carried by truck from county to county so that the condemned died in the county of conviction, was used from 1940 until a gas chamber replaced it in 1954. Willie McGee, a Black man convicted of rape on doubtful evidence, died in it in 1951.

Chapter 71

  • “the child strangled by the umbilical cord”: Vera pictured Marie hanging and her unborn baby hanging by its umbilical cord. Pregnant Black women were among the many victims of lynching during the era of racial terror in the United States. While the exact number is not known, the case of Mary Turner is one of the most widely documented instances of this particularly brutal violence. In May 1918, a white farmer named Hampton Smith was killed by one of his Black employees, Sidney Johnson, in Brooks County, Georgia. An enraged white mob began a week-long rampage, killing several Black people, including Mary Turner’s husband, Hayes Turner. After her husband was lynched, a grieving Mary Turner, who was eight months pregnant, publicly denounced the murder and threatened to have the mob members arrested. Her statement enraged the mob, which turned its fury on her. On May 19, 1918, a mob of hundreds of people captured Turner and dragged her to Folsom Bridge over the Little River. There, they tied her ankles, hung her upside down from a tree, and set her on fire. While she was still alive, a man cut open her abdomen with a knife, causing her unborn baby to fall to the ground. A mob member then stomped the baby to death. Turner’s body was then riddled with hundreds of bullets. No one was ever held accountable for the murders of Mary Turner and her unborn child. The grotesque nature of her lynching revealed the level of dehumanization and impunity with which Black women were treated during this period. Her case was widely publicized by the NAACP and became a symbol in the anti-lynching movement. The lynching of Black women is a less-documented aspect of racial terror, but historians have uncovered evidence that it was not uncommon. The violence against Black women, especially pregnant women like Mary Turner, served as a tool of white supremacy to terrorize the Black community and suppress any form of dissent. The sexualized and gendered violence inflicted upon women’s bodies was also used to communicate power and control. Many instances of women being lynched were underreported or not documented at all. The details of Mary Turner’s lynching only became widely known because of the investigation by Walter F. White of the NAACP and the subsequent national anti-lynching campaign. The murder of Mary Turner remains a potent and horrific symbol of the racial and gender-based violence that was inflicted upon Black women during the era of racial terror.
  • Prejudice against Italian immigrants ran deep: in 1891 a New Orleans mob lynched eleven Italian Americans, the largest mass lynching in American history, and in 1927 Massachusetts executed the anarchists Sacco and Vanzetti after a trial many believed unjust.
  • “They want an American Pope”: Vatican conspiracy theories are conspiracy theories that concern the Pope or the Roman Catholic Church. A majority of the theories allege that the Church and its representatives are secretly controlling secular society with a Satanic agenda for global domination. In the 1920s the Ku Klux Klan in Indiana enrolled perhaps a quarter of a million members, preaching against Catholics, Jews, and Black Americans and holding the state government until its leader, D. C. Stephenson, was convicted in 1925 of the rape and murder of Madge Oberholtzer.
  • “There are no Negroes in this county, for the sun will not set on a Negro’s head here”: Such places were called sundown towns: Black people had to be gone by nightfall or risk violence. Indiana had scores of them. See the Kentucky lynching in the Chapter 68 resources.

Chapter 77

  • “exhibit N, a Negro, the night, a noose”: The night, the noose, and the rope that follows at R: the alphabet calls up lynching. The Tuskegee Institute recorded 4,743 lynchings in the United States from 1882 to 1968; 3,446 of the dead were Black.
  • “But he only dealt with the deaths of little white children”: When Young wrote this the civil rights movement had been going on since 1954.

Chapter 80

  • “He had fled for fear the white people would see him and kill him”: Interracial marriage in the United States has only been legal since the 1967 U.S. Supreme Court decision Loving v. Virginia that held anti-miscegenation laws were unconstitutional by the 14th Amendment established in 1868. The court’s landmark decision has been commemorated and celebrated every year on the Loving Day, June 12th. The number of interracial marriages in 1967 was three percent. The first interracial marriage in what is today the United States was that of Pocahontas, who married tobacco planter John Rolfe in 1614. The first ever law prohibiting interracial marriage was passed by Maryland in 1691. The Quaker Zephaniah Kingsley married, outside the US, a black enslaved woman that he bought in Cuba. He also had three black common-law enslaved wives. He freed all four. They had to flee Florida for Haiti when it became a US territory. The prospect of black men marrying white women terrified many Americans before the Civil War. It was magnified into the greatest threat to society. The first legal black-white marriage in the United States was that of African-American professor William G. Allen and a white student, Mary King, in 1853. When their plans to marry were announced, Allen narrowly escaped being lynched. Their marriage was secret, and they left the country immediately for England, never to return. In 1957 actor Sammy Davis Jr. faced backlash for his relationship with a white woman, actress Kim Novak. In 1958, Davis briefly married a black woman, actress and dancer Loray White, to protect himself from mob violence.
  • “He had gone farther North”: In the Great Migration, some six million Black Southerners moved north and west between 1910 and 1970, fleeing lynching and Jim Crow.
  • “they had tried to hang him from a white-blossoming tree”: Jo Reed was an African American man who was lynched in Nashville, Tennessee, on April 30, 1875, where he was taken by a white mob from the county jail after being arrested for killing a police officer in a confrontation. He was hanged from a suspension bridge but, after the rope broke, Reed survived the attempted lynching, escaped via the river, and left Nashville to go West. A reference to part of the history of lynching in America is included at the end of this chapter. In 1955 the brutal lynching of fourteen year old Emmett Till for allegedly flirting with a white woman was a catalyst for the Civil Rights Movement after his mother permitted an open casket and photographs were published nationwide.

Chapter 2

  • There are several resources for reading about opium throughout history and its use in the US online. By the late 1800s women made up sixty percent of opium addicts. In the 1900s wealthy, white men and women were consumers of opium.

Chapter 3

  • Australian Bushmen have a complicated history within the Boer Wars and Australian military. It also refers to men who spend most of their life in the outback of Australia. It does not usually refer to Australian Indigenous people. There were no head-hunters in Australia (except where possibly done in burial/spiritual ceremonies) but there were in New Zealand. He is a wild, primitive figure with a surprising touch of grace and aspiration. His obsessive admiration for Miss MacIntosh, coupled with his cultural and personal dislocation, make him a symbol of alienation and the tensions between civilization and savagery. Miss MacIntosh’s disdain and rejection of him underline her role as a practical, grounded counterpoint to the novel’s dreamlike and chaotic elements. This character enriches the novel’s exploration of identity, otherness, and the boundaries of social acceptance. The Australian Bushman symbolizes a primitive, untamed force, a disruption within the otherwise orderly and practical world that Miss MacIntosh represents. His "wild mien" and "calculated, incalculable eloquence" reflect a tension between civilization and savagery, rationality and irrationality. The chapter suggests that he is out of place in the refined and wealthy environment of the invalid's house, likening his presence to a scandal or an intrusion on social norms. The bushman serves as a foil to Miss MacIntosh. While she embodies sobriety, practicality, and a clear-eyed acceptance of reality, he represents fantasy, confusion, and the disruptive power of illusion and unfulfilled ambition. His presence heightens the contrast between the grounded nursemaid and the fantastical, opium-induced world of the invalid and her acquaintances.

Chapter 5

  • Boxwood and cedarwood evoke the desire for stability and lasting truth, as embodied by Miss MacIntosh and the grounded aspects of Vera’s search for reality, while wormwood represents the bitterness, loss, and spiritual malaise that haunt Vera’s life and her mother’s opium-induced coma.

Chapter 7

  • Edward A Hannegan was a politician from Indiana. He murdered his brother-in-law in a drunken rage and was acquitted. He later developed a morphine habit as he continued in politics.

Chapter 11

  • “her opiate voyage through nowhere”: Thomas De Quincey’s opium dreams in Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1821) carried him to Egypt and the East: “I was buried, for a thousand years, in stone coffins, with mummies and sphinxes.”

Chapter 14

  • Alectryomancy is a form of divination involving roosters and a method of seeking answers or predictions by observing the behavior of roosters.
  • “a palimpsest of many hieroglyphic writings”: A palimpsest is a parchment scraped and written over, the old text still faintly showing. Thomas De Quincey called the human brain one in “The Palimpsest of the Human Brain” (1845).

Chapter 22

  • “Hong Kong funds were frozen, and the British were rank imperialists”: Britain took Hong Kong in the First Opium War, fought to force the opium trade on China (Treaty of Nanking, 1842).
  • “Mr. Chandelier, Mr. Res Tacamah”: Catherine’s companions, Mr. Res Tacamah “who was the drug bottle.”

Chapter 24

  • “my mother’s opium dreams”: Before 1900, the typical opiate addict in America was an upper-class or middle-class white woman. As long as the opium user was a sick old lady there was no push to punish users.

Chapter 26

  • “by the opium doses, by the needle points”: The hypodermic syringe (Alexander Wood, 1853) brought injected morphine into nineteenth-century medicine and addiction.

Chapter 26 · Opium and Narcotics

  • Reflect escape, oblivion, and the tension between retaining memory or seeking peace through forgetfulness.

Chapter 27

  • “her mind distilled by the juices of languorous poppy flowers”: Opium is the dried latex of the opium poppy, Papaver somniferum.

Chapter 35

  • “in no drugged moments outside of time such as the opium lady might indulge in”: The opium lady is Catherine herself. Young drew her from Minna K. Weissenbach, “the opium lady of Hyde Park” (David O. Dowling, “The Guru,” in A Delicate Aggression: Savagery and Survival in the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, Yale University Press, 2019).

Chapter 37

  • “her face darkening and contorted like the face of a drowning woman”: Opium slows breathing. Signs of an overdose include slow or stopped breathing, blue or purple lips and face, and pinpoint pupils.

Chapter 38

  • “by nightshade and bella donna”: Deadly nightshade, Atropa belladonna, enlarges the pupils and blurs the sight. Italian women are said to have used it to make their eyes beautiful, hence bella donna, “beautiful lady.”

Chapter 39

  • “how opium had poisoned all pleasures at their source”: Thomas De Quincey turned from “The Pleasures of Opium” to “The Pains of Opium” in Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1821).
  • “Is it God’s drug”: Karl Marx famously described religion as “the opium of the people” (Karl Marx, A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right, 1844), suggesting that it numbs the pain of social inequality and exploitation. Lenin called it “a sort of spiritual booze” (Vladimir Lenin, “Socialism and Religion,” 1905). Religion may be used to maintain the status quo and discourage social change. This view might assert that religion offers easy answers to complex questions about the universe, life, and death. It may appeal to those who lack resources and/or education to form different perspectives. The novel suggests that religion, like opium, can be both a source of comfort and a form of escapism or a way to cope with the harshness and uncertainties of mortal life. Catherine’s opium paradise, filled with angels and ethereal visions, embodies this duality: it is an enchantment that extends her life beyond the physical but also confines her to a dreamlike state, disconnected from concrete reality. This resonates with the Marxist critique of religion as “the opium of the people,” implying a narcotic that dulls awareness and delays confrontation with real suffering. However, Young also complicates this view by showing that such illusions, whether religious or drug-induced, can be necessary for survival amid profound existential despair. In Chapter 1, Miss MacIntosh’s critique highlights the need to face reality soberly and practically, warning against being seduced by illusions that reject nature and the “bare face” of existence.
  • “the porcelain drug bottle with very large ears”: Tacamahac, or tacamahaca, is an aromatic resin once sold by apothecaries, and Mr. Res Tacamah may take his name from it. The “glowering genii” recall the Arabian Nights tale of the fisherman who uncorks a brass bottle from the sea and lets out a jinni.

Chapter 61

  • “brigantines of the opium trade”: Boston and Salem fortunes were made in the China trade. Russell & Company, run largely by Boston families such as the Forbeses and the Delanos, was the leading American firm in the opium trade with China.

Chapter 63

  • “the Emperor Constantine or King Canute or Crispin or Clarence or Cuthbert”: King Canute, or Cnut, ruled England, Denmark, and Norway. Miss MacIntosh invokes him against those who “waste our lives in the vain expectation of that which might never happen,” dreaming of “what was not, of what would never be.” Catherine names Canute too, in her opium dreams, and Miss MacIntosh insists the “opium paradise was never God’s way of life.” The story of Canute setting his throne on the shore and bidding the tide stand still, to show his courtiers that no king commands the sea, comes from Henry of Huntingdon (twelfth century).

Chapter 64

  • “their perfidious opium paradise”:

Chapter 66

  • “the opium dreams my mother dreamed”: Psychoactive substances and paranormal activity have been reported for over a thousand years. In the documentary Super High Me in 2007 Doug Benson smokes pot for thirty days straight. He took a series of tests before and after. His Psychic ESP test went from 1/25 to 7/25.

Chapter 71

  • “she had promised to finance a Revolution”: “Revolution” serves as a metaphor for a transformative change or upheaval Catherine imagines or aspires to finance. It aligns with the novel’s broader themes of disillusionment, social change, and the tension between dreams and reality. The Revolution here can be interpreted as a symbol of radical change (personal, social, or political) that Catherine contemplates amidst her dreamlike, drug-induced state and the decaying world around her. The promise to finance a Revolution is less about a concrete political movement and more about Catherine’s fantasy or symbolic gesture of power, influence, and change in a world she perceives as lost or slipping away.

Chapter 82

  • “how my mother, after many years of sleeping, arose from her bed and walked”: So did Weissenbach. She “had been able to get out of bed after many, many years, but this is what killed her, so that she turned old overnight. She had never shown the mark of time.” She died in 1943 in New York, and Young, who kept writing to her, learned of it months later from her daughter: “as long as you kept writing to Mother and I read your letters, I felt as if my mother was somehow alive” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).

Chapter 6

  • Maternal mortality rates were 30-40% higher before Roe v. Wade according to New York State, which saw maternal mortality fall by that much after New York legalized abortion in 1970, three years before Roe v. Wade. Depending on the state, maternal and infant mortality rates are rising due to inconsistent access to abortion. Some states that restrict abortion, rather than face the rise in mortality, have simply stopped reporting or disbanded the councils that were meant to monitor mortality rates in women and infants.

Chapter 6

  • “for she died in giving birth”: At the time Young started this book maternal mortality was pervasive for multiple reasons. Around 1900 six to nine women died for every thousand births, and rates stayed highest through 1930. They fell 71% between 1939 and 1948 with the move to hospital births, antibiotics, and safe blood transfusions.

Chapter 34

  • “My mother’s beauty was already fading”: In 2017 the Pew Research Center found that, among those who see differences, 61 percent of men said it was biology that determined what things men and women excel at in the workplace, while 65 percent of women said it was due to societal expectations (Pew Research Center, “Americans are divided on whether differences between men and women are rooted in biology or societal expectations,” December 5, 2017). One of those expectations is that women are valued for their physical beauty and nurturing. In July 2022, at the Turning Point USA Student Action Summit in Tampa, Representative Matt Gaetz asked why “the women with the least likelihood of getting pregnant” were “the ones most worried about having abortions” and said, “Nobody wants to impregnate you if you look like a thumb.” That May he had called abortion-rights protesters “over-educated, under-loved millennials” (Matt Gaetz, Twitter, May 4, 2022).

Chapter 71

  • “forceps, and something which looked like a tuning fork”: Obstetric forceps were invented in the 1600s by the Chamberlen family of London, who kept them a family secret for more than a century. René Laennec invented the stethoscope in 1816.
  • “Why was Sarah laughing?”: “Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?” (Genesis 18:12, KJV): the old woman who laughed at the promise of a child.

Chapter 72

  • “all the Fallopian tubes”: Fallopian tubes (in a female mammal) is either of a pair of tubes along which eggs travel from the ovaries to the uterus. They are named for Gabriele Falloppio, the Italian anatomist who described them in 1561.
  • “had never had to take a stitch”: “The stitch” may refer to a procedure called an episiotomy, also known as perineotomy and is a surgical incision of the perineum and the posterior vaginal wall generally done by a midwife or obstetrician. It was in the 50s in the US called the “husband stitch” because it was believed to return a woman’s vaginal opening to its original size. The routine is no longer recommended for vaginal births except in emergencies. Despite this, it is one of the most common surgical procedures specific to women.
  • “buried layettes laid out in long white boxes”: Young’s first poem, written at sixteen, “was about preparing a layette for my unborn fatherless baby,” and “it does become the character of Esther Longtree in Miss Macintosh, My Darling, many decades later.” An English teacher told her “that a young girl should not have such thoughts on her mind” (Marguerite Young, interview, WNYC radio, New York). On a train to Chicago a man told her of a cocker spaniel whose false pregnancy was eased only by giving “her toys to play with as if the baby were really there” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “She had never eaten ergot”: Ergot is a fungus that in the 1930s companies marketed to women whose pregnancy was not progressing since abortion, drugs that aborted a fetus and birth control devices were illegal. The FTC deemed the pills unsafe and ineffective and stopped their sale. In 1774 it is documented that midwives used ergot to ease delivery of a baby. In 1808 the New York doctor John Stearns published his use of ergot, “pulvis parturiens,” to hasten labor.
  • “a breech birth”: A breech birth occurs when a baby is positioned feet or bottom down instead of head-down near the end of pregnancy (around 36-37 weeks). While most babies turn head-down, about 3-5% remain in this position, which carries a higher risk for vaginal delivery, often requiring a C-section.

Chapter 73

  • “In her vast super-fecundation”: In medicine, superfecundation is the fertilizing of two or more eggs from one cycle in separate acts of intercourse, so that twins may have different fathers.
  • “the birth control devices littering the bare ground”: Before 1965, birth control in the US relied on barriers, withdrawal, and, later, hormonal methods, with access heavily restricted by the Comstock Act of 1873. Common methods included condoms (vulcanized rubber by 1839), diaphragms, spermicides, and dangerous, ineffective douches marketed as “feminine hygiene.” The first oral contraceptive pill was approved in 1960.
  • “the old Chicago detective was trying to find the proof”: England’s Act to Prevent the Destroying and Murthering of Bastard Children (1624) presumed that an unmarried mother who hid the death of her newborn had murdered it, unless she could prove “by one witness at the least” that the child was born dead; the penalty was death. It stood until 1803. In Massachusetts Hannah Piggen was reportedly the last woman hanged for concealing a birth, in 1785 (Wikipedia). Concealment of birth is still a crime in many states.
  • “she might endure the birth of nothing”: “We have been with child, we have been in pain, we have as it were brought forth wind” (Isaiah 26:18, KJV).

Chapter 74

  • “she had lost her toxic condition”: Toxemia of pregnancy, now called preeclampsia, brings high blood pressure, swelling, and sometimes convulsions (eclampsia); before modern prenatal care it was one of the great killers of mothers.
  • “a woman abortionist who enjoyed police protection”: Abortion was a crime in Illinois from 1867 until 1973. In Chicago, the historian Leslie J. Reagan found, the state prosecuted chiefly abortionists, most often after a woman had died, and police questioned dying women about their abortionists and lovers to obtain “dying declarations.” Reagan, When Abortion Was a Crime (1997).

Chapter 75

  • “Often, she pondered upon difficult questions”: “...pondered upon difficult questions, some legal, some illegal… often, was raped when there was no one present but a ghostly, mean, mean child… She could not always blame men for her disappointments. Sometimes she blamed the child…” The children ruined her body and “...her raped, wounded sky, the whole world?” During and after pregnancy, a woman’s body undergoes significant changes, including increased blood volume and heart rate, breast enlargement, and skin changes like stretch marks. Postpartum, the uterus shrinks, abdominal muscles may separate (diastasis recti), and some muscles may be weakened, potentially leading to urinary incontinence. Other common after-effects include changes in shoe size, wider hips, and hair loss after an initial period of thicker hair. During pregnancy, organs like the uterus, stomach, and intestines are pushed and shifted by the growing fetus to make room. After pregnancy, these organs gradually return to their pre-pregnancy positions over several weeks or months. Vaginal stretching happens as the baby moves down the birth canal. As the baby’s head descends, it interacts with the vaginal walls and pelvic floor, causing the tissues and muscles to stretch significantly. Computer models show that some pelvic floor muscles can stretch to more than three times their normal resting length.
  • “it might be a benign tumor, this growth”: In pseudocyesis, false or phantom pregnancy, a woman believes she is pregnant and her body follows: the menses stop, the belly swells, she feels the child move. Mary Tudor, Queen of England, believed herself pregnant in 1554 and 1555; London rang its bells for a prince who was never born.
  • “she ate geraniums and paper and string”: Pica, the craving to eat things that are not food (clay, chalk, paper, ice, starch), is common in pregnancy and has been described since antiquity; the word is Latin for magpie, the bird that will eat anything.

Chapter 76

  • “no rubber corporation or Wall Street corporation”: Esther means she never used a condom. Rubber condoms followed Goodyear’s vulcanization of rubber (1844); thinner latex condoms came in the 1920s. Under the Comstock Act of 1873 mailing contraceptives or information about them was a federal crime.
  • “had murdered her twin by kicking it out early”: Physicians have long known that one twin may die early in pregnancy and be shed or reabsorbed. With ultrasound in the 1970s this “vanishing twin” proved far more common than anyone had guessed.

Chapter 77

  • “was natural and a mother should suffer”: This may refer to Genesis 3:16 as Eve and women’s punishment for being cast out of the Garden of Eden. “In sorrow thou shalt bring forth children” (Genesis 3:16, KJV).
  • “pregnant in her dreams even though there was neither child nor father”: Esther may be suffering from False pregnancy or pseudocyesis. It is the appearance of clinical or subclinical signs and symptoms associated with pregnancy although the individual is not physically carrying a baby. The mistaken impression that one is pregnant includes signs and symptoms such as tender breasts with secretions, abdominal growth, delayed menstrual periods, and subjective feelings of a moving fetus. False pregnancy has a prominent psychiatric component as well as physical manifestations of pregnancy. It can be caused by physical or mental trauma, a chemical imbalance of hormones, and some medical conditions. See pseudocyesis in the Chapter 75 resources.

Chapter 78

  • “She would turn, bend, spill a baby”: A precipitate labor, three hours or less from the first contractions to birth, can deliver a baby before the mother has time to lie down.

Chapter 79

  • “a spoon having been used as the instrument to impregnate her mother”: Artificial insemination is the deliberate introduction of sperm into a female’s cervix or uterine cavity for the purpose of achieving a pregnancy through in vivo fertilization by means other than sexual intercourse or in vitro fertilisation. It is a fertility treatment for humans, and is common practice in animal breeding. The first recorded case of artificial insemination was John Hunter in 1790, who helped impregnate a linen draper’s wife. The first reported case of artificial insemination by a donor occurred in 1884 when William H. Pancoast, a professor in Philadelphia, took sperm from a handsome student in his class to inseminate an anesthetized woman without her knowledge. The incident was not published until twenty-five years later in a medical journal. The sperm bank was developed in Iowa starting in the 1950s in research conducted by University of Iowa medical school researchers Jerome Sherman and Raymond Bunge. In the United Kingdom, the British obstetrician Mary Barton founded one of the first fertility clinics to offer donor insemination in the 1930s. Mary Barton and her first husband were medical missionaries in pre-partition India, then still ruled by Britain. She witnessed the way in which women would be punished or even killed for being childless. At the time, it was taboo to suggest that it might be the husband, and not the wife, who was infertile, not only on the Indian subcontinent but also in the United Kingdom. Barton understood that both men and women could be infertile and in 1943 was the lead author on an article for the British Medical Journal. It was signed by many of the researchers active in the field in Great Britain at that time. With her second husband, Bertold Wiesner, Mary Barton successfully inseminated an estimated 1500 women, the majority with sperm provided from Wiesner, some 100-200 from neuroscientist Derek Richter as well as an unknown number from as yet unidentified donors. It is estimated that Wiesner is the biological father of around 600 children born following these procedures, although some believe this figure could be as high as 1000. When Barton and Wiesner published their paper on the procedure it was publicly condemned by the Pope who called it a sin, and the Archbishop of Canterbury who called for the British parliament to make human artificial insemination illegal. Although it was not criminalized it was not legalized either and therefore the status of artificial insemination was ambiguous. Consequently, the activities of Barton and Wiesner at the fertility clinic were conducted in secrecy and all inseminated women were instructed to tell nobody about it. (Wikipedia)
  • “This third person, this dark woman”: A “dark woman” who assisted with births may refer to the following: 1) the Biblical midwife Shiphrah, one of the “Hebrew midwives” of Exodus 1:15, though some readers have taken her and Puah for Egyptians. Shiphrah, along with her colleague Puah, defied the Pharaoh’s order to kill newborn Hebrew males. 2) Biddy Mason, who was born into slavery, was a midwife and advocate for other enslaved people in 19th-century California. After gaining her freedom, she became a successful entrepreneur and philanthropist. 3) Margaret Charles Smith was an African American midwife in Alabama who delivered over 3,000 babies during a career spanning over 30 years, often in rural areas with limited healthcare access. 4) Mary Francis Hill Coley was a midwife from Georgia who delivered over 3,000 babies during her career. Her work was featured in the 1952 documentary, All My Babies. 5) Susie Carey was a third-generation midwife featured in a photograph at the National Museum of African American History and Culture. 6) Sarah Hudson Grant was a Black Southern midwife whose work is remembered today.
  • “the birth of Esther was hard, requiring instruments”: Instruments to assist with childbirth have evolved from rudimentary tools for destructive purposes in antiquity to sophisticated instruments like forceps and vacuum extractors today. Early interventions included destructive tools for delivering stillborn fetuses and instruments for procedures like symphysiotomy, a painful procedure to widen the pelvis. Modern forceps, introduced by the Chamberlen family in the 16th century, were a breakthrough for delivering living infants, and their use, along with vacuum extractors, remains a vital part of modern obstetrics.

Chapter 80

  • “pregnant only with the yeast of her own dreams”: There are two famous pseudocyesis cases (phantom pregnancies): Mary Tudor, Queen of England, experienced a well-documented false pregnancy, where she showed physical symptoms, and her doctors and court prepared for a birth, even drafting announcement letters with blanks for the date and sex. Anna O, the patient of Freud’s colleague Josef Breuer, experienced a false pregnancy where she believed she was in labor with her therapist’s child. Anna O was Bertha Pappenheim, who went on to found the League of Jewish Women (1904) and fought the trafficking of women.
  • Esther fits the pattern later called neonaticide: a young, unmarried mother who does not recognize or denies her pregnancy, gives birth alone, and kills the newborn in panic within the first day. The psychiatrist Phillip Resnick named it in 1970.

Chapter 81

  • “birth control devices”: The inclusion of these items is particularly striking, pointing to themes of sexuality, control over reproduction, and perhaps the anxieties or deliberate choices related to creating or preventing life. In a novel deeply concerned with motherhood, loss, and the nature of existence, these devices symbolize attempts to manage or deny natural processes, or the consequences of such interventions in the American context.
