Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • John Milton wrote the epic poem Paradise Lost. He was blind when he dictated it to people including his daughters.

Chapter 3

  • John Milton's Paradise Lost, where the Devil famously declares as he grapples with his new reality in Hell. He suggests that even in the depths of despair, one's mindset can determine their experience, "The mind is its own place, and in itself can make a heaven of hell, a hell of heaven". This quote highlights the power of the mind to influence one's perception of reality and experience, suggesting that our internal state can transform even the most adverse external circumstances into something positive or negative.

Chapter 7

  • “He’s rolling in the flood”: John Milton, Paradise Lost (1.324): “To adore the conqueror, who now beholds / Cherub and seraph rolling in the flood.” The expression metaphorically conveys that old Doc is submerged in a kind of existential or spiritual flood: caught in the overwhelming currents of his own disordered mind or possibly in the waters of death itself. It suggests that Doc is drowning or engulfed by his circumstances, unable to escape his fate. The flood represents a chaotic, engulfing force that traps Doc, reflecting his mental confusion and the dissolution of his medical practice and life.

Chapter 8

  • “going to dance the light fantastic”: John Milton’s poem L’Allegro (The Happy Man), written about 1631 and published 1645, has the lines “Come, and trip it as ye go / On the light fantastic toe.” It is a pastoral poem, which has from its first appearance been paired with the contrasting pastoral poem, Il Penseroso (The Melancholy Man), which depicts a similar day spent in contemplation and thought. (Wikipedia) L’Allegro is the poem of the happy man, and Moses gives its dance to the dying Jacqueline.

Chapter 10

  • “St. Michael and of all the holy angels”: The list comes out of Milton’s Paradise Lost, which gives Hell “Gorgons and Hydras, and Chimaeras dire” (2.628) and seats Chaos as umpire with “high arbiter Chance” who “governs all” (2.907-910).
  • “Porpoises shall eat the drowned sailor. The waters of this world shall close over his head”: The preacher gives the bride and groom a sailor’s burial at sea. Milton’s “Lycidas” (1638) mourns a friend drowned in the Irish Sea, and Ariel sings of a drowned father in The Tempest: “Full fathom five thy father lies.” The line foreshadows Miss MacIntosh lost in the waves.

Chapter 21

  • “once he sat at the right hand of the throne of God and was a favorite son of Heaven”: “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” (Isaiah 14:12). Milton’s Satan was “of the first, / If not the first Archangel, great in power” (Paradise Lost 5.659-660).

Chapter 22

  • “He was fallen from morning until seven o’clock, from evening until morning”: Milton’s fallen angel Mulciber: “from Morn / To Noon he fell, from Noon to dewy Eve, / A Summer’s day” (Paradise Lost 1.742-744). Luke has Satan fall “as lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18).

Chapter 34

  • “with his golden-footed compass moving across a clouded sky”: “He took the golden compasses, prepared / In God’s eternal store, to circumscribe / This universe” (Milton, Paradise Lost 7.225-227). Blake drew it as The Ancient of Days (1794), and Plutarch reports Plato’s saying that “God always geometrizes.”

Chapter 39

  • “great leviathans rolling, lifting like islands in the flood”: “Leviathan, which God of all his works / Created hugest that swim the ocean stream,” is taken for an island by the pilot of a night-foundered skiff (John Milton, Paradise Lost 1.201-208, 1667).

Chapter 40

  • Pandemonium is a wild uproar among a crowd of people. John Milton invented the name in Paradise Lost for the capital of Hell. (Paradise Lost 1.756).

Chapter 56

  • “tremulous as clouds with silver linings”: “Was I deceived, or did a sable cloud / Turn forth her silver lining on the night?” (John Milton, Comus, 1634).
  • “Had he not given birth to death”: In Milton’s Paradise Lost, Sin springs full-grown from the head of Satan, and she later bears his son, Death (Book 2, 1667).

Chapter 63

  • “It would be impractical for the infernal spirits to conceive their own damnation”: “The mind is its own place, and in itself / Can make a Heav’n of Hell, a Hell of Heav’n” (John Milton, Paradise Lost, 1.254-255, 1667).

Chapter 66

  • “Yet once more, Miss MacIntosh, my darling, and once more”: Vera’s elegy echoes Milton’s “Lycidas” (1637), his lament for a friend drowned at sea: “Yet once more, O ye laurels, and once more”; “He must not float upon his watery bier”; “Whilst thee the shores and sounding seas / Wash far away”; “Visit’st the bottom of the monstrous world”; “So sinks the day-star in the ocean bed”; “With nectar pure his oozy locks he laves.”

Chapter 68

  • “I would see her shining through every cloud”: Compare Milton’s Comus (1634): “Was I deceived, or did a sable cloud / Turn forth her silver lining on the night?,” the source of every cloud’s silver lining.

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • Troy is a city that was besieged for ten years and eventually conquered by King Agamemnon. The war and siege was written in Homer’s “Iliad.”

Chapter 5

  • Penelope is a character in Homer's Odyssey. The reference to Penelope highlights themes of waiting, fidelity, and steadfastness amid uncertainty and absence. Penelope, the faithful wife of Odysseus in Greek mythology, is renowned for her patience and loyalty, waiting many years for her husband’s return from the Trojan War while warding off numerous suitors. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 6

  • “She was Morality, and I was Honesty”: Homer Capehorn shares the poet’s name. Homer’s works (the Iliad and the Odyssey) present a complex picture of morality and honesty, reflecting the values and norms of ancient Greek society. In the Odyssey, Odysseus frequently uses lies and deception for survival and self-preservation, particularly when disguised. He tailors his falsehoods to specific situations and individuals, demonstrating his cleverness and resourcefulness. While Odysseus’s actions are often portrayed as strategic and necessary for his survival, they can also be viewed as ethically problematic. Despite the prevalence of deception, Homer also portrays honesty as a valuable trait. Odysseus drops his disguise at last to Penelope and to his father, and honesty brings him home.

Chapter 11

  • “Penelope’s web”: In the Odyssey, Penelope weaves a shroud for Laertes by day and unravels it by night to hold off the suitors.

Chapter 13

  • “We both step and do not step into the same river, we both are and are not” (Heraclitus Homericus, Homeric Allegories)

Chapter 21

  • “A man who is a pig is still a man”: Circe turns Odysseus’s men into swine, but “their minds were as before” (Odyssey 10).

Chapter 22

  • “it was a wise child who knew his own father”: “It is a wise father that knows his own child” (The Merchant of Venice 2.2). Telemachus says, “My mother says I am his son; but I know not, for no man knows his own father” (Odyssey 1).

Chapter 23

  • “Ulysses, if ever he had seen Penelope under electric lights”: Ulysses is the Roman name for Odysseus, a hero in ancient Greek literature. Penelope is the wife of Ulysses and is an example of a faithful wife because she waits for her husband to return and tricks suitors who wish to marry her. Penelope wove a shroud by day and unwove it by night to put off her suitors (Odyssey 2).

Chapter 29

  • “Homeric butterflies which were like persons who had passed through many unknown forms of being”: Io Vanessa is the Peacock butterfly. The Aphrodite Fritillary and the Apollo (Parnassius apollo) are named for gods. Morpheus, “the fashioner,” shapes dreams in Ovid’s Metamorphoses 11. The Atlas moth is among the largest moths in the world. Papilio homerus of Jamaica is the largest swallowtail in the Americas, and Papilio antimachus is the largest butterfly in Africa.
  • “the old Diomedes with planets and half moons”: Diomedes (Deudorix) is a butterfly found in Africa.

Chapter 32

  • “the sleepy myrmidons who did my mother’s bidding”: The Myrmidons were the soldiers Achilles led to Troy in Homer’s Iliad. Ovid tells that Zeus made them from ants for King Aeacus (Metamorphoses 7). The word came to mean a follower who obeys without question.

Chapter 36

  • “despotic, one-eyed ogres in darkened rooms”: The one-eyed ogre recalls Polyphemus, the Cyclops who penned Odysseus and his men in his dark cave (Homer, Odyssey 9).

Chapter 38

  • “the rescue of pale ladies held by one-eyed ogres”: See the Polyphemus entry in the Chapter 36 resources.

Chapter 41

  • “Had she not made a man into a tortoise with stars upon his back?”: Circe turns Odysseus’s men into swine (Odyssey 10).
  • “came no more storming at these ivory gates”: “For two are the gates of shadowy dreams, and one is fashioned of horn and one of ivory. Those dreams that pass through the gate of sawn ivory deceive men, bringing words that find no fulfillment” (Odyssey 19.562-565, trans. A. T. Murray, 1919). Aeneas leaves the underworld by the ivory gate (Aeneid 6.893-898). Hannah no longer storms the gates of Catherine’s false dreams.
  • “She should have eaten lotus flowers”: Whoever of Odysseus’s men “ate the honey-sweet fruit of the lotus, had no longer any wish to bring back word or to return” (Odyssey 9.94-95, trans. A. T. Murray, 1919). Tennyson’s mariners come “unto a land / In which it seemed always afternoon” (Alfred Tennyson, “The Lotos-Eaters,” 1832).
  • “drugged with that nepenthe”: Nepenthe is a fictional medicine for sorrow that is mentioned in Greek literature and mythology. In the Odyssey, Helen “cast into the wine of which they were drinking a drug to quiet all pain and strife, and bring forgetfulness of every ill” (Odyssey 4.220-221, trans. A. T. Murray, 1919). See Nepenthe in the Chapter 43 vocabulary.

Chapter 42

  • “fields of mountain asphodel”: In the Odyssey, Hermes leads the souls of the dead suitors down to the meadow of asphodel, where the spirits of the dead dwell (Odyssey 24).
  • “she being that ivory door”: See the gates of horn and ivory in the Chapter 41 resources.

Chapter 44

  • “Who knocks now at the ivory gates?”: See the gates of horn and ivory, the gates of false dreams, in the Chapter 41 resources.
  • “the long fingers of rosy light reaching through the clouds at dawn”: Homer’s dawn is “rosy-fingered,” rhododaktylos Eos, throughout the Iliad and the Odyssey.

Chapter 48

  • “He was the dog barking at the Dog star in the cloud”: The Dog star is Sirius in the constellation, Canis Major, the Greater Dog. Homer calls Sirius the dog of Orion, the brightest of stars but a sign of evil (Iliad 22.26-31).

Chapter 49

  • “the wine dark sea”: Homer’s sea is oinops pontos, “wine-faced,” the wine-dark sea, in the Iliad and the Odyssey.

Chapter 51

  • “a man of many gates, gates of ivory, gates of gold”: “There are two gates through which these unsubstantial fancies proceed; the one is of horn, and the other ivory. Those that come through the gate of ivory are fatuous, but those from the gate of horn mean something to those that see them” (Homer, Odyssey 19, trans. Samuel Butler, 1900).
  • “drank the waters of nepenthe”: Nepenthe is a drug described in Homer’s Odyssey as banishing grief: Helen drugs the wine “with an herb that banishes all care, sorrow, and ill humour” (Odyssey 4, trans. Samuel Butler, 1900). A stirrup cup is a last drink taken in the saddle before riding off.

Chapter 59

  • “What was more pitiful than man?”: When the immortal horses of Achilles weep for Patroclus, Zeus pities them: “for of all creatures that live and move upon the earth there is none so pitiable as he is” (Homer, Iliad, Book 17, trans. Samuel Butler, 1898).

Chapter 61

  • “He had pulled out his hair by the handfuls”: Ancient mourning tore the hair and beat the breast. When Achilles hears that Patroclus is dead, he pours dust on his head and tears his hair with his hands (Homer, Iliad, Book 18).

Chapter 75

  • “through the ivory portals”: In the Odyssey (Book 19) Penelope says that dreams come through two gates: those through the gate of ivory deceive, those through the gate of horn come true. Virgil sends Aeneas back from the underworld through the ivory gate (Aeneid 6).

Chapter 76

  • “who hovered at the ivory gates between life and death”: See the gates of horn and ivory in the Chapter 75 resources.
  • “She was always knitting and unravelling the black hood”: Penelope, waiting twenty years for Odysseus, wove a shroud for his father by day and unravelled it by night to put off her suitors (Odyssey, Book 2).

Chapter 82

  • “One drop more of nepenthe”: Nepenthe is a mythical, ancient Greek potion or drug used to induce forgetfulness of pain, sorrow, or grief. In Homer’s Odyssey (Book 4), Helen had it as a gift from Polydamna of Egypt and mixed it into the wine to ease the grief of Menelaus and his guests.

In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 4, Chapter 5, Chapter 8, Chapter 18, Chapter 26, Chapter 33, Chapter 37, Chapter 41, Chapter 42, Chapter 44, Chapter 48

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • Edgar Allen Poe wrote the poem, The Raven, as a narrative, without intentional allegory or didacticism. The main theme of the poem is one of undying devotion. The scholar experiences a perverse conflict between desire to forget and desire to remember. He seems to get some pleasure from focusing on loss. He assumes that the word "Nevermore" is the raven's "only stock and store", and, yet, he continues to ask it questions, knowing what the answer will be. His questions, then, are purposely self-deprecating and further incite his feelings of loss. Poe leaves it unclear whether the raven actually knows what it is saying or whether it really intends to cause a reaction in the poem's narrator. The scholar begins as "weak and weary", becomes regretful and grief-stricken, before passing into a frenzy and, finally, madness. Christopher F. S. Maligec suggests the poem is a type of elegiac paraclausithyron, an ancient Greek and Roman poetic form consisting of the lament of an excluded, locked-out lover at the sealed door of his beloved. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 4

  • “the silver, the golden, never the leaden bells”: Bells in this chapter symbolize the presence of death and the funeral rites permeating the house, the relentless passage of time and the cycle of life and death, a link between the material and spiritual worlds, calling attention to the unseen and the spectral, the deep, underlying melancholy that shadows the characters' lives and the house itself. Edgar Allan Poe’s poem “The Bells” (1849) moves through the same stages of life, from silver sleigh bells and golden wedding bells to brazen alarm bells and the iron bells of the funeral.

Chapter 5

  • “He had been told of people buried alive and crying in their graves”: While there appears to be an overestimation of the number of people buried alive accidentally in this chapter, in 1885 a victim was found inside his coffin with much of his hair pulled out. The fear was widespread in the nineteenth century. Poe’s story “The Premature Burial” (1844) turns on it, and inventors patented “safety coffins” with bells, air tubes, and flags so that anyone who woke underground could signal.

Chapter 8

  • “that dream within the dream”: This may refer to Edgar Allan Poe’s poem “A Dream within a Dream” (1849), which says, “All that we see or seem / Is but a dream within a dream.” This dream within a dream is a recurring theme throughout the book. The idea that life is a dream goes back to Plato, Aristotle, and Descartes. The first stanza ends with that statement, and the last stanza turns it into a question: “Is all that we see or seem / But a dream within a dream?” This symbolizes the recursive, elusive quality of existence in the novel: a reality constantly refracted through multiple dreamlike states that challenge the notion of a fixed, singular truth.

Chapter 18

  • Edgar Allan Poe’s “A Dream Within a Dream” explores the cyclical nature of dreams and the illusion of reality, further reinforcing the idea of life as a dream.

Chapter 26

See the maelstrom entry in the Chapter 2 resources.

  • “All that we see or seem / Is but a dream within a dream” (Edgar Allan Poe, “A Dream Within a Dream,” 1849).

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • The Egyptian Sailor may refer to the “Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor.” A shipwrecked traveller engages upon a spiritual endeavour or quest, journeying through the cosmos, to meet a primordial god, providing to the traveller a gift of moral vision with which to return to Egypt. Further, Richard Mathews writes that this "oldest fantasy text contains archetypal narrative of the genre: an uninitiated hero on a sea journey is thrown off course by a storm, encounters an enchanted island, confronts a monster, and survives, wiser for the experience…” The tale itself begins with a framing device in which an attendant ("follower" or "the sailor") tries to comfort his master, who is returning from an apparently failed expedition and is anxious about how the king will receive him. (Wikipedia) (The Land of Punt was an ancient kingdom, likely located in the Horn of Africa, that traded extensively with ancient Egypt. It was a source of valuable goods like gold, ebony, ivory, and aromatic resins, which were highly sought after by the Egyptians. While the exact location remains debated, current evidence points towards a coastal region encompassing parts of present-day Somalia, Djibouti, Eritrea, and northeast Sudan. The kingdom's existence is primarily known through Egyptian records and depictions, particularly from the Middle and New Kingdom periods.) An attendant reassures him, advising him on how to behave before the king, and repeating the proverb, “The mouth of a man saves him.” To encourage his master, he tells a tale of a previous voyage of his in which he overcame disaster, including meeting with a god and the king. The tale ends with the master saying, “Do not make the excellent (that is, do not act arrogantly) my friend; why give water to a goose (literally, bird) at dawn before its slaughtering in the morning?” A Middle Kingdom text, "The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor," describes a star falling to earth, which led to the extinction of giant serpents on an island. This is sometimes interpreted as a folk memory of a meteorite impact as in the Netflix series Ancient Apocalypse. The sailor’s voyage appears to be a type of Otherworld Journey, a dangerous crossing-over to a divine or magical realm beyond the edge of the known world. “William K. Simpson observes that the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor is ...one of the most interesting, straightforward, and yet puzzling compositions of ancient Egyptian literature. A curious emphasis is placed on numbers, the height of the wave, the dimensions of the ship, the number of sailors, the length of the serpent’s hood, the number of months of the sailor’s stay, and so on. It is almost as if the tale is an allegory involving the movement of stars. The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor is considered to contain esoteric knowledge, much of it related to the serpent’s story. Whatever its meaning, this tragedy is enshrined as the central motif of the narrative: it is element X in a structure A-B-C-X-C'-B'-A'. Unlike all of the other motifs, its form is mythic rather than folkloric; it seems to be a religious allegory. As a mythic island (X) set in the dead centre of a sea of folktale elements (A-C and A'-C'), it may even be the “payload” of the whole story.”

Chapter 2

  • Hieroglyph was a character of the ancient Egyptian writing system.

Chapter 3

  • Cheops to the ancient Greeks was an ancient Egyptian monarch.

Chapter 7

  • Manasseh was the eldest son of Joseph and the Egyptian Asenath.

Chapter 11

  • Menpehtyre Ramesses I (or Ramses) was the founding pharaoh of ancient Egypt’s 19th Dynasty. The dates for his short reign are not completely known but the timeline of late 1292-1290 BC is frequently cited as well as 1295-1294 BC. While Ramesses I was the founder of the 19th Dynasty, his brief reign mainly serves to mark the transition between the reign of Horemheb, who had stabilized Egypt in the late 18th Dynasty, and the rule of the powerful pharaohs of his own dynasty, in particular his son Seti I, and grandson Ramesses II. (Wikipedia)
  • Ramesses II, commonly known as Ramesses the Great, was an Egyptian pharaoh. He was the third ruler of the Nineteenth Dynasty. Along with Thutmose III of the Eighteenth Dynasty, he is often regarded as the greatest, most celebrated, and most powerful pharaoh of the New Kingdom, which itself was the most powerful period of ancient Egypt. (Wikipedia)
  • Usermaatre Meryamun Ramesses III was the second pharaoh of the Twentieth Dynasty in ancient Egypt. Some scholars date his reign from 26 March 1186 to 15 April 1155 BC, and he is considered the last pharaoh of the New Kingdom to have wielded substantial power. (Wikipedia) He took Ramesses II’s throne name and modeled his temple at Medinet Habu on Ramesses II’s, one king dreaming another’s dreams.
  • “Rameses I, II, III”: The royal mummies were found in 1881 in a hidden tomb at Deir el-Bahri, where priests had moved and rewrapped them, some in other kings’ coffins. Shelley’s “Ozymandias” (1818) takes its name from the Greek form of Ramesses II’s throne name, User-maat-re.
  • “partitioned into many selves without his knowing it”: The Egyptians held that a person was made of many parts: the ka, the life force; the ba, the soul that flies from the tomb; the name; the shadow; and the heart, weighed at judgment.
  • “pyramid-shaped ices”: Ices were molded into shapes for grand dinners. The pyramids Catherine serves come just before the pharaoh arrives.

Chapter 11 · Rameses I, II, III

  • Symbolize fragmented identities and the confusion of time within the dream.
  • The pharaoh unwrapping himself reveals the layered nature of self and memory.

Chapter 17

  • “old pharaohs voyaging to heaven upon clouds of incense”: The Pyramid Texts tell of the king rising to heaven on the smoke of incense.

Chapter 20

  • “the itinerary of the children of Israel from Egypt to Canaan”: The Israelites’ journey from Egypt to Canaan involved a circuitous route through the wilderness, lasting approximately 40 years. The Israelites’ long journey is often attributed to their disobedience, doubt, and lack of faith in God’s leadership. God led them by a longer route to protect them from enemies and allow them time to develop their faith and trust: “God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near; for God said, Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war” (Exodus 13:17), and “your children shall wander in the wilderness forty years” (Numbers 14:33).

Chapter 22

  • “Where is Cleopatra’s Needle?”: Cleopatra’s Needle is the popular name for each of a pair of ancient Egyptian obelisks re-erected in London and New York City during the nineteenth century.

Chapter 26

  • “the reincarnation of Cleopatra”: Cleopatra VII (69-30 BC), the last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt and Mark Antony’s lover. Belief in reincarnation runs through Hinduism, and through Theosophy, founded in New York in 1875.
  • “a Sphinx in her garden… a greater pyramid than her neighbor could afford”: The Great Sphinx and the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza. Egyptian Revival garden ornaments were a fashion after Napoleon’s expedition to Egypt (1798).
  • “Egyptian securities, and New England shipping”: Egypt’s foreign debts led to the Anglo-French Dual Control (1876) and the British occupation of 1882. Egyptian bonds were a favorite of cautious Victorian investors.
  • “eating from golden dishes fit for the dead pharaohs”: In ancient Egypt, cats were sacred to the goddess Bastet and were mummified by the hundreds of thousands.
  • “like an old mummified pharaoh wrapped in his body which was his boat”: Pharaohs were buried with boats to carry them through the afterlife. Khufu’s cedar ship was found beside the Great Pyramid in 1954.

Chapter 26 · The Siamese Cats

  • Symbolize mystery, immortality, and the blurred boundary between life and death. Their dominance in the Boston lady’s house reflects ongoing life amid death.

Chapter 26 · The Pyramid and the Sphinx

  • Represent ancient legacies, riddles of existence, and the enigmatic nature of identity and memory.
  • These are Egyptian sphinxes, built in rival Boston gardens by two old women who each believed she was the reincarnation of Cleopatra.

Chapter 29

  • “many other gods, the god of the sun, the goddess of the moon, the judge of the dead, the busy clerk of the underworld”: The gods are Egyptian. Osiris judged the dead, and Thoth, the scribe of the gods, recorded the weighing of the heart (Book of the Dead, spell 125). Young’s list goes on to “the goddess with the head of a cat” (Bastet) and “the jackal god who was the conductor of the dead” (Anubis).
  • “the bed of Charlemagne, the amethyst bed of Catherine the Great”: Historical people in the chapter are symbolic bridges between the personal and the universal, the real and the mythic, the past and the present. They enrich the novel’s exploration of identity, memory, mortality, and the elusive nature of reality, reinforcing its complex, dreamlike atmosphere and thematic depth.

Chapter 30

  • Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub or Saladin was the founder of the Ayyubid dynasty. Hailing from a Kurdish family, he was the first sultan of both Egypt and Syria. He was an important figure of the Third Crusade. At the height of his power, the Ayyubid realm spanned Egypt, Syria, Upper Mesopotamia, the Hejaz, Yemen, and Nubia. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 39

  • “bevies including the Egyptians and the Florentines”: Egyptians are from Egypt.
  • “a skull grinning at a banquet table”: At Egyptian banquets, Herodotus says, a man carried round a wooden corpse in a coffin to remind the guests that they would be like it when dead (Histories 2.78).

Chapter 40

  • “the language of the Nubian boy”: Nubians are an ethnolinguistic group of people indigenous to what is now present-day Sudan and Egypt.
  • “the hieroglyphic language of the drowned Egyptian sailor”: Egyptian sailor may refer to the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor. The proverbs from this story are: the mouth of a man saves him; do not act arrogant; why give water to a bird before it is slaughtered. It is interpreted as a shipwrecked traveler goes on a spiritual quest through the cosmos and meets a primordial god that provides the traveler with a moral vision to return home with.
  • “so many pharaohs in swan boats passing with the sentinel moon”: The pharaohs’ boats recall the solar barque of Ra, which carried the sun god across the sky by day and through the underworld by night.

Chapter 42

  • “an ancient pharaoh sleeping in a swan boat”: See the solar barque of Ra in the Chapter 40 resources.

Chapter 43

  • “Did she lift her veil embroidered with the stars”: The veiled goddess of Sais declared, “I am all that has been, and is, and shall be, and my robe no mortal has yet uncovered” (Plutarch, On Isis and Osiris 9, trans. Frank Cole Babbitt, 1936).

Chapter 48

  • “a small pharaoh in his tomb or boat”: The pharaoh was buried with a boat to sail with the sun through the underworld. In 1954 the cedar ship of Khufu, 143 feet long, was found dismantled in a sealed pit beside the Great Pyramid.

Chapter 49

  • “the cat miaowed”: “Miaow” is the older spelling of the cat’s cry; earlier forms miaow, miau, and meaw date from the 1630s, and “meow” is recorded from 1842 (Online Etymology Dictionary). It is miau in Spanish and German and miaou in French. Cats in Ancient Egypt were called mau, after their cry.
  • “But why should any man weep if the heavens wept for him?”: In the Bible God grieves and Jesus weeps: “it grieved him at his heart” (Genesis 6:6); “Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears” (Jeremiah 9:1); “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). In the Book of Moses of the Latter-day Saints, “the God of heaven looked upon the residue of the people, and he wept” (Moses 7:28). The Quran says of Pharaoh’s drowned people, “And the heaven and the earth wept not for them” (44:29, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, 1930), and the Egyptians said the Nile rose with the tears of Isis for Osiris (Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.32.18).
  • “the porphyry clouds”: Porphyry, from the Greek porphyra, purple, is an igneous rock with large crystals set in a fine-grained matrix, the mark of two-stage cooling. The purple porphyry of Egypt was prized by Rome and Byzantium for imperial sculpture and architecture, since purple was the color of royalty, and a Byzantine emperor’s child born in the palace’s porphyry chamber was porphyrogenitus, “born in the purple.” See Porphyry of Tyre, above.

Chapter 50

  • “not even the book of death”: The Egyptian Book of the Dead, the Book of Coming Forth by Day, was a collection of spells written on papyrus and buried with the dead from about 1550 BCE to guide them through the underworld.

Chapter 51

  • “more hieroglyphs to the alphabet of reality”: Egyptian hieroglyphs could not be read until Jean-François Champollion deciphered them from the Rosetta Stone in 1822.

Chapter 52

  • Saint Maurice, commander of the Theban Legion raised in Roman Egypt, was martyred in the late third century at Agaunum, now Saint-Maurice in the Swiss canton of Valais, for refusing orders to persecute Christians; his historicity is not certain. A statue of about 1240 in Magdeburg Cathedral is the earliest known depiction of him as a Black African knight in armor, and he was venerated across Europe. Black knights could also be called this because of the color of their armor. A black knight is a literary stock character who masks his identity and that of his liege by not displaying heraldry. Black knights are usually portrayed as villainous figures who use this anonymity for misdeeds. They are often contrasted with the knight-errant (white knight). The character appeared in Arthurian literature and has been adapted by various authors, in film and popular culture, and is sometimes associated with death or darkness.

Chapter 53

  • “a man who was a Bridge of Sighs, a Bridge of Lies, a lake of fire”: Bridge of Sighs is a bridge in Venice, Italy. Built about 1600 over the Rio di Palazzo, it led prisoners from the Doge’s Palace to the prisons, and their sighs at a last view of Venice gave it its name. Bridge of Lies is a legendary pedestrian bridge in Sibiu, Transylvania, Romania. Lake of fire is a place of after-death punishment in Egyptian and Christian religions. “And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death” (Revelation 20:14, KJV).
  • Evidence suggests that ancient Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans utilized various forms of punching bags for combat training. These bags were often crafted from materials like leather and filled with sand or other readily available materials. Ancient Chinese and Japanese civilizations also used animal skin punching bags filled with sand or grain for martial arts training. Indian wrestling traditions also employed practice equipment called “mukha dhanda,” which were essentially hanging leather pouches filled with sand, pebbles, or grain.
  • “old Egyptian wrestling holds”: Ancient Egyptian wrestling, depicted in tomb paintings and sculptures, showcased a variety of holds and techniques, many of which are still recognizable in modern wrestling styles. These depictions, particularly those at Beni Hasan, reveal over 4000-year-old techniques, including throws, takedowns, and ground grappling, emphasizing both athletic prowess and strategic combat training.

Chapter 55

  • “a mere hieroglyph which had dropped from the alphabet of heaven”: “hieroglyph” a stylized picture of an object representing a word, syllable, or sound, as found in ancient Egyptian and other writing systems.

Chapter 57

  • “a Sphinx had settled on his coat sleeve”: This sphinx is a sphinx moth, or hawk moth, named for the caterpillar’s habit of rearing up its head like the Great Sphinx. See The Life of the Sphinx Moth in the Chapter 55 resources.

Chapter 61

  • “The Egyptians had put their dead into swan boats under the sand”: Boats were buried with Egyptian kings for the voyage of the dead; Khufu’s cedar boat, buried beside the Great Pyramid, was found in 1954.

Chapter 63

  • “this, the missing breast which gave her the pain”: The Edwin Smith Papyrus, an Egyptian surgical text of about 1600 BC copying older sources, describes bulging tumors of the breast and says there is no treatment.

Chapter 64

  • The Egyptian Book of the Dead is an ancient Egyptian funerary text generally written on papyrus and used from the beginning of the New Kingdom (around 1550 BCE) to around 50 BCE.

Chapter 65

  • “Weep not, Hagar, for thy little son”: According to the Bible, Hagar was the Egyptian slave of Sarah, Abram’s wife. Sarah had been barren for a long time and sought a way to fulfill God’s promise that Abram would be father of many nations, especially since they had grown old, so she offered Hagar to Abram to be his concubine. Hagar bore Abraham’s son, Ishmael. “What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not” (Genesis 21:17, KJV). Where the King James has “he will be a wild man” (Genesis 16:12), the Hebrew reads “a wild ass of a man,” as Mr. Bonebreaker has it; see Ishmael in the Chapter 62 resources.
  • “the Egyptians were spoiled”: “And they spoiled the Egyptians” (Exodus 12:36, KJV): the Israelites, leaving Egypt, carried off the Egyptians’ silver and gold.
  • “he had dwelled for a long time in the Land of Ham”: In the Psalms the land of Ham is Egypt: “Israel also came into Egypt; and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham” (Psalm 105:23, KJV).

Chapter 66

  • “that a path would open through the sea for her”: “And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea… and made the sea dry land, and the waters were divided” (Exodus 14:21, KJV).
  • “a pillar of clouds by day, a pillar of fire by night”: “And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud, to lead them the way; and by night in a pillar of fire, to give them light” (Exodus 13:21, KJV).

Chapter 71

  • “The Cow Who Jumped over the Moon”: The Cow Who Jumped over the Moon is the English nursery rhyme “Hey Diddle Diddle.” There are numerous theories about the origin of the rhyme. James Orchard Halliwell suggested that it was a corruption of ancient Greek, probably advanced as a result of a deliberate hoax. It was connected with Hathor worship. It refers to various constellations (Taurus, Canis Minor, etc.). It describes the Flight from Egypt (the Exodus) or the founding myth of the Israelites. It depicts Elizabeth, Lady Katherine Grey, and her relationships with the earls of Hertford and Leicester. It deals with anti-clerical feeling over injunctions by Catholic priests for harder work. It describes Catherine of Aragon or Catherine I of Russia, the wife of Peter the Great or Canton de Fidèle, a supposed governor of Calais and the game of cat, an old English bat-and-ball game. This profusion of unsupported explanations was satirized by J. R. R. Tolkien in his fictional explanations of “The Man in the Moon Stayed Up Too Late.” Most scholarly commentators consider these to be unproven and state that the verse is probably meant to be simply nonsense. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 73

  • Ancient Egyptian civilization, emerging around 3100 B.C. after the unification of Upper and Lower Egypt, thrived for over 3,000 years along the Nile River. Known for pharaohs, hieroglyphs, and monumental architecture like the pyramids. This advanced society was sustained by the Nile’s predictable floods. The history is divided into Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms.

Chapter 76

  • “not like Cleopatra”: Cleopatra may refer to Cleopatra VII Philopator who was Queen of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt and its last active ruler. Her death in 30 B.C., by the bite of an asp smuggled in a basket of figs as Plutarch tells it, is history’s most famous unsolved case of murder or suicide.

Chapter 79

  • “This third person, this dark woman”: A “dark woman” who assisted with births may refer to the following: 1) the Biblical midwife Shiphrah, one of the “Hebrew midwives” of Exodus 1:15, though some readers have taken her and Puah for Egyptians. Shiphrah, along with her colleague Puah, defied the Pharaoh’s order to kill newborn Hebrew males. 2) Biddy Mason, who was born into slavery, was a midwife and advocate for other enslaved people in 19th-century California. After gaining her freedom, she became a successful entrepreneur and philanthropist. 3) Margaret Charles Smith was an African American midwife in Alabama who delivered over 3,000 babies during a career spanning over 30 years, often in rural areas with limited healthcare access. 4) Mary Francis Hill Coley was a midwife from Georgia who delivered over 3,000 babies during her career. Her work was featured in the 1952 documentary, All My Babies. 5) Susie Carey was a third-generation midwife featured in a photograph at the National Museum of African American History and Culture. 6) Sarah Hudson Grant was a Black Southern midwife whose work is remembered today.

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • The Headless Horseman has appeared in folklore around the world since the Middle Ages.

Chapter 3

  • “Like the princess, I would let down my hair, and he should climb it as if it were a rope.” - may refer to Rapunzel like folklore and fairytales. Many scholars have interpreted "Maiden in the Tower" stories, which Rapunzel is a part of, as a metaphor for the protection of young women from premarital relationships by overzealous guardians. Scholars have drawn comparisons of the confinement of Rapunzel in her tower to that of a convent, where women's lives were highly controlled and they lived in exclusion from outsiders. Scholars have also noted the strong theme of love conquering all in the story, as the lovers are united after years of searching in all versions after Persinette and are ultimately happily reunited as a family. The "Maiden in the Tower" archetype has drawn comparisons to a possible lost matriarchal myth connected to the sacred marriage between the prince and the maiden and the rivalry between the maiden, representing life and spring, and the crone, representing death and winter.

Chapter 6

  • “her little shoes which danced and danced without her”: In “The Red Shoes” (1845) by Hans Christian Andersen a vain girl is condemned to dance even after she dies. The red shoes represent Madge’s precarious balance between appearance and reality, innocence and corruption, freedom and constraint. They are a vivid symbol of her tragic, conflicted condition as she rides the bus toward an uncertain fate. In the tale the executioner cuts off Karen’s feet, and the red shoes dance away with them, much as Jacqueline dances “on one foot.”
  • “Tell them Papa’s gone a-hunting the rabbits”: Rabbits can symbolize good luck, prosperity, and abundance. The symbol of rabbits in the chapter encompasses innocence, vulnerability, lost youth, and the pervasive presence of death that shadows life in the novel. The nursery rhyme runs, “Bye, baby Bunting, / Daddy’s gone a-hunting, / Gone to get a rabbit skin / To wrap the baby Bunting in.”
  • “leading the dance in your little glass shoes”: Cinderella’s glass slipper comes from Charles Perrault’s tale (1697), and Madge travels in “glass-heeled shoes.”
  • “this sleeping beauty who never dreamed of her”: In Perrault’s and the Grimms’ tale a kiss wakes the sleeping princess. Here the bridegroom sleeps, and Madge says later, “Your kiss will not restore her beauty.”
  • “Ding, dong, bell”: Ariel’s song for a drowned father in The Tempest: “Full fathom five thy father lies . . . Ding-dong, bell.” Madge’s father drowned. The nursery rhyme “Ding, dong, bell, / Pussy’s in the well” also ends in drowning.
  • “Everyone pays the piper”: In the tale of the Pied Piper of Hamelin, the town that would not pay the piper lost its children.
  • “Jack Frost who paints the window pane white”: The nursery rhyme runs, “Jack be nimble, Jack be quick, / Jack jump over the candlestick.” Madge’s string of Jacks, Jack Robinson, Jack Frost, little Jack Fleet, Jack White, Jack-in-the-pulpit, and later Homer’s jack-in-the-box, all circle back to Jackie.
  • “Death is an old hunter. Wait until you hear his winding horn”: In the legend of the Wild Hunt a ghostly huntsman rides through the winter sky with baying hounds, and to hear him meant death.

Chapter 7

  • “The stork knoweth her times”: “Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times” (Jeremiah 8:7). Hans Christian Andersen’s “The Storks” (1838) helped spread the story that storks bring babies, a fit verse for a doctor of births.
  • “somebody saying it looked like the phoenix”: The phoenix burns itself and rises from its own ashes.
  • “Her children played ring-around-a-rosy”: The rhyme was first printed in 1881. The story that it describes the plague is a twentieth-century invention.
  • “Little pitchers have big ears”: The proverb is in John Heywood’s collection of 1546.

Chapter 8

  • “Who killed the old horse? Who killed the sparrows?”: The nursery rhyme asks, “Who killed Cock Robin? / I, said the Sparrow.”

Chapter 10

  • Lucifer “who was the brightest and is fallen farthest” is the name of different figures in folklore associated with the planet Venus. “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” (Isaiah 14:12).
  • “live happily ever after as in an old fairy tale”: The fairy-tale ending, “and they lived happily ever after.”
  • “Her face was certainly not her fortune”: The nursery rhyme’s milkmaid answers, “My face is my fortune, sir, she said.”

Chapter 11

  • “Rimski-Korsakov who never came except in Mr. Spitzer’s absence”: Rimski-Korsakov was a prominent Russian composer, a member of the Mighty Handful, five composers who drew on Russian folk music, and a significant figure in shaping Russian classical music. He is known for his operas, orchestral pieces like Scheherazade (1888), named for the bride who tells a tale night after night to stay alive, and Capriccio Espagnol. He sailed around the world as a young naval officer.
  • “the sister ravens, the brother doves”: The Grimms’ “The Seven Ravens” and Giambattista Basile’s “The Seven Doves” (1634-36) both tell of brothers changed into birds and a sister who saves them. Young makes the ravens sisters.
  • “a wild swan absent, one wild swan more”: In Andersen’s “The Wild Swans” (1838), eleven brothers are turned into swans, and their sister weaves nettle shirts to free them. The last shirt is unfinished, and the youngest is left with a swan’s wing.

Chapter 12

  • “twelve white swans like brothers or suitors bewitched”: Andersen’s eleven brothers turned into swans, and the bewitched swan maidens of Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake (1877).
  • “headless horsemen ride about in purple fog”: Washington Irving’s “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow” (1820).
  • “her face was not, it was simply not her fortune”: The nursery rhyme’s milkmaid: “My face is my fortune, sir, she said.”

Chapter 15

  • “the grasshoppers are always surprised by winter”: Aesop’s “The Ant and the Grasshopper,” and “Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise” (Proverbs 6:6).
  • “the crooked crab which can never be taught to walk a way that is not crooked”: Aesop’s “The Crab and Its Mother,” in which the mother tells her child to walk straight and cannot do it herself.

Chapter 16

  • “riding my black pony, Falada”: In the Brothers Grimm fairy tale “The Goose Girl” (1815), a princess is sent off to marry with her magical horse Falada, who can talk, and a waiting maid. The maid forces the princess to change places with her and, once she is the bride, has the prince kill Falada so he cannot tell. The princess has the horse’s head nailed under the dark gateway, and each morning it speaks to her as she passes: “Alas, young Queen, how ill you fare! / If this your tender mother knew, / Her heart would surely break in two.” In the end the king learns the truth and the false bride is punished. Falada means “spoken” in Portuguese.

Chapter 23

Chapter 26

  • “held it against him that he did not rescue her, carry her away as Peron might have done”: Catherine is expecting a man to save her, which is the damsel in distress. This is a narrative device in which one or more men must rescue a woman who has been kidnapped or placed in other peril. The “damsel” is often portrayed as beautiful, popular, and of high social status; she is usually depicted as a princess in works with fantasy or fairy tale settings. Kinship, love, lust or a combination of those motivate the male protagonist to initiate the narrative. Critics have linked the helplessness of these women to societal views that women as a group need to be taken care of by men and treated nicely. Throughout the history of the trope, the role of the woman as the victim in need of a male savior has remained constant, but her attackers have changed to suit the tastes and collective fears of the period: “monsters, mad scientists, Nazis, hippies, bikers, aliens…” (Wikipedia)

They often symbolize the soul, death, rebirth and transformation and, to some, good luck and messengers from the spirit world. Psyche, in Greek mythology a goddess of the soul, is often depicted with butterfly wings, symbolizing her connection to the soul and transformation.

The good fairy, realizing that the princess would be frightened if alone when she awakens, uses her wand to put every living person and animal in the palace asleep, to awaken when the princess does. The early versions, Giambattista Basile’s “Sun, Moon, and Talia” (1634) and Charles Perrault’s “The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood” (1697), involve rape, cannibalism, and Sleeping Beauty giving birth to children while she is asleep (similar to noncanonical books, as in the Gnostic Hypostasis of the Archons, in which the rulers of the world rape Eve). No one wakes Catherine.

The “glowering genii” recall the Arabian Nights tale of the fisherman who uncorks a brass bottle from the sea and lets out a jinni.

Margaret Hunt, 1884). See the Sleeping Beauty in the Chapter 29 resources.

In James Hilton’s Lost Horizon (1933), Lo-Tsen leaves Shangri-La and reaches the outside world an ancient woman. Washington Irving’s Rip Van Winkle (1819) wakes after twenty years (see the Chapter 36 resources).

Margaret Hunt, 1884). Hannah’s girl is “white as the snow upon the mountains,” and “Black was my true love’s heart though white was her skin.”

Here the keys belong to the wife, who fought for those “imprisoned by their cruel husbands and lords.”

Chapter 52

  • “a thieving robin redbreast such as accompanies lone travellers”: The robin redbreast of this line is the European robin, which follows gardeners and travellers for the insects they turn up; the American robin is a larger thrush named after it. A children’s poem and a legend explain that the robin’s breast was reddened by fanning the fire to keep the infant Jesus warm in the manger. In the old ballad The Children in the Wood (1595), robins cover the two lost children with leaves when they die in the forest. Many cultures have different meanings for robins, from death to the coming of spring to messengers of the spirits.
  • It may refer to The Frog Prince; or, Iron Henry, a German fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm and published in 1812 in Grimm’s Fairy Tales. In the forest, a selfish princess accidentally drops her golden ball into a well. A frog offers to retrieve it in exchange for her friendship. She agrees but goes back on her word after getting the ball back and runs to her castle. The next day, she is eating with her father when the frog knocks on the door and requests to be let in. The king tells his daughter that she must keep her promise and she reluctantly obeys. The frog sits next to her and eats from her plate, then desires to sleep in the princess’s bed. She is disgusted at the idea of sleeping with the frog, but her father angrily chastises her for loathing someone who helped her in a time of need. She picks up the frog and places him in the corner of her bedroom, but he hops up to her bed and demands to sleep as comfortably as the princess. Furious, she throws the frog against the wall, but as he falls to the floor he has transformed into a handsome prince. He explains that he was cursed by a wicked witch and the spell could only be broken with the princess’s help. The next day, the two go to the prince’s kingdom where they will be married. In modern versions, the transformation is triggered by the princess kissing the frog (a motif that apparently first appeared in English translations). In other early versions, it was sufficient for the frog to sleep for three nights on the princess’ pillow. The frog prince also has a loyal servant named Henry who had three iron bands affixed around his heart to prevent it from breaking from sadness when his master was cursed. When the frog prince reverts to his human form, Henry’s overwhelming happiness causes the bands to break, freeing his heart from its bonds. (Wikipedia)
  • Both are in folklore and literature. The Alp is a supernatural being, often likened to a demon, vampire, or incubus. It can be a spirit summoned by a witch or an evil person or can be a human or animal that transforms into an Alp during the night. Known for shapeshifting, sometimes appearing as a cat, pig, dog, snake, or even a small white butterfly. It wears a magical hat which grants powers like invisibility. The Alp may also possess an “evil eye” that causes illness and misfortune. Primarily known for attacking sleeping victims, causing nightmares and difficulty breathing, similar to sleep paralysis. They may also drink blood or milk from their victims. Can be warded off by placing a broomstick under a pillow, iron horseshoes on the bedpost, or shoes with toes pointing towards the door. Trapping them indoors by plugging holes and keeping a light on at night are also mentioned as protective measures. A White Witch is generally considered a benevolent or sympathetic magic practitioner, focusing on healing and/or helping others. In C.S. Lewis’s “The Chronicles of Narnia,” specifically “The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe,” Jadis, the White Witch, is the main antagonist, a powerful and malevolent sorceress who usurped the throne of Narnia. She is not human but rumored to be half-Jinn and half-Giantess. Described as tall with skin “white like snow or paper or icing-sugar,” with a very red mouth. She casts a spell of eternal winter, turns her enemies to stone, and is defeated by Aslan, who stands for Christ. (Wikipedia)
  • “a lost bride who had played a game of hide-and-seek with the bridegroom”: The old romance is “The Mistletoe Bough,” a legend claimed by several English country houses and best known from Thomas Haynes Bayly’s ballad of the 1830s: on her wedding day a bride hides in an old oak chest during a game of hide-and-seek, the lid locks shut, and her skeleton in its wedding dress is found years later. Samuel Rogers told the same tale of the Italian bride Ginevra in his poem Italy (1822).

Chapter 59

  • “the barkings of red-eyed dogs accompanying dead souls to Hades”: In northern English folklore the Gabriel Hounds, or Gabble Ratchets, were a spectral pack heard yelping overhead at night, and their cry foretold a death; the sound was probably wild geese in passage.
  • “the revolving castles of the dead, the glass castles, the spiral castles”: In the Welsh poem Preiddeu Annwfn (The Spoils of Annwn, Book of Taliesin, early fourteenth century), Arthur sails with three shiploads of men to the fortresses of the otherworld, among them a Glass Fortress, and only seven come back. Caer Sidi, the otherworld fortress of another Taliesin poem, has been translated “Revolving Castle.”

Chapter 63

  • “My sisters had long ropes of hair. A man could climb them”: “Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair” (Brothers Grimm, 1812).

Chapter 68

  • “Something fell and rolled along the ground, and yet the bough broke not”: The hangman’s riddle turns the nursery rhyme “Rock-a-bye, baby,” printed in Mother Goose’s Melody (about 1765): “When the bough breaks, the cradle will fall.” Marie feared she had conceived again.
  • “The Bluebeards, he was speaking of them”: In Charles Perrault’s “Bluebeard” (1697), a wife finds the bodies of the wives before her in a locked room. Henri Landru, the “French Bluebeard,” was guillotined in 1922 for murdering ten women.
  • “the mandrakes screaming when they are pulled up by the roots”: This folklore is based on the mandrake plant which is a hallucinogenic and narcotic. It is said that it grows from the blood of a hanged man and the tuber can resemble a human form. Forensic medicine does record erection and the discharge of semen in some deaths by hanging, and the folklore of the gallows mandrake grew from it. Juliet fears “shrieks like mandrakes’ torn out of the earth” (Romeo and Juliet 4.3), and in Genesis Rachel trades for Leah’s mandrakes to bear a child (Genesis 30:14-16).

Chapter 71

  • “The Three Bears”: The Three Bears is a 19th-century British fairy tale of which three versions exist. The original version of the tale tells of a not-so-polite old woman who enters the forest home of three bachelor bears while they are away. She sits in their chairs, eats some of their porridge, sits down on one of their chairs and breaks it, and sleeps in one of their beds. When the bears return and discover her, she wakes up, jumps out of the window, and is never seen again. The second version replaced the old woman with a little girl named Goldilocks, and the third and by far best-known version replaced the original bear trio with Papa Bear, Mama Bear, and Baby Bear. What was originally a frightening oral tale became a cozy family story with only a hint of menace. (Wikipedia) Robert Southey published the first printed version in 1837.
  • “The Cow Who Jumped over the Moon”: The Cow Who Jumped over the Moon is the English nursery rhyme “Hey Diddle Diddle.” There are numerous theories about the origin of the rhyme. James Orchard Halliwell suggested that it was a corruption of ancient Greek, probably advanced as a result of a deliberate hoax. It was connected with Hathor worship. It refers to various constellations (Taurus, Canis Minor, etc.). It describes the Flight from Egypt (the Exodus) or the founding myth of the Israelites. It depicts Elizabeth, Lady Katherine Grey, and her relationships with the earls of Hertford and Leicester. It deals with anti-clerical feeling over injunctions by Catholic priests for harder work. It describes Catherine of Aragon or Catherine I of Russia, the wife of Peter the Great or Canton de Fidèle, a supposed governor of Calais and the game of cat, an old English bat-and-ball game. This profusion of unsupported explanations was satirized by J. R. R. Tolkien in his fictional explanations of “The Man in the Moon Stayed Up Too Late.” Most scholarly commentators consider these to be unproven and state that the verse is probably meant to be simply nonsense. (Wikipedia)
  • “Little Tom Thumb”: Little Tom Thumb is a character of English folklore. Tom Thumb may have been a real person born around 1519, as there is a grave purporting to be his. It is set into the floor adjacent to the font of the main chapel in Holy Trinity Church at Tattershall, Lincolnshire, UK. On the tombstone it reads that T. Thumb was 101 years old. He died in 1620 and the grave measures just sixteen inches in length. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 72

  • “Who killed cock robin?”: Who Killed Cock Robin is an English nursery rhyme. Although the earliest known record of the song is from the mid-eighteenth century, there is some evidence that it is much older. Versions of the story appear to exist in other countries, including Germany. There are a number of theories that have been advanced to explain the meaning of the rhyme. According to Celtic traditions, Lugh, the sun god who dies as the nights get longer after the summer solstice, is marked in the old Celtic pictographic calendar with a bow-and-arrow shape. Lugh was the primary god representing the red sun and was also known in Welsh as Coch Rhi Ben, which when anglicized would mean Cock Robin (coch meaning red, rhi meaning lord, ben meaning leader) This may be a reference to the belief that souls became birds after death. The sparrow who kills him with his bow and arrow may represent Brân the Blessed, the god of winter in the form of a raven. (Wikipedia) Its answer, first printed in Tommy Thumb’s Pretty Song Book (1744), is “I, said the Sparrow, / With my bow and arrow.” Esther’s last words echo it: “Ah, I knew, she saw, who killed him!”
  • “Was there a babe lost in the woods, a babe lost in the snow?”: In the ballad of the Babes in the Wood (1595), two orphaned children, abandoned by their wicked uncle, die in the forest and are covered with leaves by robins.

Chapter 73

  • “dead robin redbreast under a ten-foot snowdrift”: See “Who killed cock robin?” and the Babes in the Wood, covered with leaves by robins, in the Chapter 72 resources.

Chapter 74

  • “of the babes who were murdered in the woods”: See the Babes in the Wood in the Chapter 72 resources.
  • “The birth veil had perhaps never been lifted from her face”: A child born with the caul, the birth membrane, over the face was said to have second sight and never to drown; sailors bought cauls as charms.

Chapter 75

  • “While dangling a red geranium for bait”: A red geranium may be herb Robert (Geranium robertianum), the small wild red cranesbill, also called red robin, stinking Bob, and death-come-quickly; folk magic linked it with luck and fertility. Geranium comes from the Greek geranos, crane, for the beak-shaped seed pods, and in German the plant is Stinkender Storchschnabel, stinking stork’s-bill. Because the stork was already an established European symbol of birth, family, and new babies, people linked the stork’s-bill herb to conception and depicted it alongside storks in folk art.
  • “wearing its birth veil like a bridal veil”: See the caul in the Chapter 74 resources.
  • “Sometimes it was a mud baby”: Mud baby may refer to Tar-Baby in the second of the Uncle Remus stories published in 1881. It is about a doll made of tar and turpentine used by the villainous Brer Fox to entrap Brer Rabbit. The more that Brer Rabbit fights the Tar-Baby, the more entangled he becomes.The term tar baby has come to refer to a problem that is exacerbated by attempts to struggle with it, or by extension to a situation in which mere contact can lead to becoming inextricably involved. Although the term “tar baby” is documented as coming from a folktale of African origin, its modern meaning in America is different. Many consider tar baby to be a racial term for African Americans.
  • “some little windowpeeper”: In the Coventry legend, Peeping Tom, the tailor who looked out at Lady Godiva as she rode naked through the town, was struck blind.
  • “Was she a maypole or what”: A maypole is a tall wooden pole erected as a part of various European folk festivals, around which a maypole dance often takes place. The festivals may occur in May or Pentecost, although in some countries it is instead erected at Midsummer.

Chapter 76

  • “her pupa, her Little Tom Thumb”: Little Tom Thumb may refer to Tom Thumb, a character in English folklore. The History of Tom Thumb was published in 1621 and was the first fairy tale printed in English. Tom Thumb may have been a real person born around 1519, as there is a grave purporting to be his. The grave measures just 16 inches in length.
  • “who had not killed cock robin”: Who Killed Cock Robin is an English nursery rhyme. The earliest record of the rhyme is in Tommy Thumb’s Pretty Song Book. A number of theories have been advanced to explain the meaning of the rhyme: a mythological event, such as the death of the god Balder from Norse mythology, or the ritual sacrifice of a king figure; a parody of the death of King William II, who was killed by an arrow while hunting, and who was known as William Rufus, which means red; the fall of Robert Walpole’s government in 1742, since Robin is a diminutive form of Robert and the first printing is close to the time of the events mentioned. Some folklore readings make the rhyme a seasonal myth, with the red-breasted robin as Lugh, the Irish god of light, skill, and kingship, killed at the turn of the year by winter. In Celtic studies Lugh is often paired with Brân the Blessed, the Welsh giant-king whose name means “Raven” and who was “crowned king over this Island” (Britannica).

Chapter 77

  • “cock robin had killed cock robin”: Some folklore readings connect Who Killed Cock Robin with the mythology of Lugh, a warrior, a king, a master craftsman and a savior. The Romans identified him with Mercury, and his slaying of Balor has been compared with the death of the Norse god Baldr. In Celtic studies he is often paired with Brân the Blessed, the Welsh giant-king whose name means “Raven.” St. Mologa has been theorized to be a Christian continuation of Lugh. “Cock robin” appears seven times in Esther Longtree’s chapters. “Who killed Cock Robin?” repeatedly asked in the novel is not just about a single culprit but a symbol of the pervasive and inscrutable nature of death, loss, and guilt. It is a question without a definitive answer, reflecting the novel’s exploration of mystery, suffering, and the silent tragedies that haunt Esther and the world she inhabits.
  • “hiding his head under his wing”: “The north wind doth blow, / And we shall have snow, / And what will poor Robin do then, poor thing? / He’ll sit in a barn, / And keep himself warm, / And hide his head under his wing, poor thing.”

  • “old angel Gabriel blowing his tin horn”: Gabriel is an archangel in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Gabriel announces the births of John the Baptist and of Jesus (Luke 1:19, 26), fit company for a doctor of births. The Bible does not name the angel of the last trumpet; the spiritual “Blow Your Trumpet, Gabriel,” printed in Slave Songs of the United States (1867), gives it to Gabriel.
