Chapter 7

  • Mediator is someone who acts as an intermediary, a go-between, or a peacemaker between two or more parties, particularly between God and humanity. Jesus Christ is the ultimate mediator, reconciling humanity with God through his sacrifice and subsequent exaltation. Easton’s Bible Dictionary (1897) defines a mediator as “one who intervenes between two persons who are at variance, with a view to reconcile them,” and 1 Timothy 2:5 reads, “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” (Galatians 3:19; 1 Timothy 2:5; Hebrews 8:6, 9:15, 12:24).

Chapter 10

  • “the rites for the burial of the dead”: Funeral rites originated from Jewish and Roman customs. The Order for the Burial of the Dead in the Book of Common Prayer is the service the preacher slides into.

Chapter 10

  • “the dreadful Day of Judgment”: The Day of Judgment belongs to eschatology, the part of theology that deals with the ultimate destiny of humans. It is found in Judaism, Christianity, Islam, and Zoroastrianism. The golden thrones and “the sea shall turn to glass” come from Revelation 4:4-6: “a sea of glass like unto crystal.”

Chapter 20

  • “the digit or fingerbreadth, the tophach or handbreadth, the cubit, the fathom, the reed, the foot”: Miss MacIntosh’s lessons follow the tables of measures, weights, months, and Exodus stations printed in the back of many old Bibles.
  • “the value of the Attic drachma, the gerah, the beka, the maneh, the talent”: The coins and weights of the Greeks and Hebrews, part of humanity’s effort to impose order and meaning on life.
  • “I would learn the Jewish calendar”: The Jewish calendar is a lunisolar calendar, which means it’s based on both the moon and the sun. It has 12 months, with each month containing either 29 or 30 days. To keep it in step with the solar year, a leap month is added seven times in every 19 years, the Metonic cycle. The months are Nisan, Iyar, Sivan, Tammuz, Av, Elul, Tishrei, Heshvan, Kislev, Tevet, Shevat, and Adar. In leap years, Adar becomes Adar II and another month, Adar I, is added before it. (Wikipedia) The civil year begins on Rosh Hashanah, but Nisan is the first month of the religious year: “This month shall be unto you the beginning of months” (Exodus 12:2). “Jyar” is an old spelling of Iyar. The calendar’s structure ensures that Jewish holidays take place in the correct season. It is significant as a motif of disciplined learning, historical consciousness, and the search for order in a world otherwise marked by instability and dreamlike disorientation.

Chapter 22

  • “What cared she for Issachar, Aaron, Absalom, Togarmah?”: The significance of these names is to situate the novel’s meditation on mortality, loss, and the passing of time within a biblical and mythic framework, underscoring the themes of decay and the search for meaning in the face of inevitable death.

Chapter 29

  • “the Happy Isles, the Fortunate Isles, the Isles of the Blessed”: The list runs from the Happy Isles to Aldebaran, Venus, the Garden of the Hesperides, the third and seventh heavens, Valhalla, Nirvana, and the happy hunting grounds, and ends: “God was not God in Himself, Mr. Spitzer believed, but in these pitiful images of God.”
  • “God, it had been said, was the True Vine”: The list mixes titles of Christ from the Bible and Christian devotion (the True Vine, the Bread of Life, the Door, the Good Shepherd, the Light of the World, the Man of Sorrows, the Prince of Peace) with the Great Spirit of many Native American traditions, and Young sums it up: “God was many things to many people.”

Chapter 31

  • “draped by veils of black chiffon in memory of some earlier death”: Mirrors were covered in houses of mourning, in Victorian custom and in the Jewish shiva.

Chapter 33

  • “except that the door was closed”: The Parable of the Ten Virgins (Matthew 25:1-13). It symbolizes spiritual readiness, and those that are able to enter the wedding feast. This imagery is rooted in Jewish wedding customs, where the bridegroom’s arrival was a central event, and the bride and her attendants would go out to meet him. The bridegroom came, “and the door was shut” (Matthew 25:10). “Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh” (Matthew 25:13).

Chapter 34

  • “a seven-branched crystal candelabra”: The menorah of the Tabernacle had seven branches (Exodus 25:31-37).

Chapter 36

  • “Had she not ridden from Minsk to Pinsk”: “From Minsk to Pinsk” is a common trope in classic Jewish humor, used to evoke a long, arduous, or circular journey within the Russian Empire. It is less a single specific joke between two businessmen than a setting for numerous different stories, often featuring Jewish peddlers or paupers and other travelers. Minsk and Pinsk are cities in Belarus. (Wikipedia)
  • Seven heavens are named in the Talmud (Chagigah 12b), and in Islamic tradition Muhammad climbed through the seven heavens on the Night Journey, the Mi’raj, a word that means ladder.

Chapter 38

  • “seven deathless eternities”: “Seven deathless eternities” may recall Dante’s Divine Comedy, where the seven terraces of Purgatory purge the seven deadly sins. Seven heavens are found in Judaism and Islam, and Hindu cosmology has seven upper worlds, the lokas. The seven virtues join the four cardinal virtues of Greek philosophy to the three theological virtues of Paul (1 Corinthians 13:13).

Chapter 39

  • “wandering Jews”: Wandering Jew is a mythical, immortal man whose legend began to spread in Europe in the 13th century. Young explained her interpretation in the essay “The Artist as Wanderer” (Marguerite Young, Inviting the Muses: Stories, Essays, Reviews, Dalkey Archive Press, 1994), where to her this represents the external and internal wandering of an artist.

Chapter 40

  • “that she listened for hours to Ahaseuris, the Wandering Jew”: Ahaseuris or Ahasuerus is the name of a king, the husband of Esther, in the Book of Esther from the Bible. A German pamphlet of 1602 gave the same name to the Wandering Jew, and Young follows it.
  • “as she preferred to think of him, the Everlasting Jew”: Der ewige Jude, the Everlasting Jew, is the German name of the Wandering Jew. The Everlasting Jew is also the title of a modern collection of the writings of Rabbi Isaac Lichtenstein (1825-1908), ed. D. Thomas Lancaster (First Fruits of Zion, 2013). Lichtenstein who after an encounter with the Gospel became an outspoken disciple of Yeshua (Jesus) of Nazareth, but he remained in his post as district rabbi for several years. Despite pressure from rabbinic authorities, Jewish believers, and Christian leaders, he could not be compelled to renounce Judaism or his devotion to the Torah. He is regarded as a pioneer of the Messianic Jewish movement.

Chapter 44

  • “Judas cock”: The Judas cock may refer to the Book of the Cock/Rooster which was probably written in the 400s or 500s in Arabic or Greek and used by Ethiopian Christians who have and use the text during Holy Week activities. It describes the final three days of Jesus’s life, including a sequence where he reanimated a previously roasted rooster that He sent to spy on Judas Iscariot when he (Judas) was plotting to betray Jesus. The rooster informed Jesus and his disciples of the plan. Among other events, the Book of the Rooster describes Saul of Tarsus’ participation in the arrest, abuse and crucifixion of Jesus, the betrayal of Jesus by a female relative of Judas, a debate between Pilate and Herod about the culpability of Jesus, Mary’s grief, John the Evangelist witnessing the crucifixion of Jesus, the conversations Jesus had with the two thieves he was crucified alongside Gestas (Awsēmobyā) and Demas (Salikonilidākki) and references to other miracles that Jesus performed during his life. The rooster may be based on the Ziz of Jewish mythology, a giant bird. Like the Gospel of Judas from the second century, the Book of the Rooster attempts to explain the betrayal of Judas before the Last Supper, an act which is traditionally seen as abrupt or lacking reason (Wikipedia).

Chapter 46

  • “the mirrors were rheumed with frost”: In Jewish mourning, and in many Victorian houses, the mirrors were covered after a death.

Chapter 47

  • “some small Moses in his mollusk boat”: “And when she could not longer hide him, she took for him an ark of bulrushes… and she laid it in the flags by the river’s brink” (Exodus 2:3). Moses is an important prophet in Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Druze faith, Baha’i faith and other Abrahamic religions.

Chapter 49

  • “But why should any man weep if the heavens wept for him?”: In the Bible God grieves and Jesus weeps: “it grieved him at his heart” (Genesis 6:6); “Oh that my head were waters, and mine eyes a fountain of tears” (Jeremiah 9:1); “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). In the Book of Moses of the Latter-day Saints, “the God of heaven looked upon the residue of the people, and he wept” (Moses 7:28). The Quran says of Pharaoh’s drowned people, “And the heaven and the earth wept not for them” (44:29, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall, 1930), and the Egyptians said the Nile rose with the tears of Isis for Osiris (Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.32.18).

Chapter 51

  • “Perhaps he was twelve cloaks”: Mr. Spitzer cannot define himself; he shifts between roles and images. Twelve cloaks suggest concealment, disguise, and many layers of identity, the number perhaps recalling the twelve apostles or the twelve signs of the zodiac. The islands of flowers in the flood are beauty and fragility amid chaos, isolated havens like the pockets of meaning he makes in a world of flux. The stalled sail is stagnation, the sail breaking into flame sudden and violent change. The ram’s horn, the shofar, is a call to awakening, remembrance, and the divine, and “metamorphosed” makes him not a fixed entity but a being always changing.
  • “A flaw in the creation had permitted this creation”: In the Kabbalah of Isaac Luria (sixteenth century), the vessels that held God’s light shattered at the creation, the shevirat ha-kelim, the breaking of the vessels, so that the world was made through a break. Mr. Spitzer’s errors “had never evolved from an original sin,” Augustine’s doctrine of the sin inherited from Adam.

Chapter 53

  • This may refer to Genesis 32 that describes Jacob wrestling with a “man” throughout the night. In the Book of Hosea, this figure is explicitly called an “angel.” During the struggle, Jacob is injured, specifically having the socket of his hip put out of joint. This injury left him with a limp. Jacob is considered a foundational figure in Judaism and the patriarch from whom the nation of Israel descends. “Yea, he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him” (Hosea 12:4, KJV).

Chapter 57

  • “for the table was always set for the wanderer”: Compare the old custom of setting an extra place at the table for the unexpected guest or wanderer, kept in Poland on Christmas Eve, and the cup poured for the prophet Elijah at the Passover seder.

Chapter 61

  • “like a cabalistic language few could understand”: The Kabbalah is the Jewish mystical tradition that reads hidden meanings in the letters and numbers of Scripture; “cabalistic” came to mean secret and hard to understand.

Chapter 65

  • “the star of the dirty Jew”: “Dirty Jew” is a widely recognized and offensive antisemitic slur with historical roots in hate speech and discrimination. The term is a standard antisemitic taunt used in real-world attacks and verbal abuse against Jewish people. During the Holocaust, the yellow Star of David identification marker that Jews were forced to wear encouraged people to use slurs like “dirty Jew” and to harass them. The phrase draws on ancient anti-Jewish themes that falsely associated Jews with filth or spreading disease. Miss MacIntosh objects, “quite flatly,” that the Jews should not be singled out.
  • In Chicago the Jewish neighborhood around Maxwell Street on the Near West Side was known from the 1880s as the ghetto.

Chapter 66

  • “For otherwise, where would they go?”: At the Évian Conference of July 1938, thirty-two nations met over the Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Germany, and nearly all refused to take more. In 1939 the ship St. Louis, carrying 937 passengers, most of them Jewish refugees, was turned away by Cuba, the United States, and Canada.
  • Peter Stuyvesant, the Dutch director-general of New Amsterdam, is buried there (1672). In 1654 he tried to turn away twenty-three Jewish refugees from Brazil, and the Dutch West India Company overruled him; he also held enslaved Africans.

Chapter 70

  • “one of those European refugees who had come from a town filled with storks”: There are “Stork Villages” such as: Ruhstadt, Germany, Zywkowo, Poland, Pentowo, Poland, Cigoc, Croatia, Alsace France, and Trujillo, Spain. These villages may also refer to the nearly 1000 Jewish Holocaust survivors brought to Fort Ontario in Oswego, New York by President Roosevelt in 1944 as America’s only World War II refugee shelter, known as “guests” offering a temporary sanctuary from Nazi Europe before World War II ended. They lived behind barbed wire, couldn’t work, and had to promise to return to Europe after the war, though most eventually stayed in the US.
  • “It would admit both Jews and Negroes”: Catherine’s hotel “would admit both Jews and Negroes.” Jews and African Americans could not freely stay in hotels in the US until the passage of federal and state laws that banned discrimination in public accommodations, which was enforced with the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was a landmark piece of legislation that explicitly prohibited racial discrimination in public places, such as hotels, and this was the first time that Jewish people were also protected from discrimination in public places. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibited discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in public accommodations like hotels, restaurants, and theaters. In the pre-1964 era, many hotels openly discriminated against both African Americans and Jews, often barring them from the premises entirely or requiring them to stay in separate, inferior accommodations. This was particularly true in the South, where discriminatory practices were widespread, even after the Civil War. In 1877 the banker Joseph Seligman was turned away from the Grand Union Hotel at Saratoga Springs because he was a Jew, and resorts advertised themselves as “restricted.” From 1936 Black travelers carried Victor Hugo Green’s Negro Motorist Green Book to find where they could sleep.

Chapter 71

  • “The other doctor, Simeon”: Simeon is derived from Simeon, son of Jacob and Leah, patriarch of the Tribe of Simeon. The text of Genesis 29:33 argues that the name refers to Leah’s belief that God had heard that she was hated by Jacob, in the sense of not being as favored as Rachel. “Because the LORD hath heard that I was hated, he hath therefore given me this son also: and she called his name Simeon” (Genesis 29:33, KJV). Thousands of refugee doctors fled Nazi Europe for the United States, and many were kept from practice by state licensing rules and by antisemitism.
  • “Hitler ran him out of Germany”: Adolf Hitler was an Austrian-born German politician who was the dictator of Germany from 1933 until his death in 1945. He rose to power as the leader of the Nazi Party. During his dictatorship, he initiated World War II in Europe by invading Poland on 1 September 1939. He was closely involved in military operations throughout the war and was central to the perpetration of the Holocaust, the genocide of about six million Jews and millions of other victims. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 72

  • In his last years Luther turned on the Jews in On the Jews and Their Lies (1543), a tract the Nazis reprinted.

Chapter 73

  • “worse than the Chaldeans”: In the Bible the Chaldeans are the Babylonians of Nebuchadnezzar, who burned the Temple and carried the people of Judah into captivity (2 Kings 25). Habakkuk calls them “that bitter and hasty nation” (Habakkuk 1:6, KJV), and in Daniel they are the king’s astrologers: “the magicians, and the astrologers, and the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans” (Daniel 2:2, KJV). For a Jewish fighter, no people could be worse.
  • “the brave little Jew, hard as rock”: Jewish fighters ruled American boxing in the first half of the twentieth century: twenty-six Jewish world champions between 1910 and 1940, most of them wearing the Star of David on their trunks. Abe Attell held the featherweight title from 1906 to 1912 (he first claimed it in 1901) and was later tied to the fixing of the 1919 World Series. Benny Leonard was lightweight champion from 1917 to 1925, and Barney Ross, raised in Chicago, held titles in the 1930s.
  • Doctors sent consumptives west for the dry, high air, and Denver filled with them. National Jewish Hospital for Consumptives opened there in 1899 under the motto “None may enter who can pay, none can pay who enter” (University of Denver Libraries, “Chasing the Cure”), and the Jewish Consumptives’ Relief Society opened at Lakewood in 1904.
  • “a fighter in the Jewish family, beginning with those who had fought the angels”: “And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day” (Genesis 32:24, KJV). The man renamed him Israel, “for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed” (Genesis 32:28, KJV); Hosea says “he had power over the angel, and prevailed” (Hosea 12:4, KJV). Joe’s last bout, with God on a peak above the clouds, is Jacob’s, and he is losing it.

Chapter 74

  • “to be let alone outside the pale of law”: The Pale was the English-ruled ground around Dublin; to be beyond the pale was to be outside the law and its protection. The Pale of Settlement (1791 to 1917) was the land at the western edge of the Russian Empire where Jews were forced to live.
  • “a shroud with many, many pockets”: “Shrouds have no pockets”: what is hidden in life cannot be carried into death. An Italian proverb in English print since 1854, it is also a Yiddish saying.

Chapter 77

  • “the Song of Songs of the sterility which is the creation”: The Song of Songs is an erotic poem. It is unique within the Hebrew Bible in that it celebrates sexual love. The two are in harmony, each desiring the other and rejoicing in sexual intimacy. Jewish tradition reads it as an allegory of the relationship between God and Israel In Christianity, it is treated as an allegory celebrating the love between God and Church or Christ and his bride, the Church. The Christian church’s interpretation of the Song is evidence of God’s love for his people, both collectively and individually. Over time a moral element and the bride as Virgin Mary were added. It is unique in that these conclusions are not found in the overtly theological books of the Bible. Those books reveal an imbalance in the relationship between God and man, but Song of Songs is a theological metaphor in which the two partners are equals, bound in a committed relationship. In modern times the poem has attracted the attention of feminist biblical critics, with Phyllis Trible’s “Depatriarchalizing in Biblical Interpretation” (1973) and the Feminist Companion to the Bible series edited by Athalya Brenner and Carole Fontaine.

Chapter 79

  • “This third person, this dark woman”: A “dark woman” who assisted with births may refer to the following: 1) the Biblical midwife Shiphrah, one of the “Hebrew midwives” of Exodus 1:15, though some readers have taken her and Puah for Egyptians. Shiphrah, along with her colleague Puah, defied the Pharaoh’s order to kill newborn Hebrew males. 2) Biddy Mason, who was born into slavery, was a midwife and advocate for other enslaved people in 19th-century California. After gaining her freedom, she became a successful entrepreneur and philanthropist. 3) Margaret Charles Smith was an African American midwife in Alabama who delivered over 3,000 babies during a career spanning over 30 years, often in rural areas with limited healthcare access. 4) Mary Francis Hill Coley was a midwife from Georgia who delivered over 3,000 babies during her career. Her work was featured in the 1952 documentary, All My Babies. 5) Susie Carey was a third-generation midwife featured in a photograph at the National Museum of African American History and Culture. 6) Sarah Hudson Grant was a Black Southern midwife whose work is remembered today.

Chapter 81

  • The whole human race “turned into smoke” may also call up the crematoria of the death camps, where six million Jews were murdered.
  • The concept of a “Jewish conspiracy” is an antisemitic myth with roots in medieval Europe that became the foundation for modern political antisemitism. These conspiracy theories falsely allege that Jewish people secretly manipulate institutions, banks, the media, and governments for malevolent purposes, such as achieving world domination. It is a dangerous and debunked fiction used throughout history to justify discrimination, persecution, and violence against Jews. In the Middle Ages, hostility toward Jews was often rooted in religious prejudice and false accusations, which served as a basis for later conspiracy myths. The antisemitic myth of blood libel emerged in the 12th century with the story of William of Norwich. It falsely claimed that Jews ritually murdered Christian children to use their blood for religious rituals, particularly for Passover matzah. This accusation frequently led to violent massacres and expulsions of Jewish communities. During the Black Death in the mid-14th century, Jews were used as scapegoats and falsely accused of poisoning wells to cause the plague. This led to the destruction of hundreds of Jewish communities across Europe. Due to restrictions that prevented Jews from owning land or joining certain trades, many worked as moneylenders. This created resentment and gave rise to stereotypes of Jews as greedy and obsessed with money, which later fueled secular conspiracy theories about Jewish wealth and control. In the 19th century, antisemitic ideas evolved from religious prejudice into modern political and racial theories of antisemitism, giving rise to more elaborate conspiracy narratives. German novelist Hermann Goedsche published Biarritz, which featured a fictional scene of a secret rabbinical cabal meeting in a Jewish cemetery to discuss a plot for world domination. This work was a commercial success and was later plagiarized to create The Protocols of the Elders of Zion (circa 1903), this fabricated document is the most infamous antisemitic text. It was a forgery created by the Russian secret police to stir up antisemitism and deflect from public discontent with the Tsarist regime. The Protocols claim to be the minutes of secret meetings held by Jewish leaders outlining a plan to take over the world. Though repeatedly exposed as a hoax, it continues to circulate and influence conspiracy theories to this day. Antisemitic conspiracy myths played a central role in the rise of Nazism and the Holocaust. Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party adopted the Protocols as proof of a “Jewish world conspiracy.” They used it to justify their persecution and extermination of six million Jews. They falsely claimed that Jews were behind communism, capitalism, and Germany’s loss in World War I. The American industrialist Henry Ford distributed massive quantities of antisemitic material, including articles based on the Protocols, through his newspaper, The Dearborn Independent. He later retracted and apologized for his publications following a lawsuit, but the damage was already done. Following the Russian Revolution, an antisemitic conspiracy theory known as “Jewish Bolshevism” or Żydokomuna claimed that Jews controlled the Soviet Union and international communist movements. This false notion was promoted by anti-communist factions and heavily used by Nazi propaganda. In the modern era, antisemitic conspiracy theories have adapted to contemporary fears and platforms, continuing to spread hatred. “ZOG” theory (Zionist Occupation Government) theory, promoted by some white nationalists, claims that Jews secretly control Western governments. “Great Replacement” theory is a white nationalist conspiracy theory, which has influenced mass shootings, and claims that Jews are orchestrating a demographic “replacement” of white people through immigration. At the 2017 Charlottesville rally, participants chanted “Jews will not replace us.” The internet and social media have facilitated the widespread dissemination of antisemitic conspiracy theories, with groups like QAnon promoting versions of the myth. These online forums and platforms amplify old lies and connect them to new global events, continuing the cycle of prejudice and misinformation. Antisemitism remains part of American life. On October 27, 2018, a gunman who blamed Jews for immigration killed eleven worshipers at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh, the deadliest attack on Jews in American history; another killed a worshiper at the Chabad of Poway synagogue in California in 2019, and in 2022 a gunman held a rabbi and three congregants hostage in Colleyville, Texas. The Anti-Defamation League, which has tracked incidents since 1979, counted a record 9,354 antisemitic incidents in 2024 and 6,274 in 2025, when assaults rose to 203. That year two staff members of the Israeli embassy were shot dead outside the Capital Jewish Museum in Washington, D.C. (May 21, 2025); a firebombing in Boulder, Colorado, killed an 82-year-old woman; and an arsonist set fire to Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro’s residence on the first night of Passover. The FBI counted 1,528 anti-Jewish hate crimes in 2025, 63 percent of all religion-based hate crimes, though Jews are about two percent of the population. Like many forms of prejudice and bigotry in the United States, antisemitism is still being reckoned with. Flag: after 1964, the events from 2017 to 2025.

Chapter 5

  • The folk song "Go Tell Aunt Rhody" (also known as "The Old Gray Goose is Dead") has a rich history rooted in both European and American traditions. The melody originated as a gavotte in Jean-Jacques Rousseau's 1752 opera Le Devin du Village. An English version of the opera was produced in London in 1766, and the tune subsequently inspired various English lyrics, including "Sweet Melissa". Around 1825, the tune began appearing in U.S. hymnals, and the Aunt Rhody version, a common American folk song, has appeared in numerous song anthologies. The lyrics tell the story of a gray goose that is being saved to make a feather bed, but dies. The song's lyrics are often interpreted as expressing grief or loss, specifically the death of a loved one, but it's also been suggested that the goose's death is a matter of gain for those who need feathers for their beds. (Wikipedia) In prison slang, "grey goose" refers to the prison bus that transports inmates. "The old gray goose is dead" symbolizes the pervasive presence of death and the fragility of life in the narrative. It underscores the chapter’s mood of desolation, the cyclical nature of existence, and perhaps the inevitability of loss that haunts the characters on their journey.

Chapter 6

  • “the pale girl dancing herself to death”: In the ballet Giselle (1841) the wilis are the ghosts of brides who died before their weddings and dance men to death.
  • “They were playing taps for the World War soldiers”: General Daniel Butterfield set “Taps” in 1862, and it became the bugle call at military funerals.
  • “Jenny Lind”: The “Swedish Nightingale” toured America for P. T. Barnum in 1850-1852.
  • “Little Sir Echo! How do you do?”: The children’s song (1917) was a hit again in 1939. In myth the nymph Echo pined for Narcissus until only her voice was left.
  • “taking them all over the hill and far away”: “Over the Hills and Far Away” is an old soldiers’ song, sung in The Beggar’s Opera (1728).
  • “Death was always the bridegroom”: Death and the Maiden, the skeleton embracing the girl, was a favorite subject of Renaissance painters and of Schubert’s song (1817).
  • “The sunny side of the street”: “On the Sunny Side of the Street” (1930) was a Depression-era hit.

Chapter 7

  • “He said it was Mozart”: Mozart was a prolific and influential composer of the Classical period. Despite his short life, his rapid pace of composition and proficiency from an early age resulted in more than 800 works representing virtually every Western classical genre of his time. (Wikipedia) Mozart died at thirty-five in 1791 while writing his Requiem.
  • “the fringe is frozen on the surrey top”: “The Surrey with the Fringe on Top,” from Oklahoma! (1943).
  • “a hot time in the old town next Saturday night”: “A Hot Time in the Old Town” (1896) became the marching song of the Spanish-American War.

Chapter 8

  • “Where was Miss MacIntosh, my darling, now aloud I cried?”: The novel’s title may echo the old ballad “Oh My Darling, Clementine,” whose Clementine is lost beneath the water.

Chapter 9

  • “Pythagoras who had a golden thigh”: Pythagoras was an ancient Greek philosopher. It is believed his teachings were metempsychosis, that every soul is immortal and after death enters another body, and musica universalis where the planets move according to mathematical equations and create an inaudible symphony of music. Legend says he showed a golden thigh at Olympia as a sign of his divinity.
  • “What makes you think they are not one?”: Love and death as one is the Liebestod, the love-death of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde (1865).
  • “the Islands of the Dead”: Arnold Böcklin’s painting Isle of the Dead (1880-1886), a rocky island of cypresses with a white-draped figure arriving by boat, inspired Rachmaninoff’s tone poem (1909).

Chapter 10

  • “it was a funeral march which was played at a perfect wedding”: Chopin’s Funeral March (Piano Sonata No. 2, 1839) in place of Mendelssohn’s Wedding March (1842) or Wagner’s “Here Comes the Bride” (Lohengrin, 1850).

Chapter 11

  • “Rimski-Korsakov who never came except in Mr. Spitzer’s absence”: Rimski-Korsakov was a prominent Russian composer, a member of the Mighty Handful, five composers who drew on Russian folk music, and a significant figure in shaping Russian classical music. He is known for his operas, orchestral pieces like Scheherazade (1888), named for the bride who tells a tale night after night to stay alive, and Capriccio Espagnol. He sailed around the world as a young naval officer.

Chapter 12

  • “the reincarnation of Chopin”: Chopin wrote some sixty mazurkas, the Polish dance. The polka is Czech, and he wrote none.

Chapter 14

  • The teaching most securely identified with Pythagoras is the “transmigration of souls” or metempsychosis, which holds that every soul is immortal and, upon death, enters into a new body. He may have also devised the doctrine of musica universalis, which holds that the planets move according to mathematical equations and thus resonate to produce an inaudible symphony of music. (Wikipedia)
  • “the plural melody which was not Mr. Spitzer’s composition or choice”: His “melody moving or attended by one or more related but independent arrangements of sounds” is nearly the dictionary definition of polyphony, or counterpoint, several independent melodies sounding at once.
  • “the funeral gondola with the corrugated angel at its helm”: Venice carries its dead by black gondola to the cemetery island of San Michele. Liszt wrote “La lugubre gondola” (1882) foreseeing Wagner’s death in Venice, and Wagner’s body left by gondola in 1883.

Chapter 19

  • “the bust of Martin Luther”: Martin Luther (1483-1546) was a German professor of theology, priest, Augustinian monk, and hymn writer, and the central figure of the Reformation. (Wikipedia) His “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God” (c. 1529) is still sung in Protestant churches. Luther himself opposed the image-breakers of 1522, but the Reformation he began stripped many churches bare, as Miss MacIntosh strips her room. Miss MacIntosh quoted a line attributed to him at dawn in Chapter 18.

Chapter 24

  • “Sir Christopher Wren and Jenny Lind were to be put into the rose”: Sir Christopher Wren was a highly acclaimed English architect, astronomer, and mathematician, the builder of St Paul’s Cathedral (1675-1710). Jenny Lind, “the Swedish Nightingale,” was a Swedish opera singer of the 19th century who toured America for P. T. Barnum in 1850-52.

Chapter 25

  • “for they were as fickle as wind or water or woman”: The Duke’s aria in Verdi’s Rigoletto (1851): “La donna è mobile / qual piuma al vento” (“Woman is fickle, like a feather in the wind”).
  • “the lost chords, the silent keys, the broken strings”: Adelaide Procter’s poem “A Lost Chord” (1858), set by Arthur Sullivan as “The Lost Chord” (1877): “I struck one chord of music, / Like the sound of a great Amen.”

Chapter 26

  • “A cat had walked up and down on the piano keys, playing a little tune from the works of one of the more obscure eighteenth-century musical composers”: Domenico Scarlatti’s Sonata in G minor, K. 30, has been called “The Cat’s Fugue” since the nineteenth century, after the story that his cat walked across the keyboard.

Chapter 29

  • “Only his silent music”: There is such a thing as “silent music” that was done by several musicians as experimental. John Cage’s 4’33” (1952) is an example. Mr. Spitzer “had written only silent music, that which, for many years now, no one else had ever heard.”
  • “He swore that their chant would be almost Gregorian”: Gregorian chant is a form of monophonic, unaccompanied sacred song in Latin of the Roman Catholic Church. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 33

  • “these dream fugues, these polyphonic compositions”: A fugue is a composition in which voices enter one after another on the same theme, as in Bach’s The Art of Fugue. In psychiatry a fugue is also a flight from one’s own identity.

Chapter 35

  • “the dance of the hours”: In Greek myth the Horae, the Hours, were goddesses of the seasons and of order. Ponchielli’s ballet “Dance of the Hours,” from his opera La Gioconda (1876), shows the hours of dawn, day, evening, and night.

Chapter 36

  • “Not every lost chord could be resolved”: “Seated one day at the organ, / I was weary and ill at ease… But I struck one chord of music, / Like the sound of a great Amen” (Adelaide Anne Procter, “A Lost Chord,” 1858). Arthur Sullivan set it as “The Lost Chord” in 1877.

Chapter 38

  • “a funeral gondola black as a blackbird”: Franz Liszt wrote La lugubre gondola, “the funeral gondola,” in Venice in 1882, and the next year a gondola carried Wagner’s coffin down the Grand Canal.
  • “her grand idée fixe”: An idée fixe is an obsession. Berlioz gave the name to the melody that haunts his Symphonie fantastique (1830).
  • “Mr. Spitzer writing now his nocturne in memory of her”: The nocturne, a night piece for piano, was invented by John Field in 1812 and perfected by Chopin.

Chapter 40

  • “lutenists who had known Mozart who had not known them”: By Mozart’s day the lute had nearly fallen out of use.
  • “the errant somnambulist”: In Bellini’s opera La Sonnambula (1831), the sleepwalking Amina crosses the high, broken bridge of a mill.

Chapter 42

  • “He had sought for the elements of harmony, but this was chaos”: Aristoxenus wrote the Elements of Harmony in the fourth century BC, the oldest Greek treatise on music to survive.
  • “Here comes the bride”: The tune is the Bridal Chorus from Wagner’s Lohengrin (1850).
  • “how fickle, how irresponsible this great lady was”: Francis I, King of France, is credited with saying, “Woman is always fickle; foolish is he who trusts her.” Brantôme says Francis I scratched “Souvent femme varie, bien fol est qui s’y fie” on a window at Chambord. Victor Hugo gave the line to the king in Le roi s’amuse (1832), and Verdi turned it into “La donna è mobile” in Rigoletto (1851).
  • “What mad dance was life, and what madder dance was death”: The dance of death, the medieval Danse Macabre, in which Death leads every rank of the living, became Saint-Saëns’s tone poem Danse macabre (1874).
  • “the strength of this snow maiden”: In the Russian tale of Snegurochka, the Snow Maiden, she melts when love enters her heart (Alexander Ostrovsky’s play, 1873; Rimsky-Korsakov’s opera, 1882).

Chapter 43

  • “this pale Don Juan beneath her mask”: Don Juan is a legendary, fictional Spanish literature character. He first appeared in a 1630 play, Tirso de Molina’s The Trickster of Seville, and probably most famously in the opera Don Giovanni by Mozart. He was a libertine, womanizer, arrogant, unrepentant, and was punished for these sins. Mr. Spitzer wonders whether Hannah had always been “this pale Don Juan beneath her mask,” the great seducer hidden inside the woman who refused love.
  • “my wild swan girl”: In folklore the swan maiden sheds her feathered robe to become a woman, and whoever steals the robe can keep her. Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake (1877) gives the story its best-known form.
  • “Are those the music-makers”: “We are the music makers, / And we are the dreamers of dreams” (Arthur O’Shaughnessy, “Ode,” 1873).

Chapter 44

  • “a musician whose baton had gotten loose from him”: Goethe’s “The Sorcerer’s Apprentice” (1797) starts a magic he cannot stop. Paul Dukas set it to music (1897), and in Disney’s Fantasia (1940) Mickey Mouse dreams that he conducts the stars and the waves.
  • “Must not the lover die of love?”: See the Liebestod, the love-death of Wagner’s Tristan und Isolde, in the Chapter 9 resources.

Chapter 45

  • “There was a rift in his lute.”: “It is the little rift within the lute, / That by and by will make the music mute” (Alfred Tennyson, “Merlin and Vivien,” Idylls of the King, 1859).
  • “His music was made almost entirely of lost chords.”: See Adelaide Procter’s “The Lost Chord” in the Chapter 25 resources.

Chapter 47

  • “Death was that dark lover who drew her down”: See Death and the Maiden in the Chapter 33 resources.

Chapter 48

  • “Perhaps the greatest music was that which had no meaning”: “All art constantly aspires towards the condition of music” (Walter Pater, “The School of Giorgione,” The Renaissance, 1873), the art in which form and meaning cannot be told apart.

Chapter 49

  • “perhaps only one grace note”: A grace note is a musical ornament, a brief note that precedes and embellishes the main note in a musical passage.
  • “His was this barcarolle heard not by the singer”: A barcarolle is a Venetian gondolier’s song in a rocking rhythm, like Offenbach’s Barcarolle in The Tales of Hoffmann (1881); he “had rocked them on the waves.”
  • “What cenotaph was there for him”: Mozart was buried in 1791 in a common grave at St. Marx in Vienna whose place was soon lost; a memorial stands near the likely spot, and a monument was raised to him in Vienna’s Central Cemetery in 1891.

Chapter 50

  • “So he had written this nocturne”: The Irish composer John Field published the first nocturnes in 1812, and Chopin made the form his own. The chapter closes on this night music.

Chapter 51

  • “two pianos in the silence”: John Cage’s 4′33″ (1952), first played by the pianist David Tudor, is four minutes and thirty-three seconds in which the performer plays nothing, so that the music is the sound of the room.
  • “the squawking of a fire bird”: Igor Stravinsky’s ballet The Firebird (1910) is the tale of a magical glowing bird of Russian folklore.
  • “the most famous music critics were the deaf”: Beethoven was nearly deaf when his Ninth Symphony was first played in 1824, and he had to be turned around to see the applause.

Chapter 52

  • “that old knight Tancred”: Tancred, a hero of the First Crusade, is the knight of Torquato Tasso’s epic Jerusalem Delivered (1581). He loves the pagan warrior maiden Clorinda and, not knowing her in her armor, kills her in single combat at night, baptizing her as she dies. In Canto 13, when the crusaders need timber from an enchanted forest, Tancred strikes a tall cypress; blood flows from the cut, and Clorinda’s voice cries from inside the tree that he wounds her still. Claudio Monteverdi set the duel as Il combattimento di Tancredi e Clorinda (1624). Clorinda was never Tancred’s wife; Young makes her one.

Chapter 53

  • It may refer to the Danse Macabre, the Dance of Death, which spread in late medieval art after the Black Death: Death, often a skeleton, leads people of every rank in a dance to the grave, the great equalizer. Hans Holbein the Younger’s woodcuts (1538) are the best known, and Camille Saint-Saëns wrote the symphonic poem Danse Macabre (1874).

Chapter 54

  • It is an American song published in 1926, with music by Ray Henderson and lyrics by Mort Dixon. Gene Austin’s recording topped the charts, and Josephine Baker’s 1927 recording in Paris made it popular in Europe. During World War II the German propaganda band Charlie and His Orchestra set new words to it to demoralize Allied troops, and some segregationists later played it to harass civil rights marchers. It returned in the films The Eddie Cantor Story (1954) and Pete Kelly’s Blues (1955), and Miles Davis’s 1956 recording on ’Round About Midnight made it a jazz standard; Peggy Lee, Ringo Starr, and Paul McCartney recorded it too. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 55

  • “The other great composers had written only their ninth symphonies”: Curse of the ninth is a superstition connected with classical music. It is the belief that the ninth symphony is destined to be the composer’s last. After finishing it the composer is fated to die before finishing a tenth. Beethoven, Dvořák, and Bruckner each died with nine numbered symphonies, and Gustav Mahler, who feared the curse, left his Tenth unfinished at his death in 1911.
  • “The divine Melba sings”: The divine Melba sings may refer to Dame Nellie Melba who was an operatic soprano.
  • “Jenny Lind will sing tonight”: Jenny Lind may refer to Johanna Maria “Jenny” Lind who was a Swedish opera singer. P. T. Barnum brought her to America for a tour that opened at Castle Garden, New York, in September 1850.
  • “First American performance of Ole Bull”: Ole Bull may refer to Ole Bornemann Bull who was a Norwegian virtuoso violinist and composer. He first toured America in 1843 and in 1852 founded Oleana, a short-lived Norwegian colony in Pennsylvania.
  • “when he had found himself talking to Mozart”: “Mozart” Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a prolific and influential composer of the Classical period. Despite his short life, his rapid pace of composition and proficiency from an early age resulted in more than 800 works representing virtually every Western classical genre of his time. (Wikipedia) Born in Salzburg in 1756, he played keyboard and violin and composed by the age of five, and toured Europe as a child with his father, Leopold, and his sister, Nannerl. In Vienna from 1781 he wrote The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni, Così fan tutte, The Magic Flute, the Jupiter Symphony, and many piano concertos, and he died at 35 in 1791, leaving his Requiem unfinished. Nannerl was a celebrated keyboard prodigy whose touring career ended at 17, when she was kept at home; she later taught and performed in Salzburg. She is known to have composed works of music, though no manuscripts survive. In her later years she contributed to the biographical study of her late brother. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 56

  • “though music should describe, his brother had so often reminded him, no image”: The quarrel is real. Eduard Hanslick argued in On the Beautiful in Music (1854) that music represents no images, only “tonally moving forms,” while program music painted scenes: in Saint-Saëns’s Danse macabre (1874), Death plays his fiddle in the graveyard at midnight and the oboe crows the cock’s crow at dawn.
  • “the golden cockerel weathervane”: In Pushkin’s “The Tale of the Golden Cockerel” (1834), a golden cockerel on a spire crows to warn the tsar of danger; Rimsky-Korsakov made it an opera (1909).

Chapter 57

  • “the music of the hurdy-gurdy”: The true hurdy-gurdy is a stringed instrument sounded by a cranked wheel; in America the name went to the barrel organs of street musicians.

Chapter 58

  • “a minor composition by one of the lesser-known nineteenth-century composers”: Young names no piece; the waltz is lost, remembered only by Mr. Spitzer.
  • “embalmed in old music boxes”: The Geneva watchmaker Antoine Favre made the first comb-and-pin music movement in 1796, and Swiss cylinder music boxes carried the waltzes and opera airs of the nineteenth century into parlors everywhere.
  • “such as he might have composed for a black keyboard only”: In Chopin’s “Black Key” Étude (Opus 10, No. 5, 1830) the right hand plays only on the black keys.

Chapter 59

  • “old torch singers singing under the city arc lamps”: A torch song is a lament for a love that is not returned; to “carry a torch” is to go on loving someone who does not love back. Helen Morgan, Libby Holman, and Ruth Etting were famous torch singers of the 1920s and 1930s.
  • “the bells of the drowned cathedrals”: In Breton legend the city of Ys was drowned for its sins, and on calm mornings its cathedral rises from the sea with its bells tolling. Claude Debussy set the legend in “La cathédrale engloutie” (“The Sunken Cathedral,” Préludes, Book 1, 1910).
  • “the sign marking the beginning or the end of a repeat”: Young defines the segno, the sign in a score that marks where a repeat begins or ends; “dal segno” (D.S.) means “from the sign.”
  • “that old cue-ball musician who was writing a symphony for musical billiard balls”: Composers have long played with chance. The Musikalisches Würfelspiel, a dice game for composing waltzes, was published under Mozart’s name in 1792, and John Cage composed his Music of Changes (1951) by tossing coins according to the I Ching. Mr. Spitzer’s verdict: “And if chance, it was not music.”

Chapter 60

  • “whistle like Mozart in the silent hours”: See Mozart in the Chapter 55 resources. At fourteen Mozart heard Allegri’s Miserere in the Sistine Chapel and wrote it out from memory (1770).
  • “like an unfinished fugue running through his mind”: A “fugue” has two main meanings: a complex musical composition where a theme is repeated and interwoven by multiple voices, and a temporary mental state of amnesia and wandering, often associated with dissociative disorders. Musically, it involves a single theme being introduced by one voice and then imitated by others in a structured, imitative style. Psychologically, a dissociative fugue is a condition where an individual forgets their past and may travel, only to have no memory of the period later. Bach’s Art of Fugue breaks off in its last fugue; he died in 1750 before finishing it.
  • “many antiphonies”: “Antiphonies” are a type of responsive singing or music between two groups, creating a “call and response” effect. The term can also refer to a verse sung before and after a psalm or hymn, often used in religious services.

Chapter 61

  • “an Enrico Caruso among the frogs”: Enrico Caruso was a famous Italian operatic tenor. His records made him the first great star of the phonograph; he died in 1921.
  • “an idee fixe”: In Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique (1830), the idée fixe is the melody that stands for the beloved and returns, changed, in every movement.

Chapter 62

  • “many golden cockerels flapping their wings and crowing on singing weathervanes”: Compare Rimsky-Korsakov’s opera The Golden Cockerel (first performed 1909), whose golden bird crows warnings from its perch.
  • “he was the great conductor conducting the water music”: Handel’s Water Music was first played on a barge on the Thames in July 1717, for King George I, who had it repeated three times.
  • “his barcarolle which was his elegy”: A barcarolle is a folk song of Venetian gondoliers, which is imitated in classical music to create a gently rocking rhythm, often in 6/8 or 12/8 time. The most famous examples are Jacques Offenbach’s “Barcarolle” from the opera The Tales of Hoffmann and Frédéric Chopin’s Barcarolle, Op. 60 for solo piano.
  • “had not many great composers written their works with visual patterns none could play”: Compare eye music, written to be seen rather than heard: Baude Cordier’s chanson “Belle, bonne, sage” (c. 1400) is written in the shape of a heart, and Renaissance composers blackened their notes for words of night and death.
  • “Pavanne for a Dead Lady”: Compare Maurice Ravel’s Pavane pour une infante défunte, “Pavane for a Dead Princess” (1899).
  • “a member of the Philadelphia Symphony”: The Philadelphia Orchestra was founded in 1900 by Fritz Scheel, evolving into one of America’s most prominent symphony orchestras. Key figures in its history include conductors Leopold Stokowski and Eugene Ormandy, who shaped its sound and recorded extensively. The orchestra is known for its history of innovation, including being a leader in orchestral recordings and tours, and for forging a close relationship with composer Sergei Rachmaninoff.

Chapter 64

  • “a barber of Seville”: The Barber of Seville is considered one of the greatest masterpieces of comedy in music known as an opera buffa. Rossini’s opera (1816) is based on Beaumarchais’s play (1775).

Chapter 65

  • “Love lifted me”: The hymn “Love Lifted Me,” written by James Rowe in 1912 with music by Howard E. Smith, tells a story of salvation using the biblical account of Peter walking on water (Matthew 14) as a metaphor for being pulled from sin by Jesus’s love, with Smith composing the melody despite severe arthritis, creating a powerful testament to divine rescue and devotion.

Chapter 67

  • “I can’t give you anything but love, baby”: I Can’t Give You Anything But Love, Baby is an American song from 1928. The idea behind the song came during a stroll Fields and McHugh were taking one evening down Fifth Avenue. They saw a young couple window-shopping at Tiffany’s. McHugh and Fields understood that the couple could not afford to buy jewelry from Tiffany’s. They heard the man say, “Gee, honey, I’d like to get you a sparkler like that, but right now, I can’t give you nothin’ but love!” Within an hour McHugh and Fields came up with the song. (Wikipedia) The lyricist was Dorothy Fields, one of the first women to succeed as a Broadway and Hollywood songwriter, with Jimmy McHugh; the song was introduced in the all-Black revue Blackbirds of 1928.
  • “Sweet Mary O’Grady”: Moses sings Sweet Mary O’Grady but the famous song is called Sweet Rosie O’Grady. “Sweet Rosie O’Grady” (1896) was written by Maude Nugent, a vaudeville singer, and “down by the old mill stream where I first met you” is from Tell Taylor’s “Down by the Old Mill Stream” (1910); Moses runs the two together.
  • “There was going to be a hot time in the old town tonight”: “There’ll Be a Hot Time in the Old Town Tonight” (1896), by Theodore Metz and Joe Hayden, became the marching song of Theodore Roosevelt’s Rough Riders in 1898.

Chapter 71

  • “the Wabash country”: The Wabash runs across Indiana to the Ohio. Paul Dresser’s “On the Banks of the Wabash, Far Away” (1897) became the state song in 1913.

Chapter 72

  • “The jukebox repairman”: The jukebox, a nickel a record, filled the taverns and diners of the 1930s and 1940s.

Chapter 74

  • “she was only a silent piano with dusty keys”: In the Chapter 72 resources Esther insists, “I am a white piano.”

Chapter 76

  • “a sunken ship of leaden sails and stone hull and stone bells”: See Debussy’s Sunken Cathedral and the drowned city of Ys, whose bells ring under the sea, in the Chapter 59 resources.
  • “the lost music of the lost echo of the lost chord”: “Seated one day at the organ, / I was weary and ill at ease, / And my fingers wandered idly / Over the noisy keys” (Adelaide Anne Procter, “A Lost Chord,” 1858). Arthur Sullivan set it in 1877 as “The Lost Chord,” one of the best-selling songs of the century.

Chapter 78

  • “being a white piano in a tinkling stream”: “I am a white piano,” Esther says in the Chapter 72 resources; in the Chapter 74 resources she is “only a silent piano with dusty keys.”

Chapter 79

  • “a gramophone was playing”: The gramophone, invented by Emil Berliner in 1887, is an early, mechanical, analog sound reproduction device that plays flat, spirally-grooved discs (shellac records). It uses a stylus and horn to amplify sound mechanically, without electricity. As a precursor to the modern turntable, it revolutionized music by allowing mass production of recordings, distinguishing itself from cylinder-based phonographs.

Chapter 81

  • “struck all the silent keys”: See “I am a white piano” in the Chapter 72 resources.
  • “more beautiful than Bach, Beethoven, or Brahms”: Johann Sebastian Bach was a German composer and musician of the late Baroque period. He is known for his prolific output across a variety of instruments and forms, including the orchestral Brandenburg Concertos; solo instrumental works such as the cello suites and sonatas and partitas for solo violin; keyboard works such as the Goldberg Variations and The Well-Tempered Clavier; organ works such as the Schübler Chorales and the Toccata and Fugue in D minor; and choral works such as the St Matthew Passion and the Mass in B minor. He is known for his mastery of counterpoint, as heard in The Musical Offering and The Art of Fugue. Felix Mendelssohn precipitated the Bach Revival with a performance of the St. Matthew Passion in 1829. Ever since, Bach has been known as one of the greatest composers of classical music.

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • The Prague astronomical clock is a medieval astronomical clock located in Prague. The clock was first installed in 1410 and is the oldest astronomical clock still operating. It has the ‘Walk of the Apostles’ which shows an hourly show of figures of the Apostles.

Chapter 9

  • “Pythagoras who had a golden thigh”: Pythagoras was an ancient Greek philosopher. It is believed his teachings were metempsychosis, that every soul is immortal and after death enters another body, and musica universalis where the planets move according to mathematical equations and create an inaudible symphony of music. Legend says he showed a golden thigh at Olympia as a sign of his divinity.
  • “Charles’s Wain, the Hair of Berenice”: Charles’s Wain is the Big Dipper. Berenice’s Hair is the queen’s hair offered to the gods and set among the stars. Cassiopeia sits in her chair.

Chapter 10

  • Lucifer “who was the brightest and is fallen farthest” is the name of different figures in folklore associated with the planet Venus. “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” (Isaiah 14:12).

Chapter 11

  • “the constellation known as the Great Ram”: The Great Ram is Aries, the first sign of the zodiac, the golden ram whose fleece Jason sought.
  • “the Pleiades”: The Pleiades are the seven daughters of Atlas, set in the sky as a star cluster in Taurus. They return at the end of the chapter in Ronsard’s Pléiade.

Chapter 14

  • “the music of the spheres, the silent music”: Boethius was a Roman senator, consul, magister officiorum, polymath, historian, and philosopher of the Early Middle Ages. He sought to reconcile the teachings of Plato and Aristotle with Christian theology. He broke logic into three parts: that which defines, that which divides, and that which deduces. There are three types of arguments: those of necessity, of ready believability, and sophistry. In De Musica there are three classifications: Musica mundana, Musica humana, Musica instrumentalis. In Dante’s Divine Comedy, the spirit of Boethius is pointed out by Saint Thomas Aquinas and is mentioned further in the poem. In his book De Institutione Musica (Fundamentals of Music) his drawings appear striking and may be an inspiration for the organization of Young’s novel. Musica universalis or music of the spheres or harmony of the spheres is a Greek philosophical concept founded by Pythagoras. This metaphysical principle stated that mathematical relationships could produce ‘tones’ of energy that could produce, among other things, sounds. Pythagoras proposed that the celestial bodies all have their own unique hum based on their orbital revolution. This idea influenced many scholars until the end of the Renaissance. Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer from the 1600s wrote extensively on the subject. (Wikipedia) Later astronomy set it aside. Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution, with its Wheel of Fortune.
  • The teaching most securely identified with Pythagoras is the “transmigration of souls” or metempsychosis, which holds that every soul is immortal and, upon death, enters into a new body. He may have also devised the doctrine of musica universalis, which holds that the planets move according to mathematical equations and thus resonate to produce an inaudible symphony of music. (Wikipedia)
  • “the twelve moons shining over Jupiter”: Galileo found four of Jupiter’s moons in 1610. The twelfth was found in 1951, so twelve was the count when Young wrote.
  • “Copernicus, the author of that great celestial revolution”: Nicolaus Copernicus formulated a model of the universe that placed the Sun rather than Earth at its center. (Wikipedia) His findings triggered the Copernican Revolution. His book was De revolutionibus (1543). Freud named Copernicus, with Darwin and psychoanalysis, as one of three blows to human pride (“A Difficulty in the Path of Psycho-Analysis,” 1917).

Chapter 18

  • “Where was Aldebaran?”: Aldebaran is a giant star in the zodiac constellation Taurus.
  • “Archimedes”: Archimedes was a Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, inventor, and astronomer. (Wikipedia) In the chapter he is a representation of reason, science, and the human quest for comprehension amidst the mystical and often inscrutable realities that Vera confronts in her dreamlike journey. His figure anchors the narrative’s oscillation between the mystical and the rational, the historical and the personal. See the Chapter 15 resources.

Chapter 20

  • “haunted rays of Aurora Borealis”: The northern lights. The Latin name, “northern dawn,” joins Aurora, the Roman goddess of the dawn, and Boreas, the north wind, and is usually credited to Galileo (1619).
  • “as a belt of stars”: Orion’s Belt: “Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?” (Job 38:31).

Chapter 22

  • “The longer the orbit, the longer the planetary year”: Kepler’s third law (Harmonices Mundi, 1619) is that the square of a planet’s orbital period is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit, meaning a larger orbit leads to a longer orbital period.
  • “two stars in the Great Bear, the lines which joined them pointing nearly toward the North star”: The Pointers, Dubhe and Merak, at the bowl’s edge of the Big Dipper.

Chapter 24

  • “one who had discovered a new planet, one who believed he dwelled on Uranus”: William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781, the first planet found with a telescope.
  • “many mock suns and moons”: Sun dogs (parhelia) and moon dogs are bright spots beside the sun or moon, made by light bending through ice crystals, often on a halo.

Chapter 25

  • “he being the ambiguous twin”: Joachim and Peron Spitzer may refer to Castor and Pollux, also known as the Dioscuri, twin brothers in Greek and Roman mythology. They are depicted as demigods, associated with horses, sports, and considered patrons of travelers, especially sailors. (Wikipedia) The constellation Gemini, the twins, in the sky is named after them. When mortal Castor died, Pollux shared his immortality with him, and the brothers took turns between Hades and Olympus, one dead while the other lived.

Chapter 26

  • “the heavenly harmonies forever fixed above the floods of time, dark time, those unmoving golden spheres”: “Musica universalis,” the music of the spheres: Boethius, in De institutione musica (c. 500), divided music into musica mundana (the music of the spheres), humana, and instrumentalis. The idea goes back to Pythagoras. Mr. Spitzer imagines “the silent music which requires neither instruments nor voices.” Mr. Spitzer, a semi-retired lawyer and composer of “silent music,” is attuned to the music of the spheres, the eternal, silent harmonies beyond earthly sounds.

Chapter 27

  • “the course of the inaccurate planets”: “Planet” is from the Greek planētēs, “wanderer.”

Chapter 29

  • “the Happy Isles, the Fortunate Isles, the Isles of the Blessed”: The list runs from the Happy Isles to Aldebaran, Venus, the Garden of the Hesperides, the third and seventh heavens, Valhalla, Nirvana, and the happy hunting grounds, and ends: “God was not God in Himself, Mr. Spitzer believed, but in these pitiful images of God.”
  • “Did it come through the strings of the golden lyre of the stars”: The constellations Lyra, Sagittarius (the archer), Argo Navis, and Centaurus. The Small Magellanic Cloud is a dwarf galaxy, named for Magellan’s crew, who described it on the first voyage around the world (1519-22).
  • “the nebulous mass of golden light like hairs surrounding the nucleus of a comet”: “Comet” comes from the Greek komētēs, “long-haired,” for the glowing coma around its nucleus.
  • “butterflies as big as the wailing lapwing”: Lapwing is a ground nesting bird found in Europe.

Chapter 30

  • “He was a blind astronomer”: Galileo went blind in 1638.
  • “Arcturus, Andromeda, rainy Hyades”: Job’s “Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades” (Job 9:9), and Tennyson’s “Ulysses” (1842): “Thro’ scudding drifts the rainy Hyades / Vext the dim sea.”

Chapter 32

  • “colder than the lunar sea”: The dark plains of the moon are dry basalt. They were named seas, maria, by Giovanni Riccioli on his map of 1651.

Chapter 33

  • “Perhaps it was in the lunar Apennines”: The Apennines are a mountain chain in Italy. The lunar Apennines, the Montes Apenninus, were named by Johannes Hevelius in 1647 after the Italian range.

Chapter 34

  • “these great concentric circles and eccentric circles and half moons and elliptical paths”: Ptolemy explained the planets with circles, eccentrics, and epicycles. Kepler showed in 1609 that their orbits are ellipses.
  • “like the other side of the moon, was never turned toward this world”: The Moon keeps one face toward the Earth. Its far side was first photographed by the Soviet Luna 3 in 1959.

Chapter 35

  • “thin as the deceptive Pleiades”: The Pleiades, the Seven Sisters, also Messier 45, is an open star cluster.

Chapter 36

  • “Our star’s light did not reach out far”: In 1823 Heinrich Olbers asked why, if the stars are endless, the night sky is dark. One answer is that the universe has a finite age, and the light of the farthest stars has not yet reached us.

Chapter 37

  • “aware of the earth which, viewed from another celestial body, would seem like a dead moon”: Seen from the Moon, the Earth goes through phases, full when the Moon is new.

Chapter 38

  • “polar lights accompanied by strong sounds”: Northern peoples and Arctic travellers have long reported that the aurora crackles, hisses, and whistles, a sound scientists long doubted.

Chapter 39

  • “great torch-bearers with streaming meteoric hair”: A comet is a long-haired star, from the Greek komētēs.

Chapter 40

  • “who else had talked to so many water carriers in clouds”: The water carrier is Aquarius, the constellation of the zodiac.
  • “a rider in the great Coffin of Stars”: Coffin of Stars may refer to Delphinus and the main group of stars called Job’s Coffin.
  • “occultations as when a star crossed the moon”: An occultation is the passing of one heavenly body in front of another, as when the moon hides a star. Catherine has it the other way round.

Chapter 41

  • “wide enough to admit a longhaired star”: A comet is a long-haired star, from the Greek komētēs.

Chapter 42

  • “Arcturus, found drifting”: Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern constellation of Bootes.

Chapter 43

  • “the golden archer turning in windy heavens”: Sagittarius, the archer of the zodiac, aims his arrow at the heart of the Scorpion, the red star Antares.
  • “If the Southern Cross should be missing”: Southern Cross or Crux is a constellation of the southern sky that has four bright stars in a cross-shape (Wikipedia).
  • “the Northern Cross should be missing”: Northern Cross is an astronomical asterism in the northern hemisphere of the celestial sphere and is much larger than the Southern Cross (Wikipedia). It is part of the constellation Cygnus, the Swan.
  • “thin as Pleiades”: Pleiades, also known as The Seven Sisters or Messier 45, is an open star cluster in the night sky visible in virtually every part of the globe (Wikipedia).

Chapter 46

  • Venus is both the morning star and the evening star, called Phosphorus and Hesperus by the Greeks. Gottlob Frege used the two names, one object with two senses, in “On Sense and Reference” (1892).
  • “She was like a dead planet wandering.”: Planet comes from the Greek planētēs, wanderer, for the stars that moved among the fixed stars.
  • “I fell when stars fell from the clouds”: On the night of November 12-13, 1833, the Leonid meteor storm filled the American sky with tens of thousands of shooting stars, and it was long remembered as “the night the stars fell.”

Chapter 48

  • “Orion flying as if it were a bird”: The Pleiades flee the hunter Orion across the sky: “when the Pleiades plunge into the misty sea to escape Orion’s rude strength” (Hesiod, Works and Days 619-620, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, 1914). The Greeks heard in their name peleiades, doves, and told that they were turned into doves to escape him.
  • “much as the evening star and the morning star”: Both “stars” are the planet Venus, seen in the east before sunrise and in the west after sunset. The Greeks called the morning star Phosphorus and the evening star Hesperus; Pythagoras or Parmenides is credited with seeing that they are one (Diogenes Laertius 8.14, 9.23), and the philosopher Gottlob Frege used the pair to show that two names may name one thing (“On Sense and Reference,” 1892).
  • “island universes”: In 1755 Immanuel Kant proposed that the nebulae were whole systems of stars like the Milky Way (Universal Natural History and Theory of the Heavens). The phrase “island universe” came later, from Ormsby MacKnight Mitchel’s 1846 translation of Johann Heinrich von Mädler’s Weltinsel in The Sidereal Messenger.
  • “like the moon which turns but one side to earth”: The moon turns once on its axis in the same time it takes to circle the earth, so the same face always looks toward the earth; its far side was first photographed by the Soviet Luna 3 in 1959.

Chapter 49

  • “Ice had formed over Arcturus”: The ice covers the constellations one by one.
  • “Aurora Borealis and Aurora Australis”: Aurora Borealis and Aurora Australis are the lights visible in high northern and southern latitudes (Northern and Southern lights).
  • “whether Ursa Major or Ursa Minor”: Ursa Major and Ursa Minor are constellations in the northern sky also known as Great Bear and Little Bear. Zeus set the nymph Callisto and her son Arcas among the stars as the two bears (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2).
  • “not even watery Venus”: Under its unbroken clouds Venus was long imagined as a warm, wet world; Svante Arrhenius pictured it as swamp and jungle (The Destinies of the Stars, 1918). Mariner 2 found its surface scorching hot in December 1962.

Chapter 50

  • “One might disappear like the Water Carrier”: The chairs vanish like constellations at dawn.
  • “the blind astronomer”: Galileo, who first turned the telescope on the heavens in 1609, was blind by 1638.
  • “the Big Dipper and the Little Dipper”: See Ursa Major and Ursa Minor in the Chapter 49 resources.
  • “the great huntsman passing at the far zenith of the glassy sky”: Orion hunts with his two dogs, Canis Major and Canis Minor; see the frozen constellations in the Chapter 49 resources.

Chapter 51

  • “the hounds of Nimrod barking through clouds”: “He was a mighty hunter before the LORD” (Genesis 10:9). A nimrod is now a skillful hunter, or, in later American slang, an inept person. The huntsman of the stars is Orion; see the Chapter 49 resources.
  • “the coal packs in the Milky Way”: The Coalsack is a dark nebula in the Southern Cross, a cloud of dust that blots out the stars behind it; there are smaller dark lanes all along the Milky Way.
  • “the sky was filled with mock moons”: Mock moons, paraselenae, are bright spots on either side of the moon made by ice crystals in high clouds.

Chapter 52

  • “the water hen which was the Pleiades”: The Pleiades, or Seven Sisters, are a cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus. Many old European names picture them as a hen with her chicks: the Vikings called them Freyja’s hens, and the old Hungarian name Fiastyúk means “a hen with chicks.” (Wikipedia)
  • “between the evening star and the morning star”: The evening star (Hesperus) and the morning star (Phosphorus, the light-bringer) are both the planet Venus, seen after sunset and before dawn; the Greeks came to know that the two were one. Gottlob Frege used the pair in “On Sense and Reference” (1892) to show that two names can have different senses yet name the same thing, a question of “the constitution of reality” into which Cousin Hannah never inquired.

Chapter 54

  • “the Aurora Borealis was the Aurora Australis”: Aurora Borealis and Aurora Australis are the northern and southern lights seen around the Arctic and Antarctic sky.
  • “the Northern Cross or the Southern Cross or Charing Cross”: The Northern Cross is the cross-shaped pattern of bright stars in the constellation Cygnus, and the Southern Cross is the constellation Crux, seen from the Southern Hemisphere. Charing Cross is a junction in London named for the Eleanor cross Edward I raised there in memory of his queen; Young slips an earthly cross among the stars.
  • “At the South Pole of the moon”: “At the South Pole of the moon, there were more mountains than at the North Pole of the moon” is not entirely accurate. The Lunar south pole of the moon has more craters that are not reached by sunlight because of the tilt of the moon’s axis.

Chapter 55

  • “the long streamers of Aurora Borealis”: See the northern and southern lights in the Chapter 54 resources.

Chapter 56

  • “the Dog star which was the brightest star of the heavens”: Sirius, the Dog Star in the constellation Canis Major, is the brightest star in the night sky.
  • “The earth was moved by the moon like the tide”: The solid earth has tides too. Twice a day the ground under a person’s feet rises and falls, by up to about a foot and a half, as the moon and sun pull on it.

Chapter 59

  • “a celestial equator making the day and night everywhere of equal length”: The celestial equator is Earth’s equator projected onto the sky. When the sun crosses it at the spring and autumn equinoxes, day and night are nearly equal everywhere on Earth.
  • “He was disturbed by galaxies colliding”: In the early 1950s Walter Baade and Rudolph Minkowski identified the strong radio source Cygnus A with what they took to be two galaxies in collision. Later work found another cause for its radio noise, but colliding galaxies are real.

Chapter 60

  • “the dim clusters of the Pleiades”: The Pleiades, the Seven Sisters, are a star cluster in Taurus; “Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?” (Job 38:31, KJV).

Chapter 62

  • “brilliant as five-pointed Arcturus”: Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern constellation of Bootes. “Canst thou guide Arcturus with his sons?” (Job 38:32, KJV).
  • “like an osculating star he crossed the face of the moon”: When the moon passes in front of a star, astronomers call it an occultation; Young’s “osculating” means kissing.
  • “North, Northwest of the Great Bear”: Northwest of Ursa Major, the Great Bear, is the constellation Camelopardalis. Camelopardalis is a large, faint constellation that borders the northwestern part of the Great Bear.
  • “the constellation Orion”: Orion is a constellation visible globally and features the famous Orion’s Belt. The Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery within it, is one of the brightest in the sky. In Greek myth, Orion was a giant and mighty hunter. His death story varies, but most legends involve his death by the bow of Artemis or a scorpion’s sting, after which he was placed in the heavens.
  • “sign of the Southern Cross”: The Southern Cross is an asterism of the Crux constellation, made up of four or five bright stars that form a distinctive cross shape. It is a key navigational tool for finding the direction south and is prominently featured on the flags of several southern hemisphere countries, including Australia and New Zealand. It is one of the smallest and most easily recognized constellations in the southern night sky.
  • “Note to Aldebaran”: Aldebaran is the red eye of Taurus the bull, near the Hyades.

Chapter 63

  • “Ursa Major, Charles’ Wain, Charybdis! Scyllal”: Ursa Major is also known as the Great Bear and is a constellation in the northern sky, whose associated mythology likely dates back into prehistory.

Chapter 66

  • “had killed twin sisters who had been hiding naked in the bushes”: Compare Actaeon, who came upon Diana bathing naked, was changed into a stag, and was torn apart by his own hounds (Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 3). The “great huntsman” of the sky is Orion, whom the Greater Dog follows.
  • “Greater dog, he said, was man”: The Dog Star is a nickname for Sirius, a star in the constellation Canis Major (Greater Dog).
  • “slightly less than two moons’ breadth from Polaris”: In the mid-twentieth century Polaris stood about one degree from the celestial pole, and the full moon is half a degree wide, so the explorer is right.
  • “It was pear-shaped”: On his third voyage Columbus wrote (1498) that the world is not round but shaped like a pear. In 1958 and 1959 measurements of the orbit of the satellite Vanguard 1 showed that the earth is in fact very slightly pear-shaped.

Chapter 70

  • “an Arctic tern with a black-rimmed eye”: The Arctic tern breeds in the Arctic and winters in the Antarctic, the longest migration of any bird, so that it sees more daylight than any other creature.

Chapter 71

  • “a star rushing toward this world, bound to collide with it”: When Halley’s Comet returned in 1910, newspapers warned that the earth would pass through its poisonous tail, and swindlers sold “comet pills.”

Chapter 72

  • “outside the precincts of the Starry Girdle, the Milky Way”: The Milky Way or Milky Way Galaxy is the galaxy that includes the Solar System, with the name describing the galaxy’s appearance from Earth: a hazy band of light seen in the night sky formed from stars in other arms of the galaxy, which are so far away that they cannot be individually distinguished by the naked eye. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 73

  • “the evening star and the morning star were one star”: The evening star and the morning star are both the planet Venus, called Hesperus at dusk and Phosphorus at dawn; the Greeks credited Pythagoras or Parmenides with discovering they were one. In 1892 the philosopher Gottlob Frege made “the morning star is the evening star” his famous example of two names with one meaning.

Chapter 76

  • “or maybe he had got to Capricorn”: Capricorn is the tenth astrological sign in the zodiac originating from the constellation of Capricornus, the horned goat. The Tropic of Capricorn, the southern line of the sun’s farthest reach, takes its name from the sign.

Chapter 82

  • “Map-makers of the heavenly bodies”: In 1930 the International Astronomical Union adopted the constellation boundaries drawn by Eugène Delporte, dividing the whole sky among 88 constellations so that no star falls outside.
