Definition from research

Chapter 1

  • Tantalus in Greek mythology was famous for his punishment: to stand in a pool of water beneath a fruit tree, the fruit never within reach and the water always receding before he could drink.

Chapter 2

  • Souls from the Underworld may refer to the Greek underworld in their mythology where Hades was god of the dead and king of the underworld and the eldest son of Cronus and Rhea.

Chapter 2

  • Centaur in Greek mythology has the upper body of a human and the lower body and legs of a horse.

Chapter 2

  • Medusa (guardian, protectress) in Greek mythology is the most famous of the monster figures known as Gorgons.

Chapter 2

  • The Minotaur is a mythical creature with the head and tail of a bull and body of a man.

Chapter 2

  • Demi Dryads are Greek mythological beings that live in trees.

Chapter 3

  • Stygian refers to the River Styx of the underworld in Greek mythology.

Chapter 3

  • Psyche is a Greek story about the overcoming of obstacles to the love between Psyche and Cupid/Amor. Psyche in this context embodies the spiritual and psychological dimensions of human life, the inner reality behind outward appearances, and the continual transformation inherent in the human condition.

Chapter 3

  • In Greek and Roman mythology Charon is the ferryman of Hades who carries souls of the newly deceased across the river Styx and Acheron that divided the world of the living from the world of the dead.

Chapter 5

  • Argus Panoptes is a many-eyed giant in Greek mythology. This is known to have generated sayings like the eyes of Argus, which means to be subject to scrutiny of one’s actions to an invasive degree. (Wikipedia) The "eyes of Argus" metaphorically convey the idea of a penetrating, multifaceted vision or insight or seeing many facets or truths simultaneously, reflecting the novel's themes of layered realities and the complex perceptions of its characters.
  • “coming like all the furies”: The Furies, or Erinyes, were the Greek goddesses of vengeance who hunted down wrongdoers.

Chapter 5

  • Penelope is a character in Homer's Odyssey. The reference to Penelope highlights themes of waiting, fidelity, and steadfastness amid uncertainty and absence. Penelope, the faithful wife of Odysseus in Greek mythology, is renowned for her patience and loyalty, waiting many years for her husband’s return from the Trojan War while warding off numerous suitors. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 5

  • Charon in Greek and Roman mythology is the ferryman to Hades or the underworld. Charon symbolizes the passage through death or the threshold between life and death, reinforcing the novel's exploration of mortality, memory, and the liminal spaces of existence.

Chapter 6

  • “If you did not know Theobald, how will you know her?”: The Ship of Theseus, also known as Theseus’s Paradox, is a paradox and a common thought experiment about whether an object is the same object after having all of its original components replaced over time, typically one after the other. In Greek mythology, Theseus, the mythical king of the city of Athens, rescued the children of Athens from King Minos after slaying the minotaur and then escaped onto a ship going to Delos. Each year, the Athenians would commemorate this by taking the ship on a pilgrimage to Delos to honor Apollo. A question was raised by ancient philosophers: If no pieces of the original made up the current ship, was it still the Ship of Theseus? Furthermore, if it was no longer the same, when had it ceased existing as the original ship? In contemporary philosophy, the thought experiment has applications to the philosophical study of identity over time. Within the contemporary philosophy of mind, it has inspired a variety of proposed solutions and concepts regarding the persistence of personal identity. (Wikipedia)
  • “he who would never again wear the laurel wreath”: Victors at Apollo’s Pythian Games wore laurel, and the two-handled loving cup became the sports trophy.
  • “He was the king of heaven, but woman was the queen of hell”: Persephone, carried off by Hades, became queen of the underworld, and winter came to the earth. “Death was her first lover. Death was her first husband and her last.”
  • “She was no Venus Adonis, no handsome girl with a broken arm”: The Venus de Milo, found in 1820, has lost her arms. Adonis was the youth Venus loved.
  • “She was no Helen of Troy, no face to launch a thousand ships”: Marlowe’s Doctor Faustus asks, “Was this the face that launched a thousand ships / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?” The Greeks entered Troy hidden in the wooden horse.
  • “Little Sir Echo! How do you do?”: The children’s song (1917) was a hit again in 1939. In myth the nymph Echo pined for Narcissus until only her voice was left.
  • “My father was the North wind”: In Greek myth the North Wind is Boreas, who carried off the girl Oreithyia to be his bride.

Chapter 8

  • “How was old Charon that rowed the boat?”: Charon is the ferryman of Hades (the underworld).
  • “Greatest kings have died. A turtle falling on your head”: The story goes that the playwright Aeschylus, father of tragedy, died when an eagle dropped a tortoise on his bald head.
  • “Was old Lethe roaring, making you forget?”: Lethe means oblivion, forgetfulness, or concealment. Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in Hades, from which the dead drank to forget their lives.
  • “Hercules, what happened to Hercules?”: Hercules is a half-god in Greek and Roman mythology famous for his strength and adventures. He died through his wife, Deianira, who gave him a shirt soaked in the centaur Nessus’s poisoned blood, believing it a love charm. Burning with it, he built his own funeral pyre, a death by a wife and by fire, like old Josh’s.
  • “Cyclops, men whose heads do grow beneath their shoulders”: Othello tells of “the Anthropophagi, and men whose heads / Do grow beneath their shoulders” (Othello 1.3). The Cyclops is the one-eyed giant of the Odyssey, like one-eyed Beatrice.

Chapter 9

  • “the Islands of the Blessed”: Islands of the Blessed or the Fortunate Isles are the winterless earthly paradise of the heroes of Greek mythology.
  • “Sit not there dreaming of Triton among the minnows”: Triton is a Greek god of the sea who later evolved into a merman. He is the messenger of his father, the god Poseidon. Wordsworth, in “The World Is Too Much with Us,” would rather be a pagan and “hear old Triton blow his wreathèd horn.” Miss MacIntosh would have none of it.
  • “Proteus who changed from fish to bird before her eyes”: Proteus was an early Greek, shape-shifting sea-god. In the Odyssey Menelaus holds him fast while he turns into a lion, a serpent, a leopard, water, and a tree.
  • “Pandora’s bottomless box”: Pandora was the first woman created and her story is used to explain why there is evil in the world. In Hesiod it was a jar. Erasmus made it a box in 1508. Only Hope stayed inside, and Miss MacIntosh says, “Hope dies hard in the human breast.”

Chapter 10

  • Chaos is the void before the forming of the universe in Greek mythology.
  • “Where is Philemon?”: Philemon was a Christian of Colossae to whom Paul wrote his letter about Onesimus, a runaway slave, asking forgiveness for him. In Ovid, Philemon and Baucis are the old married couple who asked to die at the same hour and were turned into two trees, an oak and a linden.

Chapter 10

  • Gorgons are creatures in Greek mythology. Medusa and her sisters had a gaze that turned men to stone.

Chapter 11

  • “Rhadamanthus”: Rhadamanthus, son of Zeus and Europa and brother of Minos, was a king of Crete who became a judge of the dead. In Virgil’s Aeneid (Book 6), he forces the dead to confess the crimes they hid on earth, as he finds Mr. Spitzer “guilty of many forgotten crimes.” He returns in Chapter 14.
  • “the Pleiades”: The Pleiades are the seven daughters of Atlas, set in the sky as a star cluster in Taurus. They return at the end of the chapter in Ronsard’s Pléiade.
  • “the constellation known as the Great Ram”: The Great Ram is Aries, the first sign of the zodiac, the golden ram whose fleece Jason sought.

Chapter 12

  • “no Tritons dreaming around the clock, no ladies weeping over dead birds, no sporting cupids”: French mantel clocks were crowded with gilded sea gods, nymphs, and cupids. Triton, son of Poseidon, blows a conch shell.
  • “the spot on a peacock’s tail”: Juno set the hundred eyes of the slain watchman Argus in the peacock’s tail (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1).

Chapter 14

  • “the law of gravity defied and golden apples falling upward”: Newton’s falling apple, and the golden apples of the Hesperides.
  • “a horse doctor talking as if he were an argumentative centaur”: Chiron, the wise centaur, was a healer and teacher of heroes.

Chapter 16

  • “the great mother-of-pearl mollusk which might have contained the form of Venus”: Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (c. 1485) shows the goddess rising from the sea on a scallop shell.

Chapter 17

  • “some ancient Sumerian or Greek wrestler or Roman gladiator”: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, from ancient Sumer and Babylon, Gilgamesh wrestles the wild man Enkidu, who becomes his friend.

Chapter 21

  • “A man who is a pig is still a man”: Circe turns Odysseus’s men into swine, but “their minds were as before” (Odyssey 10).

Chapter 22

  • “triple-crowned griffins with gold eggs between their gilded paws”: Herodotus tells of griffins guarding gold in the far north (Histories 3.116).
  • “the Islands of the Blessed or the Islands of the Dead”: Arnold Böcklin’s painting Isle of the Dead (1880) inspired Rachmaninoff’s tone poem (1909).
  • “Who gave a sop to Cerebus?”: Cerberus is the hound of Hades. A sop to Cerberus is an idiom meaning giving something to appease. Young spells it “Cerebus.” The Sibyl throws Cerberus a honeyed, drugged cake so that Aeneas can pass (Aeneid 6).
  • “Who was Hercules?”: Hercules is famous in Roman and Greek mythology for his strength and his numerous far-ranging adventures.

Chapter 23

  • “Was Helen of Troy ever disturbed by electric lights”: Helen of Troy in Greek mythology was said to be the most beautiful woman in the world. “Was this the face that launched a thousand ships?” (Marlowe, Doctor Faustus, 1604). Young makes it “caused a thousand ships to sail.”

Chapter 25

  • “he being the ambiguous twin”: Joachim and Peron Spitzer may refer to Castor and Pollux, also known as the Dioscuri, twin brothers in Greek and Roman mythology. They are depicted as demigods, associated with horses, sports, and considered patrons of travelers, especially sailors. (Wikipedia) The constellation Gemini, the twins, in the sky is named after them. When mortal Castor died, Pollux shared his immortality with him, and the brothers took turns between Hades and Olympus, one dead while the other lived.
  • “the cold mirrors of Lethean streams”: Lethe is one of the five rivers in Hades, with the Styx, Acheron, Cocytus, and Phlegethon. When someone drinks from this river they forget everything.
  • “stealing the lanterns of the gods”: This recalls Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods for humankind (Hesiod, Theogony).

Chapter 26

  • “cats walking about like flower-faced sibyls”: The Sibyls were the prophetesses of the ancient world, among them the Cumaean Sibyl who guides Aeneas into the underworld.
  • “in order to reach the upper world, one must first travel through the lower world”: Mr. Spitzer’s belief that people need to travel through the lower world to reach the upper world mirrors The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678) and/or Dante’s writings. Purgatory has seven terraces for the seven deadly sins, and there are seven virtues. Hell has nine circles and Heaven has nine spheres: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the fixed stars, and the primum mobile. According to Dante the cosmos depends on God, who exists in the Empyrean, an immaterial heaven beyond space and time. The Empyrean is made up of God’s love and light, and is home to angels, the blessed, and the souls of the faithful. Interesting note that the woman with the Siamese cats believes she was the reincarnation of Cleopatra and Dante meets Cleopatra in the circle of Hell called Lust (“Cleopatràs lussurïosa,” Inferno 5.63). Virgil wrote “Facilis descensus Averno,” “the descent to Avernus is easy… but to retrace one’s steps and climb back to the upper air, that is the task, that is the labor” (Aeneid 6.126-129), and Heraclitus, “The way up and the way down are one and the same.”

Chapter 26 · The Pyramid and the Sphinx

  • Represent ancient legacies, riddles of existence, and the enigmatic nature of identity and memory.
  • These are Egyptian sphinxes, built in rival Boston gardens by two old women who each believed she was the reincarnation of Cleopatra.

Chapter 26 · The Upper and Lower Worlds

  • Mr. Spitzer’s lower world of “the thief who had stolen bright jewels” and “the painted street woman leering under a lamp” must be crossed to reach the upper, a journey “endless like some of those journeys taken by my mother.”

Chapter 27

  • “for the tongue-less nightingales”: Philomela, whose tongue Tereus cut out, became the nightingale (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6).
  • “the great breakers coming in with their foaming manes and tails”: Poseidon was god of the sea and of horses, and breaking waves are still called “white horses.”

Chapter 28

  • “that spindle of creative flame which is said to sleep in the eternal darkness, weaving our bodies”: Weaving plays a significant role in the mythologies of various cultures, often symbolizing creation, destiny, and even the weaving of life itself. In many stories, weaving is attributed to deities or individuals who control fate or have supernatural abilities. For example, the Greek Moirae (Fates) spin, measure, and cut the thread of human lives, and the Norse goddess Frigg is associated with weaving and seiðr magic, which involves weaving destiny. Greek mythology: Athena, Arachne, Moirae (Fates), Penelope, Philomela. Norse mythology: Frigg, The Norns. Other mythologies: Neith, Laima, Päivätär and Kuutar, Spider Woman, Arianrhod. In Plato’s Myth of Er (Republic 10), the Spindle of Necessity turns the spheres on the knees of Necessity, and her daughters, the Fates, spin each life. In the chapter the “spindle of creative flame” weaves bodies, souls, and dreams, so that identity is woven like a tapestry from many threads of experience and memory, made of many intertwined selves rather than one.
  • “no patience to wait for the caterpillar to become the butterfly”: The Greek psychē means both “soul” and “butterfly.” In Apuleius’s The Golden Ass (2nd century AD), Psyche is the soul who marries Cupid.
  • “as of the great shell of Venus”: Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (c. 1485), the goddess rising from the sea on a scallop shell.
  • “the griffins flying over the roof-tops”: The griffin, with an eagle’s head and wings and a lion’s body, guarded gold in Greek legend (Herodotus, Histories 3.116).

Chapter 29

  • “According to the Greek, the butterfly was psyche”: Butterflies feature prominently in mythology across various cultures. They often symbolize the soul, death, rebirth and transformation and, to some, good luck and messengers from the spirit world. Psyche, in Greek mythology a goddess of the soul, is often depicted with butterfly wings, symbolizing her connection to the soul and transformation.
  • “eyes like the eyes of Argus”: Argus Panoptes was a many-eyed giant in Greek mythology who watched over a heifer-nymph Io. Hera set Argus to guard Io, and after Hermes killed him she set his hundred eyes in the peacock’s tail (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1). Young makes the same link in Chapter 5: “eyes like the eyes of Argus if he had lived, full of eyes like the peacock’s burning tail.”
  • “Did it come through the strings of the golden lyre of the stars”: The constellations Lyra, Sagittarius (the archer), Argo Navis, and Centaurus. The Small Magellanic Cloud is a dwarf galaxy, named for Magellan’s crew, who described it on the first voyage around the world (1519-22).
  • “the Milky Way, the thin stream of stars streaming from the breast of Juno”: Juno was an ancient Roman goddess. In the myth, milk spilled from Juno’s (Hera’s) breast as she nursed the infant Hercules, and became the Milky Way.
  • “butterflies in Elysium”: Elysium (Elysian Fields) is the Greek religious and philosophical concept of an afterlife.
  • “Homeric butterflies which were like persons who had passed through many unknown forms of being”: Io Vanessa is the Peacock butterfly. The Aphrodite Fritillary and the Apollo (Parnassius apollo) are named for gods. Morpheus, “the fashioner,” shapes dreams in Ovid’s Metamorphoses 11. The Atlas moth is among the largest moths in the world. Papilio homerus of Jamaica is the largest swallowtail in the Americas, and Papilio antimachus is the largest butterfly in Africa.
  • “the Stygian night”: Stygian refers to the River Styx of the underworld in Greek mythology.
  • “strange as the phoenix, the perfumed bird of Arabia arising from its ashes”: Herodotus describes the phoenix that comes from Arabia every five hundred years (Histories 2.73).
  • “Io on one wing and Io on the other wing as if they knew they had two souls”: Io was one of the mortal lovers of Zeus in Greek mythology.

Chapter 30

  • “She would rather address her solicitous remarks to Eustace”: Eustace is a name of Greek origin that means fruitful or abundant in grain. It can also mean steadfast or stable. (Wikipedia) Eustace may be Saint Eustace since she mentions “golden-antlered stags.” St. Eustace converted to Christianity while out hunting after seeing a cross between the deer’s antlers and hearing the voice of God. The golden-antlered stags also recall the Ceryneian Hind with golden antlers, Heracles’ third labor.
  • “Charon’s empty boat drifting on the midnight tide”: Charon, ferryman of the dead across the Styx.
  • “Arcturus, Andromeda, rainy Hyades”: Job’s “Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades” (Job 9:9), and Tennyson’s “Ulysses” (1842): “Thro’ scudding drifts the rainy Hyades / Vext the dim sea.”
  • “or are they the eyes of a peacock”: After Argus was killed, Hera set his hundred eyes in the peacock’s tail (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1).

Chapter 32

  • “had slain minotaurs”: Theseus killed the Minotaur in the Labyrinth of Crete. Here Death, who “had overthrown great kings,” is given the hero’s deeds.
  • “the sleepy myrmidons who did my mother’s bidding”: The Myrmidons were the soldiers Achilles led to Troy in Homer’s Iliad. Ovid tells that Zeus made them from ants for King Aeacus (Metamorphoses 7). The word came to mean a follower who obeys without question.
  • “the centaurs laying great golden eggs like moons upon the grass”: It recalls Aesop’s fable “The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs.”

Chapter 33

  • “like the sobbing of the rain upon the river Styx”: The Styx is the river of the underworld, and the gods swore their oaths by it.

Chapter 34

  • “She had worn her archery veil. Many golden arrows had sought her heart”: In Ovid, Cupid’s golden arrow kindles love and his leaden arrow puts it to flight (Metamorphoses 1).
  • “furies unnameable”: The Furies, or Erinyes, pursued wrongdoers. The Greeks feared to name them and called them the Eumenides, “the Kindly Ones.”
  • “screeching harpies, half woman and half bird”: The Harpies, “snatchers,” carried off the souls of the dead, and in the Aeneid they foul the Trojans’ feast (3).

Chapter 35

  • “room for one who had crossed dark waters”: Charon ferried the souls of the dead across the river Styx into Hades, for a coin placed with the corpse. Later Hannah is one who “would have ridden to the sable shores of Hades or even farther.”
  • “the dance of the hours”: In Greek myth the Horae, the Hours, were goddesses of the seasons and of order. Ponchielli’s ballet “Dance of the Hours,” from his opera La Gioconda (1876), shows the hours of dawn, day, evening, and night.
  • “gates guarded by minotaurs and dragons and speaking birds”: The Minotaur, half man and half bull, was kept at the center of the Cretan labyrinth until Theseus killed it.
  • “thin as the deceptive Pleiades”: The Pleiades, the Seven Sisters, also Messier 45, is an open star cluster.
  • “of Stygian night which knew no time”: Stygian refers to the River Styx in the underworld of Greek mythology.

Chapter 36

  • “despotic, one-eyed ogres in darkened rooms”: The one-eyed ogre recalls Polyphemus, the Cyclops who penned Odysseus and his men in his dark cave (Homer, Odyssey 9).
  • He wears winged sandals and a winged hat as messenger of the gods.
  • “Was she king of the living or queen of the dead”: Persephone, carried off by Hades, became queen of the dead.

Chapter 37

  • “one’s father who gave birth to the dead child”: Zeus bore Athena from his head and Dionysus from his thigh.
  • “seeing that he was a stag”: Actaeon, who saw Diana bathing, was turned into a stag and torn apart by his own hounds (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3).
  • “The last conch trumpet had already blown”: Triton blew his conch to call back the waters of the flood (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1). “In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible” (1 Corinthians 15:52).

Chapter 38

  • “the seven-stringed harp”: The seven-stringed harp is the lyre, which the poet Terpander was said to have given seven strings.
  • “these irrational, mystical, four-faced doorways”: Janus, the Roman god of doorways, had two faces, and Janus Quadrifrons, the four-faced Janus, had a temple with four doors.
  • “a lost psyche drifting down the wind”: In Greek psyche means both soul and butterfly. Apuleius tells the story of Psyche and Cupid in The Golden Ass.

Chapter 39

  • “Someone had gone from France to Hades”: Hades in Greek mythology is the god of the Greek underworld.
  • “She had slain the minotaur”: Minotaur is a large, bull-headed man in Greek mythology who is trapped in a labyrinth.
  • “beginning with Icarus who flew too near the sun”: Icarus flew on wings of feathers and wax made by his father Daedalus, flew too near the sun, and fell into the sea, which is named Icarian for him (Ovid, Metamorphoses 8).
  • Champs-Élysées means Elysian Fields, the paradise of heroes in Greek myth, which is why Young sets them “after this life is over.”

Chapter 40

  • Pan in Greek mythology is the god of the wild, shepherds and flocks, rustic music and impromptus, and companion of the nymphs. He has the hindquarters, legs, and horns of a goat, in the same manner as a faun or satyr.

Chapter 41

  • “Like furies of the avenging ghost”: In Aeschylus’s Eumenides (458 BC) the ghost of Clytemnestra rouses the sleeping Furies to hunt her son Orestes. See the Furies in the Chapter 34 resources.

Chapter 42

  • “fields of mountain asphodel”: In the Odyssey, Hermes leads the souls of the dead suitors down to the meadow of asphodel, where the spirits of the dead dwell (Odyssey 24).
  • “marine angels blowing mother-of-pearl horns”: Triton blows his conch shell to call back the waters of the flood (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.333-342).
  • “Oceanus which sank”: Oceanus was a Titan son of Uranus and Gaia and the husband of his sister Tethys in Greek mythology. He is the father of the water gods and the great river that circles the world.
  • “She was that Jason who had not found the golden fleece”: Jason and the Argonauts did win the golden fleece (Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica). Hannah, who “had not found the Holy Grail or any object of her quest,” is a Jason who failed.
  • “one Vulcan of the forge”: Vulcan, Hephaestus to the Greeks, is the smith of the gods.
  • “no one so expert as he in conducting a dying soul on its last journey”: Hermes Psychopompos, the guide of souls, led the dead to the underworld, and Charon ferried them over. See the psychopomp in the Chapter 32 resources.
  • “a dim-eyed marble Aphrodite”: Aphrodite is an ancient Greek goddess associated with love, lust, beauty, pleasure, passion and procreation. Hannah keeps her among the war trophies.
  • “huntress moon with her dogs”: Artemis, Diana to the Romans, is goddess of the moon and the hunt, and her hounds tore apart Actaeon, who saw her bathing.
  • “a few Promethean sparks of life”: Promethean means bold, creative, or life-giving, like Prometheus.

Chapter 43

  • “speaking to a blacksmith who was shoeing her wild horse”: In ancient Greece Hephaestus was the god of blacksmiths and was disabled either at birth or because of his fall from Mount Olympus. Zeus hurled him from Olympus, and he fell all day until he landed on Lemnos (Iliad 1.590-594).
  • Crete is the largest and most populous of the Greek islands. It was the home of the Minoan civilization, and in Greek myth it held the labyrinth of the Minotaur.
  • “Who blows this great Triton’s shell?”: Triton is a god of the sea in Greek mythology, the son of Poseidon. He blows a conch shell to calm or raise the waves, which is why Hannah asks, “Who blows this great Triton’s shell?” See Triton’s conch in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “Bacchus and his crew of satyrs crowned by flowers”: Bacchus, the Roman name for the Greek god Dionysus, is the god of the grape-harvest, winemaking and wine, fertility and orchards (Wikipedia). Hannah asks whether it is “Bacchus and his crew of satyrs crowned by flowers.”
  • “fields of asphodel”: Asphodel may refer to the Asphodel Meadows. It is a section of the underworld in Greek mythology where ordinary souls are sent to live after death (Wikipedia). See the meadow of asphodel in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • One of the seven sisters is said to hide her face, the lost Pleiad, for shame at marrying a mortal (Ovid, Fasti 4.169-178).
  • “Does he come to my bed?”: The goat with gold eyes and a beard recalls Pan, the goat-footed god of the wild, who pursued the nymph Syrinx until she was turned into reeds (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.689-712).

Chapter 44

  • “some old Triton’s horn”: See Triton’s shell in the Chapter 43 resources.
  • “Did I not drive a phaeton through a cloud?”: Phaëton drove the chariot of his father the sun and lost control of the horses, and Zeus struck him down (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2).
  • “mysteries greater than the Sphinx”: The Sphinx of Thebes killed all who could not answer her riddle of what walks on four legs, then two, then three, until Oedipus answered, man (Sophocles, Oedipus Rex).

Chapter 45

  • “why should they ever have thought that the blind see best”: Tiresias, the blind seer of Thebes, saw what the sighted could not.
  • “Had he not lost his butterfly”: In Greek, psyche means both the soul and the butterfly.
  • Icarus flew too near the sun and fell into the sea (Ovid, Metamorphoses 8), and “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” (Isaiah 14:12).

Chapter 46

  • “like the asphodel in fields of paradise”: See the meadow of asphodel in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “the smuggler Charon’s boat”: Charon ferries the dead across the Styx for the coin placed in the mouth of the dead.
  • “The great couturier has snipped his last thread.”: Atropos, the third of the Fates, cuts the thread of life.
  • “by no winged horse’s head or harp”: The silver coins of Corinth bore Pegasus, the winged horse, and Irish coins the harp.
  • “apples of Hesperides”: The golden apples of the Hesperides, guarded by a dragon at the edge of the world, were Heracles’s eleventh labor.

Chapter 47

  • “old Tritons blowing their ivory horns”: Triton is a Greek god of the sea. See Triton’s conch in the Chapter 42 resources and the Chapter 43 resources.
  • “satyrs like fawns”: Satyr is a male nature spirit in Greek mythology.
  • “confiding centaurs”: Centaur is a creature half human and half horse in Greek mythology.
  • “the phoenix burning”: See the burning phoenix in the Chapter 43 resources.
  • “the Stygian darkness unlighted by a star”: Stygian means of the Styx, the river of the dead in the Greek underworld. See Charon in the Chapter 46 resources.
  • “Night begot perhaps only the night”: In Hesiod, Night gives birth to her opposite: “From Chaos came forth Erebus and black Night; but of Night were born Aether and Day” (Theogony 123-124, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, 1914).
  • “the kingfisher’s eerie cry”: When Ceyx drowned, Alcyone and he were turned into kingfishers, and the calm days when they nest on the sea are the halcyon days (Ovid, Metamorphoses 11). See the halcyon in the Chapter 43 resources.

Chapter 48

  • “an arrowsmith to make that arrow which should reach this heart”: Cupid carries two arrows, one tipped with gold to kindle love and one with lead to put it to flight (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1).
  • “The mother of creation was this great abyss”: “Verily at the first Chaos came to be” (Hesiod, Theogony 116, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, 1914), and “darkness was upon the face of the deep” (Genesis 1:2). See Hesiod’s Night in the Chapter 47 resources.
  • “Orion flying as if it were a bird”: The Pleiades flee the hunter Orion across the sky: “when the Pleiades plunge into the misty sea to escape Orion’s rude strength” (Hesiod, Works and Days 619-620, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, 1914). The Greeks heard in their name peleiades, doves, and told that they were turned into doves to escape him.
  • “a golden-footed honey bee buzzing inside him”: The Greeks pictured souls as bees; Porphyry wrote that the ancients called souls bees (On the Cave of the Nymphs, trans. Thomas Taylor, 1823).
  • “the ferryman who ferried the souls of the dead”: See Charon in the Chapter 46 resources.
  • “the phoenix stars”: See the burning phoenix in the Chapter 43 resources.

Chapter 49

  • The Great Ram with its long horn is the constellation Aries, the ram of the golden fleece (see the Chapter 47 resources), and the many-stringed Lyre is Lyra, the lyre Mercury (Hermes) made from a tortoise shell. A ram is also one of Mercury’s symbols.
  • “the archer with the arrow in his breast”: may refer to Eros or Cupid who both shot gold-tipped arrows to make gods and humans fall in love. The archer may also be Sagittarius among the frozen stars, or Cupid, who in Apuleius says he “wounded myself with my own weapon” when he fell in love with Psyche (The Golden Ass, book 5).
  • “whether Ursa Major or Ursa Minor”: Ursa Major and Ursa Minor are constellations in the northern sky also known as Great Bear and Little Bear. Zeus set the nymph Callisto and her son Arcas among the stars as the two bears (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2).
  • “the griffin with its wings of gold”: Griffins were said to guard the gold of the far north (Herodotus 3.116). “The smallest worm will turn being trodden on” (Henry VI, Part 3, 2.2), but this worm never turned.
  • “a Roman head”: The coin left unpaid for the staring cab-driver is the ferryman’s fare; see Charon in the Chapter 46 resources.
  • “the Pleiades flying like birds”: See Orion and the Pleiades in the Chapter 48 resources.
  • “Venus shell”: In Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (about 1485) the goddess rises from the sea standing on a scallop shell; “Was he rising from the sea, or was he sinking?”

Chapter 50

  • The constellation Lyre or Lyra is a small one in the northern sky. It is the lyre of Orpheus; see Lyra in the Chapter 49 resources.
  • “Should a demoniac butterfly appear”: A demoniac butterfly may refer to a restricted demon or grass demon butterfly found in Asia. The Greek psyche means both soul and butterfly, and the butterfly rising from the fire is the soul leaving the body.
  • “the great huntsman passing at the far zenith of the glassy sky”: Orion hunts with his two dogs, Canis Major and Canis Minor; see the frozen constellations in the Chapter 49 resources.
  • “without paying a toll”: See Charon’s fare in the Chapter 46 resources.

Chapter 51

  • “ferried by a Charon of sea shells”: Charon is the ferryman of Hades in Greek mythology; he returns later in the chapter, reaching “with his oar upon the darkening waters.” See Charon in the Chapter 46 resources.
  • Eros is a concept in ancient Greek philosophy referring to sensual or passionate love. It has been used in philosophy and psychology as an equivalent to life energy. “Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind; / And therefore is wing’d Cupid painted blind” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream 1.1).
  • “a golden arrow driven through her breast”: Artemis, the huntress, is “of the golden arrows” in Homer, and when Actaeon saw her bathing she turned him into a stag and his own hounds tore him apart (Ovid, Metamorphoses 3).
  • “It was not the arrow of Cupid”: See Cupid’s gold and lead arrows in the Chapter 48 resources.

Chapter 52

  • “had thought of satyrs and garlanded fawns”: Satyrs in Greek mythology are male nature spirits, companions of Dionysus, with the ears and tail of a horse or goat; the Roman fauns, half goat, followed the god Faunus. Both stand for unbridled desire, which may be why Mr. Spitzer feels disloyal thinking of them in the house of the suffragette.
  • “the white bull garlanded with white flowers”: Zeus took the form of a snow-white bull to carry off Europa, who hung garlands of flowers on his horns before she climbed onto his back (Ovid, Metamorphoses 2). Bulls were also led to the altar garlanded for sacrifice.
  • “like Venus sleeping in her mother-of-pearl shell”: In Sandro Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (about 1484-1486, Uffizi, Florence), the goddess, born of the sea foam, is blown ashore standing in a scallop shell.
  • “Perhaps her butterfly had sailed out of her ear”: The Greek word psyche means both soul and butterfly, and the soul was often pictured leaving the body as a butterfly.
  • “no physician even to a centaur”: Chiron, the wise centaur, was the healer and teacher of Asclepius, Achilles, and Jason. Wounded by a poisoned arrow of Heracles that would not let him die, he gave up his immortality.
  • “two pennies, one in memory of the sun”: Coins were laid on the eyes of the dead to keep the lids closed, a custom often linked to the Greek obol placed in the mouth of the dead as Charon’s fare across the Styx. Mr. Spitzer has just pictured himself as “Charon’s ferry boat.”

Chapter 53

  • “he should knock upon all doors, all ivory doors”: Through the gate of ivory, Homer and Virgil say, come false dreams, and through the gate of horn the true. See the gates of horn and ivory in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “as if she were Venus rising from the sea”: See Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus in the Chapter 52 resources.
  • “that which he carried now in his purse for old Charon”: Charon, the ferryman of the dead in Greek myth, took a coin for the crossing of the Styx. See the coins on Cousin Hannah’s eyes in the Chapter 52 resources.
  • “why were there no cypress trees in New England?”: The cypress has been the tree of mourning since antiquity. Ovid tells of the boy Cyparissus, who killed his beloved stag by accident and was changed into a cypress so that he might grieve forever (Metamorphoses 10).
  • “the hoof of Pegasus striking water in an arid place”: The hoof of Pegasus is a myth about the winged, divine horse in Greek mythology. Wherever it stepped a water spring would burst forth. The spring he struck on Mount Helicon was Hippocrene, the horse’s spring, sacred to the Muses.
  • “the stone men upholding the roofs of the houses of the dead”: Columns carved as men holding up a roof are called atlantes, after Atlas, who bears the sky; carved women are caryatids.
  • “the clouded Argonauts”: In Greek mythology, the Argonauts were a group of heroes who, led by Jason, sailed on the ship Argo to retrieve the Golden Fleece from Colchis. The myth of the Argonauts is one of the most famous tales from Greek mythology.

Chapter 54

  • “He could whistle like the calliope”: In Greek mythology, Calliope is the name of the Muse of epic poetry, known for her eloquence and beautiful voice. Calliope can also refer to a musical instrument, a steam-powered organ with whistles, often associated with circuses and riverboats.
  • “the ferry boatman when he had crossed the dark and many-branching and many-flowing Styx”: See Charon and his fare in the Chapter 52 resources.
  • “a veritable Midas with the Midas touch”: Midas was the most famous King in Greek mythology for his ability to turn everything he touched into gold.

Chapter 55

  • “The golden fleece would have turned to a grey beard”: Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis for the Golden Fleece, the fleece of the winged ram, guarded by a dragon.
  • “his tortoise harp with the gut string stretched inside its empty shell”: The baby Hermes made the first lyre from a tortoise shell strung with gut, then gave it to Apollo (Homeric Hymn to Hermes).
  • “each with its blind boy cupid”: See blind Cupid in the Chapter 52 resources.

Chapter 56

  • “two coins in his brother’s purse so that he might pay the ferry boatman”: The Greeks buried their dead with a coin, an obol, to pay Charon, who ferried souls across the river Styx to the underworld; those left unburied or unpaid wandered the near shore for a hundred years.
  • “the great phaetons”: Phaethon, son of the sun god Helios, drove his father’s chariot, lost control, and was struck down by Zeus; the light, open phaeton carriage is named for him.
  • “but who was the spinner?”: Clotho, one of the three Fates, spins the thread of each life, Lachesis measures it, and Atropos cuts it.

Chapter 57

  • In Greek myth the golden apples grew in the garden of the Hesperides, and Eris’s golden apple, inscribed “to the fairest,” began the Trojan War.

Chapter 58

  • “such as should have awakened the deaf and caused the dust to stir”: In Greek mythology, Orpheus was a Thracian bard, legendary musician and prophet. He was also a renowned poet and, according to legend, travelled with Jason and the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece, and descended into the underworld to recover his lost wife, Eurydice. His music charmed beasts, trees, and stones.
  • “only the echo of the echo fading into silence”: In Ovid’s Metamorphoses, the nymph Echo pines for Narcissus until her body wastes away and her bones turn to stone, and only her voice is left (Book 3).
  • “might have knocked upon so many ivory doors”: See the gates of horn and ivory in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “the first rosy light of star-lit dawn”: Homer’s dawn is “rosy-fingered,” the epithet that opens many mornings in the Iliad and the Odyssey.
  • “showers of imaginary sound like golden rain”: Zeus came to Danaë, locked in a bronze tower, as a shower of gold, and she bore Perseus.
  • “that glassy flute music which brought the rocks hurtling from the sky”: In Greek myth Amphion played his lyre and the stones moved by themselves into the walls of Thebes.

Chapter 59

  • “the coin for Charon”: See coins for the dead and Charon’s fare in the Chapter 52 resources.
  • “that great flute-player who had caused the roaring avalanche”: See Amphion in the Chapter 58 resources.
  • “He was afraid of becoming an echo”: See Echo in the Chapter 58 resources.
  • “the gorgons in the mirrors”: Perseus cut off the Gorgon Medusa’s head by looking only at her reflection in his polished shield, for to meet her eyes was to turn to stone (Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 4).
  • “the Sphinx faces in the streets”: The Sphinx of Thebes killed all who failed her riddle: what walks on four feet in the morning, two at noon, and three in the evening? Oedipus answered, man.
  • “hearing the kingfisher’s cries”: In Ovid, Ceyx drowns at sea and his wife Alcyone finds his body washed ashore; the gods turn both into kingfishers, and the calm “halcyon days” are the days when the sea is still for their nesting (Metamorphoses, Book 11).
  • “cuneiform, atlas”: The atlas is the first bone of the neck, named for the Titan Atlas because it holds up the globe of the skull as he holds up the heavens. The cuneiform bones of the foot are named, like cuneiform writing, for their wedge shape (Latin cuneus).

Chapter 60

  • “the dim clusters of the Pleiades”: The Pleiades, the Seven Sisters, are a star cluster in Taurus; “Canst thou bind the sweet influences of Pleiades, or loose the bands of Orion?” (Job 38:31, KJV).
  • “tortoise-shell violin”: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, the newborn god makes the first lyre from a tortoise shell, stretching strings of sheep gut across it.
  • “for he had forgotten many fugues”: Lethe is both a river in the Greek underworld and the personification of forgetfulness and oblivion. Souls who drank from the River Lethe would forget their past lives, and this concept of forgetfulness is used in a broader, metaphorical sense as well.

Chapter 61

  • “cloud cherubim riding sea-horses with their long, gilded necks”: The sea-horses of Greek myth, the hippocamps, are horses in front and fish behind; they draw Poseidon’s chariot over the waves.
  • “a multiplicity of Tritons blowing their distant spiral horns”: “Or hear old Triton blow his wreathèd horn” (William Wordsworth, “The World Is Too Much with Us,” 1807). Triton, son of Poseidon, calms or raises the sea with his conch.

Chapter 62

  • “flying naiads”: In Greek mythology, the naiads, sometimes also hydriads, are a type of female spirit, or nymph, presiding over fountains, wells, springs, streams, brooks and other bodies of fresh water.
  • “Hyperborean bees”: Hyperborean means a member of a people in Greek mythology who lived in perpetual sunshine. The Hyperboreans lived “beyond the North Wind,” Boreas.
  • “phaeton shells”: Phaëton was the son of the sun god Helios (or Phoebus) in Greek mythology. He asked to prove his parentage by driving his father’s sun chariot, but his lack of skill caused the horses to run wild, burning the earth and creating deserts. Zeus eventually struck him with a thunderbolt to stop him. Horse-drawn light, open, four-wheeled carriage popular in the 18th and 19th centuries. It was owner-driven (no outside driver’s seat) and often had a folding top. An open-style car without fixed weather protection, similar to its horse-drawn predecessor.
  • “the constellation Orion”: Orion is a constellation visible globally and features the famous Orion’s Belt. The Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery within it, is one of the brightest in the sky. In Greek myth, Orion was a giant and mighty hunter. His death story varies, but most legends involve his death by the bow of Artemis or a scorpion’s sting, after which he was placed in the heavens.
  • “maps of wandering Cocytus”: Cocytus is the river of wailing in the underworld in Greek mythology. In Dante’s Inferno it is a lake of ice holding the traitors (Cantos 32-34).
  • “crowned griffins”: “Crowned griffins” may refer to a symbol of power in heraldry and art, an emblem used for regions like Kashubia, or a creature with a crown in a specific context like a game or a piece of jewelry. The griffin itself is a mythical beast with the body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle, symbolizing majesty and strength, which is then further emphasized by the addition of a crown.
  • “a Greek drachma of the period of Theseus”: The drachma was the official currency of modern Greece from 1832 until the launch of the euro in 2001. The ancient silver drachma was struck from the sixth century BC; Theseus, a hero of legend, is older than any coin, which is Young’s joke.
  • “the echoic ivory maiden Galatea”: In Greek mythology, Galatea was the name of the following figures: 1) a Nereid who loved the shepherd Acis, and was loved by the cyclops Polyphemus. 2) the post-antiquity name given to the statue of a woman created by Pygmalion and brought to life by Aphrodite. 3) daughter of Eurytius, son of Sparton. She married a man of good family but poor, Lamprus. When she became pregnant, Lamprus wished to have a son and told her to expose the child if it turned out to be a girl. Galatea gave birth to a girl while Lamprus was away, so she, with the advice of seers and her own dreams, told Lamprus that the baby was male, and named her Leucippus. As Leucippus grew older, her true sex became harder and harder to conceal, so Galatea went to the sanctuary of Leto and prayed to the goddess to change her daughter into a man. Leto took pity on mother and daughter and made Leucippus an actual man.

Chapter 63

  • “Where are the Hyperborean lights?”: See the Hyperboreans in the Chapter 62 resources.
  • Scylla and Charybdis are sea monsters in Greek mythology. To be “between Scylla and Charybdis” therefore means to be presented with two opposite dangers, the task being to find a route that avoids both. Odysseus passes between them in the Odyssey, Book 12.

Chapter 64

  • “a pale narcissus break through rock”: Vera imagines a “pale narcissus” breaking through rock, life and beauty in the barrenness of Miss MacIntosh’s baldness.
  • “the macintosh being not those golden apples falling upward”: Golden apples belong to Greek myth: the apples of the Hesperides that Heracles fetched, the apples Atalanta stooped for, and the apple of discord Paris gave to Aphrodite.

Chapter 65

  • “she was herself the Argus-eyed”: Argus had a hundred eyes, some always awake; Hera set him to watch Io (Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 1).

Chapter 66

  • “had killed twin sisters who had been hiding naked in the bushes”: Compare Actaeon, who came upon Diana bathing naked, was changed into a stag, and was torn apart by his own hounds (Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 3). The “great huntsman” of the sky is Orion, whom the Greater Dog follows.
  • “orchards of golden apples”: See the golden apples in the Chapter 64 resources.

Chapter 68

  • “Pandora’s”: In Hesiod’s Works and Days, Pandora opens a jar and lets loose every evil on mankind, leaving only hope inside; Erasmus turned the jar into a box in 1508.

Chapter 72

  • “a poor mule, or else everlastingly pregnant”: Esther is described as a mule laboring on and on much like the myth of Sisyphus where Zeus punished him for cheating death twice by forcing him to roll an immense boulder up a hill only for it to roll down every time it neared the top, repeating this action for eternity. Through the classical influence on modern culture, tasks that are both laborious and futile are therefore described as Sisyphean.

Chapter 73

  • “old Phoebe’s statue”: Old Phoebe was a washwoman, and the Phoebe of the Bible was a servant of the church: “I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea” (Romans 16:1, KJV; the King James spells her name Phebe). The Greek word translated “servant” is diakonos, deacon, and she is the only woman so named in the Bible; Paul trusted her to carry his letter to Rome. Where modern translations of 1 Timothy 3:11 speak of women deacons, the King James Version has “Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things.” In Greek mythology Phoebe was a Titaness, grandmother of Apollo and Artemis; the name means bright.

Chapter 74

  • “Her own childhood reproached her”: This section may refer to the death of Esther’s baby when she was young and how that traumatized her even now. Rape has been used as a plot device in literature and other media. It has been criticized for using rape as a metaphor that displaces the actual, violent and traumatic act of rape. It is considered misogynistic in the way female rape victims continue to be cast as collateral damage and the assault and rape of women is used as a plot point in a narrative that is fundamentally about men. Young is making this about Esther and showing how things would be different if she were a man. Young makes many references to mythology. The struggle to escape from sexual pursuit is one of the most popular motifs of Greek mythology: Persephone, Callisto, Daphne, Europa, Io, etc. Greek mythology depicts women as vulnerable to assault, able to escape only through death, or metamorphosis like Daphne who becomes a laurel tree. The consequence of fleeing sexual violence is another type of force on the body, the loss of the human form where women who survive sexual violence become pregnant, and when gods as the rapists, produce a hero child. The Chicago detective takes Esther for a corpse, then feels her pulse, finds her heartbeat, and rapes her. Chione in Greek mythology was said to be so beautiful that she was the object of a thousand men’s desire. Hermes put Chione into a deep sleep with his wand and proceeded to rape her. Since Young has said Esther is the mother of us all and Mr. Spitzer as the father of us all, these could be archetypes for Adam and Eve and possibly Lilith. In On the Origin of the World, part of the Nag Hammadi Library, the rulers of the world rape the earthly Eve, and she bears their children. In the midrash Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, Samael, riding the serpent, seduces Eve and fathers Cain; later Kabbalah makes Lilith, Adam’s first wife, Samael’s bride. The Talmud says that in the years Adam was apart from Eve he fathered spirits, demons, and lilin (Eruvin 18b).

Chapter 76

  • “by Cupid, the blind god of love”: In classical mythology, Cupid is the god of desire, erotic love, attraction and affection. “And therefore is wing’d Cupid painted blind” (A Midsummer Night’s Dream, 1.1).

Chapter 79

  • “Cupid had never feasted in her parents’ house”: In classical mythology, Cupid is the god of desire, erotic love, attraction and affection. He is often portrayed as the son of the love goddess Venus and the god of war Mars. See Cupid in the Chapter 76 resources.

Chapter 80

  • “But if one takes the first step downward”: “Easy is the descent to Avernus,” the Sibyl tells Aeneas, but to climb back up to the air is the labor (Virgil, Aeneid 6).
  • “The thousand nipples, the Milky Way”: In Greek myth the Milky Way is milk spilled from Hera’s breast when she pulled away from the infant Heracles.

Chapter 82

  • “One drop more of nepenthe”: Nepenthe is a mythical, ancient Greek potion or drug used to induce forgetfulness of pain, sorrow, or grief. In Homer’s Odyssey (Book 4), Helen had it as a gift from Polydamna of Egypt and mixed it into the wine to ease the grief of Menelaus and his guests.
  • “as if this were the coast of Charon”: Charon ferried the dead across the river Styx into Hades, for a coin laid in the mouth.

  • “He was as mad as a March hare”: “Mad as a March hare” is an idiom meaning extremely silly, eccentric, or crazy, originating from the frenzied, unpredictable behavior of European hares during their spring breeding season (March), which includes frantic chases, high leaps, and “boxing” matches where females swat males away to discourage unwanted advances. This phrase was popularized by Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland, featuring the eccentric March Hare at the Mad Hatter’s tea party, though the behavior itself is a real, albeit misunderstood, part of hare mating rituals, not actual madness.

Chapter 2

  • Lord Byron was an English poet and leading figure in the Romantic movement of his era. He was born with a deformity of his foot which caused him to limp. Lord Byron and Percy Bysshe Shelley along with others, his wife Mary Shelley (Frankenstein) were a close circle of poets and writers.

Marsh fever, or Roman fever, was malaria, whose name comes from the Italian mal aria, “bad air.” In Henry James’s “Daisy Miller” (1878), an American girl dies of Roman fever after a night visit to the Colosseum.

  • “Sit not there dreaming of Triton among the minnows”: Triton is a Greek god of the sea who later evolved into a merman. He is the messenger of his father, the god Poseidon. Wordsworth, in “The World Is Too Much with Us,” would rather be a pagan and “hear old Triton blow his wreathèd horn.” Miss MacIntosh would have none of it.
  • “the dark Satanic mills”: William Blake’s “Jerusalem” (1804).

  • “His memory was become like an Aeolian harp”: “Aeolian harp” (also wind harp) is a musical instrument that is played by the wind. Named after Aeolus, the ancient Greek god of the wind, the traditional Aeolian harp is essentially a wooden box including a sounding board, with strings stretched lengthwise across two bridges. It is often placed in a slightly opened window where the wind can blow across the strings to produce sounds. The strings can be made of different materials (or thicknesses) and all be tuned to the same pitch, or identical strings can be tuned to different pitches. Besides being the only string instrument played solely by the wind, the Aeolian harp is also the only string instrument that plays solely harmonic frequencies. They are recognizable by the sound which is a result of this property, which has been described as eerie and ethereal. The Aeolian harp, already known in the ancient world, was first described by Athanasius Kircher (1602-1680) in his books. It became popular as a household instrument during the Romantic era, and Aeolian harps are still hand-crafted today. Some are now made in the form of monumental metal sound sculptures located on the roofs of buildings and windy hilltops. (Wikipedia) Coleridge’s “The Eolian Harp” (1795) made it the Romantic emblem of a mind played on by nature.

Definition from research

Chapter 14

  • “King and Queen, Prince and Spade”: The horses are named like playing cards, and the aces fall later in the chapter.
  • “paper-backed dream books sold by fortunetellers”: Dream books matched dreams to numbers for the policy, or numbers, game played in poor neighborhoods, as in Aunt Sally’s Policy Players’ Dream Book (1889).
  • “The playing card dropping from his sleeve each morning had nearly always been an ace”: The “ace up the sleeve” is the cardsharp’s hidden card. In most fortune-telling, the ace of spades is the death card.
  • “The club, which was trifoliate, might be transformed into the sign of the cross”: The club suit is a trefoil, and the shamrock was said to teach the Trinity.
  • “at shrouded parimutuel windows”: The parimutuel, a betting pool shared among the winners, was invented by Joseph Oller in Paris in 1867.

Chapter 18

  • “Clubs are trumps”: The cards of Chapter 14.
  • “the joker is that card which has no face but is the highest card when it is used in euchre”: The joker was added to the deck for euchre in 1860s America as the “best bower,” the highest card, just as Miss MacIntosh says.

Chapter 19

  • “the deuce of clubs, that card which signifies the test of tears”: Cartomancy reads fortunes in ordinary playing cards. Young gives the deuce of clubs its meaning herself. Clubs were trumps the night before.
  • “the Devil’s cards are marked”: The Puritans called playing cards “the Devil’s books.” The American historian of cards Mrs. John King Van Rensselaer titled her book The Devil’s Picture-Books (1890).

Chapter 20

  • “dark as the ace of spades”: The ace of spades has long been called the death card. The deuce of clubs was “the omen of death” in Chapter 19.

Chapter 28

  • “the wastrel wheels of chance, the games of loaded dice, the croupiers”: Roulette (“little wheel”), whose croupier spins it.

Chapter 29

  • “where the turf meets the surf”: The slogan of the Del Mar racetrack, opened in 1937 by Bing Crosby and Pat O’Brien. Crosby sang “Where the Turf Meets the Surf.”

Chapter 30

  • “a game of whist or loo or poker”: Whist, whose rules Edmond Hoyle published in 1742, and loo, the gambling game of Pope’s age.

Chapter 31

  • “not one horseshoe of the red and white roses… two dice cubes in a lucky throw, seven and eleven”: Floral horseshoes and dice were set on gamblers’ graves. Seven and eleven are winning throws in craps.
  • “worth a candle’s flame in the headlong wind”: From the French proverb le jeu ne vaut pas la chandelle, “the game is not worth the candle,” from card players who paid for the candles they played by.

Chapter 35 · Cards and Games

  • The metaphor of cards and poker reflects strategy, risk, and deception.
  • Cousin Hannah is a “mean game” player; Mr. Spitzer distrusts her, believing she cheats.
  • This imagery symbolizes life’s gambits and the characters’ differing approaches to fate and challenge.

Chapter 37 · Cards and Dice

  • The snow falls “black as the ace of spades.”
  • The dead dice-throwers rattle “old bones under dimmed street lamps, and their skulls were their dice cups.”
  • Hannah is “one whose last card long ago was played.”

Chapter 42

  • “was solitary as the ace of hearts”: Hearts is the suit of love. See the ace of spades under “he who had played his last spade,” below.
  • “he who had played his last spade”: The ace of spades has long been called the death card. Peron was a gambler: in Young’s first draft “Mr. Spitzer knew that he was really Peyron the gambler.”

Chapter 45

  • “the universe was something shaken out of a dice box”: Einstein wrote to Max Born on December 4, 1926, that he was convinced God “does not throw dice.” Peron the gambler believed the opposite.

Chapter 46

  • “All was not over so long as there was one card out”: See the ace of spades and the ace of hearts in the Chapter 42 resources.

Chapter 47

  • “Should the reprobate be pure as snow”: “Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18), and “If I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean; yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch” (Job 9:30-31). See the ace of spades in the Chapter 42 resources.

Chapter 48

  • “neither spade nor heart nor diamond nor club”: The four French suits date from fifteenth-century France. See the ace of spades and the ace of hearts in the Chapter 42 resources.

Chapter 49

  • “only an old night porter riding with her”: Pullman sleeping-car porters were almost all Black men, many of them formerly enslaved or the sons of the enslaved; passengers called every porter “George,” after George Pullman, and they worked long hours for low pay and tips until they organized the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters under A. Philip Randolph in 1925. “Black as the ace of spades” was a common racist simile; see the ace of spades in the Chapter 42 resources.

Chapter 51

  • “the great planetary wheel turning like a ferris wheel”: George Ferris built the first Ferris wheel for the Chicago World’s Fair of 1893. Fortune’s wheel is older: in Boethius, Fortune says, “I turn the wheel that spins. I delight to see the high come down and the low ascend” (The Consolation of Philosophy 2.2, trans. W. V. Cooper, 1902).
  • “Never should he see his brother’s face”: Mr. Spitzer can see his brother only “through all the mazed images of the dead, through all the differences.” He lives through death no more miraculously than “some crazy old gambler who had thrown his last dice,” and he tries “to go legal,” as biased as “a left-handed portrait painter in a world of right-handed portrait painters.” “His effort to go straight had made him crooked,” and his way is “finally circular.” He practices only “in the courts which were paved with the moonstones of lost cases under a firmament of lost stars,” and he prefers “the seething silence to the sound, preferring mystery to exposure, preferring a cloak to nakedness.”

Chapter 52

  • “Mr. Spitzer had trembled like a gambler”: The opening lines immediately establish a world governed by chance. Mr. Spitzer trembling “like a gambler” suggests a life where outcomes are unpredictable and determined by forces beyond individual control. This aligns with existentialist themes of the absurdity of existence and the lack of inherent meaning. The “faceless card” and “star of no known number” symbolize the limits of human knowledge. No one can fully grasp the forces shaping a life, and there will always be elements of the unknown. This resonates with the existentialist emphasis on the limits of reason. The line “Yes, there was an external world, he knew now as it departed” is crucial. It indicates a loss of faith in an objective reality. The world is not fixed but is constantly slipping away, emphasizing the subjective experience. “He gave his belief when there was no reason for his belief” highlights a rejection of rationalism. Spitzer’s faith is not based on evidence or logic but on something deeper, perhaps a Kierkegaardian “leap of faith” into the absurd. “For he reserved his credulity for the grand occasions eliciting the skepticism of others. Their skepticism was his faith” is a complex statement. It suggests that Spitzer finds meaning in what others reject. This could be interpreted as a form of contrarianism, or as a deeper understanding that truth often lies in challenging conventional wisdom.

Chapter 53

  • “People were indifferent to those things which interested Mr. Spitzer”: Young drew Peron’s world from her own reading: “I’ve read a great many books on gambling, and I’ve been interested in it since early childhood, because I knew gamblers in early childhood.” Of her research she said, “Baseball, gambling, vaudeville, burlesque jokes, all this became part, as well as Moby Dick, the Bible” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “the old shell games in which the victim had no chance”: In the shell game, or thimblerig, a pea is shuffled under three shells or thimbles and the operator palms it, so the mark can never win.
  • “what was a playing card with eight pips”: A playing card with eight pips is any of the four eights in a standard deck. Each suit (hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades) contains an 8 card with eight corresponding suit symbols (pips) on the face.
  • “what was an act of trumping”: Trump comes from triumph, the name of an old card game, which is why the musician first thinks of an angel blowing a trumpet.
  • “who was the jack of discs, who was the jack of cups”: The Latin suits of Italian and Spanish cards and of the tarot are cups, coins, swords, and batons; in tarot the coins are often drawn as discs or pentacles. A jack of cups is the knave of that suit.
  • “the bird cage, of course, has something to do with gambling”: “birdcage” typically refers to Chuck-a-Luck, a dice game played with a distinctive hourglass-shaped cage containing three dice. The game is also known as “birdcage” or “sweat rag.” Players bet on the outcome of the dice roll after the dealer flips the cage and the dice come to rest.
  • “acorns, hearts, bells, and leaves”: are associated with German-suited playing cards, a traditional card system used in Central Europe. These suits predate the more internationally recognized French suits (hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades). German-suited cards typically feature 32 or 36 cards with these four suits. The acorns suit is one of the oldest. Leaves is another of the original suits. Hearts are the same in both the German and French systems. Bells are a distinctive German suit. German suits are believed to have influenced the development of the French suits. For example, the French “clubs” are thought to be derived from the German “acorns.” German-suited cards are still used in many parts of Central Europe.

Chapter 54

  • “a famous sportsman had been laid away”: Young told Studs Terkel that she “had such fun with the gambling part of the book, especially the gambler’s funeral, because Mr. Spitzer provided a marvelous funeral for his brother.” Terkel was reminded of Jack Teagarden singing “Gambler’s Blues,” a version of “St. James Infirmary” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 55

  • “a dead cue-ball artist”: See the billiards legend of Louis Fox in the Chapter 53 resources.
  • “twirled the bare-ribbed bird-cages”: In chuck-a-luck, also called birdcage, three dice tumble in an hourglass-shaped wire cage, and players bet on the numbers that come up.
  • “an old croupier, perhaps at the wrong wheel”: A croupier is the person in charge of a gaming table, gathering in and paying out money or tokens.
  • “could not and never had been able to distinguish between two spots and three spots”: The spots are the pips on dice and playing cards.
  • “In every gambler’s make-up”: Gambling or betting or gaming is the wagering of something of value on an event with an uncertain outcome with the intent of winning something else of value. Gambling dates back to the Paleolithic period, before written history. Financial Investments are generally not considered gambling when they meet certain criteria. Studies show that though many people participate in gambling as a form of recreation or to earn an income, gambling, like any behavior involving variation in brain chemistry, can become a behavioral addiction. Behavioral addiction can occur with all the negative consequences in a person’s life minus the physical issues faced by people who compulsively engage in drug and alcohol abuse. Problem gambling has multiple symptoms. Gamblers often gamble to try to win back money they have lost, and some gamble to relieve feelings of helplessness and anxiety. Gamblers may exhibit a number of cognitive and motivational biases that distort the perceived odds of events and that influence their preferences for gambles. Addiction by Design by Natasha Dow Schull shows how the manipulation of gambling pulls players into a trancelike state in which daily worries, social demands, and even bodily awareness fade away. Once in the zone, gambling addicts play not to win but simply to keep playing, for as long as possible, even at the cost of physical and economic exhaustion. Gamblers seek to lose themselves while the gambling industry seeks profit. Schull describes how the industry designs systems to profit from the maximum amount from gamblers and manipulates human psychology. Flag: after 1964, Natasha Dow Schüll’s Addiction by Design (2012).
  • “playing the bones”: Dice were first made of bone, so gamblers still call them bones; to play or roll the bones is to shoot dice.
  • “crazy as the old bank-teller or parimutuel man”: Parimutuel is a betting system in which all bets of a particular type are placed together in a pool; taxes and the house-take, or vigorish, are deducted, and payoff odds are calculated by sharing the pool among all winning bets. In some countries it is known as the tote after the totalisator, which calculates and displays bets already made. The parimutuel system is used in gambling on horse racing, greyhound racing, jai alai, and other sporting events of relatively short duration in which participants finish in a ranked order. A modified parimutuel system is also used in some lottery games. Parimutuel betting differs from fixed-odds betting in that the final payout is not determined until the pool is closed, in fixed-odds betting, the payout is agreed at the time the bet is made. Parimutuel gambling is frequently state-regulated, and it is offered in many places where gambling is otherwise illegal. Parimutuel gambling is often also offered at off-track facilities, where players may bet on the events without actually being present to observe them in person. (Wikipedia) The Paris entrepreneur Joseph Oller invented it in 1867.

Chapter 56

  • “both with only sevens and elevens”: In craps, a seven or eleven on the first roll is an automatic win, a “natural.” Peron is buried with dice that cannot lose.
  • “He had paid an old billiard hall artist to come and take one last shot”: See the billiards legend of Louis Fox in the Chapter 53 resources.

Chapter 57

  • “to bet with a penny which had heads upon both sides”: The two-headed coin is the oldest of gamblers’ tricks: whoever calls heads cannot lose.

Chapter 58

  • “the rattle of dice in an ivory box”: See playing the bones in the Chapter 55 resources.

Chapter 59

  • “played the starter music at the shining glow-worm tracks”: At American racetracks a bugler sounds the “Call to the Post” to bring the horses onto the track.
  • “the records of euchre”: Euchre is a trick-taking card game commonly played in English speaking countries. The joker was added to the American deck around the 1860s as the top trump in euchre, the “best bower.”

Chapter 60

  • “the ace of clubs falling like a swallow from his sleeve”: A card sharp hides an ace up his sleeve, the source of the phrase for a secret advantage.
  • Compare Paul Cézanne’s Card Players (1890s) and Pablo Picasso’s Card Player (winter 1913-14, Museum of Modern Art), in which the player and his cards break into flat, overlapping planes.

Chapter 61

  • The Dodgers were founded in 1883 as the Brooklyn Atlantics. The team was known alternatively as the Bridegrooms, Grooms, Superbas, Robins, and Trolley Dodgers before officially becoming the Brooklyn Dodgers in the 1930s. The team moved to Los Angeles in 1958. They were the Robins from 1914 to 1931, named for their manager, Wilbert Robinson.

Chapter 65

  • “playing solitaire with a pack of the old playing cards”: Solitaire originated in Europe in the late 18th century, likely in Germany or Scandinavia, with early versions potentially used for fortune-telling. The game, also known as Patience, spread to France and England in the 19th century, with the first rule books appearing around the 1870s. See the solitary player in the Chapter 60 resources.

  • “in a bullish or a bearish market”: A bull expects prices to rise, a bear expects them to fall; both terms come from the London exchanges of the eighteenth century.
  • “or could corner all the gold”: On Black Friday, September 24, 1869, Jay Gould and Jim Fisk’s attempt to corner the gold market collapsed, ruining many speculators.

Chapter 66 · Stock Exchange

  • A place of illusionary wealth and human folly; also a site where she confronts capitalism and socialism.

Chapter 72

  • “the oldest pinochle player”: Pinochle originated in 19th-century Germany from the French game Bezique, evolving from Binokel, with its name possibly meaning “eyeglasses” (from the Queen of Spades and Jack of Diamonds combo). German immigrants brought it to America, where it became hugely popular in the late 1800s and early 1900s, especially in the Midwest, growing into a beloved game rivaling poker and bridge, featuring unique melding and trick-taking mechanics with a special 48-card deck.

Chapter 81

  • “There were also four ugly gamblers”: May refer to the “Big Four” Allied powers during World War II, who led the fight against the Axis, were the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union (USSR), and China. These nations formed the core of the alliance, with China fighting Japan since 1937 and the others joining later.

revelation-and-the-apocalypse:
Revelation and the Apocalypse

Home

In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 3, Chapter 5, Chapter 13, Chapter 14, Chapter 15, Chapter 17, Chapter 20, Chapter 21, Chapter 22, Chapter 29, Chapter 34, Chapter 35, Chapter 36, Chapter 38, Chapter 39, Chapter 40, Chapter 41, Chapter 42, Chapter 46, Chapter 49, Chapter 50, Chapter 52, Chapter 53, Chapter 61, Chapter 63, Chapter 65, Chapter 68, Chapter 69, Chapter 72, Chapter 74, Chapter 75, Chapter 77, Chapter 81

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • The Egyptian Sailor may refer to the “Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor.” A shipwrecked traveller engages upon a spiritual endeavour or quest, journeying through the cosmos, to meet a primordial god, providing to the traveller a gift of moral vision with which to return to Egypt. Further, Richard Mathews writes that this "oldest fantasy text contains archetypal narrative of the genre: an uninitiated hero on a sea journey is thrown off course by a storm, encounters an enchanted island, confronts a monster, and survives, wiser for the experience…” The tale itself begins with a framing device in which an attendant ("follower" or "the sailor") tries to comfort his master, who is returning from an apparently failed expedition and is anxious about how the king will receive him. (Wikipedia) (The Land of Punt was an ancient kingdom, likely located in the Horn of Africa, that traded extensively with ancient Egypt. It was a source of valuable goods like gold, ebony, ivory, and aromatic resins, which were highly sought after by the Egyptians. While the exact location remains debated, current evidence points towards a coastal region encompassing parts of present-day Somalia, Djibouti, Eritrea, and northeast Sudan. The kingdom's existence is primarily known through Egyptian records and depictions, particularly from the Middle and New Kingdom periods.) An attendant reassures him, advising him on how to behave before the king, and repeating the proverb, “The mouth of a man saves him.” To encourage his master, he tells a tale of a previous voyage of his in which he overcame disaster, including meeting with a god and the king. The tale ends with the master saying, “Do not make the excellent (that is, do not act arrogantly) my friend; why give water to a goose (literally, bird) at dawn before its slaughtering in the morning?” A Middle Kingdom text, "The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor," describes a star falling to earth, which led to the extinction of giant serpents on an island. This is sometimes interpreted as a folk memory of a meteorite impact as in the Netflix series Ancient Apocalypse. The sailor’s voyage appears to be a type of Otherworld Journey, a dangerous crossing-over to a divine or magical realm beyond the edge of the known world. “William K. Simpson observes that the Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor is ...one of the most interesting, straightforward, and yet puzzling compositions of ancient Egyptian literature. A curious emphasis is placed on numbers, the height of the wave, the dimensions of the ship, the number of sailors, the length of the serpent’s hood, the number of months of the sailor’s stay, and so on. It is almost as if the tale is an allegory involving the movement of stars. The Tale of the Shipwrecked Sailor is considered to contain esoteric knowledge, much of it related to the serpent’s story. Whatever its meaning, this tragedy is enshrined as the central motif of the narrative: it is element X in a structure A-B-C-X-C'-B'-A'. Unlike all of the other motifs, its form is mythic rather than folkloric; it seems to be a religious allegory. As a mythic island (X) set in the dead centre of a sea of folktale elements (A-C and A'-C'), it may even be the “payload” of the whole story.”

Chapter 2

  • The number twelve has been significant in religions and nature. In nature there are twelve lunations in the solar year, in the full cycle of Jupiter, in the Western and Chinese zodiac. In ancient Greek there are twelve Olympians, twelve Titans, Hercules carries out twelve labors and Athena summons twelve citizens to sit as a jury which is still common to this day in a trial by jury in the US. In Christianity Ishmael has twelve sons and Jacob twelve sons who are the progenitors of the twelve tribes of Israel, twelve Apostles, in the Book of Revelation there are many references to the number twelve, and the twelve days of Christmas.

Chapter 2

  • Seven has many cultural and religious meanings: it is a significant number in almost every major religion (Christianity, God rested on the seventh day; seven symbolizes the unity of the four corners of the Earth with the Holy Trinity; it is repeated in the book of Revelations); it is associated with luck and magical properties; people retain roughly seven items of information in their short-term memory; our attention holds approximately seven pieces of information.

Chapter 3

  • “the black-winged angels of mortality falling into the burning sea” - Revelation 8:8

Chapter 3

  • The philosophy of the end of the world, or "apocalyptic philosophy," explores the concept of the world's end, often involving catastrophic events, societal collapse, or human extinction, and examines its implications for ethics, meaning, and our understanding of existence. Philosophers have considered various end-of-world scenarios, from natural disasters to societal collapse, prompting reflection on human mortality, the nature of time, and the value of life.

Chapter 5

  • “old fool gives up his sceptre and his crown of stars and his golden throne” - Scepter is a staff or wand held in the hand by a ruling monarch as an item of royal insignia. A crown of stars is a circle of stars often representing unity, solidarity and harmony in flags, seals, and signs and is also in motifs related to the Woman of the Apocalypse and Baroque allegorical art depicting the Crown of Immortality. The Crown of Immortality is a metaphorical symbolic representation of eternal life, often depicted in art and literature. It's a traditional symbol of honor, achievement, and immortality, often associated with religious or spiritual concepts. It can be visualized as a laurel wreath or a circle of stars. A golden throne symbolizes divine authority, high status, and opulence. In various cultures, it represents the power and majesty of rulers, deities, or figures of significance. The use of gold, a precious and revered metal, further enhances this symbolism, connecting it to concepts of wealth, divinity, and triumph. The phrase captures a theme of resistance to inevitable change, the stubbornness of old power figures, and the futility of clinging to decaying authority in a world that moves on. It underscores the chapter’s atmosphere of decay, entrapment, and social criticism expressed through the bus-driver’s bitter, drunken monologue.

  • Jezebel is in the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. She is known for violently purging the prophets of God from Israel and instituting the worship of Baal and Asherah. She was later put to death by defenestration or being thrown from a high place or window. In the Book of Revelations she is symbolically associated with false prophets. (Wikipedia) "Jezebel" in this context represents a symbol of moral judgment and inner conflict within the bus-driver's troubled psyche during a moment of dark reflection and suffering.
