Chapter 3

  • Coal mining labor history in the United States is marked by dangerous work, exploitation, and the struggle for workers' rights, driven by waves of immigration, the Civil War, and industrialization. Early laborers were diverse, including enslaved and free African Americans, and later, large numbers of immigrants from Great Britain, Ireland, and Eastern and Southern Europe were drawn to the industry by recruiters. The United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) was founded in 1890 to fight for better wages, safer conditions, and benefits, leading to significant labor conflicts and hard-won reforms like the eight-hour workday and pensions. The coal industry was marked by a series of violent conflicts and massacres, often stemming from labor disputes between striking workers (many of whom were immigrants) and mine owners who hired private security forces or leveraged local law enforcement to suppress union organizing efforts. Lattimer Massacre (September 10, 1897): In Lattimer, Pennsylvania, a sheriff's posse opened fire on a march of unarmed striking immigrant anthracite miners, mostly of Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, and German descent. At least 19 miners were killed, and many more were wounded. The sheriff and his deputies were later tried but acquitted. Battle of Virden (October 1898): In Virden, Illinois, a gun battle erupted when the Chicago-Virden Coal Company attempted to bring in African-American strikebreakers with armed guards. Eight strikers and six guards/strikebreakers were killed. Ludlow Massacre (April 20, 1914): During a major strike in Colorado, the Colorado National Guard and guards from the Colorado Fuel & Iron Company attacked a tent colony of 1,200 striking miners and their families. The assault resulted in the deaths of approximately 19 people, including women and children, many of whom were burned to death when the camp was set on fire. Matewan Massacre (May 19, 1920): A deadly shootout occurred in Matewan, West Virginia, between Baldwin-Felts detective agency guards (hired by mine owners to evict striking workers from company-owned housing) and local residents, including the mayor and police chief, who supported the miners. Ten people died in the clash (seven detectives, two miners, and the mayor). Herrin Massacre (June 21-22, 1922): In Herrin, Illinois, a violent confrontation occurred between union miners and strikebreakers at a strip mine. After a gunfight and a subsequent surrender under the promise of safe passage, union miners murdered 20 strikebreakers and mine guards, and three union men also died. The incident is considered one of the most violent labor disputes in US history. Battle of Blair Mountain (August/September 1921): The culmination of the West Virginia Mine Wars, this was the largest armed insurrection in U.S. history since the Civil War. Thousands of union miners fought against local law enforcement and company-hired forces. Federal troops were eventually sent in by President Harding to quell the uprising, which involved the use of airplanes to drop bombs. At least 10 to 33 people were killed in the fighting. Columbine Mine Massacre (November 21, 1927): In Serene, Colorado, striking miners were met with machine-gun fire from the Colorado Rangers and guards from the Rocky Mountain Fuel Company during a strike, resulting in the deaths of six miners. These events, part of the broader "Coal Wars" (roughly 1890-1930), were pivotal in the struggle for better wages, safer working conditions, and the right to unionize in the U.S. coal industry.

  • Historically, the term "Black Republican" has had different meanings: 1) Before the Civil War, it was used as a derogatory term for abolitionist members of the Republican Party. 2) During Reconstruction the term was also used for Republicans who supported legislation that favored African Americans. 3) During and after the Civil War the term was used to refer to members of the Negro Republican Party, a faction of the Republican Party in the South that was predominantly made up of Black Americans. 4) From the 1870s to the 1960s it was associated with the "black-and-tan faction" of the Republican Party in the South, which opposed the segregationist "lily-white movement".

  • “Sheridan’s March”: Sheridan’s March may join two campaigns of 1864: Sheridan’s Ride, Philip Sheridan’s gallop to rally his army at Cedar Creek, told in Thomas Buchanan Read’s poem “Sheridan’s Ride” (1864), and William Tecumseh Sherman’s March to the Sea through Georgia.

Chapter 52

  • “some who were the beardless boys”: Many young people served as soldiers in the Civil War, with estimates suggesting that around 10% of Union soldiers were under 18. Some were as young as 10 years old, and many served as musicians, messengers, or even in combat roles. While the official minimum enlistment age was 18, many boys lied about their age to join the military, and some were even encouraged by recruiters. William Black: At age 12, he was wounded in battle, making him the youngest known wounded soldier, according to Nashville.gov. Johnny Clem: He joined the Union Army at age 10 and became a drummer boy. Johnny Cook: He was 15 when he volunteered as a cannoneer at the Battle of Antietam and received the Medal of Honor for his bravery, according to the National Park Service. Young soldiers faced the same dangers and hardships as older soldiers, including combat, disease, and imprisonment.
  • The 1850s and 1860s in the US were a period of intense national division and conflict, culminating in the Civil War. The central issue was slavery and its expansion, which led to political realignment, violence, and ultimately, secession and war. The decade of the 1850s saw escalating tensions surrounding slavery, with political compromises failing to resolve the issue and the nation moving closer to the brink of war. The Civil War itself, fought from 1861 to 1865, resulted in the end of slavery and Northern victory, but at a tremendous cost in human lives and national unity. Compromise of 1850 attempted to address the issue of slavery in newly acquired territories, but ultimately failed to quell the growing divide. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 introduced the concept of “popular sovereignty,” allowing residents of territories to decide on slavery, leading to violence and conflict in Kansas (“Bleeding Kansas”). Existing political parties fractured, and new ones emerged, such as the Republican Party, dedicated to preventing the expansion of slavery. The movement to abolish slavery gained momentum, with figures like Harriet Beecher Stowe and her novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin further inflaming anti-slavery sentiment. Dred Scott Decision (1857) where the Supreme Court ruled that enslaved people were not citizens and Congress could not prohibit slavery in the territories, further exacerbating tensions. Abraham Lincoln’s election as president in 1860, without a single Southern electoral vote, led to the secession of several Southern states. The Civil War (1861-1865) was fought between the Union (North) and the Confederacy (South), resulting in immense loss of life and widespread destruction. Major battles like Gettysburg and Vicksburg marked turning points in the war. Emancipation Proclamation (1863) declared enslaved people in Confederate-held territory to be free. New York City draft riots (1863) discontent with the draft laws during the Civil War led to violent protests. The 13th Amendment (1865) officially abolished slavery in the United States. Reconstruction (1865-1877) after the Civil War focused on rebuilding the South and integrating formerly enslaved people into society. This era was marked by successes and failures in achieving true equality.

Chapter 53

  • “this traditional Republican”: A traditional Republican may refer to the original Republican Party that emerged in the 1850s, founded by anti-slavery activists who opposed the expansion of slavery into US territories. During the 19th century, the party was strongly associated with the abolition of slavery and the preservation of the Union.

Chapter 54

  • “a Civil War silver dollar”: “Civil War silver dollar” may refer to the Seated Liberty Dollar. The Civil War caused widespread hoarding of the coins due to their value. They were made of 90% silver. This led to a coin shortage in 1862. The government issued paper Demand Notes and later minted silver dollars which were stored in a vault for future use. The Seated Liberty Dollar was the design in use for U.S. silver dollars before and during the Civil War. A law in 1865 allowed the motto “In God We Trust” to be added to coins, and it was placed on the Seated Liberty dollar in 1866. The Seated Liberty dollar was the first coin struck at the Carson City Mint in Nevada, beginning in 1870, with thousands of these coins stored in Treasury vaults.

Chapter 57

  • “reconstructing the Civil War—the Battle of Appomattox”: The Battle of Appomattox Court House, fought in Appomattox County, Virginia, on the morning of April 9, 1865, was one of the last battles of the American Civil War. It was the final engagement of Confederate General in Chief, Robert E. Lee, and his Army of Northern Virginia before they surrendered to the Union Army of the Potomac under the Commanding General of the United States Army, Ulysses S. Grant. (Wikipedia) Lee did not surrender in a tent but in the parlor of Wilmer McLean’s house at Appomattox Court House.
  • “the flags of the Confederacy”: Refers to several flags used by the Confederate States of America during the Civil War (1861-65), with the most recognizable being the Battle Flag of the Army of Northern Virginia. It was created for battlefield use to distinguish it from the Union flag and later became a symbol for the Lost Cause narrative of Southern heritage, though its use also became tied to white supremacy and racist groups. The flag’s controversial meaning, representing both Southern heritage and a symbol of racism and slavery, has led to ongoing public debates and the removal of official displays.
  • “the flags of the Grand Union Army”: Young’s Grand Union Army is the Union army of the Civil War, whose veterans formed the Grand Army of the Republic in 1866. The Grand Union Flag, by contrast, was the first flag of the Continental Army, flown from 1775 until the Stars and Stripes was adopted in 1777.

Definition from research

Chapter 1

  • Harold Bloom says Don Quixote is the first modern novel, and that the protagonist is at war with Freud's reality principle, which accepts the necessity of dying. Bloom says that the novel has an endless range of meanings, but that a recurring theme is the human need to withstand suffering. Edith Grossman, who wrote and published a highly acclaimed English translation of the novel in 2003, says that the book is mostly meant to move people into emotion using a systematic change of course, on the verge of both tragedy and comedy at the same time. Grossman has stated: The question is that Quixote has multiple interpretations [...] and how do I deal with that in my translation. I'm going to answer your question by avoiding it [...] so when I first started reading the Quixote I thought it was the most tragic book in the world, and I would read it and weep [...] As I grew older [...] my skin grew thicker [...] and so when I was working on the translation I was actually sitting at my computer and laughing out loud. This is done [...] as Cervantes did it [...] by never letting the reader rest. You are never certain that you truly got it. Because as soon as you think you understand something, Cervantes introduces something that contradicts your premise. The novel's structure is episodic in form. The full title is indicative of the tale's object, as ingenioso (Spanish) means "quick with inventiveness", marking the transition of modern literature from dramatic to thematic unity. The novel takes place over a long period of time, including many adventures united by common themes of the nature of reality, reading, and dialogue in general. Although burlesque on the surface, the novel, especially in its second half, has served as an important thematic source not only in literature but also in much of art and music, inspiring works by Pablo Picasso and Richard Strauss. The contrasts between the tall, thin, fancy-struck and idealistic Quixote and the fat diddy, world-weary Panza is a motif echoed ever since the book's publication, and Don Quixote's imaginings are the butt of outrageous and cruel practical jokes in the novel. Even faithful and simple Sancho is forced to deceive him at certain points. The novel is considered a satire of orthodoxy, veracity and even nationalism. In exploring the individualism of his characters, Cervantes helped lead literary practice beyond the narrow convention of the chivalric romance. He spoofs the chivalric romance through a straightforward retelling of a series of acts that redound to the knightly virtues of the hero. The character of Don Quixote became so well known in its time that the word quixotic was quickly adopted by many languages. Characters such as Sancho Panza and Don Quixote's steed, Rocinante, are emblems of Western literary culture. The phrase "tilting at windmills" to describe an act of attacking imaginary enemies (or an act of extreme idealism), derives from an iconic scene in the book. It stands in a unique position between medieval romance and the modern novel. The former consists of disconnected stories featuring the same characters and settings with little exploration of the inner life of even the main character. The latter are usually focused on the psychological evolution of their characters. In Part I, Quixote imposes himself on his environment. By Part II, people know about him through "having read his adventures", and so, he needs to do less to maintain his image. By his deathbed, he has regained his sanity, and is once more "Alonso Quixano the Good".

Chapter 8

  • “that old knight errant curing them all”: Don Quixote, the mad knight errant who rides out to help people who never asked to be rescued.

Chapter 37

  • “There would be suddenly a whirling windmill”: The whirling windmill may recall the windmills that Don Quixote takes for giants (Cervantes, Don Quixote 1.8, 1605).

Chapter 45

  • “challenged icebergs, driving against them with her sword”: Don Quixote charges the windmills, taking them for giants (Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, 1605, chapter 8).

Chapter 49

  • “he had seen the other side of the tapestry”: “Translating from one language into another… is like looking at Flemish tapestries on the wrong side; for though the figures are visible, they are full of threads that make them indistinct” (Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, Part II, chapter 62, trans. John Ormsby, 1885). The chapter ends with Mr. Spitzer as the weaver woven into his own tapestry.

Chapter 65

  • “Chasing windmills—Miss MacIntosh had always been chasing windmills”: Miss MacIntosh told Vera she had been chasing Dutch windmills. Another character, Mrs. Hogden, claims to have lived in a Dutch windmill. Moses Hunnecker, the bus driver of Chapter 1, is also imagined as “some mad Don Quixote chasing windmills.” Windmills in the Dutch style stand in the United States too, among them the Fabyan Windmill outside Chicago and the two in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park (1903, 1908), the two cities of Miss MacIntosh’s solitaire. Tilting at windmills is an idiom for attacking imaginary enemies from the novel Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes. It is a founding book in Western literature and is labeled the first modern novel. Antonio Rivas of Dickinson College called it “a very good reminder of why we read, why we watch movies, why we need fiction and imagination” (“Chasing Windmills,” Dickinson College, April 21, 2015). According to Mark Aldrich of Dickinson College, in a video for the novel’s 400th anniversary (Dickinson College, 2015, YouTube), Don Quixote is the story of an older man who has lost his mind over his obsession with literature and decides to go and live these adventures of time past. Little by little through his friendship with his companion he recovers his mind. It is ultimately the journey of one man finding out who he really is. Quixote is the highest aspirations of human beings. It pits the world of imagination against the terrible reality of modern life. It highlights the challenges of understanding one’s identity. There is a parallel between Don Quixote and Miss MacIntosh My Darling in that it is not a book of issues but of tissues, like an onion, you find layer after layer upon subsequent rereadings. Don Quixote stands for change and renovating society. He wants to help the poor and the oppressed.

Chapter 70

  • “Oh, she was a creature compounded of illusions”: Mrs. Hogden strongly embodies Quixotic characteristics through her elaborate self-deception and unwavering optimism in the face of a stark reality.

Chapter 79

  • “Some, she knew, were born with silver spoons in their mouths”: The idiom, to be born with a silver spoon in their mouth, means someone born into a wealthy family or someone who has a prosperous background or is of a well-to-do family environment, often with the connotation that the person does not fully realize or appreciate the value of his or her advantage, its having been inherited rather than earned. It first appeared in print in English as early as 1719, in the translation of the novel Don Quixote. (Wikipedia)

In the research: Chapter 11, Chapter 40, Chapter 49, Chapter 53

Definition from research

Chapter 11

  • “Sir Walter Raleigh in his marvelous white satin suit embroidered with seed pearls”: Sir Walter Raleigh (c. 1552-1618) was an English statesman, soldier, spy, writer, poet, and explorer. (Wikipedia) He was famous at Elizabeth’s court for the pearls and jewels on his clothes, even his shoes.
  • Raleigh’s poetry is known as the plain style. His writing contains strong personal treatments of themes such as love, loss, beauty, and time. Most of his poems are short lyrics that were inspired by actual events. In poems Raleigh expresses a contempt-of-the-world attitude more characteristic of the Middle Ages than of the dawning era of humanistic optimism. But his lesser-known long poem, The Ocean’s Love to Cynthia, expresses a melancholy sense of history. The poem was written during his imprisonment in the Tower of London. (Wikipedia) Raleigh answered Christopher Marlowe’s “The Passionate Shepherd to His Love” with “The Nymph’s Reply to the Shepherd.” Raleigh gives an almost line-for-line refutation of Marlowe’s sentiments. Centuries later, William Carlos Williams added “Raleigh Was Right” (1940) to the conversation. It begins, “We cannot go to the country / for the country will bring us / no peace.”
  • “when he removed his white plumed hat, removed also his head”: Raleigh was beheaded at Westminster on October 29, 1618. Of the axe he said, “This is sharp medicine, but it is a physician for all diseases.” His widow kept his embalmed head for the rest of her life. The poem he wrote the night before begins, “Even such is Time, that takes in trust / Our youth, our joys, our all we have, / And pays us but with earth and dust.”
  • “his intimate name, Ocean or Water”: Elizabeth called him “Water.” Spenser named him “the Shepherd of the Ocean” in Colin Clouts Come Home Againe (1595), and Raleigh wrote The Ocean’s Love to Cynthia, with the Queen as the moon who rules the tides.
  • “a society of night devoted exclusively to atheistic propositions”: “The school of night” comes from Love’s Labour’s Lost (4.3): “Black is the badge of hell, / The hue of dungeons and the school of night.” The phrase became a name for Raleigh’s circle with Thomas Harriot and Christopher Marlowe, men accused of doubting Genesis and God. In 1594 an inquiry at Cerne Abbas examined charges of atheism against Raleigh’s circle.

Chapter 11 · Sir Walter Raleigh

  • Imagined with a white satin suit embroidered with pearls and gems.
  • His decapitation and request to be called “Ocean or Water” suggest themes of transformation, fluidity, and martyrdom or sacrifice.
  • Raleigh was beheaded in 1618.
  • Represents atheistic propositions and philosophical skepticism within the dream.

Chapter 40

  • “which was Greek shepherd singing to his flock”: Greek shepherd may refer to several references listed. The Passionate Shepherd to His Love is a poem by Christopher Marlowe which was responded to by Raleigh in Nymph’s Reply to the Shepherd and later by different poets over the years.

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • Dante Alighieri was an Italian poet who wrote the Divine Comedy.

Chapter 8

  • “that same old one-eyed Beatrice”: Beatrice is a name derived from the French name Béatrice, which came from the Latin Beatrix, which means “she who makes happy.” The popularity of the name spread because of Dante Alighieri’s poetry about the Florentine woman Beatrice Portinari. Dante presents Beatrice as being worthy of speaking for God, making her a holy individual. Beatrice “Bice” di Folco Portinari was an Italian woman who has been commonly identified as the principal inspiration for Dante Alighieri’s Vita Nuova, and is also identified with the Beatrice who acts as his guide in the last book of his narrative poem the Divine Comedy, Paradiso, and during the conclusion of the preceding Purgatorio. Within the Comedy, Beatrice is symbolic of divine grace and theology. (Wikipedia) Young’s Beatrice, a one-eyed washerwoman called a whore, is the opposite of Dante’s guide to heaven. Yet she too lives where the road divides, the graveyard on one side and the village of “promise through eternity” on the other.

Chapter 11

  • “Roland who was killed at Roncevalles”: Roland was a military leader under Charlemagne who died at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778, when Basques ambushed Charlemagne’s rear guard. The Song of Roland (c. 1100) turns them into Saracens and has Roland blow his horn too late. In Dante’s Divine Comedy, Roland is named Orlando and placed in the Heaven of Mars with others who fought for the faith (Paradiso 18).

Chapter 14

  • “the music of the spheres, the silent music”: Boethius was a Roman senator, consul, magister officiorum, polymath, historian, and philosopher of the Early Middle Ages. He sought to reconcile the teachings of Plato and Aristotle with Christian theology. He broke logic into three parts: that which defines, that which divides, and that which deduces. There are three types of arguments: those of necessity, of ready believability, and sophistry. In De Musica there are three classifications: Musica mundana, Musica humana, Musica instrumentalis. In Dante’s Divine Comedy, the spirit of Boethius is pointed out by Saint Thomas Aquinas and is mentioned further in the poem. In his book De Institutione Musica (Fundamentals of Music) his drawings appear striking and may be an inspiration for the organization of Young’s novel. Musica universalis or music of the spheres or harmony of the spheres is a Greek philosophical concept founded by Pythagoras. This metaphysical principle stated that mathematical relationships could produce ‘tones’ of energy that could produce, among other things, sounds. Pythagoras proposed that the celestial bodies all have their own unique hum based on their orbital revolution. This idea influenced many scholars until the end of the Renaissance. Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer from the 1600s wrote extensively on the subject. (Wikipedia) Later astronomy set it aside. Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution, with its Wheel of Fortune.

Chapter 17

  • “as if I were entombed in fields of everlasting ice”: At the bottom of Dante’s Hell, the traitors are frozen in the ice of Cocytus (Inferno 32-34). Vera is about to feel betrayed.

Chapter 20

  • “a babe cast into purgatory”: Catholic tradition placed unbaptized infants not in purgatory but in limbo, at the edge of Hell, where Dante puts the virtuous unbaptized (Inferno 4).

Chapter 23

  • “where the dead souls wandered like flames”: This may recall Dante’s flames, each wrapping a soul, among them Ulysses (Inferno 26).

Chapter 26

  • “wandering through the intricate streets of a dark city in perhaps the underworld”: Dis, the walled city of Hell in Dante’s Inferno (cantos 8-9).
  • “in order to reach the upper world, one must first travel through the lower world”: Mr. Spitzer’s belief that people need to travel through the lower world to reach the upper world mirrors The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678) and/or Dante’s writings. Purgatory has seven terraces for the seven deadly sins, and there are seven virtues. Hell has nine circles and Heaven has nine spheres: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the fixed stars, and the primum mobile. According to Dante the cosmos depends on God, who exists in the Empyrean, an immaterial heaven beyond space and time. The Empyrean is made up of God’s love and light, and is home to angels, the blessed, and the souls of the faithful. Interesting note that the woman with the Siamese cats believes she was the reincarnation of Cleopatra and Dante meets Cleopatra in the circle of Hell called Lust (“Cleopatràs lussurïosa,” Inferno 5.63). Virgil wrote “Facilis descensus Averno,” “the descent to Avernus is easy… but to retrace one’s steps and climb back to the upper air, that is the task, that is the labor” (Aeneid 6.126-129), and Heraclitus, “The way up and the way down are one and the same.”

Chapter 26 · The Upper and Lower Worlds

  • Mr. Spitzer’s lower world of “the thief who had stolen bright jewels” and “the painted street woman leering under a lamp” must be crossed to reach the upper, a journey “endless like some of those journeys taken by my mother.”

Chapter 29

  • “the last infernal circle of this Divine Comedy”: Divine Comedy (c. 1308-21) is a long Italian narrative poem by Dante Alighieri. It depicts the afterlife according to the Western Church medieval world view of the time. (Wikipedia) Like The Pilgrim’s Progress (1678) it is a journey from sin to heaven.

Chapter 30

  • “where Childe Roland had blown his horn before a dark tower”: Childe Roland is a character in a poem by Robert Browning. The character Roland in the poem makes a journey to the Dark Tower much like the journey of Pilgrim’s Progress and the Divine Comedy. The name Child Roland comes from the Shakespeare play King Lear Act 3 Scene 4 Lines 195-197. Browning’s poem is “Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came” (1855), and it ends with the horn: “Dauntless the slug-horn to my lips I set, / And blew. ‘Childe Roland to the Dark Tower came.’” The horn also recalls Roland of The Song of Roland, who blew his horn Oliphant at Roncevaux (778).

Chapter 37

  • “the tormented whirlwinds turning upon spindles”: “The infernal hurricane that never rests / Hurtles the spirits onward in its rapine” (Dante, Inferno 5, trans. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, 1867), the circle of the lovers.

Chapter 38

  • “seven deathless eternities”: “Seven deathless eternities” may recall Dante’s Divine Comedy, where the seven terraces of Purgatory purge the seven deadly sins. Seven heavens are found in Judaism and Islam, and Hindu cosmology has seven upper worlds, the lokas. The seven virtues join the four cardinal virtues of Greek philosophy to the three theological virtues of Paul (1 Corinthians 13:13).

Chapter 40

  • “the bird king whose head was turned backward upon his shoulders”: In Dante’s Inferno 20 the diviners walk with their heads twisted backward: “For tow’rds the reins the countenance was turned, / And backward it behoved them to advance” (trans. Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, 1867).
  • “ageless Dante”: Dante or Durante di Alighiero degli Alighieri was a Florentine poet, writer and philosopher.

Chapter 44

  • “a great cone reversed, standing on its apex”: Dante’s Hell is a funnel, a great cone reversed, narrowing circle by circle to its point at the center of the earth (Inferno).

Chapter 45

  • “the infernal mountains of frozen furies”: The lowest circle of Dante’s Hell is not fire but ice, the frozen lake of Cocytus (Inferno 32-34).

Chapter 54

  • “this music of Inferno”: Inferno is the first part of Italian writer Dante Alighieri’s 14th-century narrative poem The Divine Comedy, followed by Purgatorio and Paradiso. The Inferno describes the journey of a fictionalized version of Dante himself through Hell, guided by the ancient Roman poet Virgil. In the poem, Hell is depicted as nine concentric circles of torment located within the Earth; it is the “realm [...] of those who have rejected spiritual values by yielding to bestial appetites or violence, or by perverting their human intellect to fraud or malice against their fellowmen.” As an allegory, the Divine Comedy represents the journey of the soul toward God, with the Inferno describing the recognition and rejection of sin.
  • “an old uncle in Paradiso”: Paradiso is the third and final part of Dante’s Divine Comedy, following the Inferno and the Purgatorio. It is an allegory telling of Dante’s journey through Heaven, guided by Beatrice, who symbolizes theology. In the poem, Paradise is depicted as a series of concentric spheres surrounding the Earth, consisting of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Fixed Stars, the Primum Mobile and finally, the Empyrean. It was written in the early 14th century. Allegorically, the poem represents the soul’s ascent to God.

Chapter 62

  • “maps of wandering Cocytus”: Cocytus is the river of wailing in the underworld in Greek mythology. In Dante’s Inferno it is a lake of ice holding the traitors (Cantos 32-34).

Chapter 71

  • “an old steel engraving of Dante wooing Beatrice”: Dante’s “wooing” of Beatrice was not a traditional courtship but an idealized love he expressed through poetry, famously documented in his book Vita Nuova. He fell in love with her at a very young age, and although he encountered her only a couple of times, she became his lifelong muse, representing a spiritual and intellectual ideal. The term “courtly love” was applied to their relationship, a concept involving an idealized and often unattainable love that inspires poetry and virtue. Henry Holiday’s painting Dante and Beatrice (1883), of Dante meeting her on a Florentine bridge, was reproduced in countless engravings.

Deafness and Sign Language

Home

In the research: Chapter 1, Chapter 9, Chapter 13, Chapter 29, Chapter 49, Chapter 51, Chapter 61, Chapter 81, Chapter 82

Definition from research

Chapter 1

  • “because of a deaf musician” This figure introduces the theme of communication and isolation. A deaf musician cannot hear the music he creates or the world around him, symbolizing a disconnect or failure of connection, similar to the unanswered questions Vera faces.

Chapter 9

  • “A blind violinist and a deaf dancer”: There are many blind, deaf, and mute people in the book. This could be a play on the Three Wise Monkeys. The Three Wise Monkeys are a Japanese folk representation of the proverb “see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil.” They symbolize prudence and purity, and are often seen as a call for discretion or willful ignorance. The three monkeys are Mizaru (see no evil), Kikazaru (hear no evil), and Iwazaru (speak no evil). The concept originates in Japan, with statues of the monkeys found in temples and shrines. The proverb “see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil” is often interpreted as a way to avoid negative experiences or situations by choosing to ignore them. In Japan, the monkeys are seen as attendants of Koshin, the God of Roads, and their message is used to teach prudence and purity. In the West, the proverb is often used sarcastically to criticize those who deliberately ignore wrongdoing. The idea is rooted in Confucius: “Look not at what is contrary to propriety; listen not to what is contrary to propriety; speak not what is contrary to propriety” (Analects 12.1, trans. James Legge). Some representations include a fourth monkey, Sezaru, who “does no evil.” (Wikipedia) One misses the train by seeing it but not hearing its whistle, the other by hearing but not seeing.

Chapter 13

  • “not even the creaking of starlight”: Aristotle reports the Pythagorean answer: the spheres do make music, and people do not hear it because they have heard it since birth (On the Heavens 2.9). Lorenzo tells Jessica, “Such harmony is in immortal souls; / But whilst this muddy vesture of decay / Doth grossly close it in, we cannot hear it” (The Merchant of Venice 5.1).
  • “a subdued roaring, a noise which came from the head only”: Tinnitus, a ringing or roaring in the ears with no outside source. Beethoven described it in the Heiligenstadt Testament (1802).

Chapter 29

  • “It was his own personal theory that a butterfly could hear”: Science has found membranes on some butterfly wings that allow it to hear. The hearing organ on the wings of some butterflies is called Vogel’s organ, after Richard Vogel, who described it in 1912. His own “dead ear” is from Chapter 25.

Chapter 49

  • “Their yesterday was a pointing backward over the shoulder”: Young seems to use actual ASL sign language gestures but some seem to have changed over time. In American Sign Language time runs along the body: the past is signed behind, over the shoulder, and the future ahead.

Chapter 51

  • “Seldom did he meet with anyone who did not suffer from some form of complex illusion beyond necessity”: Most people Mr. Spitzer meets suffer “some form of complex illusion beyond necessity”: the old woman who believes she is a bird cage, the piano-tuner declaring foreheads “hollow.” Blindness and deafness become metaphors for the limits of perception: the blind portrait painter, the blind war veteran in the galleries of Europe, the deaf music critics who hear every error without hearing a note, judgment resting on something other than the senses. “One great dream informing all dreamers and all dreams” recalls a collective unconscious or universal mind, or Plato’s Form of the Good, the source all strive toward behind the shadows of sense. Happiness is fleeting as a snowflake; “three minutes of happiness seemed perhaps all there might be,” and “the greatest happiness might come through the sorrow of waiting, of postponement.” The passage holds the absurdity of existence and, through Mr. Spitzer’s work for the dead, the responsibility of making sense of their lives.
  • “the most famous music critics were the deaf”: Beethoven was nearly deaf when his Ninth Symphony was first played in 1824, and he had to be turned around to see the applause.

Chapter 61

  • “many signs which Mr. Spitzer had not understood”: American Sign Language grew from the school that Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet and the deaf French teacher Laurent Clerc opened in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1817.
  • “hearing with their eyes, their skin, their hair”: Studies of deaf adults find heightened attention to the edges of the visual field and to touch (Daphne Bavelier and others, “Do deaf individuals see better?” 2006, after 1964).
  • “a silent attendant to a Turk”: The Ottoman sultans kept mutes, the dilsiz, at the Topkapı Palace; they spoke among themselves in signs and sometimes served as executioners. See the Kafes in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “a Spanish deaf mute lip-reader in Boston”: Boston was a center of oralism, which taught deaf children to read lips and speak and drove out sign language. Alexander Graham Bell taught his Visible Speech at the Boston School for Deaf Mutes in 1871, and the Milan congress of 1880 voted to ban signing in deaf schools.
  • “he was born deaf but had been made mute”: Most deaf people have working voices. The old word “deaf-mute” came from the fact that a child born deaf did not learn speech by ear, and many Deaf people today reject the term.

Chapter 81

  • Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist. One of the most revered figures in the history of Western music, his works rank among the most performed of the classical music repertoire and span the transition from the Classical to the Romantic era. Beethoven’s early period, during which he forged his craft, is typically considered to have lasted until 1802. From 1802 to around 1812, his middle period showed an individual development from the styles of Joseph Haydn and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, and is sometimes characterised as heroic. During this time, Beethoven began to grow increasingly deaf. In his late period, from 1812 to 1827, he extended his innovations in musical form and expression.

Chapter 82

  • “Little boidies don’t have no tits”: The stone-deaf man was Young’s friend Howard Mitcham, a deaf painter in Greenwich Village. “He used to love to sing this, little boydies don’t have no tits. Little boydies don’t have no umbilical cords,” and “he knew that I was putting him in” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). For a magazine article on the deaf she interviewed deaf leaders in New York and heard the Lord’s Prayer in sign language at St. Mark’s (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

  • “the garden of the blind”: Fragrance gardens for the blind were planted to be touched and smelled. The Brooklyn Botanic Garden opened one in 1955. Vera and Miss MacIntosh walk through this garden in Chapter 3.
  • “sweet william, cosmos, rose geranium, phlox, nasturtium, nicotiana”: Scented garden flowers. Rose geranium gives off its scent at a touch, and nicotiana, flowering tobacco, opens and perfumes the air at night.
  • “flowers of the old Jerusalem, flowers of the new Jerusalem”: “I am the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Solomon 2:1), and the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down “as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2).

Chapter 13

  • “The mist flowers drooped their purple, langorous heads”: Mistflower, a real wildflower of the American South, blooms in soft purple heads in late summer.

Chapter 14

  • “a horseshoe of white roses”: Floral horseshoes and saddles of roses honored racing men. Since 1932 the Kentucky Derby winner has worn a garland of roses.
  • “the Battle of the Roses”: The Wars of the Roses (1455-1487) were a series of civil wars in England between the houses of York, with its white rose, and Lancaster, with its red.

Chapter 15

  • “bayberry and beach rose and meadows of billowing Queen Anne’s lace”: Bayberry wax made the colonists’ Christmas candles. Legend says Queen Anne pricked her finger making lace, and the one dark floret at the center of the flower is her drop of blood.
  • “the fairest flower is plucked the earliest”: The Passionate Pilgrim (1599), published under Shakespeare’s name, has “Sweet rose, fair flower, untimely pluck’d, soon vaded.”

Chapter 15 · Nature’s Contrasts

  • The “humped, naked dunes” with “seaweed,” “Queen Anne’s lace,” and “wild grass” represent the wildness and beauty of life.
  • The “low, stunted, blackened spruce and hemlock” suggest decay and resilience simultaneously.

Chapter 18

  • “the last rose of the last summer on earth”: “The Last Rose of Summer” is a poem by the Irish poet Thomas Moore, published in 1813 and written while staying at Jenkinstown Castle in County Kilkenny, Ireland, where he was said to have been inspired by the China rose ‘Old Blush.’ (Wikipedia) It poignantly represents the final vestiges of youth, vitality, and love, standing on the brink of disappearance, much like the characters grappling with mortality and
  • “the last rose of the last summer on earth”: “The Last Rose of Summer” is a poem by the Irish poet Thomas Moore, published in 1813 and written while staying at Jenkinstown Castle in County Kilkenny, Ireland, where he was said to have been inspired by the China rose ‘Old Blush.’ (Wikipedia) It poignantly represents the final vestiges of youth, vitality, and love, standing on the brink of disappearance, much like the characters grappling with mortality and the fading of dreams.

Chapter 19 · Broken Cherubim and Fallen Alabaster Rose

  • Fragments of lost innocence or beauty.

Chapter 22

  • “cabbage roses such as grew, if not in What Cheer, Iowa”: Miss MacIntosh’s hometown.

Chapter 24

  • “the bronze-colored chrysanthemums which are the flowers for the dead”: In France and Italy, chrysanthemums are laid on graves on All Saints’ Day.

Chapter 25

  • “The white tuberose or the white carnation in his buttonhole”: Both white flowers were worn or sent in mourning. The white carnation became the emblem of a mother who has died when Anna Jarvis founded Mother’s Day (1908).

Chapter 25 · The Rose in the Buttonhole

  • Initially a symbol of life and vitality, it is doubted: Mr. Spitzer concedes it may be “in all probability a lady’s ear,” and to Catherine it may be a door knob.
  • Highlights the instability of perception.

Chapter 26

  • “a bouquet of winter violets”: Ophelia’s “I would give you some violets, but they withered all when my father died” (Hamlet 4.5). Violets were a flower of faithfulness.

Chapter 27

  • “his high silk hat and black necktie and rosebud with maidenhair”: Maidenhair fern (Adiantum) was the usual green set behind a buttonhole rose.

Chapter 37 · The Cross and Rose

  • Symbolize transformation and the intertwining of suffering and beauty, life and death.

Chapter 41

  • “trooping her suffrage colors of rose on white”: The real suffrage colors were purple, white, and gold for the National Woman’s Party, yellow for the National American Woman Suffrage Association, and purple, white, and green for the British suffragettes. In Tennessee in August 1920, when the last state needed ratified the Nineteenth Amendment, “Supporters of suffrage wore yellow roses in public; the anti-suffragists wore red roses,” in “what became known as the War of the Roses” (National Constitution Center, “The man and his mom who gave women the vote”). Hannah’s “red rose of her blood” was, in Tennessee, the flower of her enemies.

Chapter 42 · The Bridegroom and Withered Flowers

  • Represent unfulfilled love and abandonment, contrasting with Cousin Hannah’s militant independence and loneliness.

Chapter 44

  • “snowdrops delicate as a wraith of mist”: The snowdrop flowers through the snow at Candlemas and stands for hope, but an old English belief held that a snowdrop brought into the house foretold a death (Roy Vickery, Oxford Dictionary of Plant-Lore, 1995).

Chapter 44 · Snowdrops and Snow

  • Represent purity, fragility, and the coldness of death. The melting snowdrops in her hand symbolize fading life and lost love.

Chapter 47 · White Rose

  • Purity, love, and mourning.

Chapter 56

  • “only the red rose by which he should be recognized”:
  • “many winter aconites”: Winter aconites is a flower in the buttercup family that grows in France, Italy, and the Balkans. It flowers yellow in late winter, often through the snow.
  • “the dew drop trembling on the lip of the helmet flower”: Helmet flower is monkshood, Aconitum, named for its hooded upper petal; every part of it is poisonous.

Chapter 56 · White and Red Roses

  • The white rose worn by Mr. Spitzer symbolizes passing beyond life (death or transcendence), while Peron’s red rose is a signifier of identity and remembrance.

Chapter 57

  • “there should be a red rose and a white rose growing on a single bush”: Young’s hybrid exists. The York and Lancaster rose, a damask rose grown since the sixteenth century, bears pink and white flowers on the same bush and is named for the red rose of Lancaster and the white rose of York, whose Wars of the Roses ended when Henry VII joined the two in the Tudor rose.

Chapter 57 · The Rose (Red and White)

  • Represents memory, fidelity, and duality. Mr. Spitzer imagines a rose named after himself and his brother, red and white together, symbolizing their intertwined fates and memories. The symbolism of red and white flowers together generally represents unity, harmony, and the balance of opposing concepts like passion and purity. This meaning is most common in Western traditions and varies significantly depending on the cultural context and the specific flowers chosen. The Tudor rose joined the red rose of Lancaster and the white rose of York after the Wars of the Roses, two houses in one flower, as Mr. Spitzer joins himself and his brother.

Chapter 59

  • “the red rose of the sun or the white rose of the moon”: Compare the Temple Garden scene of Henry VI, Part 1, where the lords of York pluck white roses and the lords of Lancaster red, the start of the Wars of the Roses (William Shakespeare, 2.4).

Chapter 61

  • “meadows of Queen Anne’s lace”: Queen Anne’s lace is the wild carrot. Legend says Queen Anne pricked her finger while making lace, and the single dark red floret at the center of the white flower head is her drop of blood.
  • “perhaps of mignonette”: Mignonette (Reseda odorata), “little darling” in French, is a small, sweet-scented garden flower long loved for nosegays.

Chapter 61 · The Rose

  • The red rose dropped into the frog’s grave symbolizes immortality, resurrection, and eternal life.

Chapter 74

  • “an old maid plucking at a daisy’s petals”: “He loves me, he loves me not.” In French the game is effeuiller la marguerite, plucking the daisy, and marguerite is the French for daisy.
  • “some old preacher or jack-in-the-pulpit”: The jack-in-the-pulpit is a woodland wildflower whose spadix stands under a hooded spathe like a preacher in his pulpit; the Johnny-jump-up is the wild pansy, the four o’clock opens in late afternoon, and shepherd’s purse is named for its heart-shaped seed pods.
  • “a moss rosebud brown as a mushroom”: The moss rose, its buds furred with green moss, was a favorite of Victorian gardens.

Chapter 74 · The Old Rosebud

  • Placed on Esther’s body, symbolizing innocence, death, or a token of remorse.

Chapter 75

  • “While dangling a red geranium for bait”: A red geranium may be herb Robert (Geranium robertianum), the small wild red cranesbill, also called red robin, stinking Bob, and death-come-quickly; folk magic linked it with luck and fertility. Geranium comes from the Greek geranos, crane, for the beak-shaped seed pods, and in German the plant is Stinkender Storchschnabel, stinking stork’s-bill. Because the stork was already an established European symbol of birth, family, and new babies, people linked the stork’s-bill herb to conception and depicted it alongside storks in folk art.

Chapter 75 · The Funeral Wreath

  • Symbolizes death and mourning; it appears on the dead baby and connects to Esther’s fears about paternity and legacy.

Chapter 78

  • “She was the red, red rose”: “O my Luve’s like a red, red rose, / That’s newly sprung in June” (Robert Burns, 1794).

Chapter 79 · Nature (Clouds, Stars, Flowers)

  • Contrasts with the harshness of Esther’s birth, representing purity, innocence, and the natural cycle of life.
  • The “clouds filled with holes” evoke fragility and vulnerability.

Chapter 81 · Black Mourning Band and Old Rosebud

  • Symbols of death, mourning, and lost beauty.

In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 6, Chapter 9, Chapter 12, Chapter 27, Chapter 36, Chapter 39, Chapter 41, Chapter 42, Chapter 45, Chapter 46, Chapter 47, Chapter 48, Chapter 57, Chapter 65, Chapter 66, Chapter 68, Chapter 69, Chapter 71, Chapter 79

Definition from research

Chapter 2 · The Clock and Time

  • The twelve goblets and chairs represent the passage of time and the ritualized nature of existence.
  • Time is both suspended and fragmented in Catherine’s world.

Chapter 6

  • “She was watching the old town clock very closely now”: Clocks can signify: time, schedules, business, modern man, new beginnings, endings, and the transitory nature of human beings. In Tudor times a clock could mean truth unveiled by time. Clocks in this chapter are not merely instruments measuring time but serve as potent symbols of the instability of human experience, the blending of reality and dream, and the inexorable flow of time that ultimately eludes human control.
  • “She dreamed that she was a sundial in a ruined garden”: Old sundials carry the motto “I count only the sunny hours.”

Chapter 9 · Time and Watches

  • The silver dollar watch worn by Miss MacIntosh symbolizes the relentless march of time and the pressure of discipline.
  • Miss MacIntosh frequently refers to time as deceptive and insists on punctuality and the urgency of preparing for the future, reinforcing the theme of control versus Vera’s dreams.

Chapter 12 · Clocks and Time

  • Clocks stopped at different hours symbolize frozen moments, hesitation, or the past lingering in the present.
  • The Big Ben, “Old Reliable,” wound daily by Miss MacIntosh, stands against the stopped clocks of Catherine’s retreat.

Chapter 12

  • “the Big Ben alarm clock”: The Big Ben was the Western Clock Company’s alarm clock, sold from 1909 and the first alarm clock advertised across the country (1910). It takes its name from the great bell in London.
  • “no Tritons dreaming around the clock, no ladies weeping over dead birds, no sporting cupids”: French mantel clocks were crowded with gilded sea gods, nymphs, and cupids. Triton, son of Poseidon, blows a conch shell.
  • “each clock having been stopped at a different hour”: In Dickens’s Great Expectations (1861), Miss Havisham stops every clock at twenty minutes to nine, the hour she was jilted, and never leaves her room. Mourners once stopped the clocks at a death.
  • “It did not repeat the hours”: Repeater clocks and watches chime the last hour again at the pull of a cord or the press of a button, so the hour can be heard in the dark.

Chapter 27

  • “Any old silver-dollar stop watch should have done for him”: Miss MacIntosh’s “silver-dollar watch,” which she always wears (Chapters 3, 9, and 22). Ingersoll’s Yankee (1896), sold for a dollar, was “the watch that made the dollar famous.”
  • “more accurate than the sundials in the windy gardens”: The sundial motto “Horas non numero nisi serenas,” “I count only the sunny hours.”

Chapter 27 · Watches

  • Mr. Spitzer wears both his own watch and his brother’s. Miss MacIntosh also has a watch, her “old dollar watch which was given to her by her dead love” (Chapter 22).
  • The brother’s unbroken, elegant watch contrasts with Mr. Spitzer’s broken, dust-clogged timepiece.
  • Watches symbolize the passage and distortion of time, memory, and connection between the brothers.

Chapter 36 · Clocks and Watches

  • Mr. Spitzer would “consult his broken watch.”
  • Hannah “could not have been persuaded to stay beyond her hour or half hour or quarter hour, the strikings of distraught, fantastic cuckoo clocks.”

Chapter 39 · Clocks

  • She passes “faces like old town clocks seen through a blowing mist, each clock striking a different deranged hour.”
  • Lord Burdock is “striking like a dozen distraught city clocks,” “striking thirteen bells far out at sea where no time was.”

Chapter 41

  • “so many little cuckoo clock Swiss villages”: The cuckoo clock comes from Germany’s Black Forest, where clockmakers built it from the eighteenth century, not from Switzerland. Its Swiss home is a tourist’s, and a film’s: in The Third Man (1949) Harry Lime says Switzerland had “five hundred years of democracy and peace, and what did that produce? The cuckoo clock.”

Chapter 42

  • “if he knew the longitude, then he did not know the latitude”: Latitude can be read from the sun and stars, but longitude needs the exact time. The problem was solved by John Harrison’s marine chronometer H4 (1761), after the British Longitude Act of 1714 offered a prize. Mr. Spitzer carries “two wrist watches.”
  • “the crystalization of one sad, wild moment”: Miss Havisham stopped her clocks at the moment she was jilted.

Chapter 45

  • “No sundial marked her hour”: Sundials often carry the motto “Horas non numero nisi serenas,” “I count only the sunny hours.”
  • “Pigeons had stopped an old town clock.”: On August 12, 1945, a flock of starlings settled on the minute hand of Big Ben and slowed it by several minutes.

Chapter 46

  • “The great steeplechase is over.”: The first steeplechase was run in Ireland in 1752, from the church steeple at Buttevant to the steeple at Doneraile, by Cornelius O’Callaghan and Edmund Blake. Here it is run by the clock’s “tall jockey” and “short jockey.”

Chapter 47

  • “But time could not tell him the time”: Clocks and calendars mark time, but they cannot tell Mr. Spitzer where he stands in it. He consults “his broken watch… a watch with no numbers to the hours,” the sundial, the starfish, the kingfisher’s cry. His memory is fractured, and time has become ambiguous, perhaps cyclical, perhaps illusory: “To ask of time the time was like asking of the thief—Where is the jewel you stole?”

Chapter 47 · The Ambiguity of Identity and Time

  • Mr. Spitzer’s reflections reveal confusion about who he is, when he is, and how identity persists or dissolves across time and death.

Chapter 48

  • “after he had consulted his broken watch”: See “his broken watch… a watch with no numbers to the hours” in the Chapter 47 resources.

Chapter 57 · Timepieces (Two Wrist Watches)

  • Represent duality and the conflicting measures of time, cosmic and earthly, highlighting Mr. Spitzer’s fractured perception of time.

Chapter 65

  • “the great, loud-ticking watch, luminous and waterproof”: Luminous dials were painted with radium paint from the 1910s. The young women who painted them, the Radium Girls, were poisoned by pointing their brushes between their lips; in Ottawa, Illinois, the Radium Dial Company’s painters won their case in 1938, and their fight helped establish workers’ right to compensation for occupational disease.

Chapter 65 · The Watch and Biblical Quotations

  • Mr. Bonebreaker’s watch symbolizes time running out, the urgency of salvation, and the inevitability of the end.

Chapter 66

  • “Her man’s watch ticking on her shoulder”: Mr. Bonebreaker’s watch.

Chapter 68

  • “No clock struck”:

Chapter 69 · Mr. Weed’s Watch

  • A “world within a world,” symbolizing time, fate, or the inevitability of death.

Chapter 71

  • “All the clocks in the house having been stopped at a different time”: Compare Miss Havisham in Dickens’s Great Expectations (1861), who stopped every clock in her house at the minute she was jilted.

Chapter 71 · The Calendar and Books

  • Symbols of time, knowledge, and the passage from order to chaos.
  • The calendar stuck 20 years ago symbolizes frozen time and lost opportunity.

Chapter 79 · Symbolic Use of Time

  • The seven-year conception period symbolizes prolonged suffering and anticipation.
  • The anniversary visit to the other woman reflects attempts to reconcile past trauma.

Definition from research

Chapter 1 · Household Items on the Moving Van

  • Everyday objects gaining symbolic, almost surreal significance.

Chapter 1 · The Opulent but Empty House

  • Represents illusion, decay, and the failure of grandeur without truth.

Chapter 2 · The House and Its Rooms

  • Described as a shifting, labyrinthine space full of illusions, secret doors, and changing places.
  • Symbolizes Catherine’s mind and the shifting nature of reality.

Chapter 4 · Driftwood House and Fire on the Beach

  • Symbolize Vera’s fragile hope and attempt to reach out to Miss MacIntosh or the lost past.

Chapter 8 · The Old Tin House and Flooded Yard

  • The dilapidated house and refuse-strewn yard symbolize decay, neglect, and the harsh realities hidden behind appearances.

Chapter 10 · Twin Iron Bedsteads

  • Represent memory, duality, and the coexistence of past and present selves (Mr. Spitzer and his deceased brother).

Chapter 15 · The House and Its Contents

  • The “old, sea-blackened house” with “empty paddocks,” “marble statues,” and “granite birds” reflects decay, history, and the passage of time.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s sparse bedroom symbolizes emotional barrenness and detachment.

Chapter 16 · The House as a Tomb and Water Castle

  • The grand house is described with imagery of tombs, water, and underwater life, creating a sense of mystery and timelessness. The references to the phoenix and musical tomb further emphasize themes of death and rebirth.

Chapter 16 · Miss MacIntosh’s Bedroom Scene

  • Vera charges in on horseback, and Miss MacIntosh stands silent by the window, changed. This scene contrasts the fantastical ride with a stark moment of reality.

Chapter 18 · Curtains Blowing, Shutters Banging, Weathercocks Creaking

  • Create an atmosphere of instability and eerie music; symbolize the chaotic forces of change and the unknown.

Chapter 19 · Miss MacIntosh’s Bedroom

  • A large, sparsely furnished chamber, described as “barely furnished” with no dust-catchers, no hanging tapestries, no floating angels, reflecting a deliberate plainness.

Chapter 19 · Decor

  • Broken cherubim heads around a blackened fireplace, a bust of Martin Luther on a pedestal, a large sea shell used as a door stopper, cracked walls, and stained ceiling with broken cornices.

Chapter 19 · Details

  • Objects are scattered about her room: her red wig on a hat rack, a whale-boned corset, a silver-dollar watch pinned to a curtain, false teeth in a jeweled water glass, stockings, patches, knitting, a porcelain chamber pot, an empty picture frame, a broken ship’s compass, a chained Bible, and a Pullman towel.

Chapter 22 · The Breakfast Table

  • The ornately set table contrasts with the characters’ modest lives, symbolizing lost grandeur or unrealized potential.

Chapter 25 · The Twin Iron Beds and Golden Cradles

  • Symbolize the intertwined destinies of Mr. Spitzer and his brother.
  • Represent infancy, death, and the passage of time.

Chapter 31 · The Empty Mansion

  • The empty house, the broken lanterns, the snow-covered garden, and the silent rooms evoke a ghostly atmosphere of abandonment and mourning.
  • The Empty Mansion represents absence, memory, and the passage of time. The desolation and decay of the mansion mirror Cousin Hannah’s death and the fading of her presence.

Chapter 39

  • “my mother’s soul was like a many-spiraling house with many rooms”: “In my Father’s house are many mansions” (John 14:2). Teresa of Ávila pictured the soul as a castle of diamond or clear crystal with many rooms, as in heaven there are many mansions (The Interior Castle, 1577).

Chapter 39 · The Infinite House

  • Catherine’s soul is compared to a vast, labyrinthine house with many rooms and doorways.
  • Each room is a partial reflection of another, symbolizing fragmented consciousness.
  • “In every room, there was someone missing. There was something missing.”

Chapter 41 · The House

  • A living, shifting entity with invisible servants, moving through time and space.
  • Represents Catherine’s mind or inner world, harboring ghosts, memories, and dreams.

Chapter 42 · Mirrors and Reflections

  • The house with rooms of mirrors and endless reflections represents the multiplicity of perspectives and the elusive nature of truth and self.

Chapter 48 · The House

  • A metaphor for the realm between life and death or consciousness; its doors and windows are mysterious passageways.

Chapter 55 · The Twin House and Mirroring Rooms

  • Symbolize the divided self and fractured identity; also the attempt to impose order on life’s chaos.

Chapter 69 · Fire Escape Room

  • Symbolizes escape but also confinement, a place between safety and danger.

Definition from research

Chapter 6

  • “Quit barking up the wrong tree”: The phrase is American, from the 1830s, for a hunting dog barking at a tree its quarry has already left.
  • “all dressed like British lords in scarlet coats”: Fox-hunters’ red coats are called “hunting pink.”
  • “Death is an old hunter. Wait until you hear his winding horn”: In the legend of the Wild Hunt a ghostly huntsman rides through the winter sky with baying hounds, and to hear him meant death.

Chapter 14

  • “the barkings of spotted coach dogs running beside the wheels”: Dalmatians were bred to run beside carriages, clearing the road and guarding the horses.
  • “her Seeing Eye dogs”: The Seeing Eye, the first American guide dog school, was founded in 1929.
  • “knew that the dog was Socrates”: Socrates was a Greek philosopher who wrote no texts of his own but is credited as one of the founders of Western philosophy. In the work Republic, written by Plato, there is a Socratic dialogue. In it Socrates argues that the dog is very much like a philosopher because the dog distinguishes the face of a friend and of an enemy only by the criterion of knowing and not knowing. (Wikipedia) Socrates swore “By the dog, the god of the Egyptians” (Gorgias 482b).

Chapter 15

  • “The old sheep dog barking in the night had not barked for nothing”: The proverb is “An old dog barks not in vain,” from George Herbert’s Outlandish Proverbs (1640).

Chapter 16

  • “the effigy of a sleeping marble boy lying on his tomb”: Medieval tomb effigies often rest their feet on a dog, the sign of fidelity.

Chapter 18

  • “Why bark if one keeps a dog?”: “Why keep a dog and bark yourself?” (1583).

Chapter 21

  • “the old, blind sheep dog running ahead of us on three legs”: The dog still “guarding the pasture which was no more against the thief who would not come.”

Chapter 22

  • “An old dog barks at nothing”: This turns around the proverb of Chapter 15, “An old dog barks not in vain.”

Chapter 31

  • “the old St. Bernard”: The monks of the Great St. Bernard Hospice bred their dogs to find travelers lost in Alpine snow. Barry (1800-1814) is said to have saved forty lives. The brandy cask was the invention of the painter Edwin Landseer (1820).

Chapter 33

  • “the fashionable dog fancier”: A dog fancier breeds and shows pedigree dogs. The Westminster Kennel Club held its first show in New York in 1877.

Chapter 34

  • “she had been married by a St. Bernard dog, an Alpine retriever”: The hospice dogs of the Great St. Bernard Pass.

Chapter 34 · The St. Bernard Dog

  • A prophetic figure in Catherine’s dreams, symbolizing guidance, loss, and perhaps spiritual rites.

Chapter 35

  • The Persian hound is likely the saluki, also called the Persian greyhound.

Chapter 40

  • “the long-bodied coach dogs barking at the wheels”: Coach dogs, usually Dalmatians, ran beside carriages to guard the horses.

Chapter 48

  • “He was the dog barking at the Dog star in the cloud”: The Dog star is Sirius in the constellation, Canis Major, the Greater Dog. Homer calls Sirius the dog of Orion, the brightest of stars but a sign of evil (Iliad 22.26-31).

Chapter 59

  • “the barkings of red-eyed dogs accompanying dead souls to Hades”: In northern English folklore the Gabriel Hounds, or Gabble Ratchets, were a spectral pack heard yelping overhead at night, and their cry foretold a death; the sound was probably wild geese in passage.

Chapter 62

  • “running coach dogs running silently”: The Dalmatian was the coach dog, bred to trot beside or beneath carriages and guard the horses; fire engines kept the custom.

Chapter 66

  • “Greater dog, he said, was man”: The Dog Star is a nickname for Sirius, a star in the constellation Canis Major (Greater Dog).
  • “He told her that he was a Great Dane”: “Great Dane” is a German breed of large mastiff-sighthound, which descends from hunting dogs of the Middle Ages used to hunt bears, wild boar, and deer. This expresses the Arctic Explorer’s tough, solitary character marked by loss and endurance, a man who carries dog-like loyalty and survival instincts but is also physically and emotionally wounded. The explorer is a pun: a great Dane.
  • “she had known a dog who had been Greater Man”: The explorer calls himself harmless, “Greater Dog,” and Miss MacIntosh recalls a dog in What Cheer who had been “Greater Man,” for he had eaten his drunken master, to whom he was chained and who had frozen to death in the Arctic cold.

Chapter 68

  • “his heels had been nipped by an old hound pursuing him through oceanic storms”: Compare Francis Thompson’s “The Hound of Heaven” (1890), on a soul pursued by God: “I fled Him, down the nights and down the days.”
  • “They were playing blind man’s buff behind the hill”: In blind man’s buff, a blindfolded player gropes to catch the others, as the children had blindfolded the blind dog.

Chapter 68 · The Blindfolded Dog

  • Innocence and cruelty intertwined, reflecting on blindness to suffering.
  • The village is described as dilapidated and eerie, with details like rusted machinery, broken wheels, and a sign “Gentle Incline —Bride Ahead—” which is a false reading for “Bridge Ahead,” evoking a sense of decay and death.
  • The Tavern, built in 1827 by “God’s servants,” is a gloomy, sprawling hotel with mildewed brick, claw-like vines, and a haunting presence. Its interior surpasses Vera’s imagination, filled with human-faced wasps and thin walls that seem to hear everything.
  • The atmosphere is filled with silence, shadows, and a slow, suffocating sense of inevitability, preparing the reader for the philosophical and existential meditations that follow.

Chapter 71

  • “this was a dogs’ graveyard”: America’s oldest pet cemetery, at Hartsdale, New York, opened in 1896.

Chapter 71 · The Dogs’ Graveyard

  • Represents death, loyalty, and the neglect of forgotten beings, mirroring the hotel’s decay.

Chapter 82 · The Silent Dog and Barking

  • Represent intuition and knowledge beyond human perception, especially about death.
