Definition from research

Chapter 12

  • “put his bet on the dark horse”: The phrase comes from Disraeli’s The Young Duke (1831): “a dark horse, which had never been thought of.”

Chapter 14 · The Black Coachman and the Family Carriage

  • Symbolizes continuity beyond death, the passage of time, and the family’s legacy, Catherine’s conscience and body.
  • The mystery of his grave and whether he was buried with his horses signifies Catherine’s fear of disruption and loss.

Chapter 14 · White Horses (King, Queen, Prince, Spade)

  • These horses have personified names and represent stability and tradition.
  • Their fate is ambiguous, mirroring the uncertainty in the narrative.

Chapter 14

  • “the four white horses”: White horses in mythology are often associated with the sun chariot, warrior-heroes, fertility, and an end-of-time savior. The white horses symbolize the solemn, mystical journey of the soul from life into death and beyond, carrying Catherine through the shifting landscapes of memory, dream, and existence by her will. They are a powerful emblem of transition, purity, fate, and the ethereal nature of mortality in the novel. In Revelation, “behold a white horse: and he that sat on him had a bow; and a crown was given unto him” (Revelation 6:2).
  • “the barkings of spotted coach dogs running beside the wheels”: Dalmatians were bred to run beside carriages, clearing the road and guarding the horses.
  • “King and Queen, Prince and Spade”: The horses are named like playing cards, and the aces fall later in the chapter.
  • “the coachman was her conscience”: The Katha Upanishad: “Know the Self as the lord of the chariot, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, the mind as the reins, and the senses as the horses.” In Plato’s Phaedrus, the soul is a charioteer driving two horses.
  • “driving a coach and six through a legal statute”: Attributed to the Irish judge Stephen Rice in the 1680s: “I will drive a coach and six through the Act of Settlement.”
  • “a horseshoe of white roses”: Floral horseshoes and saddles of roses honored racing men. Since 1932 the Kentucky Derby winner has worn a garland of roses.

Chapter 16

  • “The fierce, exultant pride that was mine”: In “What Is It with Women and Horses?” (Intelligent Horsemanship, 2019), Dr. Rosie Jones-McVey, drawing on her PhD research among British horsewomen, writes: “In Victorian novels, as well as in the more modern genre of pony-girl books, it is often aboard a horse that girls find their wings, often proving some snot-nosed boy wrong in the process, or enabling them to escape various romantic dramas and find solace in the barn. Just like the pony-girl books, many of my participants’ life stories entwined horseyness with coming-of-age stories. Horses were the means through which many women first acted in a truly independent way, often pursuing equestrian endeavours despite/without their parents, or else, proudly taking up adult-like responsibilities in being the teacher, pilot, and carer of their ponies, rather than the one being looked after and told what to do.” She argues that horses give many women a space for independence and self-assertion that their everyday lives do not.
  • “It was a steeplechase, and we would jump over all the church steeples”: The first steeplechase (1752) was a race across Irish country from one church steeple to the next.
  • “I was a bareback rider, wearing a plume, a pair of pink tights”: Philip Astley’s London circus (1768) began as trick riding in a ring, and the bareback equestrienne in tights became the star of American circuses.
  • “Falada could dance on his hind feet”: The levade and capriole of the Lipizzaners of Vienna’s Spanish Riding School, where horses rear and leap on command.
  • “served as a model for merry-go-round horses because of his grace in keeping all fours off the earth at once”: In 1878 Eadweard Muybridge photographed Leland Stanford’s horse Sallie Gardner and proved that a galloping horse lifts all four hooves at once, though not stretched out, as on carousel horses.
  • “the cabriole, the furniture of good Queen Anne’s day, whole forests of Chippendale”: Queen Anne furniture stands on curved cabriole legs, shaped like an animal’s leg. The name comes from the French cabriole, a goat’s leap. In dressage, the capriole is the horse’s leap with all four feet off the ground. Thomas Chippendale published his Director in 1754.
  • “following the movements of an imaginary polo ball”: Polo came to England from India with British cavalry officers in the 1860s, and Vera wears her “polo hat cocked back at a jaunty angle.”

Chapter 16 · Falada

  • Falada, the little black pony given to Vera by Mr. Spitzer, carries rich symbolic meaning that intertwines with Vera’s inner world and her journey.
  • Falada is described as an old, tired, wind-broken pony, light as a spirit, with a sagging back, a scrappy mane, and a knotted tail. Despite his physical frailty and advanced age, Falada moves with grace and seems almost magical, responding to Vera’s desires as if he were her own intelligence or head. The pony is said to be descended from a horse that inspired the jewel-studded horses of merry-go-rounds and carousels, connecting him to themes of childhood innocence and the cyclical nature of life and dreams.
  • Falada embodies a loyal, gentle companion who carries Vera through her internal struggles and the uncertain landscapes of her life. His responsiveness to her unspoken commands suggests an intimate connection between Vera’s mind and her means of navigating reality and illusion.
  • Although Falada is physically frail, he continues to carry Vera with grace and resilience. This mirrors Vera’s own vulnerability and strength as she faces the challenges of growing up and understanding complex realities.
  • Falada’s origin as a model for carousel horses evokes childhood fantasy and cyclical repetition, resonating with Vera’s oscillation between dream and reality. His presence blurs the lines between the tangible and the imaginary, reflecting the novel’s themes of perception and illusion.
  • Given by Mr. Spitzer, Falada also symbolizes a connection to a past that is both real and mythical, and perhaps a hope for guidance and stability amid chaos. His lineage to historical and artistic forms evokes continuity and the search for meaning.
  • Falada is described as seeming like Vera’s head or intelligence, suggesting that the pony is an extension or manifestation of her self-awareness and agency, her “headless rider” identity where the horse seems to guide the rider as much as the rider guides the horse.
  • Falada is a potent symbol of Vera’s complex inner life: her innocence, her challenges, her search for identity and direction, and the interplay between dream and reality that defines her experience in the novel.

Chapter 16 · Other Motifs

  • Falada represents freedom, imagination, and the link between past and present.
  • Moon and Stars are symbols of mystery, guidance, and the unconscious.
  • Marble Statues and Tombs are symbols of death, memory, and permanence.
  • Water and Sea Motifs represent transition, silence, and the unknown.
  • The entire ride is a metaphor for Vera’s inner journey. The horse is described as “almost only an idea,” and the house is likened to a tomb and an underwater castle.
  • References to historical furniture styles (Queen Anne, Chippendale), mythological creatures (phoenix, Triton), and fairy tales (the fairy tale of Falada, which Mr. Spitzer calls Arabic) enrich the novel’s layers.
  • The setting is a magical, moonlit garden and a grand, mysterious house filled with symbolic statues and motifs.

Chapter 17

  • “It was a horse ballet, a Spanish carousel with many mirrors”: Baroque courts staged horse ballets, and the carrousel was first a tournament of horsemen, like Louis XIV’s Grand Carrousel of 1662.

Chapter 17 · Animal Imagery

  • Falada, Vera’s old pony, a present from Mr. Spitzer, represents loyalty and alertness but is powerless.
  • Vera’s comparison of Miss MacIntosh to a “codfish swept up upon a barren shore” and “old man” adds to the grotesque transformation.

Chapter 18 · The Rider and the Horse

  • Metaphor for the unity of self and illusion, indicating the inseparability of dream and dreamer.
  • Vera wonders if she has “become Falada,” with Miss MacIntosh now the rider.

Chapter 18

  • “as if I myself had become Falada”: Vera’s pony of Chapter 16, named for the horse in the Grimm tale.

Chapter 22

  • “has won the famous steeplechase at Aintree where is the dreaded water-jump”: Master Robert, who had once pulled a plow, won the Grand National at Aintree in 1924.

Chapter 24

  • “Some had seen the black coachman”: The coachman and the white horses of Chapter 14.

Chapter 24 · Black and White Horses and Coachman

  • Black and white horses and coachman symbolize the passage between realms, possibly life and death, or reality and illusion. Earlier (Chapter 14) Catherine said the white horses were her will and the coachman was her conscience.

Chapter 26

  • “the great crowds of Derby Day”: The Derby at Epsom, run since 1780. William Powell Frith painted its crowds in “The Derby Day” (1858).

Chapter 27

  • “the great breakers coming in with their foaming manes and tails”: Poseidon was god of the sea and of horses, and breaking waves are still called “white horses.”

Chapter 32

  • “should have been employed by the old Pony Express”: Relays of riders carried the mail between St. Joseph, Missouri, and Sacramento, California, from April 1860 until the telegraph replaced them in October 1861.
  • “the black horses who wore black plumes”: Victorian hearses were drawn by black horses wearing tall plumes of black ostrich feathers.
  • “a riderless horse white as snow came through the window”: A riderless horse follows the coffin in state funerals. Lincoln’s horse, Old Bob, was led behind his hearse in Springfield in 1865, and Black Jack followed John F. Kennedy’s coffin in 1963.

Chapter 32 · The Riderless White Horse and Rider Imagery

  • The image of a riderless white horse “white as snow” coming through the window, bringing snow and cold with it, is a powerful symbol of death or the passing of Cousin Hannah.
  • The white horse traditionally symbolizes a harbinger of death or a psychopomp figure in literature, and here it represents the transition from life to death for this warrior woman.

Chapter 33 · The Black Coachman and Carriage

  • Symbolize passage, possibly death or transition.
  • The carriage on the streets of Boston, after years of absence, signals a disruption of normal order.
  • In Chapter 14 Catherine said her body was the carriage and “the coachman was her conscience.”

Chapter 35 · Horses and Riders

  • “She would have ridden naked through the gale. She would have ridden through the storm of years.”
  • She “had ridden horseback through many distant capitals already evacuated and was like a great stone horseman with a stone helmet.”
  • Mr. Spitzer thought “the fearful captain of the horse quite gloomy.”

Chapter 36 · Animals and Nature

  • Birds (blackbirds, seagulls), horses, and natural phenomena (fog, wind, fireflies) evoke transformation, freedom, and the boundary between worlds.
  • The black coachman lies where “the white manes of the running horses” streak the waves.

Chapter 37

  • “Had not the riderless horse already come”: A riderless horse with boots reversed in the stirrups follows the coffin in a military funeral, as Black Jack did at John F. Kennedy’s funeral in November 1963. In Chapter 32 a riderless horse “white as snow came through the window” the day Hannah died.

Chapter 37 · The Black Coachman

  • A symbol of death or transition. In Chapter 14 Catherine likens the coachman to “her dead consciousness fantastically dreaming.”

Chapter 37 · The Riderless Horse and Conch Trumpet

  • Symbolize death’s arrival and the end of an era or life. The horse comes “to signify that the great postilion was dead.”

Chapter 40

  • “She was struck by moon blindness”: Catherine claims to have moon blindness even though she knew it affected horses and not humans. Moon blindness or equine recurrent uveitis is the leading cause of blindness in horses with the specific cause unknown.
  • “A horse knew what the horseman did not know”: Balaam’s ass saw what Balaam could not: “And the ass saw the angel of the LORD standing in the way, and his sword drawn in his hand” (Numbers 22:23).

Chapter 40 · The Horse and Rider

  • Symbolize unity and inseparability of entities, reflecting on identity and consciousness.
  • “Sometimes she thought she was riding on her own back… she did not know whether she was the horse or the rider, the carrier or the carried.”

Chapter 42

  • “the four alabaster horses”: The four alabaster horses of the opening become “the eight long-necked horses” a few lines later.

Chapter 42 · Glass Carriage and Alabaster Horses

  • Symbolize the ethereal, dreamlike journey between worlds or states of being. The horses’ heads turning like foam and their journey through clouds evoke a passage beyond the physical.

Chapter 46

  • “remembered in no stud book of mountain-climbing”: The General Stud Book, begun by James Weatherby in 1791, records the pedigree of every English thoroughbred.
  • “The great steeplechase is over.”: The first steeplechase was run in Ireland in 1752, from the church steeple at Buttevant to the steeple at Doneraile, by Cornelius O’Callaghan and Edmund Blake. Here it is run by the clock’s “tall jockey” and “short jockey.”

Chapter 48

  • “He was always posting, trotting, gaiting”: These are the paces of a riding horse. Posting is rising and falling with the trot; the rack and the slow single-foot are the extra gaits of the five-gaited American Saddlebred.

Chapter 51

  • “glimmering hedgerow of stars all must jump”: See the steeplechase in the Chapter 46 resources.
  • “if reality had been a horse”: Mr. Spitzer thinks that if reality was a horse or a ship he would only know one small part of the thing. This is similar to the Blind Men and the Elephant parable whose moral is that humans have a tendency to claim absolute truth based on their limited, subjective experience and they ignore others’ limited, subjective experiences which may be equally true. The parable is told in the Buddhist Udana (6.4) and in John Godfrey Saxe’s poem “The Blind Men and the Elephant” (1872).

Chapter 55 · The Coach and Horses

  • Symbolize the journey of life and death; Joachim often finds himself in the wrong carriage, lost in time and space.

Chapter 56

  • “the brougham which was named after Lord Brougham”: Henry Brougham (1778-1868), Lord Chancellor from 1830 to 1834, helped pass the Reform Act of 1832 and the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833, which ended slavery in most of the British Empire. The brougham, a light closed carriage, was built to his design in 1838. Young’s dates for him are right.
  • “the great phaetons”: Phaethon, son of the sun god Helios, drove his father’s chariot, lost control, and was struck down by Zeus; the light, open phaeton carriage is named for him.
  • “lost in the horse latitudes”: The horse latitudes, about thirty degrees north and south of the equator, are belts of calm where sailing ships could lie becalmed for weeks; the legend says sailors threw horses overboard there to save water.

Chapter 57

  • “landaus, barouches, phaetons like great sea shells”: A landau is a four-wheel luxury carriage with a roof that can be let down.

Chapter 60

  • “passing the horse fountains”: Between 1902 and 1915 Hermon Lee Ensign’s National Humane Alliance gave about 125 granite watering troughs to American cities, for horses, dogs, cats, and people.

Chapter 62

  • “running coach dogs running silently”: The Dalmatian was the coach dog, bred to trot beside or beneath carriages and guard the horses; fire engines kept the custom.
  • “old trot, trot sheet music”: The “trot, trot” is the cab horse’s gait in Pick’s Fiakerlied, the song of a Viennese fiacre driver.
  • Anna Sewell’s Black Beauty (1877) was written partly to end the cruelty of the bearing rein, which held a horse’s head painfully high.

Chapter 64

  • “Driving each day a team of great Percherons”: The Percheron is a breed of draft horse that originated in the Huisne river valley in western France.

Chapter 72

  • “being that being from which no mortal issue comes”: The mule, foaled of a male donkey and a mare, is almost always sterile. The mule embodies a threshold or boundary between life and death, fertility and barrenness, creative potential and its cessation. In the broader context of the novel, which often interweaves themes of decay, loss, and the boundaries between reality and dreams, this image can be interpreted as a symbol of stagnation or an end point in the cycle of life. It also resonates with the novel’s attention to characters who are trapped in states of limbo or arrested development, such as the doctor delivering imaginary babies or the hangman haunted by the children of the hanged. The passage conveys a mood of desolation and quiet warning about reaching a place where creation and renewal cease, urging the narrator (and the reader) to recognize the significance of this boundary in the unfolding narrative and in life itself.
  • Wild ponies have run on Assateague Island, off Virginia and Maryland, for centuries; legend makes them survivors of a Spanish shipwreck. Marguerite Henry’s Misty of Chincoteague (1947) made them famous.
  • “the wild white mothers be fecundated by the wind”: There are myths about animals, not just mares, being impregnated by the wind. Pliny and Virgil told it of the mares of Lusitania. See the wind-made mares in the Chapter 71 resources.

Chapter 72 · The grey mule and manure wagon

  • Symbolize burden, endurance, and the dead-end nature of Esther’s existence.

Chapter 73

  • “The old grey mule had stood with head hanging over a fence”: See the barren mule in the Chapter 72 resources.

Chapter 74

  • “a crazy old mule in heat”: See the barren mule in the Chapter 72 resources and the Chapter 73 resources.
  • “God, she was not mulish!”: Esther insisted that she was not “mulish.” Being mulish means to be stubborn.

Chapter 77

  • “a wild, pregnant mare horsing around in the courtroom”: See the wild mares made pregnant by the wind in the Chapter 72 resources.

Chapter 78

  • “Poor Little Jackass, stinging inside”: See Balaam’s ass and the barren mule in the Chapter 72 resources.

Chapter 79

  • “that would be a treacling mill”: A mule walking in an endless circle turned the rollers of a cane mill, pressing sorghum or sugar cane for molasses, or treacle; a merry-go-round of mules would be such a mill.

Chapter 80

  • “an old sporting page that had to do with the Kentucky race-horses”: “Kentucky racehorses” Horse racing in Kentucky predates statehood (1792), with organized racing occurring in Louisville as early as 1783. All Kentucky thoroughbreds trace their lineage back to three foundation sires: the Darley Arabian, the Godolphin Arabian, and the Byerly Turk. On May 17, 1875, the first Kentucky Derby was held at Churchill Downs (then the Louisville Jockey Club). It was won by Aristides, trained by Ansel Williamson and ridden by Black jockey Oliver Lewis. In the first 28 runnings of the Derby, Black jockeys won 15 times. Notable jockeys included Isaac Murphy (three-time winner) and the aforementioned Oliver Lewis. Key winners included Vagrant (1876), the first gelding winner, and Hindoo (1881). In 1902, a syndicate led by Col. Matt Winn took over Churchill Downs, transforming it into a premier racing venue. In 1919, Sir Barton became the first horse to win the Kentucky Derby, Preakness, and Belmont Stakes, though the term “Triple Crown” was not commonly used until 1930 with Gallant Fox. Exterminator (1918) was a fan favorite who won despite being a last-minute substitute. Calumet Farm became the dominant force in American racing, with winners like Whirlaway (1941), Pensive (1944), Ponder (1949), and Hill Gail (1952). Often considered one of the greatest horses of all time, Citation won the Triple Crown and became the first horse to win $1 million.

Chapter 82

  • “seeming to be scaling like the moon”: Here “scaling” means flaking off in scales, as old paint or skin does: the old white horse is “streaked with grey and scaling, flaking like the moon.”
  • “the old nag turning into the golden mare”: Young read about racehorse “ringers” painted to race under false colors: “I read of one marvelous case at Saratoga Springs when it was a rain storm in the midst of the race, and people with absolute horror looked out to see the old nag turning into the speeder, losing the mottled coat.” She also read lives of John W. “Bet-a-Million” Gates and Diamond Jim Brady (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 82 · The Old White Horse and Surrey

  • Symbolize the passage toward death and the journey between worlds. The horse turning into silver, blue, green, and gold hints at transformation and transcendence.

In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 3, Chapter 8, Chapter 9, Chapter 10, Chapter 11, Chapter 14, Chapter 15, Chapter 16, Chapter 18, Chapter 19, Chapter 21, Chapter 22, Chapter 27, Chapter 30, Chapter 36, Chapter 37, Chapter 39, Chapter 42, Chapter 43, Chapter 44, Chapter 45, Chapter 47, Chapter 49, Chapter 50, Chapter 54, Chapter 56, Chapter 58, Chapter 59, Chapter 61, Chapter 62, Chapter 63, Chapter 64, Chapter 65, Chapter 66, Chapter 68, Chapter 74, Chapter 75, Chapter 76, Chapter 79, Chapter 81, Chapter 82

Definition from research

Chapter 2 · The Sea and Water Imagery

  • Catherine is often associated with water, tides, and drowning.
  • Symbolizes her immersion in dreams, unconsciousness, and the fluidity of existence.

Chapter 3 · Sea and Surf

  • Represent the uncontrollable forces of nature and time.
  • The beach is the boundary between worlds and the place where Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance occurs.

Chapter 8 · The Broken Windshield Wiper and Flooded Road

  • Symbolize vulnerability and the overwhelming forces of nature or fate that the characters cannot control.

Chapter 8 · The Old Tin House and Flooded Yard

  • The dilapidated house and refuse-strewn yard symbolize decay, neglect, and the harsh realities hidden behind appearances.

Chapter 9 · Sea and Water Imagery

  • The sea, waves, tides, fog, and shore recur repeatedly as symbols of life’s uncertainty, danger, and transition.
  • The sea represents the unknown, the subconscious, and the boundary between life and death.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s identity as a “land-locked sailor” who “could not swim an inch” but who constantly talks in nautical terms symbolizes a life caught between stability and the wild, uncontrollable forces of nature.

Chapter 10

  • “Porpoises shall eat the drowned sailor. The waters of this world shall close over his head”: The preacher gives the bride and groom a sailor’s burial at sea. Milton’s “Lycidas” (1638) mourns a friend drowned in the Irish Sea, and Ariel sings of a drowned father in The Tempest: “Full fathom five thy father lies.” The line foreshadows Miss MacIntosh lost in the waves.

Chapter 11

  • “his intimate name, Ocean or Water”: Elizabeth called him “Water.” Spenser named him “the Shepherd of the Ocean” in Colin Clouts Come Home Againe (1595), and Raleigh wrote The Ocean’s Love to Cynthia, with the Queen as the moon who rules the tides.

Chapter 14 · Imagery of Water, Snow, and Night

  • Recurring references to water, foaming seas, snowflakes, and darkness evoke a liminal, otherworldly atmosphere.
  • These natural elements symbolize change, decay, and the boundary between life and death.

Chapter 15 · The Sea

  • Symbolizes life’s vastness, mystery, and power.
  • The “black, whirling waters” and “primal memories” suggest subconscious depths and timeless forces.
  • The sea’s roar and the waves breaking evoke both danger and excitement.

Chapter 15

  • “my body gleaming with finny phosphorescence”: Late summer seas glow with bioluminescent plankton when the water is stirred.

Chapter 16

  • “the great mother-of-pearl mollusk which might have contained the form of Venus”: Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus (c. 1485) shows the goddess rising from the sea on a scallop shell.
  • “the shell which was the great turbaned Turk, the phaeton, the winding stairway”: These are real shells. The turban shell is one, and the wentletrap takes its name from the Dutch for “winding staircase.”
  • “I should be the umbrella medusa rising to the surface”: The jellyfish’s bell is called its umbrella, and its free-swimming stage is the medusa.

Chapter 16 · The House as a Tomb and Water Castle

  • The grand house is described with imagery of tombs, water, and underwater life, creating a sense of mystery and timelessness. The references to the phoenix and musical tomb further emphasize themes of death and rebirth.

Chapter 18 · The Sea, Waves, and Tides

  • Evoke transience, the unconscious, and the relentless movement of life and death.

Chapter 19

  • “a clump of blackened seaweed hanging on a nail on the door”: “much like some other wig.” Miss MacIntosh will be lost to the sea.

Chapter 21 · Sea and Light

  • The sea light covering the scene suggests mystery, change, and the vastness of life’s experience.

Chapter 22

  • “the sea is full of wrinkles, though it has neither age nor grey hairs”: “Time writes no wrinkle on thine azure brow: / Such as creation’s dawn beheld, thou rollest now” (Byron, Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage IV, 1818).

Chapter 22 · Memory and Forgetfulness

  • The sea, a recurring motif, is described as both full of “wrinkles” and yet possibly without memory. This paradox symbolizes the blurred lines between remembering and forgetting, life and oblivion.

Chapter 22 · The Sea

  • Represents memory, oblivion, and the passage of time. It is both a life source and a graveyard, swallowing ships and memories alike.

Chapter 27

  • “the great breakers coming in with their foaming manes and tails”: Poseidon was god of the sea and of horses, and breaking waves are still called “white horses.”

Chapter 30 · Ships and Seas

  • Metaphors for passage between life and death, reality and dream.

Chapter 36 · Water and the Sea

  • Recurring images of water, surf, tides, and waves symbolize fluidity, change, and the unconscious.
  • Water is associated with identity shifts and the impermanence of life.
  • The ground under Mr. Spitzer’s feet is “the nightmare ocean where all must change identities.”
  • Hannah has crossed “the shoreless sea of which there was no end.” “There was no sea.”

Chapter 37 · Sea and Waves

  • The sea is a motif for transformation, fluidity, and the unconscious.

Chapter 39

  • Gloucester has lost thousands of fishermen to the sea. Its Fisherman’s Memorial (1925) bears the words “They that go down to the sea in ships” (Psalm 107:23).
  • “striking thirteen bells far out at sea”: A ship’s bell strikes at most eight bells, at the end of each four-hour watch. Thirteen bells is no time at all.

Chapter 39 · Sea and Shore

  • The meeting of sea and land as a metaphor for the interface between life and death, reality and dream.

Chapter 42

  • “one eye burning to starboard, one to larboard”: Larboard, the old word for the left side of a ship, sounded so much like starboard that the Royal Navy replaced it with “port” in 1844.

Chapter 42 · Lost Ships and Stars

  • Ships represent journeys, lost hopes, and the passage of souls. Stars symbolize guidance, memory, and the unreachable. Mr. Spitzer’s cataloging of lost ships parallels the attempt to map lost lives and loves.

Chapter 43 · Skirt of Clouds and Waters

  • Symbolizes beauty, identity, and the suffragette’s fading presence.

Chapter 44

  • “the dead heart was like a sea shell carrying its own roaring”: The roar in a sea shell is not the sea. The shell gathers the sounds around it and echoes them back.

Chapter 45

  • “great krakens curling around the helms of boats”: “Below the thunders of the upper deep, / Far, far beneath in the abysmal sea, / His ancient, dreamless, uninvaded sleep / The Kraken sleepeth” (Alfred Tennyson, “The Kraken,” 1830).

Chapter 45 · Sea Shell/Sea

  • Memory, the call of the unknown, the eternal sea of life and death.

Chapter 47 · Stars, Moons, and Waves

  • Cosmic cycles, impermanence, and spiritual journeying (throughout).

Chapter 49

  • “the mermaid giving milk to her young”: Manatees and dugongs, which nurse their young at the breast, are often named as a source of mermaid legends. Columbus saw three “mermaids” off Hispaniola in January 1493 and wrote that they “were not so beautiful as they are painted.”

Chapter 49 · Water and Ice

  • Recurring images of frozen waters, ice domes, and watery graves symbolize stasis, death, and the frozen moment between life and death.
  • Water also represents fluidity, dream states, and the passage between worlds.

Chapter 50

  • “trembling mirages piling up like mountainous waves”: The castles that appear and vanish over the water recall the Fata Morgana, the mirage of towers and castles seen above the Strait of Messina and named for Morgan le Fay.
  • “there was neither starboard nor larboard”: Larboard, the left side of a ship, was replaced by “port” because it was too easily confused with starboard; the Royal Navy made the change official in 1844.
  • “false signal lights luring him out of his depths”: Wreckers of Cornish legend were said to show false lights on the cliffs to lure ships onto the rocks for plunder.
  • “a light upon the water”: “Who layeth the beams of his chambers in the waters: who maketh the clouds his chariot: who walketh upon the wings of the wind” (Psalm 104:3).

Chapter 50 · Water and Tides

  • Represent flux, the movement between life and death, progress and retreat, echoing the ebb and flow of existence.

Chapter 54 · The Sea and Water Imagery

  • The sea symbolizes the unconscious, the fluidity of reality, and the passage between life and death. Underwater fountains, sea’s burning gold, and submerged cities evoke a dreamlike state and loss.

Chapter 56 · Clouds, Sea, and Tides

  • Recurring natural motifs representing impermanence, change, and the fluid boundary between life and death.

Chapter 58

  • “sea shells buzzing like bees”: The sea heard in a shell is the noise of the room around it, echoing in the shell’s hollow, which sounds some pitches more than others.
  • “an oyster bed invaded by a starfish derby”: Starfish are the oysterman’s plague: a starfish pulls an oyster’s shell open with its tube feet and turns its own stomach inside out into the shell to digest it.
  • “the star lilies swimming through dark waters”: Young’s star lilies are crinoids, sea lilies and feather stars, animals that look like flowers. A feather star begins life on a stalk like a lily and then breaks free and swims. Their “sea-change” is Ariel’s: “Nothing of him that doth fade / But doth suffer a sea-change / Into something rich and strange” (William Shakespeare, The Tempest, 1.2).
  • “a dead sea shell was not dead but only sleeping”: Some sea shells do strike. Cone snails harpoon their prey with a venomous tooth, and the sting of the geography cone has killed people.

Chapter 59

  • “roaring like the cockles of his heart”: The “cockles of the heart,” its innermost depths, is often traced to the Latin cochleae cordis, the ventricles of the heart, or to the heart-shaped cockle shell.

Chapter 61

  • “the lute turtle sleeping in the mud”: The leatherback sea turtle is also called the lute turtle, or luth, for the ridges along its shell, which reminded French naturalists of a lute.
  • “he is wrapped in his sail and should have had a sea burial”: At sea the dead were sewn into a hammock or a length of sail, weighted with shot, and slid over the side while the captain read the burial service; by sailors’ custom the last stitch went through the nose.
  • “moving by summation”: A sea anemone’s nerve net acts by summation: one touch may do nothing, but repeated touches add up until the animal contracts. A medusa, or jellyfish, swims by pulsing its bell.
  • “to be the great conchologist”: A conchologist is a person who studies and collects shells, typically those of marine mollusks.

  • Symbolize journeys, the passage of time, and the blending of past, present, and future.

Chapter 62

  • “there were great fiddler crabs following the boats”: The male fiddler crab has one enormous claw, which he waves like a fiddler’s bow to court females and warn off rivals.

  • “east of almighty Taurus like a great wentletrap”: Wentletraps are small, often white, very high-spired, predatory or ectoparasitic sea snails, marine gastropod mollusks in the family Epitoniidae. These snails are sometimes also called “staircase shells,” and “ladder shells.” Precious wentletraps once sold for great sums, and Chinese counterfeits are said to have been molded from rice paste.
  • “dreams of fishes sleeping in anemones like birds in nests”: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, protected by a coat of mucus.

  • Metaphors for the flow of life, time, and reality. The river transforms from fire to ice, representing change and the cyclical nature of existence.

  • Symbolize the passage of time, death, and the subconscious.

  • Quotes and allusions to Ovid and Greek perspectives on beauty and hair enhance the classical depth of the novel.

Chapter 21

  • “The Devil does not always wear horns”: In Goethe’s Faust (1808), Mephistopheles tells the witch that the devil has given up his horns, tail, and claws to keep up with the times.
  • “the Devil wore a red coat and a pair of green breeches”: Folklore often makes the Devil a gentleman and a dancer. In Burns’s “Tam o’ Shanter” (1791), “auld Nick” plays the pipes for the witches’ dance.
  • “The Devil, she had said when opening her black umbrella in the sunlight, is God’s ape”: The devil as God’s ape, simia Dei, who mocks God by imitating Him, is an old Christian saying, often traced to the Church Fathers and used by Luther.   • “the groupings of beats or pulses into equal measures, accelerated or delayed”: Meter and tempo: accelerando and ritardando.
  • “the holding over of one or more tones of a chord into the following chord”: In music, a suspension is a note held over from one chord into the next. It clashes, then resolves, and here the resolution never comes.

Chapter 41

  • “thousands and ten thousands of piano keys”: Hermann von Helmholtz likened the inner ear to a piano whose strings each answer to one pitch, proposing first the arches of Corti and then the fibers of the basilar membrane as the tuned strings (Hermann von Helmholtz, On the Sensations of Tone, 1863, trans. Alexander J. Ellis, 1875).

Chapter 43 · Music (Lute, Harp, Bells)

  • Represents the ethereal, transcendent aspects of life and death; the music continues even as life fades.

Chapter 43 · Bellrope / Bells

  • Represent the passage of time, calling, and the inevitability of death.

Chapter 44

  • “Who rung these changes?”: In change ringing, a band of bell-ringers rings a set of bells in every possible order without repeating. To ring the changes is to try every variation. See the bells in the Chapter 59 resources.

Chapter 44 · Music and Sound

  • Mr. Spitzer often parallels his thoughts to music, hearing the “roaring of the long-tongued surf” and “race-track music,” symbolizing the ongoing passage of time and memory.

Chapter 45 · Bell/Bells

  • Calls to attention, spiritual awakening, and auditory hallucinations connected to death and memory.

Chapter 46

  • “to play the ranz des vaches”: The ranz des vaches is the call of the Swiss herdsmen to their cattle. Rousseau wrote that it was forbidden to sing it near Swiss soldiers in foreign service, since it made them so homesick that they deserted or died (Dictionnaire de musique, 1768). Rossini set it in the overture to William Tell (1829).
  • “all those lutes played by the angels of heaven”: Painters gave heaven the instruments of earth, as in the music-making angels of Fra Angelico’s Linaioli Triptych (1433).

Chapter 46 · Alpenhorn

  • Represents a call to lost love and memory; a connection to the mountains and the past. Its presence in a flat coastal landscape symbolizes the displacement of memory and the difficulty of preserving legacy in an unresponsive world.

Chapter 46 · Music and Bells

Chapter 47 · Music and Silence

  • Life’s complexity and death’s silence.

Chapter 48 · Music and the Score

Chapter 51

  • “Man might be the finest musician”: A person may have great gifts, but without connection, engagement, or the response of others those gifts fall silent, like an instrument no one plays, “an empty wooden box like the coffin of music strung with a few cat-gut strings.” Life gains meaning through being expressed, “even if played upon only by the fingers of the wind.”

  • The funeral bugler and violinist evoke the ceremonial aspect of death and a connection to the past.

Chapter 59

  • “the old bell-ringer’s change ringing”: Young defines change ringing in her own aside. Fabian Stedman’s Tintinnalogia (1668, with Richard Duckworth) and Campanalogia (1677) set out the art, and Stedman’s method is still rung. See change ringing in the Chapter 44 resources.

Chapter 59 · Bells and Horns

  • Bells represent the passage of time and change ringing without repetition, symbolizing life’s unpredictability.
  • Horns, especially the old horn-blower, signify calls or signals between life and death, reality and illusion.

Chapter 59 · Music and Notes

  • Musical notes written on Mr. Spitzer’s shirt cuff are his elegy and memory, fragments of his lost self.
  • The metaphor of music as elusive and ephemeral highlights the fragility of life and consciousness.

Chapter 60

  • “the pedal note prolonged and crying above a choir”: A pedal note, or pedal point, is a long-held note, usually in the bass, sounding on while the harmonies above it change; on the organ it is played with the feet.
  • “Why should he think he was an authority on the harpsichord?”: The harpsichord plucks its strings with quills rather than striking them with hammers like the piano.
  • “the all black harpsichord with the all black keys”: Many old harpsichords reverse the piano’s colors, with black natural keys and white sharps; Young’s is black throughout. See Chopin’s “Black Key” Étude in the Chapter 58 resources.
  • “the viola da gamba”: The viola da gamba, or viol, is the “viol for the leg,” held between the knees and bowed underhand. It has frets and usually six strings. The viols are a separate family from the violins; they flourished in the Renaissance and Baroque and were revived in the twentieth century.
  • “tortoise-shell violin”: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, the newborn god makes the first lyre from a tortoise shell, stretching strings of sheep gut across it.
  • “many winding horns”: “Winding horns” are a type of wind instrument, historically made from animal horns or metal, used for signaling over long distances in activities like hunting, battle, and ceremonies. Also known as blowing horns or war horns, they produce a single note, and different meanings are conveyed through rhythms and speed.

Chapter 60 · The All Black Harpsichord and Instruments

  • Represent lost artistic potential and the melancholic beauty of forgotten music.
  • The “all black keys” and “viola da gamba” suggest a somber, elegiac tone.

Chapter 61

  • In America “mouth harp” usually means the harmonica.
  • “music for the wind harp”: The wind harp, or Aeolian harp, is a box of strings set in a window or a tree for the wind to play; “And what if all of animated nature / Be but organic Harps diversely fram’d” (Samuel Taylor Coleridge, “The Eolian Harp,” 1795).

Chapter 62

  • “members of some great orchestra following with violins and lutes painted with human faces”: The instruments serve as a rich symbolic network that conveys the novel’s deep meditation on the nature of existence, the limits of human understanding, the transient beauty of life and art, and the enduring but often silent music of the soul. The musical imagery ties together themes of memory, loss, death, creativity, and the eternal quest for meaning amidst chaos and silence.
  • “glass harmonicas”: Benjamin Franklin invented the glass armonica in 1761, a row of nested glass bowls turning on a spindle and played with wet fingers; Mozart wrote for it in 1791.
  • “the great wind horn, water horn, submarine flower winding around his neck”: Compare the helicon and the sousaphone, brass basses that wrap around the player’s body.
  • “four horse hairs drawn from the tail of a white Siberian horse”: A violin bow is strung with 150 to 200 hairs from the tails of white stallions, the best long held to come from Siberia and Mongolia.

  • Represent creation, communication, and the ineffable aspects of life. Music is described as complex, sometimes unplayable, and deeply tied to natural phenomena like waves, wind, and stars.

Chapter 62 · The Old Violinist Who Never Touched Strings

  • A powerful metaphor for the paradox between appearance and reality in art, and the pain of exclusion for breaking the illusion.

Chapter 62 · Music of Silence and Memory

  • Explores the impossibility of perfect memory and the idea that music, like life, is ephemeral and incomplete, and that silence may be the truest form of music.

Chapter 68

  • “A Jew’s harp is not Jewish”: The Jew’s harp, a twanging mouth instrument known in Asia for more than two thousand years, has nothing to do with Jews; the English name dates from the sixteenth century, and no one knows its origin.

Chapter 68 · The Jew’s Harp

  • Mr. Spitzer’s identity as Peron and his music represent communication beyond words and the connection between the living and the dead.

Chapter 1 · The Double-Headed Man

  • A mysterious figure by the roadside symbolizing fragmented identity or duality.

Chapter 2 · Two Sister Ravens

  • The ravens appear symbolically and thematically as mysterious, almost otherworldly figures that contribute to the surreal, dreamlike atmosphere surrounding Catherine and her suspended existence between life and death.
  • The ravens are described as "two sister ravens who had created the universe" This description situates the ravens not merely as birds but as powerful, almost divine entities involved in cosmic creation and the shaping of reality itself.
  • Their role emphasizes Catherine’s immersion in a realm where boundaries between reality and illusion, life and death, are blurred.
  • The ravens, linked with creation, suggest a world that is constantly in flux, shaped by mysterious forces beyond ordinary human perception.
  • The ravens contribute to Catherine’s perception of her own life as “more monstrous than hers and terribly extra-human,” reflecting her alienation from the normal flow of time and human relations.
  • Their presence as mythic creators contrasts with Catherine’s physical stasis and withdrawal, underlining the tension between dynamic cosmic forces and her horizontal, dream-bound existence.
  • Ravens traditionally symbolize mystery, death, and prophecy in literature and myth, fitting well with Catherine’s liminal state caught between life and death, and her visions of phantoms, spirits, and the dead.
  • Their “sister” relationship may also suggest duality and companionship in a lonely, spectral world where Catherine resides, further personifying the enigmatic and haunting nature of her dreams.

Chapter 3 · Two Pennies

  • Found in her purse, symbolizes her humility and the little she possessed.
  • Also a poignant reminder of her mortality and disappearance.

Chapter 10 · Twin Iron Bedsteads

  • Represent memory, duality, and the coexistence of past and present selves (Mr. Spitzer and his deceased brother).

Chapter 12

  • “perhaps with two Mr. Spitzers, one who had died, one who had lived”: Joachim and Peron Spitzer, the twins.
  • “She had not two faces”: Janus, the Roman god of doorways and beginnings, looks two ways at once.

Chapter 13

  • “his brother had not been buried anywhere on this vast, amorphous estate”: Peron Spitzer, Joachim’s twin, lies elsewhere and is not among Catherine’s dead guests.

Chapter 14

  • “their cosmic union in the womb of time”: “There are many events in the womb of time which will be delivered” (Othello 1.3).
  • “the case of Spitzer versus Spitzer”: A case in which he “must appear as both the defender and the accuser.”

Chapter 25

  • “In the still chambers which had never bisected life from death, its twin”: In Hesiod’s Theogony, Sleep and Death are twin brothers, the sons of Night.
  • “he being the ambiguous twin”: Joachim and Peron Spitzer may refer to Castor and Pollux, also known as the Dioscuri, twin brothers in Greek and Roman mythology. They are depicted as demigods, associated with horses, sports, and considered patrons of travelers, especially sailors. (Wikipedia) The constellation Gemini, the twins, in the sky is named after them. When mortal Castor died, Pollux shared his immortality with him, and the brothers took turns between Hades and Olympus, one dead while the other lived.

Chapter 25 · Life and Death, Liminality

  • Mr. Spitzer exists in a state between life and death, embodying the ambiguity of human existence.
  • The chapter explores death as both a physical end and a metaphysical continuum.
  • The interplay between living and dead, memory and oblivion, is central.

Chapter 25 · Identity and Duality

  • The twin brothers symbolize duality: life/death, faith/faithlessness, decisiveness/hesitation.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s identity is fractured, as he carries both his own life and that of his dead brother.
  • The confusion over who he is and who he might become reflects existential uncertainty.

Chapter 25 · The Twin Iron Beds and Golden Cradles

  • Symbolize the intertwined destinies of Mr. Spitzer and his brother.
  • Represent infancy, death, and the passage of time.

Chapter 26 · Duality of Human Nature

  • Through the contrast between Joachim and his twin brother Peron, the duality of restraint versus impulsiveness, order versus chaos, and life versus death is examined.

Chapter 26 · The Dead Brother

  • A symbol of lost potential, memory, and the haunting presence of the past in the present.

Chapter 27

  • “they had always suffered, except for this final accident, the same accidents, one not falling unless the other fell”: The twins, like Castor and Pollux in Chapter 25.

Chapter 28

  • “the butterfly perching upon the flower had seemed as identical to the flower as twin to twin”: Zhuangzi (c. 300 BC) dreamed he was a butterfly, and woke to write: “Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly, dreaming I am a man” (trans. Herbert Giles, 1889).

Chapter 28 · Contrast Between Mr. Spitzer and His Brother Peron

  • Peron is portrayed as a man focused on the immediate, material world, indifferent to spiritual or afterlife concepts, and unconcerned with the delicate beauty Mr. Spitzer values.
  • Peron’s death, “by accident or suicide,” marks a turning point for Mr. Spitzer, leading to the end of many of his pursuits and a deepening of his introspection.

Chapter 29

  • “the similitude of death, its twin brother”: Sleep and Death are twins in Hesiod (Chapter 25), and sleep is “death’s counterfeit” in Macbeth 2.3.
  • “Io on one wing and Io on the other wing as if they knew they had two souls”: Io was one of the mortal lovers of Zeus in Greek mythology.

Chapter 29 · Multiplicity of the Soul

  • The idea of multiple souls or a divided self, reflecting Mr. Spitzer’s sense of identity and the presence of his brother’s spirit within him.

Chapter 33

  • “even her funeral, as he remembered his”: Mr. Spitzer remembers his own funeral because he buried his twin. Young said, “Grief was so great that he thought the wrong brother died” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 36

  • “if there had been no dead brother with his identical face”: The chapter portrays a triangular relationship between Peron, Joachim, and Catherine, marked by unfulfilled love, contrasting lives, and the tragic consequences of loss. Catherine’s preference for Peron and her rejection of Joachim create a dynamic of longing and sorrow that defines the emotional core of the narrative. Joachim embodies steadfastness and grief, while Peron represents passion and escape, and Catherine is caught between these polarities, her own existence fragile and dreamlike.

Chapter 36 · Rivalry and Envy

  • “His envy had never died, having outlived its subject or its object.”
  • Without a dead brother “with his identical face,” he “would have been a rival to himself and still unsatisfied.”
  • “He was this obstacle, this darkness between my mother and her love, her dead love, it little mattering who that dead love might be.”

Chapter 48

  • “the portmanteau personality carrying another soul within his soul”: Portmanteau is a large trunk or suitcase opening into two halves, or a word blending the sounds and combining the meanings of two others, a sense Lewis Carroll gave it: “You see it’s like a portmanteau—there are two meanings packed up into one word” (Through the Looking-Glass, 1871, chapter 6).

Chapter 50

  • “There was no twin star to this”: The twin star is the lost brother; see Peron, who “would not live” beyond Mr. Spitzer.

Chapter 51

  • “Had he given birth to his dead twin”: See Peron Spitzer.

Chapter 53

  • “the one chance in a million”: Young told Studs Terkel, “Mr. Spitzer is really two people. There are two Mr. Spitzers. One is a musical composer who has lived in memory of his gambling brother, the suicide, and who since his brother’s death has never composed a music which can be heard.” Peron “is a gay gambler, an impresario in the world of games and sports,” who describes himself “as the gambler who took one chance in a million, committed suicide, and lived.” In the third draft she realized “that it was not just a case of twins, but the two parts of the same man… a beautiful case of duality, which might be in all of us, like left and right, shadow and sunlight” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 53 · Identity and Duality

  • The chapter explores the paradox of the two brothers’ overlapping identities. Joachim as the “pale replica” of Peron, and Peron as an elusive, many-personality figure. The idea that Joachim might be Peron and vice versa underlines the instability of self and questions the fixity of identity.

Chapter 55 · The Twin House and Mirroring Rooms

  • Symbolize the divided self and fractured identity; also the attempt to impose order on life’s chaos.

Chapter 57 · Identity and the Double

  • Mr. Spitzer’s identity is fluid and fragmented. He sometimes confuses himself with his brother, dreams of being the tailor, or living a double existence. His struggle to reconcile these selves reflects the complexity of human identity, especially after trauma or death.

Chapter 57 · Timepieces (Two Wrist Watches)

  • Represent duality and the conflicting measures of time, cosmic and earthly, highlighting Mr. Spitzer’s fractured perception of time.

Chapter 59 · Skeleton and Bones

  • The alien skeleton inhabiting Mr. Spitzer’s body symbolizes the uncertainty of identity and the fracturing of the self.
  • His bones creaking and speaking imply the body’s betrayal or the intrusion of something foreign within him.
  • This is also foreshadowing of his true identity.

Chapter 62

  • “his brother’s milky blue stone ring and ticking jeweled wrist watch”: The right hand that signs the lawyer’s will wears Peron’s ring and Peron’s ticking watch, while the left hand signs as the musician; the twins divide Mr. Spitzer’s body between them.

Chapter 76

  • “What twin accused his twin whom he had murdered”: This seems to refer to Joachim and Peron Spitzer and here Esther is saying that Peron killed Joachim and took his identity.
  • “had murdered her twin by kicking it out early”: Physicians have long known that one twin may die early in pregnancy and be shed or reabsorbed. With ultrasound in the 1970s this “vanishing twin” proved far more common than anyone had guessed.

Chapter 78

  • “Poor, poor little thing, poor little other one who would have loved her mother so much, Rosemary”: “There’s rosemary, that’s for remembrance; pray, love, remember” (Ophelia, Hamlet, 4.5). Esther’s mother remembers Rosemary all her life.

In the research: Chapter 13, Chapter 28, Chapter 29, Chapter 30, Chapter 31, Chapter 35, Chapter 37, Chapter 42, Chapter 45, Chapter 47, Chapter 49, Chapter 50, Chapter 51, Chapter 52, Chapter 55, Chapter 56, Chapter 57, Chapter 58, Chapter 59, Chapter 61, Chapter 62, Chapter 63, Chapter 72, Chapter 77

Definition from research

Chapter 13

  • “flew away like luna moths”: The pale green luna moth lives about a week as an adult and has no mouth to eat with.

Chapter 28

  • “no patience to wait for the caterpillar to become the butterfly”: The Greek psychē means both “soul” and “butterfly.” In Apuleius’s The Golden Ass (2nd century AD), Psyche is the soul who marries Cupid.
  • “the Hesperides like spirit messengers”: Hesperides in Greek mythology are nymphs of the evening. They guarded the golden apples at the western edge of the world. The skippers, a family of butterflies, are the Hesperiidae, named for them.
  • “the harlequins, the painted ladies fluttering through the darkness”: Harlequin was the patched, masked trickster of the commedia dell’arte. The Painted Lady (Vanessa cardui) is a butterfly, and “painted lady” was also slang for a woman of the streets. Young lets both meanings fly at once.
  • “watching the amazed birth of a butterfly, the first tremblings of the feeble, dew-lit wings”: The emergence of the butterfly from the chrysalis is called eclosion.

Chapter 28 · Butterflies as a Symbol

  • Butterflies serve as a powerful metaphor for fleeting beauty, transformation, and the ephemeral nature of life and memory.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s passion for collecting butterflies reflects his attempt to capture and preserve moments of beauty and meaning amid loneliness and loss.
  • The novel details the vividness and variety of butterflies he treasured, symbolizing spiritual messengers or incarnations of beauty in various realms.
  • His butterfly collection and memories also contrast with the pragmatic and mundane approach of his brother Peron, who dismissed such ethereal concerns.

Chapter 28 · Butterflies

  • Represent transformation, beauty, and the fleeting nature of life.
  • Emblematic of Mr. Spitzer’s desire to preserve ephemeral moments amid existential uncertainty.

Chapter 29 · Butterflies as Symbols of the Soul and Immortality

  • Butterflies represent the psyche or soul, echoing the Greek notion where “psyche” means both soul and butterfly.
  • They symbolize transformation, immortality, and the elusive nature of life and death.
  • Despite their mortality, butterflies are portrayed as perfect images of immortality, transcending their ephemeral physical existence.

Chapter 29 · Butterflies

  • Transformation, resurrection, soul, ephemeral beauty, and immortality.
  • Seen as voyagers between stars, realms, and states of being.
  • Metaphors for memory, identity, and the human condition.

Chapter 29 · On Butterfly and Moth Distinctions and Flight Times (Day versus Night)

  • The ambiguous boundary and symbolic contrast between butterflies and moths, day and night, happiness and sorrow.

Chapter 29 · Butterflies as Psyche and Their Cosmic Journeys

  • The belief that butterflies wander seeking immortal love and may journey through the stars.

Chapter 29 · Mr. Spitzer’s Butterfly Collection as Memory and Identity

  • The collection holds symbolic and emotional weight, paralleling memories of his brother and his own identity.

Chapter 29 · Butterfly Names and Mythological Associations

  • Butterflies named after gods (Aphrodite, Apollo, Morpheus, Leto), mythological figures (Io, Atlas), and symbolic concepts.
  • These names embed butterflies in a rich symbolic and cultural context.
  • The rich tapestry of cultural and mythological references deepens the symbolism.

Chapter 30

  • “the suicidal butterfly-chaser chasing himself with his butterfly net”: Mr. Spitzer’s butterflies of Chapters 28 and 29.

Chapter 31

  • “his calling card embossed with the butterfly which was his sign of resurrection”: Mr. Spitzer’s calling card.

Chapter 31 · The Butterfly Card

  • The “great eye” of the planet, the “butterfly” symbol of resurrection, and references to historical and exotic locations enhance the dreamlike and timeless atmosphere.

Chapter 35

  • “the blind moth fluttered with jewels upon its wings”: “The desire of the moth for the star, / Of the night for the morrow” (Percy Bysshe Shelley, “One word is too often profaned,” 1821).

Chapter 37

  • “to death’s-head moths”: The death’s-head hawkmoth, Acherontia atropos, bears a skull on its thorax and is named for the Fate who cuts the thread of life.

Chapter 42

  • “Perhaps it was the lackey moth.”: The lackey moth is named for its caterpillar’s bright stripes, like a footman’s livery.

Chapter 45

  • “Had he not lost his butterfly”: In Greek, psyche means both the soul and the butterfly.

Chapter 45 · Butterflies

  • Transformation, fleeting perceptions and the fragility of life and consciousness.

Chapter 47

  • “an armada of white peacock butterflies”: White peacock butterflies are found in the southeastern United States, Central and South America.
  • “the Atlas moth containing its spirit in the cloud”: See the Atlas moth, among the largest moths in the world, in the Chapter 29 resources.

Chapter 49

  • “the star might be drawn by the moth”: Young reverses Shelley: “The desire of the moth for the star, / Of the night for the morrow” (Percy Bysshe Shelley, “One word is too often profaned,” 1824).

Chapter 50

  • “Should a demoniac butterfly appear”: A demoniac butterfly may refer to a restricted demon or grass demon butterfly found in Asia. The Greek psyche means both soul and butterfly, and the butterfly rising from the fire is the soul leaving the body.
  • “butterfly was sequestered like this mourning cloak”: The mourning cloak butterfly, dark with a pale border, sleeps through the winter as an adult hidden in bark and crevices.

Chapter 51

  • “drawers of his dead brother’s butterfly correspondence”: See Peron’s butterflies in the Chapter 29 resources.

Chapter 52 · Birds and Butterflies

  • Symbols of transformation, fleeting beauty, and the soul’s journey. The butterfly sailing out of the ear (a door) suggests escape or transcendence.

Chapter 55

  • “his great emperors and queens, his pearl-bordered moths”: Young’s collection is made of real butterflies and moths: the purple emperor, the queen, the pearl-bordered fritillary, the pebble prominent, the marbled white, and the mourning cloak, which the English call the Camberwell beauty.
  • “his little salts and peppers winging through the mist”: The peppered moth is speckled black and white like salt and pepper; in sooty industrial England a black form all but replaced it, a famous case of natural selection.

Chapter 55 · The Butterfly Collection and Stamps

  • Represent delicate beauty, memory, and past achievements, threatened by Peron’s recklessness.

Chapter 56

  • “the quivering bodies of dead luna moths”: The adult luna moth has no mouth and does not eat; it lives about a week, long enough to mate.

Chapter 57

  • “or perhaps he was the measuring worm”: The measuring worm, or inchworm, is the caterpillar of the geometer moths, whose name means earth-measurers; it moves by looping, as if measuring the ground.
  • “a Sphinx had settled on his coat sleeve”: This sphinx is a sphinx moth, or hawk moth, named for the caterpillar’s habit of rearing up its head like the Great Sphinx. See The Life of the Sphinx Moth in the Chapter 55 resources.

Chapter 58

  • The Sphingidae are a family of moths commonly called sphinx moths, also colloquially known as hawk moths, with many of their caterpillars known as hornworms. It includes about 1,450 species. It is best represented in the tropics, but species are found in every region. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 59

  • “his escape from this chrysalis”: The Greek word psyche means both soul and butterfly, and a butterfly leaving its chrysalis was an ancient image of the soul leaving the body.
  • “was not the moth married to the star which had extinguished it”: See Shelley’s “desire of the moth for the star” in the Chapter 57 resources.

Chapter 61

  • “flowers pale as tussock moths”: Tussock moths are found on every continent except Antarctica.

Chapter 62

  • “pearl-bordered fritillaries”: Fritillaries are a type of butterfly and a genus of flowering plants known for their checkered patterns.
  • “The death’s-head smiling, inviting pity for the moth”: The death’s-head hawkmoth carries a skull on its back and squeaks when handled.

Chapter 63

  • “Purple emperor!”: The purple emperor is a butterfly of European oak woods; imperial purple, dyed from Tyrian shellfish, was the color of emperors such as Constantine.

Chapter 72 · Fireflies, moths, and butterflies

  • Represent fleeting life, transformation, and the ethereal nature of existence.

From the resources

Chapter 77 · Birds (Robins, Blackbirds, Moths)

  • Represent life, death, innocence, and societal neglect.
  • Blackbirds especially tie to racial themes and death ignored by authorities.

In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 12, Chapter 15, Chapter 16, Chapter 19, Chapter 22, Chapter 31, Chapter 37, Chapter 55, Chapter 59, Chapter 62, Chapter 65, Chapter 68, Chapter 82

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • Molyneux’s problem, posed by the Irish scientist William Molyneux in a letter to John Locke in 1688, asked whether a man who had been born blind and who learned to distinguish and name a globe and a cube by touch, would be able to distinguish and name these objects simply by sight, once he had been enabled to see. (Wikipedia) Catherine’s blind mother keeps the world of sight in her mind and speaks “of the appearances, the visions, the beautiful world of light.”

Chapter 12 · The Garden of the Blind

  • Represents a sensory world without sight, emphasizing the importance and limitations of perception.

Chapter 12 · Eyes and Eyelashes

  • Represent the function and fragility of vision and perception; Vera meditates on their biological and symbolic significance.

Chapter 12

  • “The eyeball was made to see with”: William Paley’s Natural Theology (1802) made the eye his proof of design: “there is precisely the same proof that the eye was made for vision, as there is that the telescope was made for assisting it.” The book opens with a watch found on a heath.
  • “dead men are usually found with their eyes open”: “Joseph shall put his hand upon thine eyes” (Genesis 46:4). The living close the eyes of the dead and once weighted them with coins.
  • “Leonardo had forgotten to give eyebrows to his Mona Lisa”: The Mona Lisa (c. 1503-1519) is a half-length portrait by Leonardo da Vinci. (Wikipedia) The painting shows no eyebrows or lashes, though Giorgio Vasari (1550) praised its eyebrows, “the manner in which the hairs spring from the flesh.”
  • “the garden of the blind”: Fragrance gardens for the blind were planted to be touched and smelled. The Brooklyn Botanic Garden opened one in 1955. Vera and Miss MacIntosh walk through this garden in Chapter 3.
  • “the stumbling stone to the blind”: “Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14).
  • “the Braille texture of flowers”: Louis Braille, blinded as a child, published his raised-dot alphabet in 1829.

Chapter 12 · The Role and Limits of the Senses

  • There is an extended meditation on the human senses (sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch) as the means by which humans experience reality.
  • Vera highlights the design and function of eyes, eyelashes, eyelids, and hair as protective and sensory mechanisms.
  • The garden of the blind symbolizes a world without vision, emphasizing other ways of perceiving such as touch (Braille, texture), and questioning how place and perception influence sorrow and happiness.

Chapter 15

  • “my grandmother’s mahogany dressing table with its three stained mirrors”: The blind grandmother of the garden of the blind in Chapter 12.

Chapter 16

  • “a path that made a circle like an eye through the garden of the blind”: The grandmother’s garden of the blind.
  • “angels who restored sight to the blind and hearing to the deaf”: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped” (Isaiah 35:5). The gardens of the blind and of the deaf were Chapters 12 and 13.

Chapter 19

  • “my grandmother’s rocking chair”: The blind grandmother of the garden of the blind.

Chapter 22

  • “My mother’s mother’s blindness had been only physical”: The blind grandmother of Chapter 12.

Chapter 31 · Eyes and the Keyhole

  • “…he would be overwhelmed by the increasing certainty that there was another great, rounded eye staring at him…” The imagery of eyes symbolizes observation, mystery, and the interplay between seen and unseen forces.

Chapter 37 · Eyes and Faces

  • Eyes symbolize perception and identity; the theme of masks and hidden skulls suggests mortality beneath appearances.

Chapter 55

  • “could certainly never have employed a Seeing Eye bookkeeper”: The Seeing Eye, the first guide dog school in the United States, was founded in 1929 by Dorothy Harrison Eustis, who had trained German shepherds for the Swiss army and police; it moved to Morristown, New Jersey, in 1931.
  • “He suffered from retinal rivalry”: In binocular, or retinal, rivalry, when each eye sees a different image the brain does not fuse them but switches back and forth between them; Charles Wheatstone described it in 1838.

Chapter 55 · Visual Impairments

  • Joachim’s double vision and shifting perspectives symbolize his mental confusion and the instability of perception.

Chapter 59 · Illusion and Reality

  • The blurred perceptions of Mr. Spitzer, including his dim eyesight and confusion about colors and sounds, symbolize the difficulty of discerning reality.
  • The chapter explores illusions (revolving doors, glass walls, and shifting clouds) as metaphors for life’s uncertainties and transformations.

Chapter 62 · The Old Oil Lamp with Bull’s-Eye

  • Represents the faint, fragile light of consciousness and creativity amid darkness.

Chapter 65

  • “much like the blind leading the blind”: “And if the blind lead the blind, both shall fall into the ditch” (Matthew 15:14, KJV).
  • “Love is blind”: The saying, meaning that love overlooks faults, is ancient; Plato wrote that the lover is blind about the beloved (Laws 731e). In English, Chaucer has “For love is blynd alday, and may nat see” (“The Merchant’s Tale”), and Shakespeare’s Jessica says, “But love is blind, and lovers cannot see / The pretty follies that themselves commit” (The Merchant of Venice, 2.6).

Chapter 68

  • “They were playing blind man’s buff behind the hill”: In blind man’s buff, a blindfolded player gropes to catch the others, as the children had blindfolded the blind dog.

Chapter 68 · The Blindfolded Dog

  • Innocence and cruelty intertwined, reflecting on blindness to suffering.
  • The village is described as dilapidated and eerie, with details like rusted machinery, broken wheels, and a sign “Gentle Incline —Bride Ahead—” which is a false reading for “Bridge Ahead,” evoking a sense of decay and death.
  • The Tavern, built in 1827 by “God’s servants,” is a gloomy, sprawling hotel with mildewed brick, claw-like vines, and a haunting presence. Its interior surpasses Vera’s imagination, filled with human-faced wasps and thin walls that seem to hear everything.
  • The atmosphere is filled with silence, shadows, and a slow, suffocating sense of inevitability, preparing the reader for the philosophical and existential meditations that follow.

Chapter 82

  • “With Braille, he teaches”: Louis Braille, blinded as a child, published his raised-dot alphabet in 1829. The Seeing Eye, the first American school for guide dogs, was founded in 1929 by Dorothy Harrison Eustis.
