In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 3, Chapter 4, Chapter 5, Chapter 6, Chapter 7, Chapter 8, Chapter 9, Chapter 11, Chapter 12, Chapter 13, Chapter 14, Chapter 15, Chapter 16, Chapter 18, Chapter 27, Chapter 28, Chapter 29, Chapter 32, Chapter 33, Chapter 34, Chapter 35, Chapter 36, Chapter 37, Chapter 39, Chapter 40, Chapter 41, Chapter 42, Chapter 45, Chapter 46, Chapter 48, Chapter 49, Chapter 52, Chapter 56, Chapter 57, Chapter 59, Chapter 60, Chapter 61, Chapter 62, Chapter 63, Chapter 69, Chapter 70, Chapter 72, Chapter 73, Chapter 74, Chapter 75, Chapter 76, Chapter 77, Chapter 78, Chapter 79, Chapter 82

Definition from research

Chapter 2 · The Canary

  • Life and hope in a cage; fragile and drugged, paralleling Catherine’s own condition.
  • Symbolic of the precariousness of existence and the illusion of continuity.

Chapter 2 · Two Sister Ravens

  • The ravens appear symbolically and thematically as mysterious, almost otherworldly figures that contribute to the surreal, dreamlike atmosphere surrounding Catherine and her suspended existence between life and death.
  • The ravens are described as "two sister ravens who had created the universe" This description situates the ravens not merely as birds but as powerful, almost divine entities involved in cosmic creation and the shaping of reality itself.
  • Their role emphasizes Catherine’s immersion in a realm where boundaries between reality and illusion, life and death, are blurred.
  • The ravens, linked with creation, suggest a world that is constantly in flux, shaped by mysterious forces beyond ordinary human perception.
  • The ravens contribute to Catherine’s perception of her own life as “more monstrous than hers and terribly extra-human,” reflecting her alienation from the normal flow of time and human relations.
  • Their presence as mythic creators contrasts with Catherine’s physical stasis and withdrawal, underlining the tension between dynamic cosmic forces and her horizontal, dream-bound existence.
  • Ravens traditionally symbolize mystery, death, and prophecy in literature and myth, fitting well with Catherine’s liminal state caught between life and death, and her visions of phantoms, spirits, and the dead.
  • Their “sister” relationship may also suggest duality and companionship in a lonely, spectral world where Catherine resides, further personifying the enigmatic and haunting nature of her dreams.

Chapter 3

  • “all these fine-feathered birds of paradise”: The birds of paradise of New Guinea reached Europe in the 1500s as trade skins with their feet removed, and naturalists concluded that they had no feet and lived their whole lives in the air, feeding on dew, until they fell to earth at death. Linnaeus named one species Paradisaea apoda, “footless.”
  • “an Arctic tern stopping upon the rocks”: The Arctic tern makes the longest migration of any animal, flying each year from its Arctic breeding grounds to the Antarctic and back, and so sees two summers and more daylight than any other creature.

Chapter 4 · Red Hair and Red Rooster’s Wing

  • Symbolizes vitality, passion, and the vividness of Miss MacIntosh’s presence.

Chapter 5 · Stormy Petrels, Woodpeckers, Red-winged Blackbirds

  • Represent chaos, disturbance, and the persistence of nature amid decay.

Chapter 6 · The Stuffed Bird on Madge’s Hat

  • Symbolizes fragile consciousness, the artificiality of appearance, and the precariousness of Madge’s situation.

Chapter 6

  • “little red-winged blackbirds where the snow was falling”: Blackbirds can symbolize different things depending on the culture: death, change, magic, and mystery. Specifically in Christianity it is a symbol of temptation and carnal pleasure. Blackbirds in the chapter are multifaceted symbols embodying death, the haunting past, sorrow, and the thin veil separating life and death, reinforcing the novel’s pervasive atmosphere of melancholy and existential uncertainty.

Chapter 7 · Feathers and Wings

  • The fragile boundary between life and death, the ephemeral nature of existence, spiritual transition, decay, and the vulnerability of identity and innocence. They create an atmosphere of haunting delicacy and the inevitability of loss and change.

Chapter 8 · Birds (Woodpeckers, Bluejays, Mockingbirds)

  • Birds appear repeatedly, symbolizing nature, communication, and, perhaps, the persistence of life amid decay

Chapter 9 · Bird Imagery, Especially Seagulls

  • Seagulls appear as recurring natural motifs connected with care and injury. They may symbolize vulnerability and healing, but also freedom and the natural world.
  • The death of the seagull “when its wound was healed” suggests a paradox of survival and loss, or the cost of recovery.

Chapter 11

  • “Queen Charlotte Islands”: The Queen Charlotte Islands, off the Pacific coast of Canada, were named in 1787 for the ship Queen Charlotte, which was named for George III’s queen. They are the home of the Haida and are now called Haida Gwaii.
  • “a wild swan absent, one wild swan more”: In Andersen’s “The Wild Swans” (1838), eleven brothers are turned into swans, and their sister weaves nettle shirts to free them. The last shirt is unfinished, and the youngest is left with a swan’s wing.
  • “the sister ravens, the brother doves”: The Grimms’ “The Seven Ravens” and Giambattista Basile’s “The Seven Doves” (1634-36) both tell of brothers changed into birds and a sister who saves them. Young makes the ravens sisters.

Chapter 12

  • “the spot on a peacock’s tail”: Juno set the hundred eyes of the slain watchman Argus in the peacock’s tail (Ovid, Metamorphoses 1).
  • “Mr. Chandelier or Mr. Chanticleer”: Chanticleer is the proud rooster of Chaucer’s “The Nun’s Priest’s Tale” and the fables of Reynard the Fox. Mr. Chandelier is Catherine’s companion from Chapter 2.
  • “a rooster crowing when there was no rooster”: “Before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice” (Matthew 26:34).
  • “twelve white swans like brothers or suitors bewitched”: Andersen’s eleven brothers turned into swans, and the bewitched swan maidens of Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake (1877).

Chapter 13

  • “One should see the bird and the shadow of the bird, but one should not hear the song”: Wallace Stevens, “Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird” (1917): “The blackbird whistling / Or just after.”

Chapter 14

  • “the golden cock perched at the foot of her bed, that it was really Pythagoras shedding his golden feathers”: In Lucian’s dialogue “The Dream, or the Cock,” a cobbler’s rooster reveals that it is Pythagoras reborn. Pythagoras was said to have a golden thigh. Rimsky-Korsakov’s opera The Golden Cockerel (1909), from Pushkin’s tale (1834), has a golden cock that warns a tsar.
  • “her peacocks”: Aristotle referred to the peacock’s vain reputation. The Roman poet Ennius, following the Pythagorean teaching of rebirth, dreamed that Homer’s soul had passed into a peacock and then into himself.

Chapter 15

  • “as crazy as loons”: The loon’s wild, laughing cry gave the phrase.

Chapter 16

  • “the phoenix rising from those cold ashes of the dream”: The phoenix, which dies in fire and rises from its own ashes.
  • “the stuffed lute birds”: The lyrebird of Australia, named for its lyre-shaped tail.

Chapter 18 · Feather Pillow

  • Used by Miss MacIntosh to cover Vera’s head, symbolizing an attempt to induce forgetfulness, sleep, or escape from harsh realities.

Chapter 27

  • “for the tongue-less nightingales”: Philomela, whose tongue Tereus cut out, became the nightingale (Ovid, Metamorphoses 6).
  • “storks’ nests on the roof-tops”: In northern Europe a stork’s nest on the roof brought luck, and storks brought babies. Hans Christian Andersen’s “The Storks” (1838).

Chapter 28

  • “a booming sound like that of the loud sea bittern”: The bittern, a marsh heron, is known for its deep, booming call.
  • “more precious than the cuckoo singing as it flies”: Wordsworth’s “To the Cuckoo” (1807): “No bird, but an invisible thing, / A voice, a mystery.”

Chapter 29

  • “butterflies as big as the wailing lapwing”: Lapwing is a ground nesting bird found in Europe.

Chapter 32

  • “the stately mating dance of the whooping cranes”: Whooping cranes court with leaps, bows, and wing-flapping. By 1941 only about fifteen wild birds remained.

Chapter 33

  • “Owls, great horned owls hooting above the lonely church steeples”: “From yonder ivy-mantled tow’r / The moping owl does to the moon complain” (Thomas Gray, “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard,” 1751). Young named Gray’s Elegy as a model for Angel in the Forest (Marguerite Young, interview with Charles Ruas and Joan Schwartz, WBAI radio, New York).

Chapter 33 · The Blackbird and the Door

  • She tells someone to open the door, and the voice answers that it is already open, though the door is closed. She is talking to a human-sized blackbird.
  • These images portray the overlap of the real and the imaginary.

Chapter 34 · The Cock Crowing

  • Symbolizes awakening, sovereignty, and perhaps the harsh reality that disrupts illusions.

Chapter 35

  • “great gold-eyed white ptarmigans”: Ptarmigans are medium-sized game birds in the grouse family.

Chapter 36 · Animals and Nature

  • Birds (blackbirds, seagulls), horses, and natural phenomena (fog, wind, fireflies) evoke transformation, freedom, and the boundary between worlds.
  • The black coachman lies where “the white manes of the running horses” streak the waves.

Chapter 37

  • “the footless messengers”: Birds of paradise were believed to have no feet and never to land, because their skins reached Europe with the feet cut off. Linnaeus named the greater bird of paradise Paradisaea apoda, “footless,” in 1758.

Chapter 37 · The Hawk and Birds

  • Represent death, predation, and perhaps the inevitability of mortality. “Her head was eaten by great birds. Great birds had plucked out her eyes.”

Chapter 39

  • “the stormy petrels flying”: Petrels are said to be named for St. Peter, because they seem to walk on the water (Matthew 14:29).

Chapter 40

  • “screaming contests of Platan rails like the human voice exerted to its utmost pitch”: Young’s source is W. H. Hudson, who describes the giant wood rails, the ypecaha, of La Plata: “This is a tremendous screaming concert,” and “The screams they utter have a certain resemblance to the human voice, exerted to its utmost pitch” (W. H. Hudson, The Naturalist in La Plata, 1892, chapter 19, “Music and Dancing in Nature”).
  • “Would the sheathbills have told”: Sheathbills are Antarctic shore scavengers, ruddy turnstones are wading shorebirds, and stormy petrels are seabirds of the open ocean. See the petrel entry in the Chapter 39 resources and Birds.

Chapter 41

  • “One lost one’s magnetic sense, such as migratory birds are perhaps guided by”: Young’s “perhaps” came just before the proof. In 1965 Friedrich Merkel and Wolfgang Wiltschko showed that caged European robins orient by the earth’s magnetic field (“Magnetismus und Richtungsfinden zugunruhiger Rotkehlchen,” Die Vogelwarte 23, 1965, 71-77).
  • “the snow-white whetsaw owls”: Whetsaw owls may refer to the Saw-whet owl found in North America and one of the smallest owl species. Its name comes from its call, said to sound like a saw being whetted on a stone.

Chapter 42

  • “Ptarmigan, swallowed”: Ptarmigan is a bird in the grouse subfamily.
  • “never by robin redbreast covering him with the autumn leaf”: “Call for the robin-red-breast and the wren, / Since o’er shady groves they hover, / And with leaves and flowers do cover / The friendless bodies of unburied men” (John Webster, The White Devil 5.4, 1612). In the ballad of the Babes in the Wood, robins cover the dead children with leaves.

Chapter 45

  • “the great snowy ptarmigan”: The ptarmigan turns white in winter to vanish against the snow.
  • “Pigeons had stopped an old town clock.”: On August 12, 1945, a flock of starlings settled on the minute hand of Big Ben and slowed it by several minutes.
  • “the pigeon with the Red Cross upon its snow-white breast”: Carrier pigeons served in both world wars. Cher Ami carried the message that saved the “Lost Battalion” in the Argonne in 1918, though shot through the breast, and France awarded the bird the Croix de Guerre.
  • “the Bleeding Heart”: The bleeding-heart dove of the Philippines has a white breast with a blood-red patch at its center, as if it had been wounded.
  • “passenger pigeons now extinct”: Audubon watched a flight of passenger pigeons pass for three days in 1813, “the light of noon-day” obscured “as by an eclipse” (John James Audubon, Ornithological Biography, 1831). The last, Martha, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914. See Martha in the Chapter 49 resources.
  • “no trumpeter swan could accompany her”: The trumpeter swan was nearly gone but not extinct. In 1932 only 69 were counted in the United States outside Alaska, and the Red Rock Lakes refuge was set aside for them in 1935.

Chapter 46

  • “like the light-winged cranes”: Pliny wrote that cranes “ballast themselves with coarse sand” before crossing the Black Sea, choose a leader, and post sentinels that each hold “a little stone in its claw” (Natural History 10.30, trans. John Bostock and H. T. Riley, 1855).

Chapter 48

  • “goose barnacles”: Goose barnacles were long believed to hatch into barnacle geese, since no one had seen the geese nest; Gerald of Wales reported it in his Topographia Hibernica (about 1188), and the barnacle goose is named for the belief.
  • “having mistaken the lighthouse for the star”: Birds migrating at night are drawn to lighthouse beams and strike the glass, and keepers long recorded the dead birds found at the foot of the tower in the morning.

Chapter 49

  • “the last passenger pigeon known to earth”: Martha died at the Cincinnati Zoo on the afternoon of September 1, 1914, a month after the First World War began, alone since her last companions died in 1910. Young gives the date as September 14, 1918, the last year of the war, at one o’clock. Mr. Spitzer mourns her as the last of her kind: once something is lost, whether a species, a person, or a moment, it cannot be recovered, and mourning for her is mourning for all that is irretrievably gone. Aldo Leopold wrote for the monument to the pigeon at Wyalusing State Park in Wisconsin: “We have erected a monument to commemorate the funeral of a species. It symbolizes our sorrow” (“On a Monument to the Pigeon,” 1947).
  • “trapped by nets like the fishes of the sea”: Netters lured whole flocks with a captive pigeon tied to a perch or stool, the origin, it is said, of “stool pigeon.” At the last great nesting near Petoskey, Michigan, in 1878, hunters killed an estimated 50,000 birds a day for nearly five months, netting, shooting, and smothering them with burning sulfur, and shipped them to city markets.
  • “If there were no pigeons, could there be people”: Here pigeons stand for life, presence, and continuity, bound up with dawn and twilight, the passage between night and day, life and death. The mottled “pigeon-colored dawn” is complex and uncertain rather than a clear moment, and “He had lost all sense of the hour”: his time is fractured like his identity, and even the dawn is indistinct to him.
  • “had no soul, the old caretaker said”: John James Audubon painted a pair of passenger pigeons for The Birds of America (plate 62, 1827-1838), and Mark Catesby before him in The Natural History of Carolina, Florida and the Bahama Islands (1731-1743).
  • “whistle all the way from here to Labrador”: The Labrador duck, last recorded in 1878, was the first North American bird known to go extinct after European settlement.
  • “the whooping crane and the lute bird”: By 1941 only about twenty whooping cranes were left in the world, the wild flock wintering at Aransas on the Texas coast. The lute bird may be the lyrebird of Australia, named for the lyre shape of the male’s tail and famous for imitating any sound.
  • “He was this old fan-tail fanning his tail”: Darwin bred fancy pigeons and opened On the Origin of Species (1859) with them: the fantail with thirty or forty tail feathers spread upright and the pouter with its swollen crop. Mr. Spitzer is “pouter-breasted” too.

Chapter 49 · Birds (Pigeons, Blackbirds, Fireflies)

  • Birds symbolize life, freedom, and the passage of souls.
  • The extinction of the passenger pigeon is a metaphor for loss and the fragility of existence.
  • Fireflies and moths symbolize faint, fragile light, hope, memory, or the soul’s flicker.

Chapter 52 · Birds and Butterflies

  • Symbols of transformation, fleeting beauty, and the soul’s journey. The butterfly sailing out of the ear (a door) suggests escape or transcendence.

Chapter 56

  • “the night-crowned heron wader”: The black-crowned night heron fishes at dusk and by night. See the night-crowned kingfisher in the Chapter 55 resources.
  • “the mantling hawk”: In falconry, a hawk mantles when it spreads its wings and tail over its prey to hide it.
  • “The great barnacle birds in the clouds”: Medieval naturalists believed that barnacle geese grew from goose barnacles on driftwood, since no one had seen them nest; Gerald of Wales described it in 1188.

Chapter 57

  • “how many black swans following the white midnight”: Europeans long used the black swan as a byword for the impossible, after the Roman poet Juvenal’s “rara avis in terris nigroque simillima cygno,” a bird as rare on earth as a black swan (Satires 6.165), until the Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh found black swans in western Australia in 1697.

Chapter 59

  • “the barkings of red-eyed dogs accompanying dead souls to Hades”: In northern English folklore the Gabriel Hounds, or Gabble Ratchets, were a spectral pack heard yelping overhead at night, and their cry foretold a death; the sound was probably wild geese in passage.
  • “hearing the kingfisher’s cries”: In Ovid, Ceyx drowns at sea and his wife Alcyone finds his body washed ashore; the gods turn both into kingfishers, and the calm “halcyon days” are the days when the sea is still for their nesting (Metamorphoses, Book 11).
  • “ossifrage, the breaking of his bones”: Ossifrage means bone-breaker, from the Latin os, bone, and frangere, to break. It is the old name of the bearded vulture, which drops bones on rocks to split them for the marrow; the King James Bible lists “the ossifrage” among the unclean birds (Leviticus 11:13).

Chapter 59 · Birds and Migratory Patterns

  • Migratory birds symbolize movement between worlds, the passage of souls, and the patterns of life and death.
  • The cries of birds are likened to music and the fleeting nature of human emotion.

Chapter 60

  • “the great gold-eyed snow owl”: The snowy owl of the Arctic has yellow eyes; in some winters snowy owls come south in numbers to fields, shores, and airports.
  • “calling the wild ducks out of the clouds”: The different references to ducks are multifaceted symbols that evoke loss, innocence, mourning, and the liminal state between life and death. They enrich the emotional landscape, highlighting suffering and the fragile nature of existence amidst the novel’s broader themes of decay, memory, and transcendence.
  • “the polysyllabic horns of the wild ducks”: Young’s “polysyllabic horns” are the ducks’ calls of many syllables, which hunters imitate with wooden duck calls.
  • “a flight of mandarins driven by non-adventitious winds far off their usual course”: The mandarin duck of East Asia is the most brilliantly colored of ducks, the drake crested and with orange “sails” on his back. In China a pair of mandarin ducks stands for faithful married love.
  • “those poor birds of passage who, with their eyes blinded by the light”: Lighthouse keepers reported hundreds of migrating birds killed against the lantern in a single foggy night; the light draws night migrants, above all in fog.

Chapter 60 · Wild Ducks

  • Represent migration, passage, and the ephemeral beauty of life.
  • Their “crested heads and veiled gold eyes” suggest exoticism and a mystical presence.
  • Their flight and honking are likened to a “wild sonata,” connecting nature with music.

Chapter 61

  • “the great bitterns booming in the clouds”: The American bittern’s booming spring call carries far across the marsh; country people called the bird the thunder-pumper and the stake-driver.
  • “the black-crowned night heron splashed”: The black-crowned night heron feeds at dusk and by night; its call is a flat “quok.”
  • “the shadow of the mantling hawk”: In falconry a hawk mantles when it spreads its wings over its prey, or stretches a wing and a leg down one side.
  • “in cloud cuckooland”: In Aristophanes’s The Birds (414 BC), the birds build Cloudcuckooland, a city in the air between gods and men.
  • “the hermit thrush’s speckled breast”: The hermit thrush sings the elegy in Walt Whitman’s “When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d” (1865), his poem on the death of Lincoln.
  • “sound of the water ouzel”: A water ouzel is the traditional name for the American Dipper, a medium-sized, gray songbird known for its aquatic lifestyle, as it dives into cold, fast-moving streams to hunt for food. It is the only North American songbird that forages underwater, where it walks along the stream bed to catch aquatic insects and other prey. John Muir wrote it a hymn of praise, “The Water-Ouzel” (The Mountains of California, 1894).
  • “the great Arctic birds who round this globe each year, going from pole to pole”: The Arctic tern flies each year from its Arctic nesting grounds to the Antarctic and back, the longest migration of any bird.

Chapter 62

  • “for this was his swan song, his silent song, the swan being mute”: The mute swan is not truly mute; it hisses, snorts, and grunts. See the swan song in the Chapter 61 resources.
  • “many golden cockerels flapping their wings and crowing on singing weathervanes”: Compare Rimsky-Korsakov’s opera The Golden Cockerel (first performed 1909), whose golden bird crows warnings from its perch.
  • “the secretive egg of some great bird like the sea gannet”: The sea gannet is a large seabird, most commonly referring to the Northern Gannet, known for its spectacular plunge-diving to catch fish. These birds are white with black and gold markings and spend their lives at sea, only coming to land to nest.
  • “dance of the golden cock-of-the-rock”: The cock-of-the-rock is a real bird of South American cloud forests; the brilliant orange males gather at leks, where they dance and display to win the females.
  • “screaming coradicorns”: Young’s “coradicorns” are likely the Coraciiformes, the order of rollers, kingfishers, bee-eaters, and motmots, in which hornbills and hoopoes were also long classed.
  • “hornbills, hoopoes, motmots”: The hoopoe leads the birds on their pilgrimage in Attar’s Conference of the Birds (1177), and in Aristophanes’s The Birds it is the transformed king Tereus. See Cloudcuckooland in the Chapter 61 resources.
  • “wild screamings of stormy petrels”: Sailors named the storm petrel for Saint Peter, because it seems to walk on the water as it feeds (Matthew 14:29).
  • “loon soul crying as the light faded”: The common loon’s wailing night call carries for miles across northern lakes.
  • “apivorous birds”: Apivorous is an adjective that means “feeding on bees.” It describes animals, particularly birds, that eat bees as a food source. Bee-eaters and the honey buzzard are among them.

Chapter 63

  • “A screech owl flew by just then”: The screech owl’s cry was long taken for an omen of death.

Chapter 69 · Turkey Buzzards/Canaries

  • Represent death and the grotesque in the everyday world.

Chapter 70

  • “an Arctic tern with a black-rimmed eye”: The Arctic tern breeds in the Arctic and winters in the Antarctic, the longest migration of any bird, so that it sees more daylight than any other creature.

Chapter 72

  • “breeding lovebirds”: Lovebirds, are small parrots native to Africa and Madagascar, with nine distinct species identified. Known for their intense social bonding and “allo-preening” behavior, they were popularized in Europe during the 1800s as pets. Early records date to the 1600s, though they were extensively trapped and traded in the 19th and 20th centuries.
  • “Who killed cock robin?”: Who Killed Cock Robin is an English nursery rhyme. Although the earliest known record of the song is from the mid-eighteenth century, there is some evidence that it is much older. Versions of the story appear to exist in other countries, including Germany. There are a number of theories that have been advanced to explain the meaning of the rhyme. According to Celtic traditions, Lugh, the sun god who dies as the nights get longer after the summer solstice, is marked in the old Celtic pictographic calendar with a bow-and-arrow shape. Lugh was the primary god representing the red sun and was also known in Welsh as Coch Rhi Ben, which when anglicized would mean Cock Robin (coch meaning red, rhi meaning lord, ben meaning leader) This may be a reference to the belief that souls became birds after death. The sparrow who kills him with his bow and arrow may represent Brân the Blessed, the god of winter in the form of a raven. (Wikipedia) Its answer, first printed in Tommy Thumb’s Pretty Song Book (1744), is “I, said the Sparrow, / With my bow and arrow.” Esther’s last words echo it: “Ah, I knew, she saw, who killed him!”

Chapter 73

  • “dead robin redbreast under a ten-foot snowdrift”: See “Who killed cock robin?” and the Babes in the Wood, covered with leaves by robins, in the Chapter 72 resources.
  • “a white feather of some far-flying Arctic bird”: To show the white feather is to show cowardice, from the cockpit, where a white feather in a gamecock’s tail was taken as the mark of a poor fighter. The feather falls for the featherweight, the golden cock.

Chapter 74

  • “the poisoned blackbirds falling from the sky”: Blackbird control programs in the US aimed at reducing large roosting populations often involved, albeit with limited success, the use of toxic baits in open or plowed fields. These efforts often caused accidental mortality of non-target wildlife species.

Chapter 74 · Birds (Blackbirds, Sobbing Bird)

  • Represent sorrow, the passage of time, and the fragility of life.

Chapter 75

  • “hear the lovebirds crying for their mother”: See Esther’s lovebirds in the Chapter 72 resources.

Chapter 76

  • “who had not killed cock robin”: Who Killed Cock Robin is an English nursery rhyme. The earliest record of the rhyme is in Tommy Thumb’s Pretty Song Book. A number of theories have been advanced to explain the meaning of the rhyme: a mythological event, such as the death of the god Balder from Norse mythology, or the ritual sacrifice of a king figure; a parody of the death of King William II, who was killed by an arrow while hunting, and who was known as William Rufus, which means red; the fall of Robert Walpole’s government in 1742, since Robin is a diminutive form of Robert and the first printing is close to the time of the events mentioned. Some folklore readings make the rhyme a seasonal myth, with the red-breasted robin as Lugh, the Irish god of light, skill, and kingship, killed at the turn of the year by winter. In Celtic studies Lugh is often paired with Brân the Blessed, the Welsh giant-king whose name means “Raven” and who was “crowned king over this Island” (Britannica).

Chapter 77

  • “cock robin had killed cock robin”: Some folklore readings connect Who Killed Cock Robin with the mythology of Lugh, a warrior, a king, a master craftsman and a savior. The Romans identified him with Mercury, and his slaying of Balor has been compared with the death of the Norse god Baldr. In Celtic studies he is often paired with Brân the Blessed, the Welsh giant-king whose name means “Raven.” St. Mologa has been theorized to be a Christian continuation of Lugh. “Cock robin” appears seven times in Esther Longtree’s chapters. “Who killed Cock Robin?” repeatedly asked in the novel is not just about a single culprit but a symbol of the pervasive and inscrutable nature of death, loss, and guilt. It is a question without a definitive answer, reflecting the novel’s exploration of mystery, suffering, and the silent tragedies that haunt Esther and the world she inhabits.
  • “hiding his head under his wing”: “The north wind doth blow, / And we shall have snow, / And what will poor Robin do then, poor thing? / He’ll sit in a barn, / And keep himself warm, / And hide his head under his wing, poor thing.”

Chapter 77 · Birds (Robins, Blackbirds, Moths)

  • Represent life, death, innocence, and societal neglect.
  • Blackbirds especially tie to racial themes and death ignored by authorities.

Chapter 78 · Birds and Nests

  • Birds (woodpeckers, bluejays, blackbirds) symbolize freedom, nature, and sometimes fragility. The blackbirds’ nest with pale blue eggs and gold hair suggests innocence and the preciousness of life, as well as the shadow of loss.

Chapter 79

  • “the grey hen crowing on the bed-post”: A crowing hen was an omen of ill luck: “A whistling woman and a crowing hen / Are neither fit for God nor men.”

Chapter 82

  • “like a jackdaw picking up sticks”: A jackdaw is a small, highly social bird in the crow family, known for its striking pale-gray eyes and a distinctive silver-gray “shawl” on the back of its head. It is commonly found in urban areas, farmland, and woodlands across Europe, Asia, and North Africa.
  • “Snow-breasted gannets and Arctic terns”: Gannets are seabirds, closely related to boobies. They are known as ‘solan’ or ‘solan goose’ in Scotland. A common misconception is that the Scottish name is ‘guga’ but this is the Gaelic name referring to the chicks only. (Wikipedia)
  • “golden chanticleer”: Chauntecleer is the proud rooster of Chaucer’s “Nun’s Priest’s Tale,” nearly carried off by the fox.
  • “like an albatross”: The sailor who shot the albatross wears it around his neck: “Instead of the cross, the Albatross / About my neck was hung” (Coleridge, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, 1798).

Chapter 11 · Mr. Res Tacamah

Chapter 28 · The Role of the Narcotic and Hallucinatory World

  • Mr. Spitzer is drawn each evening to a place shaped by Catherine’s narcotic dreams, a surreal, enchanted world filled with fantastical figures (e.g., Russian bishops, lighthouse keepers, moon-faced duchesses) and imagery (snow owls, serpents, music boxes).

Definition from research

Chapter 5 · Stormy Petrels, Woodpeckers, Red-winged Blackbirds

  • Represent chaos, disturbance, and the persistence of nature amid decay.

Chapter 36

  • “The sky was pearl grey streaked by mare’s-tails”: Mares’ tails are high cirrus clouds.

Chapter 37 · Fog and Clouds

  • These represent uncertainty, the unknown, and the boundary between states of being.

Chapter 38 · Clouds, Whirlwinds, and Stars

  • Reflect the fluidity of time, memory, and identity; also Catherine’s dreamlike mental state.

Chapter 40 · Clouds, Stars, and Celestial Imagery

  • Frequently used to evoke dreamlike states, mystery, and the vastness of time and space.

Chapter 43 · Storm, Snow, Desert, Mountains

  • Represent the suffragette’s internal struggle and the vast unknown of death.

Chapter 43 · Skirt of Clouds and Waters

  • Symbolizes beauty, identity, and the suffragette’s fading presence.

Chapter 44 · Mountains, Clouds, Icebergs

  • Evoke the harshness and isolation of her inner world and struggles.
  • The iceberg imagery suggests overwhelming, unseen dangers and emotional coldness.

Chapter 44 · The Whirlwind and Darkness

  • Represent confusion, chaos, and the unknowability of the human heart.

Chapter 45 · Clouds and Snow

  • Ambiguity, transition, death, and the veil between life and afterlife.

Chapter 52 · Clouds and Snow

  • Represent mystery, concealment, and transformation. They are often described as moving, shifting, and obscuring identity and reality.

Chapter 55

  • “from vastly towering cumulo-nimbus to darkening alto-stratus”: Cumulonimbus are the towering thunderheads; altostratus is the grey sheet of mid-level cloud that comes before steady rain or snow. The Latin cloud names go back to Luke Howard’s Essay on the Modifications of Clouds (1803).

Chapter 56

  • “tremulous as clouds with silver linings”: “Was I deceived, or did a sable cloud / Turn forth her silver lining on the night?” (John Milton, Comus, 1634).
  • “the sky streaked with silvery mares’-tails”: Mares’ tails are wispy cirrus clouds, high ice clouds that often come before a change of weather; sailors said, “Mackerel sky and mares’ tails make lofty ships carry low sails.”

Chapter 56 · Clouds, Sea, and Tides

  • Recurring natural motifs representing impermanence, change, and the fluid boundary between life and death.

Chapter 57

  • “these were clouds without water”: “clouds they are without water, carried about of winds” (Jude 1:12, KJV).

  • “the oldest pinochle player in town”: German immigrants brought pinochle to America, and it filled Midwestern taverns and kitchens.

Chapter 7

  • “We all have to turn in our checks some time”: Poker players cash in their checks, or chips, when they leave the game, so the phrase came to mean dying.

  • Symbolize the complexity and hidden order of life’s movements and events despite apparent confusion.

Chapter 13

  • “the life-sized chessmen”: In Lewis Carroll’s Through the Looking-Glass (1871), Alice crosses a countryside laid out as a chessboard with living pieces. The chessmen have stood in this garden since Chapter 1.

  • The four aces that drop from Mr. Spitzer’s sleeve symbolize the four Mr. Spitzers and the layered selves.

Chapter 14

  • “The playing card dropping from his sleeve each morning had nearly always been an ace”: The “ace up the sleeve” is the cardsharp’s hidden card. In most fortune-telling, the ace of spades is the death card.

Chapter 19 · Playing Cards (Deuce of Clubs)

  • Represents the “test of tears” and omen of death; a paradox considering her moral stance against gambling.

Chapter 35

  • “unlike his brother, who had always had an ace in the hole”: In stud poker the hole card is dealt face down. An ace in the hole is a hidden winning card, and by the early 1900s the phrase meant any hidden advantage.

Chapter 35 · Cards and Games

  • The metaphor of cards and poker reflects strategy, risk, and deception.

  • Symbolizes strategic life moves, fate, and chance. Spitzer’s timidness as a chess player echoes his fear of making irreversible decisions.

  • “the wild fool, the solitary player playing on and on”: The joker, the fool of the deck, is often played wild; a card game for one is solitaire, or patience. See the joker in euchre in the Chapter 59 resources.

  • Symbolize chance, fate, and the gamble of life.

In the research: Chapter 1, Chapter 3, Chapter 6, Chapter 9, Chapter 10, Chapter 11, Chapter 14, Chapter 17, Chapter 19, Chapter 21, Chapter 27, Chapter 30, Chapter 32, Chapter 39, Chapter 41, Chapter 42, Chapter 43, Chapter 44, Chapter 45, Chapter 47, Chapter 51, Chapter 52, Chapter 53, Chapter 54, Chapter 56, Chapter 57, Chapter 58, Chapter 59, Chapter 60, Chapter 61, Chapter 62, Chapter 65, Chapter 69, Chapter 71, Chapter 74, Chapter 81

Definition from research

Chapter 1 · Mist and Grey Landscape

  • Representing ambiguity, the unknown, and the dissolution of familiar reality.

Chapter 1 · Miss MacIntosh’s Whaler’s Hat and Umbrella

  • Symbols of groundedness and practicality against the backdrop of illusion.

Chapter 3 · Corset

  • Represents discipline and the necessary constraints of life.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s tight corset is a physical embodiment of her moral and mental self-control.

Chapter 6 · The Stuffed Bird on Madge’s Hat

  • Symbolizes fragile consciousness, the artificiality of appearance, and the precariousness of Madge’s situation.

Chapter 6 · Madge’s dress and accessories

  • Madge’s dress and accessories are a kaleidoscope of symbols portraying a young woman caught in the painful tension between societal expectations and her grim reality.
  • Her artificial makeup and mismatched finery mask a deeper denial and despair about her pregnancy and future, while the sports motifs and exposed sexuality reflect a conflicted desire for life and normalcy.
  • The decayed and ill-fitting garments evoke the disintegration of her life and identity, and her restless sleep gestures toward her psychological torment and tragic fate.
  • These symbolic details richly underscore the themes of denial, vulnerability, and the tragic loss of innocence in Madge’s character within the novel.

Chapter 9 · The Party Dress and the Birthday Celebration

  • The party dress, described as filmy, sleeveless, and embroidered with seed pearls, symbolizes both Vera’s coming of age and the tension between innocence and emerging sexuality.
  • The empty birthday party and Vera dancing alone highlight loneliness, unfulfilled expectations, and the absence of community or connection.

Chapter 10 · Veil and Mustache

  • Play with gender roles and identity, challenging traditional expectations.

Chapter 10 · Old Empty Shoe

  • Could represent emptiness, absence, or abandonment.

Chapter 11

  • “made of pure Brussels lace”: Brussels lace is well known for its delicacy and beauty. Originally it was only made from the finest spun linen thread, which was spun in dark damp rooms to keep the thread from becoming too brittle. Only one ray of light was allowed into the room, and it was arranged so that it fell upon the thread. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 14 · Mr. Spitzer’s Hat and Garments

  • The black cape, high silk hat, silver buttons evoke the image of the coachman, suggesting blurred identities and roles.

Chapter 17

  • “her corset stays sticking out like the quills of an angry porcupine”: The Ghost tells Hamlet his tale would make “each particular hair to stand on end, / Like quills upon the fretful porpentine” (Hamlet 1.5). A few lines later, “My hair crawled,” and soon Vera’s hair stands “on end.”
  • “someone who wore a jumbo corset whale-boned”: Corsets were stiffened with whalebone, the baleen from the mouths of whales.

Chapter 17 · Corset and Armor

  • Miss MacIntosh’s metallic corset is described like a battleship or wrestler’s gear, symbolizing restraint, protection, and conflict readiness.

Chapter 19

  • “Her whale-boned, salmon-colored corset”: The “salmon-colored monstrosity” of Chapter 18, stiffened with whalebone.
  • “a grey fedora”: The fedora takes its name from Victorien Sardou’s play Fédora (1882), in which Sarah Bernhardt wore a soft, creased, brimmed hat. It was a woman’s hat first, and then a man’s.

Chapter 21 · The Party Dress

  • Represents innocence and celebration. Miss MacIntosh declares it beyond mending, though Vera “could not see a hole in it” or “a seed pearl which was not in its place.”
  • The destruction of the dress symbolizes the loss of innocence and the inevitability of change.

Chapter 27

  • “his high silk hat and black necktie and rosebud with maidenhair”: Maidenhair fern (Adiantum) was the usual green set behind a buttonhole rose.

Chapter 30

  • “Because of the loss of a skirt”: Young told Studs Terkel that this came from an Alpine story in which two bloomer girls shed their skirts at a summit, and the younger, going back for hers, was lost: “the lady lost her life for a skirt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See the Chapter 31 resources.
  • A white skirt often symbolizes purity, innocence, mourning (in some cultures), new beginnings, versatility, symbol of femininity. Suffragettes wore white as a symbol of the movement to represent purity and unity.

Chapter 30 · Skirts and Whispers

  • Symbolize femininity, mystery, loss, and redemption.

Chapter 32 · The Veils, Parasols, and Skirts as Symbols of Femininity and Defense

  • The chapter richly describes feminine accouterments like “great garden hats decked with billowing plumes,” “secretive veils,” “frilled parasols,” and “great hoop skirts flounced with ribbons and lace.” These symbolize traditional femininity, societal expectations, and also the subtle weapons and shields women use in social and gender conflicts.
  • Cousin Hannah’s urging for women to wield their parasol “as her sword or her shield” and to “fly her skirts as her banners in her war against tyrannical man” transforms these delicate objects into instruments of rebellion. The parasol becomes a metaphor for female agency in a world dominated by men.

Chapter 39

  • He “changed his personality whenever he changed his high silk mourner’s hat.” Young told Studs Terkel, “William James made a beautiful statement, man is body, soul, and clothing” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 41

  • “She looked like a domino”: Patches of black silk or velvet, called mouches, flies, in France, were worn in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries to hide smallpox scars and to set off the whiteness of the skin. Addison reported Whig and Tory ladies at the opera patching on opposite sides of their faces (Joseph Addison, The Spectator, no. 81, June 2, 1711). A domino is the hooded cloak worn with a half mask at masquerades, and the game pieces, black with white spots, share the name. Catherine reverses them, a white face with black patches.

Chapter 42

  • “Cousin Hannah as the great bloomer girl”: Amelia Bloomer’s The Lily promoted the loose trousers worn under a short skirt in 1851, and the costume took her name. See Young’s account to Studs Terkel of the bloomer girls who shed their skirts, in the Chapter 38 resources.
  • “wearing an old boater and striped shirt”: The straw boater and the shirtwaist were the uniform of the New Woman and the Gibson Girl of the 1890s.
  • “creeping under some great skirt or crinoline”: See the crinoline in the Chapter 41 resources.

Chapter 43

  • “that high silk hat which was almost his only God”: The high silk hat used to be a clear symbol of authority and status in society. It represented wealth and prestige. Culturally it also represented capitalism, enterprise, and ambition. The first top hats were made of beaver fur felt. From the 1840s silk plush replaced beaver, which gave the silk hat its name. For Mr. Spitzer the hat is “almost his only God.”
  • Bloomers are divided women’s garments for the lower body. They were developed in the 19th century as a healthful and comfortable alternative to the heavy, constricting dresses worn by American women (Wikipedia). They take their name from their best-known advocate, the women’s rights activist Amelia Bloomer. It became a symbol of women’s rights in the early 1850s. See Amelia Bloomer in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “Is that my love, my skirt moving through clouds”: Skirt has long been slang for a woman, as in “a bit of skirt.” The skirt Hannah lost “so long ago” may be both the garment she gave up for the cause and the woman she lost. See Young’s account of the bridal trousseaus under “a secret woman, a bride” in the Chapter 42 resources.

Chapter 43 · High Silk Hat & Black Cape (Mr. Spitzer)

  • Symbols of mourning, ritual, and his ambiguous status between life and death.

Chapter 43 · Skirt of Clouds and Waters

  • Symbolizes beauty, identity, and the suffragette’s fading presence.

Chapter 44

  • “that great bloomer girl”: Lucy Stone and other suffragists adopted the Bloomer costume, which consisted of a knee-length skirt worn over trousers or pantaloons, in the early 1850s. Stone loved the comfort and practicality of the outfit and wore it both at home and in public for about three years. However, the Bloomer costume attracted significant public scrutiny and ridicule, and critics of the women’s rights movement often focused on the reformers’ attire rather than their arguments for suffrage and other reforms. By late 1853, many prominent suffragists, including Elizabeth Cady Stanton, abandoned the Bloomer costume due to the negative attention it generated. Stanton persuaded Stone to follow suit. Stone resumed wearing long skirts, although she never again wore the restrictive corsets and voluminous dresses of the fashionable style. Other notable suffragists like Susan B. Anthony also stopped wearing Bloomers around the same time. Amelia Bloomer, the editor of The Lily newspaper and namesake of the costume, continued to wear it until 1858. Only Elizabeth Smith Miller, who had helped popularize the style, continued to wear bloomers longer, until 1861 (Wikipedia). See Amelia Bloomer in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “I must find my skirt”: This is the Alpine story Young told Studs Terkel, of two bloomer girls who shed their skirts at a summit, and the younger, going back for hers, was lost: “the lady lost her life for a skirt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “Was not this Mt. Blanc always in my heart?”: Mont Blanc, the “white mountain,” was first climbed by a woman, Marie Paradis, in 1808. Henriette d’Angeville climbed it in 1838 in men’s trousers, and Mark Twain teased that she “cramped their utility by adding her petticoat” (A Tramp Abroad, 1880).

Chapter 44 · Skirts, Laces, Petticoats

  • Symbolize femininity, freedom, and perhaps the burden of societal expectations. Cousin Hannah’s paradoxical final request for her skirt contrasts with her life’s advocacy for shedding such encumbrances.
  • Her lost love turned back on the mountain for her skirt: “I must find my skirt, my love. Farewell, farewell, my love.”

Chapter 45 · Skirt/Flounces

  • The lost love or spirit, something elusive that the suffragette seeks but cannot find.

Chapter 47

  • “What could he do for that old bloomer girl”: See Amelia Bloomer in the Chapter 42 resources.
  • “In the East where men wore skirts”: In much of Asia and the Middle East men wear wrapped or flowing garments: the sarong, the lungi, the dhoti, the thobe.

Chapter 47 · Symbolism of Clothing and Veils

  • The recurring motif of skirts, shrouds, and veils points to concealment, mystery, and the social/cultural framing of death and identity.

Chapter 47 · Skirt/Shroud

  • The veil of death, love hidden, mystery of identity.

Chapter 51

  • “He feared the naked valet who had clothed him”: The “naked valet” and the “mad couturier” who clothes him “with the colors of a dream” are outside forces shaping the perception of self and world, as in Plato’s cave, and Thomas Carlyle’s philosophy of clothes in Sartor Resartus (1833-1834) makes the body and the world garments of the spirit. “For the dream of life, even like that of death, must ever contain within it an element of the unrealized, the unrealizable—else all would be complete”: imperfection and the unattainable are part of existence, as existentialist thought holds. Mr. Spitzer fears eviction from the womb, the “citadel” where he heard “the beating of another heart above his heart,” and birth into a world where he will miss the smell of the rose, and the mother who is “a bearded man armored” unsettles fixed ideas of gender. The old jockey who dies of shock when his dream proves real shows the power of the unconscious, as in Freud. “We lived by an imperfect concatenation” echoes the Buddhist teaching of impermanence and the illusory self.

Chapter 51 · The Mantle and Cape

  • Mr. Spitzer’s mantle or cape is described as growing with him, winding like mother-of-pearl around his consciousness and unconsciousness, symbolizing the weight of existence and the intertwining of life and death.

Chapter 52 · Skirts and Veils

  • The suffragette’s lost skirt embroidered with forget-me-nots symbolizes lost love and identity. Veils and skirts also signify the blurred boundaries of gender and self.

Chapter 53 · The Black Cloak and Ivory Cane

  • Emblems of mourning, identity, and secondary intelligence. The cane serves as an extension of Spitzer’s self and his cautious, measured approach to life.

Chapter 54 · The Black Cape and High Silk Hat

  • These identify Mr. Spitzer’s figure as a ghostly, almost theatrical presence, marking him as an outsider and a man out of time.

Chapter 56

  • “many tailored suits from Savile Row”: Savile Row is a street in Central London that was originally famous for men’s tailoring.
  • “innumerable fine Steinkirk thrice-winding scarves”: Steinkirk is a kind of neckcloth worn in a loose and disorderly fashion. It is named for the Battle of Steenkerque (1692), where French officers, surprised by the enemy, went into battle with their cravats wound loosely and tucked through a buttonhole.
  • “huntsmen’s jackets, both green and red”: Fox hunters wear scarlet coats, called hunting pink, while those who hunt hares with beagles and harriers traditionally wear green.

Chapter 56 · Clothing and Tailoring

  • Represent identity, social roles, and continuity/death. Peron’s lavish suits contrast with Mr. Spitzer’s threadbare suit, symbolizing life and decay.

Chapter 57

  • “an insistently polite, threatening note from his brother’s tailor”:

Chapter 57 · The Black Funeral Suit and Tailor’s Bill

  • Symbolizes unresolved debts, both literal and metaphorical. The suit represents Peron’s dignity and the past that Mr. Spitzer attempts to honor and settle.

Chapter 58

  • “his pearl-buttoned spats”: Pearl-buttoned spats were a popular, elegant fashion accessory for both men and women from the late 19th century to the 1920s. Originally designed to protect footwear from dirt on unpaved roads, they became a symbol of social status and high fashion, especially during the Victorian and Edwardian eras. Spats faded in the late 1920s, as paved streets and motorcars made them unnecessary and men’s dress grew more casual.

Chapter 58 · The Black Cape

  • Mr. Spitzer’s attire symbolizes his somber, reflective nature and his boundary state between darkness and light, life and death.

Chapter 59

  • “his long white Steinkirk”: See the Steinkirk scarf in the Chapter 56 resources.

Chapter 60

  • “dresses of bone lace or bird-cages”: Bone lace is bobbin lace, worked on a pillow with bobbins once carved from bone. A bird-cage was the hooped steel crinoline of the 1850s and 1860s.

Chapter 61

  • The Congress gaiter is an ankle boot with elastic gussets in its sides, patented by J. Sparkes Hall in 1837.

Chapter 62

  • “From all his musical rags, future musicians must stitch together a musical coat”: Compare the philosophy of clothes in Thomas Carlyle’s Sartor Resartus (1831), “the tailor retailored.”
  • “the long white Stein-kirk”: See the Steinkirk scarf in the Chapter 56 resources.

Chapter 65 · Mutilated Crockery and Black Gloves

  • Symbols of care, brokenness, and preparation for hardship or death.

Chapter 69 · Fire Escape Room

  • Symbolizes escape but also confinement, a place between safety and danger.

Chapter 71 · Shoes

  • The doctor’s office is littered with mateless women’s shoes from all eras, symbolizing lost or fragmented lives, unfulfilled journeys, and the absence of order.

Chapter 74

  • “a shroud with many, many pockets”: “Shrouds have no pockets”: what is hidden in life cannot be carried into death. An Italian proverb in English print since 1854, it is also a Yiddish saying.

Chapter 74 · The Shroud with Many Pockets

  • Symbolizes the secrets Esther keeps, the hidden aspects of her identity and history.

Chapter 81

  • “a little man wearing a bowler hat”: The bowler hat, or “derby” in the US, is a hard felt hat with a, rounded crown and slightly curled brim, originally designed in 1849 by Thomas and William Bowler for British gamekeepers to provide durable, close-fitting head protection. It became an iconic symbol of 19th-century British, and later American Western, style.
  • “under his rain-streaked ulster”: An ulster is a long, loose overcoat, often with a cape, first made of rough Irish frieze in Belfast and named for the province. Ulster is one of the four historical provinces of Ireland, located in the north of the island. It traditionally comprises nine counties: six form Northern Ireland (Antrim, Armagh, Down, Fermanagh, Londonderry, and Tyrone), which is part of the United Kingdom, while three (Cavan, Donegal, and Monaghan) are part of the Republic of Ireland.

Chapter 81 · Black Mourning Band and Old Rosebud

  • Symbols of death, mourning, and lost beauty.

Chapter 4 · Frozen Iowa and Dead Star

  • The moon and stars symbolize time, fate, and the inevitability of death.
  • “Dead birds singing” and “falling star” evoke loss and the ephemeral nature of life.

Chapter 12 · Moonlight and Mist

  • The pregnant moonlight and mist create an atmosphere of mystery, illumination, and ambiguity.

Chapter 12

  • “baying like a dog at the moon”: “I had rather be a dog, and bay the moon, / Than such a Roman” (Julius Caesar 4.3).

Chapter 13

  • “fixed like the North star”: “But I am constant as the northern star, / Of whose true-fix’d and resting quality / There is no fellow in the firmament” (Julius Caesar 3.1).

Chapter 15 · The Moon

  • Described as “bloodless,” “white,” and like a “thin skull,” symbolizing death, the passage of time, and the eerie, detached observer of human life.
  • The moon, sea, and death imagery function symbolically to explore deeper themes.

Chapter 16 · The Moonlit Ride

  • The ride through the dark garden, past statues, fountains, and old tennis courts, symbolizes a journey through memory and imagination, a “circle like an eye through the garden of the blind.”

Chapter 16 · The Night and the Grounds

  • The story is set at night, under the moonlight, creating a dreamlike atmosphere.
  • The surroundings include dark allées, stunted trees, an old stable, gardens, fountains, statues, and a large, mysterious house with marble pillars, tapestries, and grand stairways.
  • The moonlit garden resembles a “garden of the blind,” and the house is described like a “water castle” with sea motifs and underwater imagery.
  • The atmosphere is eerie yet magical, with references to stars, fireflies, and phantoms.
  • Rich sensory descriptions evoke visual, tactile, and auditory experiences.

Chapter 17 · Moonlight and Darkness

  • The moonlight creates a cold, distant atmosphere.
  • The interplay of light and shadow symbolizes the tension between knowledge and ignorance, reality and illusion.

Chapter 17

  • “the moon which draws the waves in its wake and has no life of its own”: The moon raises the tides and shines only by reflected sunlight.

Chapter 23 · Stars and Natural Light

  • Symbolize the eternal, natural order, and the divine presence.

Chapter 24 · Snow Crystals and Halos

  • Snow crystals and halos are visual symbols of the dreamlike, kaleidoscopic nature of Catherine’s world, with multiple suns, moons, and shapes reinforcing the surreal atmosphere.

Chapter 30 · Stars and Celestial Bodies

  • Symbols of guidance, mystery, and the infinite.

Chapter 31 · Storms, Deserts, Snow, and Stars

  • Storms, deserts, snow, castles, veils, horses, swords, and stars.
  • These images underscore the mystical, elusive, and epic qualities of the characters’ inner lives.

Chapter 31 · The Great Water Eye

  • The “Great Water Eye” of the planet is a recurring symbolic image that links the characters’ personal dramas to the vastness of the universe.

Chapter 33 · Stars and Celestial Imagery

  • Stars and heavens often represent unreachable or eternal realms.
  • Catherine refuses to marry Mr. Spitzer “not while the stars shone in the glassy heavens,” linking love and fate to cosmic forces.

Chapter 35 · Light and Darkness

  • Light (stars, jewel reflections, candles) contrasts with darkness (shadows, fog, cosmic darkness).
  • Cousin Hannah is connected with shining stars and blazing eyes, symbolizing her enduring spirit.
  • Darkness often surrounds Mr. Spitzer and Catherine’s fragmented self.
  • “Like a shooting star which probably knows not its destination when it starts… she would have overshot her mark.”

Chapter 36 · Stars and the Sky

  • Stars symbolize distant memories, lost souls, or unreachable ideals.
  • The motif of stars falling or being connected across time suggests cosmic continuity despite human fragmentation.
  • “Our star’s light did not reach out far, did not illumine the entirety of space, was feeble as one firefly in the heavens of the universe.”

Chapter 38

  • “Lunacy reigned supreme”: Lunacy comes from the Latin luna, the moon, which was long believed to cause madness.

Chapter 38 · Clouds, Whirlwinds, and Stars

  • Reflect the fluidity of time, memory, and identity; also Catherine’s dreamlike mental state.

Chapter 38 · Music of the Spheres

  • Mr. Spitzer’s cosmic music imagery symbolizes the ineffable and eternal aspects of existence beyond human comprehension.

Chapter 39 · Stars, Moons, and Light

  • Celestial imagery emphasizes timelessness, otherworldliness, and Catherine’s ethereal state.
  • Light and darkness interplay to suggest knowledge, madness, and mystery.

Chapter 40 · Clouds, Stars, and Celestial Imagery

  • Frequently used to evoke dreamlike states, mystery, and the vastness of time and space.

Chapter 41 · Pearls and Planets

  • Pearls counted by Catherine symbolize worlds, memories, or selves; counting them leads to loss or dissolution.

Chapter 42 · Lost Ships and Stars

  • Ships represent journeys, lost hopes, and the passage of souls. Stars symbolize guidance, memory, and the unreachable. Mr. Spitzer’s cataloging of lost ships parallels the attempt to map lost lives and loves.

Chapter 43 · Firefly Light / Star

In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 21, Chapter 32, Chapter 38, Chapter 41, Chapter 42, Chapter 46, Chapter 54, Chapter 71, Chapter 72, Chapter 82

Definition from research

Chapter 2 · Jewels and Pearls

  • Pearls run through her fingers, symbolizing beauty, fragility, and the passage of time.
  • Jewelry also symbolizes wealth and burden, hinting at Catherine’s inheritance and social position.

Chapter 21

  • “this great head which was the secret pearl”: The merchant “who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matthew 13:46).

Chapter 32

  • “sapphires which turned to rubies, rubies which turned to sapphires”: Ruby and sapphire are the same mineral, corundum. A trace of chromium turns it red, and that red stone is ruby.

Chapter 38 · Iron Keys and Jeweled Sword

  • Represent authority, battle, and mystery. Hannah walked back and forth, “rattling great iron keys, striking against a stone wall, striking against the empty air, or fighting a mirror with her jeweled sword.”

Chapter 41 · Pearls and Planets

  • Pearls counted by Catherine symbolize worlds, memories, or selves; counting them leads to loss or dissolution.

Chapter 42

  • “all orient pearls”: Orient pearls are the most lustrous, once brought from the East: “Ransack the ocean for orient pearl” (Christopher Marlowe, Doctor Faustus 1.1).

Chapter 46

  • The voice is a sand grain: “Because of me there grew this great pearl.” A natural pearl grows when an oyster coats an irritant with nacre, more often a parasite than a grain of sand.

Chapter 54 · Jewels and Coins

  • Gems and coins appear repeatedly, symbolizing value, loss, and illusion. Mr. Spitzer refuses real jewels, preferring glass ones which is a metaphor for preferring illusion over reality.

Chapter 71

  • “the necklace of pearls that had been my mother’s”: The pearls are repeatedly connected to Vera’s mother and her legacy. They represent the “lost estate” of her mother, something precious yet intangible that Vera inherits and wears, symbolizing the remnants of the past and the enduring connection to her mother’s life and identity. The pearls are described as “real pearls which... would bring no more than cultivated pearls” in the market, suggesting a contrast between their material and symbolic value. The pearls also symbolize continuity amid loss and the passing of time. Vera’s mother believed that the pearls could not be lost or stolen, and that their number paradoxically increased with loss, implying an infinite or eternal quality beyond physical reality. This suggests a theme of immortality or persistence beyond death, where loss in one sense begets gain in another “the more pearls there were” despite losses in life. The novel often blurs the line between dream and reality, and pearls, like many other images, are part of this interplay. Pearls are associated with the ephemeral and the eternal, with illusions and truths mingling. They appear alongside motifs of opium dreams, ghosts, and phantoms, symbolizing the fragile and shifting nature of existence and memory. The pearls are linked to the theme of identity, as something that persists yet changes, much like Vera’s mother herself, who is simultaneously present and absent, real and dreamlike. The pearls become a metaphor for what remains of a person’s essence when all else has faded or been lost. The imagery of pearls dripping or cascading like tears, linked to the mother’s lifeless but radiant hands, suggests mourning and the cycle of life and death. Pearls are connected to sorrow (“the pity, pity, pity of nothing, of something”), highlighting their role as symbols of grief and the preciousness of what is gone.

Chapter 71 · Pearls

  • Vera’s mother’s real pearls symbolize inheritance, lost estate, and the eternal amidst transience.

Chapter 72 · The pearl-like raindrops that never fall

  • Reflect suspended time and unfulfilled potential.
  • Esther Longtree may symbolize the sexual revolution in the United States by considering her character’s embodiment of themes such as fertility, sexuality, societal repression, and the struggle for female autonomy.
  • Esther is depicted as “everlastingly pregnant,” carrying multiple stillborn children, representing an ongoing, unresolved fertility and reproductive issue. She is physically swollen, with symptoms of pregnancy (morning sickness, evening sickness, swollen breasts) but no viable birth occurs. This paradox of constant pregnancy without fulfillment can symbolize the tension in the 1960s between traditional expectations of women centered on motherhood and the emerging desire for sexual freedom and reproductive control. Esther’s “everlasting pregnancy” may reflect the societal burden placed on women to reproduce and the frustration when that role is unfulfilled or controlled by external forces like sterile fathers or societal norms.
  • Esther is described as robustly alive and free in some ways like her hair that flows loose “at whatever cost to sanitation,” and she tosses it regularly as if to preserve her freedom. This image evokes a woman resisting social constraints, symbolic of the sexual liberation movement where women began to assert control over their own bodies and sexuality. Yet, she is also trapped in a “womb” that is both a restaurant and a grave, a liminal space between life and death, fertility and barrenness, reflecting the societal repression of female sexuality and the stigma around pregnancy out of wedlock or outside accepted norms.
  • The numerous stillborn children Esther carries (hidden under leaves, buds, snow, rivers) represent unrealized potential, lost possibilities, and the silencing of female sexual and reproductive expression. The fact that the fathers are “sterile” or “impotent” men, often traveling salesmen or transient figures, can symbolize the failure of patriarchal structures to support or recognize women’s full sexual agency. The stillborns haunt Esther, much like the repressed desires and consequences of sexual control haunt society during the sexual revolution.
  • Esther is simultaneously described as “brilliant but dumb,” “ugly outside... but beautiful inside,” “experienced and sought after” yet also an “old maid” misunderstood by her own parents. This duality reflects the conflicted social status of women during this time who were beginning to break free from traditional roles but still faced judgment, misunderstanding, and marginalization. Esther’s education and cultural refinement contrast with her physical and social marginalization, symbolizing the new woman’s struggle to reconcile intellect, sexuality, and societal acceptance.
  • Esther’s “immortal medical case” status, with the old doctor predicting she will “be pregnant until the stars had fallen,” suggests the ongoing, unresolved nature of women’s sexual liberation. The “everlasting pregnancy” can metaphorically represent the period of social transformation as an era pregnant with possibilities but fraught with struggle, loss, and hope. Her hopefulness despite repeated disappointments mirrors the spirit of the sexual revolution, which challenged existing norms and sought new forms of expression and liberation.
  • Her affinity with natural and mythical elements (wild mares pregnant by the wind, the great skull, the starry heavens, the moon, and the stars) links Esther to a broader symbolic framework of fertility, creation, and cosmic forces. This elevates her personal reproductive tragedy to a universal level, reflecting the countercultural embrace of naturalism, mysticism, and a redefinition of human sexuality as part of a cosmic order or liberation from mechanistic, repressive traditions.
  • Esther Longtree symbolizes the complexities and contradictions of the sexual revolution in America: the tension between fertility and barrenness, freedom and repression, hope and despair, tradition and change. Her character embodies the social anxieties about female sexuality, the quest for autonomy, and the redefinition of womanhood during a period of profound cultural upheaval.
  • Her story encapsulates the bodily, social, and legal struggles over reproduction, economic survival, and patriarchal oppression that shaped the conditions the women’s rights movement sought to change through activism.

In the research: Chapter 4, Chapter 5, Chapter 12, Chapter 17, Chapter 18, Chapter 19, Chapter 20, Chapter 21, Chapter 22, Chapter 63, Chapter 64, Chapter 65, Chapter 66, Chapter 68, Chapter 72

Definition from research

Chapter 4 · Red Hair and Red Rooster’s Wing

  • Symbolizes vitality, passion, and the vividness of Miss MacIntosh’s presence.

Chapter 5 · Hair

  • Symbolizes identity, resistance, and the last vestige of personal freedom.
  • The bus-driver’s hair grows uncontrollably, reflecting his wild imagination and refusal to conform.

Chapter 12 · Hair

  • Symbolic of protection and sensitivity; also connected to historical and biblical references.
  • The meditation on hair foreshadows Miss MacIntosh’s baldness in Chapter 17.

Chapter 12

  • “the hair raising to warn us of our mortal danger”: “Then a spirit passed before my face; the hair of my flesh stood up” (Job 4:15).
  • “The most beautiful ladies of history had been noted for their hair”: Queen Berenice gave her hair to the gods for her husband’s safe return, and it was set among the stars as Coma Berenices.
  • “Absalom was caught among the apple boughs and hanged by his hair”: In 2 Samuel 18:9, Absalom’s “head caught hold of the oak.” Vera makes it an apple tree. His heavy hair was cut once a year (2 Samuel 14:26).
  • “Leonardo had forgotten to give eyebrows to his Mona Lisa”: The Mona Lisa (c. 1503-1519) is a half-length portrait by Leonardo da Vinci. (Wikipedia) The painting shows no eyebrows or lashes, though Giorgio Vasari (1550) praised its eyebrows, “the manner in which the hairs spring from the flesh.”

Chapter 17

  • “she was bald. She was bald as the egg”: Alopecia, the total loss of hair, was popularly blamed on “some sudden shock or amazement or illness.” The hair passage of Chapter 12 prepared for this, and in Chapter 19 Vera finds Miss MacIntosh’s red wig.

Chapter 17 · Baldness

  • Represents loss, emptiness, exposure, and transformation.
  • Compared to “the egg,” “the rock where nothing grows,” “the rose stripped of all its petals,” and “bare as the winter winds,” emphasizing barrenness and desolation.

Chapter 18 · Baldness of Miss MacIntosh

  • Represents the stripping away of illusion, revealing raw and uncomfortable truth.
  • Symbolizes mortality, vulnerability, and the loss of pretense.

Chapter 18

  • “The bald head is soonest shaved”: Miss MacIntosh turns old jokes about baldness on herself, here and in “No grass grows on a busy street.”

Chapter 19

  • “Her red wig, almost purple”: The wig Vera saw “upon the carven chair post” in Chapter 18.
  • “the lashless eyelids”: Alopecia universalis is the loss of all hair on the body, including the brows and lashes.

Chapter 19 · Red Wig

  • A mask or false identity, “perched like a rare tropical bird on the hat rack… within easy reach of her gnarled hand,” ready but separate from her true self.

Chapter 20

  • “There was no crowning glory of woman’s hair”: “If a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for her hair is given her for a covering” (1 Corinthians 11:15).
  • “Ugly is a field without grass, a plant without leaves, a head without hair, according to Ovid”: Ovid, The Art of Love (3.249-250): “Turpe pecus mutilum, turpe est sine gramine campus, / et sine fronde frutex, et sine crine caput” (“Ugly is a hornless bull, ugly a field without grass, a bush without leaves, and a head without hair”). The lines come in his advice to women on hiding the loss of hair, which includes buying false hair.
  • “Hair adds beauty to a good face and terror to an ugly one, according to the Greek”: Plutarch’s Life of Lycurgus (22) explains that the Spartans wore their hair long, remembering a saying of their lawgiver Lycurgus “that a fine head of hair made the handsome more comely still, and the ugly more terrible.”
  • “Was God bald, too”: Children mocked Elisha, “Go up, thou bald head” (2 Kings 2:23), and the Ancient of Days has “the hair of his head like the pure wool” (Daniel 7:9).

Chapter 20 · Hair and Baldness

  • Hair symbolizes beauty, identity, and vitality; baldness represents loss, vulnerability, and exposure.
  • Absence of hair is described as a “barren, impoverished landscape without flower or bush or hedge.”

Chapter 21 · Bald Head

  • Symbolizes raw truth, vulnerability, and the stripping away of superficial identity.

Chapter 21 · Miss MacIntosh’s Morning Appearance

  • Miss MacIntosh’s appearance contrasts sharply with the earlier portrayal of vulnerability, showing her resilience and normalcy despite suffering.

Chapter 22

  • “Take time by the forelock!”: The saying means to act quickly and decisively, especially to take advantage of an opportunity. It comes from the Greek Kairos, Opportunity, carved by Lysippus with a forelock in front and bald behind, so that he can be seized only as he comes. The Roman fabulist Phaedrus tells it of Occasio (Fables 5.8).
  • “Baldness is no cure for sorrow”: Cicero tells the philosopher Bion’s joke about the king who tore out his hair in grief, “as though baldness were a cure for sorrow” (Tusculan Disputations 3.62).

Chapter 63

  • “she with her fire red hair gleaming like the lights in a fiery furnace”: The three young men thrown into Nebuchadnezzar’s fiery furnace came out unharmed: “nor was an hair of their head singed” (Daniel 3:27, KJV).
  • “How does it happen that you have no hair along your skin?”: Alopecia universalis is considered an autoimmune disease where the person does not grow any hair on any part of their body but is otherwise healthy.
  • “Shall I tear my hair?”: See mourning that tears the hair in the Chapter 61 resources.
  • “Long hair is short wisdom”: An old German proverb said of women, “Lange Haare, kurzer Sinn,” long hair, short sense; the bald Miss MacIntosh turns it back.
  • “Where’s my hair, that woman’s glory?”: “But if a woman have long hair, it is a glory to her: for her hair is given her for a covering” (1 Corinthians 11:15, KJV).
  • “My sisters had long ropes of hair. A man could climb them”: “Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair” (Brothers Grimm, 1812).
  • “It is woman who makes man’s life so short and robs him of his hair”: “And she made him sleep upon her knees; and she called for a man, and she caused him to shave off the seven locks of his head” (Judges 16:19, KJV). Delilah’s shears took Samson’s strength.

Chapter 63 · The Wig and Baldness

  • Miss MacIntosh’s wig symbolizes the facade of social norms and appearances, which she ultimately reveals as a protective but deceptive covering. Young described the wig as the illusion itself, “the dream by which she lived” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965), and the hair it replaces as “the symbol of the dream and of the feminine in life that she never had” (Marguerite Young, interview with Duncan MacDonald, Observation Point, 1965).
  • Her baldness, exposed in a moment of vulnerability, represents raw truth, mortality, and the stripping away of illusions.

Chapter 64

  • “A barber in Chicago told me he could do nothing”: Young asked her beauty operator whether a bald woman had ever come in. One had, he said: “This lady came in, lifted her wig, and there was this head as bald as a billiard ball. And she said, what can you do for me? And he said, I couldn’t grow one hair on your head for a million dollars. And if I could, I wouldn’t need a million dollars.” Young said, “I have Miss McIntosh go to a Chicago barber and have this exact scene in the book” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “Bald I came into this world, and bald I will go out of it”: “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither” (Job 1:21, KJV).
  • “this was the universal baldness and sign of mourning”: In the Bible, shaving the head is a sign of mourning: “Make thee bald, and poll thee for thy delicate children; enlarge thy baldness as the eagle” (Micah 1:16, KJV).
  • “She should walk in narrow ways with her head covered”: “But every woman that prayeth or prophesieth with her head uncovered dishonoureth her head: for that is even all one as if she were shaven” (1 Corinthians 11:5, KJV). Paul’s rule fell hardest on a girl born bald.

Chapter 64 · Baldness

  • Represents vulnerability, difference, and mourning. It is a physical manifestation of Miss MacIntosh’s inner loneliness and social alienation.

Chapter 64 · Wig

  • The wig symbolizes the mask people wear to hide their true selves and conform to societal expectations. Miss MacIntosh’s frequent removal and replacement of the wig depict her struggle with identity. Young described the wig as the illusion itself, “the dream by which she lived” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 65

  • “and the numbers of the hairs in her head, and the least sparrow”: “But the very hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matthew 10:30, KJV), said to a woman who has none.
  • “To hoar hairs will I carry you”: “And even to hoar hairs will I carry you” (Isaiah 46:4, KJV). Miss MacIntosh cannot say that she has none.
  • “Her head was filled with dew, he said”: Mr. Bonebreaker courts her with the Song of Solomon: “my head is filled with dew” (5:2), “thy hair is as a flock of goats” (4:1), “Thy neck is as a tower of ivory” (7:4), “Many waters cannot quench love” (8:7), and Job’s “eyelids of the morning” (41:18), all KJV. Every compliment is to her hair or her beauty.
  • “Instead of a girdle, there would be a rent”: “And it shall come to pass, that instead of sweet smell there shall be stink; and instead of a girdle a rent; and instead of well set hair baldness” (Isaiah 3:24, KJV).
  • “He himself had often said, quoting the Bible, that the wife should stand forth before her husband”: “Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold… But let it be the hidden man of the heart” (1 Peter 3:3-4, KJV).

  • The physical condition of Miss MacIntosh (her baldness, lost breast, and scars) are central to the narrative.
