Chapter 4 · Nature’s Cruelty and Funeral Wreaths

  • The natural world is depicted not as nurturing but cold and indifferent.
  • Funeral wreaths and deaf old people symbolize death, silence, and abandonment.

Chapter 6 · The Wedding and Funeral Imagery

  • Madge’s “wedding” is a funeral; marriage equals death in her experience.
  • The absence of traditional wedding symbols intensifies the sense of loss and unrealized hopes.

Chapter 6

  • “until Death did them part”: The phrase comes from the marriage vows of the Book of Common Prayer (1549), which read “till death us depart”; the wording later became “till death us do part.” The same vows promise “for better for worse.”
  • “her little wedding cake bridegroom with his polished mustache”: Cake toppers of a tiny bride and groom became fashionable in the United States in the early twentieth century.
  • “this circle of creation, all of one piece having no beginning and no end”: The wedding ring has long stood for eternity. It is worn on the fourth finger, where an old belief placed a vein running to the heart.
  • “a handful of rice or confetti or white rose petals”: Rice was thrown for fertility, a bride wore “something old” such as her mother’s veil, and the bride who caught the bouquet would be the next to marry.
  • “to carry her across the threshold”: The custom goes back to Rome. A bride who stumbled at the door brought bad luck, and Madge “had stumbled on her way to the altar.”
  • “the Justice of the Peace to tie the knot”: A justice of the peace could perform a civil marriage without a church or guests.
  • “love, honor, and obey”: The older prayer book vows had only the bride promise to “obey.” Madge throws the word at Homer.
  • “She carried the yellow tuberoses at the commencement”: Tuberoses, heavily fragrant, were favorite flowers at Victorian funerals.
  • “Death comes to every wedding feast”: In Holbein’s Dance of Death (1538) a skeleton drums ahead of a newly married couple.

Chapter 7 · The Graveyard

  • A place of refuge and sustenance for Musidora and her children, representing the blurred line between life and death. One of the last public places where people can gather.

Chapter 8 · The Graveyard Hill

  • Represents the boundary between life and death, a literal and figurative crossroads on the journey.

Chapter 8 · Names on Tombstones

  • Names like Stonecipher, Longtree, Thistlewaite, Chesterfield, and others evoke lineage, memory, and the passage of generations, underscoring the permanence of death. Longtree is Esther’s last name, a character at the end of the novel.

Chapter 9 · Marriage and Reproduction Imagery

  • Miss MacIntosh’s lectures on marriage, ovaries, and reproduction are laden with symbolic meaning about societal expectations, femininity, and the passage into adulthood.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s comparison (flowers impregnated only by the wind are colorless, “but with a woman, there must be a man, not merely the wind”) symbolizes the necessity of union and procreation in life, reflecting the cultural norms around marriage and gender roles.

Chapter 10 · Wedding/Funeral Ceremony

  • Symbolizes the intertwined nature of beginnings and endings, union and separation.

Chapter 10

  • “pots and pans jangling in my ears”: A shivaree, or charivari, was the old custom of banging pots and pans outside newlyweds’ windows on their wedding night.
  • “we are gathered here in the sight of God and of this company to join man and woman together”: The Book of Common Prayer opens the marriage service, “Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation, to join together this man and this woman in holy matrimony.”
  • “Do either of ye know of an impediment to this marriage”: The phrase is from the Book of Common Prayer, which drew on the Sarum rite. It reads, “I require and charge you both, as ye will answer at the dreadful day of judgment when the secrets of all hearts shall be disclosed, that if either of you know any impediment . . . ye do now confess it,” and calls on anyone who knows a cause to “speak, or else hereafter for ever hold his peace.”
  • “Unadvisedly or lightly, marriage should not be entered in”: The prayer book says marriage is “not by any to be enterprised, nor taken in hand, unadvisedly, lightly . . . but reverently, discreetly, advisedly, soberly.”
  • “the rites for the burial of the dead”: Funeral rites originated from Jewish and Roman customs. The Order for the Burial of the Dead in the Book of Common Prayer is the service the preacher slides into.
  • “the turtle Solomon and the red geranium and an old, empty shoe”: An old shoe was thrown after the bride or tied to the carriage for luck.

Chapter 14 · The Funeral and the Graveyard

  • The funeral scenes, especially Mr. Spitzer’s brother’s funeral, symbolize mourning, loss, and the passage of time.
  • Catherine’s absence from funerals and the details of the mourning rituals emphasize her detachment and the fragmented nature of her existence.

Chapter 14

  • “the funeral gondola with the corrugated angel at its helm”: Venice carries its dead by black gondola to the cemetery island of San Michele. Liszt wrote “La lugubre gondola” (1882) foreseeing Wagner’s death in Venice, and Wagner’s body left by gondola in 1883.

Chapter 15

  • “is always the bridegroom”: The old image of Death and the Maiden, set to music by Schubert.
  • “wedlock is padlock”: From John Ray’s English Proverbs (1670).
  • “one should keep one’s eyes open, but after marriage, one should keep them half shut”: Poor Richard: “Keep your eyes wide open before marriage, half shut afterwards” (1738).

Chapter 16

  • “the black funeral gondola”: Venice’s black funeral gondolas.

Chapter 16 · The House as a Tomb and Water Castle

  • The grand house is described with imagery of tombs, water, and underwater life, creating a sense of mystery and timelessness. The references to the phoenix and musical tomb further emphasize themes of death and rebirth.

Chapter 17

  • “visualizing her with a red, curled mustache, that I had been right in assigning to her the role of the bridegroom”: The red mustache of Chapter 9 and the wedding dream of Chapter 10.

Chapter 18

  • “every heart is married to death who is the bridegroom and the bride”: Death as the bridegroom, as in Chapter 15. It means that human life is fundamentally intertwined with death. Death is not an external threat but a constant, intimate presence in life. It emphasizes the tragic and inevitable nature of mortality that defines and shapes human existence, love, and relationships. This theme is woven throughout the novel, in the narrator’s reflections on life, death, and illusion.

Chapter 20

Chapter 21

  • “as when Mr. Spitzer had taken it out of its long white box”: The dress of Chapter 9. Mr. Spitzer promised, “Fair as a bride I should be,” and Miss MacIntosh complained of its low neck and lack of sleeves.

Chapter 32

In Chapter 6 “she had no bridal trousseau, no negligee ribbons, no clothes to come to child-bed with, no dance programs, no suitors, no husband.”

Chapter 32 · Death as a Wedding and Wedding as Death

  • The narrative blurs the boundaries between life milestones and death: “weddings are funerals, and funerals are weddings.” This imagery underscores the theme of transformation and loss inherent in marriage and life.
  • Catherine’s vague, elusive descriptions of her marriage (to a phantom, a porpoise, a star, an iceberg) symbolize the illusory or absent nature of her union and love. Marriage here is a symbolic death of the self or an eternal separation, while death is the final union.

Chapter 33 · The Wedding and Bridegroom(s)

Chapter 33 · The Wedding Memories

  • White symbolizes innocence and first marriage; black, “as befitted one who should be married twice,” signifies death, mourning, and a second marriage.

Chapter 34 · The Funeral and the King of France

  • Represents grandeur, loss, and the blending of significant life events into one confusing memory.

Chapter 42 · The Bridegroom and Withered Flowers

  • Represent unfulfilled love and abandonment, contrasting with Cousin Hannah’s militant independence and loneliness.

  • The suffragette’s lost skirt embroidered with forget-me-nots symbolizes lost love and identity. Veils and skirts also signify the blurred boundaries of gender and self.

Chapter 61

  • The Sarcophagus of the Spouses from Cerveteri (c. 520 BC, Villa Giulia, Rome) shows a husband and wife reclining together as if at a banquet; Etruscan tombs held engraved bronze mirrors.
  • “a paid mourner at a funeral, walking behind the corpse”: In England the hired attendants who stood at the door and walked before the hearse were called mutes; Oliver Twist is put to work as one for the undertaker Mr. Sowerberry (Charles Dickens, Oliver Twist, 1838).

  • “Drape all the mirrors with black”: Mirrors in a house of mourning were covered, by Jewish custom during shiva and in Victorian homes, so the soul of the dead would not be caught or the living distracted by vanity.

Chapter 64

  • “Before her body she committed to the deep”: “We therefore commit his body to the deep” (Book of Common Prayer, burial at sea). Vera, writing afterward, already knows how Miss MacIntosh will die.
  • “Whom God hath created, let God not put away”: Compare the marriage service: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Matthew 19:6, KJV).

Chapter 65

  • “handing out cards promising quick and easy divorces”: In 1931 Nevada cut its residency for divorce to six weeks, and Reno became the divorce capital.

  • Symbolizes the irreversible bond with death and the complexity of human relationships.

  • Represents death, loyalty, and the neglect of forgotten beings, mirroring the hotel’s decay.

  • Symbolizes death and mourning; it appears on the dead baby and connects to Esther’s fears about paternity and legacy.

Definition from research

Chapter 15

Listed as: The old, blind sheep dog

  • The sheep dog’s barking is repeatedly mentioned as an ominous sign, something that "had not barked for nothing," unlike a young dog who barks merely for pleasure. This suggests that the dog's barking is a deliberate warning of danger lurking nearby, perhaps a threat to Vera's innocence or safety.
  • Miss MacIntosh explicitly warns Vera to be careful because "someone who would take a young girl by the hair and drag her into the shadows where her cries should not be heard" might be near.
  • The dog’s barking seems to symbolize a protective instinct, alerting to the presence of real dangers in the night that Vera might be tempted to ignore or not fully understand.
  • The dog is described as "old" and "blind," which adds complexity to its symbolism. Blindness here can be interpreted as a metaphor for the limitations of perception that come with age or experience.
  • While the dog cannot see, it still hears and senses danger, which may suggest that wisdom or vigilance does not solely depend on sight or youthful alertness.
  • The dog’s blindness could also represent the older generation’s partial understanding of dangers, aware but not fully able to prevent them. This aligns with Vera’s reflections on how older people, including Miss MacIntosh, fail to grasp the "heart of youth" and the deeper currents of life and death.
  • The dog’s old age and blindness also evoke mortality and the approach of death, consistent with the chapter’s pervasive meditation on death as a "bridegroom" and the many faces of death.
  • The old blind sheep dog is isolated in the night, barking at waves and wind, much like Vera’s own sense of separation from the older generation and their "adult fantasies."
  • On a narrative level, the dog's barking serves as a tension-building device. It punctuates the chapter’s meditative and philosophical tone with a concrete, audible signal of danger. It brings the abstract themes of death, danger, and innocence into a tangible presence, grounding Vera's lofty reflections in the physical reality of the night and the environment.
  • “The old sheep dog barking in the night had not barked for nothing”: The proverb is “An old dog barks not in vain,” from George Herbert’s Outlandish Proverbs (1640).

It may function as a potent symbol of failing protection, limited perception, and the human struggle to confront elusive and overwhelming existential truths. Its presence underscores the chapter’s meditation on vulnerability, loss, and the elusive nature of reality and memory.
  • Vera hears him barking “perhaps at a spar, perhaps at the last falling star… or some danger greater than any I could have imagined.”

Definition from research

Chapter 1

Listed as: Miss Georgia MacIntosh

  • Vera’s lost companion and moral anchor, embodying simplicity, truth, and steadfastness.
  • Young saw this common sense as a disguise: “Her whole life is an impersonation. She’s by no means sensible. It’s just her verbalism that makes her seem sensible” (Marguerite Young, interview with Duncan MacDonald, Observation Point, 1965). “Miss Macintosh was the one illusionist in her assumption that there was a simple foundation of truth” (Marguerite Young, interview, WNYC radio, New York).

Chapter 3

Listed as: Miss (Georgia) MacIntosh

  • A nursemaid who embodies practicality, common sense, and moral certainty.
  • Described physically with "marcelled red hair," "greyish, greenish eyes," and a robust constitution.
  • She is a symbol of stability, reality, and groundedness amidst chaos and confusion.
  • Rejects illusions, fantasies, and idle dreams; values labor, discipline, and the present moment.
  • Wears simple, durable clothing; disdains luxury and extravagance.
  • Has a brusque, rough demeanor, often compared to an old sailor.
  • She is industrious, always busy, and advocates physical exercise and self-forgetfulness.
  • Holds a strict moral code, emphasizing honesty, self-control, and acceptance of life's hardships.
  • Originates from What Cheer, Iowa, a simple town, and contrasts sharply with the opulent, dreamlike environment of the household.
  • Maintains distance from others, avoids intimacy, and does not indulge in self-pity.
  • Ultimately disappears under mysterious circumstances, leaving behind only her clothes and belongings on the beach.
  • Mentions she has a brother Richard, who disappeared while being a missionary.

Chapter 4

  • The lost love, symbolizing a "normal life" and idealized domesticity.
  • Her disappearance is mysterious and traumatic.
  • Associated with innocence and unattainable dreams.

Chapter 9

  • Vera’s guardian, strict and practical, embodying discipline and austere values.
  • Holds strong beliefs about women’s roles, marriage, and responsibility.
  • Comes from a harsh, unprivileged background in What Cheer, Iowa.
  • Acts as a maternal figure but also as a controlling authority.
  • Is caring yet unyielding, knowledgeable yet evasive.

Chapter 10

  • An older woman, practical and resigned to a life without love or marriage.
  • She is portrayed as colorless, ordinary in appearance, yet capable and domestically inclined.
  • In the dream, she assumes the role of bridegroom, further blurring gender and identity.

Chapter 11

  • Her denial of “those things which did not exist” is the lesson Vera leans on to tell dream from reality.

Chapter 12

  • The practical, no-nonsense caretaker who keeps the "Old Reliable" clock.
  • Represents pragmatism, moral clarity, and a grounded worldview.
  • Cautions against illusion and flight of fancy; emphasizes duty and reality.
  • Her perspective contrasts with Vera’s imaginative nature.
  • “The most beautiful ladies of history had been noted for their hair”: Queen Berenice gave her hair to the gods for her husband’s safe return, and it was set among the stars as Coma Berenices.
  • “the first vision would also be the last”: Foreshadowing of Chapter 17, when Vera finds Miss MacIntosh bald.
  • “her lips turned blue and her skin lost its natural color, turning to saffron”: Blue lips and short breath are signs of a failing heart or lungs, a warning Vera does not read.
  • Her short breath, blue lips, and stone-grey skin are signs Vera does not yet read.
  • She threatens to retire, taps Vera with a silver thimble carved “Juliet, 1899,” and saves soap coupons “to exchange for crockery.”

Chapter 13

  • Miss MacIntosh, once a fixed star in Vera’s life, becomes like a "perfect stranger."
  • “a perfect stranger I had lived with for seven years”: “From my seventh to my fourteenth birthday” (Chapter 9).
  • Lips blue and face “pale and twisted with unuttered pain,” she walked through cloudbursts on her constitutional.
  • Her rote questions: “Where is North Dakota, and what is a monsoon, and what is a mirage, Vera Cartwheel?”

Chapter 13 · Miss MacIntosh

  • Initially a symbol of stability and ordinariness, she transforms into a mysterious figure, representing the unknowability of others and the fragile nature of relationships.

Chapter 15

  • Represents the adult world’s order, prudence, and caution, but also coldness and emotional distance.
  • She is methodical, practical, and somewhat resigned, embodying a worldview that emphasizes survival and control over passion or mystery.
  • Her repeated warnings about danger and death show concern but also a limiting worldview.
  • Her peculiar habits suggest underlying fragility or unresolved fears.
  • “She could not swim a stroke”: Foreshadowing of Miss MacIntosh’s death in the sea.
  • She cannot swim, keeps her windows open in winter, and sleeps in a bare room under a harp-framed bed with “no angels to play these harps.”
  • She answers every personal question with a date, such as “the sinking of the Titanic.”

Chapter 16

  • Miss MacIntosh is her caretaker, described as an “old witch” by Vera, who holds a controlling influence over Vera’s life.
  • “Miss MacIntosh was an old witch who kept me enchained in a dark tower”: Rapunzel, locked in a tower by a witch.
  • Her door, “usually locked and barred from the inside,” opens of itself, and she stands by the window, “greatly changed… unbelievably not herself.”

Chapter 17

  • Initially described as a familiar and trusted figure, a nursemaid, a guardian.
  • Transforms into a bald, expressionless, ghostly figure, described as “bald as the egg or as the rock where nothing grows,” symbolizing loss, change, or an unsettling void.
  • Portrayed with contradictory imagery: both fragile and monstrously strong, spectral yet physically violent.
  • Vera struggles to reconcile this apparition with the Miss MacIntosh she knew, suspecting deception and a hidden identity.
  • Symbolizes a “bald pretender,” a false self, or a shadowy force challenging Vera.
  • “she was bald. She was bald as the egg”: Alopecia, the total loss of hair, was popularly blamed on “some sudden shock or amazement or illness.” The hair passage of Chapter 12 prepared for this, and in Chapter 19 Vera finds Miss MacIntosh’s red wig.
  • “I knew her by her broken nose”: The broken nose from the Spokane bus.
  • “this old man who had only one breast”: Halsted’s radical mastectomy (1894), which removed the breast and the muscles beneath it, was the standard treatment for breast cancer for most of the twentieth century. Chapter 19 confirms the loss. In Chapter 10, Vera imagined “claws upon her forehead like the claws of a lobster,” and cancer takes its name from the crab.
  • She has “only one breast,” and Vera knows her only “by her broken nose” from the Spokane bus (Chapter 9).

Chapter 18

  • Initially perceived as a plain, red-headed nursemaid.
  • Transforms into a bald, frightening figure symbolizing raw truth and loss.
  • Acts as a guide or interlocutor, mixing sternness with intimacy.
  • Represents both nurturing and harsh realities of life, death, and change.
  • Embodies themes of charity, mortality, and the limits of human understanding.
  • “Who was that old rapist if not Miss MacIntosh”: Imagery in this chapter hints that either physically, emotionally, or psychologically a rape took place. Vera because of her age and experience does not have the words to fully explain what has happened to her.
  • “The left breast is already gone”: Miss MacIntosh talks about losing her left breast. William Halsted performed his first radical mastectomy in New York in 1882 and described the operation in 1894. There is no clear record of how earlier women survived the operation, or for how long.
  • “the heavy, claw-shaped mark of her hand upon my forehead”: In Chapter 10, Vera imagined “claws upon her forehead like the claws of a lobster.” Now the claw marks Vera.
  • “that hers was that knob where the breast was missing”: In the AMC series Dietland (2018), based on Sarai Walker’s novel, the character Julia (Tamara Tunie) reveals to Plum that she has had a double mastectomy, after a life of wearing “a mask,” as Tunie put it: “the hair, the makeup, the clothes.”
  • Her red wig hangs on the chair post, and she mourns the left breast “already gone.”
  • She threatens to kill Vera if she tells, then says she lost her hair in Vera’s service.

Chapter 19

  • Bald head cold as marble, veined limbs, a missing breast (amputated), thin, ascetic mouth with “not one soft fuzz of hair upon the upper lip,” red wig resembling a tropical bird, gnarled hands.
  • Wears a baseball cap or old caps in the morning and a green ribbon in the evenings.
  • Always carries a whistle around her neck.
  • Wears a veil-tied hat outdoors, sometimes layered with heavy veiling.
  • Carries an old black umbrella indoors and outdoors, like a shield.
  • Sleeps lightly, alert to the slightest noise.
  • Yet this morning she sleeps on with “a kind of abandon,” “singularly unaware of my scrutiny.”
  • Has a strong Christian faith, critical of gambling, “the crafty Devil’s handiwork.”
  • Exhibits physical and emotional contradictions: shifting skin color, blushing for no apparent reason, and trying to resist external forces (“bucking against the broncho wind”).
  • The playing cards, especially the “deuce of clubs,” symbolize fate, death, or a trial by tears, despite her rejection of gambling.
  • Her patched clothing and worn items reflect hardship and resilience.
  • “her dim mackintosh”: The Scottish chemist Charles Macintosh patented his rubberized waterproof cloth in 1823, and the raincoat took his name. It is her name, too.
  • “one breast had been amputated”: The Halsted operation of Chapters 17 and 18.

Chapter 20

  • A figure of strength and common sense, yet marked by profound physical and existential deprivation.
  • Described as “hale and hearty, a red-headed nursemaid” in the past, yet now revealed in a state of vulnerability and loss.
  • Her condition is a mystery to Vera, who struggles to reconcile her external robustness with the internal and physical ravages revealed by the light.
  • She embodies the tension between resilience and suffering, denial and revelation.
  • Vera resolves to “protect her from the knowledge of herself.”
  • She had never wished to travel or see the world, “for she had seen enough of it,” and she was “cryptic as to any forlorn romance of the past.”
  • “Not that she would ever really die, of course!”: Her disappearance into the sea is told in Chapter 6.
  • “the missing breast like a door knob”: The “knob where the breast was missing” of Chapter 18.

Chapter 21

  • Portrayed as a strong yet vulnerable figure, marked physically by baldness, scars, and loss, which symbolize deeper suffering.
  • Despite her condition, she maintains a robust and kind demeanor, showing resilience. She is depicted with vivid details like her red hair, green ribbon, and practical attire.
  • She embodies the tension between appearance and inner reality, strength and vulnerability.
  • Her sayings on the Devil: he “does not always wear horns,” can “quote his Scriptures,” and is “God’s ape.”

Chapter 22

  • A forthright, practical woman with a strong sense of duty, she is Vera’s caretaker and disciplinarian.
  • She is resistant to illusions and ghosts, skeptical of sentimentality, and focused on maintaining order.
  • Despite her harshness, she harbors her own doubts and vulnerabilities, reflected in her philosophical musings and physical frailty.
  • She counts the days of creation from Sunday, works every day of the week, and blames the Emperor Constantine for the Christian Sunday.
  • Her “old dollar watch… was given to her by her dead love.”

Chapter 23

  • Miss MacIntosh is portrayed as fiercely grounded in what she calls “common sense,” valuing the “middle brow,” the “middle way,” and the “average life,” a disposition she prides herself on as her “greatest love,” even if others despise it.
  • This common sense coexists with a pervasive skepticism toward accepted truths such as history, geography, and law, which she dismisses as unstable, uncertain, or outright falsehoods.
  • She challenges grand narratives, like that of Caesar crossing the Rubicon or the veracity of historical figures, suggesting that time has neither accumulated nor taught wisdom.
  • This skeptical realism reveals a character who questions the foundations of knowledge and human pretensions but does so without despair; rather, she seems to accept human limitations with a certain weary humor and irony.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s discourse centers on her criticism of modern inventions, especially electric lights. She associates electricity, notably Benjamin Franklin’s experiments, as a disruptive force that has destroyed natural rhythms, privacy, and the quietness of night. She laments electric lights for erasing darkness, which she sees as essential for sleep, privacy, and even mystery in human relationships, particularly marriage. Electric lights, she argues, expose flaws and imperfections that were once safely hidden in darkness, thereby damaging marriages and social harmony.
  • Her detailed critique extends to “electric trains,” “electric irons,” “fluorescent lamps,” and “two-way lighting systems” as unnatural intrusions into life’s natural order.
  • This stance encapsulates her resistance to tampering with “old, damaged creation” and her preference for simpler, older ways such as “bayberry candles,” “snuffers,” and natural starlight. Her view is that the modern world’s brightness is a form of extravagant excess that impoverishes human experience and dignity.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s practical nature is emphasized by descriptions of her appearance and habits. She dresses plainly, in worn, practical clothing: a grey baseball sweater with a ravelling sleeve, stout shoes, and a patched salt-and-pepper tweed coat.
  • She carries her “rigging” everywhere, including an old black umbrella likened to a sail and a whale-boned ice-breaker corset, symbolizing her preparedness and no-nonsense approach to life on a “rough shore.”
  • She rejects frivolities such as filmy dresses or adornments, even on significant occasions like weddings or funerals, signaling her seriousness and focus on the immediate, tangible world rather than on dreams or illusions.
  • Despite her talk of cosmic and remote issues like glaciers, submerged continents, and the first days of creation, Miss MacIntosh reveals little of her personal emotions or vulnerabilities.
  • She claims her consciousness ceases during sleep and that she cannot remember dreams, not even her own, suggesting a detachment from inner emotional life or a guardedness.
  • Her conscience “kept guard” as a “lonely vigil,” indicating solitude and perhaps a self-imposed emotional isolation.
  • She evades personal disclosures and remains impassive, almost austere, in her demeanor.
  • This emotional reserve contrasts with the vastness of the cosmic themes she invokes, highlighting a tension between the grand and the personal.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s reflections often shift from the mundane to the cosmic and from daily life and societal critiques to the “first starfish upon the first beach” and “the first moon drawing the first tide.” This oscillation suggests that she perceives human life as part of a vast, impersonal natural order that transcends immediate existence.
  • She uses cosmic imagery to mask what she does not want to reveal: her fears, losses, or inner life.
  • This duality makes her a somewhat enigmatic figure, connecting the earthly and the universal while remaining personally elusive.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s thoughts about the coming winter, the colorlessness of the world under snow and ice, and the need to prepare with warm clothing and supplies reveal a keen awareness of mortality and the cycles of life.
  • Winter symbolizes death or hardship, and her sober preparation indicates acceptance rather than fear. Yet, she also acknowledges the subtle beauty of winter’s muted colors, reflecting a nuanced appreciation of life’s phases and transitions.
  • Her concern with time’s passing, the loss inherent in change, and the persistence of “dimmed colors” in hardship underscore a mature, grounded philosophy.
  • Throughout her discourse, Miss MacIntosh repeatedly condemns human vanity, illusions of grandeur, and false hopes.
  • She refers to “vain man” in multiple historical and contemporary contexts, from Emperor Constantine and Caesar to Benjamin Franklin, pointing out the futility of human pretensions to immortality or mastery.
  • She warns against illusions, falsehoods that may mask other truths, and the human tendency to stumble blindly in the “broad daylight which God has lighted.”
  • Her repeated invocation of vanity and illusion underscores a theme of human limitation and the importance of humility and realism.

Chapter 24

  • Practical, grounded, and coarse-grained, she offers contrast to Catherine and the servants’ fantastical world.
  • She is a companion to Vera and represents the voice of reality amidst chaos.

Chapter 27

  • “Any old silver-dollar stop watch should have done for him”: Miss MacIntosh’s “silver-dollar watch,” which she always wears (Chapters 3, 9, and 22). Ingersoll’s Yankee (1896), sold for a dollar, was “the watch that made the dollar famous.”

Chapter 35

  • “She had not been merely another old maid dreaming with her ivory-boned knitting needles”: Cousin Hannah is contrasted with Miss MacIntosh, whose “knitting needles of ivory bone” click in Chapter 1. Young’s old maid, with her balls of grey yarn and her looks at the alarm clock, lives in “empty servitude.” Cousin Hannah is the opposite: she journeyed to far and dangerous places and fought for women’s rights and freedom.

Chapter 38

  • “action was no necessary criterion or measure of life”: Those that take action, do things, and are preoccupied with accomplishments are rewarded. The mid-western, Protestant work ethic is set in these standards. The Protestant work ethic is implicitly reflected through the character of Miss MacIntosh and her attitudes toward life, labor, and morality (Max Weber, The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism, 1905). In 2021 young people in China began “lying flat” (Elsie Chen, “These Chinese Millennials Are ‘Chilling,’ and Beijing Isn’t Happy,” New York Times, July 3, 2021). It recalls Diogenes the Cynic, a Greek philosopher, who lived in a large storage jar in Athens, often called a barrel, scorning comfort and convention. Work is considered “a false idol” and people instead rest, exercise, and relax as a form of “resistance.”

Chapter 39

  • “Is it God’s drug”: Karl Marx famously described religion as “the opium of the people” (Karl Marx, A Contribution to the Critique of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right, 1844), suggesting that it numbs the pain of social inequality and exploitation. Lenin called it “a sort of spiritual booze” (Vladimir Lenin, “Socialism and Religion,” 1905). Religion may be used to maintain the status quo and discourage social change. This view might assert that religion offers easy answers to complex questions about the universe, life, and death. It may appeal to those who lack resources and/or education to form different perspectives. The novel suggests that religion, like opium, can be both a source of comfort and a form of escapism or a way to cope with the harshness and uncertainties of mortal life. Catherine’s opium paradise, filled with angels and ethereal visions, embodies this duality: it is an enchantment that extends her life beyond the physical but also confines her to a dreamlike state, disconnected from concrete reality. This resonates with the Marxist critique of religion as “the opium of the people,” implying a narcotic that dulls awareness and delays confrontation with real suffering. However, Young also complicates this view by showing that such illusions, whether religious or drug-induced, can be necessary for survival amid profound existential despair. In Chapter 1, Miss MacIntosh’s critique highlights the need to face reality soberly and practically, warning against being seduced by illusions that reject nature and the “bare face” of existence.

Chapter 63

  • Miss MacIntosh is described as the “Rock of Ages” in a crumbling world, a symbol of stability, clarity, and common sense.
  • She embodies straightforwardness, rejecting illusions and fantasies, and insists on living within a “framework” of reality.
  • Her physical appearance symbolizes her internal struggle: her ruddy hair like a “sunset burning with bees,” a broken nose, and eventually revealed baldness, all reflecting her life’s hardships and resilience.
  • The black umbrella she carries indoors and out is, in Young’s words, “a kind of canopy between her and reality. You don’t get too close to her” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). It “always casts a shadow around her and forbids intimacy” (Marguerite Young, interview, WNYC radio, New York).
  • Miss MacIntosh is a moral mentor and nursemaid figure who values practicality over imagination.
  • She is skeptical of dreams, illusions, and modern distractions, such as electric lights, which she believes disturb natural life rhythms and privacy.
  • She is combative and sharp, not hesitating to scold even divine figures like Emperor Constantine or God Himself for what she sees as excess or failure.
  • Despite her stern exterior, she has a deep, incorruptible sense of humor and reveals moments of vulnerability, especially when discussing her baldness and personal losses.

Chapter 64

  • The central figure of the chapter, an orphanage matron who has suffered lifelong baldness.
  • She is portrayed as a strong yet vulnerable woman, bearing the weight of loneliness and social alienation.
  • Her baldness is both a physical condition and a metaphor for her isolation and difference from others.
  • Miss MacIntosh evolves from a figure shrouded in mystery to a deeply human character marked by resilience and vulnerability.
  • Her storytelling reveals layers of her personality, from pride and courage to sadness and regret.
  • “A barber in Chicago told me he could do nothing”: Young asked her beauty operator whether a bald woman had ever come in. One had, he said: “This lady came in, lifted her wig, and there was this head as bald as a billiard ball. And she said, what can you do for me? And he said, I couldn’t grow one hair on your head for a million dollars. And if I could, I wouldn’t need a million dollars.” Young said, “I have Miss McIntosh go to a Chicago barber and have this exact scene in the book” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “a pair of old black gloves”: Young had Miss MacIntosh walk into the sea in black gloves “which she had carefully darned the night before.” Unsure what they meant, she asked a psychiatrist friend, who explained “all the meanings of the word black and gloves in relation to psychology and guilt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Charles Ruas, WBAI radio, New York). Two or three years after she wrote the scene, a man killed himself off Long Island: “He wore only a pair of black gloves,” which made her feel “I had struck something in reality there, too” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 65

  • A woman of many moods and contradictions, both physically and emotionally marked by her ailments.
  • She is bald, missing a breast, and wears wigs to mask her reality.
  • Profoundly lonely and marked by a sense of loss, she is simultaneously resigned and hopeful.
  • She embodies a “pilgrim’s progress from nowhere to nowhere,” with a simple, austere view of life and death.
  • Her internal conflict centers on her past, her physical condition, and her tenuous relationship with faith and society.
  • She is portrayed as both vulnerable and strong, practical yet mystical.
  • Young claimed descent from John Knox on her mother’s side. While writing the novel she “discovered that the Macintoshes, this really astonished me, were descendants from a prince, a bald prince, who was washed up on the shores of Scotland,” so that “Miss Macintosh is really a bald prince, disguised with a red wig and the woman’s gear” (Marguerite Young, interview, WNYC radio, New York).

Chapter 66

  • A strong, eccentric woman who dresses for storms and long voyages. She is bald, always wearing a red wig, which is a hidden truth only discovered later. Her voice is booming and manly, and she exhibits contradictory traits: a resolute socialist with disdain for wealth and extravagance but also an astute student of finance.
  • Represents resilience, the burden of loneliness, and the struggle for self-identity. Her baldness symbolizes vulnerability and a unique form of naked truth.
  • She harbors dreams of love, adventure, and escape from societal norms, but also suffers from deep isolation and self-awareness of her physical and emotional amputations.
  • Acts as a strict, demanding teacher who pushes Vera to learn relentlessly, even amid storms and symbolic death.

Chapter 82

  • “Thou hast wrapped me in Thy fleece”: The hymns Miss MacIntosh sings reveal a profound spiritual dimension to her character. While she keeps her doubt to herself (“Her doubt was her own wound”) and will not be “the stumbling block in another’s path,” these songs from her childhood represent an enduring, if conflicted, faith. They expose her inner struggles with vulnerability, physical and emotional wounds, and the existential human condition of being lost and in need of guidance. These moments of singing, even as she performs mundane tasks, highlight the tension between her practical life and her deep, unarticulated spiritual longings, demonstrating that her common sense and brusqueness are often a defense against profound personal suffering and a search for meaning in a chaotic world.
  • “My beginning was my end, and my end was my beginning”: Mary, Queen of Scots, embroidered the motto “En ma fin gît mon commencement” (“In my end is my beginning”); T. S. Eliot’s “East Coker” (1940) opens “In my beginning is my end” and closes “In my end is my beginning.”
  • Miss MacIntosh: Vera acknowledges that her love for Miss MacIntosh came late, only when she saw beyond the surface of her character. Vera realizes that Miss MacIntosh’s apparent mediocrity hid a phantasmagoric dream. Vera understands that despite Miss MacIntosh’s seemingly sensible nature, she was drawn to the ocean’s depths and eventually drowned.

In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 12, Chapter 22, Chapter 25, Chapter 27, Chapter 29, Chapter 34, Chapter 36, Chapter 43, Chapter 49, Chapter 51, Chapter 52, Chapter 64

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • Mr. Chandelier can be seen as an anthropomorphized object, a personification of the chandelier itself.
  • Catherine imagines him as her companion, “not always faithful,” suggesting a capricious, elusive presence that mirrors the instability and unreliability of her dream world.
  • This personification transforms an inanimate object into a character with agency and presence in her inner life, blurring the boundaries between reality and imagination.
  • Mr. Chandelier is described with almost ghostly qualities: he has “seven lighted candles in his seven crystal hands,” an image evoking mysticism and ritual, linking him to the theme of ritualistic control and orthodoxy that pervades Catherine’s background, especially considering her father’s “fantastic rituals each hour of day or night.”
  • The seven candles may also evoke the idea of illumination, yet in her world, this illumination is shadowed, uncertain, part of the “eternal twilight” that envelops her perception.
  • Mr. Chandelier’s presence also serves as a counterpoint to Catherine’s physical paralysis and mental wandering. While she lies “horizontal,” immobile, he is often depicted as moving between stillness and motion, reality and dream. This duality reflects Catherine’s own suspended state between life and death, consciousness and oblivion.
  • Mr. Chandelier is an emblematic figure embodying the interplay of light and shadow, life and death, presence and absence in her opium-induced limbo.
  • Mr. Chandelier’s “seven crystal hands” holding candles may symbolize the multiplicity of facets in Catherine’s fractured consciousness and fragmented reality. Each candle can be interpreted as a flickering point of awareness, a fragile beacon in the “glass surface” of her uncertain existence. Yet these lights are also delicate and impermanent, just as her world is “a play of illusion” where “all forms must change their shapes.”

Chapter 22

  • “Mr. Chandelier, Mr. Res Tacamah”: Catherine’s companions, Mr. Res Tacamah “who was the drug bottle.”

Chapter 25

  • “only Mr. Chandelier”: Catherine’s companion of the candles.

Chapter 27

  • “even the company of Mr. Chandelier”: Catherine’s companion of the candles.

Chapter 29

  • “the expanding crystals of Mr. Chandelier”: Catherine’s companion of the candles.

Chapter 34

  • Cousin Hannah seemed as strange “as Mr. Chandelier or a seven-branched crystal candelabra glittering in a far heaven.”

Chapter 36

  • “Had not her way been lighted by Mr. Chandelier, the rock crystal branches lighting a dark sky, moving as she moved?”

Chapter 43

Chapter 73

  • Phoebe is mentioned in the context of a graveyard, specifically as “the old washwoman’s grave” with a statue that has a bulbous nose, warts, wrinkles, and a sunbonnet. Joe Goldberg names her statue in his letters as proof that he was in the graveyard with Esther.

  • Phoebe is a symbolic figure within the narrative, evoking themes of death, memory, and the passage of time.
  • “old Phoebe’s statue”: Old Phoebe was a washwoman, and the Phoebe of the Bible was a servant of the church: “I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea” (Romans 16:1, KJV; the King James spells her name Phebe). The Greek word translated “servant” is diakonos, deacon, and she is the only woman so named in the Bible; Paul trusted her to carry his letter to Rome. Where modern translations of 1 Timothy 3:11 speak of women deacons, the King James Version has “Even so must their wives be grave, not slanderers, sober, faithful in all things.” In Greek mythology Phoebe was a Titaness, grandmother of Apollo and Artemis; the name means bright.

Definition from research

Chapter 64

  • “she having refused the hand of the true King of Sweden”: King of Sweden refers to Mr. Bonebreaker and his belief that he was descended from royalty.

Chapter 65

  • A passionate, zealous Gospel salesman from Missouri, characterized by his fervor and eccentricity.
  • He preaches about the impending end of the world, salvation, and the need for repentance.
  • He is physically gaunt and stoop-shouldered, with distinctive features like a beaked nose and bright eyes.
  • Despite his religious zeal, he is inconsistent and flawed (e.g., his diet, brushes with police, personal hygiene).
  • He represents religious fanaticism and the human desire for meaning and redemption amid decay and despair.
  • His relationship with Miss MacIntosh is complex: he idealizes her, but ultimately fails to accept her fully.
  • His preaching is openly racist and antisemitic: Black men are to be shipped back to Africa as “the sons of Ham,” and each Jew he saves earns him a star twice as bright. Miss MacIntosh disagrees with him, “quite flatly.”
  • His first name may refer to Titus the Roman emperor from 79 to 81 AD, who was also a celebrated military general. He is known for leading the Roman army to victory in the First Jewish-Roman War, which resulted in the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple. His brief reign as emperor is notable for the eruption of Mount Vesuvius and the opening of the Colosseum. Titus is also the companion to whom Paul wrote the Epistle to Titus.
  • “just as she had done to the King of Sweden”: See the King of Sweden in the Chapter 64 resources, and Mr. Bonebreaker below.
  • “Mr. Bonebreaker, a Gospel salesman, saw her reeling”: The surname Bonebrake is an Americanized version of the German name Beinbrech and means “bone break.” The original Beinbrech family lineage began in Switzerland in the 17th century, and the name evolved through various spellings before becoming Bonebrake in America. The name likely served as a metonymic occupational name for a herbalist, possibly referring to medicinal plants.
  • “the bar sinister”: The bar sinister, properly a bend or baton sinister, is popularly taken as the heraldic mark of illegitimate birth. Mr. Bonebreaker believes it shut him out from a throne, and decides that all the kings who sit on thrones are crossed by it as he is.

Chapter 66

Listed as: Mr. Bonebreaker

  • Miss MacIntosh reflects that Mr. Bonebreaker belonged to an old religion where women must kneel before men, similar to the customs of What Cheer, Iowa, where women wash men’s feet. She contrasts this with her own situation, noting her baldness and lack of traditionally feminine features, which prevent her from fulfilling such a role.
  • Mr. Bonebreaker seems to represent a lost opportunity for love and connection in Miss MacIntosh’s life. He is associated with the idea that she could never kneel before a man, implying a rejection of traditional gender roles and a sense of isolation.
  • It is said that Mr. Bonebreaker fled leaving his umbrella behind.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s baldness is a significant factor in her perception of her relationship with Mr. Bonebreaker. She believes her lack of hair and other physical attributes made her unattractive and contributed to the failure of their relationship.
  • Mr. Bonebreaker is mentioned as one of the people who knew Miss MacIntosh was bald.
  • “Had she not once had a love affair with the King of Sweden”: Mr. Bonebreaker, who believed he was the true King of Sweden.
  • “But Mr. Bonebreaker had belonged to that old religion”: This passage critiques patriarchal traditions by illustrating the extreme expectations placed on women to be subservient to men, using vivid, almost grotesque imagery of kneeling and hair used as a towel for washing men’s feet. “that old religion” and its description here refers to patriarchy of which Christianity is a part and instances of the changes from a matrilineal society and traditions to a patrilineal one are in the Bible (Marilyn French, From Eve to Dawn: A History of Women in the World, 2002). Patriarchy entitles men to admiration, sex, consent, and domestic labor from women. Men also receive better medical care and pain management and overall focus of health science for their bodies. Men also are able to practice bodily control which is often and routinely denied women. Misogyny and sexism go hand in hand with patriarchy although it is possible for men to practice one or the other and both need not be present at the same time. Sexism is the theoretical and ideological branch where beliefs, ideas and assumptions are used to rationalize and naturalize patriarchal norms and expectations. Misogyny is the “law enforcement” branch of patriarchy which polices and enforces gendered norms and expectations for girls and women (Kate Manne, Down Girl, 2017, and Entitled, 2020). Gerda Lerner documented men’s withholding knowledge and power from women through denying education for centuries (The Creation of Feminist Consciousness, 1993). Young upends many of these gendered norms in the novel.

Chapter 68

  • “a dead man’s hat”: Mr. Weed mirrors Mr. Bonebreaker, who also wears dead people’s clothes: a dead waiter’s coat and “a dead man’s shoes.”

Chapter 81

  • “Until the world blew up”: This mirrors Mr. Bonebreaker who is also looking forward to the end of the world. This also may refer to the development of the atomic bomb and its use during WWII.

Chapter 30

Listed as: Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden

  • In stark contrast to Catherine, she is a robust, adventurous, and mercurial woman.
  • Known for her vast, almost mythical experiences across the globe, including deserts, mountains, and ancient cities.
  • Has a reputation for prescience, having foreseen many historical assassinations and events.
  • Skilled in various martial and survival arts: archery in Persia, dueling in France, mountain climbing, horseback riding, balloon ascensions.
  • Has traveled extensively in disguise, infiltrated hostile territories, and defied dangers.
  • Represents a force of action, clarity, and determination, dedicated to overthrowing dreams and illusions.
  • Symbolizes a bridge between myth and history, reality and fantasy, embodying strength and resilience.
  • She rode in Arab disguise against Spanish soldiers to defend a caravan of Riffs, for “her proud heart could not endure injustice of any kind in this world.”
  • She is buried in a New England churchyard, “her jeweled sword at her side,” in “her old grey army coat” worn in “wars for the emancipation of woman.”
  • Young built her from two true stories: Charles Studin’s suffragist “battle-axe,” “one of the original bloomer girls,” whose sealed trunks held “a complete bridal trousseau” each, and two bloomer girls on an Alpine summit, the younger lost going back for her skirt (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • She “had never cared for the Spitzer boys,” predicted they “would come to no good end,” and called both brothers “profligates.”
  • Catherine sees her as “an emancipated extension of herself,” who might “rescue my mother from the opium dreams of her dead loves.”
  • “Because of the loss of a skirt”: Young told Studs Terkel that this came from an Alpine story in which two bloomer girls shed their skirts at a summit, and the younger, going back for hers, was lost: “the lady lost her life for a skirt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See the Chapter 31 resources.

Chapter 31

  • A formidable, adventurous woman, a “great captain” with a suffrage warrior’s spirit.
  • Known for her directness, fiery temper, and refusal to accept illusions or evasion.
  • Lived a nomadic life filled with symbolic and literal journeys across deserts, mountains, and forbidden cities.
  • She opposed Catherine’s love for the shadow, believing in facing harsh realities.
  • After death, she remains a spectral presence, her memory both revered and shrouded in secrecy.
  • Despite her public life and campaigns, she kept a secret of sorrow, which others hesitate to speak of.
  • Cousin Hannah disapproves of Catherine’s dreams and love for the “shadow.” Their conflict is ideological: directness and confrontation versus evasion and mystical longing.
  • She is portrayed as a mythic figure battling external foes and internal demons.
  • Her life and death symbolize the struggle between illusion and reality, love and loss.
  • The chapter describes her as a figure who fought battles greater than those recorded, with imagery of deserts, storms, and crusades.
  • She sent not one flower to Peron’s grave, neither a horseshoe of roses nor “two dice cubes in a lucky throw,” and ignored Joachim “as if it were he who had died.”
  • She called both brothers “equally insecure, as unsubstantial as flame and water.”
  • “Here lies one who searched all her life for her dead love, a body covered by the snow”: Young told Studs Terkel that Cousin Hannah came partly from an Alpine story in which two bloomer girls shed their skirts at a summit, and the younger, going back for hers, was lost: “the lady lost her life for a skirt.” She also drew on Margaret Fuller, who drowned off Fire Island in 1850 within reach of a sandbar (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). See the Chapter 30 resources.
  • “Death snatched away her beautiful bride”: Young’s other source for Cousin Hannah was a story told by Charles Studin, a founder of the NAACP, about a suffragist “battle-axe” who fought men all her life, “one of the original bloomer girls,” yet for forty years brought home sealed trunks that proved at her death to hold “a complete bridal trousseau” each. “She had a dream too” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). In another telling the lawyer found “fifty wedding gowns,” and Young added that she “had read the histories of mountain climbers, of suffragette captains, of travelers to the Middle East” (Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs, “A Conversation with Marguerite Young,” Review of Contemporary Fiction 23, no. 1, Spring 2003 (1989 original)).

Chapter 32

  • Cousin Hannah is portrayed as a powerful, uncompromising woman who never concedes or softens her standards, even for strategic reasons. She advances by open hostility and brandishes her symbolic sword like a cane, even when there is no opponent.
  • She is deeply committed to the cause of women’s suffrage and liberation from male oppression. Cousin Hannah fights against man as the cruelest oppressor of beauty and womanhood, advocating for women to use their own “weapons” such as parasols and skirts as symbols of resistance.
  • She is described as a swift, meteoric figure, always on the move and engaged in battles and journeys that span deserts, mountains, and foreign lands. She is likened to a great courier of storms and a weathervane signaling change.
  • Despite her vigor, Cousin Hannah is also seen as ancient, worn by time, and somewhat removed from the natural cycles of life and love. She is described as never having fully experienced youth, romance, or the mating seasons of life.
  • She dies not on a distant battlefield but in obscurity after years of frostbite and semi-invalidism. Her deathbed confession reveals a shift in belief that the greatest battles are fought domestically, in the struggles between man and woman at home.
  • She left her suitor at the church door with a white bouquet in his hands, and “it was said that after that he had subscribed heavily to the suffrage movement.”
  • She had “ravaged, burning eyes, a saber wound upon her cheek, a grizzled chin.”
  • “challenging the conductor to a duel”: Studin’s suffragist “challenged a British prime minister to a duel and the prime minister refused to bear arms against the lady” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “She had left him at the church door with a white bouquet in his hands”: Young told Studs Terkel that when Cousin Hannah “abandons the bridegroom at the church door,” “she goes to a numerologist who advises her as to how she should spell her name in the future and adds the hyphen just at the time when she dramatically becomes a hyphenated personality” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). The hyphen is the one in Freemount-Snowden.

  • A formidable, almost mythical figure symbolizing strength and independence.
  • She challenges Catherine’s illusions and urges her to face reality.
  • Known for her fiery spirit, sharp wit, and relentless energy, she is both a source of inspiration and tension.
  • Her distrust of men and disdain for conventional womanhood provide a counterpoint to Catherine’s experiences.
  • She “had always worn around her belt numerous iron keys which had jangled, giving off dissonant music.”
  • At the sound of a cock crowing she danced “a weird dance, giving off showers of metallic sparks.”
  • “Her contempt for old Joachim had remained necessarily boundless, like her indifference.”
  • “It was said that she was jealous of Mt. Blanc.”

  • She is remembered as someone who never sought pity or protection and who had no time for courtly graces or domestic bliss.
  • Her life was devoted to overthrowing man’s dominance, both socially and domestically.
  • She represents emancipation, freedom, and unyielding resolve.
  • Even in death, she remains vivid and influential, symbolized by images of snowy mountains and celestial journeys.

Definition from research

Chapter 1

  • Vera and seeker, deeply introspective and philosophical, haunted by loss and the search for truth.

Chapter 3

  • A child who has escaped from her mother’s “opium paradise.”
  • Looks up to Miss MacIntosh as a guide and protector.
  • Observes and reflects on the strange atmosphere and characters around her.

Chapter 4

  • Deeply affected by Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance or death.
  • Battles between despair, illusions, and the desire for a meaningful life.
  • Struggles with her mother’s (Catherine) perception of her sanity.
  • Embodies themes of mourning, hope, and transformation.

Chapter 5

  • Vera watches the bus-driver and the other passengers, including Madge, capturing their physical and emotional states with a keen, almost clinical eye. She notes Madge's moaning and accusing, Moses's erratic behavior and long hair, and the desolate landscape outside. Her observations are detailed, conveying a sense of decay, confusion, and suspended time.
  • Vera's narration is imbued with philosophical undertones. She reflects on themes of life and death, creation and destruction, reality and illusion.
  • She engages with the bus-driver's thoughts and conversations, especially his long monologue about his hair, politics, and existential musings.
  • Vera seems to understand the symbolic weight of the bus-driver's hair as a metaphor for identity, resistance to corruption, and his connection to life amid death.
  • Vera's narration conveys a sense of uncertainty about the reality of their situation. The bus-driver himself seems caught between dreaming and waking, life and death, and Vera shares this ambiguity.
  • She hints that the bus-driver may be dead or dreaming, trapped in a liminal space where time loops and places vanish. This uncertainty colors her perspective, making her more contemplative and less definitive in her judgments.
  • Vera is empathetic to the people around her. She also maintains a certain detachment. She does not intervene or change the course of events but rather records them with a mixture of sorrow, irony, and resignation. Her tone suggests an understanding of the tragic absurdity of their journey and the existential plight of the characters.
  • Vera functions as a bridge between the reader and the symbolic, almost hallucinatory world of the chapter and for the rest of the novel. Through her narration, the reader gains access to the bus-driver's inner turmoil, the desolate landscape, and the metaphysical questions raised.
  • Vera's bus trip exists in a liminal space between reality and dream, serving as a profound metaphor for her search for life and truth amid the illusions and uncertainties that surround her.

Chapter 8

  • Her descriptions are richly metaphorical and poetic, often blending natural imagery with existential or mythic overtones.
  • She imparts a sense of transition or passage not just through physical space but through states of being or time.
  • She frequently distances herself from the events, perceiving them as if in a vision or dream.
  • She is grappling with realities that are elusive, fragmented, or overwhelming.
  • She contemplates mortality, memory, and identity. This reflects an engagement with themes of impermanence and the unknowability of ultimate fate.
  • While observing others on the bus, Vera remains somewhat apart, bearing witness to their stories and conflicts without fully participating.

  • The stopping of the bus at a fork, one path leading to a graveyard hill and the other to a mysterious village of promise, serves as a potent symbol for her liminal condition. This reflects an internal or spiritual threshold, not merely a physical one.

  • The crossing into awareness is described as a moment of death and rebirth, forever altering perception: "Everything... would be different... the simplest gesture having a different meaning".
  • Following this awakening, Vera experiences a profound fragmentation of reality, where the familiar world loses its coherence and reliability.
  • The surrounding environment, including natural elements like moons, stars, and waters, fails to provide reassurance.
  • Vera explicitly bids farewell to “old moralities,” “proverbial wisdom,” and “the past and its illusion,” highlighting a rejection of previously accepted truths and a plunge into existential uncertainty.
  • Her farewell to the past is not simple nostalgia but a confrontation with the past as a “dream” that must be “laid bare like a corpse.”
  • This suggests a critical and almost forensic examination of memory, recognizing that the past is layered with deception as well as unexpected truths. Vera anticipates surprise and shock in discovering the absence of qualities once assumed and the presence of others previously unrecognized.
  • Vera’s reflections are imbued with elaborate, poetic imagery. These images evoke a dreamlike, liminal space between reality and illusion, life and death, sound and silence.

  • Vera wrestles with themes of presence and absence, sound and silence, life and death.
  • Throughout the chapter, Vera’s tone is melancholic, marked by a sense of loss, estrangement, and an almost mournful awareness of change.

Chapter 19

She seems caught between the realms of dream and waking, reality and imagination, as shown by her uncertainty about whether she is truly awake despite the vividness of the dawn light and surroundings.
  • She meticulously catalogues the objects and conditions in Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom, from the “crumbling heads of cherubim” to the “red wig, almost purple,” and the “jeweled water glass” holding false teeth. This detailed observation indicates a careful, almost forensic attention to detail, suggesting a mind that seeks to understand and piece together the significance of the environment and the person within it.
  • There is a tone of gentle curiosity in Vera’s internal questioning about Miss MacIntosh’s peculiarities: her missing eyebrows, the changing colors of her skin, her habitual wearing of hats and a whistle, and the careful way she avoids showing vulnerability (the umbrella carried “like a shield uplifted where there was no gale”). These questions are posed with “studied detachment,” as if Vera is trying to maintain emotional distance while simultaneously probing deeply into the character of Miss MacIntosh.

She notices intimate, tender details such as the fact that “one breast had been amputated,” describing what remains as “no bigger than a baby’s,” which evokes a sense of vulnerability and loss. This reveals an underlying empathy and a recognition of Miss MacIntosh’s suffering and resilience.
  • Vera recalls Miss MacIntosh’s sayings that “the Devil’s cards are marked” and that she “knew not… of these dualities in one heart, these double motions.”
  • Vera’s detailed description of Miss MacIntosh’s room (with its broken, bare, and patched furnishings, barred door, and scattered personal effects) reflects a broader sense of isolation, hardship, and complexity. She seems attuned to this atmosphere of loneliness and endurance, which may mirror her own inner state or the broader themes of the narrative.

Chapter 70

  • Vera emerges as a deeply introspective, highly imaginative, and somewhat detached individual whose internal world often blurs with external reality.
  • She explicitly states that Mrs. Hogden, a central figure in this chapter, is someone she “never saw,” but rather a “trick of my imagination, this substituting of the one for the other.” Vera acknowledges Mrs. Hogden as a “substitute... for the dream life I wanted” and even calls her “my mind’s betrayal of my mind.” Figures like Mrs. Hogden go “waddling in and out of my dreams.” She can “see” Mrs. Hogden by simply “closing my eyes, by concentrating.” Vera’s consciousness is the lens through which the narrative unfolds, making her a subjective and unreliable narrator.
  • Vera’s character is also deeply shaped by her past and the figures who influenced her upbringing, particularly Miss MacIntosh and her mother. Miss MacIntosh, Vera’s former nursemaid, “brought me up to understand that my mother’s way of life was far from average and was not to be imitated by a good woman such as she saw me becoming, a woman like herself, simple and average and clear-eyed.” This suggests that Miss MacIntosh tried to instill a sense of conventionality in Vera, despite Vera’s inherent imaginative tendencies (night-dreaming, too, “she would have disapproved of, most ardently”). That Vera “escaped from my mother’s house” further indicates a strained relationship with her mother, who is portrayed as eccentric and prone to “frenzied dreaming.” Vera keeps comparing Mrs. Hogden to Miss MacIntosh, even after Miss MacIntosh’s death.
  • Despite her imaginative immersion, Vera demonstrates a keen observational and analytical mind, though often applied to her internal world. She meticulously describes Mrs. Hogden’s outlandish appearance and actions, down to the “smashed hat with a wilted ostrich feather” and the “row of Javanese temple bells.” She also notices the “evidence left by Mrs. Hogden” in the playroom, such as “derelict whiskey bottles, empty coat hangers, withered apple cores, broken egg shells, dead flies,” distinguishing even an “artificial eyelash.” Her philosophical reflections, such as her belief in a “small, warped flower growing... outside the consciousness of God,” reveal a mind that questions universal truths and finds significance in anomalies.
  • Vera also conveys a sense of loneliness and a search for meaning or connection. She explicitly states, “The life I required was the life which required, like his, a lost companion —not merely this self-centered affliction of the right hand loving the left.” Her observation that “Everybody is lonely” suggests a deep, shared human experience she identifies with. Mrs. Hogden, as an imagined companion, could be seen as Vera’s attempt to fill this void, even while acknowledging the illusion.
  • Vera’s identity appears somewhat fluid and permeable. Mrs. Hogden mistakenly supposes Vera to be Lisa Lunde, and Vera herself often blurs the lines between her own experiences, her mother’s dreams, and the fabricated reality of Mrs. Hogden.

Chapter 71

  • An observer and participant, reflecting on the surreal and tragic elements of the setting.
  • Vera, the narrator, emerges as a deeply contemplative and psychologically complex figure, marked by a blend of wakefulness, memory, and a searching, somewhat haunted awareness.
  • Vera is awake in the cold, grey morning, unable or unwilling to sleep despite the silence and stillness around her. Her state is described as “stiff with wakefulness, with ceaseless memory” and “wide awake, alert, watchful,” showing a restless mind that is both physically and mentally active rather than at rest. This wakefulness seems not merely physical but also symbolic, representing a state of consciousness probing the mysteries and uncertainties of her surroundings and her own psyche.
  • Throughout the chapter, Vera’s thoughts drift into rich, imaginative flights and reflections. She muses on the Christian hangman and his tragic personal history, pondering whether he might hang himself or wait for dawn because of his children playing at hanging themselves. Vera also reflects on her mother’s pearls.
  • Vera is portrayed as a traveler or outsider in this strange, desolate Indiana hotel and its surroundings. She is “some time past the ambiguity of dawn,” wearing travel-stained clothes and carrying her mother’s lace and pearls, symbols of a “lost estate” and an unrealized past. Her presence in the hotel is that of someone searching for something: wild flowers of spring, beauty, or perhaps a deeper meaning amid the decay and disorder around her. This sense of quest is tinged with uncertainty and disillusionment, as the landscape and people she encounters are far removed from her expectations or hopes.
  • Vera is a keen observer of the strange and unsettling characters she encounters, especially the doctor, Dr. O’Leary, and the hangman. She notes the doctor’s madness and the surreal disorder of his office and life, filled with instruments, scattered shoes of various types and eras, and imaginary patients. Vera reflects on the blending of reality and fantasy, the doctor’s second childhood, and the presence of “imaginary babies” and a “pregnant man.”
  • Vera listens to the angry widow who confronts her, accusing her of being a “tramp girl” who kept her awake all night, and to Tabitha, the muted chambermaid who quietly carries out her duties. Despite these confrontations and the vivid descriptions of the inhabitants’ misery and anger, Vera seems somewhat detached as an intruder or observer rather than a participant. She tries to explain herself logically but acknowledges the complexity and strangeness of the place and its people.
  • Vera’s narrative voice often becomes poetic and philosophical. She notes how the hotel room expands during sleeplessness into a vast landscape of memory and future, blending space and time.

Chapter 82

Listed as: Vera

  • Reflective and deeply emotional, Vera grapples with mourning, love, and the nature of existence.
  • “Esther Longtree would be me”: When Vera says, “Esther Longtree would be me,” the line holds deep symbolic and thematic significance. This statement reflects Vera’s identification with Esther Longtree as a representation of a universal, enduring love and connection to all forms of life and experience, especially those that are broken, silent, or marginalized. Throughout the narrative, Vera contemplates profound themes of loss, silence, death, and the complexities of human love and perception. Esther Longtree emerges as a figure who embraces life and love despite her own hardships, embodying a kind of maternal, nurturing spirit who “loved us all and all things hurt or silent or broken or dead or living.” Vera’s final identification with Esther suggests a merging of identities, where Vera aspires to embody Esther’s compassion, endurance, and openness to the multiplicity of loves and sufferings that define human existence. Esther is not presented as a traditional role model in terms of success or societal status but rather as a symbol of the “average,” the “hidden,” and the dream-like qualities of life and love that transcend ordinary perception. Vera recognizes in Esther a power and enchantment beneath the surface that she had been too wrapped up in herself to fully perceive earlier. Esther represents a bridge between the ordinary and the extraordinary, the visible and the hidden, the living and the dreaming. By choosing Esther as her role model, Vera acknowledges the importance of embracing the “average” and the “hidden” aspects of life, which can “crumble into the most phantasmagoric dream that man has dreamed” and that “all the shining waters dream beyond the surface cold and bare.” Esther’s figure embodies the theme that through acceptance of loss, silence, and the unseen dimensions of existence, one can attain a deeper, more inclusive love and one that is not dependent on words or conventional communication but flows through “tongues of silence” and “all our loves.” Vera’s statement is not merely an adoption of Esther’s persona but a profound recognition of the values Esther symbolizes: compassion for the silent and broken, an embrace of the unseen dimensions of reality, and a love that transcends ordinary understanding. It marks a transcendence of Vera’s earlier isolation and mourning toward a more universal, interconnected understanding of love and existence and an acceptance of the dream-like, silent world that Esther inhabits and loves. Vera chooses Esther Longtree as her role model because Esther represents the enduring, silent love that encompasses all life’s contradictions, sufferings, and mysteries, and through this identification, Vera finds a way to affirm her own place in the continuum of love and loss that the novel so poignantly explores.

Lisa Lunde

Home

In the research: Chapter 70

Definition from research

Chapter 70

  • Lisa Lunde is introduced as Vera’s mother’s “young companion who took my place when, carrying a large suitcase, I escaped from my mother’s house.” This immediately establishes her as a replacement for Vera and suggests a practical, perhaps less privileged, background. Indeed, she is described as a “would-be physicist working for her living in order to help support her mother who was poor and mad and dreamed that she was rich,” highlighting her sense of responsibility and pragmatic drive, contrasting with the opulence and delusion of Vera’s mother’s household.
  • Lisa Lunde is characterized by her analytical, skeptical, and often blunt nature. She “prided herself on seeing immediately through Mrs. Hogden’s pretensions” and quickly assesses Mrs. Hogden as a “very dubious character, a shoplifter or something equally vicious.” Her scientific inclination is evident in her desire to “shatter all illusions at one blow,” as when she cruelly declares “Res Tacamah... is nothing but a drug bottle.” She struggles with Mrs. Hogden’s evasiveness, conceding “she was perhaps not a shoplifter... but she did not look like a school-teacher either—there was something so evasive about her, something that evaded definition.”
  • Despite her initial skepticism and clear-sightedness, Mrs. Hogden’s unwavering self-assurance eventually sways Lisa Lunde, until she “began to believe that she had come because she was invited.” This suggests a slight vulnerability to the pervasive illusions of the house, or perhaps a weariness from constantly battling them.
  • Her role in the conflict between Vera’s mother and Mrs. Hogden is notable. When Vera’s mother blames her for Mrs. Hogden’s presence and demands she “get rid of her,” Lisa Lunde reveals a more complex, almost vindictive side. “Lisa Lunde, revengeful, began to enjoy the embarrassing situation. She ran back and forth with meaningless messages between the two, and she would do nothing to interpret either character to the other.” This shows a passive-aggressive streak, where she derives satisfaction from the escalating absurdity, perhaps as a form of rebellion against her demanding employer or simply a release from her own constrained life.
  • Lisa Lunde also acts as a voice of conventional sanity, remarking that talking to oneself is fine, “but when you get to answering your own questions—then you are crazy as a loon.” This pragmatic, somewhat judgmental perspective contrasts sharply with the eccentricities of Mrs. Hogden and the delusions of Vera’s mother.
  • Lisa Lunde serves as a grounded, albeit sometimes resentful, observer and participant in the surreal events of the household. Vera’s mother, however, consistently blames Lisa Lunde, even for “keeping Mrs. Hogden out of sight.”
  • “according to Lisa Lunde, my mother’s young companion”: Lisa Lunde is presented as a sharp, young, aspiring physicist who works to support her poor and mentally ill mother. She occupies a role of both practical caretaker and critical observer within the household, particularly when dealing with Mrs. Hogden, whom she suspects of being a dubious character, possibly a shoplifter or deceiver. Lisa Lunde is skeptical, pragmatic, and often harsh in her judgments, especially toward Mrs. Hogden’s self-assured but chaotic presence. She acts as a foil to Mrs. Hogden’s delusional optimism and to the dreamlike, unstable atmosphere surrounding Vera’s mother, Catherine. Symbolically, Lisa Lunde could represent the emerging rational, scientifically minded, and socially aware American woman or intellectual figure in the early to mid-20th century. Lisa is a “would-be physicist,” embodying the growing presence of women entering scientific and intellectual fields in the US, especially during the early 20th century when women increasingly challenged traditional gender roles. Before 1965, women in science were rare and often marginalized, but they symbolized progress, rationality, and a break from the purely domestic roles prescribed to women in earlier eras. Lisa’s role as a breadwinner and caretaker for her mentally ill mother also reflects the increasing visibility of women as both laborers and family anchors in a changing social landscape. Lisa supports her poor and “mad” mother, who dreams of wealth despite poverty, highlighting the contradictions and struggles of many working-class American families during the early to mid-20th century. Many immigrants or second-generation Americans faced such hardships, balancing ambition and survival. Lisa’s pragmatic, no-nonsense attitude may symbolize the ethos of self-reliance and skepticism toward illusions that characterized many striving Americans. Lisa exposes Mrs. Hogden as potentially a shoplifter and ridicules her pretensions, thus acting as a guardian of social order and truth in the face of delusion and fantasy. This can be read as a broader symbolic role of the rational, modern American citizen who resisted charlatanism and false pretenses in a rapidly modernizing society, especially during the post-Depression and post-war years when social realism and pragmatic attitudes gained prominence. Lisa’s critical view of Mrs. Hogden and the fanciful world around Vera’s mother points to the tension between dream and reality, illusion and fact, an important theme in American culture, especially as the country grappled with modernity, the aftermath of the Great Depression, war, and social change. Lisa embodies the scientific, empirical mindset that confronts myth and deception. Lisa’s skepticism toward the older generation’s illusions (including those of Vera’s mother and Mrs. Hogden) may symbolize the younger generation’s disillusionment with the promises of the American Dream, especially in the years before the social upheavals of the 1960s. Her practical, sometimes harsh demeanor reflects a cultural shift toward realism and away from romantic or fanciful ideals that had dominated earlier eras. Symbolically, Lisa Lunde represents the scientifically educated, pragmatic, socially aware young American woman before 1965 who challenges illusions and embodies the tensions of modernity, class struggle, and generational change in the United States. She is a figure of rationality and skepticism standing in contrast to the dreamlike, unstable figures around her, reflecting broader cultural and historical shifts in American society during the early to mid-20th century.

Listed as: Mr. Spitzer

  • The repeated motif of deafness is central to his character. While Mr. Spitzer physically experiences a kind of internal "roaring" in his right ear, a noise which "did not come from this world," he is metaphorically deaf to true communication or sound in the broader existential sense described by Catherine.
