Despite his attempts to speak and reason, he is trapped in a world where "there was no sound" and "he could not hear another’s voice, not even his own voice speaking". This frames him as a figure caught between the rational world of law and argument and a deeper, more profound silence that challenges or negates those faculties.

Mr. Spitzer tries to argue against the idea that his ear is dead, pointing out that, if she means his dead brother’s ear, his brother was not buried anywhere on the estate, yet Catherine remains insistent that "the ear was dead," emphasizing a metaphysical or symbolic deafness beyond just physical hearing.

In the research: Chapter 73, Chapter 74, Chapter 75, Chapter 76, Chapter 77

Definition from research

Chapter 73

Listed as: The Chicago detective

  • A symbolic figure representing societal judgment, scrutiny, and the external pressures faced by Esther Longtree. Though he appears only indirectly through Esther’s thoughts and fears, his presence is significant and multifaceted.
  • The detective symbolizes the potential legal and moral condemnation that Esther fears. She imagines a scenario where she might be arrested, tried, and accused of murder for the stillborn children she has carried and lost over the years. The detective’s investigation represents society’s attempt to impose order and assign blame on Esther for the tragic outcomes of her pregnancies, despite her innocence in her own mind.
  • The detective is “old” and “worm-ridden,” and he is himself one of the fathers, “another old, sterile father,” hunting proof “that she had killed his three whom she had never borne or who were born without eyes.” He stands for the many fathers who impregnated Esther and took no responsibility for the children. The detective’s search for proof and evidence reflects a broader theme of male absence and desertion, with Esther bearing the burden alone.
  • Esther fears the detective’s inquiries, which might lead to public exposure of her condition and the stillborn children. She worries about appearing before a jury while visibly pregnant, the social humiliation involved, and the invasive nature of such an investigation. This fear adds to her isolation and suffering, emphasizing the harshness of societal judgment towards women in her position.
  • The detective’s efforts to find evidence of murder or wrongdoing are ultimately futile, as Esther has hidden the stillborn children in natural places (streams, fields, under snowdrifts) making proof elusive.
  • Esther’s silence and refusal to answer inquiries, partly motivated by kindness to the dying fathers and partly by self-preservation, contrast with the detective’s probing.
  • “the old Chicago detective was trying to find the proof”: England’s Act to Prevent the Destroying and Murthering of Bastard Children (1624) presumed that an unmarried mother who hid the death of her newborn had murdered it, unless she could prove “by one witness at the least” that the child was born dead; the penalty was death. It stood until 1803. In Massachusetts Hannah Piggen was reportedly the last woman hanged for concealing a birth, in 1785 (Wikipedia). Concealment of birth is still a crime in many states.

Chapter 74

  • The father of Esther’s children: three winters he found her unconscious in the fields, took her for a corpse, felt her pulse, and raped her.
  • He hunts murderers and now accuses Esther of murdering his children, though he himself raped her and sent her the name of an abortionist “who enjoyed police protection.”
  • He represents authority, suspicion, and the complexities of truth and guilt.
  • “a Chicago detective and specialist in murder mysteries”: The Chicago Detective can be understood symbolically as a representation of a police state or police corruption through several layers of meaning revealed in the novel.
  • “This Chicago detective was creating quite a problem even now”: The detective’s suit “was based upon a real case which happened in Chicago,” which Young read about in a New York paper, “and I wove it into my story” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).

  • “for it was not her business if his wife said that he was sterile”: The detective is married, and he and his wife each say the other is sterile.

  • He is still hunting “the bleeding rapist” and says he found “his handiwork, Esther Longtree with her clothes torn and her mouth foaming”; yet in Chapter 74 Esther says the detective raped her, and here that he “had never touched her.”

Chapter 65

  • “Chasing windmills—Miss MacIntosh had always been chasing windmills”: Miss MacIntosh told Vera she had been chasing Dutch windmills. Another character, Mrs. Hogden, claims to have lived in a Dutch windmill. Moses Hunnecker, the bus driver of Chapter 1, is also imagined as “some mad Don Quixote chasing windmills.” Windmills in the Dutch style stand in the United States too, among them the Fabyan Windmill outside Chicago and the two in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park (1903, 1908), the two cities of Miss MacIntosh’s solitaire. Tilting at windmills is an idiom for attacking imaginary enemies from the novel Don Quixote by Miguel de Cervantes. It is a founding book in Western literature and is labeled the first modern novel. Antonio Rivas of Dickinson College called it “a very good reminder of why we read, why we watch movies, why we need fiction and imagination” (“Chasing Windmills,” Dickinson College, April 21, 2015). According to Mark Aldrich of Dickinson College, in a video for the novel’s 400th anniversary (Dickinson College, 2015, YouTube), Don Quixote is the story of an older man who has lost his mind over his obsession with literature and decides to go and live these adventures of time past. Little by little through his friendship with his companion he recovers his mind. It is ultimately the journey of one man finding out who he really is.   • “who could have been more robustly alive than she, Esther Longtree”: Esther Longtree emerges as a deeply tragic and complex figure who embodies themes of fertility, loss, unrecognized suffering, and resilience. Physically, she is described as large, swollen, with a deformed foot, a growing bald spot, and marked by signs of repeated pregnancies. Her body is a site of contradiction: robust and vital in some ways, yet burdened by an “everlasting pregnancy” that brings her both strength and sorrow. She is portrayed with vivid imagery (her “ponderous red lips,” “long black hair flowing free,” and swollen breasts like “milky breakers”) highlighting her physicality and her connection to life and creation, even as she suffers repeated stillbirths. Esther’s story is one of repeated loss and unfulfilled motherhood. She has borne many stillborn children, hidden their remains in various natural places, and carries the constant sorrow and haunting memory of these lost lives. Despite this, she harbors a fierce hope and determination to have a living child, the “little shadow boxer” moving inside her, symbolizing persistent life against overwhelming odds. Her repeated pregnancies symbolize both a curse and a source of identity and purpose; she is “always pregnant,” yet always losing the child before birth. This paradoxical state underscores a profound loneliness and alienation from the conventional experiences of womanhood and motherhood. Her relationships with men are fraught and ambiguous. Although she has had many “fathers” of her children (often passing salesmen and transient men) these men are sterile or absent, contributing to her losses and isolation. They remember her and sometimes send tokens or inquiries years later, but their involvement is superficial and transient. Esther’s parents also misunderstand and fail to support her, regarding her as an “old maid” and a failure, unaware of her hidden suffering and the complexity of her condition. Esther also exhibits moments of bright vitality and spirited defiance. She tosses her hair freely “at whatever cost to sanitation,” laughs uproariously despite her pain, and engages in small acts of rebellion such as knitting without thread or playing with lovebirds. These actions underscore her refusal to be wholly defeated by her circumstances, highlighting her strength and courage in face of despair. Psychologically, Esther is haunted by the “little shadow boxer,” a persistent presence and hope that sustains her. She experiences both the physical symptoms of pregnancy and the deep emotional turmoil of loss and expectation. Her mind is described as clear and luminous amid the confusion and sorrow of her body, suggesting a complex inner life where hope and despair coexist. Esther Longtree is a figure of profound maternal tragedy and endurance. She embodies the pain of unrealized potential, the mystery of fertility and loss, and the resilience of the human spirit. Her story is steeped in symbolism: her body as womb and grave, her lost children as ghosts and shadows, her struggle as a metaphor for unfulfilled creation and hope amid desolation.

Young remembered a scene in The Gold Rush (1925) in which Charlie invites a beautiful lady to dinner, “instead of that a mule arrives,” and he “entertains the mule as if it were a lady”: “Charlie has been a great inspiration to this book from start to finish” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). Esther is described as a “big, dumb-headed waitress,” slow-moving and physically altered by her condition: one foot is deformed, her womb swollen, and her body constantly expanding with what she perceives as an “everlasting pregnancy.” This physical state symbolizes her ceaseless burden and the weight of her unresolved grief. Her dark hair often drifts before her eyes, symbolizing both a literal and metaphorical veil between her and the world around her, emphasizing her isolation and internal confusion. Despite the numerous pregnancies resulting only in stillborns or incomplete births (“an eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb”) Esther remains intensely maternal. She has mothered everything from her childhood thumb and big toe to a bullfrog, underscoring her nurturing nature even in the face of continual loss. This maternal impulse is paradoxical; she is both the source of life and a witness to death and absence, which causes her embarrassment and deep sorrow. Many men, termed “fathers,” have impregnated her, yet none seem to have produced a living child. These men are generally weak, sterile, or dying, and several write to Esther as they face death, seeking acknowledgment of their supposed offspring. Esther, however, rarely answers these inquiries. She prefers to maintain silence to preserve the dignity and hope of the dying fathers, fearing the cruelty that truth would impose. This silence also protects her from the pain of confronting the truth about her stillborn children and the uncertain paternity of her current perpetual pregnancy. A significant figure in Esther’s narrative is Joe Goldberg, the champion featherweight boxer, who wrote to her desperately in his dying days. He remembers their encounter in a graveyard: he raped her there, “had taken her against her will,” “deflowered her,” and “had knocked her out, stone cold.” Despite his vivid memories and longing for recognition, Esther cannot recall him clearly, only the graveyard and the circumstances of their meeting. Joe represents the strongest of the fathers who becomes weak and ephemeral like a feather, and Esther’s inability to anchor him in her memory contrasts sharply with her vivid remembrance of the weaker men. Her story explores themes of fertility, death, memory, and the human tendency to shield others from harsh truths through silence. She stands as a poignant embodiment of suffering and endurance.

Esther’s mother accuses her repeatedly, laughing and crying, that Esther “killed” Rosemary by kicking her out of the womb, condemning Esther as a murderer even before she was born. This accusation haunts Esther throughout her life, coloring her self-perception with guilt and shame. She grows up overshadowed by the memory of Rosemary, an idealized “perfect” child who would have been obedient, delicate, and beloved, the daughter her mother longed for. Esther, by contrast, is awkward, large, and defiant, and constantly reminded of her failure to be the child her mother wanted. Esther’s relationship with motherhood and fertility is deeply fraught. She is often pregnant or swollen but has lost many children, described metaphorically as “little birds,” “snowflakes,” or “stillborn,” which reflects the repeated cycle of hope and grief she endures. She carries a secret sorrow for these lost children, which she can never openly mourn or explain, and she battles both physical and emotional pain, including an enlarged heart and a crippled foot, which further symbolize her suffering. Her internal world is haunted by shadows, rustlings, and the presence of the lost children, hinting at a mystical or spectral dimension to her grief. Esther digs holes in the earth, searching for remnants of the past, the “shadow” of her twin, and the lost children, but never fully finds peace or closure. She experiences a profound alienation, sometimes doubting her own reality and identity, wondering if she herself is the shadow or the lesser existence, while Rosemary is the “real” one who should have lived. Despite all this, Esther is not without moments of fierce joy and strength. Her laughter can be loud and powerful, shaking the snow from clouds, and she fiercely protects and claims love for the children she does carry, even if they do not survive. Her stubbornness and vitality make her a figure of tragic endurance, struggling against the “nameless grave” and the weight of familial expectations and curses. Esther Longtree is a figure of intense contradiction: strong yet vulnerable, life-affirming yet haunted by death, natural yet marked by unnatural loss. Her story in this chapter reveals themes of maternal grief, the burden of inherited trauma, and the search for identity amid family secrets and personal suffering. Her character embodies the tragic complexity of fertility and loss, the interplay of life and death, and the painful legacies passed down through generations.

Chapter 79

  • The protagonist, described as a large, muscular, and natural woman, yet burdened by the unnaturalness of her conception and birth. She embodies both physical strength and emotional vulnerability.
  • She is “illusive,” caught between life and eternity, haunted by the shadow of her stillborn twin Rosemary.
  • Known as “Little Jackass,” a nickname signifying her struggle with identity and acceptance.
  • She experiences loneliness and rejection but has a deep maternal heart.
  • Esther’s internal conflict is central, revealing layers of shame, defiance, and longing.
  • “Esther Longtree was illusive”: Esther Longtree is a deeply tragic and complex figure, embodying themes of unnatural conception, loneliness, maternal suffering, and existential isolation. Her characterization is rich with symbolism and psychological depth, revealing a woman who is both physically imposing and emotionally vulnerable. Esther is described as a large, muscular, wind-burned woman with dark skin and crossed eyes that reflect a dazzling inner light where there is no actual light. Her body is often swollen due to pregnancy, yet she carries a profound sadness and a sense of being out of place in the world. She is mulish, stubborn, and somewhat vulgar, traits that stem from her difficult origins and emotional turmoil. Despite her toughness, her heart is described as “big and leaking,” full of regrets, expectations, and memories, highlighting her emotional complexity and capacity for deep feeling. Esther’s origins are central to her character. She was conceived in a way that defies the natural order, her parents never consummated their marriage physically, and instead, a third person, an “old concubine,” using a silver spoon, facilitated her conception across a great emotional and physical distance between her parents. This unusual conception symbolizes the emotional barrenness and alienation in her family. Her parents’ marriage is described as arid and loveless, lacking the fundamental union of flesh and soul. Esther’s conception is painful, slow, and unnatural, taking seven years and involving this mysterious third woman who serves as a go-between. The figure of the “other woman,” the old concubine who carries the silver spoon and physically intervenes in the conception, is a haunting presence in Esther’s story. This woman is physically and symbolically powerful and described as large, dark, and foreign, with masculine traits. She embodies the harsh reality and cruelty of Esther’s conception and birth. She is portrayed as both cruel and strangely beautiful in an inner, invisible way, representing an essential but unsettling force in Esther’s life and origin. Esther was born kicking and afraid, a difficult birth requiring instruments. She is the only one to survive; her twin, Rosemary, was stillborn. This loss haunts Esther, who is burdened by her mother’s guilt and neglect, and by a sense of having caused harm. She carries the memory and presence of Rosemary as a kind of shadow or ghost, which deepens her loneliness and feeling of being an unnatural offspring. Esther’s relationship with her parents is fraught with pain and misunderstanding. Her mother is distant, delicate, and childlike herself (never truly matured or fulfilled) and she often blames Esther for the darkness and barrenness of their world. Her father is large, passive, and somewhat detached, calling Esther “Little Jackass,” a nickname that reflects both affection and cruelty. Both parents are emotionally unavailable, and Esther is left to navigate the world as an awkward, oversized child of a loveless union. Esther stands as a symbol of isolation born of a union that never was, a child who bridges eternity and life but belongs fully to neither. She is “cloud-like,” “illusive,” and driven to the edge of existence, a creature shaped by absence and distance. Her physical largeness contrasts with the emotional barrenness around her, making her a living paradox and a figure of existential struggle. Despite her tragic origins and the neglect she suffers, Esther has a “maternal heart” and a deep desire for love and motherhood. Yet she repeatedly experiences loss (stillbirths, shadows, unborn children) and carries the burden of these losses within her. She is a woman perpetually pregnant with doubtfulness and sorrow, embodying both fertility and barrenness simultaneously. On her seventh birthday, Esther and her mother undertake a difficult journey to visit the “other woman,” the go-between who had helped conceive Esther. This journey is symbolic, marked by hardship, loss of clothing, and the harshness of the natural and social world. The visit reveals the death and decay underlying Esther’s origin: the go-between is dying, blind, and stained by darkness, and Esther perceives her as a kind of paternal figure despite her appearance and gender. Esther is caught between life and death, reality and shadow, natural and unnatural. Her death is “gradual,” tied to her continuous experience of loss and alienation. She tries to be good despite the hatred and misunderstanding she faces, and she is marked by a profound loneliness that aligns her with the natural world’s shadows and ghosts. Her character embodies the tragic consequences of emotional and physical disconnection within a family and society. Esther Longtree in this chapter is a richly drawn figure representing the painful intersection of unnatural conception, family dysfunction, loneliness, maternal longing, and existential grief. She is a living paradox: large yet vulnerable, natural yet unnatural, maternal yet burdened by loss. Her story is woven with symbolism and mythic resonance.

  • “But I will not marry him until the child comes”: Esther Longtree is portrayed as a profoundly tragic and complex figure, embodying themes of maternal loss, guilt, and longing. Physically, Esther is described as a large, cross-eyed waitress who is perpetually pregnant or swollen, a physical manifestation of her inner burden and continuous state of expectation and sorrow. Her pregnancy is not merely biological but symbolic: it represents her ongoing attempt to atone for past mistakes and losses and to reclaim a maternal identity fractured by tragedy. A central aspect of Esther’s character is her relationship with Walter, her first-born, who, despite being “killed” in a sense, has lived on outside her awareness. Walter is both a ghostly presence and a source of endless accusation and sorrow. He haunts her conscience, asking why she killed him and where his father is, embodying Esther’s unresolved guilt and the burden of an unfinished murder. Walter’s existence outside her, his growth and vitality, contrasts sharply with the stillborn children and miscarriages that have otherwise defined her reproductive life. Her narrative reveals a deep, ambivalent love and a tragic recognition of her own limitations and mistakes as a mother, compounded by her youth, ignorance, and fear at the time of Walter’s birth. Esther’s story exposes the intersection of race and identity: Walter’s father was a black man, a “prince” from Africa, who was a fugitive and victim of racial violence. This adds layers of social and personal complexity to Esther’s grief, shame, and isolation. Her memories of this man are filled with shock and surprise, reflecting the racial tensions and prejudices surrounding her. Esther’s heart turning black metaphorically expresses her internalization of this complex legacy. Esther is shown as a woman caught between two worlds: the physical, harsh reality of her life as a waitress and the spiritual, shadowy world of her lost and unborn children, as well as the memory of Walter. She acts as a “go-between,” navigating the liminal space between life and death, presence and absence, reality and dream. This is symbolized by her making a little house of straw for the spirit to come home to, answering every knocking, and feeding the spirits as if to soothe her conscience. Her repeated pregnancies and stillbirths symbolize not only personal tragedy but also a universal theme of loss and unfulfilled potential. Esther’s life is a continual cycle of hope and despair, birth and death, presence and absence. Her laughter, sometimes convulsive or mule-like, reflects a bitter acceptance of her fate, mingled with stubborn resilience. Esther Longtree is a figure of profound maternal suffering and endurance. She is marked by a deep, unresolved guilt and grief linked to her first child, Walter, whose living presence she both mourns and fears. Her story is one of tragic memory, racial and social complexity, and the haunting persistence of loss. She is a living embodiment of the liminal space between life and death, the seen and unseen, the known and the unknowable, and her narrative richly explores themes of motherhood, identity, and redemption within the novel.

  • “the little shadow boxer, he crouched under her heart”: Esther Longtree is portrayed as a deeply complex and tragic figure whose identity is heavily shaped by themes of perpetual pregnancy, loss, and loneliness. The narrative presents her as a woman “always pregnant” with a “little shadow boxer” inside her, symbolizing both hope and despair. This endless state of pregnancy is marked by a haunting series of stillbirths and hidden children buried in various secret places, which underscores a profound maternal suffering and grief. Her body is described vividly as swollen and luminous, with breasts marked by small teeth, signifying the physical and emotional scars of her repeated losses. Esther harbors a desire for a legitimate father for her unborn child, choosing the little toy salesman as the “legal father” not because of love but for the sake of appearance and legality. This man is himself a peculiar and fragile character, described as childish, innocent, and physically weak is an echo of Esther’s own vulnerability. His presence exacerbates her anxiety and sense of fragility, as he is unable to see her obvious pregnancy and the pain it entails. Despite his flaws and oddities, Esther feels maternal towards him and plans to teach him basic emotional responses and social manners, further illustrating her longing for care and order amidst chaos. The little toy salesman is also a symbol of survival and guilt; he is the lone survivor of a great storm at sea in which all others, including children, drowned. Esther’s complex feelings toward him, both pity and accusation, reflect her broader struggle with abandonment, survival, and loss. She calls him a “murderer,” not because of direct harm, but because he survived when others, including many children, did not. His survival represents a painful exception and a haunting reminder of the deaths she has endured. His repeated visits and the spectral presence of a dead child’s hand clinging to him evoke a liminal state between life and death, memory and oblivion. Esther’s inner world is one of continuous tension between hope and despair, reality and dream, maternal love and fatal loss. She imagines a future where she might be married and her child might live, but she remains haunted by the many children who never were. Her relationship with the little toy salesman encapsulates this tension: he is both a source of comfort and a symbol of her grief and unfulfilled desires. The chapter reveals her as a figure caught in an endless cycle of pregnancy and mourning, embodying themes of fertility, death, survival, and the elusive nature of identity and belonging. Chapter 82

  • “Esther Longtree would be me”: When Vera says, “Esther Longtree would be me,” the line holds deep symbolic and thematic significance. This statement reflects Vera’s identification with Esther Longtree as a representation of a universal, enduring love and connection to all forms of life and experience, especially those that are broken, silent, or marginalized. Throughout the narrative, Vera contemplates profound themes of loss, silence, death, and the complexities of human love and perception. Esther Longtree emerges as a figure who embraces life and love despite her own hardships, embodying a kind of maternal, nurturing spirit who “loved us all and all things hurt or silent or broken or dead or living.” Vera’s final identification with Esther suggests a merging of identities, where Vera aspires to embody Esther’s compassion, endurance, and openness to the multiplicity of loves and sufferings that define human existence. Esther is not presented as a traditional role model in terms of success or societal status but rather as a symbol of the “average,” the “hidden,” and the dream-like qualities of life and love that transcend ordinary perception. Vera recognizes in Esther a power and enchantment beneath the surface that she had been too wrapped up in herself to fully perceive earlier. Esther represents a bridge between the ordinary and the extraordinary, the visible and the hidden, the living and the dreaming. By choosing Esther as her role model, Vera acknowledges the importance of embracing the “average” and the “hidden” aspects of life, which can “crumble into the most phantasmagoric dream that man has dreamed” and that “all the shining waters dream beyond the surface cold and bare.” Esther’s figure embodies the theme that through acceptance of loss, silence, and the unseen dimensions of existence, one can attain a deeper, more inclusive love and one that is not dependent on words or conventional communication but flows through “tongues of silence” and “all our loves.” Vera’s statement is not merely an adoption of Esther’s persona but a profound recognition of the values Esther symbolizes: compassion for the silent and broken, an embrace of the unseen dimensions of reality, and a love that transcends ordinary understanding. It marks a transcendence of Vera’s earlier isolation and mourning toward a more universal, interconnected understanding of love and existence and an acceptance of the dream-like, silent world that Esther inhabits and loves. Vera chooses Esther Longtree as her role model because Esther represents the enduring, silent love that encompasses all life’s contradictions, sufferings, and mysteries, and through this identification, Vera finds a way to affirm her own place in the continuum of love and loss that the novel so poignantly explores.

Chapter 70

Listed as: Mrs. Hogden/Logden/Fogden/Dogden/Bogden

  • Fat, corpulent, with bleached, plastered curls.
  • Wears multiple coats stacked over each other, eccentric hats, and carries a variety of odd objects (empty birdcage, packages, temple bells).
  • Her face is blandly expressionless except for an aggressive chin and abnormally large, unfocused eyes.
  • Smells of over-ripe apples and is associated with decay and disorder.
  • Wears a water-stained yellow satin nightgown, black fur slippers, and a frilled white night-cap with an aggressive chin bow.
  • Optimistic despite her apparent destitution and displacement.
  • Talks to herself and answers her own questions, which others interpret as madness.
  • Displays a strange serenity and is described as the “least critical human being.”
  • Has an air of maudlin dignity and commands a dubious respect.
  • Exhibits contradictory behavior: vain but neglected, hopeful but delusional.
  • Plays chess alone, often crying over imagined victories or defeats.
  • Has a strong attachment to visual education and arithmetic, though she never succeeds in teaching.
  • Claims to be descended from notable historical figures (Daniel Boone, William the Conqueror, Alexander Graham Bell).
  • Sold a Dutch windmill home to come to Catherine’s house based on a letter of employment that Catherine denies writing.
  • Possibly a shoplifter or of dubious character as viewed by Lisa Lunde, but not confirmed.
  • Mysterious in origin, with no known relatives or friends, disappearing without trace after leaving.
  • “there was a faceless woman, a Mrs. Hogden”: Mrs. Hogden is a complex, multifaceted figure who embodies disorder, decay, misplaced optimism, and the collapse of old certainties. She is a grotesque presence in the household after Miss MacIntosh’s departure, representing a stark contrast to the grounded, practical, and clear-eyed Miss MacIntosh. Mrs. Hogden is described as corpulent, overburdened with possessions, dressed in layers of ill-fitting clothes, and surrounded by chaos, both physical and mental. She clings to illusions of social status, authority, and control, despite her evident disarray and marginalization. She is simultaneously comic and tragic, a figure who inhabits a liminal space between reality and dream, presence and absence, sanity and madness. Symbolically, Mrs. Hogden could be seen as representing aspects of American society and history, especially those tied to the decline of certain old social orders and the ambiguous transition to modernity. Mrs. Hogden’s sale of her Dutch windmill, her carrying all her worldly goods in a two-door Ford, and her clinging to relics such as the beaded bag, the birdcage, and the Javanese temple bells evoke the image of a once-privileged class now reduced to decay and disarray. She could symbolize the fading of old American aristocracy or the genteel upper-middle class, who struggled to maintain dignity and status in a changing social landscape. Her presence in the house, with its priceless chairs and frozen grandeur, underscores the tension between fading grandeur and the disorder of decline. Mrs. Hogden’s peripatetic arrival, her confusion about places and people (mixing up Mr. Res Tacamah, a drug bottle, with a gentleman visitor), and her life of loneliness parallel the broader social dislocations in America, including the effects of the Great Depression, the migration from rural to urban areas, and the alienation of individuals in modern capitalist society. Her sense of being unwanted yet persisting reflects the experience of many who were left behind by rapid social and economic change. As a middle-aged woman burdened by social pretensions and personal illusions, Mrs. Hogden represents the constrained roles available to women before the feminist advances of the 1960s. Her role as a supposed “teacher of arithmetic” who never fulfills this role and instead devolves into a caricature of herself suggests the limitations and frustrations imposed on women whose identities were often tied to domestic service or caretaking roles, without autonomy or recognition. Mrs. Hogden’s refusal to acknowledge reality fully: her constant smiling despite ruin, her endless dressing and undressing, her imagining social events and parties in an empty house, and her inability to accept her own decline can be read as a metaphor for American society’s denial of its underlying problems. This denial includes racial segregation, economic inequality, and social injustice that persisted before the civil rights movements and social reforms of the 1960s. Mrs. Hogden may symbolize the marginalized individuals who existed on the peripheries of American prosperity, those who were invisible or ignored by mainstream narratives of progress. Her ambiguous identity (Mrs. Hogden, Logden, or Fogden), her lack of family or friends, and the servants’ refusal to acknowledge her expectations all point to a persona that is both part of and apart from society. Mrs. Hogden symbolically represents the decaying remnants of a bygone American social order, burdened by illusions of grandeur and authority, and caught in the liminal space between past certainties and an uncertain modern future.** She embodies the contradictions of persistence and decline, presence and invisibility, sanity and madness, reflecting the complex historical and social transformations experienced in the United States, including the decline of old aristocratic values, the dislocations of modernity, the constrained roles of women, and the societal denial of persistent inequalities.

Listed as: Mr. Weed (The Christian Hangman)

  • Central to the chapter, Mr. Weed is a professional executioner who views his work as a mission to provide a painless death.
  • He is a deeply complex character: a good father, haunted by personal tragedy (his wife Marie’s suicide), and tormented by memories and dreams.
  • He discusses his profession with a mix of bitterness, humor, and philosophical insight, revealing his tolerance and humanity despite his grim role.
  • Mr. Weed recounts various cases of crime, murder, and the inefficiency or cruelty of some executions, highlighting the moral ambiguities of justice.

  • “The Tavern, built in 1827 by God’s servants who were believers in the lamb”: The town is New Harmony, Indiana, the setting of Angel in the Forest (1945). “Very astute readers of people who have been there know that it is the same town to which Vera arrives. I left out all utopian references. It’s the same town exactly” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). The bus “stops before an old hotel where there is a tattooed landlord. And my heroine meets her first encounter with rural reality as a hangman who tells of his excellent fruit orchards. These characters appear in both books” (Marguerite Young, talk on the reissue of Angel in the Forest, 1966). George Rapp’s Harmony Society founded the town in 1814 and sold it to Robert Owen in 1825.
  • “signing in, was the Christian hangman, Mr. Weed”: “There was a Christian hangman, exactly like this, upon whom I based this story” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). Young had heard a local hangman discussed at “a dinner party in a rural district” and “had read many books on hangmen and their psychology” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965), and “every single criminal case he speaks of is based upon a real case” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).
  • Compare G. Phil Hanna (died 1948) of Epworth, Illinois, across the Wabash from New Harmony, a farmer called the humane hangman. He is said to have taken up the work after seeing a botched hanging at McLeansboro, Illinois, in 1896, so that hangings would be done without pain; he took no pay and assisted at the hanging of Rainey Bethea in 1936.

Joe Goldberg

Home

In the research: Chapter 73

Definition from research

Chapter 73

Listed as: Joe Goldberg (Champion Featherweight)

  • A once-powerful boxing champion, now frail and dying of tuberculosis.
  • Writes long, emotional letters to Esther, hoping to be remembered and to claim his child.
  • Represents strength, vulnerability, and the tragic human fight against death.
  • He raped Esther in a graveyard and remembers it as the “peak of his existence”; she remembers the graveyard but not him.
  • “the brave little Jew, hard as rock”: Jewish fighters ruled American boxing in the first half of the twentieth century: twenty-six Jewish world champions between 1910 and 1940, most of them wearing the Star of David on their trunks. Abe Attell held the featherweight title from 1906 to 1912 (he first claimed it in 1901) and was later tied to the fixing of the 1919 World Series. Benny Leonard was lightweight champion from 1917 to 1925, and Barney Ross, raised in Chicago, held titles in the 1930s.
  • “Joe Goldberg, the golden cock”: The surname Goldberg is of German/Yiddish origin, meaning “gold mountain,” formed from the German words Gold (gold) and Berg (mountain/hill). It’s a common Ashkenazi Jewish surname, used both as a habitational name from places named Goldberg and as an artificial or ornamental name, often adopted for its sound or association with wealth. Joe, the gold mountain, dies in the mountains and calls Esther the “peak of his existence among the snowy peaks.”
  • “there had been thirty rounds”: Glove fights once ran long: on July 4, 1910, in Reno, Jack Johnson, the first Black heavyweight champion, knocked out Jim Jeffries, the “Great White Hope,” in the fifteenth round of a fight scheduled for forty-five. Riots broke out in some two dozen places, most of them white mobs attacking Black Americans; between 11 and 26 people were killed, among them a Black man lynched in Wheeling, West Virginia, for driving an expensive car (Wikipedia). New York’s Walker Law of 1920 capped bouts at fifteen rounds.
  • “a white feather of some far-flying Arctic bird”: To show the white feather is to show cowardice, from the cockpit, where a white feather in a gamecock’s tail was taken as the mark of a poor fighter. The feather falls for the featherweight, the golden cock.

  • “Peron had rushed impetuously ahead, and he had fallen through a glass window on the fourteenth floor”: Peron’s death, left between suicide and accident: “this intention made to seem this irrational accident.”

Chapter 26

Listed as: Peron Spitzer (Joachim’s twin brother)

  • Impulsive, competitive, impetuous, and restless.
  • His and Joachim’s lives and deaths intertwine; Peron’s death haunts Joachim.
  • He distrusted the law and wanted only “a crooked lawyer,” one who “would fix the witness and the judge,” and he often tried to fix his brother.
  • He preferred “the great crowds of Derby Day” to any dream, and “had been afraid of death.”
  • Represents the chaotic, fleeting nature of life and human memory.
  • He would have swept Catherine “into the living sunlight,” even if the sunlight were her death.
  • “the great crowds of Derby Day”: The Derby at Epsom, run since 1780. William Powell Frith painted its crowds in “The Derby Day” (1858).

Chapter 26 · The Dead Brother

  • A symbol of lost potential, memory, and the haunting presence of the past in the present.

Chapter 27

Listed as: Peron Spitzer (Joachim’s twin brother)

  • A man of “blatant tastes” who “had worn loud checks” and preferred “low company, lapsed souls, void characters, dice-rattlers.”
  • He “laughed at Mr. Spitzer’s silence,” yet left a fine, accurate watch, which he seems to have “most thoughtfully removed” before he jumped.
  • The twins “had always suffered, except for this final accident, the same accidents, one not falling unless the other fell.”

Chapter 28

Listed as: Peron Spitzer (Joachim’s twin brother)

  • A loudmouthed, pragmatic man who embraced the cruelty of actual life and seemed indifferent to spiritual or afterlife concepts.
  • His untimely death deeply affects Mr. Spitzer’s psyche and way of life.
  • He loved “the wastrel wheels of chance, the games of loaded dice, the croupiers, the billiard hall artists… the drugged horses.”
  • He “would most certainly have seen no value, no unearthly significance as to butterflies or any other spirits.”
  • “the wastrel wheels of chance, the games of loaded dice, the croupiers”: Roulette (“little wheel”), whose croupier spins it.

Chapter 28 · Contrast Between Mr. Spitzer and His Brother Peron

  • Peron is portrayed as a man focused on the immediate, material world, indifferent to spiritual or afterlife concepts, and unconcerned with the delicate beauty Mr. Spitzer values.
  • Peron’s death, “by accident or suicide,” marks a turning point for Mr. Spitzer, leading to the end of many of his pursuits and a deepening of his introspection.

Chapter 29

Listed as: Peron Spitzer (Joachim’s twin brother, allegedly dead by suicide)

  • A mysterious, volatile figure who lived a fragmented life.
  • His death profoundly impacts Mr. Spitzer, whose mourning colors his worldview.
  • Peron’s character contrasts with Mr. Spitzer’s logical nature; he is seen as a greater mystery.
  • His funeral drew “the merriest mourners who ever were”: dice shooters, vaudeville stars, mountebanks, and “ruined gamblers.”
  • He “airily dismissed Joachim from his mind when a purpose had been served” and would have shown “not a spark of gratitude.”
  • His coffin “had been sealed, and no one had looked upon his dead brother’s shattered face.”
  • “where the turf meets the surf”: The slogan of the Del Mar racetrack, opened in 1937 by Bing Crosby and Pat O’Brien. Crosby sang “Where the Turf Meets the Surf.”

Chapter 31

  • “not one horseshoe of the red and white roses… two dice cubes in a lucky throw, seven and eleven”: Floral horseshoes and dice were set on gamblers’ graves. Seven and eleven are winning throws in craps.

Chapter 33

  • The Boston newspaper reports him “seen recently walking along Benevolent Street, peering into old doorways.”
  • “even her funeral, as he remembered his”: Mr. Spitzer remembers his own funeral because he buried his twin. Young said, “Grief was so great that he thought the wrong brother died” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 34

  • He “apparently committed suicide, taking a coward’s way out.”

Chapter 35

  • Unlike Joachim, he “had always had an ace in the hole.”
  • His “astronomical gambling losses” kept Joachim “in a state of colossal bankruptcy for years.”
  • “Peron would never have lingered here.”
  • “unlike his brother, who had always had an ace in the hole”: In stud poker the hole card is dealt face down. An ace in the hole is a hidden winning card, and by the early 1900s the phrase meant any hidden advantage.

Chapter 36

  • “His brother would never have had such patience.”
  • He is the “superficial brother who had had no powers of memory or whose memory had been only in his own behalf.”
  • “if there had been no dead brother with his identical face”: The chapter portrays a triangular relationship between Peron, Joachim, and Catherine, marked by unfulfilled love, contrasting lives, and the tragic consequences of loss. Catherine’s preference for Peron and her rejection of Joachim create a dynamic of longing and sorrow that defines the emotional core of the narrative. Joachim embodies steadfastness and grief, while Peron represents passion and escape, and Catherine is caught between these polarities, her own existence fragile and dreamlike.

Chapter 37

  • “Peron had been right—and Joachim had been wrong.”
  • Hannah is “gone where poker-faced Peron was.”

Chapter 38

  • He was “this man of great wit but little brain—no legal knowledge in his head, no intellectual pretensions whatever.”
  • Catherine believes “he had expressed his love by his silence, his distance.”
  • “Sometimes she thought that only he lived.”

Chapter 41

  • A figure symbolizing tragic melancholy and finality in death.
  • “Peron had killed himself by jumping from the tallest building in a cloud as a star flashed, as a train whistled.”

Chapter 47

  • A contrast to Mr. Spitzer, more impulsive and superstitious, who had a different view of love and death.
  • His death catalyzed Mr. Spitzer’s deep reflections and mourning: Mr. Spitzer is grateful “for the fortunate error of his suicide,” which “had not been the end of wisdom but the beginning of wisdom.”
  • “His brother had died young, but had he ever married?”
  • “give up his assumption that all things which existed should be tangible”: Peron and Joachim as materialism and immaterialism. In philosophy, materialism says that everything that exists is fundamentally physical, composed of matter and energy. All phenomena, including consciousness, are ultimately reducible to physical processes. They point to the success of science in explaining the physical world and that consciousness can be explained by brain activity. Physicalism is similar in that everything can be explained by physics. Immaterialism believes there is an existence of entities or properties that are not physical, such as minds, consciousness, or spiritual realms. Non-physical entities or properties exist alongside or instead of the material world. Idealists believe that only minds and their perceptions are real, while the material world is a construction of the mind. Peron symbolizes the external, material world with its pleasures, follies, and impermanence, while Joachim represents the internal, immaterial realm of thought, memory, and spiritual seeking. See Spinoza’s mind and body as one in the Chapter 45 resources.

Chapter 48

  • Contrasts with Mr. Spitzer by his flamboyance and willingness to “burn brightly,” symbolizing a different approach to life and death. His early death and vibrant life are a foil to Mr. Spitzer’s cautious and contemplative nature.
  • “Long before his apparent suicide, he had tempted fate in many ways of which he was unconscious even at his brightest moments.”
  • “Never was he so flamboyant as when his horse had lost… He sorrowed when he won.”

Chapter 49

  • “His brother could never have accepted an ineluctable reality such as Mr. Spitzer feared. His brother had thought that there was something he could do to change things, to make for greater hope or greater hopelessness.”
  • “They were born together.” Mr. Spitzer “did not know which brother he was, and this was the crux of his mystery.”
  • “or perhaps he was the third”: “Who is the third who walks always beside you? / When I count, there are only you and I together” (T. S. Eliot, The Waste Land, 1922).

Chapter 51

  • “the gambler had become the celestial musician”: The gambler is Peron and the musician Joachim; see Peron Spitzer.
  • “Had he given birth to his dead twin”: See Peron Spitzer.
  • “Never should he see his brother’s face”: Mr. Spitzer can see his brother only “through all the mazed images of the dead, through all the differences.” He lives through death no more miraculously than “some crazy old gambler who had thrown his last dice,” and he tries “to go legal,” as biased as “a left-handed portrait painter in a world of right-handed portrait painters.” “His effort to go straight had made him crooked,” and his way is “finally circular.” He practices only “in the courts which were paved with the moonstones of lost cases under a firmament of lost stars,” and he prefers “the seething silence to the sound, preferring mystery to exposure, preferring a cloak to nakedness.”
  • “perhaps had walked off the roof like his poor brother”: Here Peron walked off the roof of the building and not through the window as earlier, which brings to mind the 1929 stock market crash and the stories of investors and brokers jumping from buildings. The wave of such suicides is largely an urban myth, amplified by sensational newspapers and the dark humor of the time; John Kenneth Galbraith called it a legend (The Great Crash, 1929, 1955). There were suicides: a brokerage firm clerk and a member of the New York Mercantile Exchange jumped to their deaths in the financial district in the weeks after the crash, others died by gas, gun, or poison, and the suicide rate rose as the Depression deepened, from 17.0 per 100,000 people in 1929 to 21.3 in 1932. Winston Churchill, in New York at the time, wrote of a man who fell from a building near his hotel (Wikipedia). Although Miss MacIntosh pays a visit to Wall Street and invests “imaginary money,” it is not mentioned if Peron or Joachim invested in Wall Street.

Chapter 52

  • Mr. Spitzer’s dead twin is present in every list he makes, for he is “mindful always that he was two persons, himself and his dead brother, and that what appeared in one column should appear in the other.” His greatest fear is “that there might be no differing counterpart.”

Chapter 53

  • Mr. Spitzer’s brother, a gambler and more flamboyant, volatile personality.
  • Peron’s life is described as colorful, many-sided, and seemingly successful, but also transient and elusive.
  • His death creates a “rift” in Spitzer’s life and intensifies Spitzer’s struggle with his own existence and identity.

Chapter 54

  • “the interment of Peron Spitzer”:

Listed as: Peron

Chapter 57

Listed as: Peron

Listed as: Peron Spitzer (Joachim’s twin brother)

Definition from research

Chapter 2

Listed as: Catherine Helena Cartwheel (Snowden)

  • A central figure who has withdrawn from life into a dreamlike, opium-fueled existence.
  • She suffers from an invisible birthmark (a blot on her left cheek), which symbolizes hidden flaws and may represent her motivation for retreating from reality.
  • She is portrayed as a "beautiful corpse," eternally young yet fixed in a horizontal, motionless state.
  • Surrounds herself with phantoms, dreams, and visions including historical figures, spirits, and imaginary visitors.
  • She is complexly caught between sanity and madness, reality and fantasy, embodying a state of suspended animation.
  • Her retreat to bed and isolation is linked to personal trauma: an unhappy marriage (Jock Cartwheel), abandonment, social humiliation, and a controlling father.

Chapter 3

  • Living in a surreal, opium-induced environment with grand illusions and fantasies.
  • Contrasted with Miss MacIntosh’s grounded reality.

Chapter 4

  • Acts as both caretaker and enforcer of oblivion.
  • Seeks to protect Vera by encouraging a withdrawal from life.
  • Represents acceptance of death in life and resignation.

Chapter 11

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Existing in a semi-conscious, dreamlike coma.
  • Her mental state is depicted as a voyage through symbolic landscapes and figures.
  • Acts as a hostess to a surreal assembly of historical, mythological, and symbolic guests.
  • Denies loss, existing in a universe where things are lost but preserved in other forms.

Chapter 12

  • Catherine is mentioned as retiring slowly from the world, symbolized by the stopped clocks.
  • She suspects Mr. Spitzer sometimes imagines himself to be his dead brother.

Chapter 13

  • The recurring motif of the "dead ear," especially in relation to Mr. Spitzer and Catherine, underscores a world where communication fails and the essence of existence is isolated from meaning.
  • Catherine’s insistence that "the ear was dead" and that "there was not a sound to be heard" suggests a bleak vision of human experience as disembodied from relational and sensory engagement.
  • Catherine is depicted as a woman caught between life and a kind of suspended existence.
  • Catherine is enveloped in a self-imposed or circumstantial state of near-death or withdrawal from reality, an enchantment that protects her but also alienates her from the world around her.
  • The “garden of the deaf” is a powerful metaphor for Catherine’s mental and emotional state.
  • This deafness is not just literal but symbolic of a disconnection from the external world and from meaningful human interaction.
  • In this garden, "one should see the bird and the shadow of the bird, but one should not hear the song," encapsulating Catherine’s experience of perceiving the world without fully engaging with it or being able to communicate effectively.
  • Her interactions with Mr. Spitzer, an old friend and legal professional, further reveal her state of mind.
  • Despite his efforts to speak and argue, Catherine insists that the "ear was dead," and that no sound truly reaches them. This exchange highlights her detachment and the barrier she has erected between herself and others, emphasizing her internal silence and the futility of communication.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s "subdued roaring" in his ear, a noise which "did not come from this world," parallels Catherine’s own internal condition, suggesting shared but differently manifested forms of alienation.
  • Catherine’s fear of the silence "unbroken by the sound" and her particular dread "when a frog screamed" indicate deep psychological distress. The silence is oppressive, a void that she cannot endure, and the rare disruptive sounds become sources of terror rather than comfort. This paradox of fearing both silence and sudden noise points to a troubled mind caught between extremes, fragile and haunted.
  • Throughout the chapter, images of decaying flowers, fading colors, and ghostly sounds surround Catherine, reinforcing the themes of impermanence and dissolution.
  • She is part of a world slipping away from life into something spectral or unreal. This imagery parallels her mental state which is caught in a liminal space between reality and illusion, life and death.
  • Despite her distance, Catherine remains a focal figure in Vera’s consciousness. Her presence is felt strongly even as she withdraws, indicating Catherine’s paradoxical role as both a source of life and a symbol of loss and mystery.

Chapter 14

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Ailing and often delirious, she is obsessed with locating the black coachman and understanding the fate of her family’s legacy.
  • She experiences visions and hallucinations, blurring the line between reality and fantasy.
  • She is deeply distrustful of Mr. Spitzer and concerned that her last wishes have been ignored or betrayed.
  • In “codicil after codicil” she left the coachman first one thing and then “everything,” even her old, empty gowns, though he was dead or unpaid.

Chapter 19

  • “my sleeping mother who called herself the horizontal person”: Catherine, who lives lying down, “never walked except in her imagination.” Miss MacIntosh is “perpendicular.”

Chapter 20

  • “a busy Etruscan seaport. A place where the dead came and went”: The Etruscans of ancient Italy built great cities of the dead, the necropoleis of Cerveteri and Tarquinia, and Populonia was one of their seaports.

Chapter 22

  • “My mother always insisted that the hotel entertained many dead men”: Catherine’s dead guests.
  • “My mother saw everything but mistook everything she saw for something else”: What Vera describes resembles visual agnosia, a term Freud coined in On Aphasia (1891).

Chapter 24

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Central figure, caught in opium dreams, presiding over an imaginary world filled with historical, mythological, and invented guests.
  • She is fully immersed in her visionary, dream-like state, discussing grand affairs and social invitations as if real.
  • She is aware of her illusionary world but maintains a clever detachment, placing faith only in the unreal.
  • Her attempts to reach historical or imaginary figures and the failure of these calls reveal her isolation and the limits of her dream world.
  • “The horizontal lady”: Catherine’s name for herself in Chapter 19.

Chapter 25

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • A strong, discerning woman who sees through Mr. Spitzer’s facade.
  • She maintains a complex relationship with Mr. Spitzer, accusing him of falsehood yet drawing him into her dreamlike world.
  • Serves as a bulwark for Mr. Spitzer’s fragile existence.
  • Her bedroom is depicted as a magical, enchanted space where reality blurs and transformations occur.
  • She addresses him “as if he were already dead,” reminding him of “those vast areas of life he had surely missed.”

Chapter 26

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Bedridden and addicted to opium.
  • Mr. Spitzer handles her estate.
  • Represents illusions of grandeur and the persistence of the past into the present.
  • Central to Mr. Spitzer’s personal life, her illness and narcotic use create a complex emotional dynamic.
  • Embodies memory, oblivion, and the tension between awareness and escape.
  • Mr. Spitzer believes she drugs herself “so that she should not see him, this old family lawyer with his brother’s face.”

Chapter 27

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • A woman lost in opium dreams and fantasies, disconnected from reality.
  • She imagines herself in surreal, historical, or symbolic roles, often interrupting conversations with remarks addressed to absent figures.
  • Her lack of faith paradoxically makes “all things possible” for her.
  • Catherine insists on assigning significant interpretations to minor details and ignores major events, suggesting her detachment from reality.
  • She enjoys “her present sense of omniscience” about Mr. Spitzer’s goings and comings, yet ignores him “in favor of God knew whom.”
  • “perhaps Catherine the Great sleeping in a bed with pillars of twisted amethyst”: Catherine II, Empress of Russia (reigned 1762-96). Catherine Cartwheel shares her name.

Chapter 28

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • A figure whose narcotic dreams create the enchanted, surreal world Mr. Spitzer visits each evening.
  • Her “obtuse faith that he would always return” and her hallucinations sustain Mr. Spitzer’s sense of renewal and continuity despite his personal losses.
  • She sees “all these beauties which he could no more see than if he were a mole under the ground,” even when her eyes are closed.

Chapter 29

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • She believes herself “both living and dead, this animated and bejeweled corpse,” and imagines the migratory beds of the famous dead drifting to her.
  • She is imagined alongside Mr. Spitzer’s butterfly reflections, creating a shared atmosphere of mystery.
  • She “would spend hours, years talking to someone who was not there.”

Chapter 30

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Portrayed as a figure lost between reality and fantasy.
  • Engages in conversations with unreal or invisible persons such as “Eustace” who changes forms and identities.
  • She seems to live in a dreamlike state, haunted by memories and by the presence of the dead.
  • Experiences sudden emotional outbursts and imagines elaborate scenarios involving historical and mythical figures.
  • Wishes for company and distraction, often imagining card games with ghostly or imaginary partners.
  • Struggles with loss, particularly the absence of her husband, and clings to hope that he might still be found or returned.

Chapter 31

  • A dreamer, living between reality and opium dreams.
  • Holds a love for a “shadow,” a dead or unreal man, rather than a concrete person.
  • Her relationship with reality is tenuous; she is entwined with mystical and illusory elements.
  • She and Mr. Spitzer share mutual admiration for Cousin Hannah and Peron.
  • Catherine’s love is for an elusive, intangible presence rather than a real man.
  • The metaphor of man as a shadow driven by the wind highlights themes of impermanence and spiritual longing.

Chapter 32

Listed as: Catherine (Vera’s mother)

  • Catherine is described as bedridden, veiled in white lace and surrounded by an atmosphere of drifting snowflakes, candle flames, and reflections. She is physically confined and vulnerable, a “creature of such fragility” who is easily overwhelmed by the presence of Cousin Hannah and the harshness of reality. Her bed is a “floating swan bed in a dazzling cloud,” which evokes both fragility and an ethereal, almost otherworldly quality.
  • Catherine’s essential loneliness and isolation is emphasized. She is abandoned by the “mysterious bridegroom” and all her loves are imaginary: pharaohs, captains, and other ethereal figures who “had left her, and they had never been.” This abandonment extends to emotional desolation, as no one, “not even Cousin Hannah,” has ever truly touched her “cold heart,” which is “cold and hard as the mountain rock.” This coldness suggests an emotional deadness or protective numbness born from pain.
  • Catherine lives largely in a world of dreams, illusions, and shifting realities. She imagines weddings to phantoms, sailboats, stars, and icebergs, reflecting a detachment from conventional life and relationships. Her marriage is portrayed as an ambiguous event, possibly symbolic or imaginary, rather than a concrete historical fact. The wedding imagery (“blushing behind her billowing wedding veils,” “married to a phantom”) conveys a sense of being caught between life and death, reality and fantasy.
  • Catherine’s mental state is described as “changeful and capricious,” with a wandering attention and vague memories. She is inconsistent in her accounts and perceptions, which may be interpreted as a symptom of her illness, age, or psychological state. This instability contrasts strongly with Cousin Hannah’s forceful and direct manner, highlighting Catherine’s passivity and internal turmoil.
  • Catherine’s relationship with Cousin Hannah reveals much about her character. Hannah is vigorous, militant, and confrontational, while Catherine simulates emotions she does not feel and “dissemble her feelings” when Hannah visits. Catherine’s indifference masks inner panic and vulnerability. Whereas Hannah is a symbol of active struggle and outward battle, Catherine is an embodiment of internal retreat and quiet suffering. Yet, Catherine admires Hannah’s energy and persistence, even as she is overshadowed by it.
  • Catherine is associated with death-like sleep. The novel suggests that she is “already dead” in a metaphorical sense, living in a “pretense of death.” Her life is marked by a profound stasis, and she may be seen as a “sleeping lady” awaiting awakening or final rest.
  • Catherine’s marriage and attitude toward men are ambiguous. She married “that great traveller who never would return,” possibly to defy Cousin Hannah’s militant feminism or to assert independence, but the marriage was doomed. Her symbolic wedding to various natural and mystical entities rather than a man suggests rejection or transcendence of traditional romantic or marital relationships.
  • Catherine is depicted with a strong aesthetic sensibility: her fingers wear jewels that “gleaming like northern lights,” and her surroundings are rich in poetic symbolism (flutes, harps, snowflakes, candle flames). She is a “beautiful femme fatale,” but her beauty is cold and distant, more a vision than a presence.

Chapter 33

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • A once-famous beauty and socialite who has long been out of public view.
  • A complex figure, described as living in illusions and opium-induced dreams.
  • Her memories, especially of her wedding(s), are fragmented, poetic, and unreliable.
  • She is not told that a newspaper reported her death, and she sometimes thinks she was never married at all, though her husband was Jock, who “had disappeared when the mountains moved like waves.”
  • She interacts with imaginary figures and experiences reality as a blend of dream and fact.
  • “she was still entertaining Chinese mandarins”: Weissenbach, the real opium lady, “dreamed about… mandarins and… a human-sized black bird standing in the hallway” (Marguerite Young, interview with Charles Ruas, WBAI radio, New York). See the blackbird at the end of the chapter and Catherine Cartwheel.
  • “the withered harp strings played upon by nothing but the fingers of the invisible wind”: At Yaddo, Truman Capote occupied Katrina Trask’s tower, where a harp played when the door opened, and Young said, “I used that harp in my description of the Opium Lady” (Charles Ruas, Conversations with American Writers, Knopf, 1985).
  • “she was talking to a human-sized blackbird”: This was Weissenbach’s: “a human-sized black bird standing in the hallway” (Marguerite Young, interview with Charles Ruas, WBAI radio, New York). See the entry on Chinese mandarins and Catherine Cartwheel.

Chapter 34

Listed as: Catherine

  • A complex character caught between dreams and reality, longing for love but resigned to solitude.
  • Her memories and fantasies reveal her inner turmoil and sense of loss.
  • She is reflective, romantic, and somewhat nostalgic, haunted by unanswered questions about love and life.
  • She was married most often by “a St. Bernard dog, an Alpine retriever who had come to her in a prophetic dream.”
  • She yearns for “a teacher of arithmetic” so that she might know “who the geometer was.”
  • When Cousin Hannah came, she would say that she “had gone to Pisa to see the Leaning Tower.”

Chapter 35

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Catherine holds a complicated view of both Cousin Hannah and Mr. Spitzer.
  • She is reflective, sometimes “unreasonably proud” of Cousin Hannah and often alone, conversing with shadows and memories.
  • Her own life is described as fragmented, filled with multiple selves and illusions.
  • She contrasts with Cousin Hannah’s unity of character and decisiveness.
  • Catherine blends admiration, doubt, and longing.
  • Before she went to bed she had been “the most marvelous dancer.”
  • “She had always seemed to give her attention to those who were not there.”
  • “If a thing was predictable, my mother at that moment ceased to believe in it.”
  • She is “always in her swan boat,” talking to “grotesque shadows on a wall.”
  • She carries on “long conversations with triple-crowned, heron-footed King Canute.”
  • “She suffered from claustrophobia even when she thought of the moon, the sun, the stars, the pathless places.”

Chapter 36

Listed as: Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • A figure consumed by memory and imagination, struggling to distinguish between them.
  • She is radical, imaginative, and deeply invested in the past and in the memory of Cousin Hannah.
  • Her mind wanders between reality and dream, reflecting on loss and the elusive nature of death.
  • She is “an incorrigible lover of the dead.”
  • “She had always been afraid of the sad news she might read—the news that she herself was dead.”

Chapter 66

  • She is described as being “pent up in bed” and dreaming in an “over-heated room.” This suggests she is physically unwell and possibly confined to her bed for an extended period.

Chapter 70

  • Catherine, Vera’s mother, is a profoundly eccentric, wealthy invalid whose grasp on reality is tenuous and fragmented. Her character is defined by a series of contradictions, delusions, and a self-centered, often manipulative, approach to those around her.
  • Initially, Vera establishes Catherine as an unconventional figure, noting that Miss MacIntosh, Vera’s former nursemaid, raised Vera to understand that her “mother’s way of life was far from average and was not to be imitated by a good woman.” Catherine is also revealed as the “true subject of [Vera’s] dreams,” indicating her deep, almost obsessive, significance to Vera.
  • Catherine’s disconnection from reality is a dominant trait. She “dreamed that she was poor,” contrasting with Lisa Lunde’s mother who “dreamed that she was rich.” Her physical and mental state is described as one of profound invalidism, often sinking into “deeper and deeper coma” and experiencing hallucinations, such as “a huge toad was eating my mother’s face” or “the balloon fish floating over my mother’s head,” and “shadowy figures stepped out of the walls. There were moths with human faces.” She herself admits to having “lost my mind several times” and declares, “I am not responsible for my actions.” Her identity is fluid; she believes she has “killed her former self and that my mother’s former self was walking through the house while my mother lay with her hair streaked out like twilight on a pillow, for my mother was dead—added, subtracted, multiplied, divided.”
  • Despite her profound mental disarray, Catherine exhibits moments of surprising shrewdness and practicality, particularly concerning financial matters. She can display a “shrewd gleam in her eyes, the absolute efficiency with which she inquired into her financial concerns, past and present,” even seeking to collect “Old loans which she had forgotten making” from dead parties. Her instruction to meticulously inspect the house for missing items after Mrs. Hogden’s departure further underscores this trait.
  • Catherine’s interactions with Mrs. Hogden, her newly arrived companion, highlight her manipulative and self-centered nature. Initially, she feigns “profound, glazed astonishment,” denying any knowledge of Mrs. Hogden or having sent an invitation, calling her an “impostor, a liar, a day-dreamer, a thief.” Despite Mrs. Hogden possessing intimate details of Catherine’s life like “the head of Alcibiades was in the drainpipe” or “a whale swimming into my mother’s bedroom” which only Catherine could have divulged, Catherine still refuses to see her. She employs elaborate excuses, claiming to be “gone to Boston to see a podiatrist” or “to the North Pole.” She blames Lisa Lunde for Mrs. Hogden’s presence and attempts to discourage Mrs. Hogden by assigning her an uncomfortable “deserted playroom” and a “hospital cot” that was “too short and too narrow.” Her ultimate directive to Mr. Spitzer to “push her off a high building or throw her into the ocean” to get rid of Mrs. Hogden reveals a cruel and extreme impulse.
  • Catherine’s desire for an arithmetic teacher who would teach “Two and two always making four...over and over again” suggests a yearning for simple, undeniable truths in a chaotic personal reality. However, she rejects Mrs. Hogden’s attempts to teach, deeming her “mad as a loon” for repeating the lesson. She views Mrs. Hogden as a “rival invalid” and a “gross, stinking parody” of her own “distended world of shimmering, loosely woven textures,” indicating a fierce protectiveness over her unique inner world.
  • Catherine’s memory and awareness fluctuate. After Mrs. Hogden’s departure, she is “disappointed now that she had not been taught arithmetic and blamed Lisa Lunde,” even considering hiring another “lonely old woman” to teach her.
  • “this Mrs. Hogden must be my Cousin Hannah”: See Cousin Hannah, who recurs in Catherine’s dreams, in the Chapter 24 resources.

Chapter 71

  • Catherine is a figure deeply immersed in a subjective, dream-like reality, detached from the conventional world. Her character is defined by her peculiar philosophies, eccentric habits, and a luxurious but illusory existence that profoundly shapes Vera’s own journey and desires.
  • Catherine is often referred to by Vera as “my sleeping mother,” suggesting a state of perpetual dreaming or detachment from waking life. Her physical presence is limited; she “had not walked for many years because of the birthmark staining her cheek and because of her fear of the wavering floor, the sea sweeping in, and her dead past.” This immobility further anchors her to her internal world, within her great, “sea-blackened house with gold towers and cornices,” which, despite its grandeur, is described as being “gone,” implying its existence is more in memory or illusion than current reality.
  • Her unique philosophical outlook is evident in her beliefs about her “real pearls,” which, she claimed, “could not be lost or stolen or sold. Whatever the human, unhuman situation might be, those real pearls could not really be lost, and I should wear them, for they were her lost estate.” She believed that losing pearls paradoxically led to their multiplication, creating “infinities of pearls,” a concept she explained as “just simple arithmetic, simple addition.” She also held a profound view of existence, stating that it was “probably not... eternity, something everlasting, this being so temporary a world, the world already gone. Only the shadow... ever does come here.”
  • Catherine’s eccentricity is vividly illustrated through her interaction with a thief who broke into her house one winter night. Far from being alarmed, she “smilingly greeted him, extending her ivory-colored hand, asking him how far he had come, and was the world truly dead, and had offered him drugged sherry.” She engaged him in a languorous conversation, “sympathizing with her that she was rich, just as she had sympathized with him that he was poor.” In a grand, yet impractical, gesture, she offered to “finance a Revolution” with a blank check, contingent on the thief naming “an exact sum needed and an exact date,” which, caught in her “shimmering enchantment,” he could not do. Her generosity extended to outfitting the thief in an aristocratic gentleman’s costume, including a “high silk opera hat,” “long white motor coat,” and “white flowers behind his ears,” symbolizing the “coming Revolution” and making him “the melting snowman upon the first day of spring.”
  • Vera carries the tangible and intangible legacy of her mother. She wears Catherine’s “black velvet which had been her abandoned shroud,” her “lace collar and the lace cuffs,” and the “necklace of pearls.” However, Vera’s own desire for “something quite plain and poor and bare” and her search for “order, as if it were a beautiful island in the midst of life” suggest a yearning for a reality distinct from her mother’s opulent, yet ultimately vanished, dream-world.
  • “the necklace of pearls that had been my mother’s”: The pearls are repeatedly connected to Vera’s mother and her legacy. They represent the “lost estate” of her mother, something precious yet intangible that Vera inherits and wears, symbolizing the remnants of the past and the enduring connection to her mother’s life and identity. The pearls are described as “real pearls which... would bring no more than cultivated pearls” in the market, suggesting a contrast between their material and symbolic value. The pearls also symbolize continuity amid loss and the passing of time. Vera’s mother believed that the pearls could not be lost or stolen, and that their number paradoxically increased with loss, implying an infinite or eternal quality beyond physical reality. This suggests a theme of immortality or persistence beyond death, where loss in one sense begets gain in another “the more pearls there were” despite losses in life. The novel often blurs the line between dream and reality, and pearls, like many other images, are part of this interplay. Pearls are associated with the ephemeral and the eternal, with illusions and truths mingling. They appear alongside motifs of opium dreams, ghosts, and phantoms, symbolizing the fragile and shifting nature of existence and memory. The pearls are linked to the theme of identity, as something that persists yet changes, much like Vera’s mother herself, who is simultaneously present and absent, real and dreamlike. The pearls become a metaphor for what remains of a person’s essence when all else has faded or been lost. The imagery of pearls dripping or cascading like tears, linked to the mother’s lifeless but radiant hands, suggests mourning and the cycle of life and death. Pearls are connected to sorrow (“the pity, pity, pity of nothing, of something”), highlighting their role as symbols of grief and the preciousness of what is gone.

Chapter 82

Listed as: Catherine

  • Once beautiful and dreamlike, she lived in a state between life and death, sustained by drugs and illusions. Her death and the destruction of her home symbolize the dissolution of a dream or an era.
  • “how my mother, after many years of sleeping, arose from her bed and walked”: So did Weissenbach. She “had been able to get out of bed after many, many years, but this is what killed her, so that she turned old overnight. She had never shown the mark of time.” She died in 1943 in New York, and Young, who kept writing to her, learned of it months later from her daughter: “as long as you kept writing to Mother and I read your letters, I felt as if my mother was somehow alive” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).
  • “if he did not speak now, he might never speak”: Young took the scene from the death of the poet Elinor Wylie (December 16, 1928) as she remembered it: William Rose Benét explained his feelings to her at length, “and then he realized that she was sitting there dead and had never heard a word. She missed his confession” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).
  • Catherine: Vera’s view of her mother changes drastically by the end of the novel. While Vera used to see her mother as a beautiful lady sleeping in her swan boat, Vera comes to terms with her mother’s death and sees her mother as poor, as if she had been evicted from her house long before she died and wandered like a beggar through the streets. This is vastly different from the beautiful woman Vera once idolized.

Esther’s Mother
