In the research: Chapter 78, Chapter 79

Definition from research

Chapter 78

Listed as: Esther’s mother

  • She blames her for the death of her twin sister, Rosemary, who was born prematurely and dead. Esther is accused of killing this twin by kicking her in the womb, an act that haunts her throughout her life. This accusation shapes Esther’s self-perception as a murderer even before birth and contributes to her lifelong feelings of guilt and alienation.
  • She hit Esther for screaming about the bee, tied her by a rope in the yard, and “had never nursed her at those narrow breasts.”
  • “Her mother used to tie her by a rope”: Vera narrates the harsh and painful parental abuse Esther Longtree endured from a very early age. Esther’s mother is portrayed as a cold, narrow-hearted woman who blamed Esther for the death of her twin sister, Rosemary, even before Esther was born. Her mother repeatedly accused her of having “killed a little child before she was ever born,” labeling her guilty of infanticide in the womb, which created a deep sense of shame and guilt in Esther throughout her life. This accusation was a source of constant reproach and emotional cruelty, with her mother both laughing and crying as she reminded Esther of this supposed crime. The mother also expressed disappointment and resentment toward Esther, comparing her unfavorably to the lost twin, Rosemary, who was idealized as perfect, delicate, and the daughter her mother wished she had. This kept Esther in a state of embarrassment and alienation, burdened by the shadow of the lost child and her mother’s cold judgment. Esther’s mother physically abused her as a child, exemplified when she once hit Esther for screaming about a bee that had flown up her skirts, not believing her and dismissing her cries. Esther was also tied by a rope in the yard under a tree by her mother, indicating neglect and harsh treatment. The mother is described as childish in mentality and size, living in a house too small for both her and Esther, filled with fragile objects that seemed to symbolize the fragile and oppressive environment Esther was subjected to. The emotional abuse extended to lack of nurturing; Esther’s mother never nursed her at the narrow breasts or stayed to comfort her tears. She also mocked Esther’s awkwardness, physical deformities, and stubborn nature, further isolating her emotionally. The mother’s coldness was a constant presence, leaving Esther to grow up lonely and unloved, intensifying her suffering. Esther’s maternal abuse was a complex mixture of emotional cruelty, neglect, physical punishment, and harsh judgment rooted in the tragic loss of her twin and her mother’s inability to love her fully, which deeply affected Esther’s sense of self and her life trajectory.
  • “Her mother had accused her of murder”: Esther’s mothers behavior is a form of severe emotional abuse with devastating psychological consequences for the surviving child. The parent’s actions are often rooted in their own inability to cope with the trauma, grief, and feelings of helplessness surrounding the death. Individuals with narcissistic or antisocial traits may lack empathy and view their children as objects to be used to regulate their own emotions. In this context, blaming the child can serve the parent’s emotional needs rather than the child’s.

Chapter 79

  • A small, delicate, and fragile woman who yearned for a child but was unable to conceive naturally.
  • She endured the long, torturous process of conception mediated by the “other woman.”
  • Often blames Esther for the barren landscape of their lives and the shadow of Rosemary.
  • Her contradictory feelings of desire, regret, and hope illustrate the emotional complexity of motherhood under duress.
  • At the go-between’s mule farm she was held “pinioned” and saw “that it was a man”; afterward she tried, and failed, to get rid of the child. She tied Esther by a rope (“She still bore the marks of the rope”), left her “out-of-doors when it rained,” and on Esther’s birthdays, which were also Rosemary’s, baked two cakes or none.

Chapter 12

Chapter 14

  • A symbolic and somewhat mythical figure associated with the family’s carriage and horses.
  • Represents continuity, memory, and the link between life and death.
  • Catherine’s wish was for the black coachman to be buried with the carriage and horses so that she might continue to “go driving” even after death.
  • His actual fate and whereabouts are uncertain, and this uncertainty fuels much of Catherine’s anguish.
  • Catherine has also defined the Black Coachman as her conscience.
  • “but what was a name?”: “What’s in a name? That which we call a rose / By any other word would smell as sweet” (Romeo and Juliet 2.2). Catherine says it of a servant whose name no one kept.
  • “The black coachman had had no wages for years”: The history of domestic work in the United States is deeply intertwined with the exploitation of Black women, men, and immigrant laborers through systemic racism, limited economic opportunities, and discriminatory labor practices. Enslaved Black women performed essential, unpaid domestic labor before emancipation, with conditions often leading to sexual abuse and the work continuing in a similar vein after abolition. For both Black and immigrant workers, this path was one of few available options, resulting in low pay, long hours, and a lack of protections, while modern policies continue to perpetuate a cycle of vulnerability.
  • “the black coachman with the white, rolling eyes”: The “white, rolling eyes” are the stock caricature of minstrel shows and early films, which made Black servants figures of fear and comedy.
  • “what had become of the color line?”: W. E. B. Du Bois: “The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line” (The Souls of Black Folk, 1903). Catherine has just turned the coachman white and the horses black.
  • Catherine insists the burial was “the coachman’s idea, not hers,” that “money had meant nothing to him,” though he had no wages for years, the old excuses of those who kept Black servants unpaid.
  • She cannot remember his name, only his “white, rolling eyes.”

  • “this perpetual and unconsummated suicide”: The will-to-live by Schopenhauer could be used to rationalize why Mr. Spitzer did what he did and how Jock, the Black Coachman, Joachim and Peron are all the same person. Mr. Spitzer’s actions (his tireless searches, his care for others, and his internal conflicts) are driven by this fundamental will, compelling him to persist despite loss and disintegration. The multiplicity of characters such as Jock, the Black Coachman, Joachim, Peron, and Mr. Spitzer symbolically represents different manifestations of this singular will struggling within one being, blurring the lines between self and other, life and death, reality and illusion. Schopenhauer’s term is Wille zum Leben, from The World as Will and Representation (1818). “In psychology, the will to live is the drive for self-preservation, usually coupled with expectations for future improvement in one’s state in life. The will to live is an important concept when attempting to understand and comprehend why we do what we do in order to stay alive, and for as long as we can.” (Wikipedia)

In the research: Chapter 24, Chapter 45, Chapter 47, Chapter 49, Chapter 55

Definition from research

Chapter 24

  • “Spinoza and Shakespeare and Mrs. Sydington were already in the green”: Spinoza was a Dutch philosopher, author of the Ethics (1677). Shakespeare was a famous British playwright.

Chapter 45

  • “Shall love be infinitely postponed?”: may refer to Hegel. To deny something is to determine it, and to determine something is to negate it. Spinoza’s principle is “every determination is negation” (Spinoza, letter 50 to Jarig Jelles, 1674). Hegel takes this one step further by suggesting that negation itself is a process of creation, and is even the essence of positive being. By denying a certain trait or characteristic, one is implicitly acknowledging the possibility of its opposite or the existence of a different reality. For Hegel, this power of the negative, or the act of negation, is what drives progress and development. Denying a particular concept allows for the possibility of a new one to emerge, incorporating both the original concept and its negation. This is often explained through the concept of the negation of the negation, where a denial of a denial leads to a new synthesis that transcends both the original thesis and the antithesis. From an existentialist perspective denying a predefined purpose or essence allows for the possibility of individuals to create their own meaning and existence.
  • “Perhaps body and soul were one.”: Spinoza held that mind and body are one and the same thing, conceived now under the attribute of thought, now under the attribute of extension (Ethics 2, proposition 21, scholium).

Chapter 47

  • “give up his assumption that all things which existed should be tangible”: Peron and Joachim as materialism and immaterialism. In philosophy, materialism says that everything that exists is fundamentally physical, composed of matter and energy. All phenomena, including consciousness, are ultimately reducible to physical processes. They point to the success of science in explaining the physical world and that consciousness can be explained by brain activity. Physicalism is similar in that everything can be explained by physics. Immaterialism believes there is an existence of entities or properties that are not physical, such as minds, consciousness, or spiritual realms. Non-physical entities or properties exist alongside or instead of the material world. Idealists believe that only minds and their perceptions are real, while the material world is a construction of the mind. Peron symbolizes the external, material world with its pleasures, follies, and impermanence, while Joachim represents the internal, immaterial realm of thought, memory, and spiritual seeking. See Spinoza’s mind and body as one in the Chapter 45 resources.
  • “he was agonized by attributing consciousness to everything”: This may refer to panpsychism, the view that mind, or something like mind, is a fundamental and widespread feature of reality, present in some form even in its most basic elements. It has roots in ancient Greek philosophy, in Thales, who held that “all things are full of gods” (Aristotle, On the Soul 1.5), and in Plato, and later in Spinoza, Leibniz, and Schopenhauer. Mr. Spitzer suffers because he senses consciousness not only in people but in clouds, stars, waves, palings, and weathervanes, so that the line between the living and the lifeless blurs and his own sense of self grows unstable.

Chapter 49

Chapter 55

  • “sub specie aeternitatis”: Sub specie aeternitatis is Latin for under the aspect of eternity or that which is universally and eternally true.

In the research: Chapter 25, Chapter 31, Chapter 37, Chapter 39, Chapter 45, Chapter 51, Chapter 52, Chapter 59, Chapter 68, Chapter 70

Definition from research

Chapter 25

  • “What death was this which was no death?”: The philosophy of death explores the meaning of death, our relationship to it, and the various ways it impacts human existence and understanding. It delves into questions about what happens after death, the nature of consciousness, and the ethical implications of death, including suicide. The Nature of Death: Dualism (the soul continues to exist after death, potentially in a separate realm or afterlife), Materialism (death is the permanent cessation of all bodily functions, including consciousness), Annihilationism (death is the end of all conscious experience, and nothing exists after death). Philosophical Perspectives on Death: Stoicism (death is not something to be feared, as it is a natural part of life and a release from suffering), Existentialism (thinkers like Kierkegaard and Heidegger, in Being and Time, 1927, emphasized the importance of confronting our mortality to understand our own existence and the meaning of life), Nietzsche (proposed that individuals have the freedom to define their own death, suggesting it could be a conscious choice rather than an inevitable fate: “Die at the right time,” in “On Free Death,” Thus Spoke Zarathustra, 1883). Ethical Considerations: Suicide (philosophy engages with questions about the moral permissibility of suicide, including whether it’s ever justifiable).

Chapter 31

  • “Here lies one who shared our common lot of mortal frailty”: Heidegger’s “being-towards-death,” from Being and Time (1927), is a fundamental aspect of human existence, highlighting the finite nature of our being and the importance of confronting mortality to live authentically. Heidegger distinguishes between authentic and inauthentic ways of living: authentic living confronts the inevitability of death and makes choices that are meaningful to oneself, while inauthentic living is swept along by what “they” say and do (das Man). Mr. Spitzer’s epitaph names the common condition Heidegger describes: one who “shared our common lot of mortal frailty.”

Chapter 37

  • “How should death be different from life, my mother asked”: Life as a state of experience and potential: Socrates thought death might be a dreamless sleep or passage to another realm where one can converse with the dead. Existentialism believes death is an inevitable aspect of human existence and that it can lead to a heightened sense of self-awareness and responsibility. Epicureanism argues death cannot harm a person, as it’s either not yet experienced (while alive) or not experienced at all (once dead). Death is defined as the loss of the capacity to engage in vital activities and the cessation of consciousness. Wittgenstein wrote that death is not an event in life, for we do not live to experience it (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 6.4311). Schopenhauer believed that understanding death as the ultimate end of life can provide a perspective on the meaning of life itself. Freud thought the life instinct (Eros) and the death instinct (Thanatos) are fundamental forces in human behavior.

Chapter 39

  • “The personal pronoun I did not always mean”: “I AM THAT I AM” (Exodus 3:14). Jesus uses the phrase “I am” in seven distinct statements each emphasizing a specific aspect of His divine nature and purpose, connecting him to the God revealed in the Old Testament. Descartes wrote, “I think, therefore I am” (René Descartes, Discourse on Method, 1637), which then leads into Existentialism and Absurdism. Existentialism proposes the idea that people are free to choose their own meaning and are responsible for their choices, there are no inherent meaning or purpose to life and instead people are responsible for creating meaning, personal experience and subjective reality are used to shape understanding of the world, freedom, responsibility, choice, self-discovery and the absurdity of human existence are explored. Anaïs Nin wrote that Young’s work was not absurdist, because Young believed there was an inherent beauty to the world (Anaïs Nin, The Novel of the Future, Macmillan, 1968).

Chapter 45

  • “Shall love be infinitely postponed?”: may refer to Hegel. To deny something is to determine it, and to determine something is to negate it. Spinoza’s principle is “every determination is negation” (Spinoza, letter 50 to Jarig Jelles, 1674). Hegel takes this one step further by suggesting that negation itself is a process of creation, and is even the essence of positive being. By denying a certain trait or characteristic, one is implicitly acknowledging the possibility of its opposite or the existence of a different reality. For Hegel, this power of the negative, or the act of negation, is what drives progress and development. Denying a particular concept allows for the possibility of a new one to emerge, incorporating both the original concept and its negation. This is often explained through the concept of the negation of the negation, where a denial of a denial leads to a new synthesis that transcends both the original thesis and the antithesis. From an existentialist perspective denying a predefined purpose or essence allows for the possibility of individuals to create their own meaning and existence.

Chapter 51

  • Existentialism: The paragraph touches upon themes of mortality, the subjective experience of time, and the search for meaning. Mr. Spitzer reflects on the fading boundary between life and death, the retrospective understanding of the heart, and the possibility of moving from death to life. These reflections suggest an awareness of the fleeting nature of existence and the individual’s struggle to find purpose in a world seemingly devoid of inherent meaning. The questions posed, such as “why should the second journey seem longer than the first?” highlight the subjective and often paradoxical nature of human experience.

Chapter 52

  • “Mr. Spitzer had trembled like a gambler”: The opening lines immediately establish a world governed by chance. Mr. Spitzer trembling “like a gambler” suggests a life where outcomes are unpredictable and determined by forces beyond individual control. This aligns with existentialist themes of the absurdity of existence and the lack of inherent meaning. The “faceless card” and “star of no known number” symbolize the limits of human knowledge. No one can fully grasp the forces shaping a life, and there will always be elements of the unknown. This resonates with the existentialist emphasis on the limits of reason. The line “Yes, there was an external world, he knew now as it departed” is crucial. It indicates a loss of faith in an objective reality. The world is not fixed but is constantly slipping away, emphasizing the subjective experience. “He gave his belief when there was no reason for his belief” highlights a rejection of rationalism. Spitzer’s faith is not based on evidence or logic but on something deeper, perhaps a Kierkegaardian “leap of faith” into the absurd. “For he reserved his credulity for the grand occasions eliciting the skepticism of others. Their skepticism was his faith” is a complex statement. It suggests that Spitzer finds meaning in what others reject. This could be interpreted as a form of contrarianism, or as a deeper understanding that truth often lies in challenging conventional wisdom.

Chapter 59

  • “his tragic sense had been the greatest joy”: Compare Miguel de Unamuno’s The Tragic Sense of Life (Del sentimiento trágico de la vida, 1913), which finds the root of human feeling in a hunger for immortality that reason cannot satisfy.

Chapter 68

  • “there was only one definition of reality, that it was real”: The line emphasizes a tautological but deeply existential assertion: reality is defined by its own existence as experienced or known, regardless of its form. “even the unreal things were real,” points to an inclusive, perhaps subjective or phenomenological, understanding of reality where things dismissed or marginalized by society (ignored, rejected, unloved) are nonetheless part of the fabric of reality. This echoes themes of illusion versus reality, and the permeability between them, which run throughout the novel. Philosophically, this passage represents a theme often associated with existentialism and phenomenology: that reality is defined by experience and perception rather than by fixed, external definitions. It also touches on the fluidity of reality, blurring lines between dream and waking life, appearance and essence, presence and absence. The passage conveys that reality is not limited to the tangible or socially accepted but includes dreams, illusions, forgotten or rejected beings, and all forms of existence or perception. It challenges rigid dichotomies and invites a broader, more inclusive understanding of what is real.

Chapter 70

  • “the unheard music of the spheres”: The passage reflects a philosophical meditation on the unavoidability of change, the human compulsion to find or impose meaning, and the possibility that such meaning is not inherent but constructed. It challenges the belief in a fixed cosmic order and suggests that what we perceive as meaningful patterns may be self-deceptions, resonating with existentialist skepticism and the impermanence stressed in ancient and modern philosophies. Pythagoras taught that the planets sound a harmony too perfect for human ears. Compare Keats, in the ode Vera has already echoed: “Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard / Are sweeter.”

In the research: Chapter 2, Chapter 3, Chapter 6, Chapter 8, Chapter 10, Chapter 12, Chapter 13, Chapter 14, Chapter 23, Chapter 24, Chapter 28, Chapter 29, Chapter 32, Chapter 36, Chapter 37, Chapter 38, Chapter 39, Chapter 40, Chapter 44, Chapter 45, Chapter 47, Chapter 48, Chapter 49, Chapter 50, Chapter 51, Chapter 52, Chapter 53, Chapter 55, Chapter 61, Chapter 71

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • Platonism is the philosophy of Plato which affirms the existence of abstract objects, which are asserted to exist in a third realm distinct from both the sensible external world and from the internal world of consciousness. It is the opposite of nominalism.

Chapter 3

  • Plutarch was a Greek Middle Platonist philosopher, biographer, essayist, and priest at the Temple of Apollo. Plutarch functions as a symbol of the mother’s intellectual and cultural anchoring amidst her drifting consciousness, representing a link to enduring human wisdom and the complexities of love, fate, and history that permeate her visionary world.

Chapter 6

  • “You think that beauty is as beauty does”: The proverb says a person’s true beauty is in their character and actions, not their physical appearance. The older proverb is “handsome is as handsome does” (1500s). The sentiment is found in the writings of Geoffrey Chaucer in “The Wife of Bath’s Tale” (c. 1387) from The Canterbury Tales. Chaucer’s lines suggest that the most virtuous person, regardless of physical appearance, is the most beautiful. The Greek philosophers Plato and Aristotle linked beauty to virtue, order, and symmetry. This perspective influenced the development of the proverb, suggesting that inner qualities are just as important as outward appearance in determining beauty.
  • “the angels do not marry, for they are male and female in one body”: In Plato’s Symposium Aristophanes tells of the first humans, double beings later split in two, each half forever seeking the other.

Chapter 8

  • “that dream within the dream”: This may refer to Edgar Allan Poe’s poem “A Dream within a Dream” (1849), which says, “All that we see or seem / Is but a dream within a dream.” This dream within a dream is a recurring theme throughout the book. The idea that life is a dream goes back to Plato, Aristotle, and Descartes. The first stanza ends with that statement, and the last stanza turns it into a question: “Is all that we see or seem / But a dream within a dream?” This symbolizes the recursive, elusive quality of existence in the novel: a reality constantly refracted through multiple dreamlike states that challenge the notion of a fixed, singular truth.

Chapter 10

  • “What is man but a poor, two-legged animal?”: Plato defined man as a featherless biped, and Diogenes answered with a plucked chicken. Lear calls man “such a poor, bare, forked animal” (King Lear 3.4).
  • “good, true, beautiful”: Plato’s three highest ideas, the Good, the True, and the Beautiful.

Chapter 12

  • The theme of shadows runs through the novel. It brings to mind Plato’s work, The Allegory of the Cave, or Plato’s Cave. It is an allegory presented by the Greek philosopher Plato in his work, Republic. The Cave describes a group of people who have lived chained to the wall of a cave all their lives, facing a blank wall. The people watch shadows projected on the wall from objects passing in front of a fire behind them and give names to these shadows. The shadows are the prisoners’ reality, but are not accurate representations of the real world. The shadows represent the fragment of reality that can normally be perceived through the senses, while the objects under the sun represent the true forms of objects that can only be perceived through reason. The philosopher is like a prisoner who is freed from the cave and comes to understand that the shadows on the wall are actually not the direct source of the images seen. A philosopher aims to understand and perceive the higher levels of reality. However, the other inmates of the cave do not even desire to leave their prison, for they know no better life. (Wikipedia) See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “that we are not as shadows”: “What shadows we are, and what shadows we pursue” (Edmund Burke, 1780), and “our days upon earth are a shadow” (Job 8:9).

Chapter 13

  • “immortal gardens”: In Plato’s Apology, Socrates looks forward to death as a chance to converse with Orpheus, Homer, and Hesiod.

Chapter 14

  • “the music of the spheres, the silent music”: Boethius was a Roman senator, consul, magister officiorum, polymath, historian, and philosopher of the Early Middle Ages. He sought to reconcile the teachings of Plato and Aristotle with Christian theology. He broke logic into three parts: that which defines, that which divides, and that which deduces. There are three types of arguments: those of necessity, of ready believability, and sophistry. In De Musica there are three classifications: Musica mundana, Musica humana, Musica instrumentalis. In Dante’s Divine Comedy, the spirit of Boethius is pointed out by Saint Thomas Aquinas and is mentioned further in the poem. In his book De Institutione Musica (Fundamentals of Music) his drawings appear striking and may be an inspiration for the organization of Young’s novel. Musica universalis or music of the spheres or harmony of the spheres is a Greek philosophical concept founded by Pythagoras. This metaphysical principle stated that mathematical relationships could produce ‘tones’ of energy that could produce, among other things, sounds. Pythagoras proposed that the celestial bodies all have their own unique hum based on their orbital revolution. This idea influenced many scholars until the end of the Renaissance. Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer from the 1600s wrote extensively on the subject. (Wikipedia) Later astronomy set it aside. Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution, with its Wheel of Fortune.
  • “the appearance beyond the appearance”: Allegory of the Cave, Plato describes people who have spent their entire lives chained by their necks and ankles in front of an inner wall with a view of the empty outer wall of the cave. They observe the shadows projected onto the outer wall by objects carried behind the inner wall by people who are invisible to the chained “prisoners” and who walk along the inner wall with a fire behind them, creating the shadows on the inner wall in front of the prisoners. The “sign bearers” pronounce the names of the objects, the sounds of which are reflected near the shadows and are understood by the prisoners as if they were coming from the shadows themselves. Only the shadows and sounds are the prisoners’ reality, which are not accurate representations of the real world. The shadows represent distorted and blurred copies of reality that can be perceived through the senses, while the objects under the Sun represent the true forms of objects that can only be perceived through reason. Three higher levels exist: natural science; deductive mathematics, geometry, and logic; and the theory of forms. Socrates explains how the philosopher is like a prisoner freed from the cave and comes to understand that the shadows on the wall are not the direct source of the images seen. A philosopher aims to understand and perceive the higher levels of reality. However, the other inmates of the cave do not even desire to leave their prison, for they know no better life. (Wikipedia)
  • “knew that the dog was Socrates”: Socrates was a Greek philosopher who wrote no texts of his own but is credited as one of the founders of Western philosophy. In the work Republic, written by Plato, there is a Socratic dialogue. In it Socrates argues that the dog is very much like a philosopher because the dog distinguishes the face of a friend and of an enemy only by the criterion of knowing and not knowing. (Wikipedia) Socrates swore “By the dog, the god of the Egyptians” (Gorgias 482b).
  • “the coachman was her conscience”: The Katha Upanishad: “Know the Self as the lord of the chariot, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, the mind as the reins, and the senses as the horses.” In Plato’s Phaedrus, the soul is a charioteer driving two horses.

Chapter 23

  • “Poor mortals all and blind as bats in a cave”: This may echo Plato’s prisoners of the cave, who take shadows for the real (Republic 7).

Chapter 24

  • “which was already occupied by Plato’s boat”: Plato’s boat might refer to the Ship of State by Plato (Republic, Book 6). It is a metaphor comparing governing a city-state to being the captain of a ship and only philosopher kings should rule.

Chapter 28

  • “that spindle of creative flame which is said to sleep in the eternal darkness, weaving our bodies”: Weaving plays a significant role in the mythologies of various cultures, often symbolizing creation, destiny, and even the weaving of life itself. In many stories, weaving is attributed to deities or individuals who control fate or have supernatural abilities. For example, the Greek Moirae (Fates) spin, measure, and cut the thread of human lives, and the Norse goddess Frigg is associated with weaving and seiðr magic, which involves weaving destiny. Greek mythology: Athena, Arachne, Moirae (Fates), Penelope, Philomela. Norse mythology: Frigg, The Norns. Other mythologies: Neith, Laima, Päivätär and Kuutar, Spider Woman, Arianrhod. In Plato’s Myth of Er (Republic 10), the Spindle of Necessity turns the spheres on the knees of Necessity, and her daughters, the Fates, spin each life. In the chapter the “spindle of creative flame” weaves bodies, souls, and dreams, so that identity is woven like a tapestry from many threads of experience and memory, made of many intertwined selves rather than one.

Chapter 29

  • “between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow”: In philosophy, happiness and sorrow are intertwined, with sorrow often seen as a necessary component for experiencing the depth of joy and vice versa rather than as simple opposites. It can be viewed in a number of ways: a dialectical relationship (yin and yang-complementary forces where one cannot exist without the other); the contrast highlights the value of positive experiences; a catalyst for growth, introspection, and a deeper understanding of life’s complexities. Philosophical perspectives are found in Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Stoicism, Utilitarianism, Hedonism, Life Satisfaction Theory. Plato and Aristotle’s eudaimonia where flourishing and well-being are achieved by living a virtuous life, not simply experiencing happiness. Nirvana is a state of liberation from suffering and the cycle of rebirth. Equanimity is the ability to remain calm and balanced in the face of both pleasure and pain. Mr. Spitzer finds it as hard to tell butterfly from moth as “to distinguish between brother and brother or between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow,” for “Seldom did happiness and sorrow occur in pure and disrelated states.”

Chapter 32

  • “that pale cavalier who, with disheveled locks, with foaming mouth, is driven by the mare”: In Plato’s Phaedrus the soul is a charioteer with two horses, one noble and one unruly, who must master the wild one with the bit.

Chapter 36

  • “So he lived at this second remove from reality”: Plato’s imitator is “thrice removed from the king and from the truth,” an imitation of an imitation (Plato, Republic 10, trans. Benjamin Jowett).
  • “It seemed to him that she had never distinguished between imagination and memory”: Julia Shaw is a psychologist and an expert in complex autobiographical false memory (Julia Shaw, The Memory Illusion, Random House, 2016). She asserts that all memories are illusions which are similar to how quantum physicists describe reality, much as Einstein wrote that “the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion” (Albert Einstein, letter to the family of Michele Besso, March 21, 1955). It’s the same way Plato talked about prisoners in a cave confusing shadows on the wall with the reality outside the cave. A 2000 study found a robust false memory effect. However, participants were able to differentiate false memories and actual memories when using specific phenomenological tasks (Jeffrey S. Anastasi, Matthew G. Rhodes, and Marcy C. Burns, “Distinguishing between Memory Illusions and Actual Memories Using Phenomenological Measurements and Explicit Warnings,” American Journal of Psychology 113, no. 1, 2000, 1-26).
  • “for total ignorance was total knowledge”: Nicholas of Cusa called it learned ignorance, De docta ignorantia (1440): the wise man knows that he does not know. Socrates said much the same in Plato’s Apology.

Chapter 37

  • “How should death be different from life, my mother asked”: Life as a state of experience and potential: Socrates thought death might be a dreamless sleep or passage to another realm where one can converse with the dead. Existentialism believes death is an inevitable aspect of human existence and that it can lead to a heightened sense of self-awareness and responsibility. Epicureanism argues death cannot harm a person, as it’s either not yet experienced (while alive) or not experienced at all (once dead). Death is defined as the loss of the capacity to engage in vital activities and the cessation of consciousness. Wittgenstein wrote that death is not an event in life, for we do not live to experience it (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 6.4311). Schopenhauer believed that understanding death as the ultimate end of life can provide a perspective on the meaning of life itself. Freud thought the life instinct (Eros) and the death instinct (Thanatos) are fundamental forces in human behavior.
  • “as man became woman with her heaving breasts”: Gender as a social construct refers to the socially created roles, behaviors, expressions, and identities associated with being a woman, man, boy, or girl. It’s not inherently determined by biology, but rather shaped by cultural norms, societal expectations, and historical contexts. This means gender is not fixed and can vary across cultures and time. In short, it is not a biological reality: it is socially created, varies across cultures, is dynamic and fluid, and is distinct from biological sex. Philosophical thought on gender goes back to ancient Greece, where Pythagoras’s table of opposites set male against female (Aristotle, Metaphysics 1.5) and Plato argued that women could be guardians (Republic 5). Later came John Locke, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Judith Sargent Murray (“On the Equality of the Sexes,” 1790), and Mary Wollstonecraft (A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792). The chapter and novel present gender as a fluid and changeable construct rather than a rigid, innate fact, using metaphorical and dreamlike language to question fixed dichotomies between male and female, self and other, life and death.
  • “the floor of the Lost Atlantis”: Atlantis can be a metaphor for something that is no longer attainable. It is a fictional island used as an allegory for the hubris of nations in Plato’s Timaeus and Critias (about 360 BC). It has had a large influence on literature, arts, and culture.

Chapter 38

  • “the beautiful music of the spheres”: Musica Universalis (music of the spheres) concept incorporates the metaphysical principle that mathematical relationships express qualities or “tones” of energy that manifests in numbers, visual angles, shapes and sounds which are all connected within a pattern of proportion. This has been explored by Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle (he rejected the idea), Boethius developed three categories of music (musica mundana, musica humana, and musica quae in quibusdam constituta est instrumentis), Kepler expounded the idea in Harmonices Mundi (1619). Boethius’s writings were later illustrated, and Young may have taken inspiration from these illustrations for the novel.
  • “Heracleitus is supposed to say that all things are in motion and nothing at rest; he compares them to the stream of a river, and says that you cannot go into the same water twice” (Plato, Cratylus 402a, trans. Benjamin Jowett).

Chapter 39

  • Plato divided the soul into three parts, reason, spirit, and appetite (Republic 4).
  • “she knew she was insane, quite mad”: “Divine madness” or “theia mania” refers to unconventional, sometimes unpredictable behavior attributed to divine inspiration or the influence of a god, often associated with mystical experiences or spiritual practice. Plato explored the idea as a source of creativity and inspiration: “the greatest of blessings come to us through madness, when it is sent as a gift of the gods” (Plato, Phaedrus 244a, trans. Harold N. Fowler, 1925). It can take the form of “religious ecstasy” where a person has a profound connection to the divine, transcending normal perceptions and societal norms.

Chapter 40

  • In Plato’s Symposium (212d) Alcibiades bursts in drunk, crowned with ivy and violets, and praises Socrates.
  • “who should know when the dream ended”: In philosophy there is the question of dreams by Zhuangzi, Plato, and Aristotle. Descartes asked how he could know that he was not now dreaming (Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation 1, 1641), which seems to be the same question Catherine is preoccupied with. Descartes’ answer was that we cannot trust our senses in waking life without invoking a benevolent God who would not deceive us. Catherine takes this one step further at the end of Chapter 39 and asks, “What if God is dreaming?” In psychology the question “Is Life a Dream?” is answered with the coherence of the waking world does give evidence that it is not just a figment of our imagination. However, the objects that we perceive as permanent are in reality through the science of quantum physics mostly made up of empty space. In a sense people do live in a dream world that is created by the mind. When people are awake, their minds conform their dreaming to a reliable set of patterns, which they assume to be determined by a reality that exists independently of their experience of it, though they have no way of knowing that reality except through the complex ways in which it affects their dream. There is also reality that is experienced and affected by psychedelic drugs and other altered states of consciousness (Sharon Hewitt Rawlette, “Is Life a Dream?,” Psychology Today, July 31, 2019).
  • “As between the figurehead and the greatest captain of the greatest boat”: Plato’s parable of the ship (Republic 6.488), where a quarrelling crew ignores the true navigator, symbolizes the dangers of a political system not based on expertise. It is often called the Ship of State, where the ship represents a nation or government, with the crew, captain, and passengers symbolizing different social classes or politicians.

Chapter 44

  • “splitting her apart into the lover and the loved”: In Plato’s Symposium, Aristophanes tells how the first humans were split in two, so that each half seeks its other: “The women who are a section of the woman do not care for men, but have female attachments” (Symposium 191e, trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1871).

Chapter 45

  • “The deepest sleep is dreamless.”: Socrates says that if death is a dreamless sleep, “to die is gain; for eternity is then only a single night” (Plato, Apology 40d-e, trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1871). The Mandukya Upanishad names deep sleep, where the sleeper desires nothing and dreams no dream, as the third state of the self.

Chapter 47

  • “Perhaps this world was the Lost Atlantis”: Atlantis is a fictional island mentioned in an allegory on the hubris of nations in Plato’s Timaeus and Critias: “in a single day and night of misfortune… the island of Atlantis in like manner disappeared in the depths of the sea” (Timaeus 25d, trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1871).
  • “he was agonized by attributing consciousness to everything”: This may refer to panpsychism, the view that mind, or something like mind, is a fundamental and widespread feature of reality, present in some form even in its most basic elements. It has roots in ancient Greek philosophy, in Thales, who held that “all things are full of gods” (Aristotle, On the Soul 1.5), and in Plato, and later in Spinoza, Leibniz, and Schopenhauer. Mr. Spitzer suffers because he senses consciousness not only in people but in clouds, stars, waves, palings, and weathervanes, so that the line between the living and the lifeless blurs and his own sense of self grows unstable.

Chapter 48

  • “for this life was a long rehearsal of music for the silence”: Life is a rehearsal, a practice, for the silence of death. The “music” is the experience of a life, passing and temporary; the “silence” is death, where all of it ceases, and which “could surely not answer or reproach.” Socrates says that “the true philosophers, Simmias, are always occupied in the practice of dying” (Plato, Phaedo 67e, trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1871), and Montaigne titled an essay “That to philosophize is to learn to die” (Essays 1.20, 1580). Hamlet’s last words are “the rest is silence” (5.2).
  • “he who knew rhombs, circles, semicircles”: Mr. Spitzer knows the geometry of things, rhombs, circles, boxes within boxes, octahedrons, and the eclipses of light by darkness and darkness by light: the nested, overlapping forms of a reality both ordered and hidden. He calls them “the forms of a divine nature.” In Plato’s Timaeus the elements are built of regular solids, air of the octahedron (55-56), and Galileo wrote that the book of the universe “is written in the language of mathematics, and its characters are triangles, circles, and other geometric figures” (The Assayer, 1623, trans. Stillman Drake, 1957).

Chapter 49

  • Porphyry of Tyre was a Neoplatonic philosopher born in Tyre, Roman Phoenicia during Roman rule. He edited and published the Enneads, the only collection of the work of Plotinus, his teacher. He wrote original works in the Greek language on a wide variety of topics, ranging from music theory to Homer. His Isagoge or Introduction, an introduction to logic and philosophy, was the standard textbook on logic throughout the Middle Ages in its Latin and Arabic translations. Porphyry was, and still is, also well-known for his anti-Christian polemics. Through works such as Philosophy from Oracles and Against the Christians (which was banned by Constantine the Great), he was involved in a controversy with early Christians. Important works and philosophy attributed to him. His Isagoge set the question for the Middle Ages, whether genera and species exist in reality or only in the mind. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 51

Happiness is fleeting as a snowflake; “three minutes of happiness seemed perhaps all there might be,” and “the greatest happiness might come through the sorrow of waiting, of postponement.” The passage holds the absurdity of existence and, through Mr. Spitzer’s work for the dead, the responsibility of making sense of their lives.

Chapter 52

  • “Should doubt move mountains which faith had not moved”: Mr. Spitzer inverts the saying that faith can move mountains: “If ye have faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye shall say unto this mountain, Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove; and nothing shall be impossible unto you” (Matthew 17:20). The suffragette’s search for a lost skirt, which leads to the death of her lover, suggests the absurdity of human pursuits, as in existentialist thought. She cries “Long live woman! Vive la femme! Viva la donna!” in many languages, “perhaps even in Sanskrit which was the language written upon a silent snowflake,” yet there are “secret languages never to be translated into words.” Her decision to dress as a man asserts her freedom against social norms, and her practical clothing against the other climbers’ finery sets materialism against idealism. The footman cutting a golden stairway from a frozen lake to the mountains of the moon may recall the ascent from Plato’s cave toward the light, and her climbing the Transcendentalist journey beyond the material world.
  • “being that Lost Atlantis”: Plato tells of Atlantis in the Timaeus and Critias (about 360 BC), an island empire beyond the Pillars of Hercules that “in a single day and night of misfortune” disappeared in the depths of the sea (Timaeus, trans. Benjamin Jowett).

Chapter 53

  • “They probably would not have understood Mr. Spitzer’s swan song”: The legend that the swan sings most beautifully just before it dies is old; in Plato’s Phaedo (84e-85b) Socrates says swans sing at their death out of joy that they are going to the god they serve.

Chapter 55

  • “some old watered bond issues of the Lost Atlantis”: “Lost Atlantis” is a mythical island civilization described by Plato in his dialogues as a powerful, technologically advanced society that was destroyed by earthquakes and sank beneath the sea. While the story is a well-known myth and has inspired theories about real locations and even modern technological advancements, most historians and scientists believe Atlantis was a philosophical allegory created by Plato to serve as a cautionary tale against hubris.

Chapter 61

  • “A swan when it is dying has the right to sing”: The swan song myth is an ancient belief that swans, typically silent throughout their lives, sing a beautiful song just before they die. The term is now used metaphorically to describe a final, often brilliant, performance, work, or gesture before retirement or death. This myth has roots in Greek and Roman mythology, appearing in the writings of Aeschylus and Plato, and was later referenced in English literature by Chaucer. The English phrase “swan song,” a translation of the German Schwanengesang, dates from 1831; Thomas Carlyle is credited with popularizing it in his satire Sartor Resartus, written in 1831.

Chapter 71

  • “What’s Wrong with Democracy?”: What’s Wrong with Democracy? Critiques of democracy existed across a wide range of historical periods and came from diverse intellectual and social movements. These arguments addressed everything from the flaws of ancient Greek democracy to the systemic exclusions within American democracy before the Civil Rights era. Philosophers like Plato warned that in a democracy, the masses, driven by ignorance and emotion, could become susceptible to self-serving demagogues. This “rule by the mob” could lead to rash, unjust decisions, such as the execution of Socrates in ancient Athens. Later, thinkers like Thomas Hobbes argued that democracy leads to chaos and civil war, advocating for a strong, singular sovereign to prevent societal collapse. Some classical and 19th-century thinkers, including Plato, Thomas Carlyle, and John Ruskin, argued that society should be led by a knowledgeable elite rather than the common people. This perspective asserted that only a select few possessed the wisdom and virtue necessary to govern effectively, and that the majority of people were ill-equipped for the complexities of statecraft. As democracy expanded during the Industrial Revolution, critics like Carlyle, John Ruskin, and William Lecky argued that it produced anarchy and chaos within modern industrial society. They believed that democratic capitalism prioritized profit and individual self-interest over social stability and the public good. Commentators like Matthew Arnold expressed concern that democracy led to a flattening of culture and a decline in intellectual standards. He feared that the “average” tastes of the masses would displace high culture and that society would suffer from a lack of moral and intellectual leadership. Before the passage of the Civil Rights Act in 1964, critics pointed out the hypocrisy of American democracy, which systematically excluded many of its own citizens. This was particularly evident in the Jim Crow South, where discriminatory laws like poll taxes and literacy tests disenfranchised millions of African Americans and poor whites. The history of American democracy has been marked by periods of deep instability and division. Scholars point to the 1890s and the aftermath of the Compromise of 1877, which ended Reconstruction, as periods of “backsliding” where racial conflict produced significant damage to democratic ideals. This history was built on the foundation of racial exclusion, as some historians note that democratic norms only took hold among white people after racial equality was removed from the agenda. Especially during the Gilded Age (1865-1915), the rise of powerful, and often corrupt, political machines led many Americans to question the health of their democracy. Critiques focused on the manipulation of the voting process, the influence of money in politics, and the resulting feeling that elections were no longer fair or truly representative of the people. The failure of some interwar and post-WWII democratic governments, such as France’s Fourth Republic, was often cited as a failure of democracy itself. Frequent changes in government and a fractured party system led many to conclude that democracy was inherently unstable and inefficient. The Civil Rights Act marks a significant turning point in the realization of American democratic ideals.

Relativity was a revolutionary idea that changed the understanding of the universe, though few could explain it. He said in a 1929 interview that, “The meaning of relativity has been widely misunderstood. Philosophers play with the word, like a child with a doll. Chapter 47

Chapter 49

  • It emphasizes processes, relations, and transformations rather than fixed essences where time and identity are fluid. “He died at his zenith because he was at his nadir, died at his nadir because he was at his zenith” This paradoxical interpenetration suggests that universals and particulars are not static but dynamically related.

The meteorologist Edward Lorenz named the effect in a 1972 talk, “Predictability: Does the Flap of a Butterfly’s Wings in Brazil Set Off a Tornado in Texas?” Ray Bradbury had already imagined it in “A Sound of Thunder” (1952), where a time traveler steps on a butterfly and changes history. “For the chaos had its pattern.”

Schrödinger meant it to show the absurdity of applying quantum superposition to everyday objects. (Wikipedia)
  • Eugene Wigner imagined in 1961 a friend inside a laboratory who sees a measurement while Wigner, outside, must treat friend and laboratory as hovering in a blur of possible states, so that the two seem to occupy distinct realities.   • “the music of the spheres, the silent music”: Boethius was a Roman senator, consul, magister officiorum, polymath, historian, and philosopher of the Early Middle Ages. He sought to reconcile the teachings of Plato and Aristotle with Christian theology. He broke logic into three parts: that which defines, that which divides, and that which deduces. There are three types of arguments: those of necessity, of ready believability, and sophistry. In De Musica there are three classifications: Musica mundana, Musica humana, Musica instrumentalis. Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer from the 1600s wrote extensively on the subject. (Wikipedia) Later astronomy set it aside. Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution, with its Wheel of Fortune.

Definition from research

Chapter 1

  • Harold Bloom says Don Quixote is the first modern novel, and that the protagonist is at war with Freud's reality principle, which accepts the necessity of dying. Bloom says that the novel has an endless range of meanings, but that a recurring theme is the human need to withstand suffering. Edith Grossman, who wrote and published a highly acclaimed English translation of the novel in 2003, says that the book is mostly meant to move people into emotion using a systematic change of course, on the verge of both tragedy and comedy at the same time. Grossman has stated: The question is that Quixote has multiple interpretations [...] and how do I deal with that in my translation. I'm going to answer your question by avoiding it [...] so when I first started reading the Quixote I thought it was the most tragic book in the world, and I would read it and weep [...] As I grew older [...] my skin grew thicker [...] and so when I was working on the translation I was actually sitting at my computer and laughing out loud. This is done [...] as Cervantes did it [...] by never letting the reader rest. You are never certain that you truly got it. Because as soon as you think you understand something, Cervantes introduces something that contradicts your premise. The novel's structure is episodic in form. The full title is indicative of the tale's object, as ingenioso (Spanish) means "quick with inventiveness", marking the transition of modern literature from dramatic to thematic unity. The novel takes place over a long period of time, including many adventures united by common themes of the nature of reality, reading, and dialogue in general. Although burlesque on the surface, the novel, especially in its second half, has served as an important thematic source not only in literature but also in much of art and music, inspiring works by Pablo Picasso and Richard Strauss. The contrasts between the tall, thin, fancy-struck and idealistic Quixote and the fat diddy, world-weary Panza is a motif echoed ever since the book's publication, and Don Quixote's imaginings are the butt of outrageous and cruel practical jokes in the novel. Even faithful and simple Sancho is forced to deceive him at certain points. The novel is considered a satire of orthodoxy, veracity and even nationalism. In exploring the individualism of his characters, Cervantes helped lead literary practice beyond the narrow convention of the chivalric romance. He spoofs the chivalric romance through a straightforward retelling of a series of acts that redound to the knightly virtues of the hero. The character of Don Quixote became so well known in its time that the word quixotic was quickly adopted by many languages. Characters such as Sancho Panza and Don Quixote's steed, Rocinante, are emblems of Western literary culture. The phrase "tilting at windmills" to describe an act of attacking imaginary enemies (or an act of extreme idealism), derives from an iconic scene in the book. It stands in a unique position between medieval romance and the modern novel. The former consists of disconnected stories featuring the same characters and settings with little exploration of the inner life of even the main character. The latter are usually focused on the psychological evolution of their characters. In Part I, Quixote imposes himself on his environment. By Part II, people know about him through "having read his adventures", and so, he needs to do less to maintain his image. By his deathbed, he has regained his sanity, and is once more "Alonso Quixano the Good".

Chapter 3

  • “be proved, and the truth was better than the lie, even should the lie seem truer than the truth, every lie containing a seed of truth in it, no doubt, but ours was the freedom to make a choice between the truth and the lie and the truth and the truth, to do what was good and right, leaving no uncertainty.” - The passage underscores that while lies may be seductive and intertwined with truth, it is the conscious choice to pursue what is good and true that defines human freedom and moral integrity. Many cultures and thinkers have expressed the belief that, despite the potential pain or discomfort of truth, it ultimately offers a more beneficial and sustainable foundation than deception. A common African proverb states, "The bitter truth is better than a sweet lie". This highlights the idea that even if the truth is difficult to hear, it is ultimately more valuable than a comforting falsehood. Writers and thinkers like Tolstoy have emphasized the importance of truth for moral clarity and authentic relationships. They argue that while lies might offer temporary comfort, they ultimately lead to unsustainable situations and undermine trust. In contrast to the idea of truth being better, the concept of the "big lie," popularized by Adolf Hitler, suggests that people can be persuaded to believe an enormous falsehood if it is presented with sufficient audacity and repeated often enough. This highlights the potential power of lies, even if they are ultimately destructive. Mark Twain famously noted that "a lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes". This emphasizes the speed and ease with which falsehoods can spread, compared to the effort often required to establish and disseminate truth. This phrase, attributed to Mark Twain as well, highlights how statistics can be manipulated to create misleading narratives. It underscores the potential for even seemingly factual information to be used to deceive. Jung’s work strongly emphasizes the importance of truth, particularly self-truth, for psychological well-being and individuation. He believed that facing one's shadow and confronting one's inner truths, even if difficult, is crucial for personal growth and wholeness. Lying, especially to oneself, can hinder this process and lead to psychological stagnation.

Chapter 16

  • “the shock of this knowledge was but the affirmation of some older shock which had been forgotten”: Freud’s “The Uncanny” (1919) describes the uncanny as something long familiar and forgotten that returns as strange.

Chapter 18

  • “such a man as is hidden in the woman”: Jung named the woman within the man the anima, and the man within the woman the animus.

Chapter 22

  • “My mother saw everything but mistook everything she saw for something else”: What Vera describes resembles visual agnosia, a term Freud coined in On Aphasia (1891).

Chapter 37

  • “How should she know when she had crossed the invisible line of demarcation”: Descartes’ dream argument: He used the experience of dreaming to question the certainty of our perceptions and beliefs. He argued that if we cannot definitively distinguish between waking and dreaming, then our sensory experiences, which are the foundation of our knowledge, might be illusions. There is philosophical skepticism because the possibility of dreams may be genuine or a fabrication. It leads one to question the validity of knowledge of the external world. Freud believed dreams are a symbolic representation of unconscious thoughts and desires. Jung expanded on Freud’s ideas that dreams can also reveal universal, archetypal patterns in the human psyche. Some theories suggest dreams are a natural byproduct of the brain’s activity during sleep, possibly involving memory consolidation, emotional processing, or the clearing out of mental clutter. Zhuangzi asked the same question when he woke from dreaming he was a butterfly; see the Chapter 8 resources.
  • “How should death be different from life, my mother asked”: Life as a state of experience and potential: Socrates thought death might be a dreamless sleep or passage to another realm where one can converse with the dead. Existentialism believes death is an inevitable aspect of human existence and that it can lead to a heightened sense of self-awareness and responsibility. Epicureanism argues death cannot harm a person, as it’s either not yet experienced (while alive) or not experienced at all (once dead). Death is defined as the loss of the capacity to engage in vital activities and the cessation of consciousness. Wittgenstein wrote that death is not an event in life, for we do not live to experience it (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 6.4311). Schopenhauer believed that understanding death as the ultimate end of life can provide a perspective on the meaning of life itself. Freud thought the life instinct (Eros) and the death instinct (Thanatos) are fundamental forces in human behavior.

Chapter 41

  • Freud distinguished mourning, which ends, from melancholia, which clings to the lost: “In mourning it is the world which has become poor and empty; in melancholia it is the ego itself” (Sigmund Freud, “Mourning and Melancholia,” 1917, Standard Edition 14, trans. James Strachey, 1957, 246).

Chapter 42

  • “in many hysterical and nervous persons”: Since ancient Greece, hysteria was an umbrella term for numerous symptoms that reinforced harmful stereotypes about women, sex, and gender. Often it was used to pathologize everything men found unmanageable in women. See the hysteria entry in the Chapter 2 resources. Freud and Breuer published Studies on Hysteria in 1895, and the diagnosis was dropped from the American Psychiatric Association’s manual (DSM-III) in 1980.

Chapter 43

  • “pawn figures moving not only from dream to dream of the dreamer but from dreamer to dreamer”: Carl Jung believed that dreams reveal more than they conceal: dreams are “a part of nature, which harbors no intention to deceive, but expresses something as best it can” (C. G. Jung, Memories, Dreams, Reflections, 1962). They are a natural expression of the imagination and speak in the most straightforward language the mind has: mythic narratives. The parts of a person’s mythic life keep a similar structure across the whole lifespan. His collective unconscious is “identical in all men and thus constitutes a common psychic substrate of a suprapersonal nature which is present in every one of us” (C. G. Jung, The Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious, Collected Works 9, part 1, trans. R. F. C. Hull, 1959). It refers to the psychological constants shared by all societies, such as rites of passage into womanhood, or the growing fascination with death after middle age. Mr. Spitzer’s sense that the same figures pass from one dreamer to another is close to Jung’s collective unconscious.

Chapter 51

  • “Seldom did he meet with anyone who did not suffer from some form of complex illusion beyond necessity”: Most people Mr. Spitzer meets suffer “some form of complex illusion beyond necessity”: the old woman who believes she is a bird cage, the piano-tuner declaring foreheads “hollow.” Blindness and deafness become metaphors for the limits of perception: the blind portrait painter, the blind war veteran in the galleries of Europe, the deaf music critics who hear every error without hearing a note, judgment resting on something other than the senses. “One great dream informing all dreamers and all dreams” recalls a collective unconscious or universal mind, or Plato’s Form of the Good, the source all strive toward behind the shadows of sense. Happiness is fleeting as a snowflake; “three minutes of happiness seemed perhaps all there might be,” and “the greatest happiness might come through the sorrow of waiting, of postponement.” The passage holds the absurdity of existence and, through Mr. Spitzer’s work for the dead, the responsibility of making sense of their lives.
  • “He feared the naked valet who had clothed him”: The “naked valet” and the “mad couturier” who clothes him “with the colors of a dream” are outside forces shaping the perception of self and world, as in Plato’s cave, and Thomas Carlyle’s philosophy of clothes in Sartor Resartus (1833-1834) makes the body and the world garments of the spirit. “For the dream of life, even like that of death, must ever contain within it an element of the unrealized, the unrealizable—else all would be complete”: imperfection and the unattainable are part of existence, as existentialist thought holds. Mr. Spitzer fears eviction from the womb, the “citadel” where he heard “the beating of another heart above his heart,” and birth into a world where he will miss the smell of the rose, and the mother who is “a bearded man armored” unsettles fixed ideas of gender. The old jockey who dies of shock when his dream proves real shows the power of the unconscious, as in Freud. “We lived by an imperfect concatenation” echoes the Buddhist teaching of impermanence and the illusory self.

Chapter 62

  • “even as the manifest dream concealed that hidden dream”: Freud distinguished the manifest content of a dream, what the dreamer remembers, from its latent content, the hidden wish it disguises (The Interpretation of Dreams, 1899).

Chapter 76

  • “there were some little boys who were murderers, too”: The belief that “some little boys who were murderers, too, and killed their mothers, but it was only because their mothers had already killed them, in quick ways and slow ways” suggests a psychological interpretation of violence as a symptom or consequence of earlier trauma, specifically maternal harm or neglect. This resonates with psychoanalytic and developmental psychology concepts about how early childhood experiences, especially those involving caregivers, profoundly shape emotional regulation, attachment, and later behavior. Children who experience harm, whether physical, emotional, or symbolic (such as neglect or abandonment), may internalize and later reenact these patterns, sometimes violently. The phrase “mothers had already killed them, in quick ways and slow ways” can be interpreted both literally and metaphorically. Psychologically, “killing” here may represent not only physical harm but also emotional or psychological damage such as: rejection, neglect, or emotional unavailability. This “kills” parts of the child’s spirit, identity, or sense of safety. This damage can manifest later in destructive behaviors, including violence towards others, even those closest to the child. The passage underscores the difficulty in attributing simple blame in situations of cruelty and violence. It suggests a cycle where victims may become perpetrators, and cruelty can be both cause and effect. This aligns with psychological understandings of the “cycle of abuse,” where patterns of trauma perpetuate across generations or within family dynamics, making it challenging to identify clear origins or solutions. The sentence carries an existential weight, reflecting on the ambiguity and complexity of human suffering. It challenges the reader to see cruelty not as a straightforward moral failing but as part of a tangled web of pain and reaction. Psychologically, this can be related to the concept of moral injury or the struggle to reconcile acts of harm within relationships that are also sources of love and care.

Chapter 80

  • “pregnant only with the yeast of her own dreams”: There are two famous pseudocyesis cases (phantom pregnancies): Mary Tudor, Queen of England, experienced a well-documented false pregnancy, where she showed physical symptoms, and her doctors and court prepared for a birth, even drafting announcement letters with blanks for the date and sex. Anna O, the patient of Freud’s colleague Josef Breuer, experienced a false pregnancy where she believed she was in labor with her therapist’s child. Anna O was Bertha Pappenheim, who went on to found the League of Jewish Women (1904) and fought the trafficking of women.

Chapter 81

  • “He whispered into her ear that there would be a great war”: Everything would be poisoned and disappear forever. This may refer to the proliferation of nuclear weapons during the Cold War. The Cold War saw a rapid nuclear arms race that saw the U.S. and Soviet Union build massive arsenals, which fueled the proliferation of nuclear weapons to other nations like the UK, France, and China. This escalation was driven by mutual suspicion and doctrines like Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD), but was tempered by arms control efforts such as the Partial Test Ban Treaty and the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). The period is also marked by dangerous standoffs, such as the Cuban Missile Crisis, which underscored the need to prevent nuclear conflict. Little Boy was the codename for the type of atomic bomb dropped on the Japanese city of Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 during World War II. It was the first nuclear weapon used in warfare. Carl Jung had visions and dreams about carnage and thought he was going insane. From his journals it is considered a premonition of World War I.

It means that the net of divine grace or judgment is extensive and all-encompassing, offering no easy escape from one’s spiritual destiny. It underscores themes of universality, inevitability, and the encompassing nature of divine authority in the novel.
  • In Indian philosophy, Maya, literally “illusion” or “magic,” has many meanings; in later Vedic texts it connotes a “magic show, an illusion where things appear to be present but are not what they seem.” (Wikipedia)

  • “this life which was no life but a temporary incarnation, a mistaken embodiment”: Both Hinduism and Buddhism believe in reincarnation, the cycle of rebirth, but their understanding of it differs. Hinduism sees a soul (atman) that is reborn into various forms, while Buddhism views rebirth as a continuation of consciousness, not a soul, and focuses on Nirvana as a path to end suffering, not a destination for the soul. In Hinduism, liberation comes with realizing that “the eternal core of the individual (atman) and the Absolute reality (brahman) are one”; Buddhism teaches anatman, “non-self,” in which karma, not a soul, carries over into a new life (Encyclopaedia Britannica, “Reincarnation”).

Chapter 26

  • “the reincarnation of Cleopatra”: Cleopatra VII (69-30 BC), the last ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt and Mark Antony’s lover. Belief in reincarnation runs through Hinduism, and through Theosophy, founded in New York in 1875.

Chapter 29

  • “between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow”: In philosophy, happiness and sorrow are intertwined, with sorrow often seen as a necessary component for experiencing the depth of joy and vice versa rather than as simple opposites. It can be viewed in a number of ways: a dialectical relationship (yin and yang-complementary forces where one cannot exist without the other); the contrast highlights the value of positive experiences; a catalyst for growth, introspection, and a deeper understanding of life’s complexities. Philosophical perspectives are found in Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Stoicism, Utilitarianism, Hedonism, Life Satisfaction Theory. Plato and Aristotle’s eudaimonia where flourishing and well-being are achieved by living a virtuous life, not simply experiencing happiness. Nirvana is a state of liberation from suffering and the cycle of rebirth. Equanimity is the ability to remain calm and balanced in the face of both pleasure and pain. Mr. Spitzer finds it as hard to tell butterfly from moth as “to distinguish between brother and brother or between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow,” for “Seldom did happiness and sorrow occur in pure and disrelated states.”
  • “the Happy Isles, the Fortunate Isles, the Isles of the Blessed”: The list runs from the Happy Isles to Aldebaran, Venus, the Garden of the Hesperides, the third and seventh heavens, Valhalla, Nirvana, and the happy hunting grounds, and ends: “God was not God in Himself, Mr. Spitzer believed, but in these pitiful images of God.”

Chapter 37

  • “trees of enormous crystal growing with their roots in the clouded sky”: The Bhagavad Gita (15.1) speaks of an eternal fig tree, the ashvattha, with its roots above and its branches below.

Chapter 38

  • “seven deathless eternities”: “Seven deathless eternities” may recall Dante’s Divine Comedy, where the seven terraces of Purgatory purge the seven deadly sins. Seven heavens are found in Judaism and Islam, and Hindu cosmology has seven upper worlds, the lokas. The seven virtues join the four cardinal virtues of Greek philosophy to the three theological virtues of Paul (1 Corinthians 13:13).

Chapter 39

  • “And was not God dreaming, too”: In Hindu myth Vishnu sleeps on the serpent Shesha upon the cosmic ocean, and the world is said to be his dream.

Chapter 40

  • “which was Sanskrit from a holy text printed on a snowflake”: Sanskrit is a classical language of South Asia. It is the sacred language of the Vedas.

Chapter 41

  • “were there not many roads to the crown of her head”: Catherine asks “...were there not many roads to the crown of her head?” This seems to mimic a saying often called a Hindu proverb: there are many paths up the mountain, all leading to the same place. While the exact phrasing is a modern paraphrase, the underlying concept is deeply rooted in traditional Hindu texts and philosophy. A classic parallel is found in the Siva Mahimnah Stotra (verse 7): “As the different streams having their sources in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so, O Lord, the different paths which men take through different tendencies, various though they appear, crooked or straight, all lead to Thee” (as quoted by Swami Vivekananda, address at the World’s Parliament of Religions, Chicago, September 11, 1893). Ramakrishna said, “As many faiths, so many paths” (The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna, trans. Swami Nikhilananda, 1942).
  • “She was swifter than her own mind”: “That One, though motionless, is swifter than the mind. The senses can never overtake It, for It ever goes before.” “It moves and It moves not. She was within, yet she was outside.”

In Hindu tradition the god Shiva has a third eye in the center of his forehead, and when it opens it destroys. In one story Shiva burns Kama, the god of love, to ash with it. The forehead point is also the ajna chakra, the seat of inner sight, which the bindi marks. The question ties her lost love to both vision and destruction.
  • “great dancer in the infinite”: Shiva as Nataraja, Lord of the Dance, dances the universe through creation and destruction within a ring of fire (Ananda K. Coomaraswamy, “The Dance of Shiva,” 1918). See the third eye entry below.

  • “The deepest sleep is dreamless.”: Socrates says that if death is a dreamless sleep, “to die is gain; for eternity is then only a single night” (Plato, Apology 40d-e, trans. Benjamin Jowett, 1871). The Mandukya Upanishad names deep sleep, where the sleeper desires nothing and dreams no dream, as the third state of the self.

Chapter 48

  • “had gone through the door of the sun”: In the Upanishads the wise “depart free from passion through the sun to where that immortal Person dwells whose nature is imperishable” (Mundaka Upanishad 1.2.11, trans. F. Max Müller, 1884). The Sanskrit is sūrya-dvāreṇa, “by the door of the sun.” Those who return to rebirth go by the path of the moon (Chandogya Upanishad 5.10). Peron goes by the sun, Mr. Spitzer by the moon.

  • “Should not the slayer be the slain?”: “If the red slayer think he slays, / Or if the slain think he is slain, / They know not well the subtle ways / I keep, and pass, and turn again” (Ralph Waldo Emerson, “Brahma,” 1857), after the Bhagavad Gita 2.19.

Chapter 50

  • “the door of truth which was covered with a golden disc”: “The door of the True is covered with a golden disk. Open that, O Pûshan, that we may see the nature of the True” (Isa Upanishad 15, trans. F. Max Müller, 1879).

  • “he would remove every stone from a road for fear the next wayfarer might be hurt”: Ganesha is the most popular and well known Hindu deity who is the Remover of Obstacles. There are many quotes from Moliere to Zen sayings that remind people that overcoming obstacles is part of life.
  • “his circular eye which seemed to turn in his forehead”: The third-eye is a mystical and esoteric concept of a speculative invisible eye in the middle of the forehead which has perception beyond ordinary sight. In Hindu tradition it is the ajna chakra between the brows, and the third eye of Shiva burns with the fire of destruction.
  • “some old, dreaming tortoise with the stars upon his back”: In Hindu myth Vishnu as the tortoise Kurma bears the world on his back, and for the Lenape and other peoples North America is Turtle Island, the earth on a great turtle’s back.

Chapter 52

  • “the tree rooted in clouds with its branches growing downward”: The Bhagavad Gita (15.1) and the Katha Upanishad (6.1) describe the eternal ashvattha, the sacred fig, with its roots above and its branches below.

  • “What of her crown of patience?”: In Stoicism, patience is a key virtue for achieving inner tranquility and living a good life; Epictetus summed up his teaching as “bear and forbear” (Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights 17.19). In Hindu thought, patience is viewed as the capacity to wait, endure opposites, and act calmly without anxiety, anger, or resentment; in the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna to endure heat and cold, pleasure and pain, which come and go (2:14). “Patience is bitter, but its fruit is sweet,” often credited to Aristotle, comes from Rousseau’s Julie, or the New Heloise (1761), Part 1, Letter 46. Miss MacIntosh’s patience is active endurance, practical and unsentimental, daily perseverance in place of dreams and self-pity.
  • Religious food restrictions, seen across Judaism (Kashrut), Islam (Halal/Haram), Hinduism (no beef), Jainism (strict vegetarianism, no roots), and early Christianity (abstain from idol-sacrificed food, blood), have ancient roots, often linked to divine command, health/sanitation (pork, blood), ecological reasons, or cultural identity, evolving over time from specific scriptural interpretations (like Jesus declaring all foods clean) to broader ethical principles like non-violence, shaping practices from what to eat to how it’s prepared. Religions emphasizing vegetarianism include Jainism (which mandates it for non-violence), Buddhism and Hinduism (strong traditions rooted in Ahimsa or non-violence), and certain Christian denominations like the Seventh-day Adventists, alongside practices in Sikhism, some Jewish traditions, and Eastern Orthodox Christianity during fasts. The core principles often involve compassion for animals, spiritual purity, and minimal harm (Ahimsa). Vegetarians, and vegans especially, must find other sources for nutrients most plentiful in animal foods, such as vitamin B12, iron, zinc, and omega-3 fats. Some anthropologists hold that eating meat, and later cooking, fueled the growth of the human brain (Richard Wrangham, Catching Fire: How Cooking Made Us Human, 2009). It can be viewed in a number of ways: a dialectical relationship (yin and yang-complementary forces where one cannot exist without the other); the contrast highlights the value of positive experiences; a catalyst for growth, introspection, and a deeper understanding of life’s complexities. Philosophical perspectives are found in Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Stoicism, Utilitarianism, Hedonism, Life Satisfaction Theory. Plato and Aristotle’s eudaimonia where flourishing and well-being are achieved by living a virtuous life, not simply experiencing happiness. Nirvana is a state of liberation from suffering and the cycle of rebirth. Equanimity is the ability to remain calm and balanced in the face of both pleasure and pain. Mr. Spitzer finds it as hard to tell butterfly from moth as “to distinguish between brother and brother or between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow,” for “Seldom did happiness and sorrow occur in pure and disrelated states.”

There may be some kind of continuation after death but it is not a separate, conscious existence. Non-personal immortality is where philosophers and thinkers believe there may be a collective consciousness with or without an individual component.
