The core principles often involve compassion for animals, spiritual purity, and minimal harm (Ahimsa). Vegetarians, and vegans especially, must find other sources for nutrients most plentiful in animal foods, such as vitamin B12, iron, zinc, and omega-3 fats. Chapter 6

  • “You are you, and she is she. I am I, or am I?”: In metaphysics the philosophy of identity is the relation each thing bears only to itself. The notion of identity gives rise to many philosophical problems, including the identity of indiscernibles (if x and y share all their properties, are they one and the same thing?), and questions about change and personal identity over time (what has to be the case for a person x at one time and a person y at a later time to be one and the same person?). The philosophical concept concerns a relation, specifically, a relation that x and y stand in if, and only if they are one and the same thing, or identical to each other (i.e. if, and only if x = y). The law of identity originates from classical antiquity. The modern formulation of identity is that of Gottfried Leibniz, who held that x is the same as y if and only if every predicate true of x is true of y as well. (Wikipedia) Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote (Tractatus 5.5301): “That identity is not a relation between objects is obvious.” At 5.5303 he elaborates: “Roughly speaking: to say of two things that they are identical is nonsense, and to say of one thing that it is identical with itself is to say nothing.”

Chapter 18

  • Ludwig Wittgenstein wrote in a diary entry of the early 1930s: “We are asleep. Our life is like a dream. But in our better hours we wake up just enough to realize that we are dreaming.”

Chapter 37

  • “How should death be different from life, my mother asked”: Life as a state of experience and potential: Socrates thought death might be a dreamless sleep or passage to another realm where one can converse with the dead. Existentialism believes death is an inevitable aspect of human existence and that it can lead to a heightened sense of self-awareness and responsibility. Epicureanism argues death cannot harm a person, as it’s either not yet experienced (while alive) or not experienced at all (once dead). Death is defined as the loss of the capacity to engage in vital activities and the cessation of consciousness. Wittgenstein wrote that death is not an event in life, for we do not live to experience it (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 6.4311). Schopenhauer believed that understanding death as the ultimate end of life can provide a perspective on the meaning of life itself. Freud thought the life instinct (Eros) and the death instinct (Thanatos) are fundamental forces in human behavior.

Chapter 39

  • “She saw an idiot who had become a great philosopher”: Wittgenstein, despite his genius, was known for his unconventional behavior and challenging personality. He even questioned his own sanity, asking Bertrand Russell if he was an idiot. Russell asked him to write something over the vacation, and after reading it told him not to become an aeronaut (Bertrand Russell, “Ludwig Wittgenstein,” in Portraits from Memory and Other Essays, Simon and Schuster, 1956). His profound insights into philosophy, language, and logic led to his recognition as a major philosopher. The idea of a philosopher becoming an “idiot” is a common trope often referencing Diogenes of Sinope. Arthur Schopenhauer was also considered eccentric.

Chapter 47

  • “music of things unutterable”: Another of philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein’s contributions was silence: “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent” (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 7, trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922). Language has logical limits, and of things beyond them, such as metaphysical or ethical truths, one should be silent. Silence for him was a space for potential meaning and understanding, a recognition of the limits of language, and a way of acknowledging what lies beyond the grasp of words. Mr. Spitzer’s “music of things unutterable” echoes Wittgenstein.

Chapter 48

  • “Man could not see his own end, for he passed beyond his end”: No one can witness his own death, because by the time death comes the self has already passed beyond it. Epicurus: “when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not” (Letter to Menoeceus, in Diogenes Laertius 10.125, trans. R. D. Hicks, 1925). Wittgenstein: “Death is not an event of life. Death is not lived through” (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 6.4311, trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922).

Chapter 58

  • “he had always been so remarkably careful in making lists”: Mr. Spitzer’s meticulous accounting and listing is directly tied to his struggle with his identity, particularly his relationship with his deceased brother. He seeks a perfect balance, a mirrored reflection where everything in his life corresponds to his brother’s, suggesting a desire to understand himself through this dualistic lens. The fear of “no differing counterpart” speaks to the existential anxiety of lacking a defined self, relying on another for definition. This resonates with philosophical concepts of identity formation, the “self” versus the “other,” and the influence of external relationships on self-perception. Thinkers like Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir explored similar themes in existentialism. Spitzer’s obsessive listing and indexing of even the most mundane objects (pearl buttons, rusted nail heads, etc.) reflects a deep-seated need to impose order on a chaotic world. He’s trying to find patterns, connections, and a “common denominator” to make sense of existence. This aligns with the philosophical pursuit of metaphysics: trying to understand the fundamental nature of reality. The futility of Spitzer’s efforts mirrors the inherent difficulties in finding absolute order or meaning in a world often perceived as absurd or chaotic (a key theme in existentialism and absurdism). The questions about the sail (“Was the sail unwinding the same as the winding sail?”) touch on the philosophical problem of identity over time. Does something remain the same if its state changes? This is further complicated by the cyclical nature of the tides and the wagon wheels, implying a sense of eternal return or repetition. This connects to Heraclitus’s famous saying, often given as “No man ever steps in the same river twice” (Plato’s version is “you could not step twice into the same river,” Cratylus 402a), emphasizing the constant flux and change in the universe. The paragraph also hints at Nietzsche’s concept of eternal recurrence. Spitzer’s attempts to capture reality through lists and measurements are ultimately limited. His fear that “all the weight, as he had often complained, was on this weightless star” alludes to the disparity between the tangible and intangible, the concrete and abstract. He can list the physical properties of objects, but he cannot capture their essence or meaning. This is related to epistemology, the study of knowledge and its limitations. The paragraph suggests the impossibility of fully knowing or representing reality, as there will always be something missing or lost in translation. The description of Spitzer’s actions creating “division as in division there was creation,” suggests that in every act of creation, there is also an act of destruction. This mirrors the belief that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. This is connected to the concept of the “Tao” which states that everything is composed of two opposites, and that without the other, it cannot exist.

It’s not inherently determined by biology, but rather shaped by cultural norms, societal expectations, and historical contexts. This means gender is not fixed and can vary across cultures and time. In short, it is not a biological reality: it is socially created, varies across cultures, is dynamic and fluid, and is distinct from biological sex. Chapter 14

  • “the music of the spheres, the silent music”: Boethius was a Roman senator, consul, magister officiorum, polymath, historian, and philosopher of the Early Middle Ages. He sought to reconcile the teachings of Plato and Aristotle with Christian theology. He broke logic into three parts: that which defines, that which divides, and that which deduces. There are three types of arguments: those of necessity, of ready believability, and sophistry. In De Musica there are three classifications: Musica mundana, Musica humana, Musica instrumentalis. In Dante’s Divine Comedy, the spirit of Boethius is pointed out by Saint Thomas Aquinas and is mentioned further in the poem. In his book De Institutione Musica (Fundamentals of Music) his drawings appear striking and may be an inspiration for the organization of Young’s novel. Musica universalis or music of the spheres or harmony of the spheres is a Greek philosophical concept founded by Pythagoras. This metaphysical principle stated that mathematical relationships could produce ‘tones’ of energy that could produce, among other things, sounds. Pythagoras proposed that the celestial bodies all have their own unique hum based on their orbital revolution. This idea influenced many scholars until the end of the Renaissance. Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer from the 1600s wrote extensively on the subject. (Wikipedia) Later astronomy set it aside. Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy in prison awaiting execution, with its Wheel of Fortune.
  • “her peacocks”: Aristotle referred to the peacock’s vain reputation. The Roman poet Ennius, following the Pythagorean teaching of rebirth, dreamed that Homer’s soul had passed into a peacock and then into himself.

Chapter 15

  • “one swallow does not make a summer”: Aristotle uses the saying in the Nicomachean Ethics (1.7) to discuss happiness and eudaimonia (living well or flourishing). He argues that a brief period of happiness or a single good deed doesn’t make a person truly happy or blessed. Happiness, for Aristotle, is a state of being that develops over a lifetime through virtuous activity.

Chapter 21

  • “evil has many forms, and the good has only one”: Aristotle writes that “it is possible to fail in many ways… while to succeed is possible only in one way,” and quotes the line “men are good in but one way, but bad in many” (Nicomachean Ethics 2.6).

Chapter 23

  • “What was so rare a thing as common sense”: Thomas Paine’s polemical pamphlet Common Sense (1776) has been described as the most influential political pamphlet of the 18th century, affecting both the American and French revolutions. Today, the concept of common sense, and how it should best be used, remains linked to many of the most perennial topics in epistemology and ethics, with special focus often directed at the philosophy of the modern social sciences. (Wikipedia)
  • “the middle brow, the middle way”: “Middlebrow” was new in Young’s day. Russell Lynes’s “Highbrow, Lowbrow, Middlebrow” ran in Harper’s in 1949. The middle way is Aristotle’s mean, virtue as the middle between two extremes (Nicomachean Ethics 2.6).

Chapter 29

  • “between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow”: In philosophy, happiness and sorrow are intertwined, with sorrow often seen as a necessary component for experiencing the depth of joy and vice versa rather than as simple opposites. It can be viewed in a number of ways: a dialectical relationship (yin and yang-complementary forces where one cannot exist without the other); the contrast highlights the value of positive experiences; a catalyst for growth, introspection, and a deeper understanding of life’s complexities. Philosophical perspectives are found in Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Stoicism, Utilitarianism, Hedonism, Life Satisfaction Theory. Plato and Aristotle’s eudaimonia where flourishing and well-being are achieved by living a virtuous life, not simply experiencing happiness. Nirvana is a state of liberation from suffering and the cycle of rebirth. Equanimity is the ability to remain calm and balanced in the face of both pleasure and pain. Mr. Spitzer finds it as hard to tell butterfly from moth as “to distinguish between brother and brother or between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow,” for “Seldom did happiness and sorrow occur in pure and disrelated states.”
  • “the bipart soul”: Aristotle’s bipartite psychology divides the soul into two main parts: the rational soul and the non-rational soul. The rational soul is responsible for reason, intellect, and higher thinking, while the non-rational soul encompasses emotions, appetites, and bodily functions. Aristotle further subdivided the rational soul into two parts: the calculating and the scientific. He also divided the non-rational soul into vegetative and appetitive (Nicomachean Ethics 1.13, 6.1). Young sets it beside Mr. Spitzer’s divided self.

Chapter 37

  • “or there should be these reversals”: Aristotle names reversal (peripeteia) and recognition as the turning points of tragedy (Poetics 11). Baudrillard’s Principle of Reversal examines how oppositions and differences can be overturned, leading to new forms of understanding and meaning (Jean Baudrillard, Symbolic Exchange and Death, 1976). Vera’s “his night was his day” passage is in Chapter 61.
  • “this mistaken earth which was perhaps its counter-earth”: The Pythagorean Philolaus set a counter-earth, the Antichthon, beyond the Earth, always hidden from it, to bring the heavenly bodies to ten (Aristotle, On the Heavens 2.13).
  • “as man became woman with her heaving breasts”: Gender as a social construct refers to the socially created roles, behaviors, expressions, and identities associated with being a woman, man, boy, or girl. It’s not inherently determined by biology, but rather shaped by cultural norms, societal expectations, and historical contexts. This means gender is not fixed and can vary across cultures and time. In short, it is not a biological reality: it is socially created, varies across cultures, is dynamic and fluid, and is distinct from biological sex. Philosophical thought on gender goes back to ancient Greece, where Pythagoras’s table of opposites set male against female (Aristotle, Metaphysics 1.5) and Plato argued that women could be guardians (Republic 5). Later came John Locke, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Judith Sargent Murray (“On the Equality of the Sexes,” 1790), and Mary Wollstonecraft (A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792). The chapter and novel present gender as a fluid and changeable construct rather than a rigid, innate fact, using metaphorical and dreamlike language to question fixed dichotomies between male and female, self and other, life and death.

Chapter 38

  • “the beautiful music of the spheres”: Musica Universalis (music of the spheres) concept incorporates the metaphysical principle that mathematical relationships express qualities or “tones” of energy that manifests in numbers, visual angles, shapes and sounds which are all connected within a pattern of proportion. This has been explored by Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle (he rejected the idea), Boethius developed three categories of music (musica mundana, musica humana, and musica quae in quibusdam constituta est instrumentis), Kepler expounded the idea in Harmonices Mundi (1619). Boethius’s writings were later illustrated, and Young may have taken inspiration from these illustrations for the novel.
  • “Life contained death as a cloud contained a passing star”: Zeno’s paradoxes: the finite can contain the infinite. Aristotle reports Zeno’s argument “that that which is in locomotion must arrive at the half-way stage before it arrives at the goal” (Aristotle, Physics 6.9, trans. R. P. Hardie and R. K. Gaye, 1930).

Chapter 40

  • “who should know when the dream ended”: In philosophy there is the question of dreams by Zhuangzi, Plato, and Aristotle. Descartes asked how he could know that he was not now dreaming (Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation 1, 1641), which seems to be the same question Catherine is preoccupied with. Descartes’ answer was that we cannot trust our senses in waking life without invoking a benevolent God who would not deceive us. Catherine takes this one step further at the end of Chapter 39 and asks, “What if God is dreaming?” In psychology the question “Is Life a Dream?” is answered with the coherence of the waking world does give evidence that it is not just a figment of our imagination. However, the objects that we perceive as permanent are in reality through the science of quantum physics mostly made up of empty space. In a sense people do live in a dream world that is created by the mind. When people are awake, their minds conform their dreaming to a reliable set of patterns, which they assume to be determined by a reality that exists independently of their experience of it, though they have no way of knowing that reality except through the complex ways in which it affects their dream. There is also reality that is experienced and affected by psychedelic drugs and other altered states of consciousness (Sharon Hewitt Rawlette, “Is Life a Dream?,” Psychology Today, July 31, 2019).
  • “a golden mean between extremes”: Aristotle placed virtue at the mean between two extremes, as courage lies between cowardice and rashness (Nicomachean Ethics 2.6).
  • “All was water”: Thales, the first Greek philosopher, held that all things are water (Aristotle, Metaphysics 1.3).

Chapter 41

  • “Aristotle had said that the ear was the doorway to the soul”: Aristotle was a Greek philosopher. The phrase “doorway to the soul” is not found in Aristotle. The nearest is his judgment that sight serves the needs of life, “but for developing intelligence, and in its indirect consequences, hearing takes the precedence,” for “rational discourse is a cause of instruction in virtue of its being audible” (Aristotle, On Sense and the Sensible 1, trans. J. I. Beare, 1908).

Chapter 42

  • “this sublunar world”: For Aristotle, all change and decay belong to the world below the moon, while the heavens above it are unchanging (On the Heavens 1).

Chapter 49

  • “one of whom no unitary statement could be made”: The problem of universals in philosophy concerns the nature and existence of universals, qualities or properties that can be shared by multiple particular things, and how they relate to particulars. In this chapter, there are multiple reflections on identity, existence, perception, and the nature of reality that offer a profound literary meditation of this “Problem.”

Chapter 51

  • Boethius (about 477-524) was a Roman senator, consul, and philosopher who sought to translate Plato and Aristotle into Latin; largely through his translations the works of Aristotle survived. His works on arithmetic, geometry, and music, with astronomy, formed the quadrivium, the core of the medieval liberal arts, in which music was the mathematical study of harmony, ratio, and proportion rather than performance. Imprisoned by Theodoric for defending a fellow consul against charges of conspiracy, he wrote On the Consolation of Philosophy, a treatise on fortune and death, before he was tortured and executed in 524. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 55

  • “the muted murmur of the paper nautilus”: The paper nautilus, or argonaut, is an octopus whose female makes a thin, paper-white shell to carry her eggs; Aristotle and Pliny believed she raised two arms as sails and sailed the sea in it.

Chapter 61

  • “hedgehogs stand with their backs always to the sea”: Mr. Spitzer thought Aristotle said that hedgehogs always stand with their backs to the sea. Aristotle: History of Animals IX says they look out of their holes in the direction of the wind.

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • Frogs in culture can symbolize fertility, harmony, and licentiousness. In Nietzsche's philosophy, the "frog perspective" or "frog's perspective" is a metaphor for a limited, narrow, and potentially biased viewpoint, often associated with a lack of depth or critical analysis. It is a perspective from below, literally, and figuratively, suggesting a limited understanding due to a fixed position in place and time.

Chapter 22

  • “Time was circled in a single week”: Nietzsche’s eternal recurrence (The Gay Science 341, 1882): “This life as you now live it and have lived it, you will have to live once more and innumerable times more.”

Chapter 25

  • “What death was this which was no death?”: The philosophy of death explores the meaning of death, our relationship to it, and the various ways it impacts human existence and understanding. It delves into questions about what happens after death, the nature of consciousness, and the ethical implications of death, including suicide. The Nature of Death: Dualism (the soul continues to exist after death, potentially in a separate realm or afterlife), Materialism (death is the permanent cessation of all bodily functions, including consciousness), Annihilationism (death is the end of all conscious experience, and nothing exists after death). Philosophical Perspectives on Death: Stoicism (death is not something to be feared, as it is a natural part of life and a release from suffering), Existentialism (thinkers like Kierkegaard and Heidegger, in Being and Time, 1927, emphasized the importance of confronting our mortality to understand our own existence and the meaning of life), Nietzsche (proposed that individuals have the freedom to define their own death, suggesting it could be a conscious choice rather than an inevitable fate: “Die at the right time,” in “On Free Death,” Thus Spoke Zarathustra, 1883). Ethical Considerations: Suicide (philosophy engages with questions about the moral permissibility of suicide, including whether it’s ever justifiable).
  • “whether he would stare at that wild, precipitous abyss which would stare at him”: Nietzsche’s quote, “If you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss gazes also into you,” is a famous aphorism warning against becoming consumed by the things you are confronting. It suggests that prolonged engagement with negativity, suffering, or challenging ideas can have a transformative effect on the person observing them, potentially altering their perspective and even their character. Mr. Spitzer, a man whose prolonged confrontation with death, identity, and existential uncertainty has led to a profound internal transformation, shows how the abyss he peers into ultimately gazes back, shaping and haunting his very being. The aphorism is from Beyond Good and Evil (1886), §146, which begins “He who fights with monsters should be careful lest he thereby become a monster.”
  • “There had been still, it seemed, a spark of life in Mr. Spitzer”: Friedrich Nietzsche proposed the “will to power” as a driving force behind human behavior, instead of the “will to live” of his predecessor Arthur Schopenhauer. Nietzsche develops it in Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883-85), “On Self-Overcoming”: “Wherever I found a living thing, there found I Will to Power” (trans. Thomas Common). Will to live: an irrational force drives humans to strive endlessly. Will to power: a dynamic force drives humans to overcome resistance and become who they truly are. Nietzsche believed that the will to power is more useful than the will to live for explaining human behavior. He used the will to power to explain both life-affirming and life-denying impulses, as well as master and slave morality. He believed that the will to power is the expression of self-realization, and that it is a condition for growth. He held that life itself is will to power, a striving that is never done. In the chapter it reflects Nietzsche’s “will to power” through its exploration of internal conflict, the striving for control amid chaos, the tension between life and death, and the dynamic, creative force underlying human existence, as embodied in Mr. Spitzer’s character and experiences.

Chapter 29

  • “as if there were a frog in his throat”: Nietzsche’s frog is a way to metaphorically understand perspective and belief. Nietzsche believed that all knowledge and values are perspectival, meaning they are shaped by our individual experiences and values. Nietzsche himself borrowed the painters’ term: values may be seen “perhaps from below, ‘frog perspectives,’ as it were” (Beyond Good and Evil, 1886, §2, trans. Helen Zimmern). This is reflected in the idea of a “frog’s perspective,” which can be understood as a belief system that is constantly changing and shifting. The term “frog’s perspective” can also be associated with the idea of narrow-mindedness or being unable to see the bigger picture. Another metaphorical expression, “swallowing the frog” can refer to confronting unpleasant realities or difficult emotions in order to grow or achieve a higher level of understanding. This aligns with Nietzsche’s emphasis on confronting difficult truths and embracing the “unpleasantness” of life. The frog can also symbolize a sense of “being in the muck,” referring to the lower aspects of oneself that need to be overcome in order to reach a higher level of awareness. Frogs appear symbolically connected to themes of life, death, transformation, and communication beyond ordinary human experience. Mr. Spitzer encounters a mute man who uses a frog as a musical instrument, training it to croak and even mimic human speech. This mute and his frog symbolize profound voicelessness and the struggle to communicate in a world that is largely silent or deaf to certain truths. The frog’s croaking becomes an emblem of fragile, ephemeral voice amid silence, reflecting the broader motifs of mortality, loss, and elusive knowledge that permeate the novel. The frog also represents vulnerability and the liminal state between life and death. Its death mourned by Mr. Spitzer as a loss greater than many others. The mute’s deep grief over the frog’s death underscores a shared human sorrow for lost expression and connection, heightening the novel’s meditation on mortality and the persistence of memory or spirit beyond physical life. The frog’s role in the novel as a creature caught between states (mute yet singing, alive yet dying). The frog’s croaking in the mute’s mouth, its death, and burial evoke themes of metamorphosis, suffering, and the fragile boundary between existence and oblivion, which are central to Nietzschean philosophy of overcoming and transformation. It relates symbolically to liminality, transformation, and the struggle for voice and meaning amid silence and death. This aligns conceptually with Nietzsche’s frog as a figure of existential change and awakening, though Young’s usage is more focused on fragility, loss, and the ineffable aspects of human experience. The frog in the novel is a potent symbol of voicelessness, transformation, and mortality, echoing themes akin to Nietzsche’s idea of the frog as an emblem of awakening and existential transition. See the “frog perspectives” of Beyond Good and Evil (1886), §2.

Chapter 36

  • “aggrandized by the pathos of distance”: Nietzsche’s phrase, the “pathos of distance,” is the feeling of rank that sets the noble apart from those below (Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, 1886, section 257).

Chapter 37

  • “Death was this dream’s immeasurable extension”: The meaning of life in relation to death: Stoicism emphasized that facing death can lead to a deeper understanding of life’s meaning and the ephemeral nature of earthly possessions. Nietzsche used the thought experiment of eternal return (recurrence) to encourage individuals to examine the meaning and value of their lives, given the possibility of living them again and again.

Chapter 40

  • “I am dead—had not old Cousin Hannah always whispered”: Nietzsche’s phrase, “God is dead” (Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science 125, 1882), refers to the demise of traditional religious belief and the moral structures built upon it. He believed this shift opened up new possibilities for humanity to create its own values and meaning. Marcus Aurelius wrote, “Consider thyself to be dead, and to have completed thy life up to the present time” (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 7.56, trans. George Long, 1862), where one focuses on present experiences and accepts the inevitability of death, rather than clinging to the past or fearing the future.

Chapter 42

  • “Should not eternal recurrence be the one law of life”: Nietzsche calls it the “moment.” There is an eternal path ahead and behind, and what one has is this moment. He wrote about it in Thus Spoke Zarathustra, in “On the Vision and the Riddle” (Part 3, 1884), and first put the thought experiment in The Gay Science 341 (1882). If one had to live this life over again for all eternity with all its ups and downs, pains and pleasures, would it be tolerable? Would one still choose life, to live? It is a thought experiment for self-reflection and a test of how life affirming a person really is. Nietzsche had the idea of “amor fati” (love of fate) (Ecce Homo, 1888). One would come to love one’s fate, the life that one has led, with a willingness to accept all of it. The Ubermensch is Nietzsche’s concept of a higher type of human or humanity that is connected to eternal recurrence. A person who is capable of loving their life, even in its entirety, is more likely to reach this state. Nietzsche also believed that eternal recurrence would force people to confront the meaninglessness of conventional morality and encourage them to create their own values. By contemplating eternal recurrence, Nietzsche hoped to spark an interest in personal values which would lead to a more authentic and fulfilling life.

Chapter 45

  • “Who is that dwarf, a turret on his head”: May refer to Nietzsche where the dwarf represents self-doubt and the limitations of conventional thought. Zarathustra’s journey involves overcoming the dwarf, symbolizing the overcoming of self-doubt and the embrace of his philosophy, including the concept of eternal recurrence. Young gives him the rose of consciousness. According to Thomas Reid sensory information, particularly in relation to movement, contributes to our subjective experience of the world. This framework suggests that consciousness might be closely tied to our ability to interact with and act upon the world. On sensation and perception, Thomas Reid saw sensation as a primitive feeling or awareness, while perception was the process of interpreting these feelings and associating them with external objects. The ability to distinguish between sensation and perception is linked to consciousness (Thomas Reid, Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man, 1785). The turret is typically a small tower, often ornamental, that juts out from a building. It is typically found on castles, large houses, etc.

Chapter 52

  • “pivoted on nothingness like the dancer over the abyss”: Zarathustra tells the crowd, “Man is a rope stretched between the animal and the Superman—a rope over an abyss,” and a tightrope walker falls to his death before them (Friedrich Nietzsche, Thus Spake Zarathustra, Prologue 4, trans. Thomas Common, 1909).
  • “he had always been so remarkably careful in making lists”: Mr. Spitzer’s meticulous accounting and listing is directly tied to his struggle with his identity, particularly his relationship with his deceased brother. He seeks a perfect balance, a mirrored reflection where everything in his life corresponds to his brother’s, suggesting a desire to understand himself through this dualistic lens. The fear of “no differing counterpart” speaks to the existential anxiety of lacking a defined self, relying on another for definition. This resonates with philosophical concepts of identity formation, the “self” versus the “other,” and the influence of external relationships on self-perception. Thinkers like Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir explored similar themes in existentialism. Spitzer’s obsessive listing and indexing of even the most mundane objects (pearl buttons, rusted nail heads, etc.) reflects a deep-seated need to impose order on a chaotic world. He’s trying to find patterns, connections, and a “common denominator” to make sense of existence. This aligns with the philosophical pursuit of metaphysics: trying to understand the fundamental nature of reality. The futility of Spitzer’s efforts mirrors the inherent difficulties in finding absolute order or meaning in a world often perceived as absurd or chaotic (a key theme in existentialism and absurdism). The questions about the sail (“Was the sail unwinding the same as the winding sail?”) touch on the philosophical problem of identity over time. Does something remain the same if its state changes? This is further complicated by the cyclical nature of the tides and the wagon wheels, implying a sense of eternal return or repetition. This connects to Heraclitus’s famous saying, often given as “No man ever steps in the same river twice” (Plato’s version is “you could not step twice into the same river,” Cratylus 402a), emphasizing the constant flux and change in the universe. The paragraph also hints at Nietzsche’s concept of eternal recurrence. Spitzer’s attempts to capture reality through lists and measurements are ultimately limited. His fear that “all the weight, as he had often complained, was on this weightless star” alludes to the disparity between the tangible and intangible, the concrete and abstract. He can list the physical properties of objects, but he cannot capture their essence or meaning. This is related to epistemology, the study of knowledge and its limitations. The paragraph suggests the impossibility of fully knowing or representing reality, as there will always be something missing or lost in translation. The description of Spitzer’s actions creating “division as in division there was creation,” suggests that in every act of creation, there is also an act of destruction. This mirrors the belief that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. This is connected to the concept of the “Tao” which states that everything is composed of two opposites, and that without the other, it cannot exist.

Chapter 62

  • “anything which was worth happening at all was worth happening twice”: Compare Nietzsche’s eternal recurrence, the thought that this very life must be lived again innumerable times (The Gay Science, 341, 1882).

Definition from research

Chapter 1

  • Phenomenology is a philosophical study and movement largely associated with the early 20th century that seeks to objectively investigate the nature of subjective, conscious experience. It attempts to describe the universal features of consciousness while avoiding assumptions about the external world, aiming to describe phenomena as they appear to the subject, and to explore the meaning and significance of the lived experiences. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 7

  • “Am I seeing with my eyes?”: This reflects the phenomenological tradition of bodily awareness. Moses’s questions are phenomenology’s: what the senses and the body give to consciousness. Vera asked the same in Chapter 1, when the world seemed “the conspiracy of memories and dreams floating without purpose” and “The individual is the one illusion.”

Chapter 14

  • “There should be the same divisions and multiplications”: Multiplicity is a philosophical concept developed by Edmund Husserl and Henri Bergson from Riemann’s description of the mathematical concept. Bergson distinguished two kinds: a countable multiplicity of distinct parts, and a qualitative one whose parts interpenetrate. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 36

  • “heard the musician only when the music had ceased”: Edmund Husserl took a melody as his example of time-consciousness: each note, as it passes, is held in “retention” while the next sounds, so that a melody is never heard all at once (Edmund Husserl, The Phenomenology of Internal Time-Consciousness, 1928).

Chapter 36 · Time and Perception

  • Time is experienced non-linearly; sounds arrive late, events are recalled out of sequence.
  • The narrative reflects a consciousness that is “always in danger” of missing or misinterpreting life’s moments.
  • This theme underscores the instability of human experience and the elusive nature of reality.
  • “Each sound reached his dead ear always a minute late.” “His eyes were separated from his ears.”

Chapter 68

  • “there was only one definition of reality, that it was real”: The line emphasizes a tautological but deeply existential assertion: reality is defined by its own existence as experienced or known, regardless of its form. “even the unreal things were real,” points to an inclusive, perhaps subjective or phenomenological, understanding of reality where things dismissed or marginalized by society (ignored, rejected, unloved) are nonetheless part of the fabric of reality. This echoes themes of illusion versus reality, and the permeability between them, which run throughout the novel. Philosophically, this passage represents a theme often associated with existentialism and phenomenology: that reality is defined by experience and perception rather than by fixed, external definitions. It also touches on the fluidity of reality, blurring lines between dream and waking life, appearance and essence, presence and absence. The passage conveys that reality is not limited to the tangible or socially accepted but includes dreams, illusions, forgotten or rejected beings, and all forms of existence or perception. It challenges rigid dichotomies and invites a broader, more inclusive understanding of what is real.

Definition from research

Chapter 1

  • Hegel described his philosophical system as “a circle of circles.” Young described the novel the same way in the Friedman and Fuchs interview: “I always thought of Miss MacIntosh as the center of the wheel, the hub, then the spokes as the subsidiary, secondary characters, and the wheel as endlessly expanding like a universe.” Here Vera calls Miss MacIntosh “the central heart, the heart of all hearts.”

Chapter 8

  • “a realm of visionary hypothesis or uncertain speculation”: Representationalism, or indirect realism, is the philosophical theory that argues that the mind perceives only mental images (representations) of the external world, not the world itself. It is opposed to direct realism, which holds that “physical objects are after all themselves directly or immediately perceived” (Laurence BonJour, “Epistemological Problems of Perception,” Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). In his philosophy, Kant distinguishes between intuitions (immediate, sensory representations) and concepts (general, mediate representations). He also distinguishes between appearances (things as they appear to an observer) and things-in-themselves (the world as it is independently of anyone’s perception).

Chapter 14

  • “the antinomies, both true, each contradicting the other”: Kant set out four antinomies in the Critique of Pure Reason (1781). An antinomy is a real or apparent contradiction between two conclusions, both of which seem justified. It is a term used in logic and epistemology, particularly in the philosophy of Immanuel Kant. Kant’s antinomies are four: two “mathematical” and two “dynamical.” They are connected with (1) the limitation of the universe in respect of space and time (whether the universe has a beginning or is infinite), (2) the theory that the whole consists of indivisible atoms (whereas, in fact, none such exist), (3) the problem of free will in relation to universal causality (free will vs determinism), and (4) the existence of a necessary being. The first two antinomies are dubbed “mathematical” antinomies, presumably because in each case the concern is the relation between what are alleged to be sensible objects (either the world itself, or objects in it) and space and time. The second two are dubbed “dynamical” antinomies, presumably because the proponents of the thesis are not committing themselves solely to claims about spatio-temporal objects. (Wikipedia)

Chapter 20

  • “the existence which is the phenomenal beyond which we do not inquire”: Kant’s Critique of Pure Reason (1781) separates the phenomenal world, things as they appear to us, from the noumenal, things as they are in themselves, which we cannot know.

Chapter 28

  • “the phenomenal world of the butterfly in all its illusive manifestations”: For Kant, the phenomenal world is the world as it appears to us, as against the thing in itself (Critique of Pure Reason, 1781).

Chapter 45

  • “Shall love be infinitely postponed?”: may refer to Hegel. To deny something is to determine it, and to determine something is to negate it. Spinoza’s principle is “every determination is negation” (Spinoza, letter 50 to Jarig Jelles, 1674). Hegel takes this one step further by suggesting that negation itself is a process of creation, and is even the essence of positive being. By denying a certain trait or characteristic, one is implicitly acknowledging the possibility of its opposite or the existence of a different reality. For Hegel, this power of the negative, or the act of negation, is what drives progress and development. Denying a particular concept allows for the possibility of a new one to emerge, incorporating both the original concept and its negation. This is often explained through the concept of the negation of the negation, where a denial of a denial leads to a new synthesis that transcends both the original thesis and the antithesis. From an existentialist perspective denying a predefined purpose or essence allows for the possibility of individuals to create their own meaning and existence.

Chapter 48

  • “with his mind forever divided among possibilities”: In Hegel’s philosophy, negation is not simply a denial or opposition, but a dynamic and constructive force driving the development of concepts and reality. It is a key aspect of his dialectical method, where a concept (thesis) generates its opposite (antithesis), and the resolution of this opposition (synthesis) leads to a more advanced understanding. The triad of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis is closer to Fichte’s language than to Hegel’s, who seldom used it; it was popularized by Heinrich Moritz Chalybäus (Gustav E. Mueller, “The Hegel Legend of ‘Thesis-Antithesis-Synthesis,’” Journal of the History of Ideas 19, no. 3, 1958). This process of negation, or “negativity,” is essential for overcoming limitations and contradictions in thought and experience.

The phrase “island universe” came later, from Ormsby MacKnight Mitchel’s 1846 translation of Johann Heinrich von Mädler’s Weltinsel in The Sidereal Messenger.

In the research: Chapter 6, Chapter 7, Chapter 8, Chapter 25, Chapter 26, Chapter 37, Chapter 38, Chapter 39, Chapter 47

Definition from research

Chapter 6

  • “Death was birth, and birth was death”: Schopenhauer’s philosophy views death not as a final annihilation, but as the negation of the individual “will-to-live,” a fundamental force driving existence and causing suffering. He believed that life is inherently a state of suffering, a constant cycle of wanting and never truly being satisfied. Death, for him, is the end of this striving, the cessation of the individual will and a return to the underlying, impersonal Will. He argued that the fear of death is irrational, stemming from the attachment to the will-to-live. Although acknowledging the desire to escape suffering, Schopenhauer rejected suicide as a philosophical solution. He argued that suicide, like the will-to-live, is an act of will, preventing the potential for a more profound liberation through the negation of the will in death. Schopenhauer saw individuality as an illusion, a temporary manifestation of the underlying Will.

Chapter 7

  • “What is sorrow? Is it happiness?”: The exploration of happiness and sorrow may refer to Schopenhauer who provides a Western interpretation of Buddhism which includes: the will to life (why people strive to keep on living no matter what) as a major driving force; it is an error to believe people exist to be happy; his solutions are to become a monk or sage and to spend as much time as possible with art and philosophy.

Chapter 8

  • “Yet you can’t help giving him your hand when he gives his hand to you”: Schopenhauer places compassion as the foundation of his ethical system, arguing that it is the only truly moral motive because it is based on a genuine concern for the well-being of others. He sees indifference as the opposite of this, something to be overcome in order to live a moral life. Compassion allows individuals to transcend their self-centeredness and act for the benefit of others, whereas indifference is a form of egoism that hinders moral conduct. Moses mocks old Doc and still pities him: “It kind of makes your heart give.”

Chapter 25

  • “those heavenly harmonies”: The push and pull between silent music and the music of the spheres or harmonious music form much of Mr. Spitzer’s tale, particularly in light of Schopenhauer’s view of music as the highest form of art. The philosophy of silence in music is that silence can be a powerful tool for making a statement, conveying emotion, and organizing structure. The novel embodies Schopenhauer’s belief in music as the highest art through its intricate portrayal of Mr. Spitzer’s silent and profound music, the use of musical metaphors to explore existential themes, and the depiction of music’s transcendence beyond the physical and intellectual world. The novel’s deep engagement with music as both expression and mystery reflects the Schopenhauerian vision of music as the direct and ultimate language of the will. Schopenhauer sets this out in The World as Will and Representation (1818), Book 3, where music, unlike the other arts, is a copy of the will itself.
  • “this perpetual and unconsummated suicide”: The will-to-live by Schopenhauer could be used to rationalize why Mr. Spitzer did what he did and how Jock, the Black Coachman, Joachim and Peron are all the same person. Mr. Spitzer’s actions (his tireless searches, his care for others, and his internal conflicts) are driven by this fundamental will, compelling him to persist despite loss and disintegration. The multiplicity of characters such as Jock, the Black Coachman, Joachim, Peron, and Mr. Spitzer symbolically represents different manifestations of this singular will struggling within one being, blurring the lines between self and other, life and death, reality and illusion. Schopenhauer’s term is Wille zum Leben, from The World as Will and Representation (1818). “In psychology, the will to live is the drive for self-preservation, usually coupled with expectations for future improvement in one’s state in life. The will to live is an important concept when attempting to understand and comprehend why we do what we do in order to stay alive, and for as long as we can.” (Wikipedia)
  • “There had been still, it seemed, a spark of life in Mr. Spitzer”: Friedrich Nietzsche proposed the “will to power” as a driving force behind human behavior, instead of the “will to live” of his predecessor Arthur Schopenhauer. Nietzsche develops it in Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883-85), “On Self-Overcoming”: “Wherever I found a living thing, there found I Will to Power” (trans. Thomas Common). Will to live: an irrational force drives humans to strive endlessly. Will to power: a dynamic force drives humans to overcome resistance and become who they truly are. Nietzsche believed that the will to power is more useful than the will to live for explaining human behavior. He used the will to power to explain both life-affirming and life-denying impulses, as well as master and slave morality. He believed that the will to power is the expression of self-realization, and that it is a condition for growth. He held that life itself is will to power, a striving that is never done. In the chapter it reflects Nietzsche’s “will to power” through its exploration of internal conflict, the striving for control amid chaos, the tension between life and death, and the dynamic, creative force underlying human existence, as embodied in Mr. Spitzer’s character and experiences.

Chapter 26

  • “the attitude of a perpetual grief”: This may refer to the philosophy of Arthur Schopenhauer, who believed that death is a natural part of life and a return to a state of non-existence that existed before birth. He thought that individual consciousness is impermanent and that the life of an individual is meaningless. His key ideas are will-to-live (the driving force behind our attachment to life and our fear of death), knowledge (shows the meaninglessness of life and the worthlessness of living), suicide (pointless because it affirms the will-to-live, though it destroys the individual), palingenesis (the will, not the individual mind or soul, is reborn in new beings), redemption (that death is an opportunity for redemption through the negation of the will). The portrayal of Mr. Spitzer’s lifelong sorrow, his recognition of life as a series of losses and unfulfilled desires, and his contemplation of the illusory nature of reality all echo Schopenhauerian themes. The passage reflects a worldview where grief and suffering are continuous and intrinsic to life. His fullest statement is in The World as Will and Representation, vol. 2 (1844), chapter 41, “On Death and Its Relation to the Indestructibility of Our Inner Nature.”

Chapter 37

  • “How should death be different from life, my mother asked”: Life as a state of experience and potential: Socrates thought death might be a dreamless sleep or passage to another realm where one can converse with the dead. Existentialism believes death is an inevitable aspect of human existence and that it can lead to a heightened sense of self-awareness and responsibility. Epicureanism argues death cannot harm a person, as it’s either not yet experienced (while alive) or not experienced at all (once dead). Death is defined as the loss of the capacity to engage in vital activities and the cessation of consciousness. Wittgenstein wrote that death is not an event in life, for we do not live to experience it (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 6.4311). Schopenhauer believed that understanding death as the ultimate end of life can provide a perspective on the meaning of life itself. Freud thought the life instinct (Eros) and the death instinct (Thanatos) are fundamental forces in human behavior.

Chapter 38

  • Schopenhauer made music the direct image of the will: it “is as immediate an objectification and copy of the whole will as the world itself” (Arthur Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Idea 1.52, 1819, trans. R. B. Haldane and J. Kemp, 1883).

Chapter 39

  • “She saw an idiot who had become a great philosopher”: Wittgenstein, despite his genius, was known for his unconventional behavior and challenging personality. He even questioned his own sanity, asking Bertrand Russell if he was an idiot. Russell asked him to write something over the vacation, and after reading it told him not to become an aeronaut (Bertrand Russell, “Ludwig Wittgenstein,” in Portraits from Memory and Other Essays, Simon and Schuster, 1956). His profound insights into philosophy, language, and logic led to his recognition as a major philosopher. The idea of a philosopher becoming an “idiot” is a common trope often referencing Diogenes of Sinope. Arthur Schopenhauer was also considered eccentric.

Chapter 47

  • “marriage was that great lottery”: “In our monogamous part of the world, to marry means to halve one’s rights and double one’s duties” (Arthur Schopenhauer, “On Women,” Parerga and Paralipomena, 1851).
  • “he was agonized by attributing consciousness to everything”: This may refer to panpsychism, the view that mind, or something like mind, is a fundamental and widespread feature of reality, present in some form even in its most basic elements. It has roots in ancient Greek philosophy, in Thales, who held that “all things are full of gods” (Aristotle, On the Soul 1.5), and in Plato, and later in Spinoza, Leibniz, and Schopenhauer. Mr. Spitzer suffers because he senses consciousness not only in people but in clouds, stars, waves, palings, and weathervanes, so that the line between the living and the lifeless blurs and his own sense of self grows unstable.

Definition from research

Chapter 2

  • “scattered hearts like motes dancing in a sunbeam”: The Roman poet Lucretius, in On the Nature of Things, pointed to the specks of dust that dance in a sunbeam in a darkened room as a picture of the atoms, always moving, colliding, and scattering in the void.

Chapter 13

  • The Garden of Epicurus by Anatole France is a book of short essays and reflections (1894) that explores the nature of happiness, the pursuit of knowledge, and the struggle for personal freedom. France doubts that anyone can be known, even to himself: “What a foolish phrase, the ‘know thyself’ of the Greek philosopher! Why, we can never know either ourselves or others.” No one, he says, has ever told everything: “It would be so profoundly interesting to listen to a confession that was absolutely sincere! Yet since the world began, nothing of the kind has ever been heard.” The past, too, comes to us shaped by art: the historian presents facts “stripped of almost all the individual peculiarities that constitute them facts,” for “History is not a science, it is an art,” and “Beauty undraped is no beauty, and what we love the best is always the unknown” (The Garden of Epicurus, trans. Alfred Allinson, 1908, pp. 67, 93-94, 123-124, 128). One of his favorite periods was the transition from paganism to Christianity (Catharine Savage Brosman, Dictionary of Literary Biography). His English publisher called him “a pagan, but a pagan constantly haunted by the preoccupation of Christ” (John Lane, 1908).
  • The Epicurean “fourfold remedy,” handed down by Philodemus: Don’t fear the gods. Don’t worry about death. What is good is easy to get. What is terrible is easy to endure.
  • “a perpetual garden party omitting the tragic spirit”: The Epicureans met in the Garden, the school Epicurus founded in Athens.

Chapter 23

  • “One can be an epicure”: Epicurus lived chiefly on bread and water: “Send me a little pot of cheese, that when I like I may fare sumptuously” (Diogenes Laertius 10.11).

Chapter 37

  • “How should death be different from life, my mother asked”: Life as a state of experience and potential: Socrates thought death might be a dreamless sleep or passage to another realm where one can converse with the dead. Existentialism believes death is an inevitable aspect of human existence and that it can lead to a heightened sense of self-awareness and responsibility. Epicureanism argues death cannot harm a person, as it’s either not yet experienced (while alive) or not experienced at all (once dead). Death is defined as the loss of the capacity to engage in vital activities and the cessation of consciousness. Wittgenstein wrote that death is not an event in life, for we do not live to experience it (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 6.4311). Schopenhauer believed that understanding death as the ultimate end of life can provide a perspective on the meaning of life itself. Freud thought the life instinct (Eros) and the death instinct (Thanatos) are fundamental forces in human behavior.

Chapter 48

  • “Man could not see his own end, for he passed beyond his end”: No one can witness his own death, because by the time death comes the self has already passed beyond it. Epicurus: “when we are, death is not come, and, when death is come, we are not” (Letter to Menoeceus, in Diogenes Laertius 10.125, trans. R. D. Hicks, 1925). Wittgenstein: “Death is not an event of life. Death is not lived through” (Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 6.4311, trans. C. K. Ogden, 1922).

In the research: Chapter 1, Chapter 3, Chapter 6, Chapter 9, Chapter 13, Chapter 22, Chapter 30, Chapter 33, Chapter 34, Chapter 36, Chapter 39, Chapter 42, Chapter 43, Chapter 44, Chapter 45, Chapter 49, Chapter 53, Chapter 63, Chapter 65, Chapter 74, Chapter 77, Chapter 82

Definition from research

Chapter 1

  • Marguerite Young in the Dalkey Interview said she talked to coal miners in the Ozarks and it was because of them that she decided to write about New Harmony (a utopia in Angels in the Forest) and that it is based upon social consciousness.

Chapter 3

  • In an interview Young said she had no idea there was a real town by the name of What Cheer, Iowa. She thought she had made it up.

Chapter 3

  • The author Virginia Woolf who committed suicide by filling her pockets with stones and walking into the River Ouse in March 1941 only several years before Marguerite Young started writing this novel.

Chapter 6

  • Marguerite Young did comment about how all people wear masks. They have at least an inner component and an outer component that is shown to the public.

Chapter 6

  • “She was breaking into two, herself and the other, this face unknown”: Young seems to be describing through Madge a form of depersonalization-derealization that is now labeled a disorder and can be brought about by stress or trauma such as rape.

Chapter 9

  • “There are many gay deceivers”: A “gay deceiver” was an old name for a rake or seducer. Gay here could mean happy or may be in reference to homosexuals. The term gay to describe immorality or someone addicted to pleasure was in use in the 17th century. Gertrude Stein in 1922 used the word gay to specifically reference homosexuals. In 1950, the earliest reference found to date for the word gay as a self-described name for homosexuals came from Alfred A. Gross who used it in the June 1950 issue of SIR magazine. In a series of interviews with Susan S. Neville, Marguerite Young said she had lovers both male and female. There was a relationship where she would not marry him but said he could visit her every Tuesday for the rest of her life.

Chapter 13

  • Marguerite Young loved Anatole France’s writing and read him widely, in French as well as in English. When her grandmother died, her first thought was that “now she can tell Anatole France that she has a little granddaughter on Earth who adores him” (Marguerite Young, interview with Charles Ruas, “The Art of Fiction No. 66,” The Paris Review 71, Fall 1977). Anatole France was a French author, poet, and critic who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1921. His short story “Marguerite” first appeared in book form in Paris in 1920, with woodcuts by Siméon, and in J. Lewis May’s English translation in 1921 (Project Gutenberg edition of the John Lane translation, 1921). France had socialist sympathies and was an outspoken supporter of the 1917 Russian Revolution, and in 1920 he backed the newly founded French Communist Party. (Wikipedia)
  • “a perpetual garden party omitting the tragic spirit”: The Epicureans met in the Garden, the school Epicurus founded in Athens.

Chapter 22 · Technique

  • Symbolism: The chapter abounds with symbolic references to ships, storms, and phantoms, enhancing themes of memory and loss.
  • Stream of Consciousness: Vera’s thoughts flow freely between observation, memory, and philosophical reflection, emphasizing her inner turmoil. Young said both things about the method. She told Studs Terkel, “This is not a stream of consciousness novel. It’s a very controlled, rather realistic treatment of that kind of attitude” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965), and in 1983, asked whether the stream of consciousness was the method of the novel, she answered, “Yes, the stream of consciousness” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).
  • Allusion: Biblical references to creation days, historical figures (Emperor Constantine, King Canute), and biblical figures (Jeremiah) deepen thematic complexity.
  • Contrast: Between Vera’s emotional state and Miss MacIntosh’s external cheerfulness and routine.

Chapter 30

  • “Eustace, Eustace! Oh, is it you, Eustace dear”: At Iowa (1955-57), Young “would pause to greet Henry James at the door” of her classroom (David O. Dowling, “The Guru,” in A Delicate Aggression: Savagery and Survival in the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, Yale University Press, 2019). She kept portraits of dead writers on her walls. Catherine greets the invisible Eustace the same way. Young also told Studs Terkel of a friend in a New York hospital who overheard “one of the richest ladies in America,” dying, greet guests who were not there: “Eustace, turn to the left. Oh, isn’t that Mr. Henry James? How do you do, Mr. James?” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 33

  • “those who must punch time-clocks in great factories, those who must turn great wheels”: Willard Bundy patented the time clock in 1888. Chaplin’s Modern Times (1936) opens on workers at the time clock and swallows Charlie in the great wheels. Young said, “Charlie Chaplin has influenced every book I’ve ever written” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).

Chapter 34

  • “that great Crusader was not a man’s woman”: There is an uncomfortable trope about women/feminists that Young uses against Cousin Hannah. She was so vehement against men when she was so ugly that men didn’t find her attractive and so there was nothing for her to defend against. It keeps coming up even to the present day. Young admitted that “there was a tendency to be satirical about her,” but she used the Alpine story of the lost skirt to explain Hannah, and in the trousseau trunks of her real source found that “she had a dream too” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 36

  • “But who knew the hidden man, that man he might never be, neither himself nor his twin brother”: In her first draft “Mr. Spitzer knew that he was really Peyron the gambler,” which “seemed so tricky to me” that she rewrote it so that he does not know (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).

Chapter 39

  • “Oh, come in, she would say”: This is what Young would do in her classroom. At Iowa she “would pause to greet Henry James at the door” (David O. Dowling, “The Guru,” in A Delicate Aggression: Savagery and Survival in the Iowa Writers’ Workshop, Yale University Press, 2019). She told Studs Terkel of a dying lady in a New York hospital, the source for Catherine’s greetings, who greeted guests who were not there: “Oh, isn’t that Mr. Henry James? How do you do, Mr. James?” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965). That is a big clue as to what is going on here.
  • Young’s Angel in the Forest (1945) tells of New Harmony’s two utopias, the Rappites and the Owenites.

Chapter 42

  • Young said, “I thought of Margaret Fuller in relation to not only Cousin Hannah, but some of the other characters.” Fuller drowned off Fire Island in 1850 (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “a secret woman, a bride”: Young told Studs Terkel that the woman behind Cousin Hannah brought home sealed trunks for forty years, and at her death each held a bridal trousseau: “She had a dream too” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “he who had played his last spade”: The ace of spades has long been called the death card. Peron was a gambler: in Young’s first draft “Mr. Spitzer knew that he was really Peyron the gambler.”

Chapter 43

  • “the spokes of the wheel”: Young described the characters in this book as the spokes of a wheel coming out from Miss MacIntosh in the center of the story: “I always thought of Miss MacIntosh as the center of the wheel, the hub,” with the other characters as “the spokes” (Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs, “A Conversation with Marguerite Young,” Review of Contemporary Fiction 23, no. 1, Spring 2003 (1989 original)). In this chapter Mr. Spitzer lets “the spokes of the wheel” extend as far as possible before they reach “the clouded rim of doubt.”

Chapter 44

  • “I must find my skirt”: This is the Alpine story Young told Studs Terkel, of two bloomer girls who shed their skirts at a summit, and the younger, going back for hers, was lost: “the lady lost her life for a skirt” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “For all dead loves and all remembered things”: The epigraph Young gave the novel is in this chapter “For all dead loves and all remembered things. I have travelled through many seas.”

Chapter 45

  • Young said that Esther Longtree, at the end of the book, “is the mother of us all, I would say, quoting Gertrude Stein” (Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs, “A Conversation with Marguerite Young,” Review of Contemporary Fiction 23, no. 1, Spring 2003 (1989 original)). Stein’s opera The Mother of Us All (1947), with music by Virgil Thomson, is about Susan B. Anthony. Steven Shaviro also reported that Young called Mr. Spitzer the father of us all.
  • In Young’s first draft, she told Kay Bonetti, “Mr. Spitzer knew that he was really Peyron the gambler” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).
  • “We were two lone women. There was no man.”: This is Hannah’s confession, and the secret Mr. Spitzer will keep. See the bridal trousseaus Young described to Studs Terkel under “a secret woman, a bride” in the Chapter 42 resources.

Chapter 49

  • In this chapter Mr. Spitzer lives the problem of universals rather than explaining it. He is “many countries, many times, many dimensions,” with no unitary self; there is “no stone which was not a cloud”; music “was ever approximate and not actual,” and “none should live to hear its completion”; signs and gestures have “many and indeterminate meanings.” The imagery leans toward nominalism or conceptualism, with universals as shadows and reflections, yet a mystical unity remains: “He lived between the golden spokes of light. He lived between the spokes of darkness.” Young does not solve the problem; she builds a world where its terms dissolve. For more, see The Problem of Universals, Platonism and nominalism in the Chapter 2 resources, and Abelard, Roscellinus, and William of Champeaux in the Chapter 52 resources.

Chapter 53

  • “People were indifferent to those things which interested Mr. Spitzer”: Young drew Peron’s world from her own reading: “I’ve read a great many books on gambling, and I’ve been interested in it since early childhood, because I knew gamblers in early childhood.” Of her research she said, “Baseball, gambling, vaudeville, burlesque jokes, all this became part, as well as Moby Dick, the Bible” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).
  • “the one chance in a million”: Young told Studs Terkel, “Mr. Spitzer is really two people. There are two Mr. Spitzers. One is a musical composer who has lived in memory of his gambling brother, the suicide, and who since his brother’s death has never composed a music which can be heard.” Peron “is a gay gambler, an impresario in the world of games and sports,” who describes himself “as the gambler who took one chance in a million, committed suicide, and lived.” In the third draft she realized “that it was not just a case of twins, but the two parts of the same man… a beautiful case of duality, which might be in all of us, like left and right, shadow and sunlight” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

Chapter 63 · The Wig and Baldness

  • Miss MacIntosh’s wig symbolizes the facade of social norms and appearances, which she ultimately reveals as a protective but deceptive covering. Young described the wig as the illusion itself, “the dream by which she lived” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965), and the hair it replaces as “the symbol of the dream and of the feminine in life that she never had” (Marguerite Young, interview with Duncan MacDonald, Observation Point, 1965).
  • Her baldness, exposed in a moment of vulnerability, represents raw truth, mortality, and the stripping away of illusions.

Chapter 65

  • Young claimed descent from John Knox on her mother’s side. While writing the novel she “discovered that the Macintoshes, this really astonished me, were descendants from a prince, a bald prince, who was washed up on the shores of Scotland,” so that “Miss Macintosh is really a bald prince, disguised with a red wig and the woman’s gear” (Marguerite Young, interview, WNYC radio, New York).

Chapter 74

  • “an old maid plucking at a daisy’s petals”: “He loves me, he loves me not.” In French the game is effeuiller la marguerite, plucking the daisy, and marguerite is the French for daisy.
  • “This Chicago detective was creating quite a problem even now”: The detective’s suit “was based upon a real case which happened in Chicago,” which Young read about in a New York paper, “and I wove it into my story” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).

Chapter 77

  • “He had been told by his father that his father would give him the secret”: “When I started to write about New Harmony, the utopia, I was inspired to do so by an account of a flour miller who tried to pass on his thumbmark to his son. That cannot be done, and the son ended by committing suicide.” Young wrote a short story about him that failed, and “I have put that flour miller and this thumb into ‘Miss MacIntosh, My Darling’ somewhere. In fact, I’ve put that flour miller and his thumb into everything I’ve ever written since,” “the idea of identity and passage of the soul” (Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs, “A Conversation with Marguerite Young,” Review of Contemporary Fiction 23, no. 1, Spring 2003 (1989 original)).

Chapter 82

  • “how my mother, after many years of sleeping, arose from her bed and walked”: So did Weissenbach. She “had been able to get out of bed after many, many years, but this is what killed her, so that she turned old overnight. She had never shown the mark of time.” She died in 1943 in New York, and Young, who kept writing to her, learned of it months later from her daughter: “as long as you kept writing to Mother and I read your letters, I felt as if my mother was somehow alive” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).
  • “the reason no one had heard his music since Peron’s death was that he was Peron”: Young compared Mr. Spitzer’s “great impersonation in this life” to “the Titchborn claimant” (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965), Arthur Orton, who claimed in 1866 to be the lost heir Roger Tichborne and was convicted of perjury in 1874. In her first draft “Mr. Spitzer knew that he was really Peyron the gambler,” which “seemed so tricky to me” that she rewrote it so that he does not know (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983).
  • “Little boidies don’t have no tits”: The stone-deaf man was Young’s friend Howard Mitcham, a deaf painter in Greenwich Village. “He used to love to sing this, little boydies don’t have no tits. Little boydies don’t have no umbilical cords,” and “he knew that I was putting him in” (Marguerite Young, interview with Kay Bonetti, American Audio Prose Library, May 1983). For a magazine article on the deaf she interviewed deaf leaders in New York and heard the Lord’s Prayer in sign language at St. Mark’s (Marguerite Young, interview with Studs Terkel, WFMT radio, 1965).

I was very much interested in the idea of a train of memory or illusion, but I suppose I rejected a train journey for the same reason that William James didn’t want to speak of the train of memory, but rather the stream of consciousness.” Philosophers had long pictured thought as a train of linked ideas; Thomas Hobbes titled a chapter of Leviathan (1651) “Of the Consequence or Trayne of Imaginations.” William James rejected the image in The Principles of Psychology (1890): “Such words as ‘chain’ or ‘train’ do not describe it fitly. . . . It is nothing jointed; it flows. A ‘river’ or a ‘stream’ are the metaphors by which it is most naturally described.” A train runs on fixed rails from station to station. Vera’s bus wanders through the mist, and its road turns and seems “to go back the way it had gone before.”

Chapter 49

  • William James: Though James certainly agreed with Peirce and against Berkeley that general ideas exist as a psychological fact, he was a nominalist in his ontology: “From every point of view, the overwhelming and portentous character ascribed to universal conceptions is surprising. Why, from Plato and Aristotle, philosophers should have vied with each other in scorn of the knowledge of the particular and in adoration of that of the general, is hard to understand, seeing that the more adorable knowledge ought to be that of the more adorable things and that the things of worth are all concretes and singulars. The only value of universal characters is that they help us, by reasoning, to know new truths about individual things.” (William James, The Principles of Psychology, 1890, chapter 12). There are at least three ways in which a realist might try to answer James’ challenge of explaining the reason why universal conceptions are more lofty than those of particulars: the moral-political answer, the mathematical-scientific answer, and the anti-paradoxical answer. Each has contemporary or near-contemporary advocates. (Wikipedia)

  • Mysterianism, named by Owen Flanagan in 1991 and argued by Colin McGinn, holds that the human mind may be too limited to solve the mind-body problem, since the cognitive capabilities of all organisms are limited by biology. William James found this liberating in “Is Life Worth Living?” (1895), where a dog in a laboratory cannot grasp the purposes of the men around it, and wrote, “I believe rather that we stand in much the same relation to the whole of the universe as our canine and feline pets do to the whole of human life” (Pragmatism, 1907, lecture 8).

Chapter 29

  • “Were these two souls which moved through him”: The soul is the purported immaterial aspect or essence of a living being. It is typically believed to be immortal and to exist apart from the material world. The three main theories that describe the relationship between the soul and the body are interactionism, parallelism, and epiphenomenalism. Anthropologists and psychologists have found that most humans are naturally inclined to believe in the existence of the soul and that they have interculturally distinguished between souls and bodies. In philosophy, the soul has been the central area of interest since ancient times. Socrates envisioned the soul to possess a rational faculty, its practice being man’s most godlike activity. Plato believed the soul to be the person’s real self, an immaterial and immortal dweller of our lives that continues and thinks even after death. Aristotle sketched out the soul as the “first actuality” of a naturally organized body: form and matter arrangement allowing natural beings to aspire to full actualization. (Wikipedia) The chapter’s “two souls” and “three souls or the amalgamations of many souls” reflect the fragmented and overlapping nature of consciousness and existence.

Chapter 37

  • “How should she know when she had crossed the invisible line of demarcation”: Descartes’ dream argument: He used the experience of dreaming to question the certainty of our perceptions and beliefs. He argued that if we cannot definitively distinguish between waking and dreaming, then our sensory experiences, which are the foundation of our knowledge, might be illusions. There is philosophical skepticism because the possibility of dreams may be genuine or a fabrication. It leads one to question the validity of knowledge of the external world. Freud believed dreams are a symbolic representation of unconscious thoughts and desires. Jung expanded on Freud’s ideas that dreams can also reveal universal, archetypal patterns in the human psyche. Some theories suggest dreams are a natural byproduct of the brain’s activity during sleep, possibly involving memory consolidation, emotional processing, or the clearing out of mental clutter.
