Definition from research

Chapter 15

  • “man is a little soul carrying around a heavy corpse”: Marcus Aurelius is quoting Epictetus: “Thou art a little soul bearing about a corpse, as Epictetus used to say” (Meditations 4.41).

Chapter 23

  • “One can enjoy too much one’s poverty, in fact, and make a great business of it”: Seneca warns against showy poverty, “a rough cloak, unkempt hair, a slovenly beard” (Letters to Lucilius 5). Seneca was a leading Roman Stoic. The school was founded by Zeno of Citium around 300 BC. Seneca’s works discuss both ethical theory and practical advice, and Seneca stresses that both parts are distinct but interdependent. Seneca regards philosophy as a balm for the wounds of life. The destructive passions, especially anger and grief, must be uprooted, or moderated according to reason. He discusses the relative merits of contemplative life and active life, and he considers it important to confront one’s own mortality and be able to face death. One must be willing to practice poverty and use wealth properly, and he writes about favours, clemency, the importance of friendship, and the need to benefit others. The universe is governed for the best by a rational providence, and this must be reconciled with acceptance of adversity.

Chapter 25

  • “What death was this which was no death?”: The philosophy of death explores the meaning of death, our relationship to it, and the various ways it impacts human existence and understanding. It delves into questions about what happens after death, the nature of consciousness, and the ethical implications of death, including suicide. The Nature of Death: Dualism (the soul continues to exist after death, potentially in a separate realm or afterlife), Materialism (death is the permanent cessation of all bodily functions, including consciousness), Annihilationism (death is the end of all conscious experience, and nothing exists after death). Philosophical Perspectives on Death: Stoicism (death is not something to be feared, as it is a natural part of life and a release from suffering), Existentialism (thinkers like Kierkegaard and Heidegger, in Being and Time, 1927, emphasized the importance of confronting our mortality to understand our own existence and the meaning of life), Nietzsche (proposed that individuals have the freedom to define their own death, suggesting it could be a conscious choice rather than an inevitable fate: “Die at the right time,” in “On Free Death,” Thus Spoke Zarathustra, 1883). Ethical Considerations: Suicide (philosophy engages with questions about the moral permissibility of suicide, including whether it’s ever justifiable).

Chapter 29

  • “between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow”: In philosophy, happiness and sorrow are intertwined, with sorrow often seen as a necessary component for experiencing the depth of joy and vice versa rather than as simple opposites. It can be viewed in a number of ways: a dialectical relationship (yin and yang-complementary forces where one cannot exist without the other); the contrast highlights the value of positive experiences; a catalyst for growth, introspection, and a deeper understanding of life’s complexities. Philosophical perspectives are found in Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Stoicism, Utilitarianism, Hedonism, Life Satisfaction Theory. Plato and Aristotle’s eudaimonia where flourishing and well-being are achieved by living a virtuous life, not simply experiencing happiness. Nirvana is a state of liberation from suffering and the cycle of rebirth. Equanimity is the ability to remain calm and balanced in the face of both pleasure and pain. Mr. Spitzer finds it as hard to tell butterfly from moth as “to distinguish between brother and brother or between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow,” for “Seldom did happiness and sorrow occur in pure and disrelated states.”

Chapter 37

  • “Death was this dream’s immeasurable extension”: The meaning of life in relation to death: Stoicism emphasized that facing death can lead to a deeper understanding of life’s meaning and the ephemeral nature of earthly possessions. Nietzsche used the thought experiment of eternal return (recurrence) to encourage individuals to examine the meaning and value of their lives, given the possibility of living them again and again.
  • “One had laughed one’s self to death”: The Stoic Chrysippus is said to have died laughing at a donkey eating his figs (Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers 7.185).

Chapter 40

  • “I am dead—had not old Cousin Hannah always whispered”: Nietzsche’s phrase, “God is dead” (Friedrich Nietzsche, The Gay Science 125, 1882), refers to the demise of traditional religious belief and the moral structures built upon it. He believed this shift opened up new possibilities for humanity to create its own values and meaning. Marcus Aurelius wrote, “Consider thyself to be dead, and to have completed thy life up to the present time” (Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 7.56, trans. George Long, 1862), where one focuses on present experiences and accepts the inevitability of death, rather than clinging to the past or fearing the future.

Chapter 52

  • “those knockings which might have come from him”: Modern Spiritualism, popular through the Victorian age, began in 1848 when the Fox sisters of Hydesville, New York, claimed that rappings in their house were messages from the dead; in 1888 Margaret Fox confessed that the knocks were made by cracking her toe joints, though she later took the confession back. In 1920 Thomas Edison told B. C. Forbes of The American Magazine that he was working on an apparatus for communicating with the dead.

Chapter 79

  • “an old spiritualist medium”: Modern Spiritualism is widely considered to have begun in March 1848 in Hydesville, New York, following the claims of the Fox sisters, Margaret and Kate, who reported hearing mysterious rappings that they believed were spirit messages. The movement originated in an area of upstate New York known as the “Burned-over District,” which was already a center for religious fervor and movements like Millerism and Mormonism during the Second Great Awakening. The movement quickly spread, with early adherents seeking direct communication with the spirits of the deceased. By the 1850s, it had spread across the country and internationally. In the 1850s, the movement attracted the attention of scientists who began investigating the reported supernatural occurrences. The credibility of the movement was challenged, especially in 1888 when the Fox sisters confessed to faking the original rappings. However, many believers continued their faith, and the movement adapted. Influential figures like Emma Hardinge Britten, a medium and lecturer, used the platform of Spiritualism to advocate for social causes like women’s rights and temperance. Spiritualism experienced a major revival after World War I, as many people sought to connect with loved ones who had died in the war. The movement continued to develop organizations and gather followers, with communities like Cassadaga, Florida, becoming known as centers for spiritualist activities. Throughout the mid-20th century, Spiritualism persisted, adapting to new generations and social changes, and leaving a lasting impact on American religious and cultural history.
